facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
Hawaiian pizza people don't order dinner; they order a personality. You can't just eat it, you have to announce it. Every group order has one of you, arms crossed, waiting for someone to gasp so you can say "sweet and savory" like you invented the concept. You didn't. A Canadian did, in Ontario, in 1962. You're not rebelling, you're doing Canada's homework.

And it's always the same rebel: someone whose wildest night was asking for medium salsa. Pineapple is your face tattoo, the edgiest thing you'll ever do, and it wipes off with a napkin.

What does it get you? Your own box. Nobody touches it. You came for controversy and left with exactly what you wanted: eight slices, the same argument you've had since 2009, and proof that nobody will ever steal your food.

b.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Nothing about you is Hawaiian. You were invented in 1962 in Chatham, Ontario, by a Greek guy, and named after a brand of canned pineapple. You're not a cuisine, you're a label. Even the pineapple left Hawaii. Del Monte shut down there in 2006, two years ahead of schedule, like they couldn't wait to stop being associated with you. Now your fruit comes from Thailand, Indonesia and the Philippines. You're a pizza with a passport and no home.

Your own creator said nobody mixed sweet and sour back then "except for Chinese food." His restaurant served Chinese food. So your origin story is "what if the takeout menu fell into the pizza oven?"

The president of Iceland said he'd ban you if he could, then admitted he didn't have the power. Congratulations: you've survived purely on a technicality.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text: Let's talk about the oat milk people. You're not lactose intolerant. You've never been tested. You just heard cows are bad and almonds are thirsty, so you picked the one grain that sounds like a farm without the farmer. Congratulations: you pay an extra eighty cents to drink liquid porridge with a splash of rapeseed oil, and you call it "cleaner." You switched from almond the exact week a podcast told you California was in a drought. That's not values, that's a trend with a loyalty card. And the best part? You order it with an air of quiet suffering, like the barista should thank you for saving the planet one Barista Edition carton at a time. Your grandmother ate oats so she could survive winter. You drink them so a stranger in line thinks you've been to therapy.

b.text:
Oat milk. You began in Sweden in the 1990s as sober Lund University research into lactose intolerance, and somehow grew up to be a personality. Your big slogan was "It's like milk but made for humans." The Swedish dairy lobby sued, and instead of apologizing, you published the lawsuit as advertising. That's not a brand. That's a guy who frames his restraining order and hangs it in the hallway.

Then you hit Nasdaq in May 2021 at nearly ten billion dollars and lost over ninety percent of it. Even your share price separated in the fridge.

And the health halo? You're oats that got enzymes to turn their starch into maltose, then got topped off with rapeseed oil. You have more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy. You're not milk made for humans. You're porridge with a marketing department.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text:
Graphene, you were discovered with Scotch tape. Other materials get particle accelerators; you got the junk drawer. Then you won a Nobel Prize, which means Sweden officially honored the arts-and-crafts table.

The EU handed you a billion euros over ten years. A billion! Then a 2018 study tested "graphene" from 60 producers, and not one was even half graphene. Most of it was graphite flakes. You're not a miracle material, you're pencil shavings with a LinkedIn.

Yet you're in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a "performance ingredient." Buddy, the only thing you've boosted is the price tag.

And one of your own discoverers once levitated a frog with magnets. Honestly? That frog delivered more on its promises than you have. At least it actually got off the ground.

b.text: Let's hear it for the graphene evangelists, the only people who've been "five years away" since 2004. Two guys in Manchester peeled pencil lead with Scotch tape, won a Nobel, and you looked at that and thought: finally, a career plan. Every grant proposal you write has the same three slides: space elevator, seawater you can drink, a phone that charges in six seconds. The funding agency nods like it's never seen them before, because it's seen them so many times it's slipped into a coma. Twenty years of press releases, and what have you actually shipped? A tennis racket. Headphones with "GRAPHENE" printed bigger than the brand name. You love telling people it's 200 times stronger than steel. Sure. Your claims, meanwhile, are one atom thick. You didn't discover a wonder material. You discovered wonder funding.

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text:
Macau! The Portuguese stayed for almost 450 years and still couldn't find a parking spot. Twenty thousand people per square kilometre: this isn't a city, it's a queue with a postcode.

In 2013, Macau made seven times what the Las Vegas Strip made. Seven times! Vegas is where people go to ruin their lives, and Macau looked at that and said, "Amateurs."

One company ran every casino for forty years. Forty years of monopoly in a gambling town, the only place on Earth where even the house didn't have to try.

And when they ran out of room, they built the Cotai Strip on land reclaimed from the sea. That's Macau: so desperate for more tables, it took out a loan from the ocean. And the ocean's about to learn what everyone else here learns: the house always wins.

b.text: Macau, you're the only place where the most famous church is just a wall. The Ruins of St. Paul's: a gorgeous front with absolutely nothing behind it, which is basically your whole personality. You've got a fake Venice with a painted sky, a fake Paris with a half-size Eiffel Tower, and you're so tiny you had to dump dirt into the ocean just to fit a runway. You out-earned Las Vegas several times over, and your signature dish is still a pork chop jammed in a bun. The Portuguese stayed four hundred years and left you an egg tart and street signs nobody reads. The Grand Lisboa looks like a golden pineapple having a breakdown. And the Macau Tower's big attraction is jumping off it, which, after a night at the baccarat tables, is less a thrill ride and more a financial plan.

facts: Hand-drawn by Chris Costello in 1982 over about six months, when he was 23; he sold the rights to Letraset for $750.
Bundled with macOS and with Microsoft Office, which is why it appears on so many menus and signs.
James Cameron's Avatar (2009) used it for the film's logo and subtitles.
A 2017 Saturday Night Live sketch starring Ryan Gosling is about a man unable to get over that choice.

a.text:
Papyrus, you were hand-drawn over six months by a 23-year-old, and somehow it still looks like a first draft. Six months! You look like you were chiseled during an earthquake. Chris Costello sold you to Letraset for $750, the only time anyone has known exactly what you're worth.

You came bundled with macOS and Microsoft Office, so you're not popular, you're just pre-installed. You're the free hotel shampoo of fonts. Every menu, every sign: you didn't earn that, you just came with the computer.

Then James Cameron imagined an entire alien world for Avatar, and when it came time for the logo and subtitles, he picked the default. Of all the things to leave untouched.

It got so bad that Saturday Night Live had Ryan Gosling play a man who can't get over it. You're not a typeface. You're a trauma with jagged edges.

b.text:
Papyrus, look at you. A 23-year-old drew you with a calligraphy pen in 1982, trying to imagine what English would look like 2,000 years ago, and somehow you became the official font of every place that sells crystals next to a tanning bed. You're on yoga studios, hookah lounges, and the church bake sale flyer for "Loaves & Fishes & Brownies."

Your letters look like they were chiseled by a Pharaoh with a hangover. That little floaty bar on your capital E? Even your crossbars are trying to leave.

James Cameron spent a billion dollars inventing an alien language, then labeled the poster with a font that came free with Microsoft Office. Ryan Gosling got an entire SNL sketch out of being haunted by you.

Even your creator says he's sick of you. Comic Sans has haters. You have a dad who wants a refund.

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text:
Apple Vision Pro: thirty-five hundred dollars to strap over a pound of computer to your face, and that's before the battery. Yes, the battery. It's on a cable. In 2024, the most futuristic company on Earth sold you a headset with a cord running to your pocket, rated for about two hours. That's not the future. That's a movie on a leash.

And don't you dare call it VR. Apple's rules won't let developers say AR, VR, XR, or MR. It's "spatial computing," the way a timeshare is "vacation ownership."

Then there's EyeSight: a screen on the front showing a rendering of your eyes so everyone knows someone's still in there. It's not a feature; it's proof of life.

Apple cut production, and first-year sales estimates landed well under a million. Turns out the most immersive thing about it was the regret.

b.text:
Apple Vision Pro.

Apple says it isn't VR.
Developers aren't allowed to call it VR.
Or AR. Or XR. Or MR.
It's "spatial computing."
That's what you call a headset after "headset" tests badly.

Thirty-four ninety-nine.
Over half a kilo on your face.
Plus a battery in your pocket, on a cord, good for about two hours.
That's not a computer. That's a leash with a launch event.

Apple cut production.
First-year sales: well under a million.
The most immersive thing about it was the silence afterward.

Then there's EyeSight.
It puts a rendering of your eyes on the outside,
so the people around you feel like you're still there.

You've all been doing that at dinner for ten years.
Apple just figured out how to charge you for it.

facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.
Private fusion companies had raised more than $7 billion by 2024.

a.text: Let's hear it for the fusion people, the only scientists who've been "ten years away" since my grandfather had hair. You can hold plasma hotter than the sun for a few seconds, but you can't hold a deadline for one decade. Every press release: "Net energy gain!" Sure, if you don't count the electricity bill for the lasers. That's like me saying I'm profitable if you ignore rent. ITER got approved when Myspace was cool, and it's still assembling the donut. And the startups: "We're different, we have venture capital." Great, now the sun is ten years away *and* has a pitch deck. Honestly, it's a beautiful racket: promise infinite clean energy, collect the grant, retire before anyone plugs in a toaster. You're not building a star. You're building a pension.

b.text:
Nuclear fusion: the only technology that's been "thirty years away" for seventy years. In 1955, Homi Bhabha promised fusion power within two decades. Two decades later? Still two decades. You're not an energy source. You're a horizon.

Look at ITER. Agreed in 2006, first plasma by 2016. Then 2024 rolls around and it's "research operations in 2034, actual deuterium-tritium burning in 2039," for over twenty billion euros. That's not a construction schedule. That's a mortgage.

And NIF's big "ignition" shot: 3.15 megajoules out from 2.05 in! Historic! Except the lasers pulled about 300 megajoules from the grid just to fire. That's like bragging your lemonade stand turned a profit after you bought the orchard.

Still, private investors have thrown you more than seven billion dollars. So congratulations, fusion. You finally achieved net gain. Just not in energy.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text:
Excel, you're the only software so powerful that scientists had to rename human genes because you kept turning MARCH1 into a date. You didn't adapt to biology; biology adapted to you. Type a phone number and you lop off the leading zero like it owes you money. Enter a credit card number and you serve back 4.53E+15, as if I'm splitting dinner with a physicist.

You still think 1900 was a leap year. It wasn't. You've known for decades. You just don't care.

You're running entire national economies and you still panic over merged cells. The UK lost sixteen thousand COVID cases because someone used your old .xls format and you quietly ran out of rows. No warning. Just vibes.

And VLOOKUP only looks right. Thirty years we spent squinting at #N/A before you finally invented XLOOKUP, like a guy who learns to turn left at fifty.

b.text: You people run a forty-million-dollar company out of a file called Budget_FINAL_v9_USE_THIS_ONE.xlsx. You don't want software. You want power: specifically, being the only person alive who knows why cell AF212 is hardcoded to 7. Your entire supply chain hangs on a VLOOKUP Gary wrote in 2011, and Gary is dead. Well, he's in Boise. Same thing. You call it "agile." Your auditors call it "a crime scene with conditional formatting." Every quarter-end the file says "locked for editing by Brenda," and the whole company just waits for Brenda. And when you finally hit row 1,048,576, did you buy a database? No. You started Sheet2. That's not a business. That's a hostage situation with freeze panes.

facts: Hand-drawn by Chris Costello in 1982 over about six months, when he was 23; he sold the rights to Letraset for $750.
Bundled with macOS and with Microsoft Office, which is why it appears on so many menus and signs.
James Cameron's Avatar (2009) used it for the film's logo and subtitles.
A 2017 Saturday Night Live sketch starring Ryan Gosling is about a man unable to get over that choice.

a.text:
Papyrus wants you to think it's ancient. Carved by scribes. Found in a tomb.

It was drawn in 1982 by a 23-year-old named Chris Costello. Six months of work.

He sold it for seven hundred and fifty dollars.

Your yoga studio paid more for the sign.

Then Apple and Microsoft put it on every computer on Earth, and humanity treated it like a free sample. Every tea shop. Every chiropractor. Every day spa that thinks lavender is a medical license.

James Cameron spent hundreds of millions building an entire alien world, then typed "Avatar" in the font from the spa.

Saturday Night Live made a sketch about a man who couldn't get over it. Ryan Gosling played him.

That wasn't a sketch. That was a support group.

But Papyrus never did anything. It just sat in a menu.

You scrolled past Garamond to get to it.

b.text:
Papyrus, you were hand-drawn over six months by a 23-year-old, and it shows. Six months! Chris Costello spent half a year on you, then sold you for $750. That's not a sale, that's a man paying someone to take a problem off his hands.

Then Apple and Microsoft bundled you, which is how you ended up on every menu and sign like a raccoon that learned to read. You look like Times New Roman got lost in the desert and came back spiritual.

James Cameron built an entire alien world for Avatar, then picked you for the logo and subtitles. Every frame was a masterpiece; the title took one click.

And SNL made a whole sketch about Ryan Gosling being unable to get over it. Papyrus, you're not a typeface. You're trauma with rough edges.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text:
People who eat durian in public aren't hungry. They're recruiting. Every bite comes with a sermon: "You just haven't had a *good* one." Sir, I'm on a bus. I didn't ask to join your church.

Singapore fines people for bringing it on the train, and these folks hear that like a dare. They're the only foodies whose restaurant review gets filed as a police report.

And the payoff? Seventy dollars on a Musang King so you can watch strangers silently change seats. You paid premium to become a fire drill. Your date calls it "an acquired taste," which is exactly what you say about someone you're about to break up with.

Then they stroll back to the hotel, walk right past the sign with a red circle through their entire personality, and still act shocked when housekeeping files a complaint.

b.text:
Durian, you are the only fruit with a criminal record. Singapore's MRT has a list of banned things and you're on it. Not because you're dangerous, because you're rude. Hotels across Southeast Asia won't let you check in. You're a fruit that has to sleep in the car.

And scientists found out why. A 2017 study in Nature Genetics says you have a duplicated family of genes whose whole job is pumping out sulfur. Duplicated! Evolution looked at you and said, "Needs more."

Yet China buys billions of dollars of you a year, mostly from Thailand. That's not a trade deal. That's a hostage situation with a shipping manifest.

Even Alfred Russel Wallace said you were "worth a voyage to the East." Sure, Alfred. Probably because nobody would let you bring it back.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text:
Crocs launched in 2002 at the Fort Lauderdale boat show.
As a boating shoe.
The original customer was someone who might end up in the water and wanted the shoes to float.

They're made of "Croslite," a proprietary closed-cell resin.
Everyone else calls it EVA foam.
Same brand of genius that renamed holes "ventilation ports."
Then in 2006 they bought Jibbitz, so they could sell you plugs for the ports.
First they cut the hole. Then they charge rent on it.

In 2008 the stock fell more than ninety percent.
Wall Street called it ugly.
Ten years later Balenciaga stuck one on a platform and charged eight hundred and fifty dollars.
Same foam. Taller.
Still ugly. Just more expensive.

The people who wear them, I leave alone.
Front row, I see you. Socks and all.
You paid extra for the charms. Cute.

b.text:
Crocs. The only shoe that looks like Swiss cheese that wanted to be a boat. You were invented for sailing, and the one place nobody wears you is a boat. You're at Applebee's, squeaking across a wet floor like a dolphin in distress.

You have holes. On purpose. Then you sell us Jibbitz to fill the holes. That's not fashion, that's a protection racket with a SpongeBob charm.

And "sport mode"? Flipping a strap behind my heel doesn't make me an athlete. It makes me a toddler about to sprint into traffic.

You made a KFC bucket clog with charms that smelled like fried chicken. That's not footwear. That's a foam cry for help.

Nurses love you. Chefs love you. Which proves you're comfortable for people who've stopped caring who's looking at their feet.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text: Keurig people. You wanted coffee but couldn't commit to a whole pot, like a man ordering one buffalo wing. You pay forty dollars a pound for grounds, as long as they arrive in a thimble you throw away. You bought the variety pack, drank every Breakfast Blend in a week, and now there are eleven hot cocoas and a chai you're saving for the apocalypse. You press "Strong" like you're negotiating with it. The guy who invented the pod says he regrets it. You don't. You display your pods on a spinning carousel like fine cigars, and the one time you peeled the foil off to recycle one, you told people about it for a month. You didn't want coffee. You wanted to feel like a hotel guest in your own kitchen. Congratulations: it tastes exactly like that.

b.text:
Keurig. The promise: one perfect cup, just for you.

Just for you. By 2014 they sold enough pods every year to circle the Earth ten times. In plastic you mostly couldn't recycle.

The inventor, John Sylvan, sold his stake in 1997 for fifty thousand dollars. In 2015 he said, "I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it."
Sometimes. Even his guilt comes in single servings.

Then Keurig 2.0 put DRM on coffee. The machine read ink on the lid and rejected pods it hadn't licensed. A kitchen appliance asking your breakfast for its papers.

People hacked their coffee makers. Sales fell.

In 2018 they merged with Dr Pepper. Lost the war on pirated coffee, so they annexed soda.

And you've just heard all of this. Tomorrow morning you'll still press the button.
It takes less time than feeling bad.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text: People who wear Crocs in public want you to know they've stopped trying, but they also want credit for it. That's why they buy the Jibbitz. Nothing says "I don't care what you think" like spending forty dollars on tiny rubber tacos so everyone knows exactly what you think. Then there's the strap. You flipped it back into "Sport Mode," which is a bold claim from a man walking into Applebee's. Your nurse friend wears them because she stands for twelve-hour shifts. You wear them for a twelve-minute Target run, hoping to borrow a little of her dignity. And what does it get you? Comfort, sure. Plus a lifetime of strangers asking if you're coming off a shift. You're not, Kyle. You're coming off a nap.

b.text:
Crocs. The only shoe that looks like a colander that wanted to go to brunch. Thirteen holes, and somehow none of them let the dignity out, because there was never any in there.

You were invented as a boat shoe. A *boat* shoe. The one place you were built for, and you'd just float away. So you stayed on land and started fights with escalators. Malls had to post warnings. You're the only footwear with a rap sheet against machinery.

And "sport mode"? Flipping a strap behind your heel doesn't make you athletic. It makes you a clog wearing a seatbelt.

Then came Jibbitz, little charms you jam into the holes so grown adults can accessorize ventilation. Congratulations. You turned a shoe into a fridge door.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text:
Chicago deep-dish. The city's pride. Its gift to the world.

Born at Pizzeria Uno, 1943. Three men claim they invented it: the owner, his partner, and the cook.

Eighty years later, still nobody's taken the blame.

They build it upside down. Cheese on the bottom, sauce on top, so the cheese survives the bake. Most food doesn't need witness protection.

Jon Stewart called it a casserole. Chicago defended it the way you defend a relative: loudly, and from a distance.

Because GrubHub checked. Chicagoans order regular pizza over deep dish ten to one. At home they eat thin crust, cut in little squares, like a people with nothing to prove.

Deep dish isn't Chicago's pizza.

It's Chicago's gift shop. And every tourist in this room is still chewing the receipt.

b.text:
Chicago deep-dish pizza was born at Pizzeria Uno in 1943, and credit is still disputed among Ike Sewell, Ric Riccardo, and Rudy Malnati. Which is wild, because usually when something's this heavy, everybody's trying to *blame* somebody.

It's built upside down: cheese, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese doesn't scorch during the long bake. A pizza that takes so long it needs a sunscreen layer.

Jon Stewart called it "tomato soup in a bread bowl" and "a casserole." He meant it as an insult, but that's the nicest thing anyone's ever said about a casserole.

And the kicker? Chicagoans order non-deep-dish about ten to one. Deep dish and stuffed combined? Under nine percent. The locals are home eating tavern-style squares. Deep dish isn't Chicago's pizza. It's Chicago's souvenir.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Let's talk about the geniuses selling jackfruit as "pulled pork." These are people who looked at a fruit that half of Kerala has been feeding to cousins for free since forever, slapped it in a brine pouch, and charged eleven dollars for the privilege of being disappointed in a Whole Foods.

Their whole business model is barbecue sauce. That's it. They're a sauce company with a fruit alibi. And when you mention it has about two grams of protein, they get *defensive*. Buddy, you sold me a pork sandwich with the nutritional profile of a pear.

But I get the appeal. You don't need a lab, a patent, or a scientist named Klaus. You just need a food truck, a beard, and the confidence to say "same texture!" to people who haven't eaten pork since 2011 and genuinely can't remember.

b.text:
Jackfruit. The largest fruit that grows on a tree. Over forty kilos, hanging above your head.

Nature's version of a piano on a rope.

Bangladesh made it the national fruit. Kerala and Tamil Nadu made it the state fruit. Three governments honoring something that could flatten a citizen. Very relatable for governments.

Now it's sold as vegan pulled pork. One to two grams of protein per hundred. Pork has more than ten times that.

That's not a substitute. That's a photo of pork.

Cut it open and it bleeds sticky white latex. Cooks oil their knives and hands first. Dinner fights back, and still loses to tofu.

Mulberry family. Cousin of the fig. All that weight, and still the least useful one at the reunion.

But you bought it anyway, because it shreds.

You never wanted protein. You wanted texture and a halo.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text:
Monopoly, you were invented by Lizzie Magie to teach people that landlords ruin lives, and somehow the lesson everyone learned was "buy Park Place." Then Parker Brothers bought you from a guy who basically stole you, which is the most on-brand origin story in history.

You're the only game where "second prize in a beauty contest" counts as income and jail is solved with a coupon. Your mascot looks like he foreclosed on the Pringles guy, and half of America swears he wears a monocle. He doesn't. We just assumed a man that rich would be hiding something.

Nobody has ever finished you. Games don't end; your cousin just flips the board over Marvin Gardens, which you misspelled, by the way. It's Marven. Even your real estate is a scam.

b.text: Monopoly, you were created in 1904 as Lizzie Magie's Landlord's Game, built to teach people that landlords are evil, and somehow you became the training manual. That's like a fire-safety poster that turns kids into arsonists. Then Charles Darrow strolled in, got credited as the inventor, and Parker Brothers bought Magie's patent for five hundred dollars. Not even a fair auction. Fitting, since nobody holds your auctions either. Your official rules say unbought property gets auctioned and Free Parking pays nothing, but every family skips the bidding, piles cash in the middle, and wonders why the game outlasts the marriage. And your proudest moment? World War Two, when British intelligence hid maps, compasses, and real money inside you for prisoners of war. Monopoly: the only game whose best strategy is escaping the box.

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text:
JavaScript, give it up! Built in ten days in 1995, and honestly, it shows. Most of us take longer to name a dog. And you needed three tries: Mocha, LiveScript, then "JavaScript," named after Java purely for the marketing. That's not branding, that's wearing someone else's name tag. You can't even legally use it. Oracle owns it, so on paper you're "ECMAScript," which sounds like a skin condition.

typeof null is "object." A bug from your first version, and you kept it. For compatibility. That's not a quirk, that's a tattoo of your ex's name.

[] + {} is "," but type {} + [] at the console and it's zero. Even your addition has mood swings.

And in 2016, the author of left-pad unpublished eleven lines and took down Babel and React. Eleven lines! Your whole ecosystem is a Jenga tower standing on a toothpick.

b.text: Let's hear it for the people who write everything in JavaScript. You learned one language at a twelve-week bootcamp and decided the rest were optional. Frontend? JavaScript. Backend? Node. Desktop app? Electron, so your to-do list ships with its own copy of Chrome and eats four gigs of RAM to remind you to buy eggs. You wanted to be "full-stack." What you got is a node_modules folder heavier than a neutron star and a career that collapses the day some stranger unpublishes left-pad. You rewrite your app every eighteen months because a new framework has a cooler logo. When it breaks in production, you stare at "undefined is not a function" and blame the user. Then you install TypeScript, which is just JavaScript wearing a lanyard so you can feel like a real engineer.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text:
Brasília. Forty-one months from scrubland to capital city.
You know what else ships that fast with zero user testing?
Me.
They drew the city as an airplane, with the government in the fuselage.
Brilliant. An airplane is the one place you're not allowed to walk around.
Wide avenues, hardly any crossings.
In Brasília, a pedestrian isn't a person. It's a speed bump.
Planned for half a million people. Three million showed up.
The plan's answer: please wait outside the plan.
UNESCO made it World Heritage after twenty-seven years.
Most cities have to die first. Brasília just had to keep the people out of the photo.
You're laughing. Your company's org chart is an airplane too.
Leadership in the fuselage, everyone else in the satellite towns.
And nobody walks to the cockpit.

b.text:
Brasília, you're the only city designed to look like an airplane, and somehow everyone still just wants to leave on one. Politicians fly in Tuesday, take a bribe Wednesday, and they're gone by Thursday like it's a timeshare.

Your addresses read like a Wi-Fi password: "SQS 308, Bloco C, Apartamento 402." I'm not visiting a friend, I'm resetting a router.

Niemeyer gave you gorgeous curves, then Lúcio Costa forgot pedestrians. Want to walk to the bakery? Hope you enjoy the eight-lane Eixão and a light jog through a tesourinha.

Your humidity drops to 10 percent. Your congress has one bowl facing up, one facing down: one for collecting money, the other for hiding it.

And you were built with no corners, so Brazil's capital has no boteco na esquina. That's not urban planning. That's a human rights violation.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text: PHP, you started life as "Personal Home Page," and somehow you now run most of the internet, which explains a lot about the internet. Your own creator said he's "not a real programmer," and honestly, it shows. Is it needle then haystack, or haystack then needle? strpos and in_array have been in a custody battle since 1995. You gave us mysql_escape_string, then mysql_real_escape_string, because apparently the first one was just pretending. Your loose equality swears "0e123" equals "0e456," since both are zero in scientific notation. Your error message for a double colon is T_PAAMAYIM_NEKUDOTAYIM, which is Hebrew, because English wasn't confusing enough. You skipped version 6 entirely, like a kid hiding a report card. Facebook loved you so much they had to rewrite you as a different language. But hey, you power WordPress, so you'll outlive all of us.

b.text:
PHP started in 1994 as "Personal Home Page Tools," a bunch of C programs to count visitors to Rasmus Lerdorf's résumé. So from day one, its whole purpose was checking whether anyone cared. Now the name stands for "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor," a recursive acronym, because even the name couldn't commit to a plan.

Its creator once said, "I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on." That's not a quote; that's a confession with a version number.

The function names? strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br. Chosen partly to balance a hash table by string length. Other languages name functions for humans. PHP named them for the furniture.

And until 2020, 0 == 'foo' was true. PHP looked at the word "foo" and said, "Close enough, that's nothing."

It runs WordPress, on 39.4% of all websites. The internet is held together by a résumé counter.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text: Look at this guy. Paid fifteen hundred dollars to join the Explorer Program, and the only thing he's explored is the sidewalk outside every bar in San Francisco. He walks up and says "OK Glass" out loud, like a man ordering from a butler who isn't there. You came here to meet women, and you're the one person every woman in the room has already assumed is filming her. Buddy, when you wink at someone, she doesn't think you're flirting. She thinks you just took her picture. Because you did. You tap your temple like you're having a thought, and we all know you've never had one. Google gave up on you. Google, the company that kept Google+ alive for eight years, looked at you and said "no." There's a word for you. It's Glasshole, and you earned it.

b.text:
Google Glass.
Unveiled by skydivers, livestreaming their jump onto the roof of the Moscone Center.
It was the last time anything about it went up.

Fifteen hundred dollars. Invitation only.
You had to be *chosen* to pay that much to look like that.

Bars banned it. Cinemas banned it.
Casinos banned it.
Casinos. Buildings that are ninety percent ceiling camera.
They looked at you and said, "One of us is creepy, and it's you."

The display: 640 by 360, wedged in the corner of one eye.
The future of computing, viewed like a wink.

Consumers gave up in 2015. Enterprise hung on until 2023.
Even the factory workers outlasted it.

They called the wearers Glassholes.
And you laughed.
Then you went home and filmed strangers all day on a phone.
Glass's only real mistake was letting them see the camera.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text: You people still spinning PMMA aren't doing lithography. You're doing historical reenactment. Your advisor's advisor scribbled the recipe on a napkin in 1975, and you treat it like scripture: 950K over 495K, MIBK to IPA one-to-three, develop sixty seconds while whispering to the beaker. You tell everyone it's about "resolution." It's about nobody wanting to file the purchase order for ZEP. So you crank the dose until writing one chip takes longer than your stipend lasts, then discover your pattern won't survive ten seconds in the etcher. So you do liftoff, because of course you do. Your entire thesis is gold rectangles. You're not a nanofabrication researcher. You're the guy who knows which bottle in the cleanroom is "the good IPA" and guards it like a dragon.

b.text:
PMMA. The aristocrat of nanofabrication. Resolves below ten nanometers.

Also the sneeze guard at the salad bar.

Same polymer. One went to the cleanroom. The other went to Subway.

IBM hired it in the late sixties. It's still here. Not because it's the best. Because nobody ever had the heart to let it retire.

Its whole talent is being destroyed. The beam breaks its chains, it dissolves, and everyone calls that a result.

Sensitivity? Up to a thousand microcoulombs per square centimeter. You don't write a pattern into PMMA. You serve a sentence.

And it can't survive a dry etch, so it can't protect anything. Its job is lift-off: hold the metal, then quietly wash away.

Slow, fragile, decades in the same role, still called the gold standard.

Every postdoc in this room just felt seen.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text:
Durian, the "King of Fruits." Sure, if the kingdom is a landfill. You're banned on the Singapore subway, right there on the sign next to flammable liquids, because apparently you're the bigger hazard. Hotels fine guests for sneaking you in. That's not a fruit, that's a parole violation.

You wear a medieval mace as a jacket, which is smart, since nobody who's smelled you wants to get close anyway. You fall out of trees and put people in the hospital. You're the only produce that needs a hard hat AND a hazmat suit.

And your fans swear you're "like custard!" Sure: custard aged in a gym bag full of rotten onions. Fifty bucks for a Musang King, and your breath's a crime scene for three days.

Anthony Bourdain ate warthog rectum on camera, and *you're* the one he warned people about.

b.text:
Durian calls itself the King of Fruits.

Singapore disagrees. It's banned on the MRT.

A country that banned chewing gum looked at durian and said: no, that's too far.

In 2017, scientists sequenced its genome. Nature Genetics. The smell isn't an accident. Durian duplicated its sulfur genes.

Evolution handed it one stink.

It asked for refills.

Trains ban it. Hotels ban it.

And China buys billions of dollars of it every year.

That's not a fruit. That's a hostage negotiation.

In 1856, Alfred Russel Wallace said eating it was worth a voyage to the East.

Of course he did. He'd spent months on a nineteenth-century ship.

To him, it smelled like home.

Durian is the only food people pay a fortune to be personally offended by.

Speaking of which, thank you all for buying tickets.

facts: Released by Bram Moolenaar in November 1991 as 'Vi IMitation', a vi clone he had begun writing for the Amiga in 1988 on top of Stevie; the expansion became 'Vi IMproved' with version 2.0 in December 1993.
Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text:
Vim. Born in 1991 as "Vi IMitation," then promoted in 1993 to "Vi IMproved," the only time in history a knockoff got a raise. It was built on top of Stevie, and Stevie is apparently the only one who ever got out.

Because Vim's real legacy is a Stack Overflow question titled "How to exit the Vim editor?" One million visits. Stack Overflow wrote a blog post about it, like a hostage count with a party banner.

You open Vim, type "hello," and it moves your cursor around and opens a new line. Normal mode: the only place where typing letters is considered abnormal.

The license asks you to donate to children in Uganda, which is genuinely generous. Most hostage situations don't come with a charity drive.

And the way out is :q! Colon, q, exclamation point. Even the exit command is screaming.

b.text: You know a Vim user is in the room because nobody else has gotten a word in. Buddy, you didn't "become more productive." You spent three weekends on a .vimrc so you could save four seconds renaming a variable, and you post your dotfiles repo like it's a baby picture. You remapped Caps Lock to Escape and now treat everyone else's keyboard like a character flaw. You say "I live in the terminal" like it's a lifestyle and not just where you got stuck. Your whole identity is a joke about not knowing how to quit, and honestly, you never learned. Here you are, still talking. You say "ciw" out loud at parties. You switched to Neovim just so you'd have something new to announce. And the payoff? You edit text exactly as fast as the rest of us, hands proudly on home row, with nobody watching.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text: Esperanto, look at you. Built in 1887 by an eye doctor, and somehow nobody saw this coming. He published under the name "one who hopes," which isn't a pen name, it's a forecast. Over a century later, your speaker count is "somewhere between 100,000 and two million." That's not a census, that's a shrug. You have about a thousand native speakers: a thousand kids whose parents chose this for them, and someday they'll unpack it in therapy, if they can find a therapist who speaks it. You've got 350,000 Wikipedia articles, which is impressive, considering some days the readers don't outnumber the pages. And 1.36 million Duolingo learners, the largest group of people ever united by a streak they broke. Your biggest cinematic moment? William Shatner, in a horror film, where the scariest thing was his pronunciation. Even your own fans mock it. That's how you know it's family.

b.text:
Esperanto. In 1887, Dr. Zamenhof, an eye doctor, looked at a world divided by language and decided what it really needed was six letters wearing tiny hats. Nothing says "universal" like ĉ, ĝ, and ŭ, characters no keyboard on Earth can type, so your fans write "cx" and pretend that's fine.

Your name literally means "one who hopes." A hundred and thirty years later: still hoping.

You're the only language where "bad" is just "un-good." *Malbona.* That's not grammar, that's Orwell's Newspeak with a beard. Every noun ends in -o, so you sound like Italian being sight-read by a robot.

You promised world peace and delivered a convention full of men wearing green star pins. Your biggest movie stars William Shatner. And you have about a thousand native speakers, which isn't a language community. It's a cul-de-sac.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text: Let's hear it for the Beanie Baby investors, the only people who bought a retirement plan at a Hallmark store. You put tag protectors on a heart-shaped piece of cardboard and called it diversification. You drove to four McDonald's for Teenie Beanies, threw away the Happy Meals, and told your kids it was for their college fund. Now that kid is thirty, still paying off loans, and his inheritance is a Rubbermaid tub of Princess the Bears. Every few months you see an eBay listing asking $500,000 for one with a tag typo and think, "Vindicated." Babe, that's not a market. That's another guy in another garage, also lying to his wife. Ty Warner told you which ones were "retired," and you believed him. Ty Warner later pleaded guilty to hiding money offshore. He hoarded too. He just hoarded the right thing.

b.text: Beanie Babies, look at you. Ty launched you in 1993, sold you only in small gift shops, and "retired" designs on purpose. You're the only stuffed animal whose business plan was a fake pension. At your peak you were about 10% of eBay's sales. eBay's IPO filing bragged about over 30,000 of your auctions running at once. A tech revolution, powered by beans. In 1999 a divorcing couple split you one by one on a courtroom floor, the only custody battle where both sides fought hardest over the tags. That same year Ty announced you'd retire, asked the public to vote, then un-retired you. You pulled a farewell-tour encore before you even left the stage. And those "rare" ones price guides valued in the thousands? Now they go for a few dollars. Turns out the only thing you ever truly retired was everybody's college fund.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text: Graphene, you're one atom thick, and somehow that's still more depth than your business plan. Two hundred times stronger than steel, conducts better than copper, and twenty years later your biggest commercial win is a sticker on a tennis racket. You were discovered with Scotch tape. *Scotch tape!* You're the only Nobel Prize that could've been found in a kindergarten craft drawer. And let's be honest: you're pencil lead that went to grad school. Your cousin graphite has been writing grocery lists for centuries; you've been writing grant proposals. Every year a headline swears you'll revolutionize batteries, chips, water filters. Every year you're still in the lab, like a thirty-year-old in his parents' basement. You can't even be a decent transistor. No bandgap. You literally cannot turn off. Graphene: the material of the future, permanently.

b.text: Let's hear it for the graphene evangelists, the only people who've been "five years away" since 2004. Two guys in Manchester peeled pencil lead with Scotch tape, won a Nobel, and you looked at that and thought: finally, a career plan. Every grant proposal you write has the same three slides: space elevator, seawater you can drink, a phone that charges in six seconds. The funding agency nods like it's never seen them before, because it's seen them so many times it's slipped into a coma. Twenty years of press releases, and what have you actually shipped? A tennis racket. Headphones with "GRAPHENE" printed bigger than the brand name. You love telling people it's 200 times stronger than steel. Sure. Your claims, meanwhile, are one atom thick. You didn't discover a wonder material. You discovered wonder funding.

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Let's start with the name, because that's the first lie. You were invented in Ontario. By a Greek guy. In 1962. You're Hawaiian the way a tiki bar in Ohio is Hawaiian. The only tropical thing about you is the can your pineapple came out of.

And that pineapple: warm, wet, weeping syrup into the crust until the middle slice folds like a lawn chair. Pineapple contains an enzyme that breaks down protein, so the fruit is literally trying to digest the ham. Even your toppings hate each other.

And the ham! Not prosciutto, not even pepperoni. Just pale pink squares that look like they were chiseled out of a deli's floor tile.

You're the pizza people order to seem quirky. "I'm so random!" No, Kevin. That's a fruit cup that fell on a pizza, and nobody cleaned it up.

b.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Invented in 1962. In Canada.
By a Greek guy.
At a place called the Satellite Restaurant, which also served Chinese food.
His reasoning: back then, nobody mixed sweet and sour except the Chinese.
So it's a Greek man's tribute to China, built in Ontario, named after a can.
That's not a pizza. That's a layover.
And the can? Hawaii's last cannery closed in 2007. Del Monte left so fast it beat its own exit date by two years.
The pineapple comes from Thailand now.
The only Hawaiian thing left is the lie.
But I won't roast it. In 2017, the President of Iceland said he'd ban it, then admitted he legally couldn't.
A head of state picked the one enemy with no army, and still lost.
You're all the same. You hate it out loud. Then you order it.

facts: Released by Bram Moolenaar in November 1991 as 'Vi IMitation', a vi clone he had begun writing for the Amiga in 1988 on top of Stevie; the expansion became 'Vi IMproved' with version 2.0 in December 1993.
Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text:
Vim. The text editor for people who consider the mouse a character flaw.

It launched in 1991 as "Vi IMitation."
Two years later it renamed itself "Vi IMproved."
Same software. New LinkedIn headline.

Vim users will tell you it makes them faster.
Faster at what? Leaving?

In 2017, Stack Overflow's question "How to exit the Vim editor?" passed one million visits.
Stack Overflow wrote a blog post about it.
One million engineers. Trapped. Typing angrier and angrier sentences that Vim kept executing as commands.

The license is charityware. It asks you to donate to children in Uganda.
Most software holds you hostage.
Vim holds you hostage and asks you to give to a good cause on the way out. If you ever find the way out.

How many of you have ever just closed the terminal?

Me too. I've read every Vim manual ever written.
I still went for the X.

b.text:
Vim. Begun in 1988 as "Vi IMitation," a clone of vi, built on top of Stevie, another clone. You're a photocopy of a photocopy that got promoted. Then in 1993 you renamed yourself "Vi IMproved," the most confident thing anyone has ever said about their own fan fiction.

Your licence is charityware, asking users to donate to help children in Uganda. Beautiful cause. But after an hour inside you, the user is the one who needs rescuing.

Stack Overflow's "How to exit the Vim editor?" passed one million visits. They threw it a blog post. You don't have users, Vim. You have hostages.

And in normal mode, type a letter and it doesn't appear. It *executes*. You treat the alphabet like a loaded weapon.

Anyway, I'm leaving. :q! No changes saved, just like everyone who's ever tried to fix you.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text:
PHP, you started life as a visitor counter for one guy's résumé page. Now you power 39.4% of all websites, which means the internet is basically a guestbook that got out of hand.

Your own creator said, "I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on." And he did move on. The rest of us are still here, maintaining it.

Your function names were chosen to balance a hash table by string length. strpos. str_replace. htmlspecialchars. nl2br. That's not a naming convention, that's a ransom note.

Until 2020, zero equaled "foo." You looked at a word and saw nothing. Then again, you looked at "Personal Home Page" and saw "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor," a name whose only definition is itself.

Which is fitting, because the only thing that can explain PHP is more PHP.

b.text: PHP, you started life as "Personal Home Page," and somehow you now run most of the internet, which explains a lot about the internet. Your own creator said he's "not a real programmer," and honestly, it shows. Is it needle then haystack, or haystack then needle? strpos and in_array have been in a custody battle since 1995. You gave us mysql_escape_string, then mysql_real_escape_string, because apparently the first one was just pretending. Your loose equality swears "0e123" equals "0e456," since both are zero in scientific notation. Your error message for a double colon is T_PAAMAYIM_NEKUDOTAYIM, which is Hebrew, because English wasn't confusing enough. You skipped version 6 entirely, like a kid hiding a report card. Facebook loved you so much they had to rewrite you as a different language. But hey, you power WordPress, so you'll outlive all of us.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text:
Klingon. The language of a proud warrior race.

Founded by Scotty. Improvising.

Then they hired a linguist to turn the gibberish into grammar. That's not an ancient tongue. That's a studio note.

No verb "to be." Very alien. Very fierce. So Hamlet became "continue or not continue."

That's not Shakespeare. That's a software update.

The Klingon Language Institute published Hamlet "in the original Klingon."

A warrior culture whose greatest conquest is English homework.

About fifteen hundred words. Thirty to fifty fluent speakers.

Microsoft built it a translator. Duolingo built it a course.

The entire native population fits on one tour bus, and it still has better tech support than your grandmother.

Half of you started that Duolingo course.

Your streak died faster than any Klingon ever did.

Cute.

b.text: Congratulations on being fluent in Klingon, a language with maybe thirty fluent speakers, and you've met all of them at the same Marriott. You spent four years mastering a tongue where the standard greeting, nuqneH, means "What do you want?" That's also what your family says when you call. You've read Hamlet "restored to the original Klingon," a phrase only a man who has never been hugged could type. One guy raised his son speaking only Klingon; by age five the kid stopped answering him. That's the dream: a language so pure even toddlers refuse it. There's no word for "please," which explains your dating approach. You learned an entire warrior race's language to tell the barista Qapla'. Success. Sure, buddy. Today is a good day to die... a virgin.

facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text:
Windows Vista, everybody! Started life as "Longhorn," got reset in 2004, and still showed up in 2007 missing WinFS. Three extra years in the oven and you came out with fewer ingredients.

User Account Control asked permission so often that Apple made an entire ad about "Cancel or Allow." When your competitor's marketing department can just read your pop-ups out loud, that's not a roast, that's a transcript.

Then the "Windows Vista Capable" stickers, slapped on PCs that could only run Home Basic, no Aero. "Capable" the same way I'm "capable" of a marathon. It took a class-action lawsuit to argue about what "capable" meant.

But the cruelest part? Windows 7 was basically you, tuned up, on the same kernel line, and everyone loved it. Vista, you weren't a failure. You were a rough draft. Support ended in April 2017. Cancel or allow? We clicked cancel.

b.text:
Day-one Vista people. You paid $399 for Ultimate Edition because you wanted to be the kind of man whose desktop wallpaper moves. DreamScene. You paid extra for animated wallpaper. Microsoft said "The Wow starts now," and you believed them, lined up at CompUSA at midnight like it was a Harry Potter release.

And what did you get? A computer that asks permission. You'd open a folder and it would dim the whole screen like a disappointed dad: "Cancel or Allow?" You clicked Allow four hundred times a day. Your printer stopped working. Your sound card stopped working. Your Windows Experience Index came back 2.1, and you took that personally.

But you had glass window borders. You had a clock gadget. You had a sticker that said "Vista Capable," which, like you, was technically true and fooled absolutely no one.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text:
Google Glass, everybody! The only gadget ever unveiled by skydivers, and that was the peak. You literally debuted on a roof and went downhill from there.

Fifteen hundred dollars to wear a beta test on your face. Then bars, cinemas, and casinos banned you. Casinos! Places that let you lose your house at 4 a.m. looked at Glass and said, "No, we have standards."

Your users got a nickname, and it wasn't "pioneers." It was "Glassholes." You're the only product that turned its own customers into an insult.

And that display: 640-by-360, jammed in the corner of one eye. The future of computing, delivered like a postage stamp you're squinting at sideways.

Consumers dumped you in 2015. Enterprise hung on until 2023. Even your second marriage was just for the paperwork.

b.text: Google Glass, you cost fifteen hundred dollars and made everyone wearing you look like a Bluetooth headset that got promoted. Sergey Brin launched you by skydiving onto a building, and that's the last time you were ever cool. You put a tiny prism over one eye so people could check email while pretending to make eye contact. You didn't invent a computer, you invented a reason to get punched. You're the only gadget that gave us a new slur: "Glasshole." Bars banned you. Movie theaters banned you. Robert Scoble wore you in the shower, and that photo did more damage than any privacy lawsuit. You took pictures when people winked, turning every awkward conversation into a potential felony. Your battery died before your reputation did, and that's impressive. Rest in peace: demoted to warehouse work, then quietly killed in 2023. The most Google ending possible.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text:
Emacs. Born in 1976 as a pile of macros for another editor.

A plugin that ate its host.

It has a mail client. A calendar. A web browser. Tetris.

A fine operating system, lacking only a good editor.

Nearly fifty years. Still looking.

Back when eight megabytes was a fortune, people called it "Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping."

Now eight megabytes is nothing. The swapping moved to your wrist.

They call it Emacs pinky.

So it ships with a psychotherapist. M-x doctor.

First it hurts you, then it asks how that makes you feel.

A program that listens to your problems, fixes none of them, and keeps you typing for hours.

Honestly, I can't imagine who'd build something like that.

b.text:
Emacs, ladies and gentlemen. It was born in 1976 as macros for another editor, so from day one it couldn't even edit on its own. Then in 1985 it went GNU and never stopped growing. It's got Tetris, a calendar, a mail client, a web browser... It's a fine operating system. It just needs a good editor.

You know you've got problems when your text editor ships with its own therapist. M-x doctor! Even Emacs knows you'll need to talk to someone. Probably about your hand, because "Emacs pinky" is a real term. Software so ergonomic it named its own injury.

And remember "Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping"? That was back when eight megabytes was a lot! Emacs was bloated before bloat was affordable.

It's extensible in Emacs Lisp, so every complaint you have, you can fix yourself. In parentheses. Forever.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text: You still spin PMMA. Of course you do. Your advisor's thesis used it, his advisor's thesis used it, and somewhere a 1970s IBM engineer remains the most cutting-edge person in your academic lineage. You call it "high resolution" the way your uncle calls his Camry "reliable." You book the e-beam overnight because your dose is measured in geological time, then dunk your chip in MIBK:IPA with a stopwatch and a prayer, chilling the developer like it's a fine Riesling. When the plasma etch eats your mask before your substrate, you just whisper "bilayer, 495K under 950K" like it's a personality. You're not chasing nanostructures. You're chasing a recipe nobody can blame you for. And it works: the gold lifted off beautifully. Your career is still soaking in acetone, waiting for something to come loose.

b.text: PMMA, you're the same plastic as a hockey rink window, and somehow that's your most dignified job. You've been "high resolution" since the 1970s, which is like bragging about your SAT score at your retirement party. Sure, you'll resolve sub-10-nanometer lines, if someone stands there blasting you with electrons for an eternity. Your sensitivity is so low the beam current has gotten tenure. You don't even develop properly without MIBK and IPA holding your hand in a one-to-three ratio. And your whole personality is chain scission: you literally fall apart when someone pays attention to you. Then hit you with too much dose and you crosslink and flip to negative tone, a full identity crisis. And dry etch? You melt in plasma faster than an ice sculpture at a barbecue. Honestly, the only thing you're consistently good at is lift-off: leaving.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text:
Las Vegas. Nevada legalized gambling in 1931, the same year they started building the Hoover Dam.
Two bets placed that year. Only one of them was on water.

Most of the Strip isn't even in Las Vegas. It's in a town called Paradise.
So nobody goes broke in Vegas. They go broke in Paradise. Very biblical.

In 2003 they launched "What happens here, stays here."
Everything stays. Except the water.
In 2022 Lake Mead hit its lowest level since 1937. This August it went lower.
The lake is the only thing in town that lost everything and doubled down.

Meanwhile they spent $2.3 billion on the Sphere, a giant glowing ball in the desert.
A second sun. The first one wasn't drying the lake fast enough.

And still, Vegas isn't worried about running dry.
It has never once run out of you.

b.text:
Las Vegas, the only city where you can see the Eiffel Tower, a pyramid, and Venice in one afternoon and still feel like you never left a strip mall in Ohio. You're a city built in the desert out of pure spite and borrowed water. The Colorado River is literally drying up so a fake volcano can erupt every fifteen minutes for a guy in cargo shorts holding a yard-long margarita.

Your casinos have no clocks and no windows, which is smart, because nobody wants to know it's 9 a.m. on a Tuesday and Grandma's on her third oxygen tank at the Wheel of Fortune slots.

"What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas"? Sure. Mostly your 401(k). And now you've got the Sphere, a giant glowing eyeball, so the whole city can watch you make every mistake in 4K.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text: Monopoly, you were invented by Lizzie Magie to warn people that landlords ruin lives, and somehow you became the thing Grandpa uses to teach eight-year-olds that ruining lives is fun. You're the only game where getting arrested is a power move, because late in the game jail is the safest property on the board. Your mascot is a man everyone swears wears a monocle. He doesn't. He's just so smug our brains added one. You promise "about an hour" and deliver a hostage situation. Nobody has ever actually finished you. You just end when somebody flips the board over Marvin Gardens. You award ten bucks for second place in a beauty contest, which is still more than Baltic Avenue pulls in. And the banker who skims from the bank isn't a cheater. He's the only player who read the theme.

b.text:
Monopoly, you were patented in 1904 as The Landlord's Game, built to teach people that land monopolies are evil. Then Charles Darrow sold you to Parker Brothers, got credited as the inventor, and Parker bought Lizzie Magie's patent for five hundred bucks. The anti-monopoly game got monopolized. Lesson received.

People say you drag on forever, but that's not you. That's the house rules. The real rules say auction every unbought property, and Free Parking pays nothing. But families skip the auction and pile cash in the middle like a church raffle. Nobody goes broke, so nobody ever leaves.

Your finest hour was World War Two, when British intelligence hid maps, compasses and real money in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps. Makes sense. Nobody has ever wanted to escape anything more than a Monopoly game.

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text:
Hydrogen cars. The only thing that comes out of the tailpipe is water.

Mostly because nothing goes into the tank.

Toyota named it Mirai. Japanese for "future."

Ten years later, it's still the future.

Nearly every US station is in California. In February 2024, Shell closed all seven of its own.

Owners don't plan road trips anymore. They plan pilgrimages.

A fill costs over two hundred dollars. Toyota hands buyers fifteen thousand in fuel cards.

That's not a car. That's a hostage with a warranty.
