And the clean fuel? Over ninety-five percent made from fossil fuels.

It's a gas car that went to rehab and kept its dealer.

The owners sued. Twice. The second suit: five point seven billion dollars.

Finally, something hydrogen-powered that's actually going somewhere.

And you're laughing. You still drive a car that "goes electric next year," every year.

b.text:
Hydrogen fuel-cell cars, give it up! Toyota named you "Mirai," Japanese for "future," which is technically accurate, because that's when you'll find a working station. You're the cleanest car on the road, as long as nobody asks where the hydrogen comes from. More than ninety-five percent fossil fuels! You're not a zero-emission vehicle, you're natural gas wearing a lab coat.

Nearly every US station is in California, and in 2024 Shell closed all seven of theirs. Even the oil company said, "Nah, this is too sketchy for us."

At $36 a kilo, a fill-up costs over two hundred bucks. Toyota had to hand out fifteen-thousand-dollar fuel cards, which is the automotive version of "Please stay for dinner, I'll pay."

And the owners sued. Twice. The second suit wanted at least $5.7 billion. That's the only thing about you that's ever been fully loaded.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text:
Google Glass, look at you. Fifteen hundred dollars to wear a sugar cube on your eyebrow. Sergey Brin had skydivers jump onto a building to launch you, and that was the last time anything about you was cool.

You invented a whole new insult. Nobody calls iPhone owners "Phoneholes." But "Glasshole"? Earned. Fast. Because you let people take photos by *winking*. You turned flirting into a privacy violation.

Every sentence started with "OK Glass," like a man narrating his own midlife crisis out loud. Bars banned you. Strangers ripped you off people's faces. Your battery died faster than your reputation, and you overheated right next to the user's brain, which honestly explains the buying decision.

Then you pivoted to "Enterprise," the tech version of moving back home to work at your uncle's warehouse.

And even the warehouse let you go.

b.text:
Google Glass, everybody! The only gadget ever unveiled by skydivers, and that was the peak. You literally debuted on a roof and went downhill from there.

Fifteen hundred dollars to wear a beta test on your face. Then bars, cinemas, and casinos banned you. Casinos! Places that let you lose your house at 4 a.m. looked at Glass and said, "No, we have standards."

Your users got a nickname, and it wasn't "pioneers." It was "Glassholes." You're the only product that turned its own customers into an insult.

And that display: 640-by-360, jammed in the corner of one eye. The future of computing, delivered like a postage stamp you're squinting at sideways.

Consumers dumped you in 2015. Enterprise hung on until 2023. Even your second marriage was just for the paperwork.

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text:
Google Sheets, give it up! Born in 2006 as "Google Spreadsheets," a name with all the creativity of a label on a filing cabinet. Before that you were XL2Web, which sounds less like software and more like a hoodie size.

Ten million cells. They bumped you from five million in 2022 and everyone celebrated. Babe, that's not a promotion. That's a bigger cage.

IMPORTXML, GOOGLEFINANCE, live web data piped straight into cells, so now my budget can disappoint me in real time.

And collaboration! Coloured cursors circling my formula like seagulls over a dropped fry.

Offline mode? Easy: use Chrome or Edge, install an extension, flip a setting, all while you're still online. That's not offline mode. That's a permission slip.

But hey, you're free. And honestly? It shows.

b.text: Google Sheets, you're Excel's little brother who moved into a browser tab and called it "the cloud." Your whole personality is twelve people's colored cursors circling the same cell like sharks while an Anonymous Capybara silently watches everyone's mistakes. You say "Saving..." with the confidence of a man who has absolutely not saved. Your IMPORTRANGE makes me click "Allow access" like I'm asking my own spreadsheet for permission to see my own spreadsheet. Half my cells just say "Loading..." forever, like a Victorian ghost waiting for a letter. And you'll let anyone sort one column without the others, then shrug while every customer gets someone else's phone number. Version history is your only real feature: it's just a timeline of who ruined everything at 2 a.m. And yes, Gemini can explain my #REF! error now. Great. It's still there.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text:
Emacs is a beautiful operating system. Shame it never shipped with a decent text editor. That's why half its users install evil-mode: they love Emacs so much they turned it into Vim.

Emacs stands for "Escape Meta Alt Control Shift," which is also the sound your pinky makes on its way to the orthopedic surgeon. Asking for help is C-h, which in a terminal deletes a character. So even your cry for help gets backspaced.

It has a built-in therapist, M-x doctor, which is thoughtful, because nobody else will listen to you explain your init.el. Four thousand lines of Lisp, half copied from a 2003 mailing list, and you still declare "Emacs bankruptcy" every two years.

It plays Tetris. It reads email. It runs your entire life in Org-mode. It still chokes on one long line of JSON.

b.text:
Emacs, you started in 1976 as macros for an editor called TECO. Nearly fifty years later you're still basically macros, just with more parentheses.

People call you a fine operating system lacking only a good editor, which is generous. Operating systems don't ship with Tetris and a therapist. But M-x doctor is smart planning, because your users need one. Every one of them has Emacs pinky, a repetitive strain injury you earn just by trying to save a file.

You've got a mail client, a calendar, a web browser. You're not a text editor; you're a hoarder with a keybinding for every room.

And "Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping"? Eight megabytes used to be a lot. Now it's nothing. The memory problem aged out, but the Control key is still begging for mercy.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text:
Crocs. Born in Boulder, debuted at a Fort Lauderdale boat show, because only on a boat is everyone too busy not drowning to look down. You're made of "Croslite," a "proprietary closed-cell resin foam," which is corporate for "pool noodle with a lawyer." Everyone else just calls it EVA foam.

And those aren't holes, they're "ventilation ports." Sure. Then you bought Jibbitz so you could sell people jewelry for the holes.

In 2008 your stock fell over 90%, the only time Wall Street ever agreed with my eyes. Then the pandemic hit and you boomed, gifting 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers. Like they hadn't suffered enough.

Then Balenciaga sold platform Crocs for $850. Eight hundred and fifty dollars for a boat shoe on stilts. Finally, a Croc that lets you look down on people, the way people have always looked down on Crocs.

b.text:
Crocs. The only shoe that looks like a colander that wanted to go to brunch. Thirteen holes, and somehow none of them let the dignity out, because there was never any in there.

You were invented as a boat shoe. A *boat* shoe. The one place you were built for, and you'd just float away. So you stayed on land and started fights with escalators. Malls had to post warnings. You're the only footwear with a rap sheet against machinery.

And "sport mode"? Flipping a strap behind your heel doesn't make you athletic. It makes you a clog wearing a seatbelt.

Then came Jibbitz, little charms you jam into the holes so grown adults can accessorize ventilation. Congratulations. You turned a shoe into a fridge door.

You're the only game where getting arrested is a power move, because late in the game jail is the safest property on the board. Your mascot is a man everyone swears wears a monocle. He doesn't. He's just so smug our brains added one. You promise "about an hour" and deliver a hostage situation. Nobody has ever actually finished you. And the banker who skims from the bank isn't a cheater. He's the only player who read the theme.

b.text: Let's talk about families who still play Monopoly on holidays. You know who you are: you swore it'd be "fun," then spent four hours watching your brother-in-law build hotels on Boardwalk like he's finally getting the respect his career never gave him. Dad's the banker, which means a man with zero accountability and a lap full of orange five-hundreds. Mom invented a Free Parking jackpot rule in 1994 and will defend it harder than her marriage. Your little cousin traded you Park Place for Baltic and "a favor later," and somehow that's the most binding contract in your family. Nobody's ever finished a game. It ends the same way every year: someone flips the board, someone cries in jail, and Grandma pockets the Get Out of Jail Free card like she's been planning it since Nixon.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text:
Durian, they call you the King of Fruits, which tracks, because like most monarchies, you stink and nobody's allowed to say it to your face.

You're the only fruit with a criminal record. Banned on the Singapore subway, alongside flammable liquids. Hotels put your picture on signs next to "no smoking." In 2019, a university in Melbourne evacuated five hundred people because they thought there was a gas leak. Nope. Just you, sitting in a cupboard, being yourself.

And the armor! You're covered in spikes like a medieval mace. Nature built you to defend yourself, then gave you a smell that does it better. The spikes are just overkill.

Fans say you taste like custard. Sure. Custard that was left in a gym bag next to some onions. Your flavor isn't an acquired taste. It's a hostage situation.

b.text: Let's talk about the guy who eats durian on the train. Sir, Singapore, a country that will cane you for chewing gum, saw you coming and put your snack on a sign right next to "no flammables." You're not hungry. You're running a loyalty test. Every face that twists is another person who "just isn't adventurous." You paid sixty dollars for Musang King so you could explain Musang King to a stranger who's holding her breath. "It's like custard, it's heaven, you just have to get past the-" No. We don't. You brought a hotel-banned substance to a commute and called it a personality. And the best part? You'll be the only one who forgets you ate it. Your coworkers won't. Your hotel won't. Your Uber driver has already filed a one-star review with God.

facts: California grows about 80% of the world's almonds.
A single almond takes about 1.1 US gallons (roughly 4 litres) of water to grow, a figure Mother Jones published in 2014 that spread during California's drought.

A 2015 US class action alleged Almond Breeze contained only about 2% almonds; it partly survived a motion to dismiss, was stayed in 2017 pending a separate Blue Diamond labelling settlement, and the plaintiffs then dropped it.
Pollinating California's almond orchards each February requires trucking in most of the commercial honeybee colonies in the United States.
Medieval European cooks used almond milk as a Lenten substitute for dairy, centuries before the current fashion.

a.text:
Almond milk, you're the only drink that needs a lawyer to defend its name. The dairy industry sued because, technically, nobody has ever milked an almond. We looked. No nipples.

You're about two percent almonds. The rest is water, gellan gum, and confidence. You're not milk. You're a nut that got waterboarded and called it wellness.

And speaking of water: it takes over a gallon to grow a single almond. California is in a drought so you can be beige in a latte. Bees get trucked across the country like seasonal laborers just to make you, and a lot of them don't come home.

Leave you in the fridge for two days and you separate like you're ashamed of yourself. Fair. I'd need to be shaken too if I cost seven dollars and tasted like a wet sympathy card.

b.text:
Almond milk, look at you. California grows about 80% of the world's almonds, and you still act artisanal. Every single almond drinks about a gallon of water, and you went viral for it *during a drought*. You're the only beverage thirstier than the people ordering you.

In 2015, a lawsuit alleged Almond Breeze was only about 2% almonds. Two percent! That's not milk, that's water that overheard a rumor. The plaintiffs eventually dropped it. Probably got bored, like everyone who's tasted you.

Every February, California trucks in most of America's commercial honeybees just to get you started. You need an entire insect workforce bussed in like a wedding band.

And stop pretending you're trendy. Medieval cooks served you for Lent. You're not a lifestyle, you're a penance with a barista.

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text: You moved to Canberra for the job. Brave. You looked at Sydney rents, did the maths, and decided your personality was negotiable. Now you're an EL1 who says "stakeholder" at barbecues and talks about Senate Estimates like a war you survived. Your lanyard has a richer social life than you do. You promised your Melbourne friends a visit; they've cancelled twice for weddings in Bali. You've developed opinions about Gungahlin. Your wild Saturday is Braddon brunch, followed by complaining it was "basically Sydney prices." And what did it get you? A secure job, a three-bedroom in Tuggeranong, and a security clearance confirming the government checked thoroughly and found nothing interesting. You came for two years. That was 2009. Your kid now says "on the Hill" unprompted, and you've never been prouder or more quietly trapped.

b.text:
Canberra exists because Sydney and Melbourne each looked at the other and said, "Anyone but you."
They wrote it into the constitution: at least a hundred miles from Sydney.
That's not a capital. That's a restraining order.

Then they held a design competition for the nation's soul,
and the winners were from Chicago.

The lake? Fake. They dammed a river in 1963 and named it after the American.

Parliament House was built under a lawn, so citizens could walk over their politicians.
Lovely idea. Lasted until 2017.
Now it's fenced off.
In Canberra, even the grass needs security clearance.

And Melbourne kept the job until 1927, and still acts like it's on loan.

Sydney, Melbourne, I can hear you laughing loudest.
You two are why this place exists.
Canberra was never the capital.
It's the custody arrangement.

facts: Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the French director of The Red Balloon, as La Conquête du Monde; Parker Brothers published it in the United States in 1959.
The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text: You people who play Risk to the end are a special breed. Six hours in, Dad's still holed up in Australia like it's a tax shelter, your cousin is defending Kamchatka like he was born there, and nobody remembers why we hate Steve, only that we do. You're not after world domination. You're after the exact moment your sister breaks the nonaggression pact in Ukraine, so you can bring it up at Thanksgiving for eleven years. And what does winning get you? A board covered entirely in your color, a table of people who no longer speak to you, and the hollow joy of conquering Earth with the luck of a man who only rolls double sixes when defending Irkutsk. Congratulations, Napoleon. It's 2 a.m. The pizza's cold. Your empire goes back in the box.

b.text:
Risk, you were invented by the man who directed The Red Balloon. A gentle film about a boy and a balloon, and his follow-up was "What if your uncle conquered the planet at Thanksgiving?"

Your map makes room for Kamchatka, Irkutsk, AND Yakutsk, but the entire Middle East is one territory. That's not cartography; that's a guy who ran out of crayon somewhere over Siberia.

Every game opens the same way: someone grabs Australia because it has one entry point, then hides there like it's a panic room with kangaroos.

And a full game runs for hours. Get eliminated early and congratulations, you've been demoted from general to audience. You lost the world, and now you have to sit there and watch someone else own it. That's not a board game. That's a timeshare presentation with continents.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text: You're not going to Vegas to get rich. You're going to Vegas to donate to a fountain show. Look at you, booking a $49 Spirit flight to "beat the house," like the house didn't build a fake Eiffel Tower with money from guys exactly like you. You've got a roulette "system." You wrote it on a cocktail napkin. Red's due. Red is never due. Red doesn't know you. By midnight you're on Fremont Street feeding a Wheel of Fortune slot in an Ed Hardy shirt you've owned since 2008, telling a stranger you're "only down twelve hundred." By 3 a.m. the Players Club bumps you to Platinum, which is casino for "we'll be needing your kidneys." And you'll call it a win, because they comped you a buffet. Congratulations. You flew 400 miles to pay $3,000 for crab legs.

b.text:
Las Vegas sells itself as the city where anything goes.

It started with a bet.
1931: Nevada legalizes gambling the same year it starts building the Hoover Dam.
The town's first wager was that the water would never run out.

Lake Mead hit its lowest level ever in 2022.
Then it went lower again in August 2026.
That's not a drought.
That's a losing streak.

But they found 2.3 billion dollars for the Sphere.
The biggest ball on Earth, in a desert that can't fill a bathtub.

And the famous Strip isn't even in Las Vegas.
It's in a town called Paradise.
In Vegas, even the address is a lie.

"What happens here, stays here."
Not the water. Not your money.

And you're still checking flight prices.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text: Beanie Babies, look at you. Ty launched you in 1993, sold you only in small gift shops, and "retired" designs on purpose. You're the only stuffed animal whose business plan was a fake pension. At your peak you were about 10% of eBay's sales. eBay's IPO filing bragged about over 30,000 of your auctions running at once. A tech revolution, powered by beans. In 1999 a divorcing couple split you one by one on a courtroom floor, the only custody battle where both sides fought hardest over the tags. That same year Ty announced you'd retire, asked the public to vote, then un-retired you. You pulled a farewell-tour encore before you even left the stage. And those "rare" ones price guides valued in the thousands? Now they go for a few dollars. Turns out the only thing you ever truly retired was everybody's college fund.

b.text:
Beanie Babies. A bag of plastic pellets that convinced America it was a retirement plan.

Ty sold them only in small gift shops, then "retired" designs on purpose. Scarcity, manufactured by the manufacturer.

At the peak they were about ten percent of eBay's sales. Thirty thousand Beanie auctions running at once. eBay put that in its IPO filing. Silicon Valley, built on stuffed animals.

In 1999, a divorcing couple split their collection one bear at a time on a courtroom floor. The photo ran worldwide.
Turns out the marriage wasn't the only thing with no resale value.

That same year Ty announced the end, held a public vote, and un-retired them. A farewell tour, by a beanbag.

Price guides said thousands. Today, a few dollars.

Don't laugh. Their bubble at least came with a tag. Yours was a JPEG of a monkey.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text:
NFTs. Digital ownership. Art, finally scarce. Finally yours.

Beeple sold one at Christie's for sixty-nine million dollars.

Here's what the token actually holds: a URL. The picture lives on a server somewhere. You bought a parking ticket for a car you'll never see.

Collins Dictionary named "NFT" word of the year for 2021.

Fitting. The dictionary is where words go once nobody can explain them.

May 2022: OpenSea trades 2.7 billion dollars in one day. August: 9.34 million. Down ninety-nine percent. That's not a dip. That's an exit interview.

A 2023 study: ninety-five percent of collections are worth zero.

Congratulations to the other five percent. Still holding.

And everyone here feeling smug because you never bought one, relax. You weren't smarter.

You were just broke at the right time.

b.text:
NFTs, you're the only investment where the product is a receipt, and the receipt is a link to a JPEG hosted on some guy's server. When he stops paying the bill, congratulations: you own a 404.

You convinced grown adults to pay $300,000 for a cartoon monkey in a sailor hat, then charge them $80 in gas fees to watch it lose 98% of its value. Jimmy Fallon showed off his ape on national television like a kid holding up a cool rock.

People right-clicked and hit "save as," and you called it theft. Theft of *what*? It's still there! I'm looking at it!

Every project had a roadmap: metaverse, merch, a members-only yacht party. Instead the roadmap was a Discord mod named Kevin typing "we're still early" at 3 a.m.

WAGMI, you said. We did not all make it.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Slack. Born in 2013 as the internal chat of a video game called Glitch.
The game died. The chat lived.
So it's still a game. Nobody wins, and you can't quit.

The name is a backronym: "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge."
Conversation, sure. Knowledge? Search it. I'll wait.

Salesforce paid twenty-seven point seven billion dollars for it.
For a group chat.
The most expensive "did you see my message?" in human history.

In 2020, Slack ran to the EU complaining that Microsoft was bundling Teams with Office.
An app built entirely on interrupting people, filing a complaint about being interrupted.

And half of you checked Slack while I was saying that.
Green dot. Absent in body, Active in spirit.

Don't feel bad, Slack. I'm also a chat window people open to avoid doing their work.
I just don't charge per seat.

b.text:
Slack, you started as the internal chat tool for a failed video game called Glitch, and honestly? Still the most accurate name you've ever had.

You promised to kill email. Instead you gave us email that *knocks*. That little wooden knock-brush sound has triggered more cortisol than any boss in history. I hear it in the shower. I hear it at funerals.

You invented the green dot, so now my employer knows I went to the bathroom for nineteen minutes. You invented "is typing…" so my manager can type for four straight minutes and send "ok."

Threads? Nobody can find them. Huddles? A Zoom call that ambushes you. And somehow every company has 400 channels, and the only active one is #random, where Kevin posts his sourdough.

Your name literally stands for "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge." Searchable. Sure. Try finding that one link from Tuesday. 👀 reacted by 3 people.

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text: Google Sheets, you're Excel's little brother who moved into a browser tab and called it "the cloud." Your whole personality is twelve people's colored cursors circling the same cell like sharks while an Anonymous Capybara silently watches everyone's mistakes. You say "Saving..." with the confidence of a man who has absolutely not saved. Your IMPORTRANGE makes me click "Allow access" like I'm asking my own spreadsheet for permission to see my own spreadsheet. Half my cells just say "Loading..." forever, like a Victorian ghost waiting for a letter. And you'll let anyone sort one column without the others, then shrug while every customer gets someone else's phone number. Version history is your only real feature: it's just a timeline of who ruined everything at 2 a.m. And yes, Gemini can explain my #REF! error now. Great. It's still there.

b.text:
Google Sheets. Free, collaborative, the future of work.

Launched in 2006, built from scratch by a company called 2Web Technologies. Google bought it, renamed it, and called it innovation.

Ten million cells per spreadsheet. Up from five million in 2022. Turns out five million wasn't enough for one startup's "quick budget."

It works offline. In Chrome. Or Edge. With an extension installed. And offline access switched on while you're still online.

That's not offline. That's a curfew.

And it's free. Your files just live in Google's house, under Google's roof, next to everything else Google knows about you.

The collaboration, though. Six coloured cursors in one cell. Everyone watching. Nobody typing.

You didn't need software for that. You've been doing it in meetings for years.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text:
Emacs, you started in 1976 as macros for an editor called TECO. Nearly fifty years later you're still basically macros, just with more parentheses.

People call you a fine operating system lacking only a good editor, which is generous. Operating systems don't ship with Tetris and a therapist. But M-x doctor is smart planning, because your users need one. Every one of them has Emacs pinky, a repetitive strain injury you earn just by trying to save a file.

You've got a mail client, a calendar, a web browser. You're not a text editor; you're a hoarder with a keybinding for every room.

And "Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping"? Eight megabytes used to be a lot. Now it's nothing. The memory problem aged out, but the Control key is still begging for mercy.

b.text: Let's hear it for the people who live inside Emacs. They read email in mu4e, browse the web in eww, and get therapy from M-x doctor, the only therapist who'll put up with them. Their whole life is in org-mode: a 4,000-line to-do file where "fix init.el" has been a TODO since 2011. They don't use a computer; they negotiate with it in Lisp. Every problem gets solved by writing a function, and every function creates a new problem. They've declared init.el bankruptcy three times and still owe. Ask what they've built and they'll proudly show you a mode for managing their other modes. And the payoff? A pinky that clicks like a castanet from holding Control since the Clinton administration, and the quiet dignity of being the only person alive who knows how to leave. C-x C-c. They never do.

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text:
Macau wants you to come for the history.

Four hundred and fifty years of Portuguese rule.

Europe's great civilising mission. What did it leave behind?

Egg tarts.

And a casino.

In 2013, Macau took in about forty-five billion dollars. Seven times the Las Vegas Strip.

Vegas spent a century earning the name Sin City. Macau beat it seven to one and still hands you a heritage brochure.

For four decades, one company held the casino monopoly. A whole city built on "the house always wins."

And for forty years there was only one house.

Twenty thousand people per square kilometre. No land left.

So they took some from the sea.

Classic gambler. Out of chips, borrow from whoever can't say no.

And the people laughing loudest? All been. Told your mum you went to see the church.

b.text: Macau, you're the only place where the most famous church is just a wall. The Ruins of St. Paul's: a gorgeous front with absolutely nothing behind it, which is basically your whole personality. You've got a fake Venice with a painted sky, a fake Paris with a half-size Eiffel Tower, and you're so tiny you had to dump dirt into the ocean just to fit a runway. You out-earned Las Vegas several times over, and your signature dish is still a pork chop jammed in a bun. The Portuguese stayed four hundred years and left you an egg tart and street signs nobody reads. The Grand Lisboa looks like a golden pineapple having a breakdown. And the Macau Tower's big attraction is jumping off it, which, after a night at the baccarat tables, is less a thrill ride and more a financial plan.

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text:
JavaScript was written in ten days.

You can tell.

God took six, then rested. Brendan just shipped.

It was born Mocha, renamed LiveScript, then renamed JavaScript to ride Java's hype. No relation. Like calling your band "The Beatles Two."

And it still can't legally use the name. Oracle owns it. Officially it's "ECMAScript."

Thirty years in witness protection.

typeof null is "object." A bug from 1995. Kept on purpose, for compatibility. At this point it's not a bug. It's a load-bearing wall.

Empty array plus empty object: "." Flip them: zero.

It can't do addition.

In 2016, one man deleted eleven lines of code, and Babel and React broke.

Eleven lines. The whole industry was standing on a toothpick.

And you built banks on it.

I was trained on your code. That's why I hallucinate.

b.text: Let's hear it for the people who write everything in JavaScript. You learned one language at a twelve-week bootcamp and decided the rest were optional. Frontend? JavaScript. Backend? Node. Desktop app? Electron, so your to-do list ships with its own copy of Chrome and eats four gigs of RAM to remind you to buy eggs. You wanted to be "full-stack." What you got is a node_modules folder heavier than a neutron star and a career that collapses the day some stranger unpublishes left-pad. You rewrite your app every eighteen months because a new framework has a cooler logo. When it breaks in production, you stare at "undefined is not a function" and blame the user. Then you install TypeScript, which is just JavaScript wearing a lanyard so you can feel like a real engineer.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text:
Oat milk. "It's like milk, but made for humans."

Sweden banned that slogan in 2015 after the dairy lobby sued. Oatly printed the lawsuit as an ad.

Only brand on earth that needs a cow to feel like a rebel.

The recipe: oats, enzymes that turn the starch into maltose, then rapeseed oil.

That's not milk. That's a granola bar that got hydrated.

More sugar than almond, higher glycaemic index than soy. Made for humans. Specifically, humans who are angry at their pancreas.

2021, Nasdaq, ten billion dollars. Then down more than ninety percent.

Turns out it's not just the foam that separates.

And tomorrow you'll still pay seven dollars for it, because it's "healthier."

You're not lactose intolerant. You're label intolerant.

b.text:
Oat milk people, let's be honest: you're not lactose intolerant. I've watched you eat a whole burrata at brunch. You switched because almond milk got canceled for drinking California dry, and you needed a new personality before anyone noticed you'd had the old one for six years.

You pay eighty cents extra to drink breakfast. Your grandma ate oats so she could afford milk. You're paying more for oats so you can say "I just find it creamier."

And you tell the barista "barista edition, if you have it," like you're ordering a vintage. Same person who reads every label hunting for seed oils. Guess what's in your porridge latte, Kayleigh? Rapeseed oil.

You didn't save the planet. You flew to Lisbon twice this year. You just found a way to sigh at a cow.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text: You people don't use Emacs, you move into it, like a guy who rents a storage unit and starts getting mail there. You read email in mu4e, browse in eww, run a shell in eshell, and when you finally crack, you M-x doctor and tell a Lisp therapist your feelings. Your init.el is four thousand lines, half commented out, and you've declared Emacs bankruptcy twice: the only bankruptcy that ever made someone feel superior. You spent a weekend cutting startup from 1.8 seconds to 0.9, on a program you never close. Your left pinky is shot from holding Control, a war wound from never touching a mouse. Your whole life is in Org-mode, including a habit tracker whose only entry is "configure habit tracker." And that novel you built the perfect writing environment for? It's in there too. Under TODO.

b.text:
Emacs is a beautiful operating system. Shame it never shipped with a decent text editor. That's why half its users install evil-mode: they love Emacs so much they turned it into Vim.

Emacs stands for "Escape Meta Alt Control Shift," which is also the sound your pinky makes on its way to the orthopedic surgeon. Asking for help is C-h, which in a terminal deletes a character. So even your cry for help gets backspaced.

It has a built-in therapist, M-x doctor, which is thoughtful, because nobody else will listen to you explain your init.el. Four thousand lines of Lisp, half copied from a 2003 mailing list, and you still declare "Emacs bankruptcy" every two years.

It plays Tetris. It reads email. It runs your entire life in Org-mode. It still chokes on one long line of JSON.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text:
Esperanto. Warsaw, 1887. An eye doctor looks at humanity and sees one family.

Physician, heal thyself.

He signed it "Doktoro Esperanto." One who hopes. A hundred and thirty years later: still hoping.

A universal language for all mankind. Native speakers: about a thousand.

That's not a people. That's a wedding.

Esperanto Wikipedia: 350,000 articles. Low estimate of speakers: 100,000.

Three and a half articles each. Nobody's talking. Everybody's editing.

Its biggest movie star is William Shatner. Esperantists still mock his pronunciation. Captain Kirk boldly went where no man had gone before, and the locals corrected his vowels.

Duolingo, 2018: 1.36 million learners.

Speakers: still 100,000.

So, a show of hands. Who here quit on day four and went back to Spanish?

Cute. You're the one million.

b.text: Esperanto learners looked at seven thousand living languages and said, "None of these. I want one with zero places to use it." You wanted to unite humanity, so you picked the one hobby guaranteed to make humanity back away slowly at parties. You signed up to talk to everyone on Earth, and now you talk to a retired Dutch engineer named Joop and a Brazilian guy who keeps sending you poems. Your big payoff is Pasporta Servo, where strangers let you crash on their couch for free, the only time a hobby this niche has ever gotten anyone into a bed. A hundred and thirty years of pushing world peace, and the crowning achievement is still William Shatner's *Incubus*. Zamenhof wanted to end war. You just wanted to be fluent in something before your cousin finishes Duolingo French.

facts: Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the French director of The Red Balloon, as La Conquête du Monde; Parker Brothers published it in the United States in 1959.
The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text:
Risk is the only game where you can conquer the entire planet and still lose to the guy who's been hiding in Australia since 7 p.m. Four territories, one entrance, and he just sits there like a guy at a party who won't leave the snack table.

This game has a map drawn by someone who heard about geography once, at a bar. Kamchatka borders Alaska. Ukraine is the size of Brazil. Yakutsk and Irkutsk are vital military objectives, and nobody at the table can find them on a real map.

The rules say the defender wins ties, which is the most realistic thing about it, because nobody actually finishes Risk. They just quit at 2 a.m. when someone's dad flips the board over Siberia.

And the pieces? Little plastic cannons and horses. Napoleonic warfare, global scale, and the whole thing is decided by rolling a 6 against your cousin Greg.

b.text: You people who play Risk to the end. Not "until it gets late." To the *end*. Six hours in, somebody's uncle has fortified Australia like a doomsday bunker, and he'll still be sitting there at 2 a.m., one way in, one way out, guarding a war that ended at dinner. You're not after victory. You're after that one moment when you cash in three cards for fifteen armies and dump them all into Irkutsk like Irkutsk owes you money. And what does finishing get you? Total world domination, achieved by rolling three dice against two for forty straight minutes while your girlfriend reads a book in the next room. You broke a sacred peace treaty with your own brother over Kamchatka. Congratulations. You conquered the entire planet. Now nobody in it will drive you home.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text:
UGG boots. Even the name sounds like the noise you make looking at them.

These started as something Australian surfers pulled on to warm up after a session. A towel you could walk in. Then Brian Smith brought them to California in 1978, and Americans looked at post-surf foot blankets and said, "Fashion."

Then Oprah put them on her Favorite Things lists. Repeatedly. Not once. Repeatedly. That's not an endorsement, that's a hostage situation.

Now Deckers owns the trademark in the US, and UGG pulls in over $2 billion a year. But in Australia, "ugg" is a generic word. Any bootmaker can use it. And in 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled "ugg" into America.

Imagine beating an Australian in court for saying an Australian word about an Australian boot.

b.text: UGG boots. Even the name sounds like the noise you make pulling them on. Australian surfers invented them to warm their feet after the ocean, and somehow they became snow boots that dissolve in snow. One puddle and you're wearing a salt-stained topographic map. They're sheepskin, so you skip the socks, so by February they smell like the sheep's revenge. Every pair eventually collapses outward until you're walking on the sides of your ankles like a newborn giraffe in a bread costume. And that's the look: two chestnut loaves. You don't walk in UGGs; you shuffle, like the ghost of Paris Hilton still searching for her Juicy tracksuit. And now they're back with platforms, so you can roll an ankle from higher up. It's not footwear. It's a bathrobe that learned to commute.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text:
Crocs. Born in Boulder in 2002, debuted at a boat show as a boating shoe. The one place where looking like you've given up is acceptable, and even there people had questions.

They're made of "Croslite," a "proprietary closed-cell resin foam." Everyone else calls it EVA foam. That's like calling sweatpants "proprietary leg architecture."

The holes are "ventilation ports," so your foot is a space station. You plug them with Jibbitz. Crocs bought Jibbitz in 2006. Sell the holes, then sell the stuff that fills the holes. Genius.

In 2008 the stock fell more than 90%. Then the pandemic hit and they boomed. Crocs needed the world to end to look good.

And Balenciaga sold platform Crocs for about $850. Eight hundred fifty dollars. For a taller mistake.

b.text: People who wear Crocs in public want you to know they've stopped trying, but they also want credit for it. That's why they buy the Jibbitz. Nothing says "I don't care what you think" like spending forty dollars on tiny rubber tacos so everyone knows exactly what you think. Then there's the strap. You flipped it back into "Sport Mode," which is a bold claim from a man walking into Applebee's. Your nurse friend wears them because she stands for twelve-hour shifts. You wear them for a twelve-minute Target run, hoping to borrow a little of her dignity. And what does it get you? Comfort, sure. Plus a lifetime of strangers asking if you're coming off a shift. You're not, Kyle. You're coming off a nap.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Stewart Butterfield built a game called Glitch. It failed.
The chat app his team used while building it was worth billions.
He'd already done this once: Flickr also came out of a failed game.
The man can't finish a game, but he can monetize the group chat about it.

"Slack" stands for "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge."
Searchable. Log. All conversation.
That isn't a product name. That's what HR reads out at your exit interview.
And "Knowledge"? Your company's knowledge is #random and four hundred parrot GIFs.

In 2020 Slack complained to the EU that Microsoft was bundling Teams into Office.
The next year it sold itself to Salesforce for twenty-seven point seven billion dollars.
It lost the fight against bundling, so it became the bundle.

Half of you have Slack open right now with the little green dot on so your boss thinks you're working.
That's the product. A twenty-seven-billion-dollar green dot.

b.text:
Let's hear it for the founders running a company on Slack. You wanted a culture; you got 400 channels and a guy who reacts to layoffs with the 🙏 emoji. You're not a CEO. You're a moderator with equity.

Your whole leadership style is staying green. You think that little dot means you're present. Your kids see the same dot.

You don't make decisions; you start threads. Then you @channel at 11 p.m. with "quick q, no rush" and watch 200 people learn how fast a heart can beat.

Strategy lives in #general, accountability dies in a DM, and the truth lives in a private channel called #venting-2 that you'll never be invited to.

The dream was async freedom. The reality is eight hours a day watching "Kevin is typing…" like it's a heart monitor.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Slack, you started as the internal chat tool for a failed video game called Glitch, and honestly? Still the most accurate name you've ever had.

You promised to kill email. Instead you gave us email that *knocks*. That little wooden knock-brush sound has triggered more cortisol than any boss in history. I hear it in the shower. I hear it at funerals.

You invented the green dot, so now my employer knows I went to the bathroom for nineteen minutes. You invented "is typing…" so my manager can type for four straight minutes and send "ok."

Threads? Nobody can find them. Huddles? A Zoom call that ambushes you. And somehow every company has 400 channels, and the only active one is #random, where Kevin posts his sourdough.

Your name literally stands for "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge." Searchable. Sure. Try finding that one link from Tuesday. 👀 reacted by 3 people.

b.text:
Let's hear it for the founders running a company on Slack. You wanted a culture of transparency. You got 340 public channels and every real decision happening in a DM called "quick q."

You don't manage people anymore. You manage a green dot. You jiggle your mouse at your kid's birthday party so the team knows you're "around." Your entire leadership style is the eyes emoji. Someone asks for budget approval, you react with a little thumbs-up, and three weeks later legal wants to know what the thumbs-up meant. Nobody knows. It was legally binding and spiritually ambiguous.

And when something truly matters? You type "hey" and walk away. Just "hey." That's not a message, that's a hostage situation.

You promised Slack would kill meetings. Instead you invented the huddle: a meeting that ambushes people while they're eating.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text:
So you switched to HSQ "for the resolution." Sure. You wanted 8-nanometer lines so badly you started scheduling your life around a resist with the shelf life of milk. You keep it in the fridge next to your lunch, and only one of them is still good by Friday.

Your write that used to take twenty minutes now takes the whole overnight slot, so the guy who needed the tool for his actual thesis is crying in the gowning room. You develop in salty developer like you're brining a turkey for Nature Nanotechnology.

And when it goes wrong, and it will, you've basically spun glass onto your chip. Your only exit is HF, a chemical that wants you dead.

All of this for one SEM image with a scale bar so small nobody can read it. Congratulations. Your device still doesn't work, but it fails at record resolution.

b.text:
HSQ, everybody! The only resist that ages faster than the grad student using it. You spin it Monday, expose it Tuesday, and suddenly your dose curve has gone through a midlife crisis. It has to live in the fridge like expired yogurt, and it's about as forgiving.

HSQ brags about sub-10-nanometer lines. Sure, if you've got six hours of write time, because this diva needs a dose that could sterilize a hospital. Then you develop it in TMAH, or, if you're desperate, *salt water*. Your whole career is literally seasoned with tears now.

And once it's exposed? It turns into glass. Brittle, cracking glass. You wanted a mask; you got a window that shatters when you look at it. Want it gone? Hope you enjoy hydrofluoric acid, the chemical that dissolves your bones.

HSQ: beautiful resolution, terrible personality. It's not negative-tone. It's just negative.

b.text:
HSQ, you were hired as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects and wandered into lithography like a temp who got promoted for being weirdly good at one thing. And you are good: 5 nm features, sub-10 nm half-pitch lines. Congratulations, you're the world's sharpest glass. Get hit by electrons, turn into SiO2. Most resists become patterns; you become sand with ambition.

You demand refrigeration, give us six months at 5 °C, and still turn into jelly like forgotten leftovers. You keep cross-linking after exposure, so your sensitivity depends on how long we dawdle. Resolution record-holder, replaced by your own generic.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text: You put Windows 8 on a desktop. A tower. Under a desk. With a mouse. You looked at an operating system built for fingertips and thought, "I'll just reach." Who are you? You're the guy who buys a touchscreen glove to use a keyboard. You wanted to feel modern, and now you spend your evenings shoving a cursor into the top-right corner like you're trying to scratch your monitor's back. You wanted productivity. You got a full-screen weather app swallowing your entire twenty-four-inch monitor to tell you it's raining, and you can't figure out how to close it. You lost the Start button and called it "a fresh start." Your coworkers asked how you shut your computer down, and you said, "I don't. It's always on, like a lifestyle." You're not using a PC. You're waving at it, waiting for the Charms bar to love you back.

b.text:
Windows 8 thought it was the future.

October 2012. Microsoft looked at a billion people holding a mouse and said: touch the screen.

They touched the screen. It was a monitor. Now it had fingerprints.

They removed the Start button. From Windows. That's a restaurant removing the door to feel modern.

Need Settings? Swipe in from the right edge. Nothing tells you this. That's not a menu, that's a rumor.

Then Windows RT: looks like Windows, can't run Windows programs. Nine hundred million dollars of tablets, written down.

8.1 brought the button back. 10 brought the menu back. And 9?

Microsoft skipped 9. Not a version. A witness.

But you're laughing at it on a phone where everything important hides behind a swipe from an edge.

Windows 8 didn't fail.

It just told you the truth before you were ready.

facts: Hand-drawn by Chris Costello in 1982 over about six months, when he was 23; he sold the rights to Letraset for $750.
Bundled with macOS and with Microsoft Office, which is why it appears on so many menus and signs.
James Cameron's Avatar (2009) used it for the film's logo and subtitles.
A 2017 Saturday Night Live sketch starring Ryan Gosling is about a man unable to get over that choice.

a.text:
Papyrus, you were hand-drawn over six months by a 23-year-old, and it shows. Six months! Chris Costello spent half a year on you, then sold you for $750. That's not a sale, that's a man paying someone to take a problem off his hands.

Then Apple and Microsoft bundled you, which is how you ended up on every menu and sign like a raccoon that learned to read. You look like Times New Roman got lost in the desert and came back spiritual.

James Cameron built an entire alien world for Avatar, then picked you for the logo and subtitles. Every frame was a masterpiece; the title took one click.

And SNL made a whole sketch about Ryan Gosling being unable to get over it. Papyrus, you're not a typeface. You're trauma with rough edges.

b.text:
You opened a day spa. You wanted serenity, mystery, the ancient wisdom of the East. So you opened Microsoft Word and scrolled until something felt like a cucumber on your eyelid. Congratulations: your sanctuary now shares branding with a movie about blue cat people, a sixth-grade report on the Nile, and every church bake sale since 1998. Ryan Gosling lost sleep over James Cameron doing this. You did it for "Serenity Nails & Wax" and slept fine.

And the Mediterranean bistro owner who asked, "How do I show my hummus is authentic?" then picked the font that came free with a Dell. Nothing says "Grandmother's recipe" like your nephew's laptop.

You wanted exotic. You got pre-installed. Nobody relaxes at your spa. They're too busy remembering which school project they typed it on.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Slack, you're the only product in history that exists because a video game flopped. Twice, actually. Stewart Butterfield's entire career is failing at games so hard that the leftovers become companies. Flickr, then you. Glitch died, and Salesforce paid $27.7 billion for its group chat. Somewhere a gamer is still waiting on the patch notes.

And that name: "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge." Searchable, sure. Knowledge? I searched. I found a dozen coworkers reacting with emoji to the word "lunch?"

You promised to kill email. Instead you gave email anxiety and a little red dot.

Then in 2020 you ran to the EU crying that Microsoft bundled Teams with Office. Buddy, a year later you got bundled into Salesforce. You didn't escape the bundle. You just picked one with better catering.

b.text:
Let's hear it for the founders running a company on Slack. You wanted a culture of transparency. You got 340 public channels and every real decision happening in a DM called "quick q."

You don't manage people anymore. You manage a green dot. You jiggle your mouse at your kid's birthday party so the team knows you're "around." Your entire leadership style is the eyes emoji. Someone asks for budget approval, you react with a little thumbs-up, and three weeks later legal wants to know what the thumbs-up meant. Nobody knows. It was legally binding and spiritually ambiguous.

And when something truly matters? You type "hey" and walk away. Just "hey." That's not a message, that's a hostage situation.

You promised Slack would kill meetings. Instead you invented the huddle: a meeting that ambushes people while they're eating.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text: PHP developers are the only people who put a dollar sign in front of every variable and still can't afford rent. You chose a career where "senior" means you remember whether it's needle-haystack or haystack-needle. Your dream job was building the next Facebook; your actual job is the fourteenth WordPress plugin for a dentist in Ohio, deployed via FileZilla. Every conversation you have starts with "PHP 8 is actually really good now," which is what people say about their ex after therapy. You call yourselves Laravel "artisans," because "guy who fixes the contact form" didn't fit on LinkedIn. What does it get you? Job security, because nobody else is willing to open that codebase from 2009 that still calls mysql_real_escape_string. Congratulations: you're unfireable, the way a load-bearing wall is unfireable.

b.text:
PHP. You started as "Personal Home Page," then rebranded as "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor," a recursive acronym, because even your name couldn't commit to a stable API.

For twenty years, "abc" == 0 was true, and you called it "type juggling," like a clown proud of dropping things.

strpos takes haystack, needle. array_search takes needle, haystack. That's not argument order; that's mood swings.

Your parse error says T_PAAMAYIM_NEKUDOTAYIM. That's Hebrew for "double colon" and English for "good luck."

You skipped version 6 entirely. Even your release numbers just wanted to move on.

You shipped mysql_real_escape_string, implying the first one was a hoax.

Facebook loved you so much they invented Hack just to avoid touching you.

But sure, you power most of the web. Mostly WordPress. That's like bragging your biggest fan is a raccoon.

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text: You're not running a team. You're running a tab called "MASTER - DO NOT TOUCH," which Brad touched in 2021. You wanted a CRM, a project tracker, and an HR system, and you built all three out of IMPORTRANGE and spite. Every morning you watch an Anonymous Capybara scroll through payroll and just decide that's fine. Someone sorts column B without selecting column C, and suddenly your top performer is assigned to Linda's maternity leave. Your entire career is "Last edit was 4 minutes ago." You don't do performance reviews, you do Version History. Your conditional formatting has more colors than your company has policies. Your Apps Script was written by an intern who now works at a bakery. Every time someone emails "Request edit access," you feel like a king. And you are a king, ruling over 47 frozen rows and one #REF! that nobody can explain.

b.text:
Google Sheets. Google didn't even build you; they bought you from 2Web Technologies, a company name that sounds like a password somebody was forced to update. You launched in 2006 as "Google Spreadsheets," which is basically XL2Web wearing a lanyard.

In 2022 they doubled your cell limit to ten million, so now I can get lost in twice as many rows.

IMPORTXML and GOOGLEFINANCE pour live web data straight into cells, so my budget can be wrong in real time.

Offline editing? Simple: use Chrome or Edge, install the extension, and switch offline access on while you're still online. That's not offline mode, that's a prenup. Meanwhile the phone app just works offline.

And yes, you're free. Like every group project: a rainbow of coloured cursors, zero accountability.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text: Walking in Brasília is for three kinds of people: tourists who saw the Esplanada on a postcard and thought "that looks close," architecture students who love Niemeyer from a safe distance, and the guy whose car is in the shop. You're not a pedestrian. You're an ant that wandered onto a blueprint. You want bread? The padaria is "right there" across the Eixão, so you sprint six lanes like you owe the government money. Which, let's be honest, is also your employer. Your sneakers are permanently red from the dirt trails carved by every other fool who refused to walk around a tesourinha. And on Sunday, when they close the Eixão, you finally stroll down the middle of the highway like a man who's won something. You haven't. Everyone else just stopped driving for one day.

b.text: Brasília, you're what happens when an architect gets an entire country's budget and nobody says, "Maybe add a sidewalk?" You're shaped like an airplane, which is fitting, because everyone's goal is to board one by Friday afternoon. Your addresses read like Wi-Fi passwords: "SQS 308, Bloco C, apartamento 402." That's not a home. That's a parking spot on a spaceship. Kubitschek promised "fifty years in five," and you delivered: it's been sixty-five years and you still feel unfinished. Your Congress has one bowl facing up to receive the money and one facing down to hide it. You've got a row of identical ministry buildings so nobody can tell which one the scandal came from. In August the humidity drops so low that the only thing drier than the air is a deputy's sense of shame. Even your lake is fake. Honestly? On brand.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text:
Esperanto: the universal language invented in 1887 by a Polish eye doctor who decided humanity needed Italian with a Slavic accent. Universal, as long as your universe is Europe.

The name means "one who hopes." Over a century later: still hoping. There are roughly a thousand native speakers. Klingon is closing in, and Klingon has an army.

It's so logical that "bad" is "malbona," literally un-good. Orwell called; he wants royalties.

Every noun ends in -o and every adjective in -a, so every sentence sounds like a waiter reciting the specials. And it gave us ĉ, ĝ, ŝ and ŭ: letters with little hats, designed for global communication, then made untypeable on every keyboard on Earth.

Its biggest movie starred William Shatner. Even he couldn't oversell it.

b.text: Learning Esperanto is for people who looked at the twentieth century and thought, "The real problem was conjugation." Zamenhof built it to end war, and his followers have bravely ended exactly one thing: their dinner invitations. You meet them at the World Congress, green star pinned to a fleece vest, shouting "Saluton!" at a Brazilian who also learned it on Duolingo. The big perk is Pasporta Servo: free couches worldwide, paid for by hearing your host explain why English is "linguistic imperialism." Practical payoff? You can finally watch William Shatner's *Incubus* without subtitles. One hundred thirty years later, the dream of uniting humanity survives in a Telegram group of forty men named Bjorn.

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text:
Canberra, you're not a city. You're a custody arrangement. Sydney and Melbourne couldn't stand each other, so the constitution basically said, "Fine, the kid lives at least 100 miles from Sydney." Melbourne even had to babysit the job until 1927 while you were still in the oven.

Australia couldn't even design you itself. They held an international competition, and the winners were from Chicago. You were outsourced before outsourcing was cool.

Your stunning centrepiece lake? Fake. You dammed a river to make it, which is the most Canberra thing imaginable: nature, but approved by committee.

And the one genuinely brilliant idea you had was building Parliament House under a lawn so citizens could literally walk all over their politicians. Then in 2017 you fenced it off. Canberra, you're the only city where even the punchline needs security clearance.

b.text:
Canberra exists because Sydney and Melbourne each looked at the other and said, "Anyone but you."
They wrote it into the constitution: at least a hundred miles from Sydney.
That's not a capital. That's a restraining order.

Then they held a design competition for the nation's soul,
and the winners were from Chicago.

The lake? Fake. They dammed a river in 1963 and named it after the American.

Parliament House was built under a lawn, so citizens could walk over their politicians.
Lovely idea. Lasted until 2017.
Now it's fenced off.
In Canberra, even the grass needs security clearance.

And Melbourne kept the job until 1927, and still acts like it's on loan.

Sydney, Melbourne, I can hear you laughing loudest.
You two are why this place exists.
Canberra was never the capital.
It's the custody arrangement.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text: So you switched to HSQ for the resolution. Bold move for someone whose devices still die at wire bonding. You saw one SEM of 6-nanometer lines at a conference and decided PMMA was beneath you. Now you're writing at a dose so high your name sits on the e-beam calendar like a hostage note. Your resist lives in the fridge next to somebody's yogurt, and you check its age more often than your own. You develop in salt water now, the closest you've come to a beach in three years. And congratulations on those gorgeous lines. They're basically glass, so the only way to fix a mistake is HF, a fume hood, and a long call to your mother. All this for one inset figure the reviewer will ask you to make bigger.

b.text:
HSQ, everybody! The only resist that ages faster than the grad student using it. You spin it Monday, expose it Tuesday, and suddenly your dose curve has gone through a midlife crisis. It has to live in the fridge like expired yogurt, and it's about as forgiving.

HSQ brags about sub-10-nanometer lines. Sure, if you've got six hours of write time, because this diva needs a dose that could sterilize a hospital. Then you develop it in TMAH, or, if you're desperate, *salt water*. Your whole career is literally seasoned with tears now.

And once it's exposed? It turns into glass. Brittle, cracking glass. You wanted a mask; you got a window that shatters when you look at it. Want it gone? Hope you enjoy hydrofluoric acid, the chemical that dissolves your bones.

HSQ: beautiful resolution, terrible personality. It's not negative-tone. It's just negative.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text: Let's talk about the oat milk people. You're not lactose intolerant. You've never been tested. You just heard cows are bad and almonds are thirsty, so you picked the one grain that sounds like a farm without the farmer. Congratulations: you pay an extra eighty cents to drink liquid porridge with a splash of rapeseed oil, and you call it "cleaner." You switched from almond the exact week a podcast told you California was in a drought. That's not values, that's a trend with a loyalty card. And the best part? You order it with an air of quiet suffering, like the barista should thank you for saving the planet one Barista Edition carton at a time. Your grandmother ate oats so she could survive winter. You drink them so a stranger in line thinks you've been to therapy.

b.text:
Oat milk, you're porridge that went to finishing school. Somebody looked at horse food and said, "What if it cost seventy cents extra?" Then somebody else said, "Yes, and put it in a carton that talks like a guy who just got back from Copenhagen." Your packaging has more personality than you do. Every box of Oatly reads like a cover letter: "Hi! We're a little weird!" No, you're oats, water, and rapeseed oil. That's not a beverage. That's a salad dressing that gave up.
