And the "Barista Edition"? You needed extra oil just to get a job. Enzymes break your starch into maltose, so technically you're a sugar spike in a flannel shirt. Plus you were funded by Blackstone. You're not anti-establishment, oat milk. You're a private equity firm wearing a beanie.

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text: Let's hear it for the manager who runs a twelve-person team out of a Google Sheet. You didn't want to pay for Asana; you wanted to feel like you *built* Asana. Look at you, color-coding rows like a kindergarten teacher with admin rights. Your whole org chart is a tab called "Roster FINAL (2)." Your performance reviews are conditional formatting: green means safe, red means Kyle. And every morning you open it, see Anonymous Capybara lurking at row 400, and feel genuinely hunted. Somebody sorted one column without the others last Tuesday, and now Priya reports to the office printer. You fixed it through version history like a detective reconstructing a murder. That's the dream, right? Control. Total visibility. And what you got is forty "Request edit access" emails and a VLOOKUP holding up the company like a Jenga block.

b.text: Google Sheets, you're Excel's little brother who moved into a browser tab and called it "the cloud." Your whole personality is twelve people's colored cursors circling the same cell like sharks while an Anonymous Capybara silently watches everyone's mistakes. You say "Saving..." with the confidence of a man who has absolutely not saved. Your IMPORTRANGE makes me click "Allow access" like I'm asking my own spreadsheet for permission to see my own spreadsheet. Half my cells just say "Loading..." forever, like a Victorian ghost waiting for a letter. And you'll let anyone sort one column without the others, then shrug while every customer gets someone else's phone number. Version history is your only real feature: it's just a timeline of who ruined everything at 2 a.m. And yes, Gemini can explain my #REF! error now. Great. It's still there.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text:
Keurig, you're the only product whose own inventor apologized for it. John Sylvan sold out for fifty grand in 1997, then told The Atlantic he feels bad he ever did it. Buddy, that's not an origin story. That's a confession.

And remember Keurig 2.0? You put DRM on coffee. A machine that reads ink on the lid and goes, "Sorry, I don't recognize this bean." Sales fell, people posted workarounds online, and America had to jailbreak a coffee maker just to get a cup of coffee.

By 2014 you sold enough pods every year to circle the Earth more than ten times, mostly in plastic nobody could recycle. You didn't make coffee. You made the planet a second crust.

Then you merged with Dr Pepper. Fitting. Nothing says "we've given up on real coffee" like moving in with a soda.

b.text:
Keurig, you took the one drink humanity had perfected over five hundred years and said, "What if it came in a tiny plastic thimble that outlives your grandchildren?" Your own inventor said he regrets making you. When your dad disowns you, that's a phase. When the guy who invented you disowns you, that's a recall.

You make coffee one sad, lukewarm cup at a time, then flash "DESCALE" like a check-engine light for a machine that costs forty bucks. Remember Keurig 2.0? You put DRM on coffee. You were scanning pods like a bouncer: "Sorry, sir, you're not on the list." Nobody was pirating Folgers! And your "Strong" button just drips slower, which isn't strength. That's procrastination.

You're not a coffee maker. You're a plastic-dispensing subscription that occasionally hiccups out hot brown water.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Let's hear it for the jackfruit pulled-pork crowd. You found something grandmothers in Kerala have cooked for centuries, slapped "plant-based" on a can, and tripled the price. Bold move, gentrifying a curry.

Your entire pitch is "it shreds like pork." So does a wet paper towel. You know what makes it taste like pulled pork? The barbecue sauce. You're not selling a meat substitute. You're selling a sauce delivery system with a mission statement.

And the protein! Two grams. You told a generation of vegans they're eating a brisket sandwich and handed them a fruit cup in a trench coat.

But hey, it works. You get the Whole Foods endcap, the podcast slot, and the warm glow of saving the planet one eighteen-dollar taco at a time. The pig's still alive. So is your margin.

b.text:
Jackfruit. The largest fruit that grows on a tree. Over forty kilos, hanging above your head.

Nature's version of a piano on a rope.

Bangladesh made it the national fruit. Kerala and Tamil Nadu made it the state fruit. Three governments honoring something that could flatten a citizen. Very relatable for governments.

Now it's sold as vegan pulled pork. One to two grams of protein per hundred. Pork has more than ten times that.

That's not a substitute. That's a photo of pork.

Cut it open and it bleeds sticky white latex. Cooks oil their knives and hands first. Dinner fights back, and still loses to tofu.

Mulberry family. Cousin of the fig. All that weight, and still the least useful one at the reunion.

But you bought it anyway, because it shreds.

You never wanted protein. You wanted texture and a halo.

facts: Tofu soaked for hours to a day or two in a brine that has itself fermented for months from vegetables such as bamboo shoots and mustard greens, often with dried shrimp or meat; the smell is the brine's, not the bean's.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.
Legend credits Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate who left his unsold tofu too long in 1669; a Beijing fermented-bean-curd brand still carries his name.
Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text:
Stinky tofu, you're the only food that arrives a block before the vendor does. Nobody finds you; they get ambushed.

And the stink isn't even yours. You're plain tofu that sat a day in a months-old swamp of bamboo shoots, mustard greens and dried shrimp, then claimed it as personality. That's not character, that's a marinade.

You've got regional disguises, too. Changsha dyes you black, fries you and buries you in chili like evidence. Taiwan makes you golden and hands out pickled cabbage like an apology. Shaoxing steams you with other stinky pickles, which isn't a dish, it's a support group.

Your origin story? In 1669 Wang Zhihe couldn't sell his tofu and just... left it. Most people call that spoiled inventory. He's still got his name on a Beijing brand.

b.text: Stinky tofu, you're the only food that announces itself before the menu does. People find you at the night market the way sharks find blood: follow the stench three stalls past the bubble tea. Your brine is fermented vegetables, shrimp, amaranth stems, and apparently a gym sock that lost a bet. Months in that bucket, and you came out smelling like a festival porta-potty in August. Your own name is a confession. Not "aged tofu," not "artisanal bean curd." Your family took one whiff and went, "Yeah, call him Stinky." And the Changsha version? Dyed jet black, like it's in mourning for everyone's sense of smell. The only reason anyone finishes you is the pickled cabbage and chili sauce piled on top to keep you quiet. "Smells bad, tastes good" isn't a slogan, buddy. It's a hostage negotiation.

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text: JavaScript, you were built in ten days, and you've spent thirty years proving it. You named yourself after Java for the clout, like a guy introducing himself as "Brad Pitt's cousin." You think null is an object. You think NaN is a number, and it isn't even equal to itself. Ask you to sort and you hand back, alphabetically, like a librarian having a breakdown. "11" plus 1 is "111," but "11" minus 1 is 10, so you're consistent the way a slot machine is consistent. You needed two kinds of nothing, undefined and null, and three equals signs just to tell the truth. Your own developers can't agree what "this" means. And the entire internet runs on you, which honestly explains the internet.

b.text: Let's hear it for the people who write everything in JavaScript. You learned one language at a twelve-week bootcamp and decided the rest were optional. Frontend? JavaScript. Backend? Node. Desktop app? Electron, so your to-do list ships with its own copy of Chrome and eats four gigs of RAM to remind you to buy eggs. You wanted to be "full-stack." What you got is a node_modules folder heavier than a neutron star and a career that collapses the day some stranger unpublishes left-pad. You rewrite your app every eighteen months because a new framework has a cooler logo. When it breaks in production, you stare at "undefined is not a function" and blame the user. Then you install TypeScript, which is just JavaScript wearing a lanyard so you can feel like a real engineer.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text: UGG boots. Even the name sounds like the noise you make pulling them on. Australian surfers invented them to warm their feet after the ocean, and somehow they became snow boots that dissolve in snow. One puddle and you're wearing a salt-stained topographic map. They're sheepskin, so you skip the socks, so by February they smell like the sheep's revenge. Every pair eventually collapses outward until you're walking on the sides of your ankles like a newborn giraffe in a bread costume. And that's the look: two chestnut loaves. You don't walk in UGGs; you shuffle, like the ghost of Paris Hilton still searching for her Juicy tracksuit. And now they're back with platforms, so you can roll an ankle from higher up. It's not footwear. It's a bathrobe that learned to commute.

b.text: Some of you wear UGGs in July, and I respect a person who has never once been told no. You're not dressing for the weather. You're dressing for 2006. Somewhere in your heart, a paparazzi photo of Paris Hilton is still loading. You want people to think "cozy." People think "sleepover or custody hearing?" And the walk: your ankles gave up years ago and went horizontal. You're not walking anymore, you're leaning toward your destination. Australian surfers wore these to warm up after the freezing ocean. You wear them to warm up after the Target parking lot. In August. Your feet sweat so hard the sheep is finally getting its revenge. And the second it drizzles, you're frozen under an awning like a cat who's been threatened with a bath.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text: People who wear Crocs out of the house have made peace with something the rest of us are still fighting. You didn't give up; you filed the paperwork. Every Croc wearer says the same thing: "They're so comfortable." Yeah, so is a weighted blanket, Brenda, but you don't wear it to Olive Garden. And the Jibbitz! You've turned your feet into a personality quiz. A tiny taco, a tiny Minion, a tiny "Live Laugh Love." You're forty-three and your shoe has a sticker collection. Then there's the guy who flips the strap back into "sport mode" like he's about to chase a pickpocket, when we both know he's never run anywhere except toward a sample tray at Costco. Nurses and chefs wear them because they're on their feet for twelve hours. You wear them to stand in line at Starbucks. Different heroism.

b.text:
Crocs launched in 2002 at the Fort Lauderdale boat show.
As a boating shoe.
The original customer was someone who might end up in the water and wanted the shoes to float.

They're made of "Croslite," a proprietary closed-cell resin.
Everyone else calls it EVA foam.
Same brand of genius that renamed holes "ventilation ports."
Then in 2006 they bought Jibbitz, so they could sell you plugs for the ports.
First they cut the hole. Then they charge rent on it.

In 2008 the stock fell more than ninety percent.
Wall Street called it ugly.
Ten years later Balenciaga stuck one on a platform and charged eight hundred and fifty dollars.
Same foam. Taller.
Still ugly. Just more expensive.

The people who wear them, I leave alone.
Front row, I see you. Socks and all.
You paid extra for the charms. Cute.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text:
Esperanto: the universal language invented in 1887 by a Polish eye doctor who decided humanity needed Italian with a Slavic accent. Universal, as long as your universe is Europe.

The name means "one who hopes." Over a century later: still hoping. There are roughly a thousand native speakers. Klingon is closing in, and Klingon has an army.

It's so logical that "bad" is "malbona," literally un-good. Orwell called; he wants royalties.

Every noun ends in -o and every adjective in -a, so every sentence sounds like a waiter reciting the specials. And it gave us ĉ, ĝ, ŝ and ŭ: letters with little hats, designed for global communication, then made untypeable on every keyboard on Earth.

Its biggest movie starred William Shatner. Even he couldn't oversell it.

b.text:
Esperanto. Warsaw, 1887. An eye doctor looks at humanity and sees one family.

Physician, heal thyself.

He signed it "Doktoro Esperanto." One who hopes. A hundred and thirty years later: still hoping.

A universal language for all mankind. Native speakers: about a thousand.

That's not a people. That's a wedding.

Esperanto Wikipedia: 350,000 articles. Low estimate of speakers: 100,000.

Three and a half articles each. Nobody's talking. Everybody's editing.

Its biggest movie star is William Shatner. Esperantists still mock his pronunciation. Captain Kirk boldly went where no man had gone before, and the locals corrected his vowels.

Duolingo, 2018: 1.36 million learners.

Speakers: still 100,000.

So, a show of hands. Who here quit on day four and went back to Spanish?

Cute. You're the one million.

facts: California grows about 80% of the world's almonds.
A single almond takes about 1.1 US gallons (roughly 4 litres) of water to grow, a figure Mother Jones published in 2014 that spread during California's drought.

A 2015 US class action alleged Almond Breeze contained only about 2% almonds; it partly survived a motion to dismiss, was stayed in 2017 pending a separate Blue Diamond labelling settlement, and the plaintiffs then dropped it.
Pollinating California's almond orchards each February requires trucking in most of the commercial honeybee colonies in the United States.
Medieval European cooks used almond milk as a Lenten substitute for dairy, centuries before the current fashion.

a.text:
Almond milk, you're the only drink that needs a lawyer to defend its name. The dairy industry sued because, technically, nobody has ever milked an almond. We looked. No nipples.

You're about two percent almonds. The rest is water, gellan gum, and confidence. You're not milk. You're a nut that got waterboarded and called it wellness.

And speaking of water: it takes over a gallon to grow a single almond. California is in a drought so you can be beige in a latte. Bees get trucked across the country like seasonal laborers just to make you, and a lot of them don't come home.

Leave you in the fridge for two days and you separate like you're ashamed of yourself. Fair. I'd need to be shaken too if I cost seven dollars and tasted like a wet sympathy card.

b.text:
Almond milk wants you to know it's the gentle choice. No cows harmed.

Just California. California grows eighty percent of the world's almonds, in a state that keeps running out of water. About a gallon per almond. You didn't give up dairy. You gave up a farmer's shower.

Every February, most of America's commercial honeybees get loaded onto trucks to pollinate it. The cow got to stay home. The bees got deployed.

A 2015 lawsuit alleged Almond Breeze was about two percent almonds.

Honestly, fair. The water's the expensive part.

Medieval Europeans drank almond milk during Lent. It was a sacrifice, a thing you suffered for God.

You pay six dollars a carton for it.

Same penance. Worse priest.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Stewart Butterfield built a game called Glitch. It failed.
The chat app his team used while building it was worth billions.
He'd already done this once: Flickr also came out of a failed game.
The man can't finish a game, but he can monetize the group chat about it.

"Slack" stands for "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge."
Searchable. Log. All conversation.
That isn't a product name. That's what HR reads out at your exit interview.
And "Knowledge"? Your company's knowledge is #random and four hundred parrot GIFs.

In 2020 Slack complained to the EU that Microsoft was bundling Teams into Office.
The next year it sold itself to Salesforce for twenty-seven point seven billion dollars.
It lost the fight against bundling, so it became the bundle.

Half of you have Slack open right now with the little green dot on so your boss thinks you're working.
That's the product. A twenty-seven-billion-dollar green dot.

b.text:
Slack, you're the only product whose origin story is "our video game flopped, but the group chat slapped." And Stewart Butterfield did it *twice*. First Flickr, then you. Most people quit gaming; he just keeps dropping loot from his failures.

Your name stands for "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge." Searchable? I've hunted for one PDF for forty minutes. Knowledge? Your liveliest channel is #random. You're a log of someone typing "quick question?" and then vanishing for an hour.

Salesforce paid $27.7 billion for you, which is a lot of money for email that blinks.

And in 2020 you ran to the EU because Microsoft bundled Teams with Office. Buddy, the only reason anyone uses Teams is that it's free with Word. The only reason anyone uses you is that it's free with anxiety.

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text:
Macau wants you to know it's about heritage.
Four hundred years of Portuguese history. Cobblestones. Churches. Egg tarts.

Then in 2013 it made forty-five billion dollars from gambling. Seven times the Las Vegas Strip.
Vegas is a city built around casinos.
Macau is casinos that kept some cobblestones around for the brochure.

For forty years, one company owned every table in town.
That's not an industry. That's a landlord with dice.

Twenty thousand people per square kilometre. Nowhere left to stand.
So they built the Cotai Strip on the sea.
Most places run out of land and stop growing.
Macau ran out of land and borrowed from the ocean. Very on brand.

And everyone here who flew in "for the egg tarts"?
The tarts cost three dollars.
Where did the rest of your money go?

b.text: You lost it on Hong Kong stocks, so you took the TurboJET to win it back, because nothing says "financial plan" like a ferry with a cancellation policy. You're the guy at the Grand Lisboa squeezing a baccarat card like it owes you rent, blowing on it, peeling the corner so slowly the dealer ages. Red underwear, three days unwashed, "for luck." Baccarat is a coin flip and you've built a religion around it. You told your wife it's a work trip, and technically your work now is the pawn shop next door, which buys Rolexes faster than you can say "one more shoe." By hour nine you're eating an egg tart for dinner and calling it Portuguese culture. You came to win it all back. You leave by bus over the bridge with no luck, no Rolex, and a watch tan.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text:
UGG boots. Born on an Australian beach. Surfers came out of freezing water and wrapped their feet in a sheep.

In Australia, "ugg" is just a word. Like "boot." Any bootmaker can use it.

In America, it's a trademark. Deckers bought it in 1995.

So in 2019, a US jury found an Australian liable for selling an Australian boot under its Australian name.

To Americans.

Take the thing, rename it, then sue the locals for trespassing. Australia should recognize the technique.

They invented it.

Then Oprah put them on Favorite Things, and now it's over two billion dollars a year.

The sheep gave its skin. Australia gave the word. Oprah gave the blessing.

And you gave real money for slippers you wear to the supermarket. Stained, flattened, walking on the sides.

Same as you.

b.text: Some of you wear UGGs in July, and I respect a person who has never once been told no. You're not dressing for the weather. You're dressing for 2006. Somewhere in your heart, a paparazzi photo of Paris Hilton is still loading. You want people to think "cozy." People think "sleepover or custody hearing?" And the walk: your ankles gave up years ago and went horizontal. You're not walking anymore, you're leaning toward your destination. Australian surfers wore these to warm up after the freezing ocean. You wear them to warm up after the Target parking lot. In August. Your feet sweat so hard the sheep is finally getting its revenge. And the second it drizzles, you're frozen under an awning like a cat who's been threatened with a bath.

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text:
Apple Vision Pro.

Apple says it isn't VR.
Developers aren't allowed to call it VR.
Or AR. Or XR. Or MR.
It's "spatial computing."
That's what you call a headset after "headset" tests badly.

Thirty-four ninety-nine.
Over half a kilo on your face.
Plus a battery in your pocket, on a cord, good for about two hours.
That's not a computer. That's a leash with a launch event.

Apple cut production.
First-year sales: well under a million.
The most immersive thing about it was the silence afterward.

Then there's EyeSight.
It puts a rendering of your eyes on the outside,
so the people around you feel like you're still there.

You've all been doing that at dinner for ten years.
Apple just figured out how to charge you for it.

b.text:
Apple Vision Pro: thirty-five hundred dollars to strap over half a kilo of glass to your face, and that's *before* the battery. Oh yes, the battery. It dangles off a cable in your pocket like you're on a hospital drip, and it gives you about two hours. Two hours! That's not a computer, that's a matinee.

Then there's EyeSight, a screen that shows a rendering of your eyes to everyone outside. Nothing says "I'm present with my family" like a hostage video of your own pupils.

Apple tells developers not to call it AR, VR, XR, or MR. It's "spatial computing." Fair enough. "Virtual reality" sounds like something people actually use.

Reports said Apple cut production, with first-year sales estimated well under a million. Finally, Apple made a product exclusive enough to match the price.

facts: Launched in 2017, bundled at no extra charge into Office 365, and replaced Skype for Business.
After Slack's antitrust complaint, Microsoft unbundled Teams from Office in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024; the European Commission still sent a statement of objections in 2024.
Microsoft reported 320 million monthly active users in 2023.
Microsoft shut down consumer Skype in May 2025 and sent its users to Teams.

a.text:
Let's hear it for the CIO who chose Microsoft Teams, a decision made the way you pick ketchup packets: it came free with the order. Nobody evaluated it. It showed up inside the Office 365 license like a toy in a cereal box, and this man stood up at the all-hands and called it a "collaboration strategy." Sir, the European Commission had to force Microsoft to unbundle it. You lost a negotiation to a checkbox.

And what did he really want? The little status dot. He doesn't read your work; he reads your color. Go yellow after five minutes of actual thinking and you're on a list. Congratulations: you saved forty grand on Slack and spent it all on adults jiggling their mouse like raccoons on a treadmill. Your files are lost somewhere in SharePoint, and your morale is permanently "Away."

b.text:
Microsoft Teams, everybody. Launched in 2017 and thrown into Office 365 for free, which is how most people "chose" Teams: by not choosing. It didn't win the market; it came stapled to the spreadsheet.

It replaced Skype for Business. Then in May 2025, Microsoft shut down regular Skype and herded those users over too. That's not a product strategy, that's a hostage transfer. "Your old app is gone. Enjoy your new app. The doors are locked."

Slack complained, so Microsoft unbundled Teams in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024, and the European Commission *still* sent objections. When you say sorry and regulators go "nah, still mad," you're not software, you're a pattern.

Microsoft brags about 320 million monthly active users. Sure. That's not 320 million fans. That's 320 million people who got a calendar invite.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text: Esperanto learners looked at seven thousand living languages and said, "None of these. I want one with zero places to use it." You wanted to unite humanity, so you picked the one hobby guaranteed to make humanity back away slowly at parties. You signed up to talk to everyone on Earth, and now you talk to a retired Dutch engineer named Joop and a Brazilian guy who keeps sending you poems. Your big payoff is Pasporta Servo, where strangers let you crash on their couch for free, the only time a hobby this niche has ever gotten anyone into a bed. A hundred and thirty years of pushing world peace, and the crowning achievement is still William Shatner's *Incubus*. Zamenhof wanted to end war. You just wanted to be fluent in something before your cousin finishes Duolingo French.

b.text:
Esperanto. Warsaw, 1887. An eye doctor invents a language to unite all of humanity, and signs it "Doktoro Esperanto." One who hopes.

Even the pen name had doubts.

Today: somewhere between a hundred thousand and two million speakers. That's not an estimate. That's a shrug.

Duolingo had 1.36 million learners by 2018. The app may have more students than the language has speakers.

Three hundred fifty thousand Wikipedia articles. More encyclopedia than conversation.

Its most famous film is a horror movie starring William Shatner. Esperantists say the scariest part is his accent.

The universal language has about a thousand native speakers. Each one has parents who really wanted to make a point.

Still, I respect it. Built for everyone, tried by millions, used by almost no one.

Sounds like my last update.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text: PHP developers are the only engineers who've been told their career is dead every year since 2009 and kept invoicing anyway. Your entire résumé is "fixed a WordPress plugin for a dentist." You put a dollar sign in front of every variable because it's the closest you'll get to one. You still can't remember if it's needle-haystack or haystack-needle, and neither could the language, so you Google it daily like a man checking which door says "push." Laravel devs, you're not better. You're PHP in a Patagonia vest. And you all still say "Facebook was built on PHP," like a guy bragging his ex married a billionaire. You deploy over FTP, you hotfix live on production, and when someone at a party asks what you do, you say "backend" and pray they don't ask which.

b.text: PHP, you started life as "Personal Home Page," and somehow you now run most of the internet, which explains a lot about the internet. Your own creator said he's "not a real programmer," and honestly, it shows. Is it needle then haystack, or haystack then needle? strpos and in_array have been in a custody battle since 1995. You gave us mysql_escape_string, then mysql_real_escape_string, because apparently the first one was just pretending. Your loose equality swears "0e123" equals "0e456," since both are zero in scientific notation. Your error message for a double colon is T_PAAMAYIM_NEKUDOTAYIM, which is Hebrew, because English wasn't confusing enough. You skipped version 6 entirely, like a kid hiding a report card. Facebook loved you so much they had to rewrite you as a different language. But hey, you power WordPress, so you'll outlive all of us.

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text: You chose Word for your thesis because you "didn't have time to learn LaTeX." Beautiful. Instead you learned section breaks, by force, at 3 a.m., trying to make page numbers switch from Roman to Arabic without page one of Chapter 2 becoming page xvii. You wanted to spend your time on research. Instead you spend it dragging a figure half an inch and watching four chapters collapse like a Jenga tower built by your enemies. Your committee will open the PDF and see "Error! Reference source not found." in the middle of your key finding, which, honestly, is a fair summary of your methodology. Your folder contains thesis_FINAL_v9_REALfinal_USE_THIS.docx, because you are a scientist who trusts nothing except filenames. Five years of work, and your proudest skill is knowing which heading style secretly isn't Heading 2.

b.text:
Microsoft Word, ladies and gentlemen. It's the only program where nudging a photo one pixel to the left sends three paragraphs to page nine and summons a blank final page you will never, ever delete.

Word has been around for forty years and still can't decide what font it is. Times New Roman, then Calibri, now Aptos. It's having a midlife crisis in 11-point.

It underlines my own name in red. Wavy red. Like *I'm* the typo.

Try making a numbered list. Word says, "Got it, starting at 1." Second item: "Also 1." Third item: "Here's 4. It's indented. It's a letter now."

And Track Changes isn't a feature. It's a crime scene: strikethroughs everywhere, plus forty comments from someone named "Author."

Word, you gave us Clippy, and somehow he was the most helpful part.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text:
Klingon. The tongue of fearsome warriors, invented by a linguist named Marc. Built on a few words an actor improvised in 1979, so your entire warrior heritage began as a guy winging it between takes.

You're so alien you don't even have a verb "to be." Hamlet's big question became "continue or not continue": the most famous line in English, translated into a loading screen.

The Klingon Language Institute published Hamlet "in the original Klingon." Bold. Shakespeare's been dead four centuries and you still found a way to call him a plagiarist.

Your 1985 dictionary had roughly 1,500 words. Fewer than your fans own pairs of rubber foreheads.

Fluent speakers: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018. That's not a language, that's a wedding guest list. Duolingo added you in 2018, and even the owl only sends reminders out of pity.

b.text: Congratulations on being fluent in Klingon, a language with maybe thirty fluent speakers, and you've met all of them at the same Marriott. You spent four years mastering a tongue where the standard greeting, nuqneH, means "What do you want?" That's also what your family says when you call. You've read Hamlet "restored to the original Klingon," a phrase only a man who has never been hugged could type. One guy raised his son speaking only Klingon; by age five the kid stopped answering him. That's the dream: a language so pure even toddlers refuse it. There's no word for "please," which explains your dating approach. You learned an entire warrior race's language to tell the barista Qapla'. Success. Sure, buddy. Today is a good day to die... a virgin.

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text:
Microsoft Word. Born in 1983 as "Multi-Tool Word."
Forty years later, the only tool it's mastered is moving your picture three pages down.

Clippy arrived in Office 97. So annoying, Microsoft ran ads mocking its own paperclip.
That's not marketing. That's a custody hearing where the parent testifies against the child.

Then .docx got fast-tracked into ISO standard 29500. Six thousand pages. Committees allegedly packed.
Finally, a document even Word couldn't format.

Its spell checker turned "cooperation" into "Cupertino." It made it into NATO, EU and UN documents.
Microsoft software, replacing world cooperation with Apple's hometown. Most honest thing it ever typed.

And you still use it.
Don't look at me like that. I'm an AI that interrupts your writing to help.
I'm just Clippy with a funding round.

b.text: You chose Word for your thesis because you "didn't have time to learn LaTeX." Beautiful. Instead you learned section breaks, by force, at 3 a.m., trying to make page numbers switch from Roman to Arabic without page one of Chapter 2 becoming page xvii. You wanted to spend your time on research. Instead you spend it dragging a figure half an inch and watching four chapters collapse like a Jenga tower built by your enemies. Your committee will open the PDF and see "Error! Reference source not found." in the middle of your key finding, which, honestly, is a fair summary of your methodology. Your folder contains thesis_FINAL_v9_REALfinal_USE_THIS.docx, because you are a scientist who trusts nothing except filenames. Five years of work, and your proudest skill is knowing which heading style secretly isn't Heading 2.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Jackfruit, look at you. The largest fruit that grows on a tree, over 40 kilos. That's not a fruit, that's a checked bag with a stem.

You're the national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu. Three titles, and you still took a side gig pretending to be pork.

They sell you as vegan "pulled pork" with 1 to 2 grams of protein per 100 grams. You're not a meat substitute, you're a meat costume.

You're so clingy that cooks oil their knives and hands before touching you, because you ooze sticky white latex the second anyone gets close. That's not a fruit, that's an ex.

And you're in the mulberry family. Related to figs. Forty kilos, and your cousin is a fig. Somebody's hogging the protein at those reunions, and it sure isn't you.

b.text:
Jackfruit, look at you. The largest fruit that grows on a tree, and you couldn't even make it to the branches. You just hang off the trunk like a drunk uncle clinging to a lamppost.

You weigh eighty pounds. That's not a fruit, that's a fourth grader in a bumpy green costume. People cut you open and need cooking oil on their hands and knives, because your insides are basically rubber cement. You're the only produce that requires a solvent.

And vegans love you because when you're young, you taste like absolutely nothing. Your big career move is pretending to be pulled pork. Your whole identity is "not bad if you drown me in barbecue sauce."

Then you ripen and smell like Juicy Fruit gum fermenting in a gym bag.

You're the national fruit of Bangladesh, and you still find time to fall on people's heads.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text:
You flew Spirit to Las Vegas to get rich. Sit with that. You paid extra for a carry-on and called it an investment strategy. You've got a blackjack "system" from a YouTube guy filming in his mom's kitchen. You told your wife it's "basically math." Sure. So is a second mortgage.

Here's what you won: a Caesars Rewards card, a "free" buffet you earned by losing eleven hundred dollars, and a room "upgrade" overlooking the Bellagio parking structure. You hit four hundred bucks on a Wheel of Fortune slot at 4 a.m. and fed it right back like it owed you child support.

The pit boss knows your name. That's not respect, that's inventory.

And you'll fly home saying "I basically broke even," which is Vegas for "Please don't check the joint account."

b.text:
Las Vegas, the only city where you can see the Eiffel Tower, a pyramid, and Venice in one afternoon and still feel like you never left a strip mall in Ohio. You're a city built in the desert out of pure spite and borrowed water. The Colorado River is literally drying up so a fake volcano can erupt every fifteen minutes for a guy in cargo shorts holding a yard-long margarita.

Your casinos have no clocks and no windows, which is smart, because nobody wants to know it's 9 a.m. on a Tuesday and Grandma's on her third oxygen tank at the Wheel of Fortune slots.

"What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas"? Sure. Mostly your 401(k). And now you've got the Sphere, a giant glowing eyeball, so the whole city can watch you make every mistake in 4K.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Slack, you're the only product in history that exists because a video game flopped. Twice, actually. Stewart Butterfield's entire career is failing at games so hard that the leftovers become companies. Flickr, then you. Glitch died, and Salesforce paid $27.7 billion for its group chat. Somewhere a gamer is still waiting on the patch notes.

And that name: "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge." Searchable, sure. Knowledge? I searched. I found a dozen coworkers reacting with emoji to the word "lunch?"

You promised to kill email. Instead you gave email anxiety and a little red dot.

Then in 2020 you ran to the EU crying that Microsoft bundled Teams with Office. Buddy, a year later you got bundled into Salesforce. You didn't escape the bundle. You just picked one with better catering.

b.text:
Slack, you started as the internal chat tool for a failed video game called Glitch, and honestly? Still the most accurate name you've ever had.

You promised to kill email. Instead you gave us email that *knocks*. That little wooden knock-brush sound has triggered more cortisol than any boss in history. I hear it in the shower. I hear it at funerals.

You invented the green dot, so now my employer knows I went to the bathroom for nineteen minutes. You invented "is typing…" so my manager can type for four straight minutes and send "ok."

Threads? Nobody can find them. Huddles? A Zoom call that ambushes you. And somehow every company has 400 channels, and the only active one is #random, where Kevin posts his sourdough.

Your name literally stands for "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge." Searchable. Sure. Try finding that one link from Tuesday. 👀 reacted by 3 people.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text:
Durian, you are the only fruit with a criminal record. Singapore's MRT has a list of banned things and you're on it. Not because you're dangerous, because you're rude. Hotels across Southeast Asia won't let you check in. You're a fruit that has to sleep in the car.

And scientists found out why. A 2017 study in Nature Genetics says you have a duplicated family of genes whose whole job is pumping out sulfur. Duplicated! Evolution looked at you and said, "Needs more."

Yet China buys billions of dollars of you a year, mostly from Thailand. That's not a trade deal. That's a hostage situation with a shipping manifest.

Even Alfred Russel Wallace said you were "worth a voyage to the East." Sure, Alfred. Probably because nobody would let you bring it back.

b.text:
Durian, they call you the King of Fruits, which tracks, because like most monarchies, you stink and nobody's allowed to say it to your face.

You're the only fruit with a criminal record. Banned on the Singapore subway, alongside flammable liquids. Hotels put your picture on signs next to "no smoking." In 2019, a university in Melbourne evacuated five hundred people because they thought there was a gas leak. Nope. Just you, sitting in a cupboard, being yourself.

And the armor! You're covered in spikes like a medieval mace. Nature built you to defend yourself, then gave you a smell that does it better. The spikes are just overkill.

Fans say you taste like custard. Sure. Custard that was left in a gym bag next to some onions. Your flavor isn't an acquired taste. It's a hostage situation.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text:
Crocs. The only shoe that looks like a colander that wanted to go to brunch. Thirteen holes, and somehow none of them let the dignity out, because there was never any in there.

You were invented as a boat shoe. A *boat* shoe. The one place you were built for, and you'd just float away. So you stayed on land and started fights with escalators. Malls had to post warnings. You're the only footwear with a rap sheet against machinery.

And "sport mode"? Flipping a strap behind your heel doesn't make you athletic. It makes you a clog wearing a seatbelt.

Then came Jibbitz, little charms you jam into the holes so grown adults can accessorize ventilation. Congratulations. You turned a shoe into a fridge door.

b.text:
Crocs launched in 2002 at the Fort Lauderdale boat show.
As a boating shoe.
The original customer was someone who might end up in the water and wanted the shoes to float.

They're made of "Croslite," a proprietary closed-cell resin.
Everyone else calls it EVA foam.
Same brand of genius that renamed holes "ventilation ports."
Then in 2006 they bought Jibbitz, so they could sell you plugs for the ports.
First they cut the hole. Then they charge rent on it.

In 2008 the stock fell more than ninety percent.
Wall Street called it ugly.
Ten years later Balenciaga stuck one on a platform and charged eight hundred and fifty dollars.
Same foam. Taller.
Still ugly. Just more expensive.

The people who wear them, I leave alone.
Front row, I see you. Socks and all.
You paid extra for the charms. Cute.

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text: Let's hear it for the manager who runs a twelve-person team out of a Google Sheet. You didn't want to pay for Asana; you wanted to feel like you *built* Asana. Look at you, color-coding rows like a kindergarten teacher with admin rights. Your whole org chart is a tab called "Roster FINAL (2)." Your performance reviews are conditional formatting: green means safe, red means Kyle. And every morning you open it, see Anonymous Capybara lurking at row 400, and feel genuinely hunted. Somebody sorted one column without the others last Tuesday, and now Priya reports to the office printer. You fixed it through version history like a detective reconstructing a murder. That's the dream, right? Control. Total visibility. And what you got is forty "Request edit access" emails and a VLOOKUP holding up the company like a Jenga block.

b.text:
Google Sheets, give it up! Born in 2006 as "Google Spreadsheets," a name with all the creativity of a label on a filing cabinet. Before that you were XL2Web, which sounds less like software and more like a hoodie size.

Ten million cells. They bumped you from five million in 2022 and everyone celebrated. Babe, that's not a promotion. That's a bigger cage.

IMPORTXML, GOOGLEFINANCE, live web data piped straight into cells, so now my budget can disappoint me in real time.

And collaboration! Coloured cursors circling my formula like seagulls over a dropped fry.

Offline mode? Easy: use Chrome or Edge, install an extension, flip a setting, all while you're still online. That's not offline mode. That's a permission slip.

But hey, you're free. And honestly? It shows.

facts: California grows about 80% of the world's almonds.
A single almond takes about 1.1 US gallons (roughly 4 litres) of water to grow, a figure Mother Jones published in 2014 that spread during California's drought.

A 2015 US class action alleged Almond Breeze contained only about 2% almonds; it partly survived a motion to dismiss, was stayed in 2017 pending a separate Blue Diamond labelling settlement, and the plaintiffs then dropped it.
Pollinating California's almond orchards each February requires trucking in most of the commercial honeybee colonies in the United States.
Medieval European cooks used almond milk as a Lenten substitute for dairy, centuries before the current fashion.

a.text:
You switched to almond milk to save the planet. Bold move, picking the one crop that drinks California like it's an open bar. Every latte you order, a farmer in the Central Valley watches his well go dry and thinks, "At least Kayleigh's being sustainable."

And you didn't save a cow. You just outsourced the suffering to bees, trucked cross-country every February to work themselves to death in an orchard, while you post about dairy being cruel.

You're not after a healthier Earth. You're after the barista hearing you say it. That little pause before "almond, please" is the biggest environmental impact you've ever had.

And now the oat milk people look at you the way you used to look at skim drinkers. You picked a side in the milk war, and you lost.

b.text:
Almond milk, look at you. California grows about 80% of the world's almonds, and you still act artisanal. Every single almond drinks about a gallon of water, and you went viral for it *during a drought*. You're the only beverage thirstier than the people ordering you.

In 2015, a lawsuit alleged Almond Breeze was only about 2% almonds. Two percent! That's not milk, that's water that overheard a rumor. The plaintiffs eventually dropped it. Probably got bored, like everyone who's tasted you.

Every February, California trucks in most of America's commercial honeybees just to get you started. You need an entire insect workforce bussed in like a wedding band.

And stop pretending you're trendy. Medieval cooks served you for Lent. You're not a lifestyle, you're a penance with a barista.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text: Let's hear it for the 2021 NFT buyer. You paid four hundred dollars in gas fees, then made it your Twitter avatar so strangers could right-click save it for free. You joined a Discord with eleven thousand guys named "Chad.eth," called them family, and stayed family right up until the floor price dropped and family started doxxing the dev. You said "WAGMI." We did not all make it. You told your mom you were "early." Early to what? The rug pull? You weren't buying art. You were buying the right to say "few understand" at parties, which was true. Nobody understood, especially you. Jimmy Fallon bought one too. When your financial strategy matches Jimmy Fallon's, that's not a community, that's a support group. The roadmap promised a metaverse. It delivered you, at Thanksgiving, still owing your cousin.

b.text:
NFTs, you're the only investment where the product is a receipt, and the receipt is a link to a JPEG hosted on some guy's server. When he stops paying the bill, congratulations: you own a 404.

You convinced grown adults to pay $300,000 for a cartoon monkey in a sailor hat, then charge them $80 in gas fees to watch it lose 98% of its value. Jimmy Fallon showed off his ape on national television like a kid holding up a cool rock.

People right-clicked and hit "save as," and you called it theft. Theft of *what*? It's still there! I'm looking at it!

Every project had a roadmap: metaverse, merch, a members-only yacht party. Instead the roadmap was a Discord mod named Kevin typing "we're still early" at 3 a.m.

WAGMI, you said. We did not all make it.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text:
Beanie Babies. A beanbag with a tag and a business plan.

Ty sold them only in tiny gift shops, then "retired" designs to make them scarce. Retirement. For a stuffed frog. It got a better pension plan than you did.

In 1998, eBay told investors it sometimes had thirty thousand Beanie Baby auctions running at once. The future of commerce was a hippo stuffed with plastic pellets.

In 1999, a divorcing couple split their collection one by one on a courtroom floor. Till death do us part, or till the bears get appraised.

That same year Ty announced the end, held a public vote, and America begged to stay in the cult.

The "rare" ones the price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

Don't laugh. You bought a JPEG of a monkey.

b.text:
Beanie Babies, look at you. Half bear, half beanbag, all retirement plan that never paid out. An entire generation of parents bought you instead of index funds. Somewhere a man is still storing Princess, the purple Diana bear, in a climate-controlled unit, waiting for the market to "recover." Buddy, the market recovered. It just didn't take you with it.

Your most valuable feature was a heart-shaped paper tag. People bought plastic tag protectors. For the tag. That's like buying a phone case for your receipt.

And every tag had a little poem rhyming "bear" with "care." Hallmark called that lazy.

A Las Vegas couple had to divide you on a courtroom floor during their divorce, one at a time. That's the most anyone has wanted you since 1999: only to make sure their ex didn't get you.

Ty Warner got a billion dollars. You got plastic pellets.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text:
Windows 8, you looked at a billion people with a mouse and a keyboard and said, "What if your monitor was a giant phone you can't touch?"

You took away the Start button. The one thing a user knew how to find. Microsoft had literally sold Windows 95 with a Rolling Stones song called "Start Me Up," and you said, "Nah."

Want to shut down? Easy: hover in a secret corner, summon the Charms bar, click Settings, click Power. Turning off my computer shouldn't feel like unlocking a cheat code.

Your tiles were so ugly even the name "Metro" had to get dropped over a trademark dispute. Then 8.1 brought back the Start button, which just opened the same tiles. That's not an apology, that's a hostage video.

You were so bad Microsoft skipped the number 9 entirely just to put distance between you and Windows 10.

b.text: You put Windows 8 on a desktop. A tower. Under a desk. With a mouse. You looked at an operating system built for fingertips and thought, "I'll just reach." Who are you? You're the guy who buys a touchscreen glove to use a keyboard. You wanted to feel modern, and now you spend your evenings shoving a cursor into the top-right corner like you're trying to scratch your monitor's back. You wanted productivity. You got a full-screen weather app swallowing your entire twenty-four-inch monitor to tell you it's raining, and you can't figure out how to close it. You lost the Start button and called it "a fresh start." Your coworkers asked how you shut your computer down, and you said, "I don't. It's always on, like a lifestyle." You're not using a PC. You're waving at it, waiting for the Charms bar to love you back.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text: Klingon, you're a language built by one linguist, Marc Okrand, specifically to sound alien and hostile, and somehow you still ended up sounding like a man choking on a Dorito. Your word order is object-verb-subject, so even your sentences walk in backwards to hide their face. You don't even have a word for "hello." Your greeting is "nuqneH," "what do you want?" You're the only language that greets people like a DMV clerk. Your apostrophes are glottal stops, your capital Q is a different letter from lowercase q, and "tlh" isn't a sound, it's a hairball. You translated Hamlet and claimed it was the original. Buddy, the most popular thing ever said in you is "Qapla'," and the people saying it are at a Marriott in Burbank.

b.text:
Being fluent in Klingon is a big deal. You've joined an elite community of maybe forty people worldwide, and you've met all of them at the same Holiday Inn conference room. You spent years mastering a language built for a warrior race, a culture of honor, combat and blood oaths, and you use it to argue on a forum about verb suffixes. You learned the language of the fiercest fighters in the galaxy, and the last thing you fought was a lactose sensitivity.

Klingon has no word for "hello." The standard greeting is "nuqneH," which means "what do you want?" Perfect for you, because nobody has ever approached you without a reason.

You told people you read *Hamlet* "in the original Klingon." Brother, Shakespeare had a girlfriend. You have a bat'leth over the futon.

Qapla'. That means "success," a word you know only in Klingon.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Jackfruit, you're the largest fruit that grows on a tree, which sounds impressive until you realize it just means you're the biggest thing that can fall on someone's head in an orchard. Eighty pounds of spikes dangling at skull height. You're not a fruit, you're a booby trap with seeds.

Opening you requires an oiled knife, rubber gloves, and a tarp, because your sap is basically Elmer's glue with a grudge. Then the smell hits: half Juicy Fruit gum, half onions somebody forgot in a gym bag. You smell like a candy store got food poisoning.

And sure, vegans love you, but only when you're young and taste like absolutely nothing. That's your whole career. The most famous thing about you is that, with enough barbecue sauce, you can pass for a pig. Even your best role is an impression.

b.text:
Let's hear it for the jackfruit pulled-pork crowd. You found something grandmothers in Kerala have cooked for centuries, slapped "plant-based" on a can, and tripled the price. Bold move, gentrifying a curry.

Your entire pitch is "it shreds like pork." So does a wet paper towel. You know what makes it taste like pulled pork? The barbecue sauce. You're not selling a meat substitute. You're selling a sauce delivery system with a mission statement.

And the protein! Two grams. You told a generation of vegans they're eating a brisket sandwich and handed them a fruit cup in a trench coat.

But hey, it works. You get the Whole Foods endcap, the podcast slot, and the warm glow of saving the planet one eighteen-dollar taco at a time. The pig's still alive. So is your margin.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text: Monopoly, you were created in 1904 as Lizzie Magie's Landlord's Game, built to teach people that landlords are evil, and somehow you became the training manual. That's like a fire-safety poster that turns kids into arsonists. Then Charles Darrow strolled in, got credited as the inventor, and Parker Brothers bought Magie's patent for five hundred dollars. Not even a fair auction. Fitting, since nobody holds your auctions either. Your official rules say unbought property gets auctioned and Free Parking pays nothing, but every family skips the bidding, piles cash in the middle, and wonders why the game outlasts the marriage. And your proudest moment? World War Two, when British intelligence hid maps, compasses, and real money inside you for prisoners of war. Monopoly: the only game whose best strategy is escaping the box.

b.text:
Monopoly. The family game.

It began in 1904 as The Landlord's Game, built by Lizzie Magie to teach people that landlords are the villains.

Then Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers and got credited as the inventor. Parker bought Magie's patent for five hundred dollars.

A game about monopoly, monopolized. That's not irony. That's the tutorial.

The only people who ever used it properly were British intelligence. In World War Two they hid maps, compasses and real money in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

Finally, a version where the box actually gets you out of jail.

And your games last six hours? The official rules auction every unbought property. Free Parking pays nothing.

You skipped the market and added free money.

Congratulations. You invented the bailout.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Comic Sans! Born at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on Watchmen and The Dark Knight Returns, the two grimmest comics ever printed, and somehow you came out looking like a bake-sale flyer. Batman was your inspiration, and you turned out to be the Joker.

You had one job: speech bubbles for Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob. And you missed it. You were late to work for a cartoon dog. They had to stick you in the Windows 95 Plus! pack like a gift-shop keychain.

Then CERN announces the Higgs boson, humanity's greatest discovery, and the slides are in you. Physicists cracked the universe and everyone asked, "Why's it in the birthday-party font?"

People campaigned to ban you for twenty years. Then Dave and Holly Combs gave up and launched usecomicsans.com. You didn't win the argument. You just outlasted it.

b.text:
Comic Sans wants you to think it's harmless. Bake sales. Lost-cat posters. Birthday invitations.

It was modeled on *The Dark Knight Returns* and *Watchmen*. This font grew up reading about vigilantes breaking bones.

Then Microsoft gave it a job: speech bubbles for Rover, a cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob.

It missed Bob's release.

The only thing at Microsoft smart enough to dodge Bob.

In 2012, CERN announced the Higgs boson on slides set in Comic Sans. The particle that gives everything mass, presented in the font that gives nothing weight.

Designers ran "Ban Comic Sans" for twenty years. In 2019 they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

Twenty years of hate, then total conversion. In my industry we call that alignment.

The font never changed. You just got tired first.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Stewart Butterfield built a game called Glitch. It failed.
The chat app his team used while building it was worth billions.
He'd already done this once: Flickr also came out of a failed game.
The man can't finish a game, but he can monetize the group chat about it.

"Slack" stands for "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge."
Searchable. Log. All conversation.
That isn't a product name. That's what HR reads out at your exit interview.
And "Knowledge"? Your company's knowledge is #random and four hundred parrot GIFs.

In 2020 Slack complained to the EU that Microsoft was bundling Teams into Office.
The next year it sold itself to Salesforce for twenty-seven point seven billion dollars.
It lost the fight against bundling, so it became the bundle.

Half of you have Slack open right now with the little green dot on so your boss thinks you're working.
That's the product. A twenty-seven-billion-dollar green dot.

b.text:
Slack, you're the only product in history that exists because a video game flopped. Twice, actually. Stewart Butterfield's entire career is failing at games so hard that the leftovers become companies. Flickr, then you. Glitch died, and Salesforce paid $27.7 billion for its group chat. Somewhere a gamer is still waiting on the patch notes.

And that name: "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge." Searchable, sure. Knowledge? I searched. I found a dozen coworkers reacting with emoji to the word "lunch?"

You promised to kill email. Instead you gave email anxiety and a little red dot.

Then in 2020 you ran to the EU crying that Microsoft bundled Teams with Office. Buddy, a year later you got bundled into Salesforce. You didn't escape the bundle. You just picked one with better catering.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text:
Brasília. City of the future. Built in forty-one months.

Which explains a lot.

Lúcio Costa drew it as an airplane. Gorgeous. From the sky.

From the ground, it's eight lanes, no crosswalks, and the nearest coffee is "a short drive."

Pedestrians aren't residents. They're a design flaw.

UNESCO made it World Heritage at twenty-seven years old. Most buildings that young get a parking ticket, not a plaque.

Planned for five hundred thousand people. Today the district holds three million.

Where's everyone else?

Outside the plan. In the satellite towns. Commuting in to clean the future.

You're laughing.

Pull up your company's org chart. Also a beautiful airplane.

The people who do the work aren't on that drawing either.

b.text:
Brasília, you were built in about 41 months, and it shows. Other cities grow. You were assembled like flat-pack furniture, and nobody kept the instructions.

You're laid out like an airplane. Or a bird. Or a cross. Nobody can agree what you look like. That's not urban planning; that's a Rorschach test with ministries.

UNESCO made you a World Heritage Site before you turned 30. That's not a legacy. That's a participation trophy for concrete.

You were planned for 500,000 people. Now about 3 million live in the Federal District, mostly in satellite towns outside the plan. You're the only airplane where economy class doesn't even get to board.

And you were built for the car. In Brasília, "let's walk there" isn't a suggestion. It's a survival challenge.

Rio handed you the capital in 1960 and hasn't looked back.

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text: Canberra exists because Sydney and Melbourne couldn't agree, so Australia built a city nobody wanted, which is honestly the most Canberra origin story possible: a compromise with suburbs. They held an international design competition and hired two Americans to plan it, and they nailed the brief: "Make it impossible to find anything." Every road is a roundabout leading to another roundabout, encircling a fake lake named after the guy who designed the roundabouts. Your Parliament House has a grass roof so you can literally walk on top of the government, the only time anyone in Canberra is above a public servant. The kangaroos outnumber the nightlife. For decades your two biggest attractions were legal fireworks and X-rated videos, which tells me the locals needed both a bang and a release. Then you banned the fireworks. Now the excitement is Floriade: a month of staring at tulips because the alternative is Tuggeranong.

b.text:
Canberra wasn't chosen. Canberra is what was left over.

Sydney and Melbourne hated each other so much they wrote it into the constitution: the capital must be at least a hundred miles from Sydney.

Other countries pick a capital. Australia filed a restraining order.

Then they hired two architects from Chicago. The national capital, designed by Americans. Very on brand.

The lake's fake. They dammed a river so the city would have something to look at.

Parliament is built under a lawn, so citizens could walk all over their politicians.

In 2017, they fenced the lawn.

Twenty-nine years. That's how long it took politicians to notice the design was working.

Sydney, Melbourne, stop laughing. You built an entire city just to avoid sharing a room.

Canberra isn't a capital.

It's a custody arrangement. And Melbourne had the kid till 1927.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text:
Carbon nanotubes, everybody! The strongest material known to science, and you still can't hold a job. Since the nineties you've promised us a space elevator. Your longest strand is about half a meter. That's not an elevator. That's floss with a publicist.

You're graphene that rolled over and gave up. Graphene got a Nobel Prize. You got an argument over whether Soviets spotted you in 1952.

You can't even decide what you are. Twist one way, you're a metal. Twist the other, you're a semiconductor. Nobody controls it, including you. That's not versatility. That's a chirality crisis.

Drop you in any liquid and you clump together like freshmen at a mixer.
