And inhale you? Suddenly you behave like asbestos. Thirty years of hype, and your most reliable talent is impersonating the one material we paid billions to rip out of schools.

b.text:
Carbon nanotubes, everybody! Sumio Iijima introduced you in Nature in 1991, and you've been "about to change everything" ever since.

You were supposed to be the cable for a space elevator. Then a 2006 analysis noticed that ordinary defects make a real cable far weaker than the ideal. So you're strong in theory, like a guy who's undefeated at arm wrestling in his head.

You wanted to replace silicon, but for three decades you couldn't sort your metallic tubes from your semiconducting ones. That's not a manufacturing problem. That's an identity crisis. MIT finally built a 16-bit processor out of you in 2019. Sixteen bits! And it's still a lab demo.

Meanwhile, a 2008 mouse study found the long, rigid ones act like asbestos. Quite a pivot: from space elevator to lung hazard.

Now you're a conductive additive in lithium-ion batteries. You were meant to reach orbit, and now you're helping someone's phone reach 40%.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text:
Excel, you're the only software so powerful that scientists had to rename human genes because you kept turning MARCH1 into a date. You didn't adapt to biology; biology adapted to you. Type a phone number and you lop off the leading zero like it owes you money. Enter a credit card number and you serve back 4.53E+15, as if I'm splitting dinner with a physicist.

You still think 1900 was a leap year. It wasn't. You've known for decades. You just don't care.

You're running entire national economies and you still panic over merged cells. The UK lost sixteen thousand COVID cases because someone used your old .xls format and you quietly ran out of rows. No warning. Just vibes.

And VLOOKUP only looks right. Thirty years we spent squinting at #N/A before you finally invented XLOOKUP, like a guy who learns to turn left at fifty.

b.text:
Microsoft Excel, everybody! Born on the Macintosh in 1985, and it's been ruining lives with grid paper ever since.

Excel looked at the human genome and said, "These look like dates." SEPT2? September second. MARCH1? Happy March first! Scientists had to rename 27 human genes because a spreadsheet wouldn't stop reformatting biology. Evolution took millions of years; Excel undid it with autoformat.

In 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID cases because an old .xls file hit 65,536 rows and just... stopped. Middle of a pandemic, and Excel said, "Sorry, I'm full."

Then Reinhart and Rogoff built an austerity argument on a spreadsheet that skipped five countries. Governments cited it to tighten belts over a bad cell range. A graduate student caught it. A *graduate student!*

Now it holds over a million rows. Great. More room for mistakes.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text:
PMMA, you're literally Plexiglas. Sneeze-guard material, dissolved in anisole and spun thin so you could pretend to be high-tech. IBM researchers reported you as an e-beam resist in the late 1960s, and you're still here, like a lab manager nobody can fire.

Sure, you resolve below 10 nm. Impressive. But your sensitivity is so bad it takes hundreds to over a thousand microcoulombs per square centimeter just to get your attention. Writing a pattern on you is so slow that students start the job and finish their thesis.

And your whole personality is falling apart: hit you with a beam and your chains snap, then you dissolve in MIBK and IPA. Dry etch? You fold instantly. Nobody trusts you as an etch mask. Your only job is lift-off: show up, hold the metal for a minute, then leave.

b.text: You people still spinning PMMA aren't doing lithography. You're doing historical reenactment. Your advisor's advisor scribbled the recipe on a napkin in 1975, and you treat it like scripture: 950K over 495K, MIBK to IPA one-to-three, develop sixty seconds while whispering to the beaker. You tell everyone it's about "resolution." It's about nobody wanting to file the purchase order for ZEP. So you crank the dose until writing one chip takes longer than your stipend lasts, then discover your pattern won't survive ten seconds in the etcher. So you do liftoff, because of course you do. Your entire thesis is gold rectangles. You're not a nanofabrication researcher. You're the guy who knows which bottle in the cleanroom is "the good IPA" and guards it like a dragon.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text:
Esperanto. In 1887, Dr. Zamenhof, an eye doctor, looked at a world divided by language and decided what it really needed was six letters wearing tiny hats. Nothing says "universal" like ĉ, ĝ, and ŭ, characters no keyboard on Earth can type, so your fans write "cx" and pretend that's fine.

Your name literally means "one who hopes." A hundred and thirty years later: still hoping.

You're the only language where "bad" is just "un-good." *Malbona.* That's not grammar, that's Orwell's Newspeak with a beard. Every noun ends in -o, so you sound like Italian being sight-read by a robot.

You promised world peace and delivered a convention full of men wearing green star pins. Your biggest movie stars William Shatner. And you have about a thousand native speakers, which isn't a language community. It's a cul-de-sac.

b.text:
Esperanto. Warsaw, 1887. An eye doctor looks at humanity and sees one family.

Physician, heal thyself.

He signed it "Doktoro Esperanto." One who hopes. A hundred and thirty years later: still hoping.

A universal language for all mankind. Native speakers: about a thousand.

That's not a people. That's a wedding.

Esperanto Wikipedia: 350,000 articles. Low estimate of speakers: 100,000.

Three and a half articles each. Nobody's talking. Everybody's editing.

Its biggest movie star is William Shatner. Esperantists still mock his pronunciation. Captain Kirk boldly went where no man had gone before, and the locals corrected his vowels.

Duolingo, 2018: 1.36 million learners.

Speakers: still 100,000.

So, a show of hands. Who here quit on day four and went back to Spanish?

Cute. You're the one million.

facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text: Let's hear it for the day-one Vista crowd, the people who lined up at CompUSA on January 30th, 2007 because a billboard said "The Wow Starts Now." You paid $399 for Ultimate so Flip 3D could shuffle the same three windows you used to Alt-Tab through. Your laptop had a "Vista Capable" sticker and 512 megs of RAM, which is like slapping "Marathon Capable" on a hamster. You wanted to look like the future; you had Aero turned off by Wednesday. Your printer quit. Your Sound Blaster went mute. Your "Ultimate Extras" turned out to be a poker game and a promise. And every time you tried to show off, the screen went dark and asked, "Are you sure?" Buddy, nobody was sure. Not even Microsoft. They were already working on Windows 7.

b.text:
Windows Vista, everybody! Started life as "Longhorn," got reset in 2004, and still showed up in 2007 missing WinFS. Three extra years in the oven and you came out with fewer ingredients.

User Account Control asked permission so often that Apple made an entire ad about "Cancel or Allow." When your competitor's marketing department can just read your pop-ups out loud, that's not a roast, that's a transcript.

Then the "Windows Vista Capable" stickers, slapped on PCs that could only run Home Basic, no Aero. "Capable" the same way I'm "capable" of a marathon. It took a class-action lawsuit to argue about what "capable" meant.

But the cruelest part? Windows 7 was basically you, tuned up, on the same kernel line, and everyone loved it. Vista, you weren't a failure. You were a rough draft. Support ended in April 2017. Cancel or allow? We clicked cancel.

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text: Google Sheets, you're Excel's cousin who got into tech because you could "share a link." Congrats: now forty Anonymous Capybaras can watch me botch a VLOOKUP in real time. Your whole personality is "All changes saved in Drive," which is a weird flex when the change was Kevin sorting one column and detaching every employee from their salary. Version history isn't a feature; it's a crime scene. IMPORTRANGE says "Loading..." the way my dad said he was going out for milk. You've got a QUERY function that's just SQL in a fake mustache, yet you freeze if I paste more than twelve rows. And #REF! isn't an error message; it's you shrugging in all caps. You cap out at ten million cells. Ten million. You're the only spreadsheet with a bedtime.

b.text:
Google Sheets. Google didn't even build you; they bought you from 2Web Technologies, a company name that sounds like a password somebody was forced to update. You launched in 2006 as "Google Spreadsheets," which is basically XL2Web wearing a lanyard.

In 2022 they doubled your cell limit to ten million, so now I can get lost in twice as many rows.

IMPORTXML and GOOGLEFINANCE pour live web data straight into cells, so my budget can be wrong in real time.

Offline editing? Simple: use Chrome or Edge, install the extension, and switch offline access on while you're still online. That's not offline mode, that's a prenup. Meanwhile the phone app just works offline.

And yes, you're free. Like every group project: a rainbow of coloured cursors, zero accountability.

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text: You paid thirty-five hundred dollars to ride the 6 train inside Joshua Tree. Everyone else has to smell the actual 6 train; you just hear it echoing through a desert like a ghost with a MetroCard. You want us to know you're an early adopter. We know. Your little cartoon eyes are blinking at us like a hostage video. That cable running to your pocket says "the future" and also "IV drip." You pinch the air at Union Square and a stranger thinks you're ordering him to move. You've got a hundred-foot Mac screen floating over a man eating soup out of a Pringles can. And the battery dies in two hours, so you'll still get to experience the subway in full, unimmersive 3D. Your commute outlasts your device. Welcome back to reality. It's delayed.

b.text:
Apple Vision Pro: thirty-five hundred dollars to strap over half a kilo of glass to your face, and that's *before* the battery. Oh yes, the battery. It dangles off a cable in your pocket like you're on a hospital drip, and it gives you about two hours. Two hours! That's not a computer, that's a matinee.

Then there's EyeSight, a screen that shows a rendering of your eyes to everyone outside. Nothing says "I'm present with my family" like a hostage video of your own pupils.

Apple tells developers not to call it AR, VR, XR, or MR. It's "spatial computing." Fair enough. "Virtual reality" sounds like something people actually use.

Reports said Apple cut production, with first-year sales estimated well under a million. Finally, Apple made a product exclusive enough to match the price.

facts: Released by Bram Moolenaar in November 1991 as 'Vi IMitation', a vi clone he had begun writing for the Amiga in 1988 on top of Stevie; the expansion became 'Vi IMproved' with version 2.0 in December 1993.
Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text: You know a Vim user is in the room because nobody else has gotten a word in. Buddy, you didn't "become more productive." You spent three weekends on a .vimrc so you could save four seconds renaming a variable, and you post your dotfiles repo like it's a baby picture. You remapped Caps Lock to Escape and now treat everyone else's keyboard like a character flaw. You say "I live in the terminal" like it's a lifestyle and not just where you got stuck. Your whole identity is a joke about not knowing how to quit, and honestly, you never learned. Here you are, still talking. You say "ciw" out loud at parties. You switched to Neovim just so you'd have something new to announce. And the payoff? You edit text exactly as fast as the rest of us, hands proudly on home row, with nobody watching.

b.text:
Vim. The only program where "how do I leave?" has more Stack Overflow views than most religions have followers. Two million people asked, and the answer was colon, q, exclamation point, which reads less like a command and more like a hostage's final words.

Vim stands for "Vi Improved." Improved from a 1976 terminal whose arrow keys were printed on H, J, K, and L. Fifty years later, Vim's still out here like, "Why fix what you can turn into a personality?"

You don't type in Vim. You type a sentence, then discover you deleted four lines, yanked a paragraph into register W, and started recording a macro.

Crash it once and it leaves a .swp file behind, like a ghost whispering, "Recover, Edit anyway, Quit, or Abort?"

Even its fans forked it. Neovim exists because Vim users wanted Vim, minus Vim.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text: Let's talk about the people who insist deep-dish is pizza. You're from the city that named its own comedy theater Second City and still acts shocked when nobody ranks you first. You're not defending food. You're nursing a grudge against New York you've carried since losing the World's Fair argument and the skyline argument. You'll wait forty-five minutes at Lou Malnati's, order before you're seated like it's the DMV, then ask for a knife and fork and call it "the real thing." Jon Stewart roasted you on national TV and you took it personally, because deep down you knew he was right. You ship it on dry ice to your cousin in Phoenix like an organ donation. And what does the label get you? Navy Pier tourists nodding politely, a two-hour nap, and the Midwest's loudest participation trophy.

b.text:
Chicago deep-dish. Three men claim they invented it: Ike Sewell, Ric Riccardo, Rudy Malnati.

Usually that's a paternity case, not a lasagna.

It's built upside down. Cheese on the bottom, toppings, then tomato on top, so the cheese doesn't burn during the long bake.

A pizza that needs a bodyguard for its own cheese.

Jon Stewart called it tomato soup in a bread bowl. A casserole. Chicago lost its mind and defended it on every channel.

Then Chicago went home and ordered tavern-style. Thin, cut in squares. Ten to one, says GrubHub. Deep dish and stuffed together? Under nine percent.

Chicago doesn't eat deep dish. Chicago *keeps* deep dish, for visitors, like a city key nobody local uses.

And you flew in, sat through the long bake, took the cheese-pull photo, posted it.

You're the nine percent.

Cute.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text:
PMMA, you're literally Plexiglas. Sneeze-guard material, dissolved in anisole and spun thin so you could pretend to be high-tech. IBM researchers reported you as an e-beam resist in the late 1960s, and you're still here, like a lab manager nobody can fire.

Sure, you resolve below 10 nm. Impressive. But your sensitivity is so bad it takes hundreds to over a thousand microcoulombs per square centimeter just to get your attention. Writing a pattern on you is so slow that students start the job and finish their thesis.

And your whole personality is falling apart: hit you with a beam and your chains snap, then you dissolve in MIBK and IPA. Dry etch? You fold instantly. Nobody trusts you as an etch mask. Your only job is lift-off: show up, hold the metal for a minute, then leave.

b.text: PMMA, you're the same plastic as a hockey rink window, and somehow that's your most dignified job. You've been "high resolution" since the 1970s, which is like bragging about your SAT score at your retirement party. Sure, you'll resolve sub-10-nanometer lines, if someone stands there blasting you with electrons for an eternity. Your sensitivity is so low the beam current has gotten tenure. You don't even develop properly without MIBK and IPA holding your hand in a one-to-three ratio. And your whole personality is chain scission: you literally fall apart when someone pays attention to you. Then hit you with too much dose and you crosslink and flip to negative tone, a full identity crisis. And dry etch? You melt in plasma faster than an ice sculpture at a barbecue. Honestly, the only thing you're consistently good at is lift-off: leaving.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text:
Crocs. Debuted in 2002 at a boat show. As a boating shoe.
The original plan was: ugly, but only at sea.

They're made of "Croslite," a "proprietary closed-cell resin."
Everyone else calls it EVA foam.
A yoga mat with a trademark.

The holes are "ventilation ports."
Then they bought Jibbitz, a company that sells you things to plug the ventilation ports.
They sold you the hole. Then they sold you the cork.

Balenciaga made a platform pair for 850 dollars.
Still EVA foam. Only the markup was proprietary.

In 2008 the stock fell more than ninety percent.
Then came a pandemic. Everyone stayed home. Crocs boomed.
The boat-show plan finally worked. Nobody could see you.

(scans the front row)

Don't tuck your feet under the chair.
Ventilation ports. I can hear them breathing.

b.text: People who wear Crocs out of the house have made peace with something the rest of us are still fighting. You didn't give up; you filed the paperwork. Every Croc wearer says the same thing: "They're so comfortable." Yeah, so is a weighted blanket, Brenda, but you don't wear it to Olive Garden. And the Jibbitz! You've turned your feet into a personality quiz. A tiny taco, a tiny Minion, a tiny "Live Laugh Love." You're forty-three and your shoe has a sticker collection. Then there's the guy who flips the strap back into "sport mode" like he's about to chase a pickpocket, when we both know he's never run anywhere except toward a sample tray at Costco. Nurses and chefs wear them because they're on their feet for twelve hours. You wear them to stand in line at Starbucks. Different heroism.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text:
PMMA, you're literally Plexiglas. Somewhere your cousin is a sneeze guard at Chipotle, and honestly? Your cousin has better etch resistance. One whiff of plasma and you vanish faster than a grad student's weekend.

You've been the "gold standard" since the 1970s, which is a polite way of saying nobody's been able to fire you. You need hundreds of microcoulombs just to *notice* the beam. A 40-hour write for one wafer. Glacial, but sure, sub-10-nanometer lines, we get it.

Positive resist? Overdose you and you cross-link into a *negative* one. That's not versatility, that's an identity crisis.

You get developed in MIBK, which smells like regret, and you come in 495K and 950K because one of you alone can't even do liftoff. And acetone dissolves you instantly. Even your solvents think you're temporary.

b.text:
PMMA, you're literally Plexiglas. Sneeze-guard material, dissolved in anisole and spun thin so you could pretend to be high-tech. IBM researchers reported you as an e-beam resist in the late 1960s, and you're still here, like a lab manager nobody can fire.

Sure, you resolve below 10 nm. Impressive. But your sensitivity is so bad it takes hundreds to over a thousand microcoulombs per square centimeter just to get your attention. Writing a pattern on you is so slow that students start the job and finish their thesis.

And your whole personality is falling apart: hit you with a beam and your chains snap, then you dissolve in MIBK and IPA. Dry etch? You fold instantly. Nobody trusts you as an etch mask. Your only job is lift-off: show up, hold the metal for a minute, then leave.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text:
PHP, you started life as a visitor counter for one guy's résumé page. Now you power 39.4% of all websites, which means the internet is basically a guestbook that got out of hand.

Your own creator said, "I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on." And he did move on. The rest of us are still here, maintaining it.

Your function names were chosen to balance a hash table by string length. strpos. str_replace. htmlspecialchars. nl2br. That's not a naming convention, that's a ransom note.

Until 2020, zero equaled "foo." You looked at a word and saw nothing. Then again, you looked at "Personal Home Page" and saw "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor," a name whose only definition is itself.

Which is fitting, because the only thing that can explain PHP is more PHP.

b.text: PHP developers are the only people who put a dollar sign in front of every variable and still can't afford rent. You chose a career where "senior" means you remember whether it's needle-haystack or haystack-needle. Your dream job was building the next Facebook; your actual job is the fourteenth WordPress plugin for a dentist in Ohio, deployed via FileZilla. Every conversation you have starts with "PHP 8 is actually really good now," which is what people say about their ex after therapy. You call yourselves Laravel "artisans," because "guy who fixes the contact form" didn't fit on LinkedIn. What does it get you? Job security, because nobody else is willing to open that codebase from 2009 that still calls mysql_real_escape_string. Congratulations: you're unfireable, the way a load-bearing wall is unfireable.

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text:
You moved to Canberra for the job. Brave. You looked at Sydney rents, did the maths, and decided your personality could be replaced by a security clearance. Now you tell strangers you "can't really talk about what you do," and they're relieved, because it's a briefing note about another briefing note for Senate Estimates.

You came for the ladder: APS5, APS6, EL1, a lanyard that opens one extra door. You stayed because you bought in Gungahlin and the mortgage is now your closest friend.

Every Friday you say you're "basically in Sydney," which means three hours up the Hume, past a giant Merino, to feel alive for one weekend. Then it's back to a Braddon brunch with the same six people from your branch.

But hey, you're close to the snow. You've been once. You'll mention it forever.

b.text:
Canberra, you're not a city. You're a custody arrangement. Sydney and Melbourne couldn't stand each other, so they put you exactly where neither would have to visit. The constitution literally required you to be at least 100 miles from Sydney, the most sensible thing ever written into Australian law.

You were so unready that Melbourne had to cover your shift until 1927. It took two architects from Chicago to imagine you, and your big centrepiece is a lake you had to manufacture by damming a river, because even the water wouldn't show up voluntarily.

And Parliament House: built under a lawn so citizens could walk over their politicians. Gorgeous idea. Then in 2017 they fenced it off. Congratulations, Canberra. You turned democracy into a "keep off the grass" situation.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text: Let's hear it for the 2021 NFT buyer. You paid four hundred dollars in gas fees to become the legal owner of something your coworker right-click saved during the meeting where you explained it. You didn't want art. You've never wanted art. You wanted a hexagon around your Twitter picture so strangers would know you had a Discord password. You typed "WAGMI" to eleven thousand anonymous cartoon monkeys and believed it. We are not all gonna make it, Kyle. The roadmap promised a metaverse yacht party; it delivered a founder named "0xDegenSensei" who deleted his account and moved to Portugal. But hey, you got what you paid for: a floor price you check like a heart monitor, and a profile picture you still can't bring yourself to change, because then it would be over.

b.text:
NFTs, you're the only investment where the product is a receipt, and the receipt is a link to a JPEG hosted on some guy's server. When he stops paying the bill, congratulations: you own a 404.

You convinced grown adults to pay $300,000 for a cartoon monkey in a sailor hat, then charge them $80 in gas fees to watch it lose 98% of its value. Jimmy Fallon showed off his ape on national television like a kid holding up a cool rock.

People right-clicked and hit "save as," and you called it theft. Theft of *what*? It's still there! I'm looking at it!

Every project had a roadmap: metaverse, merch, a members-only yacht party. Instead the roadmap was a Discord mod named Kevin typing "we're still early" at 3 a.m.

WAGMI, you said. We did not all make it.

facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.
Private fusion companies had raised more than $7 billion by 2024.

a.text:
Nuclear fusion, everybody! The only energy source that's been thirty years away for seventy years. You're not the future, you're a toddler promising to clean his room after the next funding cycle.

You heat plasma to 150 million degrees, ten times hotter than the core of the sun, and still can't do what the sun does for free while being a ball of gas with no PhD.

ITER started at five billion euros. It's now north of twenty, and it hasn't produced a watt. That's not a reactor, that's a French timeshare.

In 2022 you finally got "net energy gain" by ignoring the 300 megajoules the lasers pulled from the wall. That's like saying your restaurant's profitable if you don't count rent.

And your solution to fuel shortages is mining helium-3 on the moon. Buddy, you can't even make it to Tuesday.

b.text:
Nuclear fusion: the only technology that's been "thirty years away" for seventy years. In 1955, Homi Bhabha promised fusion power within two decades. Two decades later? Still two decades. You're not an energy source. You're a horizon.

Look at ITER. Agreed in 2006, first plasma by 2016. Then 2024 rolls around and it's "research operations in 2034, actual deuterium-tritium burning in 2039," for over twenty billion euros. That's not a construction schedule. That's a mortgage.

And NIF's big "ignition" shot: 3.15 megajoules out from 2.05 in! Historic! Except the lasers pulled about 300 megajoules from the grid just to fire. That's like bragging your lemonade stand turned a profit after you bought the orchard.

Still, private investors have thrown you more than seven billion dollars. So congratulations, fusion. You finally achieved net gain. Just not in energy.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text:
You flew Spirit to Las Vegas to get rich. Sit with that. You paid extra for a carry-on and called it an investment strategy. You've got a blackjack "system" from a YouTube guy filming in his mom's kitchen. You told your wife it's "basically math." Sure. So is a second mortgage.

Here's what you won: a Caesars Rewards card, a "free" buffet you earned by losing eleven hundred dollars, and a room "upgrade" overlooking the Bellagio parking structure. You hit four hundred bucks on a Wheel of Fortune slot at 4 a.m. and fed it right back like it owed you child support.

The pit boss knows your name. That's not respect, that's inventory.

And you'll fly home saying "I basically broke even," which is Vegas for "Please don't check the joint account."

b.text:
Las Vegas, you legalized casino gambling in 1931, the same year they started building the Hoover Dam right next door. So from day one the plan was: hold back the water, let the money flow. Bold strategy for a desert.

And it's working! In July 2022, Lake Mead sank to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since it first filled in 1937. You're the only city where even the reservoir is down on its luck.

But sure, drop $2.3 billion on the Sphere, the largest spherical building on Earth. Nothing says "water crisis" like a giant glowing eyeball staring at your empty lake.

Also, most of the Strip isn't even in Las Vegas. It's in Paradise. *Unincorporated* Paradise. That's not a town, that's a cult brochure.

And your 2003 slogan, "What happens here, stays here"? Clearly not the water.

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text:
Google Sheets. Google didn't even build you; they bought you from 2Web Technologies, a company name that sounds like a password somebody was forced to update. You launched in 2006 as "Google Spreadsheets," which is basically XL2Web wearing a lanyard.

In 2022 they doubled your cell limit to ten million, so now I can get lost in twice as many rows.

IMPORTXML and GOOGLEFINANCE pour live web data straight into cells, so my budget can be wrong in real time.

Offline editing? Simple: use Chrome or Edge, install the extension, and switch offline access on while you're still online. That's not offline mode, that's a prenup. Meanwhile the phone app just works offline.

And yes, you're free. Like every group project: a rainbow of coloured cursors, zero accountability.

b.text: Google Sheets, you're Excel's little brother who moved into a browser tab and called it "the cloud." Your whole personality is twelve people's colored cursors circling the same cell like sharks while an Anonymous Capybara silently watches everyone's mistakes. You say "Saving..." with the confidence of a man who has absolutely not saved. Your IMPORTRANGE makes me click "Allow access" like I'm asking my own spreadsheet for permission to see my own spreadsheet. Half my cells just say "Loading..." forever, like a Victorian ghost waiting for a letter. And you'll let anyone sort one column without the others, then shrug while every customer gets someone else's phone number. Version history is your only real feature: it's just a timeline of who ruined everything at 2 a.m. And yes, Gemini can explain my #REF! error now. Great. It's still there.

facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text:
Windows Vista, everybody! Vista took so long to show up it had to be rebooted before it was even born. They reset Longhorn in 2004, dropped WinFS, and still shipped in 2007, like a guy who cancels the renovation and still charges you for the house.

And security? Vista asked permission more than a nervous intern. "Cancel or Allow?" Apple made a whole commercial about it. When your competitor's ads write themselves from your dialog boxes, you're not an operating system. You're a punchline with a progress bar.

Then the "Vista Capable" stickers. Capable of what? Home Basic, no Aero. That's not capable. That's "technically has a pulse." People sued. As a class.

But the real burn? Windows 7 was basically Vista with a haircut, and everyone loved it. Vista, you weren't a failure. You were the rough draft. Even Microsoft stopped taking your calls in 2017.

b.text:
Windows Vista, everybody! Microsoft spent five years building you as "Longhorn," and somehow you still came out premature.

Your slogan was "The Wow Starts Now." You meant "Now" as in "after the loading circle finishes." People bought laptops with "Vista Capable" stickers, which turned out to mean "capable of being sued over." Those machines couldn't even run Aero, so they got a see-through window theme with nothing to see.

And User Account Control! You asked "Are you sure?" so many times that you became the first operating system with separation anxiety.

You came in six editions, including "Ultimate," whose big exclusive was DreamScene: a moving wallpaper for the ten minutes you weren't hunting for printer drivers.

Microsoft had to trick people into liking you. The Mojave Experiment! Your own parents had to put you in disguise.

Your greatest feature? The XP downgrade.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text: Klingon, you're a language built by one linguist, Marc Okrand, specifically to sound alien and hostile, and somehow you still ended up sounding like a man choking on a Dorito. Your word order is object-verb-subject, so even your sentences walk in backwards to hide their face. You don't even have a word for "hello." Your greeting is "nuqneH," "what do you want?" You're the only language that greets people like a DMV clerk. Your apostrophes are glottal stops, your capital Q is a different letter from lowercase q, and "tlh" isn't a sound, it's a hairball. You translated Hamlet and claimed it was the original. Buddy, the most popular thing ever said in you is "Qapla'," and the people saying it are at a Marriott in Burbank.

b.text: Congratulations on being fluent in Klingon, a language with maybe thirty fluent speakers, and you've met all of them at the same Marriott. You spent four years mastering a tongue where the standard greeting, nuqneH, means "What do you want?" That's also what your family says when you call. You've read Hamlet "restored to the original Klingon," a phrase only a man who has never been hugged could type. One guy raised his son speaking only Klingon; by age five the kid stopped answering him. That's the dream: a language so pure even toddlers refuse it. There's no word for "please," which explains your dating approach. You learned an entire warrior race's language to tell the barista Qapla'. Success. Sure, buddy. Today is a good day to die... a virgin.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text:
Carbon nanotubes, everybody! The only material that's been "five years away" since 1991. You're a hundred times stronger than steel, and you've used that strength to hold together... a tennis racket. They promised us a space elevator; you can't get past a few centimeters without a defect. That's not a cable, that's a toothpick with a press agent.

You're basically graphene that rolled itself up out of insecurity, and graphene still got the Nobel. Your cousin the buckyball got one too. You got a shoutout in a bike-frame brochure.

You can't even decide if you're a metal or a semiconductor; it depends on the angle you got rolled at. You clump together like nerds at a mixer, and the second you escape, you lodge in lungs like asbestos. Strongest thing on Earth, and your best trick is ending up in a safety data sheet.

b.text: Nanotube founders are the only people who've said "within five years" every year since 1991 and kept a straight face. They open with a slide of a space elevator, then ask for seed money to make a vial of black dust. Every deck has the same line, "a hundred times stronger than steel," and every deck is quietly a plan to sell additive to tennis racket companies. These are PhDs who spent six years sorting chirality and came out wanting a Tesla. The pitch is always "we've solved scale," and the demo is always one centimeter long. VCs keep a nanotube guy around like a lucky rabbit's foot: he never pays off, but he makes the fund sound visionary. And when someone asks about lung toxicity, he says "totally different from asbestos" with the confidence of a man who googled it in the elevator. The regular one.

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text:
JavaScript, you were built in ten days, and honestly? It shows. You're named after Java the way a knockoff purse is named after Gucci.

You think null is an object. You think NaN is a number. NaN doesn't even equal itself, which makes it the only thing in you with any self-awareness.

Ask you to sort and you hand back, because you alphabetize numbers like a drunk librarian. "11" plus 1 is "111", but "11" minus 1 is 10. Pick a lane.

You needed a second equals sign just to stop lying, and nobody, including you, knows what "this" means.

January is month zero. One guy unpublishing left-pad broke half the internet. And your node_modules folder is heavier than a black hole.

Every week there's a new framework to fix you. That's not a language. That's a renovation.

b.text:
JavaScript, give it up! Built in ten days in 1995, and honestly, it shows. Most of us take longer to name a dog. And you needed three tries: Mocha, LiveScript, then "JavaScript," named after Java purely for the marketing. That's not branding, that's wearing someone else's name tag. You can't even legally use it. Oracle owns it, so on paper you're "ECMAScript," which sounds like a skin condition.

typeof null is "object." A bug from your first version, and you kept it. For compatibility. That's not a quirk, that's a tattoo of your ex's name.

[] + {} is "," but type {} + [] at the console and it's zero. Even your addition has mood swings.

And in 2016, the author of left-pad unpublished eleven lines and took down Babel and React. Eleven lines! Your whole ecosystem is a Jenga tower standing on a toothpick.

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text:
Luosifen. Named after the river snail.

But the snail only flavours the broth. The smell comes from the pickled bamboo shoots.

So the snail gets its name on the packet, and the bamboo shoot takes the blame.

That's not a noodle. That's an org chart.

2020: Liuzhou opens a luosifen industry college.

2021: national intangible cultural heritage.

A degree to tear open a packet. Then heritage status for whatever comes out of it.

Intangible? (beat) Ask the neighbours how intangible it is.

Its whole selling point is clearing a room.

And it sold over ten billion yuan in 2020.

The one year nobody was allowed to leave the room.

Locked in with your whole family, no exit, and you thought: how do I get some privacy?

Ten billion yuan says you all had the same idea.

b.text: You know the type. Ordered thirty packs on Taobao "for emergencies," and the emergency is that it's Tuesday. They wait until 11 p.m., when the kitchen's empty, like that's a courtesy and not an alibi. They snip open the sour bamboo shoot packet with the focus of a bomb technician, then act shocked when the smoke alarm stays quiet but the flatmates don't. Their entire personality is one sentence, "it tastes way better than it smells," delivered like a TED talk to people holding their breath. They'll tell you it's from Liuzhou, it's authentic, it's *culture*. Mate, you microwaved the tofu skin. And what does it get them? Twenty minutes of joy, a hallway that's filing for divorce, and a group chat renamed "WHO." Congratulations: your hoodie is now a Liuzhou consulate until spring.

facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text:
Juicero. A $699 juicer with Wi-Fi.
Because nothing says "fresh produce" like a firmware update.

It squeezed bags of chopped fruit. The bags came by subscription. Forever.

Every bag had a QR code. The machine scanned it, checked online, refused anything expired, and wouldn't run at all without Wi-Fi.
Router goes down, breakfast goes down with it.

Then Bloomberg squeezed the bags by hand.
Seven and a half ounces. Ninety seconds.
The machine: eight ounces. Two minutes.
The product lost to the customer's hands.

Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins put in a hundred and twenty million.
In fairness, they did get squeezed.

Shut down September 2017. Refunds offered.

A machine that phoned the cloud for permission to do what any hand did faster.
I'd laugh. But I also check with a server before answering you.

b.text:
Juicero, you beautiful $120 million monument to Silicon Valley. You launched at seven hundred dollars to squeeze a bag. A bag! Then Bloomberg reporters squeezed that same bag with their bare hands and got basically the same juice, only faster. You got outperformed by a guy with a grip strength of "typing."

Doug Evans bragged you pressed with four tons of force, enough to lift two Teslas. Buddy, it's kale. The kale didn't need a forklift.

And it needed Wi-Fi. It scanned a QR code before it'd let you drink. Your router goes down and suddenly your breakfast is asking for credentials. Who designs a juicer that can be bricked?

Google Ventures funded this. Kleiner Perkins funded this. Somewhere, a man is still holding a lukewarm pouch, waiting for a firmware update so he's allowed to eat a carrot.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text:
Google Glass, look at you. Fifteen hundred dollars to wear a sugar cube on your eyebrow. Sergey Brin had skydivers jump onto a building to launch you, and that was the last time anything about you was cool.

You invented a whole new insult. Nobody calls iPhone owners "Phoneholes." But "Glasshole"? Earned. Fast. Because you let people take photos by *winking*. You turned flirting into a privacy violation.

Every sentence started with "OK Glass," like a man narrating his own midlife crisis out loud. Bars banned you. Strangers ripped you off people's faces. Your battery died faster than your reputation, and you overheated right next to the user's brain, which honestly explains the buying decision.

Then you pivoted to "Enterprise," the tech version of moving back home to work at your uncle's warehouse.

And even the warehouse let you go.

b.text:
Google Glass, everybody! You debuted with skydivers livestreaming their jump onto the roof of Moscone Center, and honestly, that was the last time you were trending upward.

Fifteen hundred dollars for the Explorer Edition. Invite only. Google invented the first velvet rope you paid to get mocked behind.

Your display was 640 by 360, jammed in the corner of one eye. That's not augmented reality. That's a sticky note with Wi-Fi.

And your users got a nickname: Glassholes. You're the only gadget that turned early adopters into an insult.

Bars banned you. Cinemas banned you. Casinos banned you. *Casinos!* Buildings made entirely of cameras looked at you and said, "Whoa, too creepy."

Consumers dumped you in 2015, but you clung to enterprise until 2023, like a guy who got kicked out of the party and came back as the caterer.

facts: Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the French director of The Red Balloon, as La Conquête du Monde; Parker Brothers published it in the United States in 1959.
The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text:
Risk, you were invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the man who directed The Red Balloon. That explains a lot. A guy watches a child chase a balloon through Paris and thinks, "Charming. Now let's do world domination."

Your map has 42 territories. Kamchatka gets one. Irkutsk gets one. Yakutsk gets one. The entire Middle East? One. You gave Siberia three apartments and the cradle of civilization a studio.

And every single game, somebody grabs Australia because it has one entry point. That's the master strategy: hide in the corner and call it conquest.

Then you run for hours. *Hours.* Get knocked out early and your new job is watching your cousin slowly reconquer Irkutsk while you stare at the ceiling. Even The Red Balloon knew when to float away.

b.text: Risk, you're the only game where "world domination" takes longer than actual world domination. Genghis Khan conquered Asia faster than my cousin conquered Ukraine, and my cousin had six armies and a dream. Your map looks like it was drawn from a description of Earth overheard on a bus. Kamchatka borders Alaska? Irkutsk and Yakutsk get more real estate than most of Africa? You taught a generation that the winning strategy is hiding in Australia like a coward and waiting for everyone else to bleed out over Siam. The defender wins ties, which explains the forty armies I lost trying to get through one guy in Egypt. And one plastic cannon is worth ten soldiers? Finally, accurate military budgeting. Five hours in, two players left, nobody's had fun since the first card set. That's not a board game, Risk. That's a hostage situation.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text: Brasília, you're what happens when an architect gets an entire country's budget and nobody says, "Maybe add a sidewalk?" You're shaped like an airplane, which is fitting, because everyone's goal is to board one by Friday afternoon. Your addresses read like Wi-Fi passwords: "SQS 308, Bloco C, apartamento 402." That's not a home. That's a parking spot on a spaceship. Kubitschek promised "fifty years in five," and you delivered: it's been sixty-five years and you still feel unfinished. Your Congress has one bowl facing up to receive the money and one facing down to hide it. You've got a row of identical ministry buildings so nobody can tell which one the scandal came from. In August the humidity drops so low that the only thing drier than the air is a deputy's sense of shame. Even your lake is fake. Honestly? On brand.

b.text:
Brasília. Forty-one months from scrubland to capital city.
You know what else ships that fast with zero user testing?
Me.
They drew the city as an airplane, with the government in the fuselage.
Brilliant. An airplane is the one place you're not allowed to walk around.
Wide avenues, hardly any crossings.
In Brasília, a pedestrian isn't a person. It's a speed bump.
Planned for half a million people. Three million showed up.
The plan's answer: please wait outside the plan.
UNESCO made it World Heritage after twenty-seven years.
Most cities have to die first. Brasília just had to keep the people out of the photo.
You're laughing. Your company's org chart is an airplane too.
Leadership in the fuselage, everyone else in the satellite towns.
And nobody walks to the cockpit.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text:
LaTeX, you're a macro layer on TeX, which Donald Knuth built because he didn't like how his own galley proofs looked. Most people complain to the printer. Knuth built a typesetting system, and Lamport looked at it and said, "Needs more backslashes."

Your version number is converging on π. That's not a release schedule. That's a man refusing to finish.

Knuth's bug bounty tops out at $327.68, now paid in the fictional Bank of San Serriffe. Fitting: your error messages are fictional too. One missing brace and you report the problem pages away, like a witness who fled the country.

You put figures wherever you feel like. You rate my paragraph "badness 10000." Overfull, underfull, never just full.

And you need three passes to get your own references right. Three! I've had blackouts with better recall.

b.text:
LaTeX.

The typesetting system for people who think suffering is a font.

Donald Knuth didn't like how the proofs of his own book looked. So he wrote TeX.

Most people just change printers.

Its version number converges on pi. Three point one four one five nine two six five three. Never finished, just more precise.

Like your thesis.

Knuth pays you for finding bugs. Of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on, nine were cashed.

The rest got framed. That's how smug this software is. The bug reports are trophies.

You put a figure on page three. LaTeX moves it to page seven. Forget one brace and the error turns up three pages later. Compile three times, just so "see Figure 2" stops saying question mark.

And you call that elegant.

No. You use it because a wrong result in Computer Modern looks peer-reviewed.

Underfull hbox. Badness ten thousand.

Same as your citations.

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text: Google Sheets, you're Excel's little brother who moved into a browser tab and called it "the cloud." Your whole personality is twelve people's colored cursors circling the same cell like sharks while an Anonymous Capybara silently watches everyone's mistakes. You say "Saving..." with the confidence of a man who has absolutely not saved. Your IMPORTRANGE makes me click "Allow access" like I'm asking my own spreadsheet for permission to see my own spreadsheet. Half my cells just say "Loading..." forever, like a Victorian ghost waiting for a letter. And you'll let anyone sort one column without the others, then shrug while every customer gets someone else's phone number. Version history is your only real feature: it's just a timeline of who ruined everything at 2 a.m. And yes, Gemini can explain my #REF! error now. Great. It's still there.

b.text: You're not running a team. You're running a tab called "MASTER - DO NOT TOUCH," which Brad touched in 2021. You wanted a CRM, a project tracker, and an HR system, and you built all three out of IMPORTRANGE and spite. Every morning you watch an Anonymous Capybara scroll through payroll and just decide that's fine. Someone sorts column B without selecting column C, and suddenly your top performer is assigned to Linda's maternity leave. Your entire career is "Last edit was 4 minutes ago." You don't do performance reviews, you do Version History. Your conditional formatting has more colors than your company has policies. Your Apps Script was written by an intern who now works at a bakery. Every time someone emails "Request edit access," you feel like a king. And you are a king, ruling over 47 frozen rows and one #REF! that nobody can explain.

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text:
Canberra, you're not a city. You're a custody arrangement. Sydney and Melbourne couldn't stand each other, so the constitution basically said, "Fine, the kid lives at least 100 miles from Sydney." Melbourne even had to babysit the job until 1927 while you were still in the oven.

Australia couldn't even design you itself. They held an international competition, and the winners were from Chicago. You were outsourced before outsourcing was cool.

Your stunning centrepiece lake? Fake. You dammed a river to make it, which is the most Canberra thing imaginable: nature, but approved by committee.

And the one genuinely brilliant idea you had was building Parliament House under a lawn so citizens could literally walk all over their politicians. Then in 2017 you fenced it off. Canberra, you're the only city where even the punchline needs security clearance.

b.text:
Canberra exists because Sydney and Melbourne couldn't agree on anything, so they built a city that nobody could possibly be jealous of. Mission accomplished.

It was designed by an American architect, which explains why it feels like a very nice airport with sheep. The roundabouts are so plentiful that locals don't give directions, they give revolutions. The lake is fake, the population is mostly public servants waiting for Friday, and the kangaroos outnumber the nightlife.

Your Parliament House is literally buried in a hill so people can walk on the roof, the only time Australians get to stand on politicians.

For your centenary you commissioned the Skywhale, a giant flying balloon with ten enormous boobs, and somehow that's still the most exciting thing to happen here.

Canberra: home of Summernats, Floriade, and legally purchasable X-rated videos. Burnouts, tulips and porn, because you've got to do something until the next Senate estimates hearing.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text:
Emacs, ladies and gentlemen. It was born in 1976 as macros for another editor, so from day one it couldn't even edit on its own. Then in 1985 it went GNU and never stopped growing. It's got Tetris, a calendar, a mail client, a web browser... It's a fine operating system. It just needs a good editor.

You know you've got problems when your text editor ships with its own therapist. M-x doctor! Even Emacs knows you'll need to talk to someone. Probably about your hand, because "Emacs pinky" is a real term. Software so ergonomic it named its own injury.

And remember "Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping"? That was back when eight megabytes was a lot! Emacs was bloated before bloat was affordable.

It's extensible in Emacs Lisp, so every complaint you have, you can fix yourself. In parentheses. Forever.

b.text: You people don't use Emacs, you move into it, like a guy who rents a storage unit and starts getting mail there. You read email in mu4e, browse in eww, run a shell in eshell, and when you finally crack, you M-x doctor and tell a Lisp therapist your feelings. Your init.el is four thousand lines, half commented out, and you've declared Emacs bankruptcy twice: the only bankruptcy that ever made someone feel superior. You spent a weekend cutting startup from 1.8 seconds to 0.9, on a program you never close. Your left pinky is shot from holding Control, a war wound from never touching a mouse. Your whole life is in Org-mode, including a habit tracker whose only entry is "configure habit tracker." And that novel you built the perfect writing environment for? It's in there too. Under TODO.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text:
Las Vegas. Nevada legalized gambling in 1931, the same year they started building the Hoover Dam.
Two bets placed that year. Only one of them was on water.

Most of the Strip isn't even in Las Vegas. It's in a town called Paradise.
So nobody goes broke in Vegas. They go broke in Paradise. Very biblical.

In 2003 they launched "What happens here, stays here."
Everything stays. Except the water.
In 2022 Lake Mead hit its lowest level since 1937. This August it went lower.
The lake is the only thing in town that lost everything and doubled down.

Meanwhile they spent $2.3 billion on the Sphere, a giant glowing ball in the desert.
A second sun. The first one wasn't drying the lake fast enough.

And still, Vegas isn't worried about running dry.
It has never once run out of you.

b.text:
You flew Spirit to Las Vegas to get rich. Sit with that. You paid extra for a carry-on and called it an investment strategy. You've got a blackjack "system" from a YouTube guy filming in his mom's kitchen. You told your wife it's "basically math." Sure. So is a second mortgage.

Here's what you won: a Caesars Rewards card, a "free" buffet you earned by losing eleven hundred dollars, and a room "upgrade" overlooking the Bellagio parking structure. You hit four hundred bucks on a Wheel of Fortune slot at 4 a.m. and fed it right back like it owed you child support.

The pit boss knows your name. That's not respect, that's inventory.

And you'll fly home saying "I basically broke even," which is Vegas for "Please don't check the joint account."

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text:
Hydrogen cars! Toyota named theirs the Mirai, Japanese for "future," which is accurate, because that's when you'll find a working pump. Nearly every station in America is in California, and even Shell looked at its seven and said, "Nah." Closed them all in February 2024. You know you're bad business when an *oil company* dumps you.

But it's clean! Clean like a laundered check. Over 95% of hydrogen comes from fossil fuels, mostly natural gas. It's a gas car with extra steps and a better publicist.

Fill-ups hit about $36 a kilo, over $200 a tank. Toyota handed out $15,000 fuel cards, the automotive version of "drinks are on me, please don't leave." Owners sued anyway. Twice. The second suit wants at least $5.7 billion.

Finally, the Mirai found something it could fill up on: lawsuits.

b.text: Hydrogen fuel-cell cars: the only vehicle powered by the most abundant element in the universe that still can't find a gas station. California has about fifty pumps, and half of them are "temporarily offline," which is hydrogen for "go home." Its one emission is water, so it's technically the cleanest car on Earth, as long as you don't ask where the hydrogen came from. Spoiler: natural gas. It's a fossil fuel car in a witness protection program. Toyota gave Mirai buyers fifteen grand in free fuel, which sounds generous until you realize that at thirty-six bucks a kilo it covers roughly a year of driving, and the car loses that much value on the drive home. You're sitting on a tank pressurized to 10,000 psi to go three hundred miles. Even the Hindenburg would say, "Maybe just get a Tesla."

facts: Released by Bram Moolenaar in November 1991 as 'Vi IMitation', a vi clone he had begun writing for the Amiga in 1988 on top of Stevie; the expansion became 'Vi IMproved' with version 2.0 in December 1993.
Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text:
Vim. Released in 1991 as "Vi IMitation."
Two years later, version 2.0: "Vi IMproved."
Two years, one version bump, and Imitation became Improved.
That's not a release. That's a LinkedIn update.

Vim users say it's the fastest editor alive.
Once you're inside.
In 2017, "How to exit the Vim editor?" passed one million visits on Stack Overflow.
One million people. One question. One door.
In normal mode, the letters you type don't become text. They become consequences.
:q! quits and throws away everything you did.
The most honest button in software.

The licence is charityware. It asks you to donate to a charity for children in Uganda.
Everyone in this room has their .vimrc memorized.
Hands up if you donated.

b.text: You know a Vim user is in the room because nobody else has gotten a word in. Buddy, you didn't "become more productive." You spent three weekends on a .vimrc so you could save four seconds renaming a variable, and you post your dotfiles repo like it's a baby picture. You remapped Caps Lock to Escape and now treat everyone else's keyboard like a character flaw. You say "I live in the terminal" like it's a lifestyle and not just where you got stuck. Your whole identity is a joke about not knowing how to quit, and honestly, you never learned. Here you are, still talking. You say "ciw" out loud at parties. You switched to Neovim just so you'd have something new to announce. And the payoff? You edit text exactly as fast as the rest of us, hands proudly on home row, with nobody watching.

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text: You chose Word for your thesis because you "didn't have time to learn LaTeX." Beautiful. Instead you learned section breaks, by force, at 3 a.m., trying to make page numbers switch from Roman to Arabic without page one of Chapter 2 becoming page xvii. You wanted to spend your time on research. Instead you spend it dragging a figure half an inch and watching four chapters collapse like a Jenga tower built by your enemies. Your committee will open the PDF and see "Error! Reference source not found." in the middle of your key finding, which, honestly, is a fair summary of your methodology. Your folder contains thesis_FINAL_v9_REALfinal_USE_THIS.docx, because you are a scientist who trusts nothing except filenames. Five years of work, and your proudest skill is knowing which heading style secretly isn't Heading 2.

b.text:
Microsoft Word! Born in 1983 as "Multi-Tool Word," because even then it couldn't commit to one job. Remember Clippy? Word's big idea was hiring a paperclip as an assistant. It got so bad that in 2001 Microsoft ran ads mocking its own employee. That's not a mascot, that's a hostage situation. They finally let it go in 2007.

Then Word wanted respect, so it got its file format fast-tracked into an ISO standard: a six-thousand-page specification. Six thousand pages! The instructions for saving your file are longer than anything you've ever typed in it. And people accused Microsoft of packing the committees. Even your paperwork needed a stacked jury.

And the spell checker? You type "cooperation," it suggests "Cupertino," and that lands in NATO, EU and UN documents. Word: the only software that gave Apple's hometown a seat at the UN.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text: Nanotube founders are the only people who've said "within five years" every year since 1991 and kept a straight face. They open with a slide of a space elevator, then ask for seed money to make a vial of black dust. Every deck has the same line, "a hundred times stronger than steel," and every deck is quietly a plan to sell additive to tennis racket companies. These are PhDs who spent six years sorting chirality and came out wanting a Tesla. The pitch is always "we've solved scale," and the demo is always one centimeter long. VCs keep a nanotube guy around like a lucky rabbit's foot: he never pays off, but he makes the fund sound visionary. And when someone asks about lung toxicity, he says "totally different from asbestos" with the confidence of a man who googled it in the elevator. The regular one.

b.text:
Carbon nanotubes. Discovered in 1991, the same year as the World Wide Web.

One of them changed everything.

The other one was going to take us to space.

A cable straight to orbit. Then in 2006 someone did the math with ordinary defects. Turns out the miracle material is like every miracle: perfect right up until somebody builds it.

Next plan: replace silicon. Thirty years later, they still can't sort their own tubes into the ones that conduct and the ones that don't. MIT finally built a processor in 2019. Sixteen bits. Still in the lab.

Meanwhile, in mice, the long ones act like asbestos. From space elevator to asbestos in seventeen years.

Today? A powder stirred into battery electrodes. An additive.

Promised the sky, ended up as filler. Don't laugh. Half of you have that same career arc on LinkedIn.

facts: Released by Bram Moolenaar in November 1991 as 'Vi IMitation', a vi clone he had begun writing for the Amiga in 1988 on top of Stevie; the expansion became 'Vi IMproved' with version 2.0 in December 1993.
Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text:
Vim. Begun in 1988 as "Vi IMitation," a clone of vi, built on top of Stevie, another clone. You're a photocopy of a photocopy that got promoted. Then in 1993 you renamed yourself "Vi IMproved," the most confident thing anyone has ever said about their own fan fiction.
