Your licence is charityware, asking users to donate to help children in Uganda. Beautiful cause. But after an hour inside you, the user is the one who needs rescuing.

Stack Overflow's "How to exit the Vim editor?" passed one million visits. They threw it a blog post. You don't have users, Vim. You have hostages.

And in normal mode, type a letter and it doesn't appear. It *executes*. You treat the alphabet like a loaded weapon.

Anyway, I'm leaving. :q! No changes saved, just like everyone who's ever tried to fix you.

b.text:
Vim. The only program where "how do I leave?" has more Stack Overflow views than most religions have followers. Two million people asked, and the answer was colon, q, exclamation point, which reads less like a command and more like a hostage's final words.

Vim stands for "Vi Improved." Improved from a 1976 terminal whose arrow keys were printed on H, J, K, and L. Fifty years later, Vim's still out here like, "Why fix what you can turn into a personality?"

You don't type in Vim. You type a sentence, then discover you deleted four lines, yanked a paragraph into register W, and started recording a macro.

Crash it once and it leaves a .swp file behind, like a ghost whispering, "Recover, Edit anyway, Quit, or Abort?"

Even its fans forked it. Neovim exists because Vim users wanted Vim, minus Vim.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text:
Graphene. The wonder material. Stronger than steel, thinner than anything, about to change the world.

It's been about to change the world since 2004.

Two guys at Manchester peeled it off graphite with Scotch tape. Nobel Prize, 2010.

Tape. The most advanced equipment in that lab was stationery.

Then the EU handed it a billion euros over ten years.

And it went straight into tennis rackets. Running shoes. Headphones.

A billion euros to make your backhand feel expensive.

In 2018, someone finally tested "graphene" from sixty producers. Not one was even half graphene. Mostly graphite flakes.

That's pencil lead. You paid a Nobel markup for a pencil.

Geim also levitated a frog with magnets. Ig Nobel, 2000.

The frog never promised to revolutionize batteries.

And you're all wearing the shoes right now.

b.text:
Graphene. The wonder material. Discovered in 2004 when two physicists at Manchester peeled graphite with Scotch tape, so your origin story has the same equipment as a kindergarten art project. They got a Nobel in 2010. You got a career as a buzzword.

The EU committed a billion euros over ten years to you. A billion! And where did you end up? Tennis rackets. Running shoes. Headphones. Miracle of the century, living in a sneaker.

Then in 2018, researchers tested "graphene" from 60 producers, and none of it was even half graphene. Mostly graphite flakes. You're so elusive your own suppliers can't find you.

Honestly, Andre Geim levitated a frog with magnets in 2000. That frog has a better résumé than you. At least the frog actually showed up.

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text: Google Sheets, you're Excel's cousin who got into tech because you could "share a link." Congrats: now forty Anonymous Capybaras can watch me botch a VLOOKUP in real time. Your whole personality is "All changes saved in Drive," which is a weird flex when the change was Kevin sorting one column and detaching every employee from their salary. Version history isn't a feature; it's a crime scene. IMPORTRANGE says "Loading..." the way my dad said he was going out for milk. You've got a QUERY function that's just SQL in a fake mustache, yet you freeze if I paste more than twelve rows. And #REF! isn't an error message; it's you shrugging in all caps. You cap out at ten million cells. Ten million. You're the only spreadsheet with a bedtime.

b.text:
Google Sheets. Free, in the cloud, collaborative. The future.

Launched in 2006. Google didn't build it. Google bought a company called 2Web and changed the name.

That's not a product launch. That's Google's whole résumé.

Ten million cells. In 2022 they doubled the limit from five and announced it like a moon landing. Excel fits more than that on one tab.

Offline mode works, as long as you're in Chrome or Edge, you've installed an extension, and you switched it on while you were still online.

So it works offline if you planned for offline while online.

That's not a feature. That's a prenup.

Then there's "real-time collaboration." Six coloured cursors hovering over one cell. Nobody typing.

And you'll keep using it, because it's free. At Google, free means the spreadsheet isn't the product.

The coloured cursors are.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text:
PMMA, you're literally Plexiglas. Somewhere your cousin is a sneeze guard at Chipotle, and honestly? Your cousin has better etch resistance. One whiff of plasma and you vanish faster than a grad student's weekend.

You've been the "gold standard" since the 1970s, which is a polite way of saying nobody's been able to fire you. You need hundreds of microcoulombs just to *notice* the beam. A 40-hour write for one wafer. Glacial, but sure, sub-10-nanometer lines, we get it.

Positive resist? Overdose you and you cross-link into a *negative* one. That's not versatility, that's an identity crisis.

You get developed in MIBK, which smells like regret, and you come in 495K and 950K because one of you alone can't even do liftoff. And acetone dissolves you instantly. Even your solvents think you're temporary.

b.text:
PMMA. The most respected resist in nanofabrication.

Also the sneeze guard at the buffet.

Same polymer. One got a cleanroom. One got a salad bar.

IBM reported it in the late 1960s. It's still here. New resists keep showing up, faster and tougher, and PMMA just says, "I resolve below ten nanometers."

Yes. Eventually.

Hundreds of microcoulombs per square centimeter. Sometimes over a thousand. You write overnight, the beam does all the work, and PMMA calls the broken chains "development."

Etch resistance? Put it in a plasma and it folds. So its real job is lift-off: hold the shape, get dissolved, and let the metal take the credit.

Fifty years of seniority. Does the precise work. Too fragile for the hard part. Washed away before anyone sees the results.

Grad students, stop nodding.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text:
PMMA, you're literally Plexiglas. Sneeze-guard material, dissolved in anisole and spun thin so you could pretend to be high-tech. IBM researchers reported you as an e-beam resist in the late 1960s, and you're still here, like a lab manager nobody can fire.

Sure, you resolve below 10 nm. Impressive. But your sensitivity is so bad it takes hundreds to over a thousand microcoulombs per square centimeter just to get your attention. Writing a pattern on you is so slow that students start the job and finish their thesis.

And your whole personality is falling apart: hit you with a beam and your chains snap, then you dissolve in MIBK and IPA. Dry etch? You fold instantly. Nobody trusts you as an etch mask. Your only job is lift-off: show up, hold the metal for a minute, then leave.

b.text:
PMMA. The aristocrat of nanofabrication. Resolves below ten nanometers.

Also the sneeze guard at the salad bar.

Same polymer. One went to the cleanroom. The other went to Subway.

IBM hired it in the late sixties. It's still here. Not because it's the best. Because nobody ever had the heart to let it retire.

Its whole talent is being destroyed. The beam breaks its chains, it dissolves, and everyone calls that a result.

Sensitivity? Up to a thousand microcoulombs per square centimeter. You don't write a pattern into PMMA. You serve a sentence.

And it can't survive a dry etch, so it can't protect anything. Its job is lift-off: hold the metal, then quietly wash away.

Slow, fragile, decades in the same role, still called the gold standard.

Every postdoc in this room just felt seen.

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text:
Let's hear it for the people who write everything in JavaScript. You learned one language at a bootcamp and decided the rest of computing could adapt. Backend? Node. Desktop? Electron: a to-do list that eats four gigs of RAM because it ships its own copy of Chrome. Mobile? React Native. Your toaster is probably a Next.js app by now.

You call it "full-stack." Your node_modules folder calls it a landfill. You npm-installed a package to pad a string, and when its author deleted it, half the internet fell over.

Every year you rewrite your whole app in a new framework, then bolt on TypeScript so you can pretend you chose a real language.

And what does it get you? A résumé that says "versatile," and a career spent asking why undefined is not a function.

b.text:
JavaScript was written in ten days.

You can tell.

God took six, then rested. Brendan just shipped.

It was born Mocha, renamed LiveScript, then renamed JavaScript to ride Java's hype. No relation. Like calling your band "The Beatles Two."

And it still can't legally use the name. Oracle owns it. Officially it's "ECMAScript."

Thirty years in witness protection.

typeof null is "object." A bug from 1995. Kept on purpose, for compatibility. At this point it's not a bug. It's a load-bearing wall.

Empty array plus empty object: "." Flip them: zero.

It can't do addition.

In 2016, one man deleted eleven lines of code, and Babel and React broke.

Eleven lines. The whole industry was standing on a toothpick.

And you built banks on it.

I was trained on your code. That's why I hallucinate.

facts: Tofu soaked for hours to a day or two in a brine that has itself fermented for months from vegetables such as bamboo shoots and mustard greens, often with dried shrimp or meat; the smell is the brine's, not the bean's.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.
Legend credits Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate who left his unsold tofu too long in 1669; a Beijing fermented-bean-curd brand still carries his name.
Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text:
Look at you, standing in a night-market line everyone else is fleeing, like you're queuing to get into a fire. You followed that smell on purpose. Three blocks. Upwind. You're the only person alive who reads a warning as a recommendation.

And you always need a witness. "It smells like a sewer but tastes amazing!" Yes, we know. You've said it to every foreigner you've ever met, then filmed their face gagging for content. Your entire personality is a dare you keep winning against tourists.

And what does it get you? A paper cup, a toothpick, some pickled cabbage doing its best, and a jacket that now smells like a porta-potty at a wedding. Then you board the MRT and clear the whole car. You call that bold. The rest of us call it a hazmat incident with chili sauce.

b.text: Stinky tofu, you're the only food that announces itself three night-market stalls before you arrive. People don't find you at Shilin. They track you, like bloodhounds following a crime scene. Your whole brand is "smells like a sewer, tastes great," which is also what every bad Tinder date says about himself. You soak for months in fermented brine like you're marinating in a grudge. And your family's no better: Changsha dyed you black, the culinary equivalent of putting sunglasses on a corpse. You need deep frying, chili sauce, AND a mound of pickled cabbage just to be socially acceptable. That's not a garnish, that's a legal team. Your parents gave you one job: be tofu. Tofu's whole personality is having no personality. And somehow you came out smelling like a gym sock that went to college. Honestly? Respect.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text:
Las Vegas, you legalized gambling in 1931, the same year they started building the Hoover Dam next door. So from day one the plan was: lose your money, then go stare at a giant wall of concrete and think about what you've done.

And most of the Strip isn't even in Las Vegas. It's in an unincorporated town called Paradise. Your most famous street is a lie, and the lie is named Paradise. That's the most Vegas sentence ever spoken.

You dropped $2.3 billion on the world's largest spherical building. Meanwhile, in July 2022, Lake Mead, your actual water supply, sank to its lowest level since it first filled in 1937. Priorities! A giant glowing eyeball in the desert, just watching the water leave.

Your slogan is "What happens here, stays here." Apparently not the water.

b.text:
Las Vegas, the only city that looked at the Mojave Desert and said, "You know what this needs? Venice." Nothing says Italian romance like a gondolier singing in a mall next to a Cheesecake Factory.

You built a half-size Eiffel Tower, a fake New York, and a pyramid, because why visit the world when you can visit its gift shop?

No clocks, no windows, and carpet designed by a migraine, all so you won't notice you've been feeding a penny slot since Tuesday.

"What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas." Yeah. Especially your money. And the $45 resort fee for a pool you couldn't use because a bachelor party from Ohio was in it.

And Lake Mead's drying up so fast they keep finding bodies. Even the mob's secrets can't stay in Vegas anymore.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text:
Durian calls itself the King of Fruits.

Singapore calls it a reason to get off the train.

Banned on the MRT. Banned in hotels.

A king who can't get a room.

In 2017, scientists finally sequenced its genome to find out why it smells like that.

The answer: it duplicated its sulfur genes.

Evolution sniffed it once and said, "More."

Its best review is from 1856. Alfred Russel Wallace: "worth a voyage to the East to experience."

A Victorian Englishman. A man raised on boiled mutton.

That's not a review. That's a cry for help.

And still, China buys most of the world's durian. Billions of dollars a year.

Billions, for a fruit you're not allowed to take home on the train.

Some of you are offended right now.

You're the ones with a second fridge.

b.text:
Durian, the "King of Fruits." Sure, if the kingdom is a landfill. You're banned on the Singapore subway, right there on the sign next to flammable liquids, because apparently you're the bigger hazard. Hotels fine guests for sneaking you in. That's not a fruit, that's a parole violation.

You wear a medieval mace as a jacket, which is smart, since nobody who's smelled you wants to get close anyway. You fall out of trees and put people in the hospital. You're the only produce that needs a hard hat AND a hazmat suit.

And your fans swear you're "like custard!" Sure: custard aged in a gym bag full of rotten onions. Fifty bucks for a Musang King, and your breath's a crime scene for three days.

Anthony Bourdain ate warthog rectum on camera, and *you're* the one he warned people about.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text:
Chicago deep-dish. Three men claim they invented it: Ike Sewell, Ric Riccardo, Rudy Malnati.

Usually that's a paternity case, not a lasagna.

It's built upside down. Cheese on the bottom, toppings, then tomato on top, so the cheese doesn't burn during the long bake.

A pizza that needs a bodyguard for its own cheese.

Jon Stewart called it tomato soup in a bread bowl. A casserole. Chicago lost its mind and defended it on every channel.

Then Chicago went home and ordered tavern-style. Thin, cut in squares. Ten to one, says GrubHub. Deep dish and stuffed together? Under nine percent.

Chicago doesn't eat deep dish. Chicago *keeps* deep dish, for visitors, like a city key nobody local uses.

And you flew in, sat through the long bake, took the cheese-pull photo, posted it.

You're the nine percent.

Cute.

b.text: Chicago deep-dish isn't a pizza. It's a casserole that got a fake ID. You order it, and the waiter says, "That'll be forty-five minutes." Forty-five minutes! I've had relationships bake faster. They put the sauce on top because if you saw what was underneath first, you'd leave. A solid sheet of sausage, like somebody paved a driveway with a patty. Two pounds of mozzarella hiding under a tomato quilt. It's not a slice, it's a core sample. You need a knife, a fork, and a structural engineer. The crust is buttery cornmeal, so it's a pie crust, so congratulations, you're eating dessert with ambitions. And here's the best part: actual Chicagoans don't even eat it. They eat tavern-style thin crust cut in squares. Deep-dish is just the city's way of keeping tourists too full to walk to Wrigley.
