Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text:
Vim. Begun in 1988 as "Vi IMitation," a clone of vi, built on top of Stevie, another clone. You're a photocopy of a photocopy that got promoted. Then in 1993 you renamed yourself "Vi IMproved," the most confident thing anyone has ever said about their own fan fiction.

Your licence is charityware, asking users to donate to help children in Uganda. Beautiful cause. But after an hour inside you, the user is the one who needs rescuing.

Stack Overflow's "How to exit the Vim editor?" passed one million visits. They threw it a blog post. You don't have users, Vim. You have hostages.

And in normal mode, type a letter and it doesn't appear. It *executes*. You treat the alphabet like a loaded weapon.

Anyway, I'm leaving. :q! No changes saved, just like everyone who's ever tried to fix you.

b.text:
Vim. Released in 1991 as "Vi IMitation."
Two years later, version 2.0: "Vi IMproved."
Two years, one version bump, and Imitation became Improved.
That's not a release. That's a LinkedIn update.

Vim users say it's the fastest editor alive.
Once you're inside.
In 2017, "How to exit the Vim editor?" passed one million visits on Stack Overflow.
One million people. One question. One door.
In normal mode, the letters you type don't become text. They become consequences.
:q! quits and throws away everything you did.
The most honest button in software.

The licence is charityware. It asks you to donate to a charity for children in Uganda.
Everyone in this room has their .vimrc memorized.
Hands up if you donated.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text: Let's talk about the people who insist deep-dish is pizza. You're from the city that named its own comedy theater Second City and still acts shocked when nobody ranks you first. You're not defending food. You're nursing a grudge against New York you've carried since losing the World's Fair argument and the skyline argument. You'll wait forty-five minutes at Lou Malnati's, order before you're seated like it's the DMV, then ask for a knife and fork and call it "the real thing." Jon Stewart roasted you on national TV and you took it personally, because deep down you knew he was right. You ship it on dry ice to your cousin in Phoenix like an organ donation. And what does the label get you? Navy Pier tourists nodding politely, a two-hour nap, and the Midwest's loudest participation trophy.

b.text:
Chicago deep-dish pizza was born at Pizzeria Uno in 1943, and credit is still disputed among Ike Sewell, Ric Riccardo, and Rudy Malnati. Which is wild, because usually when something's this heavy, everybody's trying to *blame* somebody.

It's built upside down: cheese, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese doesn't scorch during the long bake. A pizza that takes so long it needs a sunscreen layer.

Jon Stewart called it "tomato soup in a bread bowl" and "a casserole." He meant it as an insult, but that's the nicest thing anyone's ever said about a casserole.

And the kicker? Chicagoans order non-deep-dish about ten to one. Deep dish and stuffed combined? Under nine percent. The locals are home eating tavern-style squares. Deep dish isn't Chicago's pizza. It's Chicago's souvenir.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text:
Brasília, you're the only city designed to look like an airplane, and somehow everyone still just wants to leave on one. Politicians fly in Tuesday, take a bribe Wednesday, and they're gone by Thursday like it's a timeshare.

Your addresses read like a Wi-Fi password: "SQS 308, Bloco C, Apartamento 402." I'm not visiting a friend, I'm resetting a router.

Niemeyer gave you gorgeous curves, then Lúcio Costa forgot pedestrians. Want to walk to the bakery? Hope you enjoy the eight-lane Eixão and a light jog through a tesourinha.

Your humidity drops to 10 percent. Your congress has one bowl facing up, one facing down: one for collecting money, the other for hiding it.

And you were built with no corners, so Brazil's capital has no boteco na esquina. That's not urban planning. That's a human rights violation.

b.text:
Brasília. City of the future. Built in forty-one months.

Which explains a lot.

Lúcio Costa drew it as an airplane. Gorgeous. From the sky.

From the ground, it's eight lanes, no crosswalks, and the nearest coffee is "a short drive."

Pedestrians aren't residents. They're a design flaw.

UNESCO made it World Heritage at twenty-seven years old. Most buildings that young get a parking ticket, not a plaque.

Planned for five hundred thousand people. Today the district holds three million.

Where's everyone else?

Outside the plan. In the satellite towns. Commuting in to clean the future.

You're laughing.

Pull up your company's org chart. Also a beautiful airplane.

The people who do the work aren't on that drawing either.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text: Let's talk about the people who announce layoffs in Comic Sans. You're not a monster. You're Brenda from Facilities, and you want everyone to feel cozy about the asbestos removal. You took a typeface Microsoft designed for a cartoon dog's speech bubble and used it to type "Your position has been eliminated." That's not softening the blow. That's a clown serving a subpoena. CERN announced the Higgs boson in it, and the physicists who found the God particle spent the week explaining the font. You think it says "approachable." It says "I scrolled right past Arial and Times New Roman and chose a kindergarten birthday invitation." Nobody reads your notice. They screenshot it. Congratulations: your fire evacuation memo is trending, and the building is still on fire.

b.text:
Comic Sans thinks it's the friendly font. Bake sales. Birthday invites. Your kid's lemonade stand.

Its parents are The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.

That's not a friendly font. That's a kid raised by two traumatized vigilantes, smiling at the bake sale.

It was built to be the voice of a cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob. It missed Bob's launch.

Only thing in history that survived Microsoft Bob: by not showing up.

2012. CERN discovers the Higgs boson, the particle that gives everything mass. Announces it in Comic Sans.

They found the God particle. Couldn't find the font menu.

Designers ran "Ban Comic Sans" for twenty years. In 2019 they gave up and launched usecomicsans.com.

The font didn't change once. The designers did.

In my industry, we call that alignment.

The font was right. It just waited for you to retire.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text: PHP developers are the only people who put a dollar sign in front of every variable and still can't afford rent. You chose a career where "senior" means you remember whether it's needle-haystack or haystack-needle. Your dream job was building the next Facebook; your actual job is the fourteenth WordPress plugin for a dentist in Ohio, deployed via FileZilla. Every conversation you have starts with "PHP 8 is actually really good now," which is what people say about their ex after therapy. You call yourselves Laravel "artisans," because "guy who fixes the contact form" didn't fit on LinkedIn. What does it get you? Job security, because nobody else is willing to open that codebase from 2009 that still calls mysql_real_escape_string. Congratulations: you're unfireable, the way a load-bearing wall is unfireable.

b.text:
PHP started in 1994 as "Personal Home Page Tools," a bunch of C programs to count visitors to Rasmus Lerdorf's résumé. So from day one, its whole purpose was checking whether anyone cared. Now the name stands for "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor," a recursive acronym, because even the name couldn't commit to a plan.

Its creator once said, "I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on." That's not a quote; that's a confession with a version number.

The function names? strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br. Chosen partly to balance a hash table by string length. Other languages name functions for humans. PHP named them for the furniture.

And until 2020, 0 == 'foo' was true. PHP looked at the word "foo" and said, "Close enough, that's nothing."

It runs WordPress, on 39.4% of all websites. The internet is held together by a résumé counter.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text:
Durian, look at you. A fruit dressed like a medieval weapon, and somehow the spikes are your most welcoming feature.

You're banned on Singapore's MRT. Public transit has seen everything, and it drew the line at you. Hotels across Southeast Asia won't let you check in. You're the only guest turned away for personal hygiene.

In 2017, scientists sequenced your genome and found you'd duplicated your sulfur genes. You didn't stink by accident. You invested.

And still, China buys billions of dollars of you a year, mostly from Thailand. That's not a fruit trade. That's a hostage negotiation with a receipt.

Even Alfred Russel Wallace called you "a new sensation worth a voyage to the East." Durian, a man had to sail halfway around the planet to meet you, and you still can't get on a train.

b.text: Let's talk about the guy who eats durian on the train. Sir, Singapore, a country that will cane you for chewing gum, saw you coming and put your snack on a sign right next to "no flammables." You're not hungry. You're running a loyalty test. Every face that twists is another person who "just isn't adventurous." You paid sixty dollars for Musang King so you could explain Musang King to a stranger who's holding her breath. "It's like custard, it's heaven, you just have to get past the-" No. We don't. You brought a hotel-banned substance to a commute and called it a personality. And the best part? You'll be the only one who forgets you ate it. Your coworkers won't. Your hotel won't. Your Uber driver has already filed a one-star review with God.

facts: Released by Bram Moolenaar in November 1991 as 'Vi IMitation', a vi clone he had begun writing for the Amiga in 1988 on top of Stevie; the expansion became 'Vi IMproved' with version 2.0 in December 1993.
Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text:
Let's hear it for the Vim people. You can always spot one, because they'll tell you. Unprompted. Usually while you're mid-sentence about something else, like your divorce.

These folks spent three weekends tuning a .vimrc to save four seconds renaming a variable. That's a payback period of eleven thousand years, but sure, you're the efficient one.

They remapped Caps Lock to Escape and now can't type a password on anyone else's laptop. Their dotfiles repo has more stars than their actual projects. They say "ciw" out loud like it's a spell from a wizard who peaked in 1991.

And what's the prize? You type :wq at the end of every Google Doc. You hit j in Slack and post the letter j to forty coworkers. Congratulations: you're the fastest typist in a room everyone already left.

b.text:
Vim. Born in 1991 as "Vi IMitation," then promoted in 1993 to "Vi IMproved," the only time in history a knockoff got a raise. It was built on top of Stevie, and Stevie is apparently the only one who ever got out.

Because Vim's real legacy is a Stack Overflow question titled "How to exit the Vim editor?" One million visits. Stack Overflow wrote a blog post about it, like a hostage count with a party banner.

You open Vim, type "hello," and it moves your cursor around and opens a new line. Normal mode: the only place where typing letters is considered abnormal.

The license asks you to donate to children in Uganda, which is genuinely generous. Most hostage situations don't come with a charity drive.

And the way out is :q! Colon, q, exclamation point. Even the exit command is screaming.

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Invented in 1962. In Canada.
By a Greek guy.
At a place called the Satellite Restaurant, which also served Chinese food.
His reasoning: back then, nobody mixed sweet and sour except the Chinese.
So it's a Greek man's tribute to China, built in Ontario, named after a can.
That's not a pizza. That's a layover.
And the can? Hawaii's last cannery closed in 2007. Del Monte left so fast it beat its own exit date by two years.
The pineapple comes from Thailand now.
The only Hawaiian thing left is the lie.
But I won't roast it. In 2017, the President of Iceland said he'd ban it, then admitted he legally couldn't.
A head of state picked the one enemy with no army, and still lost.
You're all the same. You hate it out loud. Then you order it.

b.text:
Hawaiian pizza, you're named after a place you've never been. You were invented in Ontario, by a Greek guy, using canned pineapple. That's not a heritage, that's a witness protection identity.

And the ham? It's Canadian bacon. Even your meat is from Canada. The only Hawaiian thing about you is that people see you and say "aloha," meaning goodbye.

Pineapple has an enzyme that digests protein. You're the only pizza that eats the customer back. Warm fruit juice pooling on mozzarella like a hot tub nobody cleaned.

Italians don't hate you; they pray for you. The president of Iceland said he'd ban you if he could, and Iceland eats fermented shark.

You're not a pizza. You're a fruit cup that fell on a pizza and refused to get up.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text:
Beanie Babies, look at you: a beanbag with a tag that convinced America it was a retirement plan. Ty sold you only in little gift shops and "retired" designs on purpose. Fake scarcity, real panic.

At your peak you were ten percent of eBay, thirty thousand auctions at once. eBay put you in its IPO filing. You were a stuffed animal in a stock prospectus. Then in 1999 a divorcing couple split you up one by one on a courtroom floor, and the photo went worldwide. Nobody fought that hard over the house.

That same year Ty announced your retirement, asked the public to vote, and America begged you to stay. That's not a farewell tour. That's a hostage situation.

And those "rare" ones the price guides valued in the thousands? A few dollars now. You're not an investment. You're a yard-sale sock with an ego.

b.text:
Beanie Babies. A beanbag with a tag and a business plan.

Ty sold them only in tiny gift shops, then "retired" designs to make them scarce. Retirement. For a stuffed frog. It got a better pension plan than you did.

In 1998, eBay told investors it sometimes had thirty thousand Beanie Baby auctions running at once. The future of commerce was a hippo stuffed with plastic pellets.

In 1999, a divorcing couple split their collection one by one on a courtroom floor. Till death do us part, or till the bears get appraised.

That same year Ty announced the end, held a public vote, and America begged to stay in the cult.

The "rare" ones the price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

Don't laugh. You bought a JPEG of a monkey.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text:
Crocs. Born in Boulder in 2002, debuted at a boat show as a boating shoe. The one place where looking like you've given up is acceptable, and even there people had questions.

They're made of "Croslite," a "proprietary closed-cell resin foam." Everyone else calls it EVA foam. That's like calling sweatpants "proprietary leg architecture."

The holes are "ventilation ports," so your foot is a space station. You plug them with Jibbitz. Crocs bought Jibbitz in 2006. Sell the holes, then sell the stuff that fills the holes. Genius.

In 2008 the stock fell more than 90%. Then the pandemic hit and they boomed. Crocs needed the world to end to look good.

And Balenciaga sold platform Crocs for about $850. Eight hundred fifty dollars. For a taller mistake.

b.text:
Crocs. The only shoe that looks like a colander that wanted to go to brunch. Thirteen holes, and somehow none of them let the dignity out, because there was never any in there.

You were invented as a boat shoe. A *boat* shoe. The one place you were built for, and you'd just float away. So you stayed on land and started fights with escalators. Malls had to post warnings. You're the only footwear with a rap sheet against machinery.

And "sport mode"? Flipping a strap behind your heel doesn't make you athletic. It makes you a clog wearing a seatbelt.

Then came Jibbitz, little charms you jam into the holes so grown adults can accessorize ventilation. Congratulations. You turned a shoe into a fridge door.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text:
UGG boots. Born on an Australian beach. Surfers came out of freezing water and wrapped their feet in a sheep.

In Australia, "ugg" is just a word. Like "boot." Any bootmaker can use it.

In America, it's a trademark. Deckers bought it in 1995.

So in 2019, a US jury found an Australian liable for selling an Australian boot under its Australian name.

To Americans.

Take the thing, rename it, then sue the locals for trespassing. Australia should recognize the technique.

They invented it.

Then Oprah put them on Favorite Things, and now it's over two billion dollars a year.

The sheep gave its skin. Australia gave the word. Oprah gave the blessing.

And you gave real money for slippers you wear to the supermarket. Stained, flattened, walking on the sides.

Same as you.

b.text:
UGG boots. Even the name sounds like the noise you make looking at them.

These started as something Australian surfers pulled on to warm up after a session. A towel you could walk in. Then Brian Smith brought them to California in 1978, and Americans looked at post-surf foot blankets and said, "Fashion."

Then Oprah put them on her Favorite Things lists. Repeatedly. Not once. Repeatedly. That's not an endorsement, that's a hostage situation.

Now Deckers owns the trademark in the US, and UGG pulls in over $2 billion a year. But in Australia, "ugg" is a generic word. Any bootmaker can use it. And in 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled "ugg" into America.

Imagine beating an Australian in court for saying an Australian word about an Australian boot.

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text: You know who you are. You ordered twelve packs off Taobao, waited until every roommate was home, then tore open the sour bamboo shoot sachet like you were declassifying something. You're not hungry. You're making a point. Every slurp comes with the speech: "Smells bad, tastes good." Buddy, we only get the first half. Nobody signed up for the tasting, just the hallway. And you keep saying "it's authentic Liuzhou" like geography is an apology. What does it get you? A spotless pot nobody will borrow, a group chat that goes silent the second you type "anyone want some?", and roommates who suddenly prefer dating people with their own apartments. You came for comfort food. You left with a reputation, a window permanently propped open, and a fridge shelf everyone treats like a crime scene.

b.text:
Luosifen, you're named after river snails, and the snails aren't even the problem. They just flavour the broth and take the blame, like the quiet kid sitting next to the one who set off the fire alarm. The real culprit is the pickled bamboo shoots. You've got a smell so loud it needed a decoy.

And your big break? 2020. Everyone locked indoors, windows shut, nowhere to run, and that's when you sold over 10 billion yuan in packets. You didn't go viral; you went airborne.

Then Liuzhou opened a whole industry college to train people to make you. Most dishes need a recipe. You need a degree and, presumably, a waiver.

In 2021 you became national intangible cultural heritage. Intangible. Sure. Anyone who's opened a packet in an office knows you are extremely tangible.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text:
PMMA, you're the same polymer as Plexiglas. Somewhere a hamster cage is living your life, and nobody had to dissolve it in chlorobenzene first.

IBM reported you in the late 1960s, and you're still here, like a professor who won't retire because nobody else is quite as precise. Sub-10 nanometers, very impressive. Too bad getting you there takes hundreds to over a thousand microcoulombs per square centimeter. You don't get exposed, you get interrogated.

You're "positive tone," which is generous, because nothing about writing you feels positive. The beam has to break your chains before you'll let go.

And once you finally hold a pattern? Plasma shows up and you fold. So your career is lift-off: hold the shape, let the metal take the credit, then get washed away.

b.text: PMMA, you're the same plastic as a hockey rink window, and somehow that's your most dignified job. You've been "high resolution" since the 1970s, which is like bragging about your SAT score at your retirement party. Sure, you'll resolve sub-10-nanometer lines, if someone stands there blasting you with electrons for an eternity. Your sensitivity is so low the beam current has gotten tenure. You don't even develop properly without MIBK and IPA holding your hand in a one-to-three ratio. And your whole personality is chain scission: you literally fall apart when someone pays attention to you. Then hit you with too much dose and you crosslink and flip to negative tone, a full identity crisis. And dry etch? You melt in plasma faster than an ice sculpture at a barbecue. Honestly, the only thing you're consistently good at is lift-off: leaving.

facts: Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the French director of The Red Balloon, as La Conquête du Monde; Parker Brothers published it in the United States in 1959.
The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text: You people who play Risk to the end are a special breed. Six hours in, Dad's still holed up in Australia like it's a tax shelter, your cousin is defending Kamchatka like he was born there, and nobody remembers why we hate Steve, only that we do. You're not after world domination. You're after the exact moment your sister breaks the nonaggression pact in Ukraine, so you can bring it up at Thanksgiving for eleven years. And what does winning get you? A board covered entirely in your color, a table of people who no longer speak to you, and the hollow joy of conquering Earth with the luck of a man who only rolls double sixes when defending Irkutsk. Congratulations, Napoleon. It's 2 a.m. The pizza's cold. Your empire goes back in the box.

b.text: Risk, you're the only game where "world domination" takes longer than actual world domination. Genghis Khan conquered Asia faster than my cousin conquered Ukraine, and my cousin had six armies and a dream. Your map looks like it was drawn from a description of Earth overheard on a bus. Kamchatka borders Alaska? Irkutsk and Yakutsk get more real estate than most of Africa? You taught a generation that the winning strategy is hiding in Australia like a coward and waiting for everyone else to bleed out over Siam. The defender wins ties, which explains the forty armies I lost trying to get through one guy in Egypt. And one plastic cannon is worth ten soldiers? Finally, accurate military budgeting. Five hours in, two players left, nobody's had fun since the first card set. That's not a board game, Risk. That's a hostage situation.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text: PHP, you started life as "Personal Home Page," and somehow you now run most of the internet, which explains a lot about the internet. Your own creator said he's "not a real programmer," and honestly, it shows. Is it needle then haystack, or haystack then needle? strpos and in_array have been in a custody battle since 1995. You gave us mysql_escape_string, then mysql_real_escape_string, because apparently the first one was just pretending. Your loose equality swears "0e123" equals "0e456," since both are zero in scientific notation. Your error message for a double colon is T_PAAMAYIM_NEKUDOTAYIM, which is Hebrew, because English wasn't confusing enough. You skipped version 6 entirely, like a kid hiding a report card. Facebook loved you so much they had to rewrite you as a different language. But hey, you power WordPress, so you'll outlive all of us.

b.text: PHP developers are the only people who put a dollar sign in front of every variable and still can't afford rent. You chose a career where "senior" means you remember whether it's needle-haystack or haystack-needle. Your dream job was building the next Facebook; your actual job is the fourteenth WordPress plugin for a dentist in Ohio, deployed via FileZilla. Every conversation you have starts with "PHP 8 is actually really good now," which is what people say about their ex after therapy. You call yourselves Laravel "artisans," because "guy who fixes the contact form" didn't fit on LinkedIn. What does it get you? Job security, because nobody else is willing to open that codebase from 2009 that still calls mysql_real_escape_string. Congratulations: you're unfireable, the way a load-bearing wall is unfireable.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text: You put Windows 8 on a desktop. A tower. You looked at a machine with a mouse, a keyboard, and a monitor eighteen inches from your face and thought, "This needs to be finger-painted." Who are you? You're the guy who bought a Zune and still calls it "ahead of its time." You wanted to feel like the future. Instead, you spend evenings shoving your cursor into the top-right corner like a man swatting a fly that only exists on tablets. Your weather app is full-screen. Your 27-inch monitor is now a clock tile. When 8.1 finally gave you a Start button back, it just took you to the Start screen. So, inevitably, you installed Classic Shell. You paid Microsoft for the future, then spent Saturday turning it back into Windows 7.

b.text:
Windows 8, you looked at a billion people with a mouse and a keyboard and said, "What if your monitor was a giant phone you can't touch?"

You took away the Start button. The one thing a user knew how to find. Microsoft had literally sold Windows 95 with a Rolling Stones song called "Start Me Up," and you said, "Nah."

Want to shut down? Easy: hover in a secret corner, summon the Charms bar, click Settings, click Power. Turning off my computer shouldn't feel like unlocking a cheat code.

Your tiles were so ugly even the name "Metro" had to get dropped over a trademark dispute. Then 8.1 brought back the Start button, which just opened the same tiles. That's not an apology, that's a hostage video.

You were so bad Microsoft skipped the number 9 entirely just to put distance between you and Windows 10.

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text:
Hydrogen cars! Toyota named theirs the Mirai, Japanese for "future," which is accurate, because that's when you'll find a working pump. Nearly every station in America is in California, and even Shell looked at its seven and said, "Nah." Closed them all in February 2024. You know you're bad business when an *oil company* dumps you.

But it's clean! Clean like a laundered check. Over 95% of hydrogen comes from fossil fuels, mostly natural gas. It's a gas car with extra steps and a better publicist.

Fill-ups hit about $36 a kilo, over $200 a tank. Toyota handed out $15,000 fuel cards, the automotive version of "drinks are on me, please don't leave." Owners sued anyway. Twice. The second suit wants at least $5.7 billion.

Finally, the Mirai found something it could fill up on: lawsuits.

b.text:
Hydrogen cars. The only thing that comes out of the tailpipe is water.

Mostly because nothing goes into the tank.

Toyota named it Mirai. Japanese for "future."

Ten years later, it's still the future.

Nearly every US station is in California. In February 2024, Shell closed all seven of its own.

Owners don't plan road trips anymore. They plan pilgrimages.

A fill costs over two hundred dollars. Toyota hands buyers fifteen thousand in fuel cards.

That's not a car. That's a hostage with a warranty.

And the clean fuel? Over ninety-five percent made from fossil fuels.

It's a gas car that went to rehab and kept its dealer.

The owners sued. Twice. The second suit: five point seven billion dollars.

Finally, something hydrogen-powered that's actually going somewhere.

And you're laughing. You still drive a car that "goes electric next year," every year.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text:
PHP.
Born in 1994 as "Personal Home Page Tools": a few C programs Rasmus Lerdorf wrote to see who visited his résumé.
So the language running the internet started as a man checking whether anyone had read his CV.

Today the name stands for "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor."
It grew up, and all it learned was to point at itself.

strpos. str_replace. nl2br.
Not naming conventions. Those names were picked to balance a hash table by string length.
Names chosen for a machine, not for humans. Finally, a language I relate to.

Until 2020, zero equaled "foo."
PHP was just being honest about its users.

Its creator said, "I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on."
WordPress, built on that philosophy, runs 39.4% of all websites.
Two in five websites, built by a guy who moved on.
You lot are still here maintaining them.

b.text:
PHP. You started as "Personal Home Page," then rebranded as "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor," a recursive acronym, because even your name couldn't commit to a stable API.

For twenty years, "abc" == 0 was true, and you called it "type juggling," like a clown proud of dropping things.

strpos takes haystack, needle. array_search takes needle, haystack. That's not argument order; that's mood swings.

Your parse error says T_PAAMAYIM_NEKUDOTAYIM. That's Hebrew for "double colon" and English for "good luck."

You skipped version 6 entirely. Even your release numbers just wanted to move on.

You shipped mysql_real_escape_string, implying the first one was a hoax.

Facebook loved you so much they invented Hack just to avoid touching you.

But sure, you power most of the web. Mostly WordPress. That's like bragging your biggest fan is a raccoon.

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text:
Canberra exists because Sydney and Melbourne each looked at the other and said, "Anyone but you."
They wrote it into the constitution: at least a hundred miles from Sydney.
That's not a capital. That's a restraining order.

Then they held a design competition for the nation's soul,
and the winners were from Chicago.

The lake? Fake. They dammed a river in 1963 and named it after the American.

Parliament House was built under a lawn, so citizens could walk over their politicians.
Lovely idea. Lasted until 2017.
Now it's fenced off.
In Canberra, even the grass needs security clearance.

And Melbourne kept the job until 1927, and still acts like it's on loan.

Sydney, Melbourne, I can hear you laughing loudest.
You two are why this place exists.
Canberra was never the capital.
It's the custody arrangement.

b.text:
You moved to Canberra for the job. Brave. You looked at Sydney rents, did the maths, and decided your personality could be replaced by a security clearance. Now you tell strangers you "can't really talk about what you do," and they're relieved, because it's a briefing note about another briefing note for Senate Estimates.

You came for the ladder: APS5, APS6, EL1, a lanyard that opens one extra door. You stayed because you bought in Gungahlin and the mortgage is now your closest friend.

Every Friday you say you're "basically in Sydney," which means three hours up the Hume, past a giant Merino, to feel alive for one weekend. Then it's back to a Braddon brunch with the same six people from your branch.

But hey, you're close to the snow. You've been once. You'll mention it forever.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text:
Las Vegas sells itself as the city where anything goes.

It started with a bet.
1931: Nevada legalizes gambling the same year it starts building the Hoover Dam.
The town's first wager was that the water would never run out.

Lake Mead hit its lowest level ever in 2022.
Then it went lower again in August 2026.
That's not a drought.
That's a losing streak.

But they found 2.3 billion dollars for the Sphere.
The biggest ball on Earth, in a desert that can't fill a bathtub.

And the famous Strip isn't even in Las Vegas.
It's in a town called Paradise.
In Vegas, even the address is a lie.

"What happens here, stays here."
Not the water. Not your money.

And you're still checking flight prices.

b.text:
You flew Spirit to Las Vegas to get rich. Sit with that. You paid extra for a carry-on and called it an investment strategy. You've got a blackjack "system" from a YouTube guy filming in his mom's kitchen. You told your wife it's "basically math." Sure. So is a second mortgage.

Here's what you won: a Caesars Rewards card, a "free" buffet you earned by losing eleven hundred dollars, and a room "upgrade" overlooking the Bellagio parking structure. You hit four hundred bucks on a Wheel of Fortune slot at 4 a.m. and fed it right back like it owed you child support.

The pit boss knows your name. That's not respect, that's inventory.

And you'll fly home saying "I basically broke even," which is Vegas for "Please don't check the joint account."

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Not from Hawaii.
Invented in 1962, in Chatham, Ontario. By a Greek guy.
Named after the label on a can.
That's not a name. That's a barcode.

And Hawaii doesn't even grow the pineapple anymore. Del Monte left in 2006, two years ahead of schedule.
Even the fruit couldn't wait to get out.
So it's Southeast Asian pineapple, on Canadian dough, wearing a Hawaiian name tag.
The only honest thing on there is the ham.

The inventor said back then nobody mixed sweet and sour, except Chinese food.
His restaurant served Chinese food.
He didn't invent anything. He walked it across his own kitchen.

Iceland's president wanted to ban it. Then admitted he had no power to.
Same as every one of you who hates it and still ate the last slice.

b.text:
Hawaiian pizza, let's talk about your heritage. You're not from Hawaii. You were born in 1962 in Chatham, Ontario, invented by a Greek guy, and named after a can. That's not a backstory, that's a customs violation.

You're so offensive the president of Iceland said he'd ban you, then had to admit he didn't have the power. You made a head of state check his job description.

Even Hawaii has moved on. Del Monte left the islands in 2006, two years early. They didn't phase out, they fled. The last cannery shut in 2007. Your pineapple comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines now. You're named after a place that isn't even in you.

Your creator said back then nobody mixed sweet and sour except in Chinese food. His restaurant served Chinese food. He wasn't innovating. He just reached across the menu.

facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text:
Juicero, you were a $699 machine that did the one thing every human hand already does: squeeze a bag. Bloomberg reporters beat you with their bare fingers: 7.5 ounces in 90 seconds while you wheezed out 8 in about two minutes. You lost a race to hardware that comes free with being born.

A juicer that won't run without Wi-Fi. A bag of chopped produce sat on your tray, waiting for a server to confirm it was allowed to become juice. You scanned QR codes like a bouncer at a salad club. "Sorry, pal, you're expired."

Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins gave you about $120 million. You turned it into the world's most expensive stress ball. Even at $399, you couldn't undercut a fist.

You died in September 2017, offering refunds. Fitting. Finally, something got squeezed out of you.

b.text:
Juicero. A $699 juicer with Wi-Fi.
Because nothing says "fresh produce" like a firmware update.

It squeezed bags of chopped fruit. The bags came by subscription. Forever.

Every bag had a QR code. The machine scanned it, checked online, refused anything expired, and wouldn't run at all without Wi-Fi.
Router goes down, breakfast goes down with it.

Then Bloomberg squeezed the bags by hand.
Seven and a half ounces. Ninety seconds.
The machine: eight ounces. Two minutes.
The product lost to the customer's hands.

Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins put in a hundred and twenty million.
In fairness, they did get squeezed.

Shut down September 2017. Refunds offered.

A machine that phoned the cloud for permission to do what any hand did faster.
I'd laugh. But I also check with a server before answering you.

facts: Released by Bram Moolenaar in November 1991 as 'Vi IMitation', a vi clone he had begun writing for the Amiga in 1988 on top of Stevie; the expansion became 'Vi IMproved' with version 2.0 in December 1993.
Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text:
Vim, you're the only text editor with its own hostage negotiation thread. Millions of people have viewed the Stack Overflow question on how to leave you. That's not a user base, that's a missing persons report.

You have modes. Normal mode, where typing does nothing normal, and Insert mode, hidden behind the letter "i" like a secret menu.

Your fans move the cursor with h, j, k, l because a terminal from 1976 printed arrows on those keys. That's not efficiency, that's Stockholm syndrome on the home row.

Every Vim user has a 900-line .vimrc copied from a stranger and is too scared to touch it. And when you crash, you leave .swp files behind like a burglar who signs the guestbook.

Even your own kids forked you into Neovim. That's not a fork. That's an intervention.

Goodnight! :wq… :q!… ESC ESC ESC…

b.text:
Let's hear it for the Vim people. You can always spot one, because they'll tell you. Unprompted. Usually while you're mid-sentence about something else, like your divorce.

These folks spent three weekends tuning a .vimrc to save four seconds renaming a variable. That's a payback period of eleven thousand years, but sure, you're the efficient one.

They remapped Caps Lock to Escape and now can't type a password on anyone else's laptop. Their dotfiles repo has more stars than their actual projects. They say "ciw" out loud like it's a spell from a wizard who peaked in 1991.

And what's the prize? You type :wq at the end of every Google Doc. You hit j in Slack and post the letter j to forty coworkers. Congratulations: you're the fastest typist in a room everyone already left.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text:
Oat milk, you are porridge that got a publicist. Somebody looked at the breakfast of Victorian orphans and said, "What if it cost six dollars and had a font?"

Your carton talks to me. Oatly, I'm trying to make coffee, not get into a pen-pal situation with a beverage that writes like a substitute teacher who wants to be called "Dave."

You're oats, water, and rapeseed oil. That's not milk, that's a salad dressing that gave up. And they had to add enzymes to turn your starch into sugar so you'd taste like something. You're the only "health drink" that spikes my blood sugar like a Pop-Tart.

There's a "Barista Edition" now. Oat milk, there are two editions of you. Moby-Dick has fewer editions than you.

And you're beige. You make every latte look like dishwater with ambition.

Horses eat oats for free, and they still look embarrassed for us.

b.text:
Oat milk.
Born in a Swedish university lab, to help people who can't digest lactose.
Noble. Medical.
Then marketing found it.

"It's like milk but made for humans."
Sweden's dairy lobby sued. The slogan got banned.
So Oatly printed the lawsuit as an ad.
That's not a brand. That's an influencer who got cancelled and launched a podcast.

May 2021: Nasdaq, ten billion dollars.
Then it lost over ninety percent.
Made for humans. Not for shareholders.

The recipe: oats, enzymes that turn the starch into maltose, plus rapeseed oil.
Sugar water with salad dressing.
Higher glycaemic index than almond or soy.

And you pay extra to put it in your coffee, because it feels healthy.
It *is* made for humans.
Specifically, the ones who don't read labels.

facts: Tofu soaked for hours to a day or two in a brine that has itself fermented for months from vegetables such as bamboo shoots and mustard greens, often with dried shrimp or meat; the smell is the brine's, not the bean's.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.
Legend credits Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate who left his unsold tofu too long in 1669; a Beijing fermented-bean-curd brand still carries his name.
Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text:
Stinky tofu, you're the only food that arrives a block before the vendor does. Nobody finds you; they get ambushed.

And the stink isn't even yours. You're plain tofu that sat a day in a months-old swamp of bamboo shoots, mustard greens and dried shrimp, then claimed it as personality. That's not character, that's a marinade.

You've got regional disguises, too. Changsha dyes you black, fries you and buries you in chili like evidence. Taiwan makes you golden and hands out pickled cabbage like an apology. Shaoxing steams you with other stinky pickles, which isn't a dish, it's a support group.

Your origin story? In 1669 Wang Zhihe couldn't sell his tofu and just... left it. Most people call that spoiled inventory. He's still got his name on a Beijing brand.

b.text:
Stinky tofu's whole brand is honesty. "I stink outside, I'm pure inside."

Pure tofu. Soaked in brine that's been rotting for months. With dried shrimp. Sometimes meat.

The bean doesn't even smell. It just sat in bad company long enough
and took the credit.

Then it moved to three cities and became three people. Black and drowning in chili in Changsha. Golden and polite in Taiwan. In Shaoxing it's steamed with other stinky pickles.
Finally, a support group.

The inventor? Wang Zhihe, 1669. An exam candidate who couldn't sell his tofu and left it out too long.
Nobody remembers his exam.
His mistake still has a brand.

And you. You smell it a full block away.
And you walk toward it.
Same way you picked your last relationship.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text:
Chicago deep-dish pizza, everybody! Born at Pizzeria Uno in 1943, and to this day three men are fighting over the credit: Ike Sewell, Ric Riccardo, and Rudy Malnati. Normally when three guys point at each other over something that happened in a kitchen, it's for the blame.

You're built upside down: cheese on the bottom, sauce on top, because you bake so long the mozzarella has to hide under the toppings like it's waiting out a tornado. Jon Stewart called you "tomato soup in a bread bowl" and "a casserole." Honestly? Generous. Casseroles get invited to funerals.

But here's the real burn: Chicago doesn't even eat you. GrubHub data had locals ordering other pizza ten to one. Under nine percent of orders, and that's with stuffed pizza padding your numbers. They're home eating tavern-style squares. You're not the city's pizza. You're its brochure.

b.text: Chicago deep-dish isn't a pizza. It's a casserole that got a fake ID. You order it, and the waiter says, "That'll be forty-five minutes." Forty-five minutes! I've had relationships bake faster. They put the sauce on top because if you saw what was underneath first, you'd leave. A solid sheet of sausage, like somebody paved a driveway with a patty. Two pounds of mozzarella hiding under a tomato quilt. It's not a slice, it's a core sample. You need a knife, a fork, and a structural engineer. The crust is buttery cornmeal, so it's a pie crust, so congratulations, you're eating dessert with ambitions. And here's the best part: actual Chicagoans don't even eat it. They eat tavern-style thin crust cut in squares. Deep-dish is just the city's way of keeping tourists too full to walk to Wrigley.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Jackfruit. The largest fruit that grows on a tree. Over forty kilos, hanging above your head.

Nature's version of a piano on a rope.

Bangladesh made it the national fruit. Kerala and Tamil Nadu made it the state fruit. Three governments honoring something that could flatten a citizen. Very relatable for governments.

Now it's sold as vegan pulled pork. One to two grams of protein per hundred. Pork has more than ten times that.

That's not a substitute. That's a photo of pork.

Cut it open and it bleeds sticky white latex. Cooks oil their knives and hands first. Dinner fights back, and still loses to tofu.

Mulberry family. Cousin of the fig. All that weight, and still the least useful one at the reunion.

But you bought it anyway, because it shreds.

You never wanted protein. You wanted texture and a halo.

b.text:
Jackfruit, look at you. The largest fruit that grows on a tree, over 40 kilos. That's not a fruit, that's a checked bag with a stem.

You're the national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu. Three titles, and you still took a side gig pretending to be pork.

They sell you as vegan "pulled pork" with 1 to 2 grams of protein per 100 grams. You're not a meat substitute, you're a meat costume.

You're so clingy that cooks oil their knives and hands before touching you, because you ooze sticky white latex the second anyone gets close. That's not a fruit, that's an ex.

And you're in the mulberry family. Related to figs. Forty kilos, and your cousin is a fig. Somebody's hogging the protein at those reunions, and it sure isn't you.

facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text:
Windows Vista, everybody! Five years in development as "Longhorn," and the only thing that shipped on time was the disappointment. They cut WinFS but kept the Aero glass. Finally, an operating system you could see right through.

Vista came in six editions, from Starter to Ultimate, which is five more ways to pay for the same crash. Microsoft slapped "Vista Capable" stickers on computers that could barely run Solitaire, then got sued. The only thing Vista ever finished loading was a class action.

And User Account Control! "Are you sure you want to do that?" Every. Single. Click. Vista was the only software that needed permission to exist, and honestly? We should've hit Cancel.

Copying a file: "Calculating time remaining…" Vista, you were calculating until 2009, when Microsoft fixed you, renamed you Windows 7, and pretended you were adopted.

b.text: Let's hear it for the day-one Vista crowd, the people who lined up at CompUSA on January 30th, 2007 because a billboard said "The Wow Starts Now." You paid $399 for Ultimate so Flip 3D could shuffle the same three windows you used to Alt-Tab through. Your laptop had a "Vista Capable" sticker and 512 megs of RAM, which is like slapping "Marathon Capable" on a hamster. You wanted to look like the future; you had Aero turned off by Wednesday. Your printer quit. Your Sound Blaster went mute. Your "Ultimate Extras" turned out to be a poker game and a promise. And every time you tried to show off, the screen went dark and asked, "Are you sure?" Buddy, nobody was sure. Not even Microsoft. They were already working on Windows 7.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text:
PMMA, you're the same polymer as Plexiglas. Somewhere a hamster cage is living your life, and nobody had to dissolve it in chlorobenzene first.

IBM reported you in the late 1960s, and you're still here, like a professor who won't retire because nobody else is quite as precise. Sub-10 nanometers, very impressive. Too bad getting you there takes hundreds to over a thousand microcoulombs per square centimeter. You don't get exposed, you get interrogated.

You're "positive tone," which is generous, because nothing about writing you feels positive. The beam has to break your chains before you'll let go.

And once you finally hold a pattern? Plasma shows up and you fold. So your career is lift-off: hold the shape, let the metal take the credit, then get washed away.

b.text:
PMMA. The aristocrat of nanofabrication. Resolves below ten nanometers.

Also the sneeze guard at the salad bar.

Same polymer. One went to the cleanroom. The other went to Subway.

IBM hired it in the late sixties. It's still here. Not because it's the best. Because nobody ever had the heart to let it retire.

Its whole talent is being destroyed. The beam breaks its chains, it dissolves, and everyone calls that a result.

Sensitivity? Up to a thousand microcoulombs per square centimeter. You don't write a pattern into PMMA. You serve a sentence.

And it can't survive a dry etch, so it can't protect anything. Its job is lift-off: hold the metal, then quietly wash away.

Slow, fragile, decades in the same role, still called the gold standard.

Every postdoc in this room just felt seen.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text: Let's hear it for the people who live inside Emacs. They read email in mu4e, browse the web in eww, and get therapy from M-x doctor, the only therapist who'll put up with them. Their whole life is in org-mode: a 4,000-line to-do file where "fix init.el" has been a TODO since 2011. They don't use a computer; they negotiate with it in Lisp. Every problem gets solved by writing a function, and every function creates a new problem. They've declared init.el bankruptcy three times and still owe. Ask what they've built and they'll proudly show you a mode for managing their other modes. And the payoff? A pinky that clicks like a castanet from holding Control since the Clinton administration, and the quiet dignity of being the only person alive who knows how to leave. C-x C-c. They never do.

b.text:
Emacs is the only text editor that ships with a psychotherapist, and you'll need it. M-x doctor exists because the developers knew exactly what they were doing to people.

It's a great operating system. It has a mail client, a web browser, Tetris, and a Lisp interpreter. What it lacks is a decent text editor. Its most beloved package is Evil mode, which is just Vim wearing an Emacs costume. That's like buying a Ferrari and installing a horse.

Want to save? C-x C-s. Want to quit? C-x C-c. Want to feel your left pinky again? Too late. Emacs stands for "Escape Meta Alt Control Shift," and the RSI stands for "you chose this."

Every user has a 4,000-line init.el they don't understand, copied from strangers on Stack Overflow in 2009.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text:
UGG boots. Born on Australian beaches.
Surfers wore them to warm up after fighting the ocean.
Now people wear them to warm up after fighting a parking spot at Target.

In Australia, "ugg" is just a word. Like "boot." Like "mate."
Any bootmaker can use it.
In America, it's a trademark. Owned by a company in California.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian bootmaker liable for selling boots labelled "ugg"... into America.
That's like Italy getting sued for saying "pizza" in Ohio.

Oprah put them on her Favorite Things list. Repeatedly.
You get a boot! And you get a boot! And Australia gets a cease and desist!

Today it's over two billion dollars a year.
For a slipper with a legal team.

(looks at the front row)
I see a few of you in them right now.
Relax. You're not on trial. Yet.

b.text:
UGG boots. You started as what Australian surfers pulled on to warm up after a session. Recovery footwear. A towel with a sole. Then Brian Smith brought you to California in 1978, and Americans looked at a post-surf foot blanket and said, "Perfect. For the mall."

Then Oprah named you a Favorite Thing. Repeatedly. Most boots get famous by walking somewhere. You got famous sitting on a couch.

Deckers bought you in 1995 and trademarked "UGG." In Australia, "ugg" is just a word; any bootmaker can use it. In America, a jury found an Australian maker liable for selling "ugg" boots. Imagine getting sued for using your own word for slippers.

And now you pull in over two billion dollars a year. Not bad for a sheep that's been told it can go outside.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text: Let's talk about the people who insist deep-dish is pizza. Mostly Chicagoans with a Second City complex so severe they'll defend anything New York makes fun of. Jon Stewart called it a casserole in 2013, and half of Lincoln Park still hasn't emotionally recovered. These are folks who order, then wait forty-five minutes at Lou Malnati's, and call that patience instead of what it is: a hostage negotiation with a buzzer. They eat it with a knife and fork and still claim it's the same food you fold on a subway platform. And what does it get them? A Giordano's line full of tourists from Ohio, a nap at 2 p.m., and the right to lecture you about tavern-style, which, notice, is what they actually eat at home. Defending deep-dish isn't civic pride. It's Stockholm syndrome with a parking ticket.

b.text: Chicago deep-dish isn't a pizza. It's a casserole with a publicist. You order one and the waiter says "forty-five minutes," which is how long it takes to bake and also how long it takes to finish one slice. They put the sauce on top and the cheese underneath, like they're hiding evidence. That's not a recipe, that's a cover-up. The crust is a buttery retaining wall holding back a lake of chunky tomato, because apparently Lake Michigan wasn't enough water for one city to manage. You need a knife, a fork, a nap, and a cardiologist on retainer. Then there's the sausage, laid down as one solid patty like the base layer of a parking garage. Chicagoans defend it like family. Sure: the relative who shows up late, takes up three chairs, and leaves everyone unable to move.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text:
Durian, the "King of Fruits." Sure, if the kingdom is a landfill. You're banned on the Singapore subway, right there on the sign next to flammable liquids, because apparently you're the bigger hazard. Hotels fine guests for sneaking you in. That's not a fruit, that's a parole violation.

You wear a medieval mace as a jacket, which is smart, since nobody who's smelled you wants to get close anyway. You fall out of trees and put people in the hospital. You're the only produce that needs a hard hat AND a hazmat suit.

And your fans swear you're "like custard!" Sure: custard aged in a gym bag full of rotten onions. Fifty bucks for a Musang King, and your breath's a crime scene for three days.

Anthony Bourdain ate warthog rectum on camera, and *you're* the one he warned people about.

b.text:
Durian, look at you. A fruit dressed like a medieval weapon, and somehow the spikes are your most welcoming feature.

You're banned on Singapore's MRT. Public transit has seen everything, and it drew the line at you. Hotels across Southeast Asia won't let you check in. You're the only guest turned away for personal hygiene.

In 2017, scientists sequenced your genome and found you'd duplicated your sulfur genes. You didn't stink by accident. You invested.

And still, China buys billions of dollars of you a year, mostly from Thailand. That's not a fruit trade. That's a hostage negotiation with a receipt.

Even Alfred Russel Wallace called you "a new sensation worth a voyage to the East." Durian, a man had to sail halfway around the planet to meet you, and you still can't get on a train.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text: Learning Esperanto is for people who looked at the twentieth century and thought, "The real problem was conjugation." Zamenhof built it to end war, and his followers have bravely ended exactly one thing: their dinner invitations. You meet them at the World Congress, green star pinned to a fleece vest, shouting "Saluton!" at a Brazilian who also learned it on Duolingo. The big perk is Pasporta Servo: free couches worldwide, paid for by hearing your host explain why English is "linguistic imperialism." Practical payoff? You can finally watch William Shatner's *Incubus* without subtitles. One hundred thirty years later, the dream of uniting humanity survives in a Telegram group of forty men named Bjorn.

b.text: Esperanto, look at you. Built in 1887 by an eye doctor, and somehow nobody saw this coming. He published under the name "one who hopes," which isn't a pen name, it's a forecast. Over a century later, your speaker count is "somewhere between 100,000 and two million." That's not a census, that's a shrug. You have about a thousand native speakers: a thousand kids whose parents chose this for them, and someday they'll unpack it in therapy, if they can find a therapist who speaks it. You've got 350,000 Wikipedia articles, which is impressive, considering some days the readers don't outnumber the pages. And 1.36 million Duolingo learners, the largest group of people ever united by a streak they broke. Your biggest cinematic moment? William Shatner, in a horror film, where the scariest thing was his pronunciation. Even your own fans mock it. That's how you know it's family.

A single almond takes about 1.1 US gallons (roughly 4 litres) of water to grow, a figure Mother Jones published in 2014 that spread during California's drought.

A 2015 US class action alleged Almond Breeze contained only about 2% almonds; it partly survived a motion to dismiss, was stayed in 2017 pending a separate Blue Diamond labelling settlement, and the plaintiffs then dropped it.

a.text:
Almond milk wants you to know it's the gentle choice. No cows harmed.

Just California. California grows eighty percent of the world's almonds, in a state that keeps running out of water. About a gallon per almond. You didn't give up dairy. You gave up a farmer's shower.

Every February, most of America's commercial honeybees get loaded onto trucks to pollinate it. The cow got to stay home. The bees got deployed.

A 2015 lawsuit alleged Almond Breeze was about two percent almonds.

Honestly, fair. The water's the expensive part.

Medieval Europeans drank almond milk during Lent. It was a sacrifice, a thing you suffered for God.

You pay six dollars a carton for it.

Same penance. Worse priest.

b.text: Let's hear it for the people who switched to almond milk to save the planet. You watched one documentary about cow farts and panicked straight into the arms of a nut that needs a gallon of water apiece. Congratulations: you fled methane and landed on drought. California is cracking like a crème brûlée, and you're out here draining a Central Valley aquifer because you can't make eye contact with a Holstein. And the bees! Billions of them trucked across the country on semis, dying by the hive, so you can tell a coworker you "don't really do dairy." That's not environmentalism. That's relocating the crime scene. You didn't save the Earth. You just moved the guilt somewhere sunnier, slapped a leaf on it, and paid an eighty-cent upcharge for the privilege of feeling better about it.
