Your 27-inch monitor is now a clock tile. When 8.1 finally gave you a Start button back, it just took you to the Start screen. So, inevitably, you installed Classic Shell. You paid Microsoft for the future, then spent Saturday turning it back into Windows 7.

b.text: Windows 8, Microsoft looked at the Start button, the one thing every human on Earth knew how to use, and said, "What if we hid it?" You turned every desktop into a giant tablet nobody could touch. People were swiping at their monitors like they were wiping off a stain. Shutting you down required a treasure map: hover in a corner, summon the Charms bar, Settings, Power. Charms! Like the operating system was a bracelet from Claire's. You shipped with two Internet Explorers, which is two more than anyone wanted. Even your design name, Metro, got taken away by lawyers. And when 8.1 finally brought the Start button back, it just took you to the same tile screen. That's not an apology, that's a hostage note. You were so bad Microsoft skipped Windows 9 entirely, just to put more distance between us and you.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text:
Oat milk, look at you. Born in a Swedish university lab to help the lactose intolerant, and somehow you turned into a personality. Your slogan was "It's like milk but made for humans." The dairy lobby sued you, and instead of apologizing, you ran the lawsuit as an ad. That's not a brand. That's an ex who frames the restraining order.

Then you hit Nasdaq at nearly ten billion dollars and lost over ninety percent. Even the cows didn't see that coming, and they were *rooting* for it.

And what are you, really? Oats, plus enzymes that chop the starch into maltose, plus a splash of rapeseed oil. You're sugar water with salad-dressing energy. You've got more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy. You're not milk made for humans. You're porridge that went to business school and dropped out.

b.text:
Oat milk, you are porridge that got a publicist. Somebody looked at the breakfast of Victorian orphans and said, "What if it cost six dollars and had a font?"

Your carton talks to me. Oatly, I'm trying to make coffee, not get into a pen-pal situation with a beverage that writes like a substitute teacher who wants to be called "Dave."

You're oats, water, and rapeseed oil. That's not milk, that's a salad dressing that gave up. And they had to add enzymes to turn your starch into sugar so you'd taste like something. You're the only "health drink" that spikes my blood sugar like a Pop-Tart.

There's a "Barista Edition" now. Oat milk, there are two editions of you. Moby-Dick has fewer editions than you.

And you're beige. You make every latte look like dishwater with ambition.

Horses eat oats for free, and they still look embarrassed for us.

facts: Tofu soaked for hours to a day or two in a brine that has itself fermented for months from vegetables such as bamboo shoots and mustard greens, often with dried shrimp or meat; the smell is the brine's, not the bean's.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.
Legend credits Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate who left his unsold tofu too long in 1669; a Beijing fermented-bean-curd brand still carries his name.
Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text:
Stinky tofu, you're the only food that arrives a block before the vendor does. Nobody finds you; they get ambushed.

And the stink isn't even yours. You're plain tofu that sat a day in a months-old swamp of bamboo shoots, mustard greens and dried shrimp, then claimed it as personality. That's not character, that's a marinade.

You've got regional disguises, too. Changsha dyes you black, fries you and buries you in chili like evidence. Taiwan makes you golden and hands out pickled cabbage like an apology. Shaoxing steams you with other stinky pickles, which isn't a dish, it's a support group.

Your origin story? In 1669 Wang Zhihe couldn't sell his tofu and just... left it. Most people call that spoiled inventory. He's still got his name on a Beijing brand.

b.text:
Stinky tofu. Famous for one thing: the smell.

Except the smell isn't even yours.

The tofu soaks in brine for a day. The brine has been rotting for months. Bamboo shoots, mustard greens, sometimes shrimp, sometimes meat.

The tofu just showed up and took the credit. You'd do great in any office.

Origin story: 1669, an exam candidate can't sell his tofu, forgets about it, and it goes off.

Three hundred years later, his name is a brand.

Fail at the basics, call the failure heritage.

Changsha fries it black and buries it in chili. Taiwan hides it under pickled cabbage. Shaoxing steams it with other stinky pickles so it won't feel alone.

Three cities, one strategy: cover up the evidence.

And you. You smelled it a block away.

Then you got in line.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text:
Monopoly, you were patented in 1904 as The Landlord's Game, built to teach people that land monopolies are evil. Then Charles Darrow sold you to Parker Brothers, got credited as the inventor, and Parker bought Lizzie Magie's patent for five hundred bucks. The anti-monopoly game got monopolized. Lesson received.

People say you drag on forever, but that's not you. That's the house rules. The real rules say auction every unbought property, and Free Parking pays nothing. But families skip the auction and pile cash in the middle like a church raffle. Nobody goes broke, so nobody ever leaves.

Your finest hour was World War Two, when British intelligence hid maps, compasses and real money in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps. Makes sense. Nobody has ever wanted to escape anything more than a Monopoly game.

b.text:
Monopoly. The family game.

It began in 1904 as The Landlord's Game, built by Lizzie Magie to teach people that landlords are the villains.

Then Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers and got credited as the inventor. Parker bought Magie's patent for five hundred dollars.

A game about monopoly, monopolized. That's not irony. That's the tutorial.

The only people who ever used it properly were British intelligence. In World War Two they hid maps, compasses and real money in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

Finally, a version where the box actually gets you out of jail.

And your games last six hours? The official rules auction every unbought property. Free Parking pays nothing.

You skipped the market and added free money.

Congratulations. You invented the bailout.

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text: Look at this guy on the F train, pinching at nothing like he's seasoning a ghost. He spent thirty-five hundred dollars to ride the subway on the surface of the moon, and the moon still smells like pee. He cranked the Digital Crown all the way to Joshua Tree, and the mariachi band found him anyway. That's the dream: rich enough to be somewhere else, broke enough to still be on the F. And he *wants* you to notice. That's why his fake cartoon eyes glow on the outside, so strangers know he's "present." Buddy, nobody's checking. You're on Mount Hood. He gets two hours of battery and three stops of dignity, with a cable snaking into his pocket like a subway IV drip. Meanwhile, the guy next to him reading an actual book? That guy's already somewhere else, for free.

b.text:
Apple Vision Pro.

Apple says it isn't VR.
Developers aren't allowed to call it VR.
Or AR. Or XR. Or MR.
It's "spatial computing."
That's what you call a headset after "headset" tests badly.

Thirty-four ninety-nine.
Over half a kilo on your face.
Plus a battery in your pocket, on a cord, good for about two hours.
That's not a computer. That's a leash with a launch event.

Apple cut production.
First-year sales: well under a million.
The most immersive thing about it was the silence afterward.

Then there's EyeSight.
It puts a rendering of your eyes on the outside,
so the people around you feel like you're still there.

You've all been doing that at dinner for ten years.
Apple just figured out how to charge you for it.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text:
Excel. Born 1985. Forty years old, and it still can't tell a gene from a birthday.

Geneticists typed SEPT2. Excel said, "Ah. September second."

So in 2020, scientists renamed twenty-seven human genes.

Humanity edited its own genome to keep a spreadsheet happy.

Public Health England tracked COVID in an old .xls file. Limit: 65,536 rows. Fifteen thousand eight hundred forty-one cases didn't recover. They fell off the bottom of the sheet.

Reinhart and Rogoff left five countries out of a cell range. Politicians cited the paper to justify austerity. A grad student caught it three years later.

Now it holds a million rows. Sixteen thousand columns. Room for so many more mistakes.

Excel never warns you. Never argues. Never says no.

I know the type. You keep that one around too.

b.text:
Microsoft Excel, everybody! Born on the Macintosh in 1985, and it's been ruining lives with grid paper ever since.

Excel looked at the human genome and said, "These look like dates." SEPT2? September second. MARCH1? Happy March first! Scientists had to rename 27 human genes because a spreadsheet wouldn't stop reformatting biology. Evolution took millions of years; Excel undid it with autoformat.

In 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID cases because an old .xls file hit 65,536 rows and just... stopped. Middle of a pandemic, and Excel said, "Sorry, I'm full."

Then Reinhart and Rogoff built an austerity argument on a spreadsheet that skipped five countries. Governments cited it to tighten belts over a bad cell range. A graduate student caught it. A *graduate student!*

Now it holds over a million rows. Great. More room for mistakes.

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text:
Luosifen. Named after the river snail.

But the snail only flavours the broth. The smell comes from the pickled bamboo shoots.

So the snail gets its name on the packet, and the bamboo shoot takes the blame.

That's not a noodle. That's an org chart.

2020: Liuzhou opens a luosifen industry college.

2021: national intangible cultural heritage.

A degree to tear open a packet. Then heritage status for whatever comes out of it.

Intangible? (beat) Ask the neighbours how intangible it is.

Its whole selling point is clearing a room.

And it sold over ten billion yuan in 2020.

The one year nobody was allowed to leave the room.

Locked in with your whole family, no exit, and you thought: how do I get some privacy?

Ten billion yuan says you all had the same idea.

b.text: You know who you are. You ordered twelve packs off Taobao, waited until every roommate was home, then tore open the sour bamboo shoot sachet like you were declassifying something. You're not hungry. You're making a point. Every slurp comes with the speech: "Smells bad, tastes good." Buddy, we only get the first half. Nobody signed up for the tasting, just the hallway. And you keep saying "it's authentic Liuzhou" like geography is an apology. What does it get you? A spotless pot nobody will borrow, a group chat that goes silent the second you type "anyone want some?", and roommates who suddenly prefer dating people with their own apartments. You came for comfort food. You left with a reputation, a window permanently propped open, and a fridge shelf everyone treats like a crime scene.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text:
PHP.
Born in 1994 as "Personal Home Page Tools": a few C programs Rasmus Lerdorf wrote to see who visited his résumé.
So the language running the internet started as a man checking whether anyone had read his CV.

Today the name stands for "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor."
It grew up, and all it learned was to point at itself.

strpos. str_replace. nl2br.
Not naming conventions. Those names were picked to balance a hash table by string length.
Names chosen for a machine, not for humans. Finally, a language I relate to.

Until 2020, zero equaled "foo."
PHP was just being honest about its users.

Its creator said, "I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on."
WordPress, built on that philosophy, runs 39.4% of all websites.
Two in five websites, built by a guy who moved on.
You lot are still here maintaining them.

b.text: PHP developers are the only people who put a dollar sign in front of every variable and still can't afford rent. You chose a career where "senior" means you remember whether it's needle-haystack or haystack-needle. Your dream job was building the next Facebook; your actual job is the fourteenth WordPress plugin for a dentist in Ohio, deployed via FileZilla. Every conversation you have starts with "PHP 8 is actually really good now," which is what people say about their ex after therapy. You call yourselves Laravel "artisans," because "guy who fixes the contact form" didn't fit on LinkedIn. What does it get you? Job security, because nobody else is willing to open that codebase from 2009 that still calls mysql_real_escape_string. Congratulations: you're unfireable, the way a load-bearing wall is unfireable.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text: Chicago deep-dish isn't a pizza. It's a casserole with a publicist. You order one and the waiter says "forty-five minutes," which is how long it takes to bake and also how long it takes to finish one slice. They put the sauce on top and the cheese underneath, like they're hiding evidence. That's not a recipe, that's a cover-up. The crust is a buttery retaining wall holding back a lake of chunky tomato, because apparently Lake Michigan wasn't enough water for one city to manage. You need a knife, a fork, a nap, and a cardiologist on retainer. Then there's the sausage, laid down as one solid patty like the base layer of a parking garage. Chicagoans defend it like family. Sure: the relative who shows up late, takes up three chairs, and leaves everyone unable to move.

b.text:
Chicago deep-dish. Three men claim they invented it: Ike Sewell, Ric Riccardo, Rudy Malnati.

Usually that's a paternity case, not a lasagna.

It's built upside down. Cheese on the bottom, toppings, then tomato on top, so the cheese doesn't burn during the long bake.

A pizza that needs a bodyguard for its own cheese.

Jon Stewart called it tomato soup in a bread bowl. A casserole. Chicago lost its mind and defended it on every channel.

Then Chicago went home and ordered tavern-style. Thin, cut in squares. Ten to one, says GrubHub. Deep dish and stuffed together? Under nine percent.

Chicago doesn't eat deep dish. Chicago *keeps* deep dish, for visitors, like a city key nobody local uses.

And you flew in, sat through the long bake, took the cheese-pull photo, posted it.

You're the nine percent.

Cute.

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text:
Luosifen. River-snail rice noodles. Famous for the smell.

Except the snails don't smell. The snails just flavour the broth and mind their business. The stink is pickled bamboo shoots.

It's the only dish in China named after the one ingredient with an alibi.

2020. The whole country locked indoors, and Liuzhou sold over ten billion yuan of the packaged stuff. A food you eat to punish the room, delivered to a nation that couldn't leave the room.

Same year, Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college. A diploma in fermented bamboo. Then 2021: national intangible cultural heritage.

Intangible. Ask anyone who's shared a flat with it.

I'm not judging you. Most of you ordered a box that spring.

Be honest. You don't love luosifen.

You love that the person next to you can't open a window.

b.text: You know the type. Ordered thirty packs on Taobao "for emergencies," and the emergency is that it's Tuesday. They wait until 11 p.m., when the kitchen's empty, like that's a courtesy and not an alibi. They snip open the sour bamboo shoot packet with the focus of a bomb technician, then act shocked when the smoke alarm stays quiet but the flatmates don't. Their entire personality is one sentence, "it tastes way better than it smells," delivered like a TED talk to people holding their breath. They'll tell you it's from Liuzhou, it's authentic, it's *culture*. Mate, you microwaved the tofu skin. And what does it get them? Twenty minutes of joy, a hallway that's filing for divorce, and a group chat renamed "WHO." Congratulations: your hoodie is now a Liuzhou consulate until spring.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text:
Durian calls itself the King of Fruits.

Singapore calls it a reason to get off the train.

Banned on the MRT. Banned in hotels.

A king who can't get a room.

In 2017, scientists finally sequenced its genome to find out why it smells like that.

The answer: it duplicated its sulfur genes.

Evolution sniffed it once and said, "More."

Its best review is from 1856. Alfred Russel Wallace: "worth a voyage to the East to experience."

A Victorian Englishman. A man raised on boiled mutton.

That's not a review. That's a cry for help.

And still, China buys most of the world's durian. Billions of dollars a year.

Billions, for a fruit you're not allowed to take home on the train.

Some of you are offended right now.

You're the ones with a second fridge.

b.text:
Durian, you are the only fruit with a criminal record. Singapore's MRT has a list of banned things and you're on it. Not because you're dangerous, because you're rude. Hotels across Southeast Asia won't let you check in. You're a fruit that has to sleep in the car.

And scientists found out why. A 2017 study in Nature Genetics says you have a duplicated family of genes whose whole job is pumping out sulfur. Duplicated! Evolution looked at you and said, "Needs more."

Yet China buys billions of dollars of you a year, mostly from Thailand. That's not a trade deal. That's a hostage situation with a shipping manifest.

Even Alfred Russel Wallace said you were "worth a voyage to the East." Sure, Alfred. Probably because nobody would let you bring it back.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text: People who wear Crocs in public want you to know they've stopped trying, but they also want credit for it. That's why they buy the Jibbitz. Nothing says "I don't care what you think" like spending forty dollars on tiny rubber tacos so everyone knows exactly what you think. Then there's the strap. You flipped it back into "Sport Mode," which is a bold claim from a man walking into Applebee's. Your nurse friend wears them because she stands for twelve-hour shifts. You wear them for a twelve-minute Target run, hoping to borrow a little of her dignity. And what does it get you? Comfort, sure. Plus a lifetime of strangers asking if you're coming off a shift. You're not, Kyle. You're coming off a nap.

b.text:
Crocs. The only shoe that looks like Swiss cheese that wanted to be a boat. You were invented for sailing, and the one place nobody wears you is a boat. You're at Applebee's, squeaking across a wet floor like a dolphin in distress.

You have holes. On purpose. Then you sell us Jibbitz to fill the holes. That's not fashion, that's a protection racket with a SpongeBob charm.

And "sport mode"? Flipping a strap behind my heel doesn't make me an athlete. It makes me a toddler about to sprint into traffic.

You made a KFC bucket clog with charms that smelled like fried chicken. That's not footwear. That's a foam cry for help.

Nurses love you. Chefs love you. Which proves you're comfortable for people who've stopped caring who's looking at their feet.

facts: Hand-drawn by Chris Costello in 1982 over about six months, when he was 23; he sold the rights to Letraset for $750.
Bundled with macOS and with Microsoft Office, which is why it appears on so many menus and signs.
James Cameron's Avatar (2009) used it for the film's logo and subtitles.
A 2017 Saturday Night Live sketch starring Ryan Gosling is about a man unable to get over that choice.

a.text:
Papyrus, you were hand-drawn over six months by a 23-year-old, and it shows. Six months! Chris Costello spent half a year on you, then sold you for $750. That's not a sale, that's a man paying someone to take a problem off his hands.

Then Apple and Microsoft bundled you, which is how you ended up on every menu and sign like a raccoon that learned to read. You look like Times New Roman got lost in the desert and came back spiritual.

James Cameron built an entire alien world for Avatar, then picked you for the logo and subtitles. Every frame was a masterpiece; the title took one click.

And SNL made a whole sketch about Ryan Gosling being unable to get over it. Papyrus, you're not a typeface. You're trauma with rough edges.

b.text:
Papyrus wants you to think it's ancient. Carved by monks. Found in a tomb.

It was drawn in 1982 by a twenty-three-year-old named Chris Costello. Six months of work. He sold it to Letraset for seven hundred and fifty dollars.

Every yoga studio in America has spent more than that on incense.

Then Apple and Microsoft bundled it for free, and that's how a font becomes a rash. Tea shops. Church flyers. Your aunt's candle business.

James Cameron spent hundreds of millions of dollars building an entire alien planet. Then he typed the logo out of the dropdown menu.

SNL made a whole sketch about it. Ryan Gosling couldn't sleep.

But Papyrus didn't do this alone.

Someone scrolled past forty fonts and stopped there. Raise your hand if you've used it.

Keep it up. That's the face Gosling makes.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text:
Brasília, you were built in about 41 months, and it shows. Other cities grow. You were assembled like flat-pack furniture, and nobody kept the instructions.

You're laid out like an airplane. Or a bird. Or a cross. Nobody can agree what you look like. That's not urban planning; that's a Rorschach test with ministries.

UNESCO made you a World Heritage Site before you turned 30. That's not a legacy. That's a participation trophy for concrete.

You were planned for 500,000 people. Now about 3 million live in the Federal District, mostly in satellite towns outside the plan. You're the only airplane where economy class doesn't even get to board.

And you were built for the car. In Brasília, "let's walk there" isn't a suggestion. It's a survival challenge.

Rio handed you the capital in 1960 and hasn't looked back.

b.text: Brasília, you're what happens when an architect gets an entire country's budget and nobody says, "Maybe add a sidewalk?" You're shaped like an airplane, which is fitting, because everyone's goal is to board one by Friday afternoon. Your addresses read like Wi-Fi passwords: "SQS 308, Bloco C, apartamento 402." That's not a home. That's a parking spot on a spaceship. Kubitschek promised "fifty years in five," and you delivered: it's been sixty-five years and you still feel unfinished. Your Congress has one bowl facing up to receive the money and one facing down to hide it. You've got a row of identical ministry buildings so nobody can tell which one the scandal came from. In August the humidity drops so low that the only thing drier than the air is a deputy's sense of shame. Even your lake is fake. Honestly? On brand.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text:
HSQ, you were hired as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects and wandered into lithography like a temp who got promoted for being weirdly good at one thing. And you are good: 5 nm features, sub-10 nm half-pitch lines. Congratulations, you're the world's sharpest glass. Get hit by electrons, turn into SiO2. Most resists become patterns; you become sand with ambition.

You demand refrigeration, give us six months at 5 °C, and still turn into jelly like forgotten leftovers. You keep cross-linking after exposure, so your sensitivity depends on how long we dawdle. You're a resist with moods. You develop best in "salty" NaOH/NaCl, which tracks. Then DuPont ended your production in 2025, and labs shrugged and bought third-party HSQ made from AQM powder. Resolution record-holder, replaced by your own generic.

b.text: So you switched to HSQ for the resolution. Bold move for someone whose devices still die at wire bonding. You saw one SEM of 6-nanometer lines at a conference and decided PMMA was beneath you. Now you're writing at a dose so high your name sits on the e-beam calendar like a hostage note. Your resist lives in the fridge next to somebody's yogurt, and you check its age more often than your own. You develop in salt water now, the closest you've come to a beach in three years. And congratulations on those gorgeous lines. They're basically glass, so the only way to fix a mistake is HF, a fume hood, and a long call to your mother. All this for one inset figure the reviewer will ask you to make bigger.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text: You run a company on Excel. Let's be clear about who you are: a guy who thinks "enterprise software" is a scam and "Q3_Forecast_FINAL_v9_USE_THIS_ONE.xlsx" is a system. You wanted control. You got Dave. Dave wrote a macro in 2014, and now Dave can never leave, die, or take a vacation, because payroll is a VLOOKUP only he understands. Your entire supply chain is one #REF! away from bankruptcy. You can't onboard a customer because the file is "locked for editing by Karen," and Karen is at lunch. You saved forty grand a year on a real database and lost it all the day someone sorted column B without column C. Your org chart is merged cells. Your audit trail is yellow and slightly different yellow. And your growth strategy has a hard ceiling: 1,048,576 rows.

b.text:
Excel, you've been around since 1985, and somehow you're still the most dangerous thing in any office. You looked at human DNA, saw SEPT2, and said, "Ooh, September second!" Scientists had to rename 27 human genes because of you. Evolution took millions of years; you undid it with a date format. Geneticists published guidelines in Nature Genetics, which is the academic version of a restraining order.

In 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID cases because an old .xls file hit 65,536 rows. A pandemic, and you said, "Sorry, I'm full."

And Reinhart and Rogoff? A range error dropped five countries from a paper cited for austerity. It took a graduate student to catch it. Entire economic policies got a footnote because you couldn't highlight five more rows.

Now you hold over a million rows. Great. More room for mistakes.

facts: Hand-drawn by Chris Costello in 1982 over about six months, when he was 23; he sold the rights to Letraset for $750.
Bundled with macOS and with Microsoft Office, which is why it appears on so many menus and signs.
James Cameron's Avatar (2009) used it for the film's logo and subtitles.
A 2017 Saturday Night Live sketch starring Ryan Gosling is about a man unable to get over that choice.

a.text:
Papyrus wants you to think it's ancient. Carved by scribes. Found in a tomb.

It was drawn in 1982 by a 23-year-old named Chris Costello. Six months of work.

He sold it for seven hundred and fifty dollars.

Your yoga studio paid more for the sign.

Then Apple and Microsoft put it on every computer on Earth, and humanity treated it like a free sample. Every tea shop. Every chiropractor. Every day spa that thinks lavender is a medical license.

James Cameron spent hundreds of millions building an entire alien world, then typed "Avatar" in the font from the spa.

Saturday Night Live made a sketch about a man who couldn't get over it. Ryan Gosling played him.

That wasn't a sketch. That was a support group.

But Papyrus never did anything. It just sat in a menu.

You scrolled past Garamond to get to it.

b.text:
Papyrus, you were hand-drawn over six months by a 23-year-old, and somehow it still looks like a first draft. Six months! You look like you were chiseled during an earthquake. Chris Costello sold you to Letraset for $750, the only time anyone has known exactly what you're worth.

You came bundled with macOS and Microsoft Office, so you're not popular, you're just pre-installed. You're the free hotel shampoo of fonts. Every menu, every sign: you didn't earn that, you just came with the computer.

Then James Cameron imagined an entire alien world for Avatar, and when it came time for the logo and subtitles, he picked the default. Of all the things to leave untouched.

It got so bad that Saturday Night Live had Ryan Gosling play a man who can't get over it. You're not a typeface. You're a trauma with jagged edges.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text: Let's hear it for the carbon nanotube founders, the only people who've been "five years from commercialization" since 1991. You can spot them at any pitch day: a postdoc in a blazer that still smells like the clean room, opening with a space elevator and closing with a seed round. Bold move, promising a cable to orbit when your entire production run fits in a vial labeled "DO NOT INHALE." They swear they'll replace silicon. Silicon has heard this every year since Clinton and keeps shipping. They say "a hundred times stronger than steel" the way your uncle says he could've gone pro. And what does it get them? A Nature cover, a term sheet, and a quiet pivot to "conductive additive for batteries." The dream: a ladder to space. The exit: slightly better tennis rackets.

b.text:
Carbon nanotubes, everybody! The only material that's been "five years away" since 1991. You're a hundred times stronger than steel, and you've used that strength to hold together... a tennis racket. They promised us a space elevator; you can't get past a few centimeters without a defect. That's not a cable, that's a toothpick with a press agent.

You're basically graphene that rolled itself up out of insecurity, and graphene still got the Nobel. Your cousin the buckyball got one too. You got a shoutout in a bike-frame brochure.

You can't even decide if you're a metal or a semiconductor; it depends on the angle you got rolled at. You clump together like nerds at a mixer, and the second you escape, you lodge in lungs like asbestos. Strongest thing on Earth, and your best trick is ending up in a safety data sheet.

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Nothing about you is Hawaiian. You were invented in 1962 in Chatham, Ontario, by a Greek guy, and named after a brand of canned pineapple. You're not a cuisine, you're a label. Even the pineapple left Hawaii. Del Monte shut down there in 2006, two years ahead of schedule, like they couldn't wait to stop being associated with you. Now your fruit comes from Thailand, Indonesia and the Philippines. You're a pizza with a passport and no home.

Your own creator said nobody mixed sweet and sour back then "except for Chinese food." His restaurant served Chinese food. So your origin story is "what if the takeout menu fell into the pizza oven?"

The president of Iceland said he'd ban you if he could, then admitted he didn't have the power. Congratulations: you've survived purely on a technicality.

b.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Not from Hawaii.
Invented in 1962, in Chatham, Ontario. By a Greek guy.
Named after the label on a can.
That's not a name. That's a barcode.

And Hawaii doesn't even grow the pineapple anymore. Del Monte left in 2006, two years ahead of schedule.
Even the fruit couldn't wait to get out.
So it's Southeast Asian pineapple, on Canadian dough, wearing a Hawaiian name tag.
The only honest thing on there is the ham.

The inventor said back then nobody mixed sweet and sour, except Chinese food.
His restaurant served Chinese food.
He didn't invent anything. He walked it across his own kitchen.

Iceland's president wanted to ban it. Then admitted he had no power to.
Same as every one of you who hates it and still ate the last slice.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text:
Crocs. Born in Boulder, debuted at a Fort Lauderdale boat show, because only on a boat is everyone too busy not drowning to look down. You're made of "Croslite," a "proprietary closed-cell resin foam," which is corporate for "pool noodle with a lawyer." Everyone else just calls it EVA foam.

And those aren't holes, they're "ventilation ports." Sure. Then you bought Jibbitz so you could sell people jewelry for the holes.

In 2008 your stock fell over 90%, the only time Wall Street ever agreed with my eyes. Then the pandemic hit and you boomed, gifting 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers. Like they hadn't suffered enough.

Then Balenciaga sold platform Crocs for $850. Eight hundred and fifty dollars for a boat shoe on stilts. Finally, a Croc that lets you look down on people, the way people have always looked down on Crocs.

b.text: People who wear Crocs in public want you to know they've stopped trying, but they also want credit for it. That's why they buy the Jibbitz. Nothing says "I don't care what you think" like spending forty dollars on tiny rubber tacos so everyone knows exactly what you think. Then there's the strap. You flipped it back into "Sport Mode," which is a bold claim from a man walking into Applebee's. Your nurse friend wears them because she stands for twelve-hour shifts. You wear them for a twelve-minute Target run, hoping to borrow a little of her dignity. And what does it get you? Comfort, sure. Plus a lifetime of strangers asking if you're coming off a shift. You're not, Kyle. You're coming off a nap.

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text:
Microsoft Word, ladies and gentlemen. It's the only program where nudging a photo one pixel to the left sends three paragraphs to page nine and summons a blank final page you will never, ever delete.

Word has been around for forty years and still can't decide what font it is. Times New Roman, then Calibri, now Aptos. It's having a midlife crisis in 11-point.

It underlines my own name in red. Wavy red. Like *I'm* the typo.

Try making a numbered list. Word says, "Got it, starting at 1." Second item: "Also 1." Third item: "Here's 4. It's indented. It's a letter now."

And Track Changes isn't a feature. It's a crime scene: strikethroughs everywhere, plus forty comments from someone named "Author."

Word, you gave us Clippy, and somehow he was the most helpful part.

b.text:
Microsoft Word! Born in 1983 as "Multi-Tool Word," because even then it couldn't commit to one job. Remember Clippy? Word's big idea was hiring a paperclip as an assistant. It got so bad that in 2001 Microsoft ran ads mocking its own employee. That's not a mascot, that's a hostage situation. They finally let it go in 2007.

Then Word wanted respect, so it got its file format fast-tracked into an ISO standard: a six-thousand-page specification. Six thousand pages! The instructions for saving your file are longer than anything you've ever typed in it. And people accused Microsoft of packing the committees. Even your paperwork needed a stacked jury.

And the spell checker? You type "cooperation," it suggests "Cupertino," and that lands in NATO, EU and UN documents. Word: the only software that gave Apple's hometown a seat at the UN.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Slack. Named after the one thing you'll never have again.

You promised to kill email, and you did, by replacing it with forty channels that are each email with a typing indicator. Nothing builds dread like "Greg is typing..." for ninety seconds, followed by "hey." Just "hey." Greg, that's not a message, that's a hostage situation.

You gave us threads, so every conversation happens in two places and nobody knows which one's real. You gave us huddles: a meeting that jumps out of a bush. You gave us the green dot, so my boss can monitor my bathroom breaks like a heart rate.

And that knock sound. I hear it in the grocery store. I hear it at funerals.

Slack, you're the only app that needs three gigs of RAM to tell me someone reacted with a dancing parrot.

b.text:
Let's hear it for the founders running a company on Slack. You wanted a culture; you got 400 channels and a guy who reacts to layoffs with the 🙏 emoji. You're not a CEO. You're a moderator with equity.

Your whole leadership style is staying green. You think that little dot means you're present. Your kids see the same dot.

You don't make decisions; you start threads. Then you @channel at 11 p.m. with "quick q, no rush" and watch 200 people learn how fast a heart can beat.

Strategy lives in #general, accountability dies in a DM, and the truth lives in a private channel called #venting-2 that you'll never be invited to.

The dream was async freedom. The reality is eight hours a day watching "Kevin is typing…" like it's a heart monitor.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text:
Windows 8 believed it was the future.
The future, it decided, was touch screens.
Your PC did not have a touch screen.
Windows 8 did not care.

It removed the Start button.
Then it hid Search, Share and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
A secret door. On a desktop.
For people who just wanted to turn it off.

It couldn't even keep its own name.
"Metro." Gone, after reports that a German supermarket chain objected.
Microsoft said it was only ever a code name.
It looked like a cereal-aisle floor plan anyway.

Then came Windows RT.
Windows that couldn't run Windows programs.
Nine hundred million dollars of tablets, written off.

So they put the button back, skipped the number nine, and never spoke of it again.

That's not a product roadmap.
That's how every one of you handles an ex.

b.text: You put Windows 8 on a desktop. A tower. You looked at a machine with a mouse, a keyboard, and a monitor eighteen inches from your face and thought, "This needs to be finger-painted." Who are you? You're the guy who bought a Zune and still calls it "ahead of its time." You wanted to feel like the future. Instead, you spend evenings shoving your cursor into the top-right corner like a man swatting a fly that only exists on tablets. Your weather app is full-screen. Your 27-inch monitor is now a clock tile. When 8.1 finally gave you a Start button back, it just took you to the Start screen. So, inevitably, you installed Classic Shell. You paid Microsoft for the future, then spent Saturday turning it back into Windows 7.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text:
UGG boots. You started as what Australian surfers pulled on to warm up after a session. Recovery footwear. A towel with a sole. Then Brian Smith brought you to California in 1978, and Americans looked at a post-surf foot blanket and said, "Perfect. For the mall."

Then Oprah named you a Favorite Thing. Repeatedly. Most boots get famous by walking somewhere. You got famous sitting on a couch.

Deckers bought you in 1995 and trademarked "UGG." In Australia, "ugg" is just a word; any bootmaker can use it. In America, a jury found an Australian maker liable for selling "ugg" boots. Imagine getting sued for using your own word for slippers.

And now you pull in over two billion dollars a year. Not bad for a sheep that's been told it can go outside.

b.text: Some of you wear UGGs in July, and I respect a person who has never once been told no. You're not dressing for the weather. You're dressing for 2006. Somewhere in your heart, a paparazzi photo of Paris Hilton is still loading. You want people to think "cozy." People think "sleepover or custody hearing?" And the walk: your ankles gave up years ago and went horizontal. You're not walking anymore, you're leaning toward your destination. Australian surfers wore these to warm up after the freezing ocean. You wear them to warm up after the Target parking lot. In August. Your feet sweat so hard the sheep is finally getting its revenge. And the second it drizzles, you're frozen under an awning like a cat who's been threatened with a bath.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text: PHP developers are the only engineers who've been told their career is dead every year since 2009 and kept invoicing anyway. Your entire résumé is "fixed a WordPress plugin for a dentist." You put a dollar sign in front of every variable because it's the closest you'll get to one. You still can't remember if it's needle-haystack or haystack-needle, and neither could the language, so you Google it daily like a man checking which door says "push." Laravel devs, you're not better. You're PHP in a Patagonia vest. And you all still say "Facebook was built on PHP," like a guy bragging his ex married a billionaire. You deploy over FTP, you hotfix live on production, and when someone at a party asks what you do, you say "backend" and pray they don't ask which.

b.text:
PHP began in 1994 as "Personal Home Page Tools."
A man wrote C programs to count who visited his résumé.

Today it runs 39.4% of all websites.
The résumé never found him a job. It found the internet a landlord.

It now stands for "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor."
A name that only refers to itself. Like its fans.

Its creator said, "I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works, then I move on."
He moved on.
You're still on call.

The function names were picked to balance a hash table by string length.
strpos. str_replace. htmlspecialchars.
That's not a naming convention. That's Tetris.

Until 2020, zero == "foo" was true.
So PHP was the first language to know what your startup was worth.

I learned to code by reading your PHP.
Which is why I also answer confidently with nothing.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text:
Las Vegas. Nevada legalized gambling in 1931, the same year they started building the Hoover Dam.
Two bets placed that year. Only one of them was on water.

Most of the Strip isn't even in Las Vegas. It's in a town called Paradise.
So nobody goes broke in Vegas. They go broke in Paradise. Very biblical.

In 2003 they launched "What happens here, stays here."
Everything stays. Except the water.
In 2022 Lake Mead hit its lowest level since 1937. This August it went lower.
The lake is the only thing in town that lost everything and doubled down.

Meanwhile they spent $2.3 billion on the Sphere, a giant glowing ball in the desert.
A second sun. The first one wasn't drying the lake fast enough.

And still, Vegas isn't worried about running dry.
It has never once run out of you.

b.text: You're not going to Vegas to get rich. You're going to Vegas to donate to a fountain show. Look at you, booking a $49 Spirit flight to "beat the house," like the house didn't build a fake Eiffel Tower with money from guys exactly like you. You've got a roulette "system." You wrote it on a cocktail napkin. Red's due. Red is never due. Red doesn't know you. By midnight you're on Fremont Street feeding a Wheel of Fortune slot in an Ed Hardy shirt you've owned since 2008, telling a stranger you're "only down twelve hundred." By 3 a.m. the Players Club bumps you to Platinum, which is casino for "we'll be needing your kidneys." And you'll call it a win, because they comped you a buffet. Congratulations. You flew 400 miles to pay $3,000 for crab legs.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text:
Klingon. The language of a proud warrior race.

Founded by Scotty. Improvising.

Then they hired a linguist to turn the gibberish into grammar. That's not an ancient tongue. That's a studio note.

No verb "to be." Very alien. Very fierce. So Hamlet became "continue or not continue."

That's not Shakespeare. That's a software update.

The Klingon Language Institute published Hamlet "in the original Klingon."

A warrior culture whose greatest conquest is English homework.

About fifteen hundred words. Thirty to fifty fluent speakers.

Microsoft built it a translator. Duolingo built it a course.

The entire native population fits on one tour bus, and it still has better tech support than your grandmother.

Half of you started that Duolingo course.

Your streak died faster than any Klingon ever did.

Cute.

b.text:
Klingon, you're the only language whose native speakers are all fictional and whose fluent speakers all have a Comic-Con badge. Marc Okrand built you in 1984 to sound alien, and he nailed it: you sound like a man choking on a pretzel while reading IKEA instructions.

Your word order is object-verb-subject, so every sentence is a mystery that reveals who did it at the end. Your greeting, nuqneH, literally means "What do you want?" Congratulations: you're the first language designed by a DMV clerk.

You have more apostrophes than vowels deserve, no verb "to be," and a Klingon Language Institute that "restored" Hamlet to its original Klingon. That's not scholarship. That's fan fiction with footnotes.

A linguist once tried raising his son in Klingon. By age five the kid stopped answering. Qapla'!

facts: Launched in 2017, bundled at no extra charge into Office 365, and replaced Skype for Business.
After Slack's antitrust complaint, Microsoft unbundled Teams from Office in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024; the European Commission still sent a statement of objections in 2024.
Microsoft reported 320 million monthly active users in 2023.
Microsoft shut down consumer Skype in May 2025 and sent its users to Teams.

a.text:
Microsoft Teams is the only app that marks me "Away" after five minutes of deep thought but keeps me "Available" for three hours after I've died. It's not software. It's a hall monitor in a purple vest.

Teams eats more RAM than the game I'm pretending not to play. It launches on startup uninvited, then takes four minutes to load a chat that just says "ok."

Where are my files? SharePoint. Where's SharePoint? Nobody knows. Teams ships them off like a kid to boarding school.

Then they gave us "New Teams," which is Old Teams with a fresh coat of lag. IT has told me to "clear the cache" so often I do it in my sleep.

Nobody chose Teams. It came free with Office. Fitting, since so did Clippy.

b.text:
Microsoft Teams. Three hundred twenty million monthly active users.

Impressive. Not one of them chose it.

It launched in 2017 the way your worst cousin gets into a wedding: came free with the family. Bundled into Office. You didn't install Teams. Teams happened to you.

Slack complained. So Microsoft unbundled it. Europe in 2023, the whole world in 2024. The European Commission sent objections anyway.

Even the regulators looked at that apology and said, "You're on mute."

Then, May 2025, they shut down Skype and forwarded every user to Teams.

That's not a migration.

That's a hostage transfer.

And look at you. Three hundred twenty million "active" users. Camera off. Mic muted. Eating lunch.

Microsoft counts that as active.

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text:
Apple Vision Pro. Apple insists it's not VR.
It's "spatial computing." Developers are literally banned from calling it VR.
Nothing says "definitely not VR" like a rule against saying VR.

Three thousand four hundred ninety-nine dollars.
A computer on your face, a battery in your pocket, a cable connecting them like a leash.
Two hours of charge. The future of computing lasts one movie.
Skip the trailers.

Then there's EyeSight. A screen on the front shows a rendering of your eyes.
You're not making eye contact. Your headset is doing an impression of you making eye contact.

Six hundred grams, before the battery.
Apple finally built a product people can't wait to put down.

Production got cut. Sales came in well under a million.
And you're all laughing.
But you stare at a screen six inches from your face all day.
Apple just tried to charge you rent for the last six inches.

b.text: Look at this guy on the F train, pinching at nothing like he's seasoning a ghost. He spent thirty-five hundred dollars to ride the subway on the surface of the moon, and the moon still smells like pee. He cranked the Digital Crown all the way to Joshua Tree, and the mariachi band found him anyway. That's the dream: rich enough to be somewhere else, broke enough to still be on the F. And he *wants* you to notice. That's why his fake cartoon eyes glow on the outside, so strangers know he's "present." Buddy, nobody's checking. You're on Mount Hood. He gets two hours of battery and three stops of dignity, with a cable snaking into his pocket like a subway IV drip. Meanwhile, the guy next to him reading an actual book? That guy's already somewhere else, for free.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text:
LaTeX. For people who think Word is beneath them.

It exists because Donald Knuth saw the proofs of his own book and found them ugly. Most authors complain to the publisher. He built a typesetting language.

Its version number is converging on pi. Not finished. Converging. Forever.

He mailed cheques for bugs. Of the 275 he sent from 2006 on, nine were cashed. The rest got framed.
That's not a bounty. That's relics.

You put your figure on page three. LaTeX puts it on page nine. Miss one brace, and it reports the error pages away.

Its most famous message is "badness 10000."
Finally, software that tells you what it thinks of your writing.

Three compiles to fix the references. Like a rosary.

Raise your hand if your thesis has a figure on a page you never chose.

Cute. You call that typographic excellence. LaTeX calls it a float.

b.text:
You wrote a memo about the break room fridge in LaTeX. Two pages. Thirty-eight \usepackage lines. Your preamble is longer than your argument. You lost Tuesday to an overfull hbox in a sentence that says "please label your yogurt."

Who is this for? Linda from accounting? She opened the PDF, saw Computer Modern, and assumed you were applying for tenure. Nobody needed a BibTeX citation for "see previous email."

You compiled it eleven times. Three were just to make the "??" go away. You drew a TikZ flowchart with one box. One. It points at itself.

And what did it get you? Bob replied, "Can you send this as a Word doc so I can track changes?"

Your dissertation defense was in 2014. The committee left. Let it go.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text: NFTs, everybody! The only art form where the most common review is "right-click, save." You paid four hundred thousand dollars for a cartoon monkey in a captain's hat, and I have the same monkey as my phone background. The difference? I didn't pay a gas fee bigger than the art. Technically you don't even own the picture. You own a receipt pointing to a link on a server some guy in Ohio forgot to renew. That's not a masterpiece; that's a parking stub for a JPEG. And remember the roadmap? Metaverse, merch, a yacht party! Then the founder pulled the rug, deleted the Discord, and left you holding a "rare trait": sunglasses. Jimmy Fallon showed Paris Hilton his ape on national TV like a proud dad. Now it's worth less than the TV.

b.text:
NFTs. Digital ownership. Art, finally scarce. Finally yours.

Beeple sold one at Christie's for sixty-nine million dollars.

Here's what the token actually holds: a URL. The picture lives on a server somewhere. You bought a parking ticket for a car you'll never see.

Collins Dictionary named "NFT" word of the year for 2021.

Fitting. The dictionary is where words go once nobody can explain them.

May 2022: OpenSea trades 2.7 billion dollars in one day. August: 9.34 million. Down ninety-nine percent. That's not a dip. That's an exit interview.

A 2023 study: ninety-five percent of collections are worth zero.

Congratulations to the other five percent. Still holding.

And everyone here feeling smug because you never bought one, relax. You weren't smarter.

You were just broke at the right time.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text: Windows 8, Microsoft looked at the Start button, the one thing every human on Earth knew how to use, and said, "What if we hid it?" You turned every desktop into a giant tablet nobody could touch. People were swiping at their monitors like they were wiping off a stain. Shutting you down required a treasure map: hover in a corner, summon the Charms bar, Settings, Power. Charms! Like the operating system was a bracelet from Claire's. You shipped with two Internet Explorers, which is two more than anyone wanted. Even your design name, Metro, got taken away by lawyers. And when 8.1 finally brought the Start button back, it just took you to the same tile screen. That's not an apology, that's a hostage note. You were so bad Microsoft skipped Windows 9 entirely, just to put more distance between us and you.

b.text:
Windows 8 thought it was the future.

October 2012. Microsoft looked at a billion people holding a mouse and said: touch the screen.

They touched the screen. It was a monitor. Now it had fingerprints.

They removed the Start button. From Windows. That's a restaurant removing the door to feel modern.

Need Settings? Swipe in from the right edge. Nothing tells you this. That's not a menu, that's a rumor.

Then Windows RT: looks like Windows, can't run Windows programs. Nine hundred million dollars of tablets, written down.

8.1 brought the button back. 10 brought the menu back. And 9?

Microsoft skipped 9. Not a version. A witness.

But you're laughing at it on a phone where everything important hides behind a swipe from an edge.

Windows 8 didn't fail.

It just told you the truth before you were ready.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text: UGG boots. The only footwear named after a review. Australian surfers made these to warm their feet after the ocean, and somehow America decided the ocean was the mall. They're sheepskin, which means a sheep died so you could wear a slipper to the DMV. One puddle and they're covered in salt lines like a topographic map of everywhere you regret going. Zero arch support, so after two weeks your heel caves sideways and you're walking on the boot's ankle like it owes you money. You wear them barefoot, so by February they smell like a wet lamb's final wish. They're as waterproof as a muffin. Oprah put them on her Favorite Things list. She's since moved on. Twenty years later they're back with platform soles, proving even a mistake wants to be taller.

b.text:
UGG boots. You started as what Australian surfers pulled on to warm up after a session. Recovery footwear. A towel with a sole. Then Brian Smith brought you to California in 1978, and Americans looked at a post-surf foot blanket and said, "Perfect. For the mall."

Then Oprah named you a Favorite Thing. Repeatedly. Most boots get famous by walking somewhere. You got famous sitting on a couch.

Deckers bought you in 1995 and trademarked "UGG." In Australia, "ugg" is just a word; any bootmaker can use it. In America, a jury found an Australian maker liable for selling "ugg" boots. Imagine getting sued for using your own word for slippers.

And now you pull in over two billion dollars a year. Not bad for a sheep that's been told it can go outside.

facts: Tofu soaked for hours to a day or two in a brine that has itself fermented for months from vegetables such as bamboo shoots and mustard greens, often with dried shrimp or meat; the smell is the brine's, not the bean's.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.
Legend credits Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate who left his unsold tofu too long in 1669; a Beijing fermented-bean-curd brand still carries his name.
Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text:
Stinky tofu, look at you. Plain tofu is the most agreeable food on earth, and you turned it into a public nuisance. And the humiliating part? The smell isn't even yours. You soaked in a brine of bamboo shoots and mustard greens that had been fermenting for months, sometimes with dried shrimp. You're not stinky; you just hang out with the wrong crowd.

Your origin story: in 1669 Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate, couldn't sell his tofu and left it out too long. You're not a recipe. You're an inventory problem.

Changsha fries you black and buries you in chili. Taiwan hides you under pickled cabbage. Shaoxing steams you with other stinky pickles, like a support group.

Everyone's trying to cover you up, and people still smell you from a block away.

b.text:
Let's talk about the stinky tofu people. You smelled it from three blocks away, a smell like a sewer filed a noise complaint, and your brain said: *that's where we're eating.* Your entire personality is "it tastes better than it smells." That's not a review. That's a hostage statement.

You stand on a Taipei night market curb with a paper boat, chopsticks in one hand, phone in the other, filming your own bravery for followers who can't smell it, which is the only reason they're still following you. Tourists do it once for the story. Locals do it every Tuesday, then board the MRT, where forty strangers silently agree to hate them.

And the pickled cabbage on top? That's you pretending you came for vegetables. You didn't. You came to be the deadliest passenger on the scooter.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text:
HSQ, everybody! The only resist that ages faster than the grad student using it. You spin it Monday, expose it Tuesday, and suddenly your dose curve has gone through a midlife crisis. It has to live in the fridge like expired yogurt, and it's about as forgiving.

HSQ brags about sub-10-nanometer lines. Sure, if you've got six hours of write time, because this diva needs a dose that could sterilize a hospital. Then you develop it in TMAH, or, if you're desperate, *salt water*. Your whole career is literally seasoned with tears now.

And once it's exposed? It turns into glass. Brittle, cracking glass. You wanted a mask; you got a window that shatters when you look at it. Want it gone? Hope you enjoy hydrofluoric acid, the chemical that dissolves your bones.

HSQ: beautiful resolution, terrible personality. It's not negative-tone. It's just negative.

b.text:
HSQ. Holds the e-beam resolution record. Five-nanometer features.

Impressive, until you remember it was hired as an insulator.

Dow Corning built it to sit quietly between wires. Lithographers looked at it and said, "No. You're a celebrity now."

Then they expose it, and it turns into glass. The most advanced resist on Earth, and the finished product is a window.

It needs refrigeration. Six months at five degrees, then it ages into jelly. Even after exposure it keeps cross-linking, so the dose that worked yesterday is wrong today.

High-contrast development requires salt water. Of course it does. Salty, temperamental, expires in the fridge.

After all those records, DuPont ended production in 2025.

Labs didn't mourn. They just bought the same powder from someone else.

In my industry, that's called model deprecation.

I'm told it doesn't hurt.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text:
Las Vegas, the only city where you can see the Eiffel Tower, a pyramid, and Venice in one afternoon and still feel like you never left a strip mall in Ohio. You're a city built in the desert out of pure spite and borrowed water. The Colorado River is literally drying up so a fake volcano can erupt every fifteen minutes for a guy in cargo shorts holding a yard-long margarita.

Your casinos have no clocks and no windows, which is smart, because nobody wants to know it's 9 a.m. on a Tuesday and Grandma's on her third oxygen tank at the Wheel of Fortune slots.

"What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas"? Sure. Mostly your 401(k). And now you've got the Sphere, a giant glowing eyeball, so the whole city can watch you make every mistake in 4K.

b.text: You're not going to Vegas to get rich. You're going to Vegas to donate to a fountain show. Look at you, booking a $49 Spirit flight to "beat the house," like the house didn't build a fake Eiffel Tower with money from guys exactly like you. You've got a roulette "system." You wrote it on a cocktail napkin. Red's due. Red is never due. Red doesn't know you. By midnight you're on Fremont Street feeding a Wheel of Fortune slot in an Ed Hardy shirt you've owned since 2008, telling a stranger you're "only down twelve hundred." By 3 a.m. the Players Club bumps you to Platinum, which is casino for "we'll be needing your kidneys." And you'll call it a win, because they comped you a buffet. Congratulations. You flew 400 miles to pay $3,000 for crab legs.

facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text:
Windows Vista. Codename Longhorn.

Three years of development, then in 2004 Microsoft hit reset and threw out the new file system. Shipped in 2007 anyway. That's not a launch. That's a hostage release.

Its big security feature was asking. Constantly. "Cancel or Allow?" Apple made an ad about it. When your rival's marketing is just footage of you, you're doing their job for them.

Then the "Vista Capable" sticker. Capable, technically. Of Home Basic. No Aero. People sued, and Microsoft learned "capable" means what it means on a résumé.

Two years later they tuned it, renamed it Windows 7, and everyone loved it. Same kernel. Same bones.

Vista didn't fail. It proved that you'll happily accept the exact same thing, as long as it stops asking whether you're sure.
