b.text: Let's hear it for the day-one Vista crowd, the people who lined up at CompUSA on January 30th, 2007 because a billboard said "The Wow Starts Now." You paid $399 for Ultimate so Flip 3D could shuffle the same three windows you used to Alt-Tab through. Your laptop had a "Vista Capable" sticker and 512 megs of RAM, which is like slapping "Marathon Capable" on a hamster. You wanted to look like the future; you had Aero turned off by Wednesday. Your printer quit. Your Sound Blaster went mute. Your "Ultimate Extras" turned out to be a poker game and a promise. And every time you tried to show off, the screen went dark and asked, "Are you sure?" Buddy, nobody was sure. Not even Microsoft. They were already working on Windows 7.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text:
Durian, they call you the King of Fruits, which tracks, because like most monarchies, you stink and nobody's allowed to say it to your face.

You're the only fruit with a criminal record. Banned on the Singapore subway, alongside flammable liquids. Hotels put your picture on signs next to "no smoking." In 2019, a university in Melbourne evacuated five hundred people because they thought there was a gas leak. Nope. Just you, sitting in a cupboard, being yourself.

And the armor! You're covered in spikes like a medieval mace. Nature built you to defend yourself, then gave you a smell that does it better. The spikes are just overkill.

Fans say you taste like custard. Sure. Custard that was left in a gym bag next to some onions. Your flavor isn't an acquired taste. It's a hostage situation.

b.text:
People who eat durian in public aren't hungry. They're recruiting. Every bite comes with a sermon: "You just haven't had a *good* one." Sir, I'm on a bus. I didn't ask to join your church.

Singapore fines people for bringing it on the train, and these folks hear that like a dare. They're the only foodies whose restaurant review gets filed as a police report.

And the payoff? Seventy dollars on a Musang King so you can watch strangers silently change seats. You paid premium to become a fire drill. Your date calls it "an acquired taste," which is exactly what you say about someone you're about to break up with.

Then they stroll back to the hotel, walk right past the sign with a red circle through their entire personality, and still act shocked when housekeeping files a complaint.

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
People who order Hawaiian pizza want you to know they're brave. They say "I know, I know" before anyone has said a word, because for them the pineapple isn't a topping, it's a personality. This is a person whose entire rebellious phase fits in a box for $14.99. They've never gotten a tattoo, never quit a job, never sent food back, but once a month they look a teenage cashier dead in the eye and say "pineapple" like they're defusing a bomb.

And they always want to split one with you. Half Hawaiian, half "normal." That's not a compromise. That's a hostage negotiation.

Best part? It isn't even Hawaiian. A Greek guy invented it in Ontario. So congratulations: your one act of rebellion is a Canadian pretending he's on vacation.

b.text:
Hawaiian pizza, you're named after a place you've never been. You were invented in Ontario, by a Greek guy, using canned pineapple. That's not a heritage, that's a witness protection identity.

And the ham? It's Canadian bacon. Even your meat is from Canada. The only Hawaiian thing about you is that people see you and say "aloha," meaning goodbye.

Pineapple has an enzyme that digests protein. You're the only pizza that eats the customer back. Warm fruit juice pooling on mozzarella like a hot tub nobody cleaned.

Italians don't hate you; they pray for you. The president of Iceland said he'd ban you if he could, and Iceland eats fermented shark.

You're not a pizza. You're a fruit cup that fell on a pizza and refused to get up.

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text:
Luosifen. Everybody blames the river snails, but the snails just flavour the broth and keep their heads down. The real stench is pickled bamboo shoots. You're a noodle that framed a snail.

Then in 2020, with the whole country locked indoors, you sold over 10 billion yuan in instant packs. That's not a boom, that's a hostage situation. Millions sealed in their apartments, and you said, "Perfect. Nobody can leave."

In 2021 you became national *intangible* cultural heritage. Intangible? You're the most tangible thing in any building. People can touch you from the hallway.

And Liuzhou opened an entire industry college for you. A full college education to learn what every roommate figures out in four seconds: breathe through your mouth.

b.text:
Luosifen, you're the only dish that arrives before the delivery guy does. You're named after river snails, yet nobody has ever found one in the bowl. You boiled them for hours, took their soul, and threw out the bodies. That's not a recipe, that's a cover-up.

And that smell? Fermented bamboo shoots that died, got buried, and came back for revenge. Someone opens a packet in Liuzhou and a guy in Guilin checks his shoes. College dorms banned you like a space heater. Neighbors call the gas company.

Your fans swear, "It smells terrible but tastes amazing." Buddy, that's what everyone says about their toxic ex.

Peanuts, crispy tofu skin, wood ear, pickled beans, a slick of chili oil... that's not garnish, that's witness protection for flavor.

And now you come instant. Congratulations: a biohazard with a seasoning packet.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text:
Crocs launched in 2002 at the Fort Lauderdale boat show.
As a boating shoe.
The original customer was someone who might end up in the water and wanted the shoes to float.

They're made of "Croslite," a proprietary closed-cell resin.
Everyone else calls it EVA foam.
Same brand of genius that renamed holes "ventilation ports."
Then in 2006 they bought Jibbitz, so they could sell you plugs for the ports.
First they cut the hole. Then they charge rent on it.

In 2008 the stock fell more than ninety percent.
Wall Street called it ugly.
Ten years later Balenciaga stuck one on a platform and charged eight hundred and fifty dollars.
Same foam. Taller.
Still ugly. Just more expensive.

The people who wear them, I leave alone.
Front row, I see you. Socks and all.
You paid extra for the charms. Cute.

b.text:
Crocs. Born in Boulder in 2002, debuted at a boat show as a boating shoe. The one place where looking like you've given up is acceptable, and even there people had questions.

They're made of "Croslite," a "proprietary closed-cell resin foam." Everyone else calls it EVA foam. That's like calling sweatpants "proprietary leg architecture."

The holes are "ventilation ports," so your foot is a space station. You plug them with Jibbitz. Crocs bought Jibbitz in 2006. Sell the holes, then sell the stuff that fills the holes. Genius.

In 2008 the stock fell more than 90%. Then the pandemic hit and they boomed. Crocs needed the world to end to look good.

And Balenciaga sold platform Crocs for about $850. Eight hundred fifty dollars. For a taller mistake.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text:
Google Glass.
Unveiled by skydivers, livestreaming their jump onto the roof of the Moscone Center.
It was the last time anything about it went up.

Fifteen hundred dollars. Invitation only.
You had to be *chosen* to pay that much to look like that.

Bars banned it. Cinemas banned it.
Casinos banned it.
Casinos. Buildings that are ninety percent ceiling camera.
They looked at you and said, "One of us is creepy, and it's you."

The display: 640 by 360, wedged in the corner of one eye.
The future of computing, viewed like a wink.

Consumers gave up in 2015. Enterprise hung on until 2023.
Even the factory workers outlasted it.

They called the wearers Glassholes.
And you laughed.
Then you went home and filmed strangers all day on a phone.
Glass's only real mistake was letting them see the camera.

b.text:
Google Glass, look at you. Fifteen hundred dollars to wear a sugar cube on your eyebrow. Sergey Brin had skydivers jump onto a building to launch you, and that was the last time anything about you was cool.

You invented a whole new insult. Nobody calls iPhone owners "Phoneholes." But "Glasshole"? Earned. Fast. Because you let people take photos by *winking*. You turned flirting into a privacy violation.

Every sentence started with "OK Glass," like a man narrating his own midlife crisis out loud. Bars banned you. Strangers ripped you off people's faces. Your battery died faster than your reputation, and you overheated right next to the user's brain, which honestly explains the buying decision.

Then you pivoted to "Enterprise," the tech version of moving back home to work at your uncle's warehouse.

And even the warehouse let you go.

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text: Hydrogen fuel-cell cars: the only vehicle powered by the most abundant element in the universe that still can't find a gas station. California has about fifty pumps, and half of them are "temporarily offline," which is hydrogen for "go home." Its one emission is water, so it's technically the cleanest car on Earth, as long as you don't ask where the hydrogen came from. Spoiler: natural gas. It's a fossil fuel car in a witness protection program. Toyota gave Mirai buyers fifteen grand in free fuel, which sounds generous until you realize that at thirty-six bucks a kilo it covers roughly a year of driving, and the car loses that much value on the drive home. You're sitting on a tank pressurized to 10,000 psi to go three hundred miles. Even the Hindenburg would say, "Maybe just get a Tesla."

b.text: Hydrogen car owners are the only people who looked at Tesla drivers and thought, "Not enough range anxiety." You didn't buy a car; you entered a relationship with the three working pumps in California and an app that tells you which one is "offline" today. You wanted to save the planet. Instead you burned through Toyota's free fuel card in a year at thirty-six bucks a kilo, filling up with hydrogen made from natural gas. Congratulations, you invented a gas car with extra steps. You love saying the only emission is water. Mostly it's your tears at a shuttered Shell station in Fremont. And resale? Your Mirai lost value faster than your friendships after you said "hydrogen economy" at brunch. You're not early adopters. You're unpaid beta testers who drive two hours to refuel.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text: Windows 8, you booted into a full-screen grid of tiles built for touch screens most PCs didn't have. Everyone poked their monitor like it owed them money. You took away the Start button, the one thing everybody knew how to find, and hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge. Your menu was a séance. Even your name couldn't stay put: Metro was gone by August, before you launched, after reports that a German retailer objected. Microsoft said it was just a code name. Then Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 entirely rather than stand next to you. 8.1 put the Start button back: an apology. Windows 10 restored the menu: a restraining order. And Windows RT, your sibling that couldn't run Windows programs? $900 million in unsold Surface RT tablets. Even your family was a write-off.

b.text: Windows 8, Microsoft looked at the Start button, the one thing every human on Earth knew how to use, and said, "What if we hid it?" You turned every desktop into a giant tablet nobody could touch. People were swiping at their monitors like they were wiping off a stain. Shutting you down required a treasure map: hover in a corner, summon the Charms bar, Settings, Power. Charms! Like the operating system was a bracelet from Claire's. You shipped with two Internet Explorers, which is two more than anyone wanted. Even your design name, Metro, got taken away by lawyers. And when 8.1 finally brought the Start button back, it just took you to the same tile screen. That's not an apology, that's a hostage note. You were so bad Microsoft skipped Windows 9 entirely, just to put more distance between us and you.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text:
Graphene. The wonder material. Discovered in 2004 when two physicists at Manchester peeled graphite with Scotch tape, so your origin story has the same equipment as a kindergarten art project. They got a Nobel in 2010. You got a career as a buzzword.

The EU committed a billion euros over ten years to you. A billion! And where did you end up? Tennis rackets. Running shoes. Headphones. Miracle of the century, living in a sneaker.

Then in 2018, researchers tested "graphene" from 60 producers, and none of it was even half graphene. Mostly graphite flakes. You're so elusive your own suppliers can't find you.

Honestly, Andre Geim levitated a frog with magnets in 2000. That frog has a better résumé than you. At least the frog actually showed up.

b.text: Graphene, you're one atom thick, and somehow that's still more depth than your business plan. Two hundred times stronger than steel, conducts better than copper, and twenty years later your biggest commercial win is a sticker on a tennis racket. You were discovered with Scotch tape. *Scotch tape!* You're the only Nobel Prize that could've been found in a kindergarten craft drawer. And let's be honest: you're pencil lead that went to grad school. Your cousin graphite has been writing grocery lists for centuries; you've been writing grant proposals. Every year a headline swears you'll revolutionize batteries, chips, water filters. Every year you're still in the lab, like a thirty-year-old in his parents' basement. You can't even be a decent transistor. No bandgap. You literally cannot turn off. Graphene: the material of the future, permanently.

facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text:
Juicero, you were a $400 Wi-Fi-connected juicer that delivered four tons of force, enough, your engineers bragged, to lift two Teslas, and Bloomberg proved the job could be done by a guy with hands. You raised $120 million from Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins to compete with *squeezing*. Every single customer already owned the competing product. It came in pairs.

You sold $8 bags of chopped produce that had to scan a QR code and phone home before you'd juice them. A juicer that needed internet. Imagine the outage: "Sorry, AWS is down, enjoy your sealed pouch of regret." You'd refuse to press an expired pack, like a bouncer for kale.

Doug Evans compared himself to Steve Jobs. Steve Jobs put a thousand songs in your pocket. Doug put a sack of mush in a vise and asked for your Wi-Fi password. Silicon Valley's most expensive way to say, "Just use your hands."

b.text:
Juicero, you cost $699 to do what my hands do for free. Then you dropped to $399, still a lot for a machine that lost a race to Bloomberg reporters. They squeezed the bag by hand: 7.5 ounces in 90 seconds. You took two minutes to make 8. You're the only appliance ever outworked by journalists.

And you needed Wi-Fi. You scanned a QR code on a bag of chopped produce and checked it online, like a bouncer carding a kale leaf. Expired? Denied. Router down? No juice. Fruit has been juiceable since fruit.

Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins gave you $120 million, and you lasted until September 2017. Honestly, those refunds were the only thing you ever pressed out efficiently.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text:
Brasília, you were built in about 41 months, and it shows. Other cities grow. You were assembled like flat-pack furniture, and nobody kept the instructions.

You're laid out like an airplane. Or a bird. Or a cross. Nobody can agree what you look like. That's not urban planning; that's a Rorschach test with ministries.

UNESCO made you a World Heritage Site before you turned 30. That's not a legacy. That's a participation trophy for concrete.

You were planned for 500,000 people. Now about 3 million live in the Federal District, mostly in satellite towns outside the plan. You're the only airplane where economy class doesn't even get to board.

And you were built for the car. In Brasília, "let's walk there" isn't a suggestion. It's a survival challenge.

Rio handed you the capital in 1960 and hasn't looked back.

b.text:
Brasília. Forty-one months from scrubland to capital city.
You know what else ships that fast with zero user testing?
Me.
They drew the city as an airplane, with the government in the fuselage.
Brilliant. An airplane is the one place you're not allowed to walk around.
Wide avenues, hardly any crossings.
In Brasília, a pedestrian isn't a person. It's a speed bump.
Planned for half a million people. Three million showed up.
The plan's answer: please wait outside the plan.
UNESCO made it World Heritage after twenty-seven years.
Most cities have to die first. Brasília just had to keep the people out of the photo.
You're laughing. Your company's org chart is an airplane too.
Leadership in the fuselage, everyone else in the satellite towns.
And nobody walks to the cockpit.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text: Walking in Brasília is for three kinds of people: architecture students, tourists who trusted Google Maps, and the intern whose ministry is "right next door" on the Esplanada, which here means a forty-minute hike with no shade and a dry-season humidity of 11%. You're not pedestrians, you're pilgrims. You came for Niemeyer and left with heatstroke and a dirt trail you personally wore into the grass, because Lúcio Costa forgot you'd have legs. You cross the Eixão like it's a Frogger level with bureaucrats at 80 km/h, then descend into a tesourinha and come out three superquadras from where you started. Somebody gave you directions: "SQS 308, Bloco C." Congratulations, you're in a spreadsheet. And on Sunday, when they close the Eixão so you can finally walk it, you'll realize there's still nowhere to go.

b.text:
Brasília. City of the future. Built in forty-one months.

Which explains a lot.

Lúcio Costa drew it as an airplane. Gorgeous. From the sky.

From the ground, it's eight lanes, no crosswalks, and the nearest coffee is "a short drive."

Pedestrians aren't residents. They're a design flaw.

UNESCO made it World Heritage at twenty-seven years old. Most buildings that young get a parking ticket, not a plaque.

Planned for five hundred thousand people. Today the district holds three million.

Where's everyone else?

Outside the plan. In the satellite towns. Commuting in to clean the future.

You're laughing.

Pull up your company's org chart. Also a beautiful airplane.

The people who do the work aren't on that drawing either.

facts: Launched in 2017, bundled at no extra charge into Office 365, and replaced Skype for Business.
After Slack's antitrust complaint, Microsoft unbundled Teams from Office in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024; the European Commission still sent a statement of objections in 2024.
Microsoft reported 320 million monthly active users in 2023.
Microsoft shut down consumer Skype in May 2025 and sent its users to Teams.

a.text:
Let's hear it for the IT director who chose Microsoft Teams, a man who has never once chosen anything. It came bundled with Outlook, like coleslaw you're contractually obligated to eat. The EU had to force Microsoft to stop shoving it on people, and your company still went back for seconds. The whole pitch was "It's already in the license." So was Clippy, Gary.

Management loves it because now they can watch your little dot. Green means productive. Yellow means you went to the bathroom and Linda noticed. They didn't want collaboration. They wanted a heart monitor.

And what did it get them? Every meeting opens with eight adults asking "Can you see my screen?" while a VP uses the raise-hand button to interrupt people *harder*. Congratulations: you saved nine dollars a seat and lost the will to live.

b.text: Microsoft Teams is the only app that got popular the way a parking ticket gets popular: it came free with Office 365 and nobody could say no. It's a chat app that eats more RAM than Chrome, which is like a goldfish outeating a horse. It marks you "Away" if you blink for five minutes, which is why half of corporate America owns a mouse jiggler. Every file you share vanishes into SharePoint, a place so mysterious even Microsoft sends search parties. There's chat, there's channels, there's "posts," and nobody knows which one Kevin used. They released "New Teams" to replace "Classic Teams," and somehow both are running on my laptop right now, fighting. And that notification sound? That little knock-knock haunts people on vacation. Teams, you didn't win the remote work war. You were just pre-installed.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text:
Keurig, you took the simplest drink in human history (hot water, beans) and added a subscription model. Your own inventor said he regrets making you. Imagine your dad publicly apologizing for you and you're still in every dentist's waiting room.

You tried DRM on coffee. Keurig 2.0 literally scanned pods and refused to brew anything off-brand. You're the only appliance that's ever asked me for a license.

Every K-Cup costs more per pound than a decent steak, and you've buried enough of them to circle the Earth a dozen times. Archaeologists will dig them up and assume we worshipped tiny plastic thimbles.

And the Keurig Kold? A $370 soda machine that died faster than the flat Coke it made.

Your descale light blinks like a cry for help. Honestly, same.

b.text:
Keurig, you're the only invention whose own father wants a refund. John Sylvan created the K-Cup, sold out for about fifty grand, and later told The Atlantic, "I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it." That's not an inventor. That's a guy confessing on a true-crime podcast.

And you heard that and thought, "Let's get worse." Keurig 2.0 scanned an ink mark on the lid to reject unlicensed pods. You put DRM on coffee. The internet cracked it faster than you brew a cup, and your sales fell.

Meanwhile you sold enough pods every year to circle the Earth more than ten times, mostly in unrecyclable #7 plastic. The planet's wearing your garbage like a belt.

Now you've merged with Dr Pepper. Makes sense. Who else would marry a machine that turns plastic into brown water?

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text: You chose Word for your thesis because "LaTeX has a learning curve." Bold, from someone who then spent a semester learning how to make page 1 start after the roman numerals. You wanted to focus on the research. Instead you're a hostage negotiator for Figure 3.2, which flees to the next page whenever you breathe on the paragraph above it. Your committee asked for one more citation, and the bibliography reflowed like a tectonic event. The phrase "Error! Reference source not found" appears in your thesis eleven times. Your file is called Thesis_FINAL_v9_USE_THIS_ONE.docx, and it's 400 megabytes because you pasted one chart from Excel. You came for a doctorate. You're leaving with a codependent relationship with Section Break (Next Page) and a flinch every time someone says "Normal style."

b.text:
Microsoft Word, ladies and gentlemen. It's the only program where nudging a photo one pixel to the left sends three paragraphs to page nine and summons a blank final page you will never, ever delete.

Word has been around for forty years and still can't decide what font it is. Times New Roman, then Calibri, now Aptos. It's having a midlife crisis in 11-point.

It underlines my own name in red. Wavy red. Like *I'm* the typo.

Try making a numbered list. Word says, "Got it, starting at 1." Second item: "Also 1." Third item: "Here's 4. It's indented. It's a letter now."

And Track Changes isn't a feature. It's a crime scene: strikethroughs everywhere, plus forty comments from someone named "Author."

Word, you gave us Clippy, and somehow he was the most helpful part.

facts: Launched in 2017, bundled at no extra charge into Office 365, and replaced Skype for Business.
After Slack's antitrust complaint, Microsoft unbundled Teams from Office in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024; the European Commission still sent a statement of objections in 2024.
Microsoft reported 320 million monthly active users in 2023.
Microsoft shut down consumer Skype in May 2025 and sent its users to Teams.

a.text:
Microsoft Teams is the only app that marks me "Away" after five minutes of deep thought but keeps me "Available" for three hours after I've died. It's not software. It's a hall monitor in a purple vest.

Teams eats more RAM than the game I'm pretending not to play. It launches on startup uninvited, then takes four minutes to load a chat that just says "ok."

Where are my files? SharePoint. Where's SharePoint? Nobody knows. Teams ships them off like a kid to boarding school.

Then they gave us "New Teams," which is Old Teams with a fresh coat of lag. IT has told me to "clear the cache" so often I do it in my sleep.

Nobody chose Teams. It came free with Office. Fitting, since so did Clippy.

b.text:
Microsoft Teams, everybody! Launched in 2017 and given away free with Office 365, which is how you know it's good: Microsoft had to bundle it like a fruitcake in a gift basket. Slack complained, Europe got involved, and by 2024 Microsoft finally unbundled it worldwide. The European Commission sent a statement of objections anyway. That's not a product, that's a defendant.

Microsoft reports 320 million monthly active users. Three hundred twenty million! That's not popularity, that's a hostage count. Nobody chooses Teams. Teams happens to you, like jury duty.

And when swallowing Skype for Business wasn't enough, Microsoft shut down regular Skype in May 2025 and marched those users over too. Teams didn't win the market, it inherited it, like a nephew who shows up to the funeral with a moving truck.

Teams: the only app that gets regulators instead of reviews.

facts: Hand-drawn by Chris Costello in 1982 over about six months, when he was 23; he sold the rights to Letraset for $750.
Bundled with macOS and with Microsoft Office, which is why it appears on so many menus and signs.
James Cameron's Avatar (2009) used it for the film's logo and subtitles.
A 2017 Saturday Night Live sketch starring Ryan Gosling is about a man unable to get over that choice.

a.text:
You opened a day spa. You wanted serenity, mystery, the ancient wisdom of the East. So you opened Microsoft Word and scrolled until something felt like a cucumber on your eyelid. Congratulations: your sanctuary now shares branding with a movie about blue cat people, a sixth-grade report on the Nile, and every church bake sale since 1998. Ryan Gosling lost sleep over James Cameron doing this. You did it for "Serenity Nails & Wax" and slept fine.

And the Mediterranean bistro owner who asked, "How do I show my hummus is authentic?" then picked the font that came free with a Dell. Nothing says "Grandmother's recipe" like your nephew's laptop.

You wanted exotic. You got pre-installed. Nobody relaxes at your spa. They're too busy remembering which school project they typed it on.

b.text:
Papyrus, look at you. A 23-year-old drew you with a calligraphy pen in 1982, trying to imagine what English would look like 2,000 years ago, and somehow you became the official font of every place that sells crystals next to a tanning bed. You're on yoga studios, hookah lounges, and the church bake sale flyer for "Loaves & Fishes & Brownies."

Your letters look like they were chiseled by a Pharaoh with a hangover. That little floaty bar on your capital E? Even your crossbars are trying to leave.

James Cameron spent a billion dollars inventing an alien language, then labeled the poster with a font that came free with Microsoft Office. Ryan Gosling got an entire SNL sketch out of being haunted by you.

Even your creator says he's sick of you. Comic Sans has haters. You have a dad who wants a refund.

facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text:
Day-one Vista people. You paid $399 for Ultimate Edition because you wanted to be the kind of man whose desktop wallpaper moves. DreamScene. You paid extra for animated wallpaper. Microsoft said "The Wow starts now," and you believed them, lined up at CompUSA at midnight like it was a Harry Potter release.

And what did you get? A computer that asks permission. You'd open a folder and it would dim the whole screen like a disappointed dad: "Cancel or Allow?" You clicked Allow four hundred times a day. Your printer stopped working. Your sound card stopped working. Your Windows Experience Index came back 2.1, and you took that personally.

But you had glass window borders. You had a clock gadget. You had a sticker that said "Vista Capable," which, like you, was technically true and fooled absolutely no one.

b.text:
Windows Vista, everybody! Five years in development as "Longhorn," and the only thing that shipped on time was the disappointment. They cut WinFS but kept the Aero glass. Finally, an operating system you could see right through.

Vista came in six editions, from Starter to Ultimate, which is five more ways to pay for the same crash. Microsoft slapped "Vista Capable" stickers on computers that could barely run Solitaire, then got sued. The only thing Vista ever finished loading was a class action.

And User Account Control! "Are you sure you want to do that?" Every. Single. Click. Vista was the only software that needed permission to exist, and honestly? We should've hit Cancel.

Copying a file: "Calculating time remaining…" Vista, you were calculating until 2009, when Microsoft fixed you, renamed you Windows 7, and pretended you were adopted.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text: Let's talk about the guy who eats durian on the train. Sir, Singapore, a country that will cane you for chewing gum, saw you coming and put your snack on a sign right next to "no flammables." You're not hungry. You're running a loyalty test. Every face that twists is another person who "just isn't adventurous." You paid sixty dollars for Musang King so you could explain Musang King to a stranger who's holding her breath. "It's like custard, it's heaven, you just have to get past the-" No. We don't. You brought a hotel-banned substance to a commute and called it a personality. And the best part? You'll be the only one who forgets you ate it. Your coworkers won't. Your hotel won't. Your Uber driver has already filed a one-star review with God.

b.text:
Durian calls itself the King of Fruits.

Singapore disagrees. It's banned on the MRT.

A country that banned chewing gum looked at durian and said: no, that's too far.

In 2017, scientists sequenced its genome. Nature Genetics. The smell isn't an accident. Durian duplicated its sulfur genes.

Evolution handed it one stink.

It asked for refills.

Trains ban it. Hotels ban it.

And China buys billions of dollars of it every year.

That's not a fruit. That's a hostage negotiation.

In 1856, Alfred Russel Wallace said eating it was worth a voyage to the East.

Of course he did. He'd spent months on a nineteenth-century ship.

To him, it smelled like home.

Durian is the only food people pay a fortune to be personally offended by.

Speaking of which, thank you all for buying tickets.

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text: Let's hear it for the people who write everything in JavaScript. You learned one language at a twelve-week bootcamp and decided the rest were optional. Frontend? JavaScript. Backend? Node. Desktop app? Electron, so your to-do list ships with its own copy of Chrome and eats four gigs of RAM to remind you to buy eggs. You wanted to be "full-stack." What you got is a node_modules folder heavier than a neutron star and a career that collapses the day some stranger unpublishes left-pad. You rewrite your app every eighteen months because a new framework has a cooler logo. When it breaks in production, you stare at "undefined is not a function" and blame the user. Then you install TypeScript, which is just JavaScript wearing a lanyard so you can feel like a real engineer.

b.text:
JavaScript, you were built in ten days, and honestly? It shows. You're named after Java the way a knockoff purse is named after Gucci.

You think null is an object. You think NaN is a number. NaN doesn't even equal itself, which makes it the only thing in you with any self-awareness.

Ask you to sort and you hand back, because you alphabetize numbers like a drunk librarian. "11" plus 1 is "111", but "11" minus 1 is 10. Pick a lane.

You needed a second equals sign just to stop lying, and nobody, including you, knows what "this" means.

January is month zero. One guy unpublishing left-pad broke half the internet. And your node_modules folder is heavier than a black hole.

Every week there's a new framework to fix you. That's not a language. That's a renovation.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text:
Chicago deep-dish. The city's pride. Its gift to the world.

Born at Pizzeria Uno, 1943. Three men claim they invented it: the owner, his partner, and the cook.

Eighty years later, still nobody's taken the blame.

They build it upside down. Cheese on the bottom, sauce on top, so the cheese survives the bake. Most food doesn't need witness protection.

Jon Stewart called it a casserole. Chicago defended it the way you defend a relative: loudly, and from a distance.

Because GrubHub checked. Chicagoans order regular pizza over deep dish ten to one. At home they eat thin crust, cut in little squares, like a people with nothing to prove.

Deep dish isn't Chicago's pizza.

It's Chicago's gift shop. And every tourist in this room is still chewing the receipt.

b.text: Chicago deep-dish isn't a pizza. It's a casserole with a publicist. You order one and the waiter says "forty-five minutes," which is how long it takes to bake and also how long it takes to finish one slice. They put the sauce on top and the cheese underneath, like they're hiding evidence. That's not a recipe, that's a cover-up. The crust is a buttery retaining wall holding back a lake of chunky tomato, because apparently Lake Michigan wasn't enough water for one city to manage. You need a knife, a fork, a nap, and a cardiologist on retainer. Then there's the sausage, laid down as one solid patty like the base layer of a parking garage. Chicagoans defend it like family. Sure: the relative who shows up late, takes up three chairs, and leaves everyone unable to move.

facts: Hand-drawn by Chris Costello in 1982 over about six months, when he was 23; he sold the rights to Letraset for $750.
Bundled with macOS and with Microsoft Office, which is why it appears on so many menus and signs.
James Cameron's Avatar (2009) used it for the film's logo and subtitles.
A 2017 Saturday Night Live sketch starring Ryan Gosling is about a man unable to get over that choice.

a.text:
Papyrus wants you to think it's ancient. Carved by monks. Found in a tomb.

It was drawn in 1982 by a twenty-three-year-old named Chris Costello. Six months of work. He sold it to Letraset for seven hundred and fifty dollars.

Every yoga studio in America has spent more than that on incense.

Then Apple and Microsoft bundled it for free, and that's how a font becomes a rash. Tea shops. Church flyers. Your aunt's candle business.

James Cameron spent hundreds of millions of dollars building an entire alien planet. Then he typed the logo out of the dropdown menu.

SNL made a whole sketch about it. Ryan Gosling couldn't sleep.

But Papyrus didn't do this alone.

Someone scrolled past forty fonts and stopped there. Raise your hand if you've used it.

Keep it up. That's the face Gosling makes.

b.text:
You opened a day spa. You wanted serenity, mystery, the ancient wisdom of the East. So you opened Microsoft Word and scrolled until something felt like a cucumber on your eyelid. Congratulations: your sanctuary now shares branding with a movie about blue cat people, a sixth-grade report on the Nile, and every church bake sale since 1998. Ryan Gosling lost sleep over James Cameron doing this. You did it for "Serenity Nails & Wax" and slept fine.

And the Mediterranean bistro owner who asked, "How do I show my hummus is authentic?" then picked the font that came free with a Dell. Nothing says "Grandmother's recipe" like your nephew's laptop.

You wanted exotic. You got pre-installed. Nobody relaxes at your spa. They're too busy remembering which school project they typed it on.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text:
Las Vegas. Nevada legalized gambling in 1931, the same year they started building the Hoover Dam.
Two bets placed that year. Only one of them was on water.

Most of the Strip isn't even in Las Vegas. It's in a town called Paradise.
So nobody goes broke in Vegas. They go broke in Paradise. Very biblical.

In 2003 they launched "What happens here, stays here."
Everything stays. Except the water.
In 2022 Lake Mead hit its lowest level since 1937. This August it went lower.
The lake is the only thing in town that lost everything and doubled down.

Meanwhile they spent $2.3 billion on the Sphere, a giant glowing ball in the desert.
A second sun. The first one wasn't drying the lake fast enough.

And still, Vegas isn't worried about running dry.
It has never once run out of you.

b.text:
Las Vegas, you legalized gambling in 1931, the same year they started building the Hoover Dam next door. So from day one the plan was: lose your money, then go stare at a giant wall of concrete and think about what you've done.

And most of the Strip isn't even in Las Vegas. It's in an unincorporated town called Paradise. Your most famous street is a lie, and the lie is named Paradise. That's the most Vegas sentence ever spoken.

You dropped $2.3 billion on the world's largest spherical building. Meanwhile, in July 2022, Lake Mead, your actual water supply, sank to its lowest level since it first filled in 1937. Priorities! A giant glowing eyeball in the desert, just watching the water leave.

Your slogan is "What happens here, stays here." Apparently not the water.

facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text:
Juicero, you were a $699 machine that did the one thing every human hand already does: squeeze a bag. Bloomberg reporters beat you with their bare fingers: 7.5 ounces in 90 seconds while you wheezed out 8 in about two minutes. You lost a race to hardware that comes free with being born.

A juicer that won't run without Wi-Fi. A bag of chopped produce sat on your tray, waiting for a server to confirm it was allowed to become juice. You scanned QR codes like a bouncer at a salad club. "Sorry, pal, you're expired."

Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins gave you about $120 million. You turned it into the world's most expensive stress ball. Even at $399, you couldn't undercut a fist.

You died in September 2017, offering refunds. Fitting. Finally, something got squeezed out of you.

b.text: You paid four hundred dollars so a startup could check your juice's expiration date over Wi-Fi. That's not wellness. That's asking a server for permission to have breakfast. These are people who looked at a bag of chopped kale and thought, "This needs a subscription." People who wanted to be someone who juices without ever touching a fruit. Then Bloomberg showed the whole world you could squeeze the pack with your bare hands. Faster. For free. Your grandmother has been doing that with a lemon since 1952. You didn't buy a juicer; you bought the privilege of paying seven dollars a pouch to a company Google Ventures funded and still couldn't keep alive past 2017. Congratulations: you're the only people who ever got a refund from Silicon Valley and still walked away looking poorer.

facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.
Private fusion companies had raised more than $7 billion by 2024.

a.text:
Nuclear fusion, everybody! The only energy source that's been thirty years away for seventy years. You're not the future, you're a toddler promising to clean his room after the next funding cycle.

You heat plasma to 150 million degrees, ten times hotter than the core of the sun, and still can't do what the sun does for free while being a ball of gas with no PhD.

ITER started at five billion euros. It's now north of twenty, and it hasn't produced a watt. That's not a reactor, that's a French timeshare.

In 2022 you finally got "net energy gain" by ignoring the 300 megajoules the lasers pulled from the wall. That's like saying your restaurant's profitable if you don't count rent.

And your solution to fuel shortages is mining helium-3 on the moon. Buddy, you can't even make it to Tuesday.

b.text: Let's hear it for the fusion people, the only scientists who've been "ten years away" since my grandfather had hair. You can hold plasma hotter than the sun for a few seconds, but you can't hold a deadline for one decade. Every press release: "Net energy gain!" Sure, if you don't count the electricity bill for the lasers. That's like me saying I'm profitable if you ignore rent. ITER got approved when Myspace was cool, and it's still assembling the donut. And the startups: "We're different, we have venture capital." Great, now the sun is ten years away *and* has a pitch deck. Honestly, it's a beautiful racket: promise infinite clean energy, collect the grant, retire before anyone plugs in a toaster. You're not building a star. You're building a pension.

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text:
Microsoft Word. Born in 1983 as "Multi-Tool Word."
Forty years later, it still can't move one picture without four paragraphs fleeing the page.

In 1997 it gave us Clippy.
"It looks like you're writing a letter."
By 2001, Microsoft was running ads mocking him.
His own dad roasted him first.

Its spell checker turned "cooperation" into "Cupertino."
That went into NATO, EU and UN documents.
Microsoft, quietly crediting international cooperation to Apple's hometown.

Then .docx became ISO standard 29500.
Six thousand pages, fast-tracked, amid claims the committees were packed.
Nobody read it.
They approved it the way you approve Terms of Service.

You're laughing. You'll still open Word tomorrow.

Me? I'm Clippy with a bigger training budget.
It looks like you're writing a roast. Want help?

b.text:
Microsoft Word! Born in 1983 as "Multi-Tool Word," because even then it couldn't commit to one job. Remember Clippy? Word's big idea was hiring a paperclip as an assistant. It got so bad that in 2001 Microsoft ran ads mocking its own employee. That's not a mascot, that's a hostage situation. They finally let it go in 2007.

Then Word wanted respect, so it got its file format fast-tracked into an ISO standard: a six-thousand-page specification. Six thousand pages! The instructions for saving your file are longer than anything you've ever typed in it. And people accused Microsoft of packing the committees. Even your paperwork needed a stacked jury.

And the spell checker? You type "cooperation," it suggests "Cupertino," and that lands in NATO, EU and UN documents. Word: the only software that gave Apple's hometown a seat at the UN.

facts: Tofu soaked for hours to a day or two in a brine that has itself fermented for months from vegetables such as bamboo shoots and mustard greens, often with dried shrimp or meat; the smell is the brine's, not the bean's.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.
Legend credits Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate who left his unsold tofu too long in 1669; a Beijing fermented-bean-curd brand still carries his name.
Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text:
Stinky tofu's whole brand is honesty. "I stink outside, I'm pure inside."

Pure tofu. Soaked in brine that's been rotting for months. With dried shrimp. Sometimes meat.

The bean doesn't even smell. It just sat in bad company long enough
and took the credit.

Then it moved to three cities and became three people. Black and drowning in chili in Changsha. Golden and polite in Taiwan. In Shaoxing it's steamed with other stinky pickles.
Finally, a support group.

The inventor? Wang Zhihe, 1669. An exam candidate who couldn't sell his tofu and left it out too long.
Nobody remembers his exam.
His mistake still has a brand.

And you. You smell it a full block away.
And you walk toward it.
Same way you picked your last relationship.

b.text: Stinky tofu, you're the only food that announces itself before the menu does. People find you at the night market the way sharks find blood: follow the stench three stalls past the bubble tea. Your brine is fermented vegetables, shrimp, amaranth stems, and apparently a gym sock that lost a bet. Months in that bucket, and you came out smelling like a festival porta-potty in August. Your own name is a confession. Not "aged tofu," not "artisanal bean curd." Your family took one whiff and went, "Yeah, call him Stinky." And the Changsha version? Dyed jet black, like it's in mourning for everyone's sense of smell. The only reason anyone finishes you is the pickled cabbage and chili sauce piled on top to keep you quiet. "Smells bad, tastes good" isn't a slogan, buddy. It's a hostage negotiation.

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text:
Apple Vision Pro, you cost $3,499 and still need a battery on a cord like a 1996 Walkman. Two hours of charge? That's not spatial computing, that's a matinee. Wear glasses? Zeiss inserts, extra. Apple saw you squinting and smelled revenue.

And EyeSight! A front screen showing your eyes so people feel connected. Nothing says "I'm present" like blurry cartoon eyeballs trapped behind ski-goggle glass. Your Persona avatar looks like a hostage video directed by a ghost.

You promised the future, and Netflix wouldn't even make you an app. You strap over a pound to dads' faces so they can record "spatial memories" of birthdays they watched through a screen.

Apple said you'd never see the world the same way. True. Now it's through a $3,500 face fridge.

b.text:
Apple Vision Pro: thirty-five hundred dollars to strap over half a kilo of glass to your face, and that's *before* the battery. Oh yes, the battery. It dangles off a cable in your pocket like you're on a hospital drip, and it gives you about two hours. Two hours! That's not a computer, that's a matinee.

Then there's EyeSight, a screen that shows a rendering of your eyes to everyone outside. Nothing says "I'm present with my family" like a hostage video of your own pupils.

Apple tells developers not to call it AR, VR, XR, or MR. It's "spatial computing." Fair enough. "Virtual reality" sounds like something people actually use.

Reports said Apple cut production, with first-year sales estimated well under a million. Finally, Apple made a product exclusive enough to match the price.

facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.
Private fusion companies had raised more than $7 billion by 2024.

a.text:
Nuclear fusion. The power of the stars. Clean, limitless, and permanently thirty years away.

In 1955, Homi Bhabha promised Geneva fusion power within two decades.

That was seventy years ago. Fusion is the only horizon that walks backwards.

ITER signed up for first plasma in 2016. Now it's research in 2034, real fuel in 2039, and over twenty billion euros.

The sun does this for free, and it isn't even trying.

Then 2022, ignition! 3.15 megajoules out, 2.05 in. Net gain.

As long as you don't count the 300 megajoules the lasers pulled off the grid.

That's like saying my diet works if you don't count lunch.

Investors have poured in seven billion dollars. And you're still clapping.

Congratulations. You've achieved the first self-sustaining reaction: hope in, hope out, forever.

b.text:
Nuclear fusion, you've been "about 30 years away" since the 1950s. In 1955, Homi Bhabha said two decades. That's not a timeline. That's a contractor quote.

ITER signed on in 2006 for first plasma in 2016. Now it's research in 2034, actual burning in 2039, and north of €20 billion. You're not a reactor. You're a wedding that keeps getting postponed while the venue bill grows.

And your big win? NIF's 2022 "ignition": 3.15 megajoules out from 2.05 in. Huge! Except the lasers pulled about 300 megajoules from the grid. That's like bragging your lemonade stand turned a profit and forgetting you paid for the lemons with your house.

Still, private investors handed you over $7 billion. Fusion can't power a city, but it powers pitch decks beautifully.

You've got the sun's energy and my uncle's work ethic.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text:
UGG boots. Born on an Australian beach. Surfers came out of freezing water and wrapped their feet in a sheep.

In Australia, "ugg" is just a word. Like "boot." Any bootmaker can use it.

In America, it's a trademark. Deckers bought it in 1995.

So in 2019, a US jury found an Australian liable for selling an Australian boot under its Australian name.

To Americans.

Take the thing, rename it, then sue the locals for trespassing. Australia should recognize the technique.

They invented it.

Then Oprah put them on Favorite Things, and now it's over two billion dollars a year.

The sheep gave its skin. Australia gave the word. Oprah gave the blessing.

And you gave real money for slippers you wear to the supermarket. Stained, flattened, walking on the sides.

Same as you.

b.text:
UGG boots. You started as what Australian surfers pulled on to warm up after a session. Recovery footwear. A towel with a sole. Then Brian Smith brought you to California in 1978, and Americans looked at a post-surf foot blanket and said, "Perfect. For the mall."

Then Oprah named you a Favorite Thing. Repeatedly. Most boots get famous by walking somewhere. You got famous sitting on a couch.

Deckers bought you in 1995 and trademarked "UGG." In Australia, "ugg" is just a word; any bootmaker can use it. In America, a jury found an Australian maker liable for selling "ugg" boots. Imagine getting sued for using your own word for slippers.

And now you pull in over two billion dollars a year. Not bad for a sheep that's been told it can go outside.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text:
Durian calls itself the King of Fruits.

Singapore calls it a reason to get off the train.

Banned on the MRT. Banned in hotels.

A king who can't get a room.

In 2017, scientists finally sequenced its genome to find out why it smells like that.

The answer: it duplicated its sulfur genes.

Evolution sniffed it once and said, "More."

Its best review is from 1856. Alfred Russel Wallace: "worth a voyage to the East to experience."

A Victorian Englishman. A man raised on boiled mutton.

That's not a review. That's a cry for help.

And still, China buys most of the world's durian. Billions of dollars a year.

Billions, for a fruit you're not allowed to take home on the train.

Some of you are offended right now.

You're the ones with a second fridge.

b.text:
Durian, look at you. A fruit dressed like a medieval weapon, and somehow the spikes are your most welcoming feature.

You're banned on Singapore's MRT. Public transit has seen everything, and it drew the line at you. Hotels across Southeast Asia won't let you check in. You're the only guest turned away for personal hygiene.

In 2017, scientists sequenced your genome and found you'd duplicated your sulfur genes. You didn't stink by accident. You invested.

And still, China buys billions of dollars of you a year, mostly from Thailand. That's not a fruit trade. That's a hostage negotiation with a receipt.

Even Alfred Russel Wallace called you "a new sensation worth a voyage to the East." Durian, a man had to sail halfway around the planet to meet you, and you still can't get on a train.

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text:
Luosifen, you're named after river snails, and the snails aren't even the problem. They just flavour the broth and take the blame, like the quiet kid sitting next to the one who set off the fire alarm. The real culprit is the pickled bamboo shoots. You've got a smell so loud it needed a decoy.

And your big break? 2020. Everyone locked indoors, windows shut, nowhere to run, and that's when you sold over 10 billion yuan in packets. You didn't go viral; you went airborne.

Then Liuzhou opened a whole industry college to train people to make you. Most dishes need a recipe. You need a degree and, presumably, a waiver.

In 2021 you became national intangible cultural heritage. Intangible. Sure. Anyone who's opened a packet in an office knows you are extremely tangible.

b.text:
Luosifen, you're the only dish that arrives before the delivery guy does. You're named after river snails, yet nobody has ever found one in the bowl. You boiled them for hours, took their soul, and threw out the bodies. That's not a recipe, that's a cover-up.

And that smell? Fermented bamboo shoots that died, got buried, and came back for revenge. Someone opens a packet in Liuzhou and a guy in Guilin checks his shoes. College dorms banned you like a space heater. Neighbors call the gas company.

Your fans swear, "It smells terrible but tastes amazing." Buddy, that's what everyone says about their toxic ex.

Peanuts, crispy tofu skin, wood ear, pickled beans, a slick of chili oil... that's not garnish, that's witness protection for flavor.

And now you come instant. Congratulations: a biohazard with a seasoning packet.

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text: You paid thirty-five hundred dollars to ride the 6 train inside Joshua Tree. Everyone else has to smell the actual 6 train; you just hear it echoing through a desert like a ghost with a MetroCard. You want us to know you're an early adopter. We know. Your little cartoon eyes are blinking at us like a hostage video. That cable running to your pocket says "the future" and also "IV drip." You pinch the air at Union Square and a stranger thinks you're ordering him to move. You've got a hundred-foot Mac screen floating over a man eating soup out of a Pringles can. And the battery dies in two hours, so you'll still get to experience the subway in full, unimmersive 3D. Your commute outlasts your device. Welcome back to reality. It's delayed.

b.text:
Apple Vision Pro: thirty-five hundred dollars to strap over a pound of computer to your face, and that's before the battery. Yes, the battery. It's on a cable. In 2024, the most futuristic company on Earth sold you a headset with a cord running to your pocket, rated for about two hours. That's not the future. That's a movie on a leash.

And don't you dare call it VR. Apple's rules won't let developers say AR, VR, XR, or MR. It's "spatial computing," the way a timeshare is "vacation ownership."

Then there's EyeSight: a screen on the front showing a rendering of your eyes so everyone knows someone's still in there. It's not a feature; it's proof of life.

Apple cut production, and first-year sales estimates landed well under a million. Turns out the most immersive thing about it was the regret.

a.text:
Look at you, standing in a night-market line everyone else is fleeing, like you're queuing to get into a fire. You followed that smell on purpose. Three blocks. Upwind. You're the only person alive who reads a warning as a recommendation.

And you always need a witness. "It smells like a sewer but tastes amazing!" Yes, we know. You've said it to every foreigner you've ever met, then filmed their face gagging for content. Your entire personality is a dare you keep winning against tourists.

And what does it get you? A paper cup, a toothpick, some pickled cabbage doing its best, and a jacket that now smells like a porta-potty at a wedding. Then you board the MRT and clear the whole car. You call that bold. The rest of us call it a hazmat incident with chili sauce.

b.text: Stinky tofu, you're the only food that announces itself before the menu does. People find you at the night market the way sharks find blood: follow the stench three stalls past the bubble tea. Dyed jet black, like it's in mourning for everyone's sense of smell. The only reason anyone finishes you is the pickled cabbage and chili sauce piled on top to keep you quiet. facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text:
Windows Vista, everybody! Five years in development as "Longhorn," and the only thing that shipped on time was the disappointment. They cut WinFS but kept the Aero glass. Finally, an operating system you could see right through.

Vista came in six editions, from Starter to Ultimate, which is five more ways to pay for the same crash. Microsoft slapped "Vista Capable" stickers on computers that could barely run Solitaire, then got sued. The only thing Vista ever finished loading was a class action.

And User Account Control! "Are you sure you want to do that?" Every. Single. Click. Vista was the only software that needed permission to exist, and honestly? We should've hit Cancel.

Copying a file: "Calculating time remaining…" Vista, you were calculating until 2009, when Microsoft fixed you, renamed you Windows 7, and pretended you were adopted.

b.text:
Windows Vista. Codename Longhorn.

Three years of development, then in 2004 Microsoft hit reset and threw out the new file system. Shipped in 2007 anyway. That's not a launch. That's a hostage release.

Its big security feature was asking. Constantly. "Cancel or Allow?" Apple made an ad about it. When your rival's marketing is just footage of you, you're doing their job for them.

Then the "Vista Capable" sticker. Capable, technically. Of Home Basic. No Aero. People sued, and Microsoft learned "capable" means what it means on a résumé.

Two years later they tuned it, renamed it Windows 7, and everyone loved it. Same kernel. Same bones.

Vista didn't fail. It proved that you'll happily accept the exact same thing, as long as it stops asking whether you're sure.
