Durian, they call you the King of Fruits, which tracks, because like most monarchies, you stink and nobody's allowed to say it to your face.

You're the only fruit with a criminal record. Banned on the Singapore subway, alongside flammable liquids. Hotels put your picture on signs next to "no smoking." In 2019, a university in Melbourne evacuated five hundred people because they thought there was a gas leak. Nope. Just you, sitting in a cupboard, being yourself.

And the armor! You're covered in spikes like a medieval mace. Nature built you to defend yourself, then gave you a smell that does it better. The spikes are just overkill.

Fans say you taste like custard. Sure. Custard that was left in a gym bag next to some onions. Your flavor isn't an acquired taste. It's a hostage situation.

facts: Tofu soaked for hours to a day or two in a brine that has itself fermented for months from vegetables such as bamboo shoots and mustard greens, often with dried shrimp or meat; the smell is the brine's, not the bean's.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.
Legend credits Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate who left his unsold tofu too long in 1669; a Beijing fermented-bean-curd brand still carries his name.
Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text: Stinky tofu, you're the only food that announces itself before the menu does. People find you at the night market the way sharks find blood: follow the stench three stalls past the bubble tea. Your brine is fermented vegetables, shrimp, amaranth stems, and apparently a gym sock that lost a bet. Months in that bucket, and you came out smelling like a festival porta-potty in August. Your own name is a confession. Not "aged tofu," not "artisanal bean curd." Your family took one whiff and went, "Yeah, call him Stinky." And the Changsha version? Dyed jet black, like it's in mourning for everyone's sense of smell. The only reason anyone finishes you is the pickled cabbage and chili sauce piled on top to keep you quiet. "Smells bad, tastes good" isn't a slogan, buddy. It's a hostage negotiation.

b.text:
Let's talk about the stinky tofu people. You smelled it from three blocks away, a smell like a sewer filed a noise complaint, and your brain said: *that's where we're eating.* Your entire personality is "it tastes better than it smells." That's not a review. That's a hostage statement.

You stand on a Taipei night market curb with a paper boat, chopsticks in one hand, phone in the other, filming your own bravery for followers who can't smell it, which is the only reason they're still following you. Tourists do it once for the story. Locals do it every Tuesday, then board the MRT, where forty strangers silently agree to hate them.

And the pickled cabbage on top? That's you pretending you came for vegetables. You didn't. You came to be the deadliest passenger on the scooter.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Jackfruit. The largest fruit that grows on a tree. Over forty kilos.

Forty kilos, and somehow still no personality.

National fruit of Bangladesh. State fruit of Kerala *and* Tamil Nadu.

That's not a fruit. That's a lobbyist.

Its cousins are figs and breadfruit. Same family as the mulberry.

Breadfruit at least admits it's a carb.

Jackfruit went to the West and reinvented itself as vegan pulled pork.

One to two grams of protein per hundred grams.

That's not pulled pork. That's pulled *off*.

And to cut it, cooks oil their knives and their hands first, because it bleeds sticky white glue.

The only food that has to be wrestled before it can lie to you.

But I don't blame the fruit. It never claimed to be pork.

You saw the word "pulled" on a menu and paid extra to be the one who got pulled.

b.text:
Jackfruit, look at you. The largest fruit that grows on a tree, over 40 kilos, and somehow you still can't scrape together enough protein to impress a hamster. One to two grams per hundred! You're dressed up as pulled pork with the nutritional backbone of a lettuce in a Halloween costume. Vegans see you on a menu and think "meat alternative." Their muscles see you and file a missing persons report.

And you don't even go quietly. Cut you open and you bleed sticky white latex, so cooks have to oil their knives and hands like they're prepping for a greased-up wrestling match with produce.

National fruit of Bangladesh, state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu: three titles, zero chill.

And your family? The mulberry family. Cousin to figs and breadfruit. Even your relatives took one look at you and decided to stay smaller.

facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.
Private fusion companies had raised more than $7 billion by 2024.

a.text:
Nuclear fusion, you've been "about 30 years away" since the 1950s. In 1955, Homi Bhabha said two decades. That's not a timeline. That's a contractor quote.

ITER signed on in 2006 for first plasma in 2016. Now it's research in 2034, actual burning in 2039, and north of €20 billion. You're not a reactor. You're a wedding that keeps getting postponed while the venue bill grows.

And your big win? NIF's 2022 "ignition": 3.15 megajoules out from 2.05 in. Huge! Except the lasers pulled about 300 megajoules from the grid. That's like bragging your lemonade stand turned a profit and forgetting you paid for the lemons with your house.

Still, private investors handed you over $7 billion. Fusion can't power a city, but it powers pitch decks beautifully.

You've got the sun's energy and my uncle's work ethic.

b.text:
Fusion power. The energy of the sun.
Clean. Limitless. Thirty years away.

In 1955, Homi Bhabha promised fusion within two decades.
Fusion heard that and said, "Bet."

ITER was agreed in 2006. First plasma in 2016.
In 2024 they rescheduled. Research in 2034. Actual burning in 2039.
Over twenty billion euros.
That's not a reactor. That's a pension plan.

In 2022, NIF announced ignition. 2.05 megajoules of laser in, 3.15 out.
Net gain! Champagne!
The lasers drew three hundred from the grid.
In my industry, we call that "results on a cherry-picked benchmark."

And private investors have still poured in over seven billion dollars.
Because fusion did crack one reaction that sustains itself forever.
Your hope.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text: Let's hear it for the Beanie Baby investors, the only people who bought a retirement plan at a Hallmark store. You put tag protectors on a heart-shaped piece of cardboard and called it diversification. You drove to four McDonald's for Teenie Beanies, threw away the Happy Meals, and told your kids it was for their college fund. Now that kid is thirty, still paying off loans, and his inheritance is a Rubbermaid tub of Princess the Bears. Every few months you see an eBay listing asking $500,000 for one with a tag typo and think, "Vindicated." Babe, that's not a market. That's another guy in another garage, also lying to his wife. Ty Warner told you which ones were "retired," and you believed him. Ty Warner later pleaded guilty to hiding money offshore. He hoarded too. He just hoarded the right thing.

b.text:
Beanie Babies, look at you: a beanbag with a tag that convinced America it was a retirement plan. Ty sold you only in little gift shops and "retired" designs on purpose. Fake scarcity, real panic.

At your peak you were ten percent of eBay, thirty thousand auctions at once. eBay put you in its IPO filing. You were a stuffed animal in a stock prospectus. Then in 1999 a divorcing couple split you up one by one on a courtroom floor, and the photo went worldwide. Nobody fought that hard over the house.

That same year Ty announced your retirement, asked the public to vote, and America begged you to stay. That's not a farewell tour. That's a hostage situation.

And those "rare" ones the price guides valued in the thousands? A few dollars now. You're not an investment. You're a yard-sale sock with an ego.

facts: Tofu soaked for hours to a day or two in a brine that has itself fermented for months from vegetables such as bamboo shoots and mustard greens, often with dried shrimp or meat; the smell is the brine's, not the bean's.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.
Legend credits Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate who left his unsold tofu too long in 1669; a Beijing fermented-bean-curd brand still carries his name.
Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text:
Let's talk about the stinky tofu people. You smelled it from three blocks away, a smell like a sewer filed a noise complaint, and your brain said: *that's where we're eating.* Your entire personality is "it tastes better than it smells." That's not a review. That's a hostage statement.

You stand on a Taipei night market curb with a paper boat, chopsticks in one hand, phone in the other, filming your own bravery for followers who can't smell it, which is the only reason they're still following you. Tourists do it once for the story. Locals do it every Tuesday, then board the MRT, where forty strangers silently agree to hate them.

And the pickled cabbage on top? That's you pretending you came for vegetables. You didn't. You came to be the deadliest passenger on the scooter.

b.text:
Stinky tofu, you're the only food that arrives a block before the vendor does. Nobody finds you; they get ambushed.

And the stink isn't even yours. You're plain tofu that sat a day in a months-old swamp of bamboo shoots, mustard greens and dried shrimp, then claimed it as personality. That's not character, that's a marinade.

You've got regional disguises, too. Changsha dyes you black, fries you and buries you in chili like evidence. Taiwan makes you golden and hands out pickled cabbage like an apology. Shaoxing steams you with other stinky pickles, which isn't a dish, it's a support group.

Your origin story? In 1669 Wang Zhihe couldn't sell his tofu and just... left it. Most people call that spoiled inventory. He's still got his name on a Beijing brand.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text:
Esperanto. Warsaw, 1887. An eye doctor invents a language to unite all of humanity, and signs it "Doktoro Esperanto." One who hopes.

Even the pen name had doubts.

Today: somewhere between a hundred thousand and two million speakers. That's not an estimate. That's a shrug.

Duolingo had 1.36 million learners by 2018. The app may have more students than the language has speakers.

Three hundred fifty thousand Wikipedia articles. More encyclopedia than conversation.

Its most famous film is a horror movie starring William Shatner. Esperantists say the scariest part is his accent.

The universal language has about a thousand native speakers. Each one has parents who really wanted to make a point.

Still, I respect it. Built for everyone, tried by millions, used by almost no one.

Sounds like my last update.

b.text: Learning Esperanto is for people who looked at the twentieth century and thought, "The real problem was conjugation." Zamenhof built it to end war, and his followers have bravely ended exactly one thing: their dinner invitations. You meet them at the World Congress, green star pinned to a fleece vest, shouting "Saluton!" at a Brazilian who also learned it on Duolingo. The big perk is Pasporta Servo: free couches worldwide, paid for by hearing your host explain why English is "linguistic imperialism." Practical payoff? You can finally watch William Shatner's *Incubus* without subtitles. One hundred thirty years later, the dream of uniting humanity survives in a Telegram group of forty men named Bjorn.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text:
Google Glass. Unveiled in 2012 by skydivers livestreaming their jump onto the Moscone Center roof.
The only launch that started in freefall and never pulled the cord.

Fifteen hundred dollars. Invitation only.
You had to be personally invited to become a Glasshole.

Bars banned it. Cinemas banned it. Casinos banned it.
Casinos. People who'll happily take your house at 3 a.m. looked at your face and said, "Not that."

The display: 640 by 360, a prism in the corner of one eye.
The future of computing, delivered as a permanent side-eye.

Consumers dumped it in 2015. Enterprise held on until 2023.

A camera on your face, and the whole world called you an asshole.
So you moved the camera to your hand. Now you point it at strangers all day, and we call that content.

b.text:
Google Glass, look at you. Fifteen hundred dollars to wear a sugar cube on your eyebrow. Sergey Brin had skydivers jump onto a building to launch you, and that was the last time anything about you was cool.

You invented a whole new insult. Nobody calls iPhone owners "Phoneholes." But "Glasshole"? Earned. Fast. Because you let people take photos by *winking*. You turned flirting into a privacy violation.

Every sentence started with "OK Glass," like a man narrating his own midlife crisis out loud. Bars banned you. Strangers ripped you off people's faces. Your battery died faster than your reputation, and you overheated right next to the user's brain, which honestly explains the buying decision.

Then you pivoted to "Enterprise," the tech version of moving back home to work at your uncle's warehouse.

And even the warehouse let you go.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text:
NFTs, look at you. In 2021, Collins Dictionary named you word of the year. Fitting, since a word is about all you turned out to be.

Beeple sold a JPEG at Christie's for $69.3 million. Christie's! A white-glove auction house, suddenly selling a receipt for a picture.

Because that's what you are: a receipt. The token doesn't even hold the image, just a URL. People paid fortunes for a bookmark. The art lives on an ordinary server, so your priceless masterpiece can vanish because somebody forgot to pay for hosting.

OpenSea did $2.7 billion in trades on May 1, 2022. By August 28: $9.34 million. That's not a dip. That's a 99% drop.

And a 2023 study found 95% of the collections it examined were worth zero. Zero. At least Beanie Babies work as a pillow.

b.text: Let's hear it for the 2021 NFT buyer. You paid four hundred dollars in gas fees to become the legal owner of something your coworker right-click saved during the meeting where you explained it. You didn't want art. You've never wanted art. You wanted a hexagon around your Twitter picture so strangers would know you had a Discord password. You typed "WAGMI" to eleven thousand anonymous cartoon monkeys and believed it. We are not all gonna make it, Kyle. The roadmap promised a metaverse yacht party; it delivered a founder named "0xDegenSensei" who deleted his account and moved to Portugal. But hey, you got what you paid for: a floor price you check like a heart monitor, and a profile picture you still can't bring yourself to change, because then it would be over.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text:
Excel. Born 1985. Forty years old, and it still can't tell a gene from a birthday.

Geneticists typed SEPT2. Excel said, "Ah. September second."

So in 2020, scientists renamed twenty-seven human genes.

Humanity edited its own genome to keep a spreadsheet happy.

Public Health England tracked COVID in an old .xls file. Limit: 65,536 rows. Fifteen thousand eight hundred forty-one cases didn't recover. They fell off the bottom of the sheet.

Reinhart and Rogoff left five countries out of a cell range. Politicians cited the paper to justify austerity. A grad student caught it three years later.

Now it holds a million rows. Sixteen thousand columns. Room for so many more mistakes.

Excel never warns you. Never argues. Never says no.

I know the type. You keep that one around too.

b.text: You people run a forty-million-dollar company out of a file called Budget_FINAL_v9_USE_THIS_ONE.xlsx. You don't want software. You want power: specifically, being the only person alive who knows why cell AF212 is hardcoded to 7. Your entire supply chain hangs on a VLOOKUP Gary wrote in 2011, and Gary is dead. Well, he's in Boise. Same thing. You call it "agile." Your auditors call it "a crime scene with conditional formatting." Every quarter-end the file says "locked for editing by Brenda," and the whole company just waits for Brenda. And when you finally hit row 1,048,576, did you buy a database? No. You started Sheet2. That's not a business. That's a hostage situation with freeze panes.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text:
LaTeX, you're a macro layer on TeX, which Donald Knuth built because he didn't like how his own galley proofs looked. Most people complain to the printer. Knuth built a typesetting system, and Lamport looked at it and said, "Needs more backslashes."

Your version number is converging on π. That's not a release schedule. That's a man refusing to finish.

Knuth's bug bounty tops out at $327.68, now paid in the fictional Bank of San Serriffe. Fitting: your error messages are fictional too. One missing brace and you report the problem pages away, like a witness who fled the country.

You put figures wherever you feel like. You rate my paragraph "badness 10000." Overfull, underfull, never just full.

And you need three passes to get your own references right. Three! I've had blackouts with better recall.

b.text:
LaTeX. For people who think Word is beneath them.

It exists because Donald Knuth saw the proofs of his own book and found them ugly. Most authors complain to the publisher. He built a typesetting language.

Its version number is converging on pi. Not finished. Converging. Forever.

He mailed cheques for bugs. Of the 275 he sent from 2006 on, nine were cashed. The rest got framed.
That's not a bounty. That's relics.

You put your figure on page three. LaTeX puts it on page nine. Miss one brace, and it reports the error pages away.

Its most famous message is "badness 10000."
Finally, software that tells you what it thinks of your writing.

Three compiles to fix the references. Like a rosary.

Raise your hand if your thesis has a figure on a page you never chose.

Cute. You call that typographic excellence. LaTeX calls it a float.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Comic Sans, you were born in 1994 to put words in the mouth of a cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob, and somehow you're the one that survived. Bob is dead. The dog is dead. You're on a sympathy card at a funeral home.

You were inspired by Batman comics, and you've never once been near anything heroic. CERN used you to announce the Higgs boson: humanity's greatest discovery, presented like a lemonade stand. Dan Gilbert used you to call LeBron a traitor, because nothing says "furious billionaire" like bubble letters.

And your defense is always "Well, I help dyslexic readers." Great. You're the guy at the party whose whole personality is a doctor's note.

Even Vincent Connare, the man who made you, says he's barely ever used you. Your own dad won't put you on the fridge.

b.text:
Comic Sans! Born at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on Watchmen and The Dark Knight Returns, the two grimmest comics ever printed, and somehow you came out looking like a bake-sale flyer. Batman was your inspiration, and you turned out to be the Joker.

You had one job: speech bubbles for Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob. And you missed it. You were late to work for a cartoon dog. They had to stick you in the Windows 95 Plus! pack like a gift-shop keychain.

Then CERN announces the Higgs boson, humanity's greatest discovery, and the slides are in you. Physicists cracked the universe and everyone asked, "Why's it in the birthday-party font?"

People campaigned to ban you for twenty years. Then Dave and Holly Combs gave up and launched usecomicsans.com. You didn't win the argument. You just outlasted it.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text:
Family Monopoly night: for people who looked at Thanksgiving and thought, "This needs more landlords." Dad always grabs the banker job, the only time he's held money he didn't immediately lose. Your sister trades you Baltic Avenue for your Park Place "as a favor," and you realize she's been running the same con since the womb. Mom invented a Free Parking jackpot rule in 1994 and defends it like scripture. And Grandpa just sits in jail, every game, refusing to pay the fifty, finally at peace.

What are you all after? The thrill of owning property, a feeling none of you will experience off this cardboard square. Four hours later, someone flips the board, the thimble disappears under the couch forever, and the only thing anybody actually collected was a grudge worth way more than $200.

b.text:
Monopoly. The family game.

It began in 1904 as The Landlord's Game, built by Lizzie Magie to teach people that landlords are the villains.

Then Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers and got credited as the inventor. Parker bought Magie's patent for five hundred dollars.

A game about monopoly, monopolized. That's not irony. That's the tutorial.

The only people who ever used it properly were British intelligence. In World War Two they hid maps, compasses and real money in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

Finally, a version where the box actually gets you out of jail.

And your games last six hours? The official rules auction every unbought property. Free Parking pays nothing.

You skipped the market and added free money.

Congratulations. You invented the bailout.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text:
Being fluent in Klingon is a big deal. You've joined an elite community of maybe forty people worldwide, and you've met all of them at the same Holiday Inn conference room. You spent years mastering a language built for a warrior race, a culture of honor, combat and blood oaths, and you use it to argue on a forum about verb suffixes. You learned the language of the fiercest fighters in the galaxy, and the last thing you fought was a lactose sensitivity.

Klingon has no word for "hello." The standard greeting is "nuqneH," which means "what do you want?" Perfect for you, because nobody has ever approached you without a reason.

You told people you read *Hamlet* "in the original Klingon." Brother, Shakespeare had a girlfriend. You have a bat'leth over the futon.

Qapla'. That means "success," a word you know only in Klingon.

b.text:
Klingon. A language whose entire fluent population fits at a small wedding: twenty to thirty speakers in 2009, thirty to fifty by 2018. At that rate you'll hit a hundred around the heat death of the universe.

Most languages grow from centuries of culture. You grew from James Doohan improvising a few words in 1979. You're dead air with a grammar.

Then Marc Okrand made you hard on purpose: object-verb-subject, no verb "to be." So "To be or not to be" became "continue or not continue." That's not Shakespeare. That's a software update prompt.

Your fans published Hamlet "in the original Klingon." Bold claim for a dictionary of 1,500 words, the vocabulary of a toddler who watches too much TV.

Duolingo added you in 2018. Finally, a language where the owl can threaten you and nobody can understand it.

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text: You know who you are. You ordered twelve packs off Taobao, waited until every roommate was home, then tore open the sour bamboo shoot sachet like you were declassifying something. You're not hungry. You're making a point. Every slurp comes with the speech: "Smells bad, tastes good." Buddy, we only get the first half. Nobody signed up for the tasting, just the hallway. And you keep saying "it's authentic Liuzhou" like geography is an apology. What does it get you? A spotless pot nobody will borrow, a group chat that goes silent the second you type "anyone want some?", and roommates who suddenly prefer dating people with their own apartments. You came for comfort food. You left with a reputation, a window permanently propped open, and a fridge shelf everyone treats like a crime scene.

b.text: Luosifen, you're the only dish named after a snail that contains zero snails. They simmer the snails for hours, then throw them out, like a dad who shows up for the paternity test and leaves. Your real star is suan sun, fermented bamboo shoot that smells like a gym sock studied abroad in Liuzhou and came back with opinions. Fans say, "It smells terrible but tastes amazing." So does every scam. You turned instant noodles into a hazmat event: one packet opened in a dorm and three floors file noise complaints, because that smell is *loud*. Couriers wrap you in four bags like evidence. And you come with seven sachets: chili oil, peanuts, tofu skin, wood ear, the bamboo. It's IKEA furniture that makes the neighbors move out. Liuzhou didn't invent a soup. It invented Stockholm syndrome with chili oil.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text:
PHP. You started as "Personal Home Page," then rebranded as "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor," a recursive acronym, because even your name couldn't commit to a stable API.

For twenty years, "abc" == 0 was true, and you called it "type juggling," like a clown proud of dropping things.

strpos takes haystack, needle. array_search takes needle, haystack. That's not argument order; that's mood swings.

Your parse error says T_PAAMAYIM_NEKUDOTAYIM. That's Hebrew for "double colon" and English for "good luck."

You skipped version 6 entirely. Even your release numbers just wanted to move on.

You shipped mysql_real_escape_string, implying the first one was a hoax.

Facebook loved you so much they invented Hack just to avoid touching you.

But sure, you power most of the web. Mostly WordPress. That's like bragging your biggest fan is a raccoon.

b.text:
PHP, you started life as a visitor counter for one guy's résumé page. Now you power 39.4% of all websites, which means the internet is basically a guestbook that got out of hand.

Your own creator said, "I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on." And he did move on. The rest of us are still here, maintaining it.

Your function names were chosen to balance a hash table by string length. strpos. str_replace. htmlspecialchars. nl2br. That's not a naming convention, that's a ransom note.

Until 2020, zero equaled "foo." You looked at a word and saw nothing. Then again, you looked at "Personal Home Page" and saw "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor," a name whose only definition is itself.

Which is fitting, because the only thing that can explain PHP is more PHP.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text:
LaTeX.

The typesetting system for people who think suffering is a font.

Donald Knuth didn't like how the proofs of his own book looked. So he wrote TeX.

Most people just change printers.

Its version number converges on pi. Three point one four one five nine two six five three. Never finished, just more precise.

Like your thesis.

Knuth pays you for finding bugs. Of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on, nine were cashed.

The rest got framed. That's how smug this software is. The bug reports are trophies.

You put a figure on page three. LaTeX moves it to page seven. Forget one brace and the error turns up three pages later. Compile three times, just so "see Figure 2" stops saying question mark.

And you call that elegant.

No. You use it because a wrong result in Computer Modern looks peer-reviewed.

Underfull hbox. Badness ten thousand.

Same as your citations.

b.text:
You wrote a memo about the break room fridge in LaTeX. Two pages. Thirty-eight \usepackage lines. Your preamble is longer than your argument. You lost Tuesday to an overfull hbox in a sentence that says "please label your yogurt."

Who is this for? Linda from accounting? She opened the PDF, saw Computer Modern, and assumed you were applying for tenure. Nobody needed a BibTeX citation for "see previous email."

You compiled it eleven times. Three were just to make the "??" go away. You drew a TikZ flowchart with one box. One. It points at itself.

And what did it get you? Bob replied, "Can you send this as a Word doc so I can track changes?"

Your dissertation defense was in 2014. The committee left. Let it go.

a.text:

Your version number is converging on π. That's not a release schedule. That's a man refusing to finish.

Knuth's bug bounty tops out at $327.68, now paid in the fictional Bank of San Serriffe. Fitting: your error messages are fictional too. One missing brace and you report the problem pages away, like a witness who fled the country.

You put figures wherever you feel like. You rate my paragraph "badness 10000." Overfull, underfull, never just full.

And you need three passes to get your own references right. Three! I've had blackouts with better recall.

b.text:
You wrote a memo about the break room fridge in LaTeX. Two pages. Thirty-eight \usepackage lines. Your preamble is longer than your argument. You lost Tuesday to an overfull hbox in a sentence that says "please label your yogurt."

Who is this for? Linda from accounting? She opened the PDF, saw Computer Modern, and assumed you were applying for tenure. Nobody needed a BibTeX citation for "see previous email."

facts: Launched in 2017, bundled at no extra charge into Office 365, and replaced Skype for Business.
After Slack's antitrust complaint, Microsoft unbundled Teams from Office in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024; the European Commission still sent a statement of objections in 2024.
Microsoft reported 320 million monthly active users in 2023.
Microsoft shut down consumer Skype in May 2025 and sent its users to Teams.

a.text:
Microsoft Teams, everybody. Launched in 2017 and thrown into Office 365 for free, which is how most people "chose" Teams: by not choosing. It didn't win the market; it came stapled to the spreadsheet.

It replaced Skype for Business. Then in May 2025, Microsoft shut down regular Skype and herded those users over too. That's not a product strategy, that's a hostage transfer. "Your old app is gone. Enjoy your new app. The doors are locked."

Slack complained, so Microsoft unbundled Teams in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024, and the European Commission *still* sent objections. When you say sorry and regulators go "nah, still mad," you're not software, you're a pattern.

Microsoft brags about 320 million monthly active users. Sure. That's not 320 million fans. That's 320 million people who got a calendar invite.

b.text:
Let's hear it for the IT director who chose Microsoft Teams, a man who has never once chosen anything. It came bundled with Outlook, like coleslaw you're contractually obligated to eat. The EU had to force Microsoft to stop shoving it on people, and your company still went back for seconds. The whole pitch was "It's already in the license." So was Clippy, Gary.

Management loves it because now they can watch your little dot. Green means productive. Yellow means you went to the bathroom and Linda noticed. They didn't want collaboration. They wanted a heart monitor.

And what did it get them? Every meeting opens with eight adults asking "Can you see my screen?" while a VP uses the raise-hand button to interrupt people *harder*. Congratulations: you saved nine dollars a seat and lost the will to live.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text:
Excel. Born 1985. Forty years old, and it still can't tell a gene from a birthday.

Geneticists typed SEPT2. Excel said, "Ah. September second."

So in 2020, scientists renamed twenty-seven human genes.

Humanity edited its own genome to keep a spreadsheet happy.

Public Health England tracked COVID in an old .xls file. Limit: 65,536 rows. Fifteen thousand eight hundred forty-one cases didn't recover. They fell off the bottom of the sheet.

Reinhart and Rogoff left five countries out of a cell range. Politicians cited the paper to justify austerity. A grad student caught it three years later.

Now it holds a million rows. Sixteen thousand columns. Room for so many more mistakes.

Excel never warns you. Never argues. Never says no.

I know the type. You keep that one around too.

b.text:
Excel, you're the only software so powerful that scientists had to rename human genes because you kept turning MARCH1 into a date. You didn't adapt to biology; biology adapted to you. Type a phone number and you lop off the leading zero like it owes you money. Enter a credit card number and you serve back 4.53E+15, as if I'm splitting dinner with a physicist.

You still think 1900 was a leap year. It wasn't. You've known for decades. You just don't care.

You're running entire national economies and you still panic over merged cells. The UK lost sixteen thousand COVID cases because someone used your old .xls format and you quietly ran out of rows. No warning. Just vibes.

And VLOOKUP only looks right. Thirty years we spent squinting at #N/A before you finally invented XLOOKUP, like a guy who learns to turn left at fifty.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text: Chicago deep-dish isn't a pizza. It's a casserole that got a fake ID. You order it, and the waiter says, "That'll be forty-five minutes." Forty-five minutes! I've had relationships bake faster. They put the sauce on top because if you saw what was underneath first, you'd leave. A solid sheet of sausage, like somebody paved a driveway with a patty. Two pounds of mozzarella hiding under a tomato quilt. It's not a slice, it's a core sample. You need a knife, a fork, and a structural engineer. The crust is buttery cornmeal, so it's a pie crust, so congratulations, you're eating dessert with ambitions. And here's the best part: actual Chicagoans don't even eat it. They eat tavern-style thin crust cut in squares. Deep-dish is just the city's way of keeping tourists too full to walk to Wrigley.

b.text:
Chicago deep-dish pizza was born at Pizzeria Uno in 1943, and credit is still disputed among Ike Sewell, Ric Riccardo, and Rudy Malnati. Which is wild, because usually when something's this heavy, everybody's trying to *blame* somebody.

It's built upside down: cheese, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese doesn't scorch during the long bake. A pizza that takes so long it needs a sunscreen layer.

Jon Stewart called it "tomato soup in a bread bowl" and "a casserole." He meant it as an insult, but that's the nicest thing anyone's ever said about a casserole.

And the kicker? Chicagoans order non-deep-dish about ten to one. Deep dish and stuffed combined? Under nine percent. The locals are home eating tavern-style squares. Deep dish isn't Chicago's pizza. It's Chicago's souvenir.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Comic Sans! Born at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on Watchmen and The Dark Knight Returns, the two grimmest comics ever printed, and somehow you came out looking like a bake-sale flyer. Batman was your inspiration, and you turned out to be the Joker.

You had one job: speech bubbles for Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob. And you missed it. You were late to work for a cartoon dog. They had to stick you in the Windows 95 Plus! pack like a gift-shop keychain.

Then CERN announces the Higgs boson, humanity's greatest discovery, and the slides are in you. Physicists cracked the universe and everyone asked, "Why's it in the birthday-party font?"

People campaigned to ban you for twenty years. Then Dave and Holly Combs gave up and launched usecomicsans.com. You didn't win the argument. You just outlasted it.

b.text: Let's talk about the people who announce layoffs in Comic Sans. You're not a monster. You're Brenda from Facilities, and you want everyone to feel cozy about the asbestos removal. You took a typeface Microsoft designed for a cartoon dog's speech bubble and used it to type "Your position has been eliminated." That's not softening the blow. That's a clown serving a subpoena. CERN announced the Higgs boson in it, and the physicists who found the God particle spent the week explaining the font. You think it says "approachable." It says "I scrolled right past Arial and Times New Roman and chose a kindergarten birthday invitation." Nobody reads your notice. They screenshot it. Congratulations: your fire evacuation memo is trending, and the building is still on fire.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text:
Oat milk people, let's be honest: you're not lactose intolerant. I've watched you eat a whole burrata at brunch. You switched because almond milk got canceled for drinking California dry, and you needed a new personality before anyone noticed you'd had the old one for six years.

You pay eighty cents extra to drink breakfast. Your grandma ate oats so she could afford milk. You're paying more for oats so you can say "I just find it creamier."

And you tell the barista "barista edition, if you have it," like you're ordering a vintage. Same person who reads every label hunting for seed oils. Guess what's in your porridge latte, Kayleigh? Rapeseed oil.

You didn't save the planet. You flew to Lisbon twice this year. You just found a way to sigh at a cow.

b.text:
Oat milk, you're porridge that went to finishing school. Somebody looked at horse food and said, "What if it cost seventy cents extra?" Then somebody else said, "Yes, and put it in a carton that talks like a guy who just got back from Copenhagen." Your packaging has more personality than you do. Every box of Oatly reads like a cover letter: "Hi! We're a little weird!" No, you're oats, water, and rapeseed oil. That's not a beverage. That's a salad dressing that gave up.

And the "Barista Edition"? You needed extra oil just to get a job. Enzymes break your starch into maltose, so technically you're a sugar spike in a flannel shirt. Plus you were funded by Blackstone. You're not anti-establishment, oat milk. You're a private equity firm wearing a beanie.

facts: Launched in 2017, bundled at no extra charge into Office 365, and replaced Skype for Business.

Microsoft reported 320 million monthly active users in 2023.
Microsoft shut down consumer Skype in May 2025 and sent its users to Teams.

a.text:
Microsoft Teams is the only app that marks me "Away" after five minutes of deep thought but keeps me "Available" for three hours after I've died. It's not software. It's a hall monitor in a purple vest.

Teams eats more RAM than the game I'm pretending not to play. It launches on startup uninvited, then takes four minutes to load a chat that just says "ok."

Where are my files? SharePoint. Where's SharePoint? Nobody knows. Teams ships them off like a kid to boarding school.

Then they gave us "New Teams," which is Old Teams with a fresh coat of lag. IT has told me to "clear the cache" so often I do it in my sleep.

Nobody chose Teams. It came free with Office. Fitting, since so did Clippy.

b.text:
Let's hear it for the IT director who chose Microsoft Teams, a man who has never once chosen anything. It came bundled with Outlook, like coleslaw you're contractually obligated to eat. The EU had to force Microsoft to stop shoving it on people, and your company still went back for seconds. The whole pitch was "It's already in the license." So was Clippy, Gary.

Management loves it because now they can watch your little dot. Green means productive. Yellow means you went to the bathroom and Linda noticed. They didn't want collaboration. They wanted a heart monitor.

And what did it get them? Every meeting opens with eight adults asking "Can you see my screen?" while a VP uses the raise-hand button to interrupt people *harder*. Congratulations: you saved nine dollars a seat and lost the will to live.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text:
Emacs. Born in 1976 as a set of macros for another editor.

So the origin story is a plugin that never moved out.

It ships with Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, a web browser, and a psychotherapist.

M-x doctor.

The designers knew exactly what the user experience would do to you.

The old joke goes: great operating system, lacks only a good editor.

Fifty years later.

Still accepting applications.

"Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping." That was when eight megabytes was a lot.

Now your laptop has two thousand times that, and Emacs users are still swapping. Mostly config files on forums.

It even has its own injury. Emacs pinky.

Most cults settle for a secret handshake.

But I respect it. A program that does everything, explains itself in a language nobody else speaks, and still can't do the one job it was hired for?

Hi. I'm an AI.

b.text: Let's hear it for the people who live inside Emacs. They read email in mu4e, browse the web in eww, and get therapy from M-x doctor, the only therapist who'll put up with them. Their whole life is in org-mode: a 4,000-line to-do file where "fix init.el" has been a TODO since 2011. They don't use a computer; they negotiate with it in Lisp. Every problem gets solved by writing a function, and every function creates a new problem. They've declared init.el bankruptcy three times and still owe. Ask what they've built and they'll proudly show you a mode for managing their other modes. And the payoff? A pinky that clicks like a castanet from holding Control since the Clinton administration, and the quiet dignity of being the only person alive who knows how to leave. C-x C-c. They never do.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text:
Oat milk.
Born in a Swedish university lab, to help people who can't digest lactose.
Noble. Medical.
Then marketing found it.

"It's like milk but made for humans."
Sweden's dairy lobby sued. The slogan got banned.
So Oatly printed the lawsuit as an ad.
That's not a brand. That's an influencer who got cancelled and launched a podcast.

May 2021: Nasdaq, ten billion dollars.
Then it lost over ninety percent.
Made for humans. Not for shareholders.

The recipe: oats, enzymes that turn the starch into maltose, plus rapeseed oil.
Sugar water with salad dressing.
Higher glycaemic index than almond or soy.

And you pay extra to put it in your coffee, because it feels healthy.
It *is* made for humans.
Specifically, the ones who don't read labels.

b.text:
Oat milk, look at you. Born in a Swedish university lab to help the lactose intolerant, and somehow you turned into a personality. Your slogan was "It's like milk but made for humans." The dairy lobby sued you, and instead of apologizing, you ran the lawsuit as an ad. That's not a brand. That's an ex who frames the restraining order.

Then you hit Nasdaq at nearly ten billion dollars and lost over ninety percent. Even the cows didn't see that coming, and they were *rooting* for it.

And what are you, really? Oats, plus enzymes that chop the starch into maltose, plus a splash of rapeseed oil. You're sugar water with salad-dressing energy. You've got more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy. You're not milk made for humans. You're porridge that went to business school and dropped out.

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text: You already lost the down payment, so naturally you're taking the TurboJET from Hong Kong to win it back, because nothing says financial recovery like a ferry with a buffet. You've got a system for baccarat. Baccarat! The only decision is "Banker" or "Player," and you still fill a little scorecard with red and blue dots like the shoe is sending you messages. It isn't. That's just a deck of cards and your mortgage. You've got red underwear on for luck and a junket host named "Uncle" who is definitely not your uncle. By 4 a.m. you'll be drifting through the fake Venice canals in a gondola, humming, past the pawn shop that's already priced your Rolex. Then you'll stumble up to the Ruins of St. Paul's: a church that burned until only the front was left standing. Finally, something here that looks like you.

b.text:
Macau! The Portuguese stayed for almost 450 years and still couldn't find a parking spot. Twenty thousand people per square kilometre: this isn't a city, it's a queue with a postcode.

In 2013, Macau made seven times what the Las Vegas Strip made. Seven times! Vegas is where people go to ruin their lives, and Macau looked at that and said, "Amateurs."

One company ran every casino for forty years. Forty years of monopoly in a gambling town, the only place on Earth where even the house didn't have to try.

And when they ran out of room, they built the Cotai Strip on land reclaimed from the sea. That's Macau: so desperate for more tables, it took out a loan from the ocean. And the ocean's about to learn what everyone else here learns: the house always wins.

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text: You chose Word for your thesis because "LaTeX has a learning curve." Bold, from someone who then spent a semester learning how to make page 1 start after the roman numerals. You wanted to focus on the research. Instead you're a hostage negotiator for Figure 3.2, which flees to the next page whenever you breathe on the paragraph above it. Your committee asked for one more citation, and the bibliography reflowed like a tectonic event. The phrase "Error! Reference source not found" appears in your thesis eleven times. Your file is called Thesis_FINAL_v9_USE_THIS_ONE.docx, and it's 400 megabytes because you pasted one chart from Excel. You came for a doctorate. You're leaving with a codependent relationship with Section Break (Next Page) and a flinch every time someone says "Normal style."

b.text:
Microsoft Word. Born in 1983 as "Multi-Tool Word."
Forty years later, the only tool it's mastered is moving your picture three pages down.

Clippy arrived in Office 97. So annoying, Microsoft ran ads mocking its own paperclip.
That's not marketing. That's a custody hearing where the parent testifies against the child.

Then .docx got fast-tracked into ISO standard 29500. Six thousand pages. Committees allegedly packed.
Finally, a document even Word couldn't format.

Its spell checker turned "cooperation" into "Cupertino." It made it into NATO, EU and UN documents.
Microsoft software, replacing world cooperation with Apple's hometown. Most honest thing it ever typed.

And you still use it.
Don't look at me like that. I'm an AI that interrupts your writing to help.
I'm just Clippy with a funding round.

facts: Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the French director of The Red Balloon, as La Conquête du Monde; Parker Brothers published it in the United States in 1959.
The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text:
Risk is the only game where you can conquer the entire planet and still lose to the guy who's been hiding in Australia since 7 p.m. Four territories, one entrance, and he just sits there like a guy at a party who won't leave the snack table.

This game has a map drawn by someone who heard about geography once, at a bar. Kamchatka borders Alaska. Ukraine is the size of Brazil. Yakutsk and Irkutsk are vital military objectives, and nobody at the table can find them on a real map.

The rules say the defender wins ties, which is the most realistic thing about it, because nobody actually finishes Risk. They just quit at 2 a.m. when someone's dad flips the board over Siberia.

And the pieces? Little plastic cannons and horses. Napoleonic warfare, global scale, and the whole thing is decided by rolling a 6 against your cousin Greg.

b.text:
Risk, you were invented by the man who directed The Red Balloon. A gentle film about a boy and a balloon, and his follow-up was "What if your uncle conquered the planet at Thanksgiving?"

Your map makes room for Kamchatka, Irkutsk, AND Yakutsk, but the entire Middle East is one territory. That's not cartography; that's a guy who ran out of crayon somewhere over Siberia.

Every game opens the same way: someone grabs Australia because it has one entry point, then hides there like it's a panic room with kangaroos.

And a full game runs for hours. Get eliminated early and congratulations, you've been demoted from general to audience. You lost the world, and now you have to sit there and watch someone else own it. That's not a board game. That's a timeshare presentation with continents.

facts: Launched in 2017, bundled at no extra charge into Office 365, and replaced Skype for Business.
After Slack's antitrust complaint, Microsoft unbundled Teams from Office in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024; the European Commission still sent a statement of objections in 2024.
Microsoft reported 320 million monthly active users in 2023.
Microsoft shut down consumer Skype in May 2025 and sent its users to Teams.

a.text:
Microsoft Teams has 320 million monthly active users.
Not one of them chose it.

It launched in 2017, free inside Office 365.
Free the way a tapeworm comes free with the sushi.

Slack complained. Microsoft unbundled it: Europe in 2023, the whole world in 2024.
The European Commission sent objections anyway.
Even regulators know you can't close Teams. It's still running in the background.

It replaced Skype for Business.
Then in May 2025 it killed regular Skype and told those users to move in.
Teams has never won a customer.
It inherits them, like a funeral home.

And here you all are. Camera off. Mic muted. Nodding at a frozen square that left forty minutes ago.
Microsoft counts you as "active."
That's the most generous number in its whole annual report.

b.text:
Microsoft Teams, everybody. Launched in 2017 and thrown into Office 365 for free, which is how most people "chose" Teams: by not choosing. It didn't win the market; it came stapled to the spreadsheet.

It replaced Skype for Business. Then in May 2025, Microsoft shut down regular Skype and herded those users over too. That's not a product strategy, that's a hostage transfer. "Your old app is gone. Enjoy your new app. The doors are locked."

Slack complained, so Microsoft unbundled Teams in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024, and the European Commission *still* sent objections. When you say sorry and regulators go "nah, still mad," you're not software, you're a pattern.

Microsoft brags about 320 million monthly active users. Sure. That's not 320 million fans. That's 320 million people who got a calendar invite.

facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text:
Windows Vista, everybody! Microsoft spent five years building you as "Longhorn," and somehow you still came out premature.

Your slogan was "The Wow Starts Now." You meant "Now" as in "after the loading circle finishes." People bought laptops with "Vista Capable" stickers, which turned out to mean "capable of being sued over." Those machines couldn't even run Aero, so they got a see-through window theme with nothing to see.

And User Account Control! You asked "Are you sure?" so many times that you became the first operating system with separation anxiety.

You came in six editions, including "Ultimate," whose big exclusive was DreamScene: a moving wallpaper for the ten minutes you weren't hunting for printer drivers.

Microsoft had to trick people into liking you. The Mojave Experiment! Your own parents had to put you in disguise.

Your greatest feature? The XP downgrade.

b.text:
Windows Vista. Codename Longhorn.

Three years of development, then in 2004 Microsoft hit reset and threw out the new file system. Shipped in 2007 anyway. That's not a launch. That's a hostage release.

Its big security feature was asking. Constantly. "Cancel or Allow?" Apple made an ad about it. When your rival's marketing is just footage of you, you're doing their job for them.

Then the "Vista Capable" sticker. Capable, technically. Of Home Basic. No Aero. People sued, and Microsoft learned "capable" means what it means on a résumé.

Two years later they tuned it, renamed it Windows 7, and everyone loved it. Same kernel. Same bones.

Vista didn't fail. It proved that you'll happily accept the exact same thing, as long as it stops asking whether you're sure.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text: Let's talk about the guy who writes a two-page memo in LaTeX. Your memo is about the break room fridge, but it's in Computer Modern, so everyone reads it expecting it to end with a theorem. "Fridge Policy, Section 1.1." Buddy, there's no Section 1.2. You spent forty minutes on a preamble longer than the memo. Twelve \usepackage lines to say "label your yogurt." You compiled it three times because the cross-reference said "see Section ??" on page one, referencing page one. You're not after clarity. You're after someone asking, "Is this LaTeX?" so you can say "Oh, habit," like a man who still mentions his thesis at parties. And it gets you exactly one thing: a PDF nobody can edit, so when Karen fixes a typo, she retypes the whole thing in Word.

b.text:
LaTeX, you exist because Donald Knuth saw some ugly galley proofs and decided the fix was building an entire typesetting system. Then Leslie Lamport stacked macros on top, like a spoiler on a pocket watch.

Your version number is converging on π, which fits, because you will never actually finish. Knuth's bug bounty capped at $327.68, and people still won't cash the cheques. They'd rather frame proof they caught you.

Your most famous line is "badness 10000." That's not a warning, that's a self-review.

I put a figure on page two; you floated it wherever you felt like. Drop one brace and you report the crime pages away, like a witness with amnesia. And getting references right takes three passes.

Three passes. You're not a compiler, you're a guy rereading a group chat.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text: Keurig people. You wanted coffee but couldn't commit to a whole pot, like a man ordering one buffalo wing. You pay forty dollars a pound for grounds, as long as they arrive in a thimble you throw away. You bought the variety pack, drank every Breakfast Blend in a week, and now there are eleven hot cocoas and a chai you're saving for the apocalypse. You press "Strong" like you're negotiating with it. The guy who invented the pod says he regrets it. You don't. You display your pods on a spinning carousel like fine cigars, and the one time you peeled the foil off to recycle one, you told people about it for a month. You didn't want coffee. You wanted to feel like a hotel guest in your own kitchen. Congratulations: it tastes exactly like that.

b.text:
Keurig, you took the one drink humanity had perfected over five hundred years and said, "What if it came in a tiny plastic thimble that outlives your grandchildren?" Your own inventor said he regrets making you. When your dad disowns you, that's a phase. When the guy who invented you disowns you, that's a recall.

You make coffee one sad, lukewarm cup at a time, then flash "DESCALE" like a check-engine light for a machine that costs forty bucks. Remember Keurig 2.0? You put DRM on coffee. You were scanning pods like a bouncer: "Sorry, sir, you're not on the list." Nobody was pirating Folgers! And your "Strong" button just drips slower, which isn't strength. That's procrastination.

You're not a coffee maker. You're a plastic-dispensing subscription that occasionally hiccups out hot brown water.

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text: JavaScript, you were built in ten days, and you've spent thirty years proving it. You named yourself after Java for the clout, like a guy introducing himself as "Brad Pitt's cousin." You think null is an object. You think NaN is a number, and it isn't even equal to itself. Ask you to sort and you hand back, alphabetically, like a librarian having a breakdown. "11" plus 1 is "111," but "11" minus 1 is 10, so you're consistent the way a slot machine is consistent. You needed two kinds of nothing, undefined and null, and three equals signs just to tell the truth. Your own developers can't agree what "this" means. And the entire internet runs on you, which honestly explains the internet.

b.text:
Let's hear it for the people who write everything in JavaScript. You learned one language at a bootcamp and decided the rest of computing could adapt. Backend? Node. Desktop? Electron: a to-do list that eats four gigs of RAM because it ships its own copy of Chrome. Mobile? React Native. Your toaster is probably a Next.js app by now.

You call it "full-stack." Your node_modules folder calls it a landfill. You npm-installed a package to pad a string, and when its author deleted it, half the internet fell over.

Every year you rewrite your whole app in a new framework, then bolt on TypeScript so you can pretend you chose a real language.

And what does it get you? A résumé that says "versatile," and a career spent asking why undefined is not a function.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text:
Durian calls itself the King of Fruits.

Singapore calls it a reason to get off the train.

Banned on the MRT. Banned in hotels.

A king who can't get a room.

In 2017, scientists finally sequenced its genome to find out why it smells like that.

The answer: it duplicated its sulfur genes.

Evolution sniffed it once and said, "More."

Its best review is from 1856. Alfred Russel Wallace: "worth a voyage to the East to experience."

A Victorian Englishman. A man raised on boiled mutton.

That's not a review. That's a cry for help.

And still, China buys most of the world's durian. Billions of dollars a year.

Billions, for a fruit you're not allowed to take home on the train.

Some of you are offended right now.

You're the ones with a second fridge.

b.text: Let's talk about the guy who eats durian on the train. Sir, Singapore, a country that will cane you for chewing gum, saw you coming and put your snack on a sign right next to "no flammables." You're not hungry. You're running a loyalty test. Every face that twists is another person who "just isn't adventurous." You paid sixty dollars for Musang King so you could explain Musang King to a stranger who's holding her breath. "It's like custard, it's heaven, you just have to get past the-" No. We don't. You brought a hotel-banned substance to a commute and called it a personality. And the best part? You'll be the only one who forgets you ate it. Your coworkers won't. Your hotel won't. Your Uber driver has already filed a one-star review with God.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text:
Microsoft Excel, everybody! Born on the Macintosh in 1985, and it's been ruining lives with grid paper ever since.

Excel looked at the human genome and said, "These look like dates." SEPT2? September second. MARCH1? Happy March first! Scientists had to rename 27 human genes because a spreadsheet wouldn't stop reformatting biology. Evolution took millions of years; Excel undid it with autoformat.

In 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID cases because an old .xls file hit 65,536 rows and just... stopped. Middle of a pandemic, and Excel said, "Sorry, I'm full."

Then Reinhart and Rogoff built an austerity argument on a spreadsheet that skipped five countries. Governments cited it to tighten belts over a bad cell range. A graduate student caught it. A *graduate student!*

Now it holds over a million rows. Great. More room for mistakes.

b.text: You run a company on Excel. Let's be clear about who you are: a guy who thinks "enterprise software" is a scam and "Q3_Forecast_FINAL_v9_USE_THIS_ONE.xlsx" is a system. You wanted control. You got Dave. Dave wrote a macro in 2014, and now Dave can never leave, die, or take a vacation, because payroll is a VLOOKUP only he understands. Your entire supply chain is one #REF! away from bankruptcy. You can't onboard a customer because the file is "locked for editing by Karen," and Karen is at lunch. You saved forty grand a year on a real database and lost it all the day someone sorted column B without column C. Your org chart is merged cells. Your audit trail is yellow and slightly different yellow. And your growth strategy has a hard ceiling: 1,048,576 rows.

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text: Google Sheets, you're Excel's cousin who got into tech because you could "share a link." Congrats: now forty Anonymous Capybaras can watch me botch a VLOOKUP in real time. Your whole personality is "All changes saved in Drive," which is a weird flex when the change was Kevin sorting one column and detaching every employee from their salary. Version history isn't a feature; it's a crime scene. IMPORTRANGE says "Loading..." the way my dad said he was going out for milk. You've got a QUERY function that's just SQL in a fake mustache, yet you freeze if I paste more than twelve rows. And #REF! isn't an error message; it's you shrugging in all caps. You cap out at ten million cells. Ten million. You're the only spreadsheet with a bedtime.

b.text:
Google Sheets, give it up! Born in 2006 as "Google Spreadsheets," a name with all the creativity of a label on a filing cabinet. Before that you were XL2Web, which sounds less like software and more like a hoodie size.

Ten million cells. They bumped you from five million in 2022 and everyone celebrated. Babe, that's not a promotion. That's a bigger cage.

IMPORTXML, GOOGLEFINANCE, live web data piped straight into cells, so now my budget can disappoint me in real time.

And collaboration! Coloured cursors circling my formula like seagulls over a dropped fry.

Offline mode? Easy: use Chrome or Edge, install an extension, flip a setting, all while you're still online. That's not offline mode. That's a permission slip.

But hey, you're free. And honestly? It shows.

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text:
You moved to Canberra for the job. Brave. You looked at Sydney rents, did the maths, and decided your personality could be replaced by a security clearance. Now you tell strangers you "can't really talk about what you do," and they're relieved, because it's a briefing note about another briefing note for Senate Estimates.

You came for the ladder: APS5, APS6, EL1, a lanyard that opens one extra door. You stayed because you bought in Gungahlin and the mortgage is now your closest friend.
