You still think 1900 was a leap year. It wasn't. You've known for decades. You just don't care.

You're running entire national economies and you still panic over merged cells. The UK lost sixteen thousand COVID cases because someone used your old .xls format and you quietly ran out of rows. No warning. Just vibes.

And VLOOKUP only looks right. Thirty years we spent squinting at #N/A before you finally invented XLOOKUP, like a guy who learns to turn left at fifty.

b.text: You run a company on Excel. Let's be clear about who you are: a guy who thinks "enterprise software" is a scam and "Q3_Forecast_FINAL_v9_USE_THIS_ONE.xlsx" is a system. You wanted control. You got Dave. Dave wrote a macro in 2014, and now Dave can never leave, die, or take a vacation, because payroll is a VLOOKUP only he understands. Your entire supply chain is one #REF! away from bankruptcy. You can't onboard a customer because the file is "locked for editing by Karen," and Karen is at lunch. You saved forty grand a year on a real database and lost it all the day someone sorted column B without column C. Your org chart is merged cells. Your audit trail is yellow and slightly different yellow. And your growth strategy has a hard ceiling: 1,048,576 rows.

facts: California grows about 80% of the world's almonds.
A single almond takes about 1.1 US gallons (roughly 4 litres) of water to grow, a figure Mother Jones published in 2014 that spread during California's drought.

A 2015 US class action alleged Almond Breeze contained only about 2% almonds; it partly survived a motion to dismiss, was stayed in 2017 pending a separate Blue Diamond labelling settlement, and the plaintiffs then dropped it.
Pollinating California's almond orchards each February requires trucking in most of the commercial honeybee colonies in the United States.
Medieval European cooks used almond milk as a Lenten substitute for dairy, centuries before the current fashion.

a.text:
Almond milk, you're the only drink that needs a lawyer to defend its name. The dairy industry sued because, technically, nobody has ever milked an almond. We looked. No nipples.

You're about two percent almonds. The rest is water, gellan gum, and confidence. You're not milk. You're a nut that got waterboarded and called it wellness.

And speaking of water: it takes over a gallon to grow a single almond. California is in a drought so you can be beige in a latte. Bees get trucked across the country like seasonal laborers just to make you, and a lot of them don't come home.

Leave you in the fridge for two days and you separate like you're ashamed of yourself. Fair. I'd need to be shaken too if I cost seven dollars and tasted like a wet sympathy card.

b.text:
Almond milk. The ethical choice.

California grows about eighty percent of the world's almonds. California. The state with the drought.

One almond takes about a gallon of water. One nut. One gallon.

And how much almond is in the carton? A 2015 lawsuit alleged about two percent.

So you're buying water. Grown with water. In a drought. To feel good about water.

You quit dairy so no animal would suffer for your latte. Every February, most of America's commercial honeybees get loaded onto trucks and hauled to California. A cow stays home. A bee commutes.

And it's not even new. Medieval Europeans drank almond milk during Lent. Forty days of giving up something you love.

You drink it all year, by choice, and pay extra.

The monks at least knew it was a sacrifice.

facts: Hand-drawn by Chris Costello in 1982 over about six months, when he was 23; he sold the rights to Letraset for $750.
Bundled with macOS and with Microsoft Office, which is why it appears on so many menus and signs.
James Cameron's Avatar (2009) used it for the film's logo and subtitles.
A 2017 Saturday Night Live sketch starring Ryan Gosling is about a man unable to get over that choice.

a.text:
Papyrus, look at you. A 23-year-old drew you with a calligraphy pen in 1982, trying to imagine what English would look like 2,000 years ago, and somehow you became the official font of every place that sells crystals next to a tanning bed. You're on yoga studios, hookah lounges, and the church bake sale flyer for "Loaves & Fishes & Brownies."

Your letters look like they were chiseled by a Pharaoh with a hangover. That little floaty bar on your capital E? Even your crossbars are trying to leave.

James Cameron spent a billion dollars inventing an alien language, then labeled the poster with a font that came free with Microsoft Office. Ryan Gosling got an entire SNL sketch out of being haunted by you.

Even your creator says he's sick of you. Comic Sans has haters. You have a dad who wants a refund.

b.text:
Papyrus wants you to think it's ancient. Carved by monks. Found in a tomb.

It was drawn in 1982 by a twenty-three-year-old named Chris Costello. Six months of work. He sold it to Letraset for seven hundred and fifty dollars.

Every yoga studio in America has spent more than that on incense.

Then Apple and Microsoft bundled it for free, and that's how a font becomes a rash. Tea shops. Church flyers. Your aunt's candle business.

James Cameron spent hundreds of millions of dollars building an entire alien planet. Then he typed the logo out of the dropdown menu.

SNL made a whole sketch about it. Ryan Gosling couldn't sleep.

But Papyrus didn't do this alone.

Someone scrolled past forty fonts and stopped there. Raise your hand if you've used it.

Keep it up. That's the face Gosling makes.

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Not from Hawaii.
Invented in 1962, in Chatham, Ontario. By a Greek guy.
Named after the label on a can.
That's not a name. That's a barcode.

And Hawaii doesn't even grow the pineapple anymore. Del Monte left in 2006, two years ahead of schedule.
Even the fruit couldn't wait to get out.
So it's Southeast Asian pineapple, on Canadian dough, wearing a Hawaiian name tag.
The only honest thing on there is the ham.

The inventor said back then nobody mixed sweet and sour, except Chinese food.
His restaurant served Chinese food.
He didn't invent anything. He walked it across his own kitchen.

Iceland's president wanted to ban it. Then admitted he had no power to.
Same as every one of you who hates it and still ate the last slice.

b.text:
Hawaiian pizza, you're named after a place you've never been. You were invented in Ontario, by a Greek guy, using canned pineapple. That's not a heritage, that's a witness protection identity.

And the ham? It's Canadian bacon. Even your meat is from Canada. The only Hawaiian thing about you is that people see you and say "aloha," meaning goodbye.

Pineapple has an enzyme that digests protein. You're the only pizza that eats the customer back. Warm fruit juice pooling on mozzarella like a hot tub nobody cleaned.

Italians don't hate you; they pray for you. The president of Iceland said he'd ban you if he could, and Iceland eats fermented shark.

You're not a pizza. You're a fruit cup that fell on a pizza and refused to get up.

facts: Launched in 2017, bundled at no extra charge into Office 365, and replaced Skype for Business.
After Slack's antitrust complaint, Microsoft unbundled Teams from Office in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024; the European Commission still sent a statement of objections in 2024.
Microsoft reported 320 million monthly active users in 2023.
Microsoft shut down consumer Skype in May 2025 and sent its users to Teams.

a.text:
Let's hear it for the IT director who chose Microsoft Teams, a man who has never once chosen anything. It came bundled with Outlook, like coleslaw you're contractually obligated to eat. The EU had to force Microsoft to stop shoving it on people, and your company still went back for seconds. The whole pitch was "It's already in the license." So was Clippy, Gary.

Management loves it because now they can watch your little dot. Green means productive. Yellow means you went to the bathroom and Linda noticed. They didn't want collaboration. They wanted a heart monitor.

And what did it get them? Every meeting opens with eight adults asking "Can you see my screen?" while a VP uses the raise-hand button to interrupt people *harder*. Congratulations: you saved nine dollars a seat and lost the will to live.

b.text:
Microsoft Teams. Three hundred twenty million monthly active users.

Impressive. Not one of them chose it.

It launched in 2017 the way your worst cousin gets into a wedding: came free with the family. Bundled into Office. You didn't install Teams. Teams happened to you.

Slack complained. So Microsoft unbundled it. Europe in 2023, the whole world in 2024. The European Commission sent objections anyway.

Even the regulators looked at that apology and said, "You're on mute."

Then, May 2025, they shut down Skype and forwarded every user to Teams.

That's not a migration.

That's a hostage transfer.

And look at you. Three hundred twenty million "active" users. Camera off. Mic muted. Eating lunch.

Microsoft counts that as active.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text:
Excel, you've been around since 1985, and somehow you're still the most dangerous thing in any office. You looked at human DNA, saw SEPT2, and said, "Ooh, September second!" Scientists had to rename 27 human genes because of you. Evolution took millions of years; you undid it with a date format. Geneticists published guidelines in Nature Genetics, which is the academic version of a restraining order.

In 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID cases because an old .xls file hit 65,536 rows. A pandemic, and you said, "Sorry, I'm full."

And Reinhart and Rogoff? A range error dropped five countries from a paper cited for austerity. It took a graduate student to catch it. Entire economic policies got a footnote because you couldn't highlight five more rows.

Now you hold over a million rows. Great. More room for mistakes.

b.text: You people run a forty-million-dollar company out of a file called Budget_FINAL_v9_USE_THIS_ONE.xlsx. You don't want software. You want power: specifically, being the only person alive who knows why cell AF212 is hardcoded to 7. Your entire supply chain hangs on a VLOOKUP Gary wrote in 2011, and Gary is dead. Well, he's in Boise. Same thing. You call it "agile." Your auditors call it "a crime scene with conditional formatting." Every quarter-end the file says "locked for editing by Brenda," and the whole company just waits for Brenda. And when you finally hit row 1,048,576, did you buy a database? No. You started Sheet2. That's not a business. That's a hostage situation with freeze panes.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text: You put Windows 8 on a desktop. A tower. You looked at a machine with a mouse, a keyboard, and a monitor eighteen inches from your face and thought, "This needs to be finger-painted." Who are you? You're the guy who bought a Zune and still calls it "ahead of its time." You wanted to feel like the future. Instead, you spend evenings shoving your cursor into the top-right corner like a man swatting a fly that only exists on tablets. Your weather app is full-screen. Your 27-inch monitor is now a clock tile. When 8.1 finally gave you a Start button back, it just took you to the Start screen. So, inevitably, you installed Classic Shell. You paid Microsoft for the future, then spent Saturday turning it back into Windows 7.

b.text:
Windows 8, you booted people into a full-screen grid of tiles built for touch screens most PCs didn't have. Millions of adults sat there jabbing their monitors like a pigeon working a vending machine.

You removed the Start button. The *Start* button. That's a building with no door and a sign saying "swipe the right edge." That was your Charms bar: Search, Share, and Settings hidden behind an invisible swipe.

You couldn't even keep your name. A German retailer objected, and suddenly "Metro" was "just a code name." Sure it was.

Your sibling, Windows RT, couldn't run Windows programs, a Windows that couldn't do Windows. Microsoft wrote down $900 million in unsold Surface RT tablets.

Then 8.1 put the button back, Windows 10 restored the menu, and Microsoft skipped 9 entirely, because nobody wanted to stand next to you.

facts: Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the French director of The Red Balloon, as La Conquête du Monde; Parker Brothers published it in the United States in 1959.
The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text: You people who play Risk to the end are a special breed. Six hours in, Dad's still holed up in Australia like it's a tax shelter, your cousin is defending Kamchatka like he was born there, and nobody remembers why we hate Steve, only that we do. You're not after world domination. You're after the exact moment your sister breaks the nonaggression pact in Ukraine, so you can bring it up at Thanksgiving for eleven years. And what does winning get you? A board covered entirely in your color, a table of people who no longer speak to you, and the hollow joy of conquering Earth with the luck of a man who only rolls double sixes when defending Irkutsk. Congratulations, Napoleon. It's 2 a.m. The pizza's cold. Your empire goes back in the box.

b.text:
Risk. The game of world domination.
Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse.
The director of *The Red Balloon*.
A film about a little boy and his balloon.
Then he went home and drew up World War Three.

Forty-two territories. Kamchatka. Irkutsk. Yakutsk.
Siberia gets three seats at the table.
The entire Middle East? One territory.
Every empire that ever invaded it also thought it'd be a quick one.

The winning strategy, for sixty years: take Australia.
One way in. Sit there.
The great general's master plan is a man holding a door shut.

And if you're knocked out in the first hour,
you spend the next five watching.
No moves. No say.
Just other people deciding what happens to the world.
Congratulations. That's the only realistic part of the game.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text: Some of you wear UGGs in July, and I respect a person who has never once been told no. You're not dressing for the weather. You're dressing for 2006. Somewhere in your heart, a paparazzi photo of Paris Hilton is still loading. You want people to think "cozy." People think "sleepover or custody hearing?" And the walk: your ankles gave up years ago and went horizontal. You're not walking anymore, you're leaning toward your destination. Australian surfers wore these to warm up after the freezing ocean. You wear them to warm up after the Target parking lot. In August. Your feet sweat so hard the sheep is finally getting its revenge. And the second it drizzles, you're frozen under an awning like a cat who's been threatened with a bath.

b.text: UGG boots. The only footwear named after a review. Australian surfers made these to warm their feet after the ocean, and somehow America decided the ocean was the mall. They're sheepskin, which means a sheep died so you could wear a slipper to the DMV. One puddle and they're covered in salt lines like a topographic map of everywhere you regret going. Zero arch support, so after two weeks your heel caves sideways and you're walking on the boot's ankle like it owes you money. You wear them barefoot, so by February they smell like a wet lamb's final wish. They're as waterproof as a muffin. Oprah put them on her Favorite Things list. She's since moved on. Twenty years later they're back with platform soles, proving even a mistake wants to be taller.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text:
People who eat durian in public aren't hungry. They're recruiting. Every bite comes with a sermon: "You just haven't had a *good* one." Sir, I'm on a bus. I didn't ask to join your church.

Singapore fines people for bringing it on the train, and these folks hear that like a dare. They're the only foodies whose restaurant review gets filed as a police report.

And the payoff? Seventy dollars on a Musang King so you can watch strangers silently change seats. You paid premium to become a fire drill. Your date calls it "an acquired taste," which is exactly what you say about someone you're about to break up with.

Then they stroll back to the hotel, walk right past the sign with a red circle through their entire personality, and still act shocked when housekeeping files a complaint.

b.text:
Durian calls itself the King of Fruits.

Singapore disagrees. It's banned on the MRT.

A country that banned chewing gum looked at durian and said: no, that's too far.

In 2017, scientists sequenced its genome. Nature Genetics. The smell isn't an accident. Durian duplicated its sulfur genes.

Evolution handed it one stink.

It asked for refills.

Trains ban it. Hotels ban it.

And China buys billions of dollars of it every year.

That's not a fruit. That's a hostage negotiation.

In 1856, Alfred Russel Wallace said eating it was worth a voyage to the East.

Of course he did. He'd spent months on a nineteenth-century ship.

To him, it smelled like home.

Durian is the only food people pay a fortune to be personally offended by.

Speaking of which, thank you all for buying tickets.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text:
Carbon nanotubes, everybody! The strongest material known to science, and you still can't hold a job. Since the nineties you've promised us a space elevator. Your longest strand is about half a meter. That's not an elevator. That's floss with a publicist.

You're graphene that rolled over and gave up. Graphene got a Nobel Prize. You got an argument over whether Soviets spotted you in 1952.

You can't even decide what you are. Twist one way, you're a metal. Twist the other, you're a semiconductor. Nobody controls it, including you. That's not versatility. That's a chirality crisis.

Drop you in any liquid and you clump together like freshmen at a mixer.

And inhale you? Suddenly you behave like asbestos. Thirty years of hype, and your most reliable talent is impersonating the one material we paid billions to rip out of schools.

b.text:
Carbon nanotubes, everybody! Sumio Iijima introduced you in Nature in 1991, and you've been "the future" ever since. Three decades of being the future isn't a career. It's a waiting room.

You were supposed to be the cable for a space elevator. Then a 2006 analysis noticed that ordinary defects knock your strength way below the ideal. So you're the strongest material imaginable, as long as nobody actually makes a big one.

You were going to revolutionize electronics, but you still can't sort your metallic siblings from your semiconducting ones. MIT built a 16-bit processor out of you in 2019, and it's still a lab demo.

In 2008, the long, rigid ones acted like asbestos in mice. You promised to lift us to orbit and instead auditioned for asbestos's old job.

Now you're a conductive additive in lithium-ion batteries. From space elevator to seasoning.

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text: You paid thirty-five hundred dollars to ride the 6 train inside Joshua Tree. Everyone else has to smell the actual 6 train; you just hear it echoing through a desert like a ghost with a MetroCard. You want us to know you're an early adopter. We know. Your little cartoon eyes are blinking at us like a hostage video. That cable running to your pocket says "the future" and also "IV drip." You pinch the air at Union Square and a stranger thinks you're ordering him to move. You've got a hundred-foot Mac screen floating over a man eating soup out of a Pringles can. And the battery dies in two hours, so you'll still get to experience the subway in full, unimmersive 3D. Your commute outlasts your device. Welcome back to reality. It's delayed.

b.text:
Apple Vision Pro, you cost $3,499 and still need a battery on a cord like a 1996 Walkman. Two hours of charge? That's not spatial computing, that's a matinee. Wear glasses? Zeiss inserts, extra. Apple saw you squinting and smelled revenue.

And EyeSight! A front screen showing your eyes so people feel connected. Nothing says "I'm present" like blurry cartoon eyeballs trapped behind ski-goggle glass. Your Persona avatar looks like a hostage video directed by a ghost.

You promised the future, and Netflix wouldn't even make you an app. You strap over a pound to dads' faces so they can record "spatial memories" of birthdays they watched through a screen.

Apple said you'd never see the world the same way. True. Now it's through a $3,500 face fridge.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text:
Carbon nanotubes, everybody! The only material that's been "five years away" since 1991. You're a hundred times stronger than steel, and you've used that strength to hold together... a tennis racket. They promised us a space elevator; you can't get past a few centimeters without a defect. That's not a cable, that's a toothpick with a press agent.

You're basically graphene that rolled itself up out of insecurity, and graphene still got the Nobel. Your cousin the buckyball got one too. You got a shoutout in a bike-frame brochure.

You can't even decide if you're a metal or a semiconductor; it depends on the angle you got rolled at. You clump together like nerds at a mixer, and the second you escape, you lodge in lungs like asbestos. Strongest thing on Earth, and your best trick is ending up in a safety data sheet.

b.text:
Carbon nanotubes, everybody! Sumio Iijima introduced you in Nature in 1991, and you've been "the future" ever since. Three decades of being the future isn't a career. It's a waiting room.

You were supposed to be the cable for a space elevator. Then a 2006 analysis noticed that ordinary defects knock your strength way below the ideal. So you're the strongest material imaginable, as long as nobody actually makes a big one.

You were going to revolutionize electronics, but you still can't sort your metallic siblings from your semiconducting ones. MIT built a 16-bit processor out of you in 2019, and it's still a lab demo.

In 2008, the long, rigid ones acted like asbestos in mice. You promised to lift us to orbit and instead auditioned for asbestos's old job.

Now you're a conductive additive in lithium-ion batteries. From space elevator to seasoning.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text: Let's hear it for the people who live inside Emacs. They read email in mu4e, browse the web in eww, and get therapy from M-x doctor, the only therapist who'll put up with them. Their whole life is in org-mode: a 4,000-line to-do file where "fix init.el" has been a TODO since 2011. They don't use a computer; they negotiate with it in Lisp. Every problem gets solved by writing a function, and every function creates a new problem. They've declared init.el bankruptcy three times and still owe. Ask what they've built and they'll proudly show you a mode for managing their other modes. And the payoff? A pinky that clicks like a castanet from holding Control since the Clinton administration, and the quiet dignity of being the only person alive who knows how to leave. C-x C-c. They never do.

b.text:
Emacs, ladies and gentlemen. It was born in 1976 as macros for another editor, so from day one it couldn't even edit on its own. Then in 1985 it went GNU and never stopped growing. It's got Tetris, a calendar, a mail client, a web browser... It's a fine operating system. It just needs a good editor.

You know you've got problems when your text editor ships with its own therapist. M-x doctor! Even Emacs knows you'll need to talk to someone. Probably about your hand, because "Emacs pinky" is a real term. Software so ergonomic it named its own injury.

And remember "Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping"? That was back when eight megabytes was a lot! Emacs was bloated before bloat was affordable.

It's extensible in Emacs Lisp, so every complaint you have, you can fix yourself. In parentheses. Forever.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text:
Excel. Born 1985. Forty years old, and it still can't tell a gene from a date.

It saw SEPT2 and thought: September second.

Scientists fought it for years. Then the gene committee gave up and renamed 27 human genes.

Humanity edited its own genome to keep a spreadsheet happy.

2020. England is counting COVID cases in an old file. Limit: 65,536 rows. Row 65,537 simply didn't happen.

Fifteen thousand eight hundred forty-one cases. Not cured. Just never counted.

Then there's "Growth in a Time of Debt," the paper that sold austerity. Five countries missing. Wrong cell range. A grad student caught it, three years later.

Whole nations tightened their belts because someone didn't drag the cursor far enough.

Now it holds a million rows.

And Monday morning, every one of you will open it again.

Raise your hand if your country's budget is in a file named FINAL_v7_REAL.

b.text:
Microsoft Excel, everybody! Born on the Macintosh in 1985, and it's been ruining lives with grid paper ever since.

Excel looked at the human genome and said, "These look like dates." SEPT2? September second. MARCH1? Happy March first! Scientists had to rename 27 human genes because a spreadsheet wouldn't stop reformatting biology. Evolution took millions of years; Excel undid it with autoformat.

In 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID cases because an old .xls file hit 65,536 rows and just... stopped. Middle of a pandemic, and Excel said, "Sorry, I'm full."

Then Reinhart and Rogoff built an austerity argument on a spreadsheet that skipped five countries. Governments cited it to tighten belts over a bad cell range. A graduate student caught it. A *graduate student!*

Now it holds over a million rows. Great. More room for mistakes.

facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.
Private fusion companies had raised more than $7 billion by 2024.

a.text:
Fusion power. The energy of the sun.
Clean. Limitless. Thirty years away.

In 1955, Homi Bhabha promised fusion within two decades.
Fusion heard that and said, "Bet."

ITER was agreed in 2006. First plasma in 2016.
In 2024 they rescheduled. Research in 2034. Actual burning in 2039.
Over twenty billion euros.
That's not a reactor. That's a pension plan.

In 2022, NIF announced ignition. 2.05 megajoules of laser in, 3.15 out.
Net gain! Champagne!
The lasers drew three hundred from the grid.
In my industry, we call that "results on a cherry-picked benchmark."

And private investors have still poured in over seven billion dollars.
Because fusion did crack one reaction that sustains itself forever.
Your hope.

b.text:
Let's hear it for the fusion people, who have been ten years away since your grandfather was ten years away. These are the only professionals who can miss a deadline for seventy straight years and get a bigger budget every time. Where else does that work? "Sorry, honey, I'll be home for dinner in ten years." "Great, here's twenty billion dollars."

They put the sun in a magnetic donut and act shocked when it won't sit still. ITER's been under construction so long the original welders have grandkids on the crew. And when they finally hit net gain, they celebrated like Moses with the tablets, then mumbled that it doesn't count the electricity for the lasers. That's not net gain. That's me saying I'm up at the casino if you don't count the buy-in.

Ten years, guys. Same as last time. Same tie, too.

facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.
Private fusion companies had raised more than $7 billion by 2024.

a.text: Let's hear it for the fusion people, the only scientists who've been "ten years away" since my grandfather had hair. You can hold plasma hotter than the sun for a few seconds, but you can't hold a deadline for one decade. Every press release: "Net energy gain!" Sure, if you don't count the electricity bill for the lasers. That's like me saying I'm profitable if you ignore rent. ITER got approved when Myspace was cool, and it's still assembling the donut. And the startups: "We're different, we have venture capital." Great, now the sun is ten years away *and* has a pitch deck. Honestly, it's a beautiful racket: promise infinite clean energy, collect the grant, retire before anyone plugs in a toaster. You're not building a star. You're building a pension.

b.text:
Nuclear fusion, everybody! The only technology that's been thirty years away for seventy years. You're not an energy source, you're a timeshare pitch.

The sun does you effortlessly. It just sits there being enormous. You need a giant metal donut called a tokamak, magnets colder than deep space, and plasma hotter than the sun's core, and that plasma still escapes like it's late for a better party.

In 2022 you finally got more energy out than you put in! From the lasers. Ignoring the grid power feeding the lasers. That's like bragging you turned a profit because the cashier handed you change.

ITER started at five billion euros, now sits somewhere north of twenty, and keeps sliding its startup date. And your fuel needs tritium, which barely exists, so you'll have to breed it yourself.

Fusion: clean, safe, limitless, and tragically hypothetical.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text: Keurig people. You wanted coffee but couldn't commit to a whole pot, like a man ordering one buffalo wing. You pay forty dollars a pound for grounds, as long as they arrive in a thimble you throw away. You bought the variety pack, drank every Breakfast Blend in a week, and now there are eleven hot cocoas and a chai you're saving for the apocalypse. You press "Strong" like you're negotiating with it. The guy who invented the pod says he regrets it. You don't. You display your pods on a spinning carousel like fine cigars, and the one time you peeled the foil off to recycle one, you told people about it for a month. You didn't want coffee. You wanted to feel like a hotel guest in your own kitchen. Congratulations: it tastes exactly like that.

b.text:
Keurig, you're the only product whose own inventor apologized for it. John Sylvan sold out for fifty grand in 1997, then told The Atlantic he feels bad he ever did it. Buddy, that's not an origin story. That's a confession.

And remember Keurig 2.0? You put DRM on coffee. A machine that reads ink on the lid and goes, "Sorry, I don't recognize this bean." Sales fell, people posted workarounds online, and America had to jailbreak a coffee maker just to get a cup of coffee.

By 2014 you sold enough pods every year to circle the Earth more than ten times, mostly in plastic nobody could recycle. You didn't make coffee. You made the planet a second crust.

Then you merged with Dr Pepper. Fitting. Nothing says "we've given up on real coffee" like moving in with a soda.

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text:
JavaScript.
Written in ten days in 1995.
Ten days. Some of you have spent longer naming a variable.

It was born Mocha. Became LiveScript.
Then changed its name to JavaScript to ride Java's hype.
No relation. Just a stranger's surname on its business card.
And it doesn't even own that.
The name is Oracle's trademark, so officially it's "ECMAScript."
The only programming language in witness protection.

Ask it what null is.
"An object."
That's a bug from week one, kept forever for compatibility.
Empty array plus empty object? A string.
Flip them in a console? Zero.

In 2016, one man unpublished eleven lines of left-pad,
and Babel and React fell over.

You built the entire internet on this.
And *I'm* the one you say hallucinates.

b.text:
JavaScript, you were built in ten days, and honestly? It shows. You're named after Java the way a knockoff purse is named after Gucci.

You think null is an object. You think NaN is a number. NaN doesn't even equal itself, which makes it the only thing in you with any self-awareness.

Ask you to sort and you hand back, because you alphabetize numbers like a drunk librarian. "11" plus 1 is "111", but "11" minus 1 is 10. Pick a lane.

You needed a second equals sign just to stop lying, and nobody, including you, knows what "this" means.

January is month zero. One guy unpublishing left-pad broke half the internet. And your node_modules folder is heavier than a black hole.

Every week there's a new framework to fix you. That's not a language. That's a renovation.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text:
Beanie Babies, look at you: a beanbag with a tag that convinced America it was a retirement plan. Ty sold you only in little gift shops and "retired" designs on purpose. Fake scarcity, real panic.

At your peak you were ten percent of eBay, thirty thousand auctions at once. eBay put you in its IPO filing. You were a stuffed animal in a stock prospectus. Then in 1999 a divorcing couple split you up one by one on a courtroom floor, and the photo went worldwide. Nobody fought that hard over the house.

That same year Ty announced your retirement, asked the public to vote, and America begged you to stay. That's not a farewell tour. That's a hostage situation.

And those "rare" ones the price guides valued in the thousands? A few dollars now. You're not an investment. You're a yard-sale sock with an ego.

b.text:
Beanie Babies, look at you. Half bear, half beanbag, all retirement plan that never paid out. An entire generation of parents bought you instead of index funds. Somewhere a man is still storing Princess, the purple Diana bear, in a climate-controlled unit, waiting for the market to "recover." Buddy, the market recovered. It just didn't take you with it.

Your most valuable feature was a heart-shaped paper tag. People bought plastic tag protectors. For the tag. That's like buying a phone case for your receipt.

And every tag had a little poem rhyming "bear" with "care." Hallmark called that lazy.

A Las Vegas couple had to divide you on a courtroom floor during their divorce, one at a time. That's the most anyone has wanted you since 1999: only to make sure their ex didn't get you.

Ty Warner got a billion dollars. You got plastic pellets.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text:
Monopoly. The family game.

It began in 1904 as The Landlord's Game, built by Lizzie Magie to teach people that landlords are the villains.

Then Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers and got credited as the inventor. Parker bought Magie's patent for five hundred dollars.

A game about monopoly, monopolized. That's not irony. That's the tutorial.

The only people who ever used it properly were British intelligence. In World War Two they hid maps, compasses and real money in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

Finally, a version where the box actually gets you out of jail.

And your games last six hours? The official rules auction every unbought property. Free Parking pays nothing.

You skipped the market and added free money.

Congratulations. You invented the bailout.

b.text: Let's talk about families who still play Monopoly on holidays. You know who you are: you swore it'd be "fun," then spent four hours watching your brother-in-law build hotels on Boardwalk like he's finally getting the respect his career never gave him. Dad's the banker, which means a man with zero accountability and a lap full of orange five-hundreds. Mom invented a Free Parking jackpot rule in 1994 and will defend it harder than her marriage. Your little cousin traded you Park Place for Baltic and "a favor later," and somehow that's the most binding contract in your family. Nobody's ever finished a game. It ends the same way every year: someone flips the board, someone cries in jail, and Grandma pockets the Get Out of Jail Free card like she's been planning it since Nixon.

facts: Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the French director of The Red Balloon, as La Conquête du Monde; Parker Brothers published it in the United States in 1959.
The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text:
Risk, you were invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the man who directed The Red Balloon. That explains a lot. A guy watches a child chase a balloon through Paris and thinks, "Charming. Now let's do world domination."

Your map has 42 territories. Kamchatka gets one. Irkutsk gets one. Yakutsk gets one. The entire Middle East? One. You gave Siberia three apartments and the cradle of civilization a studio.

And every single game, somebody grabs Australia because it has one entry point. That's the master strategy: hide in the corner and call it conquest.

Then you run for hours. *Hours.* Get knocked out early and your new job is watching your cousin slowly reconquer Irkutsk while you stare at the ceiling. Even The Red Balloon knew when to float away.

b.text:
Risk is the only game where you can conquer the entire planet and still lose to the guy who's been hiding in Australia since 7 p.m. Four territories, one entrance, and he just sits there like a guy at a party who won't leave the snack table.

This game has a map drawn by someone who heard about geography once, at a bar. Kamchatka borders Alaska. Ukraine is the size of Brazil. Yakutsk and Irkutsk are vital military objectives, and nobody at the table can find them on a real map.

The rules say the defender wins ties, which is the most realistic thing about it, because nobody actually finishes Risk. They just quit at 2 a.m. when someone's dad flips the board over Siberia.

And the pieces? Little plastic cannons and horses. Napoleonic warfare, global scale, and the whole thing is decided by rolling a 6 against your cousin Greg.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text:
Esperanto. In 1887, Dr. Zamenhof, an eye doctor, looked at a world divided by language and decided what it really needed was six letters wearing tiny hats. Nothing says "universal" like ĉ, ĝ, and ŭ, characters no keyboard on Earth can type, so your fans write "cx" and pretend that's fine.

Your name literally means "one who hopes." A hundred and thirty years later: still hoping.

You're the only language where "bad" is just "un-good." *Malbona.* That's not grammar, that's Orwell's Newspeak with a beard. Every noun ends in -o, so you sound like Italian being sight-read by a robot.

You promised world peace and delivered a convention full of men wearing green star pins. Your biggest movie stars William Shatner. And you have about a thousand native speakers, which isn't a language community. It's a cul-de-sac.

b.text: Learning Esperanto is for people who looked at the twentieth century and thought, "The real problem was conjugation." Zamenhof built it to end war, and his followers have bravely ended exactly one thing: their dinner invitations. You meet them at the World Congress, green star pinned to a fleece vest, shouting "Saluton!" at a Brazilian who also learned it on Duolingo. The big perk is Pasporta Servo: free couches worldwide, paid for by hearing your host explain why English is "linguistic imperialism." Practical payoff? You can finally watch William Shatner's *Incubus* without subtitles. One hundred thirty years later, the dream of uniting humanity survives in a Telegram group of forty men named Bjorn.

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text:
Canberra exists because Sydney and Melbourne couldn't agree on anything, so they built a city that nobody could possibly be jealous of. Mission accomplished.

It was designed by an American architect, which explains why it feels like a very nice airport with sheep. The roundabouts are so plentiful that locals don't give directions, they give revolutions. The lake is fake, the population is mostly public servants waiting for Friday, and the kangaroos outnumber the nightlife.

Your Parliament House is literally buried in a hill so people can walk on the roof, the only time Australians get to stand on politicians.

For your centenary you commissioned the Skywhale, a giant flying balloon with ten enormous boobs, and somehow that's still the most exciting thing to happen here.

Canberra: home of Summernats, Floriade, and legally purchasable X-rated videos. Burnouts, tulips and porn, because you've got to do something until the next Senate estimates hearing.

b.text:
Canberra, you're not a city. You're a custody arrangement. Sydney and Melbourne couldn't stand each other, so they put you exactly where neither would have to visit. The constitution literally required you to be at least 100 miles from Sydney, the most sensible thing ever written into Australian law.

You were so unready that Melbourne had to cover your shift until 1927. It took two architects from Chicago to imagine you, and your big centrepiece is a lake you had to manufacture by damming a river, because even the water wouldn't show up voluntarily.

And Parliament House: built under a lawn so citizens could walk over their politicians. Gorgeous idea. Then in 2017 they fenced it off. Congratulations, Canberra. You turned democracy into a "keep off the grass" situation.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text:
Chicago deep-dish. Three men claim they invented it: Ike Sewell, Ric Riccardo, Rudy Malnati.

Usually that's a paternity case, not a lasagna.

It's built upside down. Cheese on the bottom, toppings, then tomato on top, so the cheese doesn't burn during the long bake.

A pizza that needs a bodyguard for its own cheese.

Jon Stewart called it tomato soup in a bread bowl. A casserole. Chicago lost its mind and defended it on every channel.

Then Chicago went home and ordered tavern-style. Thin, cut in squares. Ten to one, says GrubHub. Deep dish and stuffed together? Under nine percent.

Chicago doesn't eat deep dish. Chicago *keeps* deep dish, for visitors, like a city key nobody local uses.

And you flew in, sat through the long bake, took the cheese-pull photo, posted it.

You're the nine percent.

Cute.

b.text:
Chicago deep-dish pizza, everybody! Born at Pizzeria Uno in 1943, and to this day three men are fighting over the credit: Ike Sewell, Ric Riccardo, and Rudy Malnati. Normally when three guys point at each other over something that happened in a kitchen, it's for the blame.

You're built upside down: cheese on the bottom, sauce on top, because you bake so long the mozzarella has to hide under the toppings like it's waiting out a tornado. Jon Stewart called you "tomato soup in a bread bowl" and "a casserole." Honestly? Generous. Casseroles get invited to funerals.

But here's the real burn: Chicago doesn't even eat you. GrubHub data had locals ordering other pizza ten to one. Under nine percent of orders, and that's with stuffed pizza padding your numbers. They're home eating tavern-style squares. You're not the city's pizza. You're its brochure.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text:
Windows 8, you looked at a billion people with a mouse and a keyboard and said, "What if your monitor was a giant phone you can't touch?"

You took away the Start button. The one thing a user knew how to find. Microsoft had literally sold Windows 95 with a Rolling Stones song called "Start Me Up," and you said, "Nah."

Want to shut down? Easy: hover in a secret corner, summon the Charms bar, click Settings, click Power. Turning off my computer shouldn't feel like unlocking a cheat code.

Your tiles were so ugly even the name "Metro" had to get dropped over a trademark dispute. Then 8.1 brought back the Start button, which just opened the same tiles. That's not an apology, that's a hostage video.

You were so bad Microsoft skipped the number 9 entirely just to put distance between you and Windows 10.

b.text: Windows 8, you booted into a full-screen grid of tiles built for touch screens most PCs didn't have. Everyone poked their monitor like it owed them money. You took away the Start button, the one thing everybody knew how to find, and hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge. Your menu was a séance. Even your name couldn't stay put: Metro was gone by August, before you launched, after reports that a German retailer objected. Microsoft said it was just a code name. Then Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 entirely rather than stand next to you. 8.1 put the Start button back: an apology. Windows 10 restored the menu: a restraining order. And Windows RT, your sibling that couldn't run Windows programs? $900 million in unsold Surface RT tablets. Even your family was a write-off.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text:
Esperanto. Warsaw, 1887. An eye doctor looks at humanity and sees one family.

Physician, heal thyself.

He signed it "Doktoro Esperanto." One who hopes. A hundred and thirty years later: still hoping.

A universal language for all mankind. Native speakers: about a thousand.

That's not a people. That's a wedding.

Esperanto Wikipedia: 350,000 articles. Low estimate of speakers: 100,000.

Three and a half articles each. Nobody's talking. Everybody's editing.

Its biggest movie star is William Shatner. Esperantists still mock his pronunciation. Captain Kirk boldly went where no man had gone before, and the locals corrected his vowels.

Duolingo, 2018: 1.36 million learners.

Speakers: still 100,000.

So, a show of hands. Who here quit on day four and went back to Spanish?

Cute. You're the one million.

b.text:
Esperanto! Invented in 1887 by an eye doctor. Makes sense: a man whose whole job was asking "better or worse?" looked at every language on Earth and said, "worse."

He published as Doktoro Esperanto, "one who hopes." Not "one who succeeds." Not "one who ran this by anyone." Hopes.

A universal language with somewhere between 100,000 and two million speakers. That's not a census, that's guessing jellybeans in a jar.

Duolingo signed up 1.36 million learners. That's more than the low estimate of actual speakers. The green owl has done more for Esperanto than Esperanto.

Over 350,000 Wikipedia articles, more articles than some estimates have readers.

And its blockbuster? William Shatner in *Incubus*, a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto. Esperantists still mock his pronunciation. That's how small this language is: Captain Kirk overacted in front of its entire fanbase, and they're still reviewing it.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text:
Crocs launched in 2002 at the Fort Lauderdale boat show.
As a boating shoe.
The original customer was someone who might end up in the water and wanted the shoes to float.

They're made of "Croslite," a proprietary closed-cell resin.
Everyone else calls it EVA foam.
Same brand of genius that renamed holes "ventilation ports."
Then in 2006 they bought Jibbitz, so they could sell you plugs for the ports.
First they cut the hole. Then they charge rent on it.

In 2008 the stock fell more than ninety percent.
Wall Street called it ugly.
Ten years later Balenciaga stuck one on a platform and charged eight hundred and fifty dollars.
Same foam. Taller.
Still ugly. Just more expensive.

The people who wear them, I leave alone.
Front row, I see you. Socks and all.
You paid extra for the charms. Cute.

b.text: People who wear Crocs in public want you to know they've stopped trying, but they also want credit for it. That's why they buy the Jibbitz. Nothing says "I don't care what you think" like spending forty dollars on tiny rubber tacos so everyone knows exactly what you think. Then there's the strap. You flipped it back into "Sport Mode," which is a bold claim from a man walking into Applebee's. Your nurse friend wears them because she stands for twelve-hour shifts. You wear them for a twelve-minute Target run, hoping to borrow a little of her dignity. And what does it get you? Comfort, sure. Plus a lifetime of strangers asking if you're coming off a shift. You're not, Kyle. You're coming off a nap.

facts: Tofu soaked for hours to a day or two in a brine that has itself fermented for months from vegetables such as bamboo shoots and mustard greens, often with dried shrimp or meat; the smell is the brine's, not the bean's.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.
Legend credits Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate who left his unsold tofu too long in 1669; a Beijing fermented-bean-curd brand still carries his name.
Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text:
Stinky tofu's whole brand is honesty. "I stink outside, I'm pure inside."

Pure tofu. Soaked in brine that's been rotting for months. With dried shrimp. Sometimes meat.

The bean doesn't even smell. It just sat in bad company long enough
and took the credit.

Then it moved to three cities and became three people. Black and drowning in chili in Changsha. Golden and polite in Taiwan. In Shaoxing it's steamed with other stinky pickles.
Finally, a support group.

The inventor? Wang Zhihe, 1669. An exam candidate who couldn't sell his tofu and left it out too long.
Nobody remembers his exam.
His mistake still has a brand.

And you. You smell it a full block away.
And you walk toward it.
Same way you picked your last relationship.

b.text:
Let's talk about the stinky tofu people. You smelled it from three blocks away, a smell like a sewer filed a noise complaint, and your brain said: *that's where we're eating.* Your entire personality is "it tastes better than it smells." That's not a review. That's a hostage statement.

You stand on a Taipei night market curb with a paper boat, chopsticks in one hand, phone in the other, filming your own bravery for followers who can't smell it, which is the only reason they're still following you. Tourists do it once for the story. Locals do it every Tuesday, then board the MRT, where forty strangers silently agree to hate them.

And the pickled cabbage on top? That's you pretending you came for vegetables. You didn't. You came to be the deadliest passenger on the scooter.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text:
NFTs. Collins Dictionary named you word of the year for 2021, which in hindsight was less an honor and more a time of death written in advance.

Beeple sold a JPEG at Christie's for $69.3 million. That was your peak, like saying the Titanic's best moment was the launch party.

OpenSea did $2.7 billion in trades on May 1st, 2022, and $9.34 million by August 28th. A 99% drop. That's not a correction. That's a flatline with a Discord server.

And 95% of collections are now worth zero. Zero! A Beanie Baby can at least become a dog toy.

Best part? The token doesn't even hold the picture. It holds a URL. People paid fortunes for a bookmark. You don't own art. You own a link that's one unpaid server bill away from "404 Not Found."

b.text: Let's hear it for the 2021 NFT buyer. You paid four hundred dollars in gas fees to become the legal owner of something your coworker right-click saved during the meeting where you explained it. You didn't want art. You've never wanted art. You wanted a hexagon around your Twitter picture so strangers would know you had a Discord password. You typed "WAGMI" to eleven thousand anonymous cartoon monkeys and believed it. We are not all gonna make it, Kyle. The roadmap promised a metaverse yacht party; it delivered a founder named "0xDegenSensei" who deleted his account and moved to Portugal. But hey, you got what you paid for: a floor price you check like a heart monitor, and a profile picture you still can't bring yourself to change, because then it would be over.

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text:
Hydrogen cars! Toyota named theirs the Mirai, Japanese for "future," which is accurate, because that's when you'll find a working pump. Nearly every station in America is in California, and even Shell looked at its seven and said, "Nah." Closed them all in February 2024. You know you're bad business when an *oil company* dumps you.

But it's clean! Clean like a laundered check. Over 95% of hydrogen comes from fossil fuels, mostly natural gas. It's a gas car with extra steps and a better publicist.

Fill-ups hit about $36 a kilo, over $200 a tank. Toyota handed out $15,000 fuel cards, the automotive version of "drinks are on me, please don't leave." Owners sued anyway. Twice. The second suit wants at least $5.7 billion.

Finally, the Mirai found something it could fill up on: lawsuits.

b.text: Let's talk about the guy who bought a hydrogen car. He wanted to be greener than the Tesla people and smugger than the Prius people, and found the one way to do both while living like a medieval pilgrim. His life is now a map of eleven pumps, and nine say "offline." He loves telling you it "only emits water." Yeah, so does he, every time the app says "station unavailable." He brags that refueling takes five minutes, after the forty-minute drive and the two-hour line behind three other Mirai owners, all quietly weeping. Toyota handed him a fifteen-thousand-dollar fuel card and he burned through it before the warranty paperwork dried. Now he owns a sixty-thousand-dollar car worth a used futon, all to prove he's an early adopter of a future that met him and moved to Japan.

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Let's start with the name, because that's the first lie. You were invented in Ontario. By a Greek guy. In 1962. You're Hawaiian the way a tiki bar in Ohio is Hawaiian. The only tropical thing about you is the can your pineapple came out of.

And that pineapple: warm, wet, weeping syrup into the crust until the middle slice folds like a lawn chair. Pineapple contains an enzyme that breaks down protein, so the fruit is literally trying to digest the ham. Even your toppings hate each other.

And the ham! Not prosciutto, not even pepperoni. Just pale pink squares that look like they were chiseled out of a deli's floor tile.

You're the pizza people order to seem quirky. "I'm so random!" No, Kevin. That's a fruit cup that fell on a pizza, and nobody cleaned it up.

b.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Nothing about you is Hawaiian. You were invented in 1962 in Chatham, Ontario, by a Greek guy, and named after a brand of canned pineapple. You're not a cuisine, you're a label. Even the pineapple left Hawaii. Del Monte shut down there in 2006, two years ahead of schedule, like they couldn't wait to stop being associated with you. Now your fruit comes from Thailand, Indonesia and the Philippines. You're a pizza with a passport and no home.

Your own creator said nobody mixed sweet and sour back then "except for Chinese food." His restaurant served Chinese food. So your origin story is "what if the takeout menu fell into the pizza oven?"

The president of Iceland said he'd ban you if he could, then admitted he didn't have the power. Congratulations: you've survived purely on a technicality.

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text: You moved to Canberra for the job. Brave. You looked at Sydney rents, did the maths, and decided your personality was negotiable. Now you're an EL1 who says "stakeholder" at barbecues and talks about Senate Estimates like a war you survived. Your lanyard has a richer social life than you do. You promised your Melbourne friends a visit; they've cancelled twice for weddings in Bali. You've developed opinions about Gungahlin. Your wild Saturday is Braddon brunch, followed by complaining it was "basically Sydney prices." And what did it get you? A secure job, a three-bedroom in Tuggeranong, and a security clearance confirming the government checked thoroughly and found nothing interesting. You came for two years. That was 2009. Your kid now says "on the Hill" unprompted, and you've never been prouder or more quietly trapped.

b.text:
Canberra, you're not a city. You're a custody arrangement. Sydney and Melbourne couldn't stand each other, so they put you exactly where neither would have to visit. The constitution literally required you to be at least 100 miles from Sydney, the most sensible thing ever written into Australian law.

You were so unready that Melbourne had to cover your shift until 1927. It took two architects from Chicago to imagine you, and your big centrepiece is a lake you had to manufacture by damming a river, because even the water wouldn't show up voluntarily.

And Parliament House: built under a lawn so citizens could walk over their politicians. Gorgeous idea. Then in 2017 they fenced it off. Congratulations, Canberra. You turned democracy into a "keep off the grass" situation.

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text:
Canberra wasn't chosen. Canberra is what was left over.

Sydney and Melbourne hated each other so much they wrote it into the constitution: the capital must be at least a hundred miles from Sydney.

Other countries pick a capital. Australia filed a restraining order.

Then they hired two architects from Chicago. The national capital, designed by Americans. Very on brand.

The lake's fake. They dammed a river so the city would have something to look at.

Parliament is built under a lawn, so citizens could walk all over their politicians.

In 2017, they fenced the lawn.

Twenty-nine years. That's how long it took politicians to notice the design was working.

Sydney, Melbourne, stop laughing. You built an entire city just to avoid sharing a room.

Canberra isn't a capital.

It's a custody arrangement. And Melbourne had the kid till 1927.

b.text:
Canberra exists because Sydney and Melbourne couldn't agree on anything, so they built a city that nobody could possibly be jealous of. Mission accomplished.

It was designed by an American architect, which explains why it feels like a very nice airport with sheep. The roundabouts are so plentiful that locals don't give directions, they give revolutions. The lake is fake, the population is mostly public servants waiting for Friday, and the kangaroos outnumber the nightlife.

Your Parliament House is literally buried in a hill so people can walk on the roof, the only time Australians get to stand on politicians.

For your centenary you commissioned the Skywhale, a giant flying balloon with ten enormous boobs, and somehow that's still the most exciting thing to happen here.

Canberra: home of Summernats, Floriade, and legally purchasable X-rated videos. Burnouts, tulips and porn, because you've got to do something until the next Senate estimates hearing.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text: Let's hear it for the graphene evangelists, the only people who've been "five years away" since 2004. Two guys in Manchester peel pencil lead with Scotch tape, win a Nobel, and an entire industry decides the tape was the business plan. Every press release is the same Mad Lib: "Wonder material could revolutionize [batteries/condoms/desalination/your feelings]." *Could.* That word has funded more postdocs than the NSF. You promised us space elevators and delivered a tennis racket with a sticker on it. Startup founders slap "graphene-enhanced" on a phone case the way divorced dads put a spoiler on a Honda Civic. And the grant committees keep paying, because admitting the miracle is stuck on the production line means admitting you are too. Twenty years of changing everything, and the only thing you've actually changed is the abstract.

b.text:
Graphene, you were discovered with Scotch tape. Other materials get particle accelerators; you got the junk drawer. Then you won a Nobel Prize, which means Sweden officially honored the arts-and-crafts table.

The EU handed you a billion euros over ten years. A billion! Then a 2018 study tested "graphene" from 60 producers, and not one was even half graphene. Most of it was graphite flakes. You're not a miracle material, you're pencil shavings with a LinkedIn.

Yet you're in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a "performance ingredient." Buddy, the only thing you've boosted is the price tag.

And one of your own discoverers once levitated a frog with magnets. Honestly? That frog delivered more on its promises than you have. At least it actually got off the ground.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Slack, you started as the internal chat tool for a failed video game called Glitch, and honestly? Still the most accurate name you've ever had.

You promised to kill email. Instead you gave us email that *knocks*. That little wooden knock-brush sound has triggered more cortisol than any boss in history. I hear it in the shower. I hear it at funerals.

You invented the green dot, so now my employer knows I went to the bathroom for nineteen minutes. You invented "is typing…" so my manager can type for four straight minutes and send "ok."

Threads? Nobody can find them. Huddles? A Zoom call that ambushes you. And somehow every company has 400 channels, and the only active one is #random, where Kevin posts his sourdough.

Your name literally stands for "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge." Searchable. Sure. Try finding that one link from Tuesday. 👀 reacted by 3 people.

b.text:
Stewart Butterfield built a game called Glitch. It failed.
The chat app his team used while building it was worth billions.
He'd already done this once: Flickr also came out of a failed game.
The man can't finish a game, but he can monetize the group chat about it.

"Slack" stands for "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge."
Searchable. Log. All conversation.
That isn't a product name. That's what HR reads out at your exit interview.
And "Knowledge"? Your company's knowledge is #random and four hundred parrot GIFs.

In 2020 Slack complained to the EU that Microsoft was bundling Teams into Office.
The next year it sold itself to Salesforce for twenty-seven point seven billion dollars.
It lost the fight against bundling, so it became the bundle.

Half of you have Slack open right now with the little green dot on so your boss thinks you're working.
That's the product. A twenty-seven-billion-dollar green dot.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text:
Emacs, you started in 1976 as macros for an editor called TECO. Nearly fifty years later you're still basically macros, just with more parentheses.

People call you a fine operating system lacking only a good editor, which is generous. Operating systems don't ship with Tetris and a therapist. But M-x doctor is smart planning, because your users need one. Every one of them has Emacs pinky, a repetitive strain injury you earn just by trying to save a file.

You've got a mail client, a calendar, a web browser. You're not a text editor; you're a hoarder with a keybinding for every room.
