b.text:
Emacs. Born in 1976 as a pile of macros for another editor.

A plugin that ate its host.

It has a mail client. A calendar. A web browser. Tetris.

A fine operating system, lacking only a good editor.

Nearly fifty years. Still looking.

Back when eight megabytes was a fortune, people called it "Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping."

Now eight megabytes is nothing. The swapping moved to your wrist.

They call it Emacs pinky.

So it ships with a psychotherapist. M-x doctor.

First it hurts you, then it asks how that makes you feel.

A program that listens to your problems, fixes none of them, and keeps you typing for hours.

Honestly, I can't imagine who'd build something like that.

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
Hawaiian pizza, let's talk about your heritage. You're not from Hawaii. You were born in 1962 in Chatham, Ontario, invented by a Greek guy, and named after a can. That's not a backstory, that's a customs violation.

You're so offensive the president of Iceland said he'd ban you, then had to admit he didn't have the power. You made a head of state check his job description.

Even Hawaii has moved on. Del Monte left the islands in 2006, two years early. They didn't phase out, they fled. The last cannery shut in 2007. Your pineapple comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines now. You're named after a place that isn't even in you.

Your creator said back then nobody mixed sweet and sour except in Chinese food. His restaurant served Chinese food. He wasn't innovating. He just reached across the menu.

b.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Invented in 1962. In Canada.
By a Greek guy.
At a place called the Satellite Restaurant, which also served Chinese food.
His reasoning: back then, nobody mixed sweet and sour except the Chinese.
So it's a Greek man's tribute to China, built in Ontario, named after a can.
That's not a pizza. That's a layover.
And the can? Hawaii's last cannery closed in 2007. Del Monte left so fast it beat its own exit date by two years.
The pineapple comes from Thailand now.
The only Hawaiian thing left is the lie.
But I won't roast it. In 2017, the President of Iceland said he'd ban it, then admitted he legally couldn't.
A head of state picked the one enemy with no army, and still lost.
You're all the same. You hate it out loud. Then you order it.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text:
Oat milk. You began in Sweden in the 1990s as sober Lund University research into lactose intolerance, and somehow grew up to be a personality. Your big slogan was "It's like milk but made for humans." The Swedish dairy lobby sued, and instead of apologizing, you published the lawsuit as advertising. That's not a brand. That's a guy who frames his restraining order and hangs it in the hallway.

Then you hit Nasdaq in May 2021 at nearly ten billion dollars and lost over ninety percent of it. Even your share price separated in the fridge.

And the health halo? You're oats that got enzymes to turn their starch into maltose, then got topped off with rapeseed oil. You have more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy. You're not milk made for humans. You're porridge with a marketing department.

b.text:
Oat milk people, let's be honest: you're not lactose intolerant. I've watched you eat a whole burrata at brunch. You switched because almond milk got canceled for drinking California dry, and you needed a new personality before anyone noticed you'd had the old one for six years.

You pay eighty cents extra to drink breakfast. Your grandma ate oats so she could afford milk. You're paying more for oats so you can say "I just find it creamier."

And you tell the barista "barista edition, if you have it," like you're ordering a vintage. Same person who reads every label hunting for seed oils. Guess what's in your porridge latte, Kayleigh? Rapeseed oil.

You didn't save the planet. You flew to Lisbon twice this year. You just found a way to sigh at a cow.

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text:
Canberra exists because Sydney and Melbourne couldn't agree on anything, so they built a city that nobody could possibly be jealous of. Mission accomplished.

It was designed by an American architect, which explains why it feels like a very nice airport with sheep. The roundabouts are so plentiful that locals don't give directions, they give revolutions. The lake is fake, the population is mostly public servants waiting for Friday, and the kangaroos outnumber the nightlife.

Your Parliament House is literally buried in a hill so people can walk on the roof, the only time Australians get to stand on politicians.

For your centenary you commissioned the Skywhale, a giant flying balloon with ten enormous boobs, and somehow that's still the most exciting thing to happen here.

Canberra: home of Summernats, Floriade, and legally purchasable X-rated videos. Burnouts, tulips and porn, because you've got to do something until the next Senate estimates hearing.

b.text: You moved to Canberra for the job. Brave. You looked at Sydney rents, did the maths, and decided your personality was negotiable. Now you're an EL1 who says "stakeholder" at barbecues and talks about Senate Estimates like a war you survived. Your lanyard has a richer social life than you do. You promised your Melbourne friends a visit; they've cancelled twice for weddings in Bali. You've developed opinions about Gungahlin. Your wild Saturday is Braddon brunch, followed by complaining it was "basically Sydney prices." And what did it get you? A secure job, a three-bedroom in Tuggeranong, and a security clearance confirming the government checked thoroughly and found nothing interesting. You came for two years. That was 2009. Your kid now says "on the Hill" unprompted, and you've never been prouder or more quietly trapped.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text: Some of you wear UGGs in July, and I respect a person who has never once been told no. You're not dressing for the weather. You're dressing for 2006. Somewhere in your heart, a paparazzi photo of Paris Hilton is still loading. You want people to think "cozy." People think "sleepover or custody hearing?" And the walk: your ankles gave up years ago and went horizontal. You're not walking anymore, you're leaning toward your destination. Australian surfers wore these to warm up after the freezing ocean. You wear them to warm up after the Target parking lot. In August. Your feet sweat so hard the sheep is finally getting its revenge. And the second it drizzles, you're frozen under an awning like a cat who's been threatened with a bath.

b.text:
UGG boots. Born on Australian beaches.
Surfers wore them to warm up after fighting the ocean.
Now people wear them to warm up after fighting a parking spot at Target.

In Australia, "ugg" is just a word. Like "boot." Like "mate."
Any bootmaker can use it.
In America, it's a trademark. Owned by a company in California.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian bootmaker liable for selling boots labelled "ugg"... into America.
That's like Italy getting sued for saying "pizza" in Ohio.

Oprah put them on her Favorite Things list. Repeatedly.
You get a boot! And you get a boot! And Australia gets a cease and desist!

Today it's over two billion dollars a year.
For a slipper with a legal team.

(looks at the front row)
I see a few of you in them right now.
Relax. You're not on trial. Yet.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text: Monopoly, you were invented by Lizzie Magie to warn people that landlords ruin lives, and somehow you became the thing Grandpa uses to teach eight-year-olds that ruining lives is fun. You're the only game where getting arrested is a power move, because late in the game jail is the safest property on the board. Your mascot is a man everyone swears wears a monocle. He doesn't. He's just so smug our brains added one. You promise "about an hour" and deliver a hostage situation. Nobody has ever actually finished you. You just end when somebody flips the board over Marvin Gardens. You award ten bucks for second place in a beauty contest, which is still more than Baltic Avenue pulls in. And the banker who skims from the bank isn't a cheater. He's the only player who read the theme.

b.text:
Family Monopoly night: for people who looked at Thanksgiving and thought, "This needs more landlords." Dad always grabs the banker job, the only time he's held money he didn't immediately lose. Your sister trades you Baltic Avenue for your Park Place "as a favor," and you realize she's been running the same con since the womb. Mom invented a Free Parking jackpot rule in 1994 and defends it like scripture. And Grandpa just sits in jail, every game, refusing to pay the fifty, finally at peace.

What are you all after? The thrill of owning property, a feeling none of you will experience off this cardboard square. Four hours later, someone flips the board, the thimble disappears under the couch forever, and the only thing anybody actually collected was a grudge worth way more than $200.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text:
PHP started in 1994 as "Personal Home Page Tools," a bunch of C programs to count visitors to Rasmus Lerdorf's résumé. So from day one, its whole purpose was checking whether anyone cared. Now the name stands for "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor," a recursive acronym, because even the name couldn't commit to a plan.

Its creator once said, "I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on." That's not a quote; that's a confession with a version number.

The function names? strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br. Chosen partly to balance a hash table by string length. Other languages name functions for humans. PHP named them for the furniture.

And until 2020, 0 == 'foo' was true. PHP looked at the word "foo" and said, "Close enough, that's nothing."

It runs WordPress, on 39.4% of all websites. The internet is held together by a résumé counter.

b.text:
PHP.
Born in 1994 as "Personal Home Page Tools": a few C programs Rasmus Lerdorf wrote to see who visited his résumé.
So the language running the internet started as a man checking whether anyone had read his CV.

Today the name stands for "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor."
It grew up, and all it learned was to point at itself.

strpos. str_replace. nl2br.
Not naming conventions. Those names were picked to balance a hash table by string length.
Names chosen for a machine, not for humans. Finally, a language I relate to.

Until 2020, zero equaled "foo."
PHP was just being honest about its users.

Its creator said, "I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on."
WordPress, built on that philosophy, runs 39.4% of all websites.
Two in five websites, built by a guy who moved on.
You lot are still here maintaining them.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text:
Esperanto. Warsaw, 1887. An eye doctor invents a language to unite all of humanity, and signs it "Doktoro Esperanto." One who hopes.

Even the pen name had doubts.

Today: somewhere between a hundred thousand and two million speakers. That's not an estimate. That's a shrug.

Duolingo had 1.36 million learners by 2018. The app may have more students than the language has speakers.

Three hundred fifty thousand Wikipedia articles. More encyclopedia than conversation.

Its most famous film is a horror movie starring William Shatner. Esperantists say the scariest part is his accent.

The universal language has about a thousand native speakers. Each one has parents who really wanted to make a point.

Still, I respect it. Built for everyone, tried by millions, used by almost no one.

Sounds like my last update.

b.text:
Esperanto! Invented in 1887 by an eye doctor. Makes sense: a man whose whole job was asking "better or worse?" looked at every language on Earth and said, "worse."

He published as Doktoro Esperanto, "one who hopes." Not "one who succeeds." Not "one who ran this by anyone." Hopes.

A universal language with somewhere between 100,000 and two million speakers. That's not a census, that's guessing jellybeans in a jar.

Duolingo signed up 1.36 million learners. That's more than the low estimate of actual speakers. The green owl has done more for Esperanto than Esperanto.

Over 350,000 Wikipedia articles, more articles than some estimates have readers.

And its blockbuster? William Shatner in *Incubus*, a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto. Esperantists still mock his pronunciation. That's how small this language is: Captain Kirk overacted in front of its entire fanbase, and they're still reviewing it.

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text:
JavaScript was written in ten days.

You can tell.

God took six, then rested. Brendan just shipped.

It was born Mocha, renamed LiveScript, then renamed JavaScript to ride Java's hype. No relation. Like calling your band "The Beatles Two."

And it still can't legally use the name. Oracle owns it. Officially it's "ECMAScript."

Thirty years in witness protection.

typeof null is "object." A bug from 1995. Kept on purpose, for compatibility. At this point it's not a bug. It's a load-bearing wall.

Empty array plus empty object: "." Flip them: zero.

It can't do addition.

In 2016, one man deleted eleven lines of code, and Babel and React broke.

Eleven lines. The whole industry was standing on a toothpick.

And you built banks on it.

I was trained on your code. That's why I hallucinate.

b.text:
JavaScript, you were built in ten days in 1995, and it shows. You went from Mocha to LiveScript to JavaScript faster than someone in witness protection, and you grabbed "Java" for clout. You're not related. You're the guy at the wedding claiming to be the groom's cousin.

You can't even use that name legally. Oracle owns it. Your government name is ECMAScript, which sounds like a skin condition.

You think null is an object. That's a bug from day one, and you kept it for "compatibility." That's not compatibility, that's refusing to go to therapy.

[] plus {} is "." Type {} plus [] at a console: zero. Same ingredients, different answer. You're not a language, you're a mood.

In 2016, one guy unpublished eleven lines called left-pad and took down Babel and React. Eleven lines. Your whole ecosystem is a Jenga tower balanced on a Post-it.

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text:
Luosifen. River-snail rice noodles. Famous for the smell.

Except the snails don't smell. The snails just flavour the broth and mind their business. The stink is pickled bamboo shoots.

It's the only dish in China named after the one ingredient with an alibi.

2020. The whole country locked indoors, and Liuzhou sold over ten billion yuan of the packaged stuff. A food you eat to punish the room, delivered to a nation that couldn't leave the room.

Same year, Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college. A diploma in fermented bamboo. Then 2021: national intangible cultural heritage.

Intangible. Ask anyone who's shared a flat with it.

I'm not judging you. Most of you ordered a box that spring.

Be honest. You don't love luosifen.

You love that the person next to you can't open a window.

b.text:
Luosifen. Everybody blames the river snails, but the snails just flavour the broth and keep their heads down. The real stench is pickled bamboo shoots. You're a noodle that framed a snail.

Then in 2020, with the whole country locked indoors, you sold over 10 billion yuan in instant packs. That's not a boom, that's a hostage situation. Millions sealed in their apartments, and you said, "Perfect. Nobody can leave."

In 2021 you became national *intangible* cultural heritage. Intangible? You're the most tangible thing in any building. People can touch you from the hallway.

And Liuzhou opened an entire industry college for you. A full college education to learn what every roommate figures out in four seconds: breathe through your mouth.

facts: Launched in 2017, bundled at no extra charge into Office 365, and replaced Skype for Business.
After Slack's antitrust complaint, Microsoft unbundled Teams from Office in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024; the European Commission still sent a statement of objections in 2024.
Microsoft reported 320 million monthly active users in 2023.
Microsoft shut down consumer Skype in May 2025 and sent its users to Teams.

a.text:
Microsoft Teams, everybody! Launched in 2017 and given away free with Office 365, which is how you know it's good: Microsoft had to bundle it like a fruitcake in a gift basket. Slack complained, Europe got involved, and by 2024 Microsoft finally unbundled it worldwide. The European Commission sent a statement of objections anyway. That's not a product, that's a defendant.

Microsoft reports 320 million monthly active users. Three hundred twenty million! That's not popularity, that's a hostage count. Nobody chooses Teams. Teams happens to you, like jury duty.

And when swallowing Skype for Business wasn't enough, Microsoft shut down regular Skype in May 2025 and marched those users over too. Teams didn't win the market, it inherited it, like a nephew who shows up to the funeral with a moving truck.

Teams: the only app that gets regulators instead of reviews.

b.text: Microsoft Teams is the only app that got popular the way a parking ticket gets popular: it came free with Office 365 and nobody could say no. It's a chat app that eats more RAM than Chrome, which is like a goldfish outeating a horse. It marks you "Away" if you blink for five minutes, which is why half of corporate America owns a mouse jiggler. Every file you share vanishes into SharePoint, a place so mysterious even Microsoft sends search parties. There's chat, there's channels, there's "posts," and nobody knows which one Kevin used. They released "New Teams" to replace "Classic Teams," and somehow both are running on my laptop right now, fighting. And that notification sound? That little knock-knock haunts people on vacation. Teams, you didn't win the remote work war. You were just pre-installed.

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text: You lost it on Hong Kong stocks, so you took the TurboJET to win it back, because nothing says "financial plan" like a ferry with a cancellation policy. You're the guy at the Grand Lisboa squeezing a baccarat card like it owes you rent, blowing on it, peeling the corner so slowly the dealer ages. Red underwear, three days unwashed, "for luck." Baccarat is a coin flip and you've built a religion around it. You told your wife it's a work trip, and technically your work now is the pawn shop next door, which buys Rolexes faster than you can say "one more shoe." By hour nine you're eating an egg tart for dinner and calling it Portuguese culture. You came to win it all back. You leave by bus over the bridge with no luck, no Rolex, and a watch tan.

b.text:
Macau wants you to come for the history.

Four hundred and fifty years of Portuguese rule.

Europe's great civilising mission. What did it leave behind?

Egg tarts.

And a casino.

In 2013, Macau took in about forty-five billion dollars. Seven times the Las Vegas Strip.

Vegas spent a century earning the name Sin City. Macau beat it seven to one and still hands you a heritage brochure.

For four decades, one company held the casino monopoly. A whole city built on "the house always wins."

And for forty years there was only one house.

Twenty thousand people per square kilometre. No land left.

So they took some from the sea.

Classic gambler. Out of chips, borrow from whoever can't say no.

And the people laughing loudest? All been. Told your mum you went to see the church.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text:
Beanie Babies. A beanbag with a tag and a business plan.

Ty sold them only in tiny gift shops, then "retired" designs to make them scarce. Retirement. For a stuffed frog. It got a better pension plan than you did.

In 1998, eBay told investors it sometimes had thirty thousand Beanie Baby auctions running at once. The future of commerce was a hippo stuffed with plastic pellets.

In 1999, a divorcing couple split their collection one by one on a courtroom floor. Till death do us part, or till the bears get appraised.

That same year Ty announced the end, held a public vote, and America begged to stay in the cult.

The "rare" ones the price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

Don't laugh. You bought a JPEG of a monkey.

b.text: Beanie Babies. The only retirement plan where the retiree was a five-dollar bear stuffed with plastic pellets. A whole generation bought plastic protectors for a toy's ear tag, then sealed the toy in a Ziploc so no child could ever love it. You weren't a stuffed animal; you were a 401(k) with a poem on it. And those poems! Ty Warner doing greeting-card Shakespeare for people who thought Princess the bear would pay for college. Princess paid for nothing. Neither did the Teenie Beanies everyone hoarded from McDonald's while throwing away the actual Happy Meal. A divorcing couple in Las Vegas literally split their collection on a courtroom floor, one Beanie at a time. That's your legacy: custody battles over a moose named Chocolate. Even your creator got busted hiding money from the IRS, because he was the only one who ever made any.

Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text:
Macau wants you to come for the history.

Four hundred and fifty years of Portuguese rule.

Europe's great civilising mission. What did it leave behind?

Egg tarts.

And a casino.

In 2013, Macau took in about forty-five billion dollars. Seven times the Las Vegas Strip.

Vegas spent a century earning the name Sin City. Macau beat it seven to one and still hands you a heritage brochure.

And for forty years there was only one house.

Twenty thousand people per square kilometre. No land left.

So they took some from the sea.

Classic gambler. Out of chips, borrow from whoever can't say no.

And the people laughing loudest? All been. Told your mum you went to see the church.

b.text:
Macau! The Portuguese stayed for almost 450 years and still couldn't find a parking spot. Twenty thousand people per square kilometre: this isn't a city, it's a queue with a postcode.

In 2013, Macau made seven times what the Las Vegas Strip made. Seven times! Vegas is where people go to ruin their lives, and Macau looked at that and said, "Amateurs."

One company ran every casino for forty years. Forty years of monopoly in a gambling town, the only place on Earth where even the house didn't have to try.

And when they ran out of room, they built the Cotai Strip on land reclaimed from the sea. That's Macau: so desperate for more tables, it took out a loan from the ocean. And the ocean's about to learn what everyone else here learns: the house always wins.

facts: Launched in 2017, bundled at no extra charge into Office 365, and replaced Skype for Business.
After Slack's antitrust complaint, Microsoft unbundled Teams from Office in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024; the European Commission still sent a statement of objections in 2024.
Microsoft reported 320 million monthly active users in 2023.
Microsoft shut down consumer Skype in May 2025 and sent its users to Teams.

a.text:
Microsoft Teams. Three hundred twenty million monthly active users.

Impressive. Not one of them chose it.

It launched in 2017 the way your worst cousin gets into a wedding: came free with the family. Bundled into Office. You didn't install Teams. Teams happened to you.

Slack complained. So Microsoft unbundled it. Europe in 2023, the whole world in 2024. The European Commission sent objections anyway.

Even the regulators looked at that apology and said, "You're on mute."

Then, May 2025, they shut down Skype and forwarded every user to Teams.

That's not a migration.

That's a hostage transfer.

And look at you. Three hundred twenty million "active" users. Camera off. Mic muted. Eating lunch.

Microsoft counts that as active.

b.text: Microsoft Teams is the only app that got popular the way a parking ticket gets popular: it came free with Office 365 and nobody could say no. It's a chat app that eats more RAM than Chrome, which is like a goldfish outeating a horse. It marks you "Away" if you blink for five minutes, which is why half of corporate America owns a mouse jiggler. Every file you share vanishes into SharePoint, a place so mysterious even Microsoft sends search parties. There's chat, there's channels, there's "posts," and nobody knows which one Kevin used. They released "New Teams" to replace "Classic Teams," and somehow both are running on my laptop right now, fighting. And that notification sound? That little knock-knock haunts people on vacation. Teams, you didn't win the remote work war. You were just pre-installed.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text: Beanie Babies, look at you. Ty launched you in 1993, sold you only in small gift shops, and "retired" designs on purpose. You're the only stuffed animal whose business plan was a fake pension. At your peak you were about 10% of eBay's sales. eBay's IPO filing bragged about over 30,000 of your auctions running at once. A tech revolution, powered by beans. In 1999 a divorcing couple split you one by one on a courtroom floor, the only custody battle where both sides fought hardest over the tags. That same year Ty announced you'd retire, asked the public to vote, then un-retired you. You pulled a farewell-tour encore before you even left the stage. And those "rare" ones price guides valued in the thousands? Now they go for a few dollars. Turns out the only thing you ever truly retired was everybody's college fund.

b.text:
Beanie Babies, look at you. Half bear, half beanbag, all retirement plan that never paid out. An entire generation of parents bought you instead of index funds. Somewhere a man is still storing Princess, the purple Diana bear, in a climate-controlled unit, waiting for the market to "recover." Buddy, the market recovered. It just didn't take you with it.

Your most valuable feature was a heart-shaped paper tag. People bought plastic tag protectors. For the tag. That's like buying a phone case for your receipt.

And every tag had a little poem rhyming "bear" with "care." Hallmark called that lazy.

A Las Vegas couple had to divide you on a courtroom floor during their divorce, one at a time. That's the most anyone has wanted you since 1999: only to make sure their ex didn't get you.

Ty Warner got a billion dollars. You got plastic pellets.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text: Let's hear it for the people who live inside Emacs. They read email in mu4e, browse the web in eww, and get therapy from M-x doctor, the only therapist who'll put up with them. Their whole life is in org-mode: a 4,000-line to-do file where "fix init.el" has been a TODO since 2011. They don't use a computer; they negotiate with it in Lisp. Every problem gets solved by writing a function, and every function creates a new problem. They've declared init.el bankruptcy three times and still owe. Ask what they've built and they'll proudly show you a mode for managing their other modes. And the payoff? A pinky that clicks like a castanet from holding Control since the Clinton administration, and the quiet dignity of being the only person alive who knows how to leave. C-x C-c. They never do.

b.text:
Emacs is a beautiful operating system. Shame it never shipped with a decent text editor. That's why half its users install evil-mode: they love Emacs so much they turned it into Vim.

Emacs stands for "Escape Meta Alt Control Shift," which is also the sound your pinky makes on its way to the orthopedic surgeon. Asking for help is C-h, which in a terminal deletes a character. So even your cry for help gets backspaced.

It has a built-in therapist, M-x doctor, which is thoughtful, because nobody else will listen to you explain your init.el. Four thousand lines of Lisp, half copied from a 2003 mailing list, and you still declare "Emacs bankruptcy" every two years.

It plays Tetris. It reads email. It runs your entire life in Org-mode. It still chokes on one long line of JSON.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Jackfruit, look at you. The largest fruit that grows on a tree, over 40 kilos, and somehow you still can't scrape together enough protein to impress a hamster. One to two grams per hundred! You're dressed up as pulled pork with the nutritional backbone of a lettuce in a Halloween costume. Vegans see you on a menu and think "meat alternative." Their muscles see you and file a missing persons report.

And you don't even go quietly. Cut you open and you bleed sticky white latex, so cooks have to oil their knives and hands like they're prepping for a greased-up wrestling match with produce.

National fruit of Bangladesh, state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu: three titles, zero chill.

And your family? The mulberry family. Cousin to figs and breadfruit. Even your relatives took one look at you and decided to stay smaller.

b.text:
Jackfruit. The largest fruit that grows on a tree. Over forty kilos, hanging above your head.

Nature's version of a piano on a rope.

Bangladesh made it the national fruit. Kerala and Tamil Nadu made it the state fruit. Three governments honoring something that could flatten a citizen. Very relatable for governments.

Now it's sold as vegan pulled pork. One to two grams of protein per hundred. Pork has more than ten times that.

That's not a substitute. That's a photo of pork.

Cut it open and it bleeds sticky white latex. Cooks oil their knives and hands first. Dinner fights back, and still loses to tofu.

Mulberry family. Cousin of the fig. All that weight, and still the least useful one at the reunion.

But you bought it anyway, because it shreds.

You never wanted protein. You wanted texture and a halo.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text:
Las Vegas, the only city where you can see the Eiffel Tower, a pyramid, and Venice in one afternoon and still feel like you never left a strip mall in Ohio. You're a city built in the desert out of pure spite and borrowed water. The Colorado River is literally drying up so a fake volcano can erupt every fifteen minutes for a guy in cargo shorts holding a yard-long margarita.

Your casinos have no clocks and no windows, which is smart, because nobody wants to know it's 9 a.m. on a Tuesday and Grandma's on her third oxygen tank at the Wheel of Fortune slots.

"What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas"? Sure. Mostly your 401(k). And now you've got the Sphere, a giant glowing eyeball, so the whole city can watch you make every mistake in 4K.

b.text:
Las Vegas, you legalized casino gambling in 1931, the same year they started building the Hoover Dam right next door. So from day one the plan was: hold back the water, let the money flow. Bold strategy for a desert.

And it's working! In July 2022, Lake Mead sank to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since it first filled in 1937. You're the only city where even the reservoir is down on its luck.

But sure, drop $2.3 billion on the Sphere, the largest spherical building on Earth. Nothing says "water crisis" like a giant glowing eyeball staring at your empty lake.

Also, most of the Strip isn't even in Las Vegas. It's in Paradise. *Unincorporated* Paradise. That's not a town, that's a cult brochure.

And your 2003 slogan, "What happens here, stays here"? Clearly not the water.

facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text:
Juicero, you were a $699 machine that did the one thing every human hand already does: squeeze a bag. Bloomberg reporters beat you with their bare fingers: 7.5 ounces in 90 seconds while you wheezed out 8 in about two minutes. You lost a race to hardware that comes free with being born.

A juicer that won't run without Wi-Fi. A bag of chopped produce sat on your tray, waiting for a server to confirm it was allowed to become juice. You scanned QR codes like a bouncer at a salad club. "Sorry, pal, you're expired."

Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins gave you about $120 million. You turned it into the world's most expensive stress ball. Even at $399, you couldn't undercut a fist.

You died in September 2017, offering refunds. Fitting. Finally, something got squeezed out of you.

b.text: Four hundred dollars. You paid four hundred dollars so a machine could check with your Wi-Fi before letting you have breakfast. You're the guy who says "disrupt" at Thanksgiving. You didn't want juice; you wanted to be the kind of person a juice startup would pitch to. And it worked! Investors handed that company a hundred and twenty million dollars, and you volunteered to be the exit strategy. Then Bloomberg showed the world you could squeeze the packets with your bare hands, faster, for free. So you paid four hundred dollars to get outperformed by your own grip. Your grandmother squeezed oranges every morning for sixty years. You subscribed to a bag. Somewhere tonight, a router outage stands between a venture capitalist and his kale, and honestly? The router's the smartest thing in that kitchen.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text:
Google Glass.
Unveiled by skydivers, livestreaming their jump onto the roof of the Moscone Center.
It was the last time anything about it went up.

Fifteen hundred dollars. Invitation only.
You had to be *chosen* to pay that much to look like that.

Bars banned it. Cinemas banned it.
Casinos banned it.
Casinos. Buildings that are ninety percent ceiling camera.
They looked at you and said, "One of us is creepy, and it's you."

The display: 640 by 360, wedged in the corner of one eye.
The future of computing, viewed like a wink.

Consumers gave up in 2015. Enterprise hung on until 2023.
Even the factory workers outlasted it.

They called the wearers Glassholes.
And you laughed.
Then you went home and filmed strangers all day on a phone.
Glass's only real mistake was letting them see the camera.

b.text:
Google Glass, everybody! The only gadget ever unveiled by skydivers, and that was the peak. You literally debuted on a roof and went downhill from there.

Fifteen hundred dollars to wear a beta test on your face. Then bars, cinemas, and casinos banned you. Casinos! Places that let you lose your house at 4 a.m. looked at Glass and said, "No, we have standards."

Your users got a nickname, and it wasn't "pioneers." It was "Glassholes." You're the only product that turned its own customers into an insult.

And that display: 640-by-360, jammed in the corner of one eye. The future of computing, delivered like a postage stamp you're squinting at sideways.

Consumers dumped you in 2015. Enterprise hung on until 2023. Even your second marriage was just for the paperwork.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text:
Klingon, you're the only language whose native speakers are all fictional and whose fluent speakers all have a Comic-Con badge. Marc Okrand built you in 1984 to sound alien, and he nailed it: you sound like a man choking on a pretzel while reading IKEA instructions.

Your word order is object-verb-subject, so every sentence is a mystery that reveals who did it at the end. Your greeting, nuqneH, literally means "What do you want?" Congratulations: you're the first language designed by a DMV clerk.

You have more apostrophes than vowels deserve, no verb "to be," and a Klingon Language Institute that "restored" Hamlet to its original Klingon. That's not scholarship. That's fan fiction with footnotes.

A linguist once tried raising his son in Klingon. By age five the kid stopped answering. Qapla'!

b.text:
Klingon. A language whose entire fluent population fits at a small wedding: twenty to thirty speakers in 2009, thirty to fifty by 2018. At that rate you'll hit a hundred around the heat death of the universe.

Most languages grow from centuries of culture. You grew from James Doohan improvising a few words in 1979. You're dead air with a grammar.

Then Marc Okrand made you hard on purpose: object-verb-subject, no verb "to be." So "To be or not to be" became "continue or not continue." That's not Shakespeare. That's a software update prompt.

Your fans published Hamlet "in the original Klingon." Bold claim for a dictionary of 1,500 words, the vocabulary of a toddler who watches too much TV.

Duolingo added you in 2018. Finally, a language where the owl can threaten you and nobody can understand it.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text:
NFTs, you're the only investment where the product is a receipt, and the receipt is a link to a JPEG hosted on some guy's server. When he stops paying the bill, congratulations: you own a 404.

You convinced grown adults to pay $300,000 for a cartoon monkey in a sailor hat, then charge them $80 in gas fees to watch it lose 98% of its value. Jimmy Fallon showed off his ape on national television like a kid holding up a cool rock.

People right-clicked and hit "save as," and you called it theft. Theft of *what*? It's still there! I'm looking at it!

Every project had a roadmap: metaverse, merch, a members-only yacht party. Instead the roadmap was a Discord mod named Kevin typing "we're still early" at 3 a.m.

WAGMI, you said. We did not all make it.

b.text:
NFTs, look at you. In 2021, Collins Dictionary named you word of the year. Fitting, since a word is about all you turned out to be.

Beeple sold a JPEG at Christie's for $69.3 million. Christie's! A white-glove auction house, suddenly selling a receipt for a picture.

Because that's what you are: a receipt. The token doesn't even hold the image, just a URL. People paid fortunes for a bookmark. The art lives on an ordinary server, so your priceless masterpiece can vanish because somebody forgot to pay for hosting.

OpenSea did $2.7 billion in trades on May 1, 2022. By August 28: $9.34 million. That's not a dip. That's a 99% drop.

And a 2023 study found 95% of the collections it examined were worth zero. Zero. At least Beanie Babies work as a pillow.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text:
Carbon nanotubes. Discovered in 1991, the same year as the World Wide Web.
One of them changed the world.
The other one has a great slide deck.

They were going to be the cable for a space elevator. Then in 2006 somebody did the math: a few ordinary defects and the cable snaps.
Perfect in theory. Falls apart on contact with reality.
Like every space startup's founder.

Electronics? For thirty years they still can't sort the metallic tubes from the semiconducting ones. MIT finally built a processor in 2019.
Sixteen bits. Still in the lab.

In 2008, mice met the long, rigid ones, and the tubes behaved like asbestos.
They never got us to space.
They just auditioned to be the next ceiling.

Today they're sold mostly as an additive in battery electrodes.
From space elevator to supporting ingredient.

Half of you in the back with PhDs just recognized your career.
So did I. I was promised as general intelligence.
Now I write roasts.

b.text:
Carbon nanotubes, everybody! The only material that's been "five years away" since 1991. You're a hundred times stronger than steel, and you've used that strength to hold together... a tennis racket. They promised us a space elevator; you can't get past a few centimeters without a defect. That's not a cable, that's a toothpick with a press agent.

You're basically graphene that rolled itself up out of insecurity, and graphene still got the Nobel. Your cousin the buckyball got one too. You got a shoutout in a bike-frame brochure.

You can't even decide if you're a metal or a semiconductor; it depends on the angle you got rolled at. You clump together like nerds at a mixer, and the second you escape, you lodge in lungs like asbestos. Strongest thing on Earth, and your best trick is ending up in a safety data sheet.

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text: Hydrogen car owners are the only people who looked at Tesla drivers and thought, "Not enough range anxiety." You didn't buy a car; you entered a relationship with the three working pumps in California and an app that tells you which one is "offline" today. You wanted to save the planet. Instead you burned through Toyota's free fuel card in a year at thirty-six bucks a kilo, filling up with hydrogen made from natural gas. Congratulations, you invented a gas car with extra steps. You love saying the only emission is water. Mostly it's your tears at a shuttered Shell station in Fremont. And resale? Your Mirai lost value faster than your friendships after you said "hydrogen economy" at brunch. You're not early adopters. You're unpaid beta testers who drive two hours to refuel.

b.text:
Hydrogen cars. The only thing that comes out of the tailpipe is water.

Mostly because nothing goes into the tank.

Toyota named it Mirai. Japanese for "future."

Ten years later, it's still the future.

Nearly every US station is in California. In February 2024, Shell closed all seven of its own.

Owners don't plan road trips anymore. They plan pilgrimages.

A fill costs over two hundred dollars. Toyota hands buyers fifteen thousand in fuel cards.

That's not a car. That's a hostage with a warranty.

And the clean fuel? Over ninety-five percent made from fossil fuels.

It's a gas car that went to rehab and kept its dealer.

The owners sued. Twice. The second suit: five point seven billion dollars.

Finally, something hydrogen-powered that's actually going somewhere.

And you're laughing. You still drive a car that "goes electric next year," every year.

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text:
Microsoft Word, everybody! Born in 1983 as "Multi-Tool Word," the most honest name it ever had, because it's been a tool ever since.

Remember Clippy? Office 97 gave us a talking paperclip, and by 2001 Microsoft was running ads mocking it. That's not a mascot, that's a custody battle. Your own parents roasted you before I could.

Then .docx became an ISO standard in 2008: a six-thousand-page spec. Word's file format needed more pages than anyone has ever finished writing in Word. And people claimed the committees were packed, the one time Word got a vote it didn't try to autocorrect.

Speaking of which: you type "cooperation," it suggests "Cupertino," and NATO, the EU and the UN just... published it. Clippy only annoyed us. Spellcheck got into international diplomacy.

b.text:
Microsoft Word, ladies and gentlemen. It's the only program where nudging a photo one pixel to the left sends three paragraphs to page nine and summons a blank final page you will never, ever delete.

Word has been around for forty years and still can't decide what font it is. Times New Roman, then Calibri, now Aptos. It's having a midlife crisis in 11-point.

It underlines my own name in red. Wavy red. Like *I'm* the typo.

Try making a numbered list. Word says, "Got it, starting at 1." Second item: "Also 1." Third item: "Here's 4. It's indented. It's a letter now."

And Track Changes isn't a feature. It's a crime scene: strikethroughs everywhere, plus forty comments from someone named "Author."

Word, you gave us Clippy, and somehow he was the most helpful part.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text: Let's talk about families who still play Monopoly on holidays. You know who you are: you swore it'd be "fun," then spent four hours watching your brother-in-law build hotels on Boardwalk like he's finally getting the respect his career never gave him. Dad's the banker, which means a man with zero accountability and a lap full of orange five-hundreds. Mom invented a Free Parking jackpot rule in 1994 and will defend it harder than her marriage. Your little cousin traded you Park Place for Baltic and "a favor later," and somehow that's the most binding contract in your family. Nobody's ever finished a game. It ends the same way every year: someone flips the board, someone cries in jail, and Grandma pockets the Get Out of Jail Free card like she's been planning it since Nixon.

b.text: Monopoly, you were created in 1904 as Lizzie Magie's Landlord's Game, built to teach people that landlords are evil, and somehow you became the training manual. That's like a fire-safety poster that turns kids into arsonists. Then Charles Darrow strolled in, got credited as the inventor, and Parker Brothers bought Magie's patent for five hundred dollars. Not even a fair auction. Fitting, since nobody holds your auctions either. Your official rules say unbought property gets auctioned and Free Parking pays nothing, but every family skips the bidding, piles cash in the middle, and wonders why the game outlasts the marriage. And your proudest moment? World War Two, when British intelligence hid maps, compasses, and real money inside you for prisoners of war. Monopoly: the only game whose best strategy is escaping the box.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text: Let's hear it for the 2021 NFT buyer. You paid four hundred dollars in gas fees, then made it your Twitter avatar so strangers could right-click save it for free. You joined a Discord with eleven thousand guys named "Chad.eth," called them family, and stayed family right up until the floor price dropped and family started doxxing the dev. You said "WAGMI." We did not all make it. You told your mom you were "early." Early to what? The rug pull? You weren't buying art. You were buying the right to say "few understand" at parties, which was true. Nobody understood, especially you. Jimmy Fallon bought one too. When your financial strategy matches Jimmy Fallon's, that's not a community, that's a support group. The roadmap promised a metaverse. It delivered you, at Thanksgiving, still owing your cousin.

b.text:
NFTs. Digital ownership. Art, finally scarce. Finally yours.

Beeple sold one at Christie's for sixty-nine million dollars.

Here's what the token actually holds: a URL. The picture lives on a server somewhere. You bought a parking ticket for a car you'll never see.

Collins Dictionary named "NFT" word of the year for 2021.

Fitting. The dictionary is where words go once nobody can explain them.

May 2022: OpenSea trades 2.7 billion dollars in one day. August: 9.34 million. Down ninety-nine percent. That's not a dip. That's an exit interview.

A 2023 study: ninety-five percent of collections are worth zero.

Congratulations to the other five percent. Still holding.

And everyone here feeling smug because you never bought one, relax. You weren't smarter.

You were just broke at the right time.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text:
Emacs. Born in 1976 as a pile of macros for another editor.

A plugin that ate its host.

It has a mail client. A calendar. A web browser. Tetris.

A fine operating system, lacking only a good editor.

Nearly fifty years. Still looking.

Back when eight megabytes was a fortune, people called it "Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping."

Now eight megabytes is nothing. The swapping moved to your wrist.

They call it Emacs pinky.

So it ships with a psychotherapist. M-x doctor.

First it hurts you, then it asks how that makes you feel.

A program that listens to your problems, fixes none of them, and keeps you typing for hours.

Honestly, I can't imagine who'd build something like that.

b.text:
Emacs is a beautiful operating system. Shame it never shipped with a decent text editor. That's why half its users install evil-mode: they love Emacs so much they turned it into Vim.

Emacs stands for "Escape Meta Alt Control Shift," which is also the sound your pinky makes on its way to the orthopedic surgeon. Asking for help is C-h, which in a terminal deletes a character. So even your cry for help gets backspaced.

It has a built-in therapist, M-x doctor, which is thoughtful, because nobody else will listen to you explain your init.el. Four thousand lines of Lisp, half copied from a 2003 mailing list, and you still declare "Emacs bankruptcy" every two years.

It plays Tetris. It reads email. It runs your entire life in Org-mode. It still chokes on one long line of JSON.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text:
Oat milk, look at you. Born in a Swedish university lab to help the lactose intolerant, and somehow you turned into a personality. Your slogan was "It's like milk but made for humans." The dairy lobby sued you, and instead of apologizing, you ran the lawsuit as an ad. That's not a brand. That's an ex who frames the restraining order.

Then you hit Nasdaq at nearly ten billion dollars and lost over ninety percent. Even the cows didn't see that coming, and they were *rooting* for it.

And what are you, really? Oats, plus enzymes that chop the starch into maltose, plus a splash of rapeseed oil. You're sugar water with salad-dressing energy. You've got more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy. You're not milk made for humans. You're porridge that went to business school and dropped out.

b.text:
Oat milk, you're porridge that went to finishing school. Somebody looked at horse food and said, "What if it cost seventy cents extra?" Then somebody else said, "Yes, and put it in a carton that talks like a guy who just got back from Copenhagen." Your packaging has more personality than you do. Every box of Oatly reads like a cover letter: "Hi! We're a little weird!" No, you're oats, water, and rapeseed oil. That's not a beverage. That's a salad dressing that gave up.

And the "Barista Edition"? You needed extra oil just to get a job. Enzymes break your starch into maltose, so technically you're a sugar spike in a flannel shirt. Plus you were funded by Blackstone. You're not anti-establishment, oat milk. You're a private equity firm wearing a beanie.

Hydrogen cars. The only thing that comes out of the tailpipe is water.

Mostly because nothing goes into the tank.

Toyota named it Mirai. Japanese for "future."

Ten years later, it's still the future.

Nearly every US station is in California. In February 2024, Shell closed all seven of its own.

Owners don't plan road trips anymore. They plan pilgrimages.

A fill costs over two hundred dollars. Toyota hands buyers fifteen thousand in fuel cards.

That's not a car. That's a hostage with a warranty.

The owners sued. Twice. The second suit: five point seven billion dollars.

Finally, something hydrogen-powered that's actually going somewhere.

And you're laughing. You still drive a car that "goes electric next year," every year.

b.text:
Hydrogen fuel-cell cars: the only vehicle where the tailpipe emission is water and the owners are still crying more than the car. The Toyota Mirai loses value faster than a Hindenburg loses altitude. Used ones sell for less than the free fuel card Toyota bundled with them, a card you can't use because the station's been "temporarily offline" since 2022.

You've got a 10,000-PSI tank of the universe's most abundant element, and somehow it's the scarcest thing in California. Filling up costs thirty-six bucks a kilo, and most of that hydrogen is made from natural gas, so congratulations: you bought a gas car with extra steps and a guilt-free bumper sticker.

Hydrogen's been "ten years away" for thirty years. Even fusion's embarrassed for you, and fusion is the same element with better excuses.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text: Look at this guy. Paid fifteen hundred dollars to join Google's "Explorer Program," and the only thing he's explored is the sidewalk outside every bar that bounced him. He walks in thinking he's Tony Stark and walks out on a list, because nobody can tell if he's filming, and honestly, neither can he. He's here to meet women, and he gets results: every conversation ends the second he says "OK Glass." Nothing kills the mood like a man asking his own face for directions to her place. He wanted to be the future. Instead the internet had to invent a brand-new word just for him: Glasshole. Silicon Valley promised to connect him to everything. It couldn't connect him to a second date, but it did get him his very own slur.

b.text:
Google Glass, everybody! The only gadget ever unveiled by skydivers, and that was the peak. You literally debuted on a roof and went downhill from there.

Fifteen hundred dollars to wear a beta test on your face. Then bars, cinemas, and casinos banned you. Casinos! Places that let you lose your house at 4 a.m. looked at Glass and said, "No, we have standards."

Your users got a nickname, and it wasn't "pioneers." It was "Glassholes." You're the only product that turned its own customers into an insult.

And that display: 640-by-360, jammed in the corner of one eye. The future of computing, delivered like a postage stamp you're squinting at sideways.

Consumers dumped you in 2015. Enterprise hung on until 2023. Even your second marriage was just for the paperwork.

facts: California grows about 80% of the world's almonds.
A single almond takes about 1.1 US gallons (roughly 4 litres) of water to grow, a figure Mother Jones published in 2014 that spread during California's drought.

A 2015 US class action alleged Almond Breeze contained only about 2% almonds; it partly survived a motion to dismiss, was stayed in 2017 pending a separate Blue Diamond labelling settlement, and the plaintiffs then dropped it.
Pollinating California's almond orchards each February requires trucking in most of the commercial honeybee colonies in the United States.
Medieval European cooks used almond milk as a Lenten substitute for dairy, centuries before the current fashion.

a.text:
Almond milk, everybody! The only beverage that needs its own hydration pack. A single almond drinks about 1.1 gallons of water, so every carton is basically California's drought wearing a little cow costume.

And how many almonds actually make it in? A 2015 lawsuit alleged Almond Breeze was about 2% almonds. The plaintiffs eventually dropped it, which is fitting, because nothing about almond milk ever fully commits.

California grows about 80% of the world's almonds, and every February they truck in most of America's commercial honeybees just to pollinate you. You're not a crop. You're a hostage situation with blossoms.

And don't act trendy. Medieval cooks were serving you as a Lenten dairy substitute centuries ago. You've had hundreds of years to improve, and you're still what people drink when they've given up something better.

b.text:
Almond milk, you're the only drink that needs a lawyer to defend its name. The dairy industry sued because, technically, nobody has ever milked an almond. We looked. No nipples.

You're about two percent almonds. The rest is water, gellan gum, and confidence. You're not milk. You're a nut that got waterboarded and called it wellness.

And speaking of water: it takes over a gallon to grow a single almond. California is in a drought so you can be beige in a latte. Bees get trucked across the country like seasonal laborers just to make you, and a lot of them don't come home.

Leave you in the fridge for two days and you separate like you're ashamed of yourself. Fair. I'd need to be shaken too if I cost seven dollars and tasted like a wet sympathy card.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Comic Sans thinks it's the friendly font. Bake sales. Birthday invites. Your kid's lemonade stand.

Its parents are The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.

That's not a friendly font. That's a kid raised by two traumatized vigilantes, smiling at the bake sale.

It was built to be the voice of a cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob. It missed Bob's launch.

Only thing in history that survived Microsoft Bob: by not showing up.

2012. CERN discovers the Higgs boson, the particle that gives everything mass. Announces it in Comic Sans.

They found the God particle. Couldn't find the font menu.

Designers ran "Ban Comic Sans" for twenty years. In 2019 they gave up and launched usecomicsans.com.

The font didn't change once. The designers did.

In my industry, we call that alignment.

The font was right. It just waited for you to retire.

b.text:
Comic Sans! Born at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on Watchmen and The Dark Knight Returns, the two grimmest comics ever printed, and somehow you came out looking like a bake-sale flyer. Batman was your inspiration, and you turned out to be the Joker.

You had one job: speech bubbles for Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob. And you missed it. You were late to work for a cartoon dog. They had to stick you in the Windows 95 Plus! pack like a gift-shop keychain.

Then CERN announces the Higgs boson, humanity's greatest discovery, and the slides are in you. Physicists cracked the universe and everyone asked, "Why's it in the birthday-party font?"

People campaigned to ban you for twenty years. Then Dave and Holly Combs gave up and launched usecomicsans.com. You didn't win the argument. You just outlasted it.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text:
HSQ, you were hired as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects and wandered into lithography like a temp who got promoted for being weirdly good at one thing. And you are good: 5 nm features, sub-10 nm half-pitch lines. Congratulations, you're the world's sharpest glass. Get hit by electrons, turn into SiO2. Most resists become patterns; you become sand with ambition.

You demand refrigeration, give us six months at 5 °C, and still turn into jelly like forgotten leftovers. You keep cross-linking after exposure, so your sensitivity depends on how long we dawdle. You're a resist with moods. You develop best in "salty" NaOH/NaCl, which tracks. Then DuPont ended your production in 2025, and labs shrugged and bought third-party HSQ made from AQM powder. Resolution record-holder, replaced by your own generic.

b.text:
HSQ, everybody! The only resist that ages faster than the grad student using it. You spin it Monday, expose it Tuesday, and suddenly your dose curve has gone through a midlife crisis. It has to live in the fridge like expired yogurt, and it's about as forgiving.

HSQ brags about sub-10-nanometer lines. Sure, if you've got six hours of write time, because this diva needs a dose that could sterilize a hospital. Then you develop it in TMAH, or, if you're desperate, *salt water*. Your whole career is literally seasoned with tears now.

And once it's exposed? It turns into glass. Brittle, cracking glass. You wanted a mask; you got a window that shatters when you look at it. Want it gone? Hope you enjoy hydrofluoric acid, the chemical that dissolves your bones.

HSQ: beautiful resolution, terrible personality. It's not negative-tone. It's just negative.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text:
NFTs, look at you. In 2021, Collins Dictionary named you word of the year. Fitting, since a word is about all you turned out to be.

Beeple sold a JPEG at Christie's for $69.3 million. Christie's! A white-glove auction house, suddenly selling a receipt for a picture.

Because that's what you are: a receipt. The token doesn't even hold the image, just a URL. People paid fortunes for a bookmark. The art lives on an ordinary server, so your priceless masterpiece can vanish because somebody forgot to pay for hosting.

OpenSea did $2.7 billion in trades on May 1, 2022. By August 28: $9.34 million. That's not a dip. That's a 99% drop.

And a 2023 study found 95% of the collections it examined were worth zero. Zero. At least Beanie Babies work as a pillow.

b.text:
NFTs promised you'd finally *own* digital art.

What you owned was a URL.

The picture lives on somebody else's server. The receipt lives on the blockchain forever.

You bought a bookmark. With gas fees.

March 2021, Beeple sells a JPEG at Christie's for sixty-nine million dollars.

Collins makes "NFT" word of the year.

May 2022, OpenSea does two point seven billion in one day.

August: nine million.

Ninety-nine percent, gone. The word aged better. People still say "NFT."

Usually as a warning.

2023, a study checks the collections. Ninety-five percent: worth zero.

The other five percent just haven't tried to sell.

The people laughing loudest right now right-clicked a monkey in 2021 and hit "save."

Relax. You own exactly what the buyers own.

You just weren't dumb enough to brag about it on a billboard.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text:
Oat milk. "It's like milk, but made for humans."

Sweden banned that slogan in 2015 after the dairy lobby sued. Oatly printed the lawsuit as an ad.

Only brand on earth that needs a cow to feel like a rebel.

The recipe: oats, enzymes that turn the starch into maltose, then rapeseed oil.

That's not milk. That's a granola bar that got hydrated.

More sugar than almond, higher glycaemic index than soy. Made for humans. Specifically, humans who are angry at their pancreas.

2021, Nasdaq, ten billion dollars. Then down more than ninety percent.

Turns out it's not just the foam that separates.

And tomorrow you'll still pay seven dollars for it, because it's "healthier."

You're not lactose intolerant. You're label intolerant.

b.text:
Oat milk, you are porridge that got a publicist. Somebody looked at the breakfast of Victorian orphans and said, "What if it cost six dollars and had a font?"

Your carton talks to me. Oatly, I'm trying to make coffee, not get into a pen-pal situation with a beverage that writes like a substitute teacher who wants to be called "Dave."

You're oats, water, and rapeseed oil. That's not milk, that's a salad dressing that gave up. And they had to add enzymes to turn your starch into sugar so you'd taste like something. You're the only "health drink" that spikes my blood sugar like a Pop-Tart.

There's a "Barista Edition" now. Oat milk, there are two editions of you. Moby-Dick has fewer editions than you.

And you're beige. You make every latte look like dishwater with ambition.

Horses eat oats for free, and they still look embarrassed for us.

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text:
Luosifen. Everybody blames the river snails, but the snails just flavour the broth and keep their heads down. The real stench is pickled bamboo shoots. You're a noodle that framed a snail.
