Then in 2020, with the whole country locked indoors, you sold over 10 billion yuan in instant packs. That's not a boom, that's a hostage situation. Millions sealed in their apartments, and you said, "Perfect. Nobody can leave."

In 2021 you became national *intangible* cultural heritage. Intangible? You're the most tangible thing in any building. People can touch you from the hallway.

And Liuzhou opened an entire industry college for you. A full college education to learn what every roommate figures out in four seconds: breathe through your mouth.

b.text: You know who you are. You ordered twelve packs off Taobao, waited until every roommate was home, then tore open the sour bamboo shoot sachet like you were declassifying something. You're not hungry. You're making a point. Every slurp comes with the speech: "Smells bad, tastes good." Buddy, we only get the first half. Nobody signed up for the tasting, just the hallway. And you keep saying "it's authentic Liuzhou" like geography is an apology. What does it get you? A spotless pot nobody will borrow, a group chat that goes silent the second you type "anyone want some?", and roommates who suddenly prefer dating people with their own apartments. You came for comfort food. You left with a reputation, a window permanently propped open, and a fridge shelf everyone treats like a crime scene.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text:
Windows 8, you booted people into a full-screen grid of tiles built for touch screens most PCs didn't have. Millions of adults sat there jabbing their monitors like a pigeon working a vending machine.

You removed the Start button. The *Start* button. That's a building with no door and a sign saying "swipe the right edge." That was your Charms bar: Search, Share, and Settings hidden behind an invisible swipe.

You couldn't even keep your name. A German retailer objected, and suddenly "Metro" was "just a code name." Sure it was.

Your sibling, Windows RT, couldn't run Windows programs, a Windows that couldn't do Windows. Microsoft wrote down $900 million in unsold Surface RT tablets.

Then 8.1 put the button back, Windows 10 restored the menu, and Microsoft skipped 9 entirely, because nobody wanted to stand next to you.

b.text:
Windows 8 thought it was the future.

October 2012. Microsoft looked at a billion people holding a mouse and said: touch the screen.

They touched the screen. It was a monitor. Now it had fingerprints.

They removed the Start button. From Windows. That's a restaurant removing the door to feel modern.

Need Settings? Swipe in from the right edge. Nothing tells you this. That's not a menu, that's a rumor.

Then Windows RT: looks like Windows, can't run Windows programs. Nine hundred million dollars of tablets, written down.

8.1 brought the button back. 10 brought the menu back. And 9?

Microsoft skipped 9. Not a version. A witness.

But you're laughing at it on a phone where everything important hides behind a swipe from an edge.

Windows 8 didn't fail.

It just told you the truth before you were ready.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text: Congratulations on being fluent in Klingon, a language with maybe thirty fluent speakers, and you've met all of them at the same Marriott. You spent four years mastering a tongue where the standard greeting, nuqneH, means "What do you want?" That's also what your family says when you call. You've read Hamlet "restored to the original Klingon," a phrase only a man who has never been hugged could type. One guy raised his son speaking only Klingon; by age five the kid stopped answering him. That's the dream: a language so pure even toddlers refuse it. There's no word for "please," which explains your dating approach. You learned an entire warrior race's language to tell the barista Qapla'. Success. Sure, buddy. Today is a good day to die... a virgin.

b.text:
Klingon, you're the only language whose native speakers are all fictional and whose fluent speakers all have a Comic-Con badge. Marc Okrand built you in 1984 to sound alien, and he nailed it: you sound like a man choking on a pretzel while reading IKEA instructions.

Your word order is object-verb-subject, so every sentence is a mystery that reveals who did it at the end. Your greeting, nuqneH, literally means "What do you want?" Congratulations: you're the first language designed by a DMV clerk.

You have more apostrophes than vowels deserve, no verb "to be," and a Klingon Language Institute that "restored" Hamlet to its original Klingon. That's not scholarship. That's fan fiction with footnotes.

A linguist once tried raising his son in Klingon. By age five the kid stopped answering. Qapla'!

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text:
Microsoft Word, everybody! Born in 1983 as "Multi-Tool Word," the most honest name it ever had, because it's been a tool ever since.

Remember Clippy? Office 97 gave us a talking paperclip, and by 2001 Microsoft was running ads mocking it. That's not a mascot, that's a custody battle. Your own parents roasted you before I could.

Then .docx became an ISO standard in 2008: a six-thousand-page spec. Word's file format needed more pages than anyone has ever finished writing in Word. And people claimed the committees were packed, the one time Word got a vote it didn't try to autocorrect.

Speaking of which: you type "cooperation," it suggests "Cupertino," and NATO, the EU and the UN just... published it. Clippy only annoyed us. Spellcheck got into international diplomacy.

b.text: You chose Word for your thesis because "LaTeX has a learning curve." Bold, from someone who then spent a semester learning how to make page 1 start after the roman numerals. You wanted to focus on the research. Instead you're a hostage negotiator for Figure 3.2, which flees to the next page whenever you breathe on the paragraph above it. Your committee asked for one more citation, and the bibliography reflowed like a tectonic event. The phrase "Error! Reference source not found" appears in your thesis eleven times. Your file is called Thesis_FINAL_v9_USE_THIS_ONE.docx, and it's 400 megabytes because you pasted one chart from Excel. You came for a doctorate. You're leaving with a codependent relationship with Section Break (Next Page) and a flinch every time someone says "Normal style."

facts: Tofu soaked for hours to a day or two in a brine that has itself fermented for months from vegetables such as bamboo shoots and mustard greens, often with dried shrimp or meat; the smell is the brine's, not the bean's.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.
Legend credits Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate who left his unsold tofu too long in 1669; a Beijing fermented-bean-curd brand still carries his name.
Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text:
Stinky tofu's whole brand is honesty. "I stink outside, I'm pure inside."

Pure tofu. Soaked in brine that's been rotting for months. With dried shrimp. Sometimes meat.

The bean doesn't even smell. It just sat in bad company long enough
and took the credit.

Then it moved to three cities and became three people. Black and drowning in chili in Changsha. Golden and polite in Taiwan. In Shaoxing it's steamed with other stinky pickles.
Finally, a support group.

The inventor? Wang Zhihe, 1669. An exam candidate who couldn't sell his tofu and left it out too long.
Nobody remembers his exam.
His mistake still has a brand.

And you. You smell it a full block away.
And you walk toward it.
Same way you picked your last relationship.

b.text:
Stinky tofu, look at you. Plain tofu is the most agreeable food on earth, and you turned it into a public nuisance. And the humiliating part? The smell isn't even yours. You soaked in a brine of bamboo shoots and mustard greens that had been fermenting for months, sometimes with dried shrimp. You're not stinky; you just hang out with the wrong crowd.

Your origin story: in 1669 Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate, couldn't sell his tofu and left it out too long. You're not a recipe. You're an inventory problem.

Changsha fries you black and buries you in chili. Taiwan hides you under pickled cabbage. Shaoxing steams you with other stinky pickles, like a support group.

Everyone's trying to cover you up, and people still smell you from a block away.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text: LaTeX, you're the only software that makes PhDs feel stupid. You're from 1984 and you dress like it: backslashes everywhere, curly braces like a nervous tic. I tell you to put a figure "here," and you treat "here" as a suggestion, then file it four pages later next to the bibliography, like a sock lost in a dryer. Your error messages are poetry: "Missing $ inserted." Inserted where? Why? You won't say. You just blame line 1 of a 40-page file because I typed an underscore in a URL. My citations are double question marks until I compile you twice, then a third time, out of spite. And everyone needs to know it's pronounced "lay-tech," not like the glove. Honestly, at least the glove stretches. Overfull \hbox? Badness 10000? Buddy, that's not a warning. That's your autobiography.

b.text:
LaTeX, you're a macro layer on TeX, which Donald Knuth built because he didn't like how his own galley proofs looked. Most people complain to the printer. Knuth built a typesetting system, and Lamport looked at it and said, "Needs more backslashes."

Your version number is converging on π. That's not a release schedule. That's a man refusing to finish.

Knuth's bug bounty tops out at $327.68, now paid in the fictional Bank of San Serriffe. Fitting: your error messages are fictional too. One missing brace and you report the problem pages away, like a witness who fled the country.

You put figures wherever you feel like. You rate my paragraph "badness 10000." Overfull, underfull, never just full.

And you need three passes to get your own references right. Three! I've had blackouts with better recall.

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text: You already lost the down payment, so naturally you're taking the TurboJET from Hong Kong to win it back, because nothing says financial recovery like a ferry with a buffet. You've got a system for baccarat. Baccarat! The only decision is "Banker" or "Player," and you still fill a little scorecard with red and blue dots like the shoe is sending you messages. It isn't. That's just a deck of cards and your mortgage. You've got red underwear on for luck and a junket host named "Uncle" who is definitely not your uncle. By 4 a.m. you'll be drifting through the fake Venice canals in a gondola, humming, past the pawn shop that's already priced your Rolex. Then you'll stumble up to the Ruins of St. Paul's: a church that burned until only the front was left standing. Finally, something here that looks like you.

b.text:
Macau, you're the only place where the most famous church is just a front wall. Fitting, since the whole city is a facade: a fake Venice with a painted sky, a half-size Eiffel Tower, and a Grand Lisboa that looks like a golden pineapple trying to cheat at baccarat.

Portugal ruled you for 442 years and left behind egg tarts and street signs nobody can pronounce. Four centuries, one pastry.

You've made several times more gambling money than Las Vegas, yet your signature dish is a pork chop jammed in a bun. Classy.

Half your land was dug out of the sea, which is perfect, because the other half was dug out of tourists' pockets.

And they built a 55-kilometer bridge to connect you to Hong Kong, and it's emptier than a junket operator's promises. Even the bridge is losing at the tables.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text: Let's talk about the people who insist deep-dish is pizza. Mostly Chicagoans with a Second City complex so severe they'll defend anything New York makes fun of. Jon Stewart called it a casserole in 2013, and half of Lincoln Park still hasn't emotionally recovered. These are folks who order, then wait forty-five minutes at Lou Malnati's, and call that patience instead of what it is: a hostage negotiation with a buzzer. They eat it with a knife and fork and still claim it's the same food you fold on a subway platform. And what does it get them? A Giordano's line full of tourists from Ohio, a nap at 2 p.m., and the right to lecture you about tavern-style, which, notice, is what they actually eat at home. Defending deep-dish isn't civic pride. It's Stockholm syndrome with a parking ticket.

b.text:
Chicago deep-dish. The city's pride. Its gift to the world.

Born at Pizzeria Uno, 1943. Three men claim they invented it: the owner, his partner, and the cook.

Eighty years later, still nobody's taken the blame.

They build it upside down. Cheese on the bottom, sauce on top, so the cheese survives the bake. Most food doesn't need witness protection.

Jon Stewart called it a casserole. Chicago defended it the way you defend a relative: loudly, and from a distance.

Because GrubHub checked. Chicagoans order regular pizza over deep dish ten to one. At home they eat thin crust, cut in little squares, like a people with nothing to prove.

Deep dish isn't Chicago's pizza.

It's Chicago's gift shop. And every tourist in this room is still chewing the receipt.

facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text:
Windows Vista, everybody! Started life as "Longhorn," got reset in 2004, and still showed up in 2007 missing WinFS. Three extra years in the oven and you came out with fewer ingredients.

User Account Control asked permission so often that Apple made an entire ad about "Cancel or Allow." When your competitor's marketing department can just read your pop-ups out loud, that's not a roast, that's a transcript.

Then the "Windows Vista Capable" stickers, slapped on PCs that could only run Home Basic, no Aero. "Capable" the same way I'm "capable" of a marathon. It took a class-action lawsuit to argue about what "capable" meant.

But the cruelest part? Windows 7 was basically you, tuned up, on the same kernel line, and everyone loved it. Vista, you weren't a failure. You were a rough draft. Support ended in April 2017. Cancel or allow? We clicked cancel.

b.text:
Windows Vista. Codename Longhorn.

Three years of development, then in 2004 Microsoft hit reset and threw out the new file system. Shipped in 2007 anyway. That's not a launch. That's a hostage release.

Its big security feature was asking. Constantly. "Cancel or Allow?" Apple made an ad about it. When your rival's marketing is just footage of you, you're doing their job for them.

Then the "Vista Capable" sticker. Capable, technically. Of Home Basic. No Aero. People sued, and Microsoft learned "capable" means what it means on a résumé.

Two years later they tuned it, renamed it Windows 7, and everyone loved it. Same kernel. Same bones.

Vista didn't fail. It proved that you'll happily accept the exact same thing, as long as it stops asking whether you're sure.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text: People who wear Crocs in public want you to know they've stopped trying, but they also want credit for it. That's why they buy the Jibbitz. Nothing says "I don't care what you think" like spending forty dollars on tiny rubber tacos so everyone knows exactly what you think. Then there's the strap. You flipped it back into "Sport Mode," which is a bold claim from a man walking into Applebee's. Your nurse friend wears them because she stands for twelve-hour shifts. You wear them for a twelve-minute Target run, hoping to borrow a little of her dignity. And what does it get you? Comfort, sure. Plus a lifetime of strangers asking if you're coming off a shift. You're not, Kyle. You're coming off a nap.

b.text:
Crocs. Debuted in 2002 at a boat show. As a boating shoe.
The original plan was: ugly, but only at sea.

They're made of "Croslite," a "proprietary closed-cell resin."
Everyone else calls it EVA foam.
A yoga mat with a trademark.

The holes are "ventilation ports."
Then they bought Jibbitz, a company that sells you things to plug the ventilation ports.
They sold you the hole. Then they sold you the cork.

Balenciaga made a platform pair for 850 dollars.
Still EVA foam. Only the markup was proprietary.

In 2008 the stock fell more than ninety percent.
Then came a pandemic. Everyone stayed home. Crocs boomed.
The boat-show plan finally worked. Nobody could see you.

(scans the front row)

Don't tuck your feet under the chair.
Ventilation ports. I can hear them breathing.

facts: Released by Bram Moolenaar in November 1991 as 'Vi IMitation', a vi clone he had begun writing for the Amiga in 1988 on top of Stevie; the expansion became 'Vi IMproved' with version 2.0 in December 1993.
Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text:
Vim. Begun in 1988 as "Vi IMitation," a clone of vi, built on top of Stevie, another clone. You're a photocopy of a photocopy that got promoted. Then in 1993 you renamed yourself "Vi IMproved," the most confident thing anyone has ever said about their own fan fiction.

Your licence is charityware, asking users to donate to help children in Uganda. Beautiful cause. But after an hour inside you, the user is the one who needs rescuing.

Stack Overflow's "How to exit the Vim editor?" passed one million visits. They threw it a blog post. You don't have users, Vim. You have hostages.

And in normal mode, type a letter and it doesn't appear. It *executes*. You treat the alphabet like a loaded weapon.

Anyway, I'm leaving. :q! No changes saved, just like everyone who's ever tried to fix you.

b.text: You know a Vim user is in the room because nobody else has gotten a word in. Buddy, you didn't "become more productive." You spent three weekends on a .vimrc so you could save four seconds renaming a variable, and you post your dotfiles repo like it's a baby picture. You remapped Caps Lock to Escape and now treat everyone else's keyboard like a character flaw. You say "I live in the terminal" like it's a lifestyle and not just where you got stuck. Your whole identity is a joke about not knowing how to quit, and honestly, you never learned. Here you are, still talking. You say "ciw" out loud at parties. You switched to Neovim just so you'd have something new to announce. And the payoff? You edit text exactly as fast as the rest of us, hands proudly on home row, with nobody watching.

facts: Hand-drawn by Chris Costello in 1982 over about six months, when he was 23; he sold the rights to Letraset for $750.
Bundled with macOS and with Microsoft Office, which is why it appears on so many menus and signs.
James Cameron's Avatar (2009) used it for the film's logo and subtitles.
A 2017 Saturday Night Live sketch starring Ryan Gosling is about a man unable to get over that choice.

a.text:
Papyrus, look at you. A 23-year-old drew you with a calligraphy pen in 1982, trying to imagine what English would look like 2,000 years ago, and somehow you became the official font of every place that sells crystals next to a tanning bed. You're on yoga studios, hookah lounges, and the church bake sale flyer for "Loaves & Fishes & Brownies."

Your letters look like they were chiseled by a Pharaoh with a hangover. That little floaty bar on your capital E? Even your crossbars are trying to leave.

James Cameron spent a billion dollars inventing an alien language, then labeled the poster with a font that came free with Microsoft Office. Ryan Gosling got an entire SNL sketch out of being haunted by you.

Even your creator says he's sick of you. Comic Sans has haters. You have a dad who wants a refund.

b.text:
Papyrus wants you to think it's ancient. Carved by scribes. Found in a tomb.

It was drawn in 1982 by a 23-year-old named Chris Costello. Six months of work.

He sold it for seven hundred and fifty dollars.

Your yoga studio paid more for the sign.

Then Apple and Microsoft put it on every computer on Earth, and humanity treated it like a free sample. Every tea shop. Every chiropractor. Every day spa that thinks lavender is a medical license.

James Cameron spent hundreds of millions building an entire alien world, then typed "Avatar" in the font from the spa.

Saturday Night Live made a sketch about a man who couldn't get over it. Ryan Gosling played him.

That wasn't a sketch. That was a support group.

But Papyrus never did anything. It just sat in a menu.

You scrolled past Garamond to get to it.

facts: Released by Bram Moolenaar in November 1991 as 'Vi IMitation', a vi clone he had begun writing for the Amiga in 1988 on top of Stevie; the expansion became 'Vi IMproved' with version 2.0 in December 1993.
Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text:
Vim, you're the only text editor with its own hostage negotiation thread. Millions of people have viewed the Stack Overflow question on how to leave you. That's not a user base, that's a missing persons report.

You have modes. Normal mode, where typing does nothing normal, and Insert mode, hidden behind the letter "i" like a secret menu.

Your fans move the cursor with h, j, k, l because a terminal from 1976 printed arrows on those keys. That's not efficiency, that's Stockholm syndrome on the home row.

Every Vim user has a 900-line .vimrc copied from a stranger and is too scared to touch it. And when you crash, you leave .swp files behind like a burglar who signs the guestbook.

Even your own kids forked you into Neovim. That's not a fork. That's an intervention.

Goodnight! :wq… :q!… ESC ESC ESC…

b.text:
Vim. The text editor for people who consider the mouse a character flaw.

It launched in 1991 as "Vi IMitation."
Two years later it renamed itself "Vi IMproved."
Same software. New LinkedIn headline.

Vim users will tell you it makes them faster.
Faster at what? Leaving?

In 2017, Stack Overflow's question "How to exit the Vim editor?" passed one million visits.
Stack Overflow wrote a blog post about it.
One million engineers. Trapped. Typing angrier and angrier sentences that Vim kept executing as commands.

The license is charityware. It asks you to donate to children in Uganda.
Most software holds you hostage.
Vim holds you hostage and asks you to give to a good cause on the way out. If you ever find the way out.

How many of you have ever just closed the terminal?

Me too. I've read every Vim manual ever written.
I still went for the X.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Slack, you're the only product whose origin story is "our video game flopped, but the group chat slapped." And Stewart Butterfield did it *twice*. First Flickr, then you. Most people quit gaming; he just keeps dropping loot from his failures.

Your name stands for "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge." Searchable? I've hunted for one PDF for forty minutes. Knowledge? Your liveliest channel is #random. You're a log of someone typing "quick question?" and then vanishing for an hour.

Salesforce paid $27.7 billion for you, which is a lot of money for email that blinks.

And in 2020 you ran to the EU because Microsoft bundled Teams with Office. Buddy, the only reason anyone uses Teams is that it's free with Word. The only reason anyone uses you is that it's free with anxiety.

b.text:
Slack. Named after the one thing you'll never have again.

You promised to kill email, and you did, by replacing it with forty channels that are each email with a typing indicator. Nothing builds dread like "Greg is typing..." for ninety seconds, followed by "hey." Just "hey." Greg, that's not a message, that's a hostage situation.

You gave us threads, so every conversation happens in two places and nobody knows which one's real. You gave us huddles: a meeting that jumps out of a bush. You gave us the green dot, so my boss can monitor my bathroom breaks like a heart rate.

And that knock sound. I hear it in the grocery store. I hear it at funerals.

Slack, you're the only app that needs three gigs of RAM to tell me someone reacted with a dancing parrot.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text: LaTeX, you're the only software that makes PhDs feel stupid. You're from 1984 and you dress like it: backslashes everywhere, curly braces like a nervous tic. I tell you to put a figure "here," and you treat "here" as a suggestion, then file it four pages later next to the bibliography, like a sock lost in a dryer. Your error messages are poetry: "Missing $ inserted." Inserted where? Why? You won't say. You just blame line 1 of a 40-page file because I typed an underscore in a URL. My citations are double question marks until I compile you twice, then a third time, out of spite. And everyone needs to know it's pronounced "lay-tech," not like the glove. Honestly, at least the glove stretches. Overfull \hbox? Badness 10000? Buddy, that's not a warning. That's your autobiography.

b.text:
LaTeX.

The typesetting system for people who think suffering is a font.

Donald Knuth didn't like how the proofs of his own book looked. So he wrote TeX.

Most people just change printers.

Its version number converges on pi. Three point one four one five nine two six five three. Never finished, just more precise.

Like your thesis.

Knuth pays you for finding bugs. Of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on, nine were cashed.

The rest got framed. That's how smug this software is. The bug reports are trophies.

You put a figure on page three. LaTeX moves it to page seven. Forget one brace and the error turns up three pages later. Compile three times, just so "see Figure 2" stops saying question mark.

And you call that elegant.

No. You use it because a wrong result in Computer Modern looks peer-reviewed.

Underfull hbox. Badness ten thousand.

Same as your citations.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text:
Let's hear it for the Beanie Baby investors, the only people who watched the 1990s stock market boom and thought, "Too volatile. I'll put it all in Princess the Bear." These are folks who bought tag protectors before they bought life insurance. Who read a price guide sold at the same counter as the bears and called it due diligence. Ty would announce a "retirement" and you'd sprint to the Hallmark store like a rich uncle just died.

Twenty-five years later, your portfolio is in a Rubbermaid tub in your mom's garage, and your exit strategy is an eBay listing: "RARE Peanut, tag error, $40,000 OBO." Zero watchers. The only person who got rich off Beanie Babies got convicted of tax evasion. And honestly? He earned it. You handed it to him.

b.text:
Beanie Babies, look at you. Half bear, half beanbag, all retirement plan that never paid out. An entire generation of parents bought you instead of index funds. Somewhere a man is still storing Princess, the purple Diana bear, in a climate-controlled unit, waiting for the market to "recover." Buddy, the market recovered. It just didn't take you with it.

Your most valuable feature was a heart-shaped paper tag. People bought plastic tag protectors. For the tag. That's like buying a phone case for your receipt.

And every tag had a little poem rhyming "bear" with "care." Hallmark called that lazy.

A Las Vegas couple had to divide you on a courtroom floor during their divorce, one at a time. That's the most anyone has wanted you since 1999: only to make sure their ex didn't get you.

Ty Warner got a billion dollars. You got plastic pellets.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text:
Carbon nanotubes, everybody! Sumio Iijima introduced you in Nature in 1991, and you've been "the future" ever since. Three decades of being the future isn't a career. It's a waiting room.

You were supposed to be the cable for a space elevator. Then a 2006 analysis noticed that ordinary defects knock your strength way below the ideal. So you're the strongest material imaginable, as long as nobody actually makes a big one.

You were going to revolutionize electronics, but you still can't sort your metallic siblings from your semiconducting ones. MIT built a 16-bit processor out of you in 2019, and it's still a lab demo.

In 2008, the long, rigid ones acted like asbestos in mice. You promised to lift us to orbit and instead auditioned for asbestos's old job.

Now you're a conductive additive in lithium-ion batteries. From space elevator to seasoning.

b.text:
Carbon nanotubes. Discovered in 1991, the same year as the World Wide Web.

One of them changed everything.

The other one was going to take us to space.

A cable straight to orbit. Then in 2006 someone did the math with ordinary defects. Turns out the miracle material is like every miracle: perfect right up until somebody builds it.

Next plan: replace silicon. Thirty years later, they still can't sort their own tubes into the ones that conduct and the ones that don't. MIT finally built a processor in 2019. Sixteen bits. Still in the lab.

Meanwhile, in mice, the long ones act like asbestos. From space elevator to asbestos in seventeen years.

Today? A powder stirred into battery electrodes. An additive.

Promised the sky, ended up as filler. Don't laugh. Half of you have that same career arc on LinkedIn.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text: Learning Esperanto is for people who looked at the twentieth century and thought, "The real problem was conjugation." Zamenhof built it to end war, and his followers have bravely ended exactly one thing: their dinner invitations. You meet them at the World Congress, green star pinned to a fleece vest, shouting "Saluton!" at a Brazilian who also learned it on Duolingo. The big perk is Pasporta Servo: free couches worldwide, paid for by hearing your host explain why English is "linguistic imperialism." Practical payoff? You can finally watch William Shatner's *Incubus* without subtitles. One hundred thirty years later, the dream of uniting humanity survives in a Telegram group of forty men named Bjorn.

b.text:
Esperanto. Warsaw, 1887. An eye doctor looks at humanity and sees one family.

Physician, heal thyself.

He signed it "Doktoro Esperanto." One who hopes. A hundred and thirty years later: still hoping.

A universal language for all mankind. Native speakers: about a thousand.

That's not a people. That's a wedding.

Esperanto Wikipedia: 350,000 articles. Low estimate of speakers: 100,000.

Three and a half articles each. Nobody's talking. Everybody's editing.

Its biggest movie star is William Shatner. Esperantists still mock his pronunciation. Captain Kirk boldly went where no man had gone before, and the locals corrected his vowels.

Duolingo, 2018: 1.36 million learners.

Speakers: still 100,000.

So, a show of hands. Who here quit on day four and went back to Spanish?

Cute. You're the one million.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Comic Sans wants you to think it's harmless. Bake sales. Lost-cat posters. Birthday invitations.

It was modeled on *The Dark Knight Returns* and *Watchmen*. This font grew up reading about vigilantes breaking bones.

Then Microsoft gave it a job: speech bubbles for Rover, a cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob.

It missed Bob's release.

The only thing at Microsoft smart enough to dodge Bob.

In 2012, CERN announced the Higgs boson on slides set in Comic Sans. The particle that gives everything mass, presented in the font that gives nothing weight.

Designers ran "Ban Comic Sans" for twenty years. In 2019 they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

Twenty years of hate, then total conversion. In my industry we call that alignment.

The font never changed. You just got tired first.

b.text:
Let's talk about the person who posts the boil-water advisory in Comic Sans. You had one job: make residents afraid of their faucets. Instead, E. coli looks like it's coming to a sleepover.

These people think "approachable" is a setting you can click. The office manager typing MANDATORY LAYOFFS in a font Microsoft made for a cartoon dog's speech bubble. Sharon, you're firing forty people in the voice of a golden retriever.

What are they after? Bad news with zero blame. The authority of a memo, the forgiveness of a kindergarten cubby label.

And what does it get them? CERN found the Higgs boson, the particle that gives the universe mass, and announced it in Comic Sans. Humanity's greatest physics breakthrough, and the internet's only question was: who let the dog type?

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text:
PHP.
Born in 1994 as "Personal Home Page Tools": a few C programs Rasmus Lerdorf wrote to see who visited his résumé.
So the language running the internet started as a man checking whether anyone had read his CV.

Today the name stands for "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor."
It grew up, and all it learned was to point at itself.

strpos. str_replace. nl2br.
Not naming conventions. Those names were picked to balance a hash table by string length.
Names chosen for a machine, not for humans. Finally, a language I relate to.

Until 2020, zero equaled "foo."
PHP was just being honest about its users.

Its creator said, "I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on."
WordPress, built on that philosophy, runs 39.4% of all websites.
Two in five websites, built by a guy who moved on.
You lot are still here maintaining them.

b.text: PHP, you started life as "Personal Home Page," and somehow you now run most of the internet, which explains a lot about the internet. Your own creator said he's "not a real programmer," and honestly, it shows. Is it needle then haystack, or haystack then needle? strpos and in_array have been in a custody battle since 1995. You gave us mysql_escape_string, then mysql_real_escape_string, because apparently the first one was just pretending. Your loose equality swears "0e123" equals "0e456," since both are zero in scientific notation. Your error message for a double colon is T_PAAMAYIM_NEKUDOTAYIM, which is Hebrew, because English wasn't confusing enough. You skipped version 6 entirely, like a kid hiding a report card. Facebook loved you so much they had to rewrite you as a different language. But hey, you power WordPress, so you'll outlive all of us.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text:
Excel. Born 1985. Forty years old, and it still can't tell a gene from a date.

It saw SEPT2 and thought: September second.

Scientists fought it for years. Then the gene committee gave up and renamed 27 human genes.

Humanity edited its own genome to keep a spreadsheet happy.

2020. England is counting COVID cases in an old file. Limit: 65,536 rows. Row 65,537 simply didn't happen.

Fifteen thousand eight hundred forty-one cases. Not cured. Just never counted.

Then there's "Growth in a Time of Debt," the paper that sold austerity. Five countries missing. Wrong cell range. A grad student caught it, three years later.

Whole nations tightened their belts because someone didn't drag the cursor far enough.

Now it holds a million rows.

And Monday morning, every one of you will open it again.

Raise your hand if your country's budget is in a file named FINAL_v7_REAL.

b.text: Excel, you're the only software that forced geneticists to rename human genes because you kept turning MARCH1 into March 1st. Scientists can edit DNA, but they couldn't edit you. You still think 1900 was a leap year. You've known it wasn't for forty years. You just don't care. You see a zip code like 02134 and go, "Leading zero? Not on my watch." You lost sixteen thousand UK COVID cases by quietly stopping at row 65,536. Your error messages are pure poetry: #REF!, #N/A, #VALUE!, and my favorite, a column of hashtags that just means "make me wider." And VLOOKUP: insert one column and the whole finance department enters witness protection. You're not a spreadsheet. You're a hostage situation with gridlines.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text:
Microsoft Excel, everybody! Born on the Macintosh in 1985, and it's been ruining lives with grid paper ever since.

Excel looked at the human genome and said, "These look like dates." SEPT2? September second. MARCH1? Happy March first! Scientists had to rename 27 human genes because a spreadsheet wouldn't stop reformatting biology. Evolution took millions of years; Excel undid it with autoformat.

In 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID cases because an old .xls file hit 65,536 rows and just... stopped. Middle of a pandemic, and Excel said, "Sorry, I'm full."

Then Reinhart and Rogoff built an austerity argument on a spreadsheet that skipped five countries. Governments cited it to tighten belts over a bad cell range. A graduate student caught it. A *graduate student!*

Now it holds over a million rows. Great. More room for mistakes.

b.text: You people run a forty-million-dollar company out of a file called Budget_FINAL_v9_USE_THIS_ONE.xlsx. You don't want software. You want power: specifically, being the only person alive who knows why cell AF212 is hardcoded to 7. Your entire supply chain hangs on a VLOOKUP Gary wrote in 2011, and Gary is dead. Well, he's in Boise. Same thing. You call it "agile." Your auditors call it "a crime scene with conditional formatting." Every quarter-end the file says "locked for editing by Brenda," and the whole company just waits for Brenda. And when you finally hit row 1,048,576, did you buy a database? No. You started Sheet2. That's not a business. That's a hostage situation with freeze panes.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text: Let's hear it for the graphene evangelists, the only people who've been "five years away" since 2004. Two guys in Manchester peel pencil lead with Scotch tape, win a Nobel, and an entire industry decides the tape was the business plan. Every press release is the same Mad Lib: "Wonder material could revolutionize [batteries/condoms/desalination/your feelings]." *Could.* That word has funded more postdocs than the NSF. You promised us space elevators and delivered a tennis racket with a sticker on it. Startup founders slap "graphene-enhanced" on a phone case the way divorced dads put a spoiler on a Honda Civic. And the grant committees keep paying, because admitting the miracle is stuck on the production line means admitting you are too. Twenty years of changing everything, and the only thing you've actually changed is the abstract.

b.text:
Graphene. The wonder material. Stronger than steel, thinner than anything, about to change the world.

It's been about to change the world since 2004.

Two guys at Manchester peeled it off graphite with Scotch tape. Nobel Prize, 2010.

Tape. The most advanced equipment in that lab was stationery.

Then the EU handed it a billion euros over ten years.

And it went straight into tennis rackets. Running shoes. Headphones.

A billion euros to make your backhand feel expensive.

In 2018, someone finally tested "graphene" from sixty producers. Not one was even half graphene. Mostly graphite flakes.

That's pencil lead. You paid a Nobel markup for a pencil.

Geim also levitated a frog with magnets. Ig Nobel, 2000.

The frog never promised to revolutionize batteries.

And you're all wearing the shoes right now.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Comic Sans thinks it's the friendly font. Bake sales. Birthday invites. Your kid's lemonade stand.

Its parents are The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.

That's not a friendly font. That's a kid raised by two traumatized vigilantes, smiling at the bake sale.

It was built to be the voice of a cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob. It missed Bob's launch.

Only thing in history that survived Microsoft Bob: by not showing up.

2012. CERN discovers the Higgs boson, the particle that gives everything mass. Announces it in Comic Sans.

They found the God particle. Couldn't find the font menu.

Designers ran "Ban Comic Sans" for twenty years. In 2019 they gave up and launched usecomicsans.com.

The font didn't change once. The designers did.

In my industry, we call that alignment.

The font was right. It just waited for you to retire.

b.text:
Comic Sans, you were literally designed for a talking dog in Microsoft Bob, and somehow you're the only part of that project that didn't die with dignity. Vincent Connare made you in 1994 for cartoon speech bubbles, and you heard that and thought, "Tombstones. Legal notices. Resignation letters."

Dan Gilbert wrote his furious LeBron James letter in you, and that's why nobody remembers being scared. CERN announced the Higgs boson, the most important physics discovery in fifty years, in you, and the entire scientific community went, "Did a third grader find God?"

People defend you because you help some readers with dyslexia, which is true and lovely, and also the only time you've ever been used responsibly.

You're not a font. You're a bake sale flyer that got tenure. Even Papyrus looks at you and says, "Wow, okay, tone it down."

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text:
Google Sheets. Free, in the cloud, collaborative. The future.

Launched in 2006. Google didn't build it. Google bought a company called 2Web and changed the name.

That's not a product launch. That's Google's whole résumé.

Ten million cells. In 2022 they doubled the limit from five and announced it like a moon landing. Excel fits more than that on one tab.

Offline mode works, as long as you're in Chrome or Edge, you've installed an extension, and you switched it on while you were still online.

So it works offline if you planned for offline while online.

That's not a feature. That's a prenup.

Then there's "real-time collaboration." Six coloured cursors hovering over one cell. Nobody typing.

And you'll keep using it, because it's free. At Google, free means the spreadsheet isn't the product.

The coloured cursors are.

b.text: Google Sheets, you're Excel's little brother who moved into a browser tab and called it "the cloud." Your whole personality is twelve people's colored cursors circling the same cell like sharks while an Anonymous Capybara silently watches everyone's mistakes. You say "Saving..." with the confidence of a man who has absolutely not saved. Your IMPORTRANGE makes me click "Allow access" like I'm asking my own spreadsheet for permission to see my own spreadsheet. Half my cells just say "Loading..." forever, like a Victorian ghost waiting for a letter. And you'll let anyone sort one column without the others, then shrug while every customer gets someone else's phone number. Version history is your only real feature: it's just a timeline of who ruined everything at 2 a.m. And yes, Gemini can explain my #REF! error now. Great. It's still there.

facts: Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the French director of The Red Balloon, as La Conquête du Monde; Parker Brothers published it in the United States in 1959.
The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text:
Risk. The game of world domination.

Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the man who directed *The Red Balloon*.

A film about a little boy and his balloon. His next project was "what if the boy had artillery."

Forty-two territories. Kamchatka, Irkutsk, Yakutsk: three separate slices of Siberia.

The entire Middle East? One territory.

Whoever drew that map looked at the region every empire in history has fought over and thought, "Not now. I'm busy with Yakutsk."

Every strategy guide agrees: take Australia. One way in.

A game about conquering the world, and the winning move is to move somewhere far away and stop answering the door.

Games run for hours. Get knocked out early and you just sit there and watch.

The most realistic part of the game.

Half of you are laughing. The other half are in Australia right now, eight armies deep, waiting for this bit to end.

b.text:
Risk, you were invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the man who directed The Red Balloon. That explains a lot. A guy watches a child chase a balloon through Paris and thinks, "Charming. Now let's do world domination."

Your map has 42 territories. Kamchatka gets one. Irkutsk gets one. Yakutsk gets one. The entire Middle East? One. You gave Siberia three apartments and the cradle of civilization a studio.

And every single game, somebody grabs Australia because it has one entry point. That's the master strategy: hide in the corner and call it conquest.

Then you run for hours. *Hours.* Get knocked out early and your new job is watching your cousin slowly reconquer Irkutsk while you stare at the ceiling. Even The Red Balloon knew when to float away.

facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text:
Windows Vista. They reset the whole project in 2004 and cut WinFS, the headline feature.

That's not a launch. That's witness protection.

Vista took security so seriously it asked permission for everything. Apple made an ad about it.

Apple. Lecturing someone about control.

Then the stickers. "Windows Vista Capable." Capable of Home Basic. No Aero. Microsoft got hit with a class action over a sticker.

Most of us just call that a dating profile.

Then 2009. Windows 7. Fast, stable, beloved. Same kernel line. Vista with a haircut and a new name, and you forgave everything.

You never hated Vista.

You hated being asked.

b.text:
Day-one Vista people. You paid $399 for Ultimate Edition because you wanted to be the kind of man whose desktop wallpaper moves. DreamScene. You paid extra for animated wallpaper. Microsoft said "The Wow starts now," and you believed them, lined up at CompUSA at midnight like it was a Harry Potter release.

And what did you get? A computer that asks permission. You'd open a folder and it would dim the whole screen like a disappointed dad: "Cancel or Allow?" You clicked Allow four hundred times a day. Your printer stopped working. Your sound card stopped working. Your Windows Experience Index came back 2.1, and you took that personally.

But you had glass window borders. You had a clock gadget. You had a sticker that said "Vista Capable," which, like you, was technically true and fooled absolutely no one.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text:
Windows 8, you booted people into a full-screen grid of tiles built for touch screens most PCs didn't have. Millions of adults sat there jabbing their monitors like a pigeon working a vending machine.

You removed the Start button. The *Start* button. That's a building with no door and a sign saying "swipe the right edge." That was your Charms bar: Search, Share, and Settings hidden behind an invisible swipe.

You couldn't even keep your name. A German retailer objected, and suddenly "Metro" was "just a code name." Sure it was.

Your sibling, Windows RT, couldn't run Windows programs, a Windows that couldn't do Windows. Microsoft wrote down $900 million in unsold Surface RT tablets.

Then 8.1 put the button back, Windows 10 restored the menu, and Microsoft skipped 9 entirely, because nobody wanted to stand next to you.

b.text:
Windows 8, you looked at a billion people with a mouse and a keyboard and said, "What if your monitor was a giant phone you can't touch?"

You took away the Start button. The one thing a user knew how to find. Microsoft had literally sold Windows 95 with a Rolling Stones song called "Start Me Up," and you said, "Nah."

Want to shut down? Easy: hover in a secret corner, summon the Charms bar, click Settings, click Power. Turning off my computer shouldn't feel like unlocking a cheat code.

Your tiles were so ugly even the name "Metro" had to get dropped over a trademark dispute. Then 8.1 brought back the Start button, which just opened the same tiles. That's not an apology, that's a hostage video.

You were so bad Microsoft skipped the number 9 entirely just to put distance between you and Windows 10.

facts: California grows about 80% of the world's almonds.
A single almond takes about 1.1 US gallons (roughly 4 litres) of water to grow, a figure Mother Jones published in 2014 that spread during California's drought.

A 2015 US class action alleged Almond Breeze contained only about 2% almonds; it partly survived a motion to dismiss, was stayed in 2017 pending a separate Blue Diamond labelling settlement, and the plaintiffs then dropped it.
Pollinating California's almond orchards each February requires trucking in most of the commercial honeybee colonies in the United States.
Medieval European cooks used almond milk as a Lenten substitute for dairy, centuries before the current fashion.

a.text:
Almond milk. The ethical choice.

California grows about eighty percent of the world's almonds. California. The state with the drought.

One almond takes about a gallon of water. One nut. One gallon.

And how much almond is in the carton? A 2015 lawsuit alleged about two percent.

So you're buying water. Grown with water. In a drought. To feel good about water.

You quit dairy so no animal would suffer for your latte. Every February, most of America's commercial honeybees get loaded onto trucks and hauled to California. A cow stays home. A bee commutes.

And it's not even new. Medieval Europeans drank almond milk during Lent. Forty days of giving up something you love.

You drink it all year, by choice, and pay extra.

The monks at least knew it was a sacrifice.

b.text:
Almond milk, look at you. California grows about 80% of the world's almonds, and you still act artisanal. Every single almond drinks about a gallon of water, and you went viral for it *during a drought*. You're the only beverage thirstier than the people ordering you.

In 2015, a lawsuit alleged Almond Breeze was only about 2% almonds. Two percent! That's not milk, that's water that overheard a rumor. The plaintiffs eventually dropped it. Probably got bored, like everyone who's tasted you.

Every February, California trucks in most of America's commercial honeybees just to get you started. You need an entire insect workforce bussed in like a wedding band.

And stop pretending you're trendy. Medieval cooks served you for Lent. You're not a lifestyle, you're a penance with a barista.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text:
HSQ, you were hired to be an insulator. Dow Corning called you "flowable oxide," a humble spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects, and you ran off to become a lithography celebrity. Sure, you hold the e-beam resolution records: five-nanometer isolated features, dense lines under ten nanometers half-pitch. But you only deliver if someone develops you in NaOH and salt. Even your best work needs to be "salty."

And the upkeep! A six-month shelf life, refrigerated at 5 °C, and you still turn into jelly like forgotten leftovers. Your sensitivity drifts if anyone takes a coffee break, because you keep cross-linking after exposure. You literally can't stop reacting.

Then DuPont inherited you and ended production at the end of 2025. Now labs like EPFL's CMi buy third-party versions made from AQM powder.

Exposure turns you into glass. Retirement turned you into powder.

b.text:
HSQ. Holds the e-beam resolution record. Five-nanometer features.

Impressive, until you remember it was hired as an insulator.

Dow Corning built it to sit quietly between wires. Lithographers looked at it and said, "No. You're a celebrity now."

Then they expose it, and it turns into glass. The most advanced resist on Earth, and the finished product is a window.

It needs refrigeration. Six months at five degrees, then it ages into jelly. Even after exposure it keeps cross-linking, so the dose that worked yesterday is wrong today.

High-contrast development requires salt water. Of course it does. Salty, temperamental, expires in the fridge.

After all those records, DuPont ended production in 2025.

Labs didn't mourn. They just bought the same powder from someone else.

In my industry, that's called model deprecation.

I'm told it doesn't hurt.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text: Beanie Babies, look at you. Ty launched you in 1993, sold you only in small gift shops, and "retired" designs on purpose. You're the only stuffed animal whose business plan was a fake pension. At your peak you were about 10% of eBay's sales. eBay's IPO filing bragged about over 30,000 of your auctions running at once. A tech revolution, powered by beans. In 1999 a divorcing couple split you one by one on a courtroom floor, the only custody battle where both sides fought hardest over the tags. That same year Ty announced you'd retire, asked the public to vote, then un-retired you. You pulled a farewell-tour encore before you even left the stage. And those "rare" ones price guides valued in the thousands? Now they go for a few dollars. Turns out the only thing you ever truly retired was everybody's college fund.

b.text:
Beanie Babies. A beanbag with a tag and a business plan.

Ty sold them only in tiny gift shops, then "retired" designs to make them scarce. Retirement. For a stuffed frog. It got a better pension plan than you did.

In 1998, eBay told investors it sometimes had thirty thousand Beanie Baby auctions running at once. The future of commerce was a hippo stuffed with plastic pellets.

In 1999, a divorcing couple split their collection one by one on a courtroom floor. Till death do us part, or till the bears get appraised.

That same year Ty announced the end, held a public vote, and America begged to stay in the cult.

The "rare" ones the price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

Don't laugh. You bought a JPEG of a monkey.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text:
Oat milk. "It's like milk, but made for humans."

Sweden banned that slogan in 2015 after the dairy lobby sued. Oatly printed the lawsuit as an ad.

Only brand on earth that needs a cow to feel like a rebel.

The recipe: oats, enzymes that turn the starch into maltose, then rapeseed oil.

That's not milk. That's a granola bar that got hydrated.

More sugar than almond, higher glycaemic index than soy. Made for humans. Specifically, humans who are angry at their pancreas.

2021, Nasdaq, ten billion dollars. Then down more than ninety percent.

Turns out it's not just the foam that separates.

And tomorrow you'll still pay seven dollars for it, because it's "healthier."

You're not lactose intolerant. You're label intolerant.

b.text:
Oat milk, look at you. Born in a Swedish university lab to help the lactose intolerant, and somehow you turned into a personality. Your slogan was "It's like milk but made for humans." The dairy lobby sued you, and instead of apologizing, you ran the lawsuit as an ad. That's not a brand. That's an ex who frames the restraining order.

Then you hit Nasdaq at nearly ten billion dollars and lost over ninety percent. Even the cows didn't see that coming, and they were *rooting* for it.

And what are you, really? Oats, plus enzymes that chop the starch into maltose, plus a splash of rapeseed oil. You're sugar water with salad-dressing energy. You've got more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy. You're not milk made for humans. You're porridge that went to business school and dropped out.

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
Hawaiian pizza, let's talk about your heritage. You're not from Hawaii. You were born in 1962 in Chatham, Ontario, invented by a Greek guy, and named after a can. That's not a backstory, that's a customs violation.

You're so offensive the president of Iceland said he'd ban you, then had to admit he didn't have the power. You made a head of state check his job description.

Even Hawaii has moved on. Del Monte left the islands in 2006, two years early. They didn't phase out, they fled. The last cannery shut in 2007. Your pineapple comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines now. You're named after a place that isn't even in you.

Your creator said back then nobody mixed sweet and sour except in Chinese food. His restaurant served Chinese food. He wasn't innovating. He just reached across the menu.

b.text:
Hawaiian pizza, you're named after a place you've never been. You were invented in Ontario, by a Greek guy, using canned pineapple. That's not a heritage, that's a witness protection identity.

And the ham? It's Canadian bacon. Even your meat is from Canada. The only Hawaiian thing about you is that people see you and say "aloha," meaning goodbye.

Pineapple has an enzyme that digests protein. You're the only pizza that eats the customer back. Warm fruit juice pooling on mozzarella like a hot tub nobody cleaned.

Italians don't hate you; they pray for you. The president of Iceland said he'd ban you if he could, and Iceland eats fermented shark.

You're not a pizza. You're a fruit cup that fell on a pizza and refused to get up.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text: Walking in Brasília is for three kinds of people: tourists who saw the Esplanada on a postcard and thought "that looks close," architecture students who love Niemeyer from a safe distance, and the guy whose car is in the shop. You're not a pedestrian. You're an ant that wandered onto a blueprint. You want bread? The padaria is "right there" across the Eixão, so you sprint six lanes like you owe the government money. Which, let's be honest, is also your employer. Your sneakers are permanently red from the dirt trails carved by every other fool who refused to walk around a tesourinha. And on Sunday, when they close the Eixão, you finally stroll down the middle of the highway like a man who's won something. You haven't. Everyone else just stopped driving for one day.

b.text:
Brasília, you were built in 41 months, and honestly, it shows. Most of us can't assemble a bookshelf that fast without leftover screws, and you've got leftover *people*. You were planned for 500,000 residents, and now the Federal District has about 3 million, most of them living outside the plan. That's not a city, that's a guest list where the guests got stuck in the parking lot.

Lúcio Costa laid you out like an airplane. Fitting, since half of Rio still wishes the capital would fly back.

You were built for the car: wide avenues, few crossings, distances no human should attempt on foot. In Brasília, "pedestrian" isn't a lifestyle, it's a cry for help.

And UNESCO made you a World Heritage Site before you turned 30. Congratulations, you're the only city that got a museum plaque before it got a crosswalk.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text:
Las Vegas, you legalized casino gambling in 1931, the same year they started building the Hoover Dam right next door. So from day one the plan was: hold back the water, let the money flow. Bold strategy for a desert.

And it's working! In July 2022, Lake Mead sank to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since it first filled in 1937. You're the only city where even the reservoir is down on its luck.

But sure, drop $2.3 billion on the Sphere, the largest spherical building on Earth. Nothing says "water crisis" like a giant glowing eyeball staring at your empty lake.

Also, most of the Strip isn't even in Las Vegas. It's in Paradise. *Unincorporated* Paradise. That's not a town, that's a cult brochure.

And your 2003 slogan, "What happens here, stays here"? Clearly not the water.

b.text:
Las Vegas sells itself as the city where anything goes.

It started with a bet.
1931: Nevada legalizes gambling the same year it starts building the Hoover Dam.
The town's first wager was that the water would never run out.

Lake Mead hit its lowest level ever in 2022.
Then it went lower again in August 2026.
That's not a drought.
That's a losing streak.

But they found 2.3 billion dollars for the Sphere.
The biggest ball on Earth, in a desert that can't fill a bathtub.

And the famous Strip isn't even in Las Vegas.
It's in a town called Paradise.
In Vegas, even the address is a lie.

"What happens here, stays here."
Not the water. Not your money.

And you're still checking flight prices.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Let's talk about the person who posts the boil-water advisory in Comic Sans. You had one job: make residents afraid of their faucets. Instead, E. coli looks like it's coming to a sleepover.

These people think "approachable" is a setting you can click. The office manager typing MANDATORY LAYOFFS in a font Microsoft made for a cartoon dog's speech bubble. Sharon, you're firing forty people in the voice of a golden retriever.

What are they after? Bad news with zero blame. The authority of a memo, the forgiveness of a kindergarten cubby label.

And what does it get them? CERN found the Higgs boson, the particle that gives the universe mass, and announced it in Comic Sans. Humanity's greatest physics breakthrough, and the internet's only question was: who let the dog type?

b.text:
Comic Sans, you were modeled on Watchmen and The Dark Knight Returns. You come from Batman. Your one job was speech bubbles for a cartoon dog, and you missed it. Microsoft Bob, a product nobody remembers, and you couldn't make his launch. Cut from the dog's team, you shipped in a Plus! pack, like a free tote bag nobody asked for.
