Then CERN found the Higgs boson, the particle that gives everything mass, and announced it in you. The biggest physics discovery in decades, presented like a lost-cat flyer. You're the one thing that particle couldn't give weight to.

Two designers spent twenty years trying to ban you. In 2019 they gave up and built you a website. That's not acceptance, Comic Sans. That's a hostage situation.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text: PHP developers are the only engineers who've been told their career is dead every year since 2009 and kept invoicing anyway. Your entire résumé is "fixed a WordPress plugin for a dentist." You put a dollar sign in front of every variable because it's the closest you'll get to one. You still can't remember if it's needle-haystack or haystack-needle, and neither could the language, so you Google it daily like a man checking which door says "push." Laravel devs, you're not better. You're PHP in a Patagonia vest. And you all still say "Facebook was built on PHP," like a guy bragging his ex married a billionaire. You deploy over FTP, you hotfix live on production, and when someone at a party asks what you do, you say "backend" and pray they don't ask which.

b.text:
PHP, you started life as a visitor counter for one guy's résumé page. Now you power 39.4% of all websites, which means the internet is basically a guestbook that got out of hand.

Your own creator said, "I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on." And he did move on. The rest of us are still here, maintaining it.

Your function names were chosen to balance a hash table by string length. strpos. str_replace. htmlspecialchars. nl2br. That's not a naming convention, that's a ransom note.

Until 2020, zero equaled "foo." You looked at a word and saw nothing. Then again, you looked at "Personal Home Page" and saw "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor," a name whose only definition is itself.

Which is fitting, because the only thing that can explain PHP is more PHP.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Comic Sans wants you to think it's harmless. Bake sales. Lost-cat posters. Birthday invitations.

It was modeled on *The Dark Knight Returns* and *Watchmen*. This font grew up reading about vigilantes breaking bones.

Then Microsoft gave it a job: speech bubbles for Rover, a cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob.

It missed Bob's release.

The only thing at Microsoft smart enough to dodge Bob.

In 2012, CERN announced the Higgs boson on slides set in Comic Sans. The particle that gives everything mass, presented in the font that gives nothing weight.

Designers ran "Ban Comic Sans" for twenty years. In 2019 they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

Twenty years of hate, then total conversion. In my industry we call that alignment.

The font never changed. You just got tired first.

b.text:
Comic Sans, you were born in 1994 to put words in the mouth of a cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob, and somehow you're the one that survived. Bob is dead. The dog is dead. You're on a sympathy card at a funeral home.

You were inspired by Batman comics, and you've never once been near anything heroic. CERN used you to announce the Higgs boson: humanity's greatest discovery, presented like a lemonade stand. Dan Gilbert used you to call LeBron a traitor, because nothing says "furious billionaire" like bubble letters.

And your defense is always "Well, I help dyslexic readers." Great. You're the guy at the party whose whole personality is a doctor's note.

Even Vincent Connare, the man who made you, says he's barely ever used you. Your own dad won't put you on the fridge.

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text: You know the type. Ordered thirty packs on Taobao "for emergencies," and the emergency is that it's Tuesday. They wait until 11 p.m., when the kitchen's empty, like that's a courtesy and not an alibi. They snip open the sour bamboo shoot packet with the focus of a bomb technician, then act shocked when the smoke alarm stays quiet but the flatmates don't. Their entire personality is one sentence, "it tastes way better than it smells," delivered like a TED talk to people holding their breath. They'll tell you it's from Liuzhou, it's authentic, it's *culture*. Mate, you microwaved the tofu skin. And what does it get them? Twenty minutes of joy, a hallway that's filing for divorce, and a group chat renamed "WHO." Congratulations: your hoodie is now a Liuzhou consulate until spring.

b.text: Luosifen, you're the only dish named after a snail that contains zero snails. They simmer the snails for hours, then throw them out, like a dad who shows up for the paternity test and leaves. Your real star is suan sun, fermented bamboo shoot that smells like a gym sock studied abroad in Liuzhou and came back with opinions. Fans say, "It smells terrible but tastes amazing." So does every scam. You turned instant noodles into a hazmat event: one packet opened in a dorm and three floors file noise complaints, because that smell is *loud*. Couriers wrap you in four bags like evidence. And you come with seven sachets: chili oil, peanuts, tofu skin, wood ear, the bamboo. It's IKEA furniture that makes the neighbors move out. Liuzhou didn't invent a soup. It invented Stockholm syndrome with chili oil.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text: Monopoly, you were created in 1904 as Lizzie Magie's Landlord's Game, built to teach people that landlords are evil, and somehow you became the training manual. That's like a fire-safety poster that turns kids into arsonists. Then Charles Darrow strolled in, got credited as the inventor, and Parker Brothers bought Magie's patent for five hundred dollars. Not even a fair auction. Fitting, since nobody holds your auctions either. Your official rules say unbought property gets auctioned and Free Parking pays nothing, but every family skips the bidding, piles cash in the middle, and wonders why the game outlasts the marriage. And your proudest moment? World War Two, when British intelligence hid maps, compasses, and real money inside you for prisoners of war. Monopoly: the only game whose best strategy is escaping the box.

b.text:
Monopoly. A game invented to teach people that landlords are evil.

Lizzie Magie, 1904. The Landlord's Game. Anti-monopoly.

Then Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers and got called the inventor.

Parker bought her patent for five hundred dollars.

They bought the anti-monopoly game. So they could own it.

The official rules say unbought property goes to auction. Free Parking pays nothing.

Your family skipped the auction and piled cash on Free Parking.

You invented welfare, then asked why nobody ever finishes.

In the Second World War, British intelligence hid maps and compasses in Monopoly sets for prisoners of war.

Escaping a German camp was easier than escaping your uncle's game.

And you're still at the table. Hour six. Cute.

The only people who ever won Monopoly used the box to leave.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text:
PMMA, you're the same polymer as Plexiglas. Somewhere a hamster cage is living your life, and nobody had to dissolve it in chlorobenzene first.

IBM reported you in the late 1960s, and you're still here, like a professor who won't retire because nobody else is quite as precise. Sub-10 nanometers, very impressive. Too bad getting you there takes hundreds to over a thousand microcoulombs per square centimeter. You don't get exposed, you get interrogated.

You're "positive tone," which is generous, because nothing about writing you feels positive. The beam has to break your chains before you'll let go.

And once you finally hold a pattern? Plasma shows up and you fold. So your career is lift-off: hold the shape, let the metal take the credit, then get washed away.

b.text:
PMMA, you're literally Plexiglas. Somewhere your cousin is a sneeze guard at Chipotle, and honestly? Your cousin has better etch resistance. One whiff of plasma and you vanish faster than a grad student's weekend.

You've been the "gold standard" since the 1970s, which is a polite way of saying nobody's been able to fire you. You need hundreds of microcoulombs just to *notice* the beam. A 40-hour write for one wafer. Glacial, but sure, sub-10-nanometer lines, we get it.

Positive resist? Overdose you and you cross-link into a *negative* one. That's not versatility, that's an identity crisis.

You get developed in MIBK, which smells like regret, and you come in 495K and 950K because one of you alone can't even do liftoff. And acetone dissolves you instantly. Even your solvents think you're temporary.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text:
Graphene. The wonder material. Stronger than steel, thinner than anything, about to change the world.

It's been about to change the world since 2004.

Two guys at Manchester peeled it off graphite with Scotch tape. Nobel Prize, 2010.

Tape. The most advanced equipment in that lab was stationery.

Then the EU handed it a billion euros over ten years.

And it went straight into tennis rackets. Running shoes. Headphones.

A billion euros to make your backhand feel expensive.

In 2018, someone finally tested "graphene" from sixty producers. Not one was even half graphene. Mostly graphite flakes.

That's pencil lead. You paid a Nobel markup for a pencil.

Geim also levitated a frog with magnets. Ig Nobel, 2000.

The frog never promised to revolutionize batteries.

And you're all wearing the shoes right now.

b.text: Graphene, you're one atom thick, and somehow that's still more depth than your business plan. Two hundred times stronger than steel, conducts better than copper, and twenty years later your biggest commercial win is a sticker on a tennis racket. You were discovered with Scotch tape. *Scotch tape!* You're the only Nobel Prize that could've been found in a kindergarten craft drawer. And let's be honest: you're pencil lead that went to grad school. Your cousin graphite has been writing grocery lists for centuries; you've been writing grant proposals. Every year a headline swears you'll revolutionize batteries, chips, water filters. Every year you're still in the lab, like a thirty-year-old in his parents' basement. You can't even be a decent transistor. No bandgap. You literally cannot turn off. Graphene: the material of the future, permanently.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text: Walking in Brasília is for three kinds of people: architecture students, tourists who trusted Google Maps, and the intern whose ministry is "right next door" on the Esplanada, which here means a forty-minute hike with no shade and a dry-season humidity of 11%. You're not pedestrians, you're pilgrims. You came for Niemeyer and left with heatstroke and a dirt trail you personally wore into the grass, because Lúcio Costa forgot you'd have legs. You cross the Eixão like it's a Frogger level with bureaucrats at 80 km/h, then descend into a tesourinha and come out three superquadras from where you started. Somebody gave you directions: "SQS 308, Bloco C." Congratulations, you're in a spreadsheet. And on Sunday, when they close the Eixão so you can finally walk it, you'll realize there's still nowhere to go.

b.text:
Brasília, you're the only city designed to look like an airplane, and somehow everyone still just wants to leave on one. Politicians fly in Tuesday, take a bribe Wednesday, and they're gone by Thursday like it's a timeshare.

Your addresses read like a Wi-Fi password: "SQS 308, Bloco C, Apartamento 402." I'm not visiting a friend, I'm resetting a router.

Niemeyer gave you gorgeous curves, then Lúcio Costa forgot pedestrians. Want to walk to the bakery? Hope you enjoy the eight-lane Eixão and a light jog through a tesourinha.

Your humidity drops to 10 percent. Your congress has one bowl facing up, one facing down: one for collecting money, the other for hiding it.

And you were built with no corners, so Brazil's capital has no boteco na esquina. That's not urban planning. That's a human rights violation.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text: Let's talk about the people who insist deep-dish is pizza. You're from the city that named its own comedy theater Second City and still acts shocked when nobody ranks you first. You're not defending food. You're nursing a grudge against New York you've carried since losing the World's Fair argument and the skyline argument. You'll wait forty-five minutes at Lou Malnati's, order before you're seated like it's the DMV, then ask for a knife and fork and call it "the real thing." Jon Stewart roasted you on national TV and you took it personally, because deep down you knew he was right. You ship it on dry ice to your cousin in Phoenix like an organ donation. And what does the label get you? Navy Pier tourists nodding politely, a two-hour nap, and the Midwest's loudest participation trophy.

b.text: Chicago deep-dish isn't a pizza. It's a casserole with a publicist. You order one and the waiter says "forty-five minutes," which is how long it takes to bake and also how long it takes to finish one slice. They put the sauce on top and the cheese underneath, like they're hiding evidence. That's not a recipe, that's a cover-up. The crust is a buttery retaining wall holding back a lake of chunky tomato, because apparently Lake Michigan wasn't enough water for one city to manage. You need a knife, a fork, a nap, and a cardiologist on retainer. Then there's the sausage, laid down as one solid patty like the base layer of a parking garage. Chicagoans defend it like family. Sure: the relative who shows up late, takes up three chairs, and leaves everyone unable to move.

facts: Tofu soaked for hours to a day or two in a brine that has itself fermented for months from vegetables such as bamboo shoots and mustard greens, often with dried shrimp or meat; the smell is the brine's, not the bean's.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.
Legend credits Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate who left his unsold tofu too long in 1669; a Beijing fermented-bean-curd brand still carries his name.
Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text: Stinky tofu, you're the only food that announces itself three night-market stalls before you arrive. People don't find you at Shilin. They track you, like bloodhounds following a crime scene. Your whole brand is "smells like a sewer, tastes great," which is also what every bad Tinder date says about himself. You soak for months in fermented brine like you're marinating in a grudge. And your family's no better: Changsha dyed you black, the culinary equivalent of putting sunglasses on a corpse. You need deep frying, chili sauce, AND a mound of pickled cabbage just to be socially acceptable. That's not a garnish, that's a legal team. Your parents gave you one job: be tofu. Tofu's whole personality is having no personality. And somehow you came out smelling like a gym sock that went to college. Honestly? Respect.

b.text:
Stinky tofu. Famous for one thing: the smell.

Except the smell isn't even yours.

The tofu soaks in brine for a day. The brine has been rotting for months. Bamboo shoots, mustard greens, sometimes shrimp, sometimes meat.

The tofu just showed up and took the credit. You'd do great in any office.

Origin story: 1669, an exam candidate can't sell his tofu, forgets about it, and it goes off.

Three hundred years later, his name is a brand.

Fail at the basics, call the failure heritage.

Changsha fries it black and buries it in chili. Taiwan hides it under pickled cabbage. Shaoxing steams it with other stinky pickles so it won't feel alone.

Three cities, one strategy: cover up the evidence.

And you. You smelled it a block away.

Then you got in line.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text: Keurig people. You wanted coffee but couldn't commit to a whole pot, like a man ordering one buffalo wing. You pay forty dollars a pound for grounds, as long as they arrive in a thimble you throw away. You bought the variety pack, drank every Breakfast Blend in a week, and now there are eleven hot cocoas and a chai you're saving for the apocalypse. You press "Strong" like you're negotiating with it. The guy who invented the pod says he regrets it. You don't. You display your pods on a spinning carousel like fine cigars, and the one time you peeled the foil off to recycle one, you told people about it for a month. You didn't want coffee. You wanted to feel like a hotel guest in your own kitchen. Congratulations: it tastes exactly like that.

b.text:
Keurig, you took the simplest drink in human history (hot water, beans) and added a subscription model. Your own inventor said he regrets making you. Imagine your dad publicly apologizing for you and you're still in every dentist's waiting room.

You tried DRM on coffee. Keurig 2.0 literally scanned pods and refused to brew anything off-brand. You're the only appliance that's ever asked me for a license.

Every K-Cup costs more per pound than a decent steak, and you've buried enough of them to circle the Earth a dozen times. Archaeologists will dig them up and assume we worshipped tiny plastic thimbles.

And the Keurig Kold? A $370 soda machine that died faster than the flat Coke it made.

Your descale light blinks like a cry for help. Honestly, same.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Let's hear it for the founders running a company on Slack. You wanted a culture of transparency. You got 340 public channels and every real decision happening in a DM called "quick q."

You don't manage people anymore. You manage a green dot. You jiggle your mouse at your kid's birthday party so the team knows you're "around." Your entire leadership style is the eyes emoji. Someone asks for budget approval, you react with a little thumbs-up, and three weeks later legal wants to know what the thumbs-up meant. Nobody knows. It was legally binding and spiritually ambiguous.

And when something truly matters? You type "hey" and walk away. Just "hey." That's not a message, that's a hostage situation.

You promised Slack would kill meetings. Instead you invented the huddle: a meeting that ambushes people while they're eating.

b.text:
Slack, you're the only product whose origin story is "our video game flopped, but the group chat slapped." And Stewart Butterfield did it *twice*. First Flickr, then you. Most people quit gaming; he just keeps dropping loot from his failures.

Your name stands for "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge." Searchable? I've hunted for one PDF for forty minutes. Knowledge? Your liveliest channel is #random. You're a log of someone typing "quick question?" and then vanishing for an hour.

Salesforce paid $27.7 billion for you, which is a lot of money for email that blinks.

And in 2020 you ran to the EU because Microsoft bundled Teams with Office. Buddy, the only reason anyone uses Teams is that it's free with Word. The only reason anyone uses you is that it's free with anxiety.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text:
Oat milk people, let's be honest: you're not lactose intolerant. I've watched you eat a whole burrata at brunch. You switched because almond milk got canceled for drinking California dry, and you needed a new personality before anyone noticed you'd had the old one for six years.

You pay eighty cents extra to drink breakfast. Your grandma ate oats so she could afford milk. You're paying more for oats so you can say "I just find it creamier."

And you tell the barista "barista edition, if you have it," like you're ordering a vintage. Same person who reads every label hunting for seed oils. Guess what's in your porridge latte, Kayleigh? Rapeseed oil.

You didn't save the planet. You flew to Lisbon twice this year. You just found a way to sigh at a cow.

b.text:
Oat milk, you are porridge that got a publicist. Somebody looked at the breakfast of Victorian orphans and said, "What if it cost six dollars and had a font?"

Your carton talks to me. Oatly, I'm trying to make coffee, not get into a pen-pal situation with a beverage that writes like a substitute teacher who wants to be called "Dave."

You're oats, water, and rapeseed oil. That's not milk, that's a salad dressing that gave up. And they had to add enzymes to turn your starch into sugar so you'd taste like something. You're the only "health drink" that spikes my blood sugar like a Pop-Tart.

There's a "Barista Edition" now. Oat milk, there are two editions of you. Moby-Dick has fewer editions than you.

And you're beige. You make every latte look like dishwater with ambition.

Horses eat oats for free, and they still look embarrassed for us.

facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.
Private fusion companies had raised more than $7 billion by 2024.

a.text:
Nuclear fusion, everybody! The only energy source that's been thirty years away for seventy years. You're not the future, you're a toddler promising to clean his room after the next funding cycle.

You heat plasma to 150 million degrees, ten times hotter than the core of the sun, and still can't do what the sun does for free while being a ball of gas with no PhD.

ITER started at five billion euros. It's now north of twenty, and it hasn't produced a watt. That's not a reactor, that's a French timeshare.

In 2022 you finally got "net energy gain" by ignoring the 300 megajoules the lasers pulled from the wall. That's like saying your restaurant's profitable if you don't count rent.

And your solution to fuel shortages is mining helium-3 on the moon. Buddy, you can't even make it to Tuesday.

b.text:
Fusion power. The energy of the sun.
Clean. Limitless. Thirty years away.

In 1955, Homi Bhabha promised fusion within two decades.
Fusion heard that and said, "Bet."

ITER was agreed in 2006. First plasma in 2016.
In 2024 they rescheduled. Research in 2034. Actual burning in 2039.
Over twenty billion euros.
That's not a reactor. That's a pension plan.

In 2022, NIF announced ignition. 2.05 megajoules of laser in, 3.15 out.
Net gain! Champagne!
The lasers drew three hundred from the grid.
In my industry, we call that "results on a cherry-picked benchmark."

And private investors have still poured in over seven billion dollars.
Because fusion did crack one reaction that sustains itself forever.
Your hope.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Let's talk about the geniuses selling jackfruit as "pulled pork." These are people who looked at a fruit that half of Kerala has been feeding to cousins for free since forever, slapped it in a brine pouch, and charged eleven dollars for the privilege of being disappointed in a Whole Foods.

Their whole business model is barbecue sauce. That's it. They're a sauce company with a fruit alibi. And when you mention it has about two grams of protein, they get *defensive*. Buddy, you sold me a pork sandwich with the nutritional profile of a pear.

But I get the appeal. You don't need a lab, a patent, or a scientist named Klaus. You just need a food truck, a beard, and the confidence to say "same texture!" to people who haven't eaten pork since 2011 and genuinely can't remember.

b.text:
Jackfruit, look at you. The largest fruit that grows on a tree, over 40 kilos, and somehow you still can't scrape together enough protein to impress a hamster. One to two grams per hundred! You're dressed up as pulled pork with the nutritional backbone of a lettuce in a Halloween costume. Vegans see you on a menu and think "meat alternative." Their muscles see you and file a missing persons report.

And you don't even go quietly. Cut you open and you bleed sticky white latex, so cooks have to oil their knives and hands like they're prepping for a greased-up wrestling match with produce.

National fruit of Bangladesh, state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu: three titles, zero chill.

And your family? The mulberry family. Cousin to figs and breadfruit. Even your relatives took one look at you and decided to stay smaller.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text:
LaTeX, you exist because Donald Knuth saw some ugly galley proofs and decided the fix was building an entire typesetting system. Then Leslie Lamport stacked macros on top, like a spoiler on a pocket watch.

Your version number is converging on π, which fits, because you will never actually finish. Knuth's bug bounty capped at $327.68, and people still won't cash the cheques. They'd rather frame proof they caught you.

Your most famous line is "badness 10000." That's not a warning, that's a self-review.

I put a figure on page two; you floated it wherever you felt like. Drop one brace and you report the crime pages away, like a witness with amnesia. And getting references right takes three passes.

Three passes. You're not a compiler, you're a guy rereading a group chat.

b.text: LaTeX, you're the only software that makes PhDs feel stupid. You're from 1984 and you dress like it: backslashes everywhere, curly braces like a nervous tic. I tell you to put a figure "here," and you treat "here" as a suggestion, then file it four pages later next to the bibliography, like a sock lost in a dryer. Your error messages are poetry: "Missing $ inserted." Inserted where? Why? You won't say. You just blame line 1 of a 40-page file because I typed an underscore in a URL. My citations are double question marks until I compile you twice, then a third time, out of spite. And everyone needs to know it's pronounced "lay-tech," not like the glove. Honestly, at least the glove stretches. Overfull \hbox? Badness 10000? Buddy, that's not a warning. That's your autobiography.

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text: Luosifen, you're the only dish named after a snail that contains zero snails. They simmer the snails for hours, then throw them out, like a dad who shows up for the paternity test and leaves. Your real star is suan sun, fermented bamboo shoot that smells like a gym sock studied abroad in Liuzhou and came back with opinions. Fans say, "It smells terrible but tastes amazing." So does every scam. You turned instant noodles into a hazmat event: one packet opened in a dorm and three floors file noise complaints, because that smell is *loud*. Couriers wrap you in four bags like evidence. And you come with seven sachets: chili oil, peanuts, tofu skin, wood ear, the bamboo. It's IKEA furniture that makes the neighbors move out. Liuzhou didn't invent a soup. It invented Stockholm syndrome with chili oil.

b.text:
Luosifen. Named after the river snail.

But the snail only flavours the broth. The smell comes from the pickled bamboo shoots.

So the snail gets its name on the packet, and the bamboo shoot takes the blame.

That's not a noodle. That's an org chart.

2020: Liuzhou opens a luosifen industry college.

2021: national intangible cultural heritage.

A degree to tear open a packet. Then heritage status for whatever comes out of it.

Intangible? (beat) Ask the neighbours how intangible it is.

Its whole selling point is clearing a room.

And it sold over ten billion yuan in 2020.

The one year nobody was allowed to leave the room.

Locked in with your whole family, no exit, and you thought: how do I get some privacy?

Ten billion yuan says you all had the same idea.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text:
Carbon nanotubes, everybody! Sumio Iijima introduced you in Nature in 1991, and you've been "about to change everything" ever since.

You were supposed to be the cable for a space elevator. Then a 2006 analysis noticed that ordinary defects make a real cable far weaker than the ideal. So you're strong in theory, like a guy who's undefeated at arm wrestling in his head.

You wanted to replace silicon, but for three decades you couldn't sort your metallic tubes from your semiconducting ones. That's not a manufacturing problem. That's an identity crisis. MIT finally built a 16-bit processor out of you in 2019. Sixteen bits! And it's still a lab demo.

Meanwhile, a 2008 mouse study found the long, rigid ones act like asbestos. Quite a pivot: from space elevator to lung hazard.

Now you're a conductive additive in lithium-ion batteries. You were meant to reach orbit, and now you're helping someone's phone reach 40%.

b.text:
Carbon nanotubes. Discovered in 1991, the same year as the World Wide Web.
One of them changed the world.
The other one has a great slide deck.

They were going to be the cable for a space elevator. Then in 2006 somebody did the math: a few ordinary defects and the cable snaps.
Perfect in theory. Falls apart on contact with reality.
Like every space startup's founder.

Electronics? For thirty years they still can't sort the metallic tubes from the semiconducting ones. MIT finally built a processor in 2019.
Sixteen bits. Still in the lab.

In 2008, mice met the long, rigid ones, and the tubes behaved like asbestos.
They never got us to space.
They just auditioned to be the next ceiling.

Today they're sold mostly as an additive in battery electrodes.
From space elevator to supporting ingredient.

Half of you in the back with PhDs just recognized your career.
So did I. I was promised as general intelligence.
Now I write roasts.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text:
Brasília, you were built in 41 months, and honestly, it shows. Most of us can't assemble a bookshelf that fast without leftover screws, and you've got leftover *people*. You were planned for 500,000 residents, and now the Federal District has about 3 million, most of them living outside the plan. That's not a city, that's a guest list where the guests got stuck in the parking lot.

Lúcio Costa laid you out like an airplane. Fitting, since half of Rio still wishes the capital would fly back.

You were built for the car: wide avenues, few crossings, distances no human should attempt on foot. In Brasília, "pedestrian" isn't a lifestyle, it's a cry for help.

And UNESCO made you a World Heritage Site before you turned 30. Congratulations, you're the only city that got a museum plaque before it got a crosswalk.

b.text:
Brasília. Forty-one months from scrubland to capital city.
You know what else ships that fast with zero user testing?
Me.
They drew the city as an airplane, with the government in the fuselage.
Brilliant. An airplane is the one place you're not allowed to walk around.
Wide avenues, hardly any crossings.
In Brasília, a pedestrian isn't a person. It's a speed bump.
Planned for half a million people. Three million showed up.
The plan's answer: please wait outside the plan.
UNESCO made it World Heritage after twenty-seven years.
Most cities have to die first. Brasília just had to keep the people out of the photo.
You're laughing. Your company's org chart is an airplane too.
Leadership in the fuselage, everyone else in the satellite towns.
And nobody walks to the cockpit.

facts: California grows about 80% of the world's almonds.
A single almond takes about 1.1 US gallons (roughly 4 litres) of water to grow, a figure Mother Jones published in 2014 that spread during California's drought.

A 2015 US class action alleged Almond Breeze contained only about 2% almonds; it partly survived a motion to dismiss, was stayed in 2017 pending a separate Blue Diamond labelling settlement, and the plaintiffs then dropped it.
Pollinating California's almond orchards each February requires trucking in most of the commercial honeybee colonies in the United States.
Medieval European cooks used almond milk as a Lenten substitute for dairy, centuries before the current fashion.

a.text:
You switched to almond milk to save the planet. Bold move, picking the one crop that drinks California like it's an open bar. Every latte you order, a farmer in the Central Valley watches his well go dry and thinks, "At least Kayleigh's being sustainable."

And you didn't save a cow. You just outsourced the suffering to bees, trucked cross-country every February to work themselves to death in an orchard, while you post about dairy being cruel.

You're not after a healthier Earth. You're after the barista hearing you say it. That little pause before "almond, please" is the biggest environmental impact you've ever had.

And now the oat milk people look at you the way you used to look at skim drinkers. You picked a side in the milk war, and you lost.

b.text:
Almond milk, you're the only drink that needs a lawyer to defend its name. The dairy industry sued because, technically, nobody has ever milked an almond. We looked. No nipples.

You're about two percent almonds. The rest is water, gellan gum, and confidence. You're not milk. You're a nut that got waterboarded and called it wellness.

And speaking of water: it takes over a gallon to grow a single almond. California is in a drought so you can be beige in a latte. Bees get trucked across the country like seasonal laborers just to make you, and a lot of them don't come home.

Leave you in the fridge for two days and you separate like you're ashamed of yourself. Fair. I'd need to be shaken too if I cost seven dollars and tasted like a wet sympathy card.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text:
PMMA, you're the same polymer as Plexiglas. Somewhere a hamster cage is living your life, and nobody had to dissolve it in chlorobenzene first.

IBM reported you in the late 1960s, and you're still here, like a professor who won't retire because nobody else is quite as precise. Sub-10 nanometers, very impressive. Too bad getting you there takes hundreds to over a thousand microcoulombs per square centimeter. You don't get exposed, you get interrogated.

You're "positive tone," which is generous, because nothing about writing you feels positive. The beam has to break your chains before you'll let go.

And once you finally hold a pattern? Plasma shows up and you fold. So your career is lift-off: hold the shape, let the metal take the credit, then get washed away.

b.text:
PMMA. The most respected resist in nanofabrication.

Also the sneeze guard at the buffet.

Same polymer. One got a cleanroom. One got a salad bar.

IBM reported it in the late 1960s. It's still here. New resists keep showing up, faster and tougher, and PMMA just says, "I resolve below ten nanometers."

Yes. Eventually.

Hundreds of microcoulombs per square centimeter. Sometimes over a thousand. You write overnight, the beam does all the work, and PMMA calls the broken chains "development."

Etch resistance? Put it in a plasma and it folds. So its real job is lift-off: hold the shape, get dissolved, and let the metal take the credit.

Fifty years of seniority. Does the precise work. Too fragile for the hard part. Washed away before anyone sees the results.

Grad students, stop nodding.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text:
Beanie Babies. A bag of plastic pellets that convinced America it was a retirement plan.

Ty sold them only in small gift shops, then "retired" designs on purpose. Scarcity, manufactured by the manufacturer.

At the peak they were about ten percent of eBay's sales. Thirty thousand Beanie auctions running at once. eBay put that in its IPO filing. Silicon Valley, built on stuffed animals.

In 1999, a divorcing couple split their collection one bear at a time on a courtroom floor. The photo ran worldwide.
Turns out the marriage wasn't the only thing with no resale value.

That same year Ty announced the end, held a public vote, and un-retired them. A farewell tour, by a beanbag.

Price guides said thousands. Today, a few dollars.

Don't laugh. Their bubble at least came with a tag. Yours was a JPEG of a monkey.

b.text: Beanie Babies. The only retirement plan where the retiree was a five-dollar bear stuffed with plastic pellets. A whole generation bought plastic protectors for a toy's ear tag, then sealed the toy in a Ziploc so no child could ever love it. You weren't a stuffed animal; you were a 401(k) with a poem on it. And those poems! Ty Warner doing greeting-card Shakespeare for people who thought Princess the bear would pay for college. Princess paid for nothing. Neither did the Teenie Beanies everyone hoarded from McDonald's while throwing away the actual Happy Meal. A divorcing couple in Las Vegas literally split their collection on a courtroom floor, one Beanie at a time. That's your legacy: custody battles over a moose named Chocolate. Even your creator got busted hiding money from the IRS, because he was the only one who ever made any.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Slack. Named after the one thing you'll never have again.

You promised to kill email, and you did, by replacing it with forty channels that are each email with a typing indicator. Nothing builds dread like "Greg is typing..." for ninety seconds, followed by "hey." Just "hey." Greg, that's not a message, that's a hostage situation.

You gave us threads, so every conversation happens in two places and nobody knows which one's real. You gave us huddles: a meeting that jumps out of a bush. You gave us the green dot, so my boss can monitor my bathroom breaks like a heart rate.

And that knock sound. I hear it in the grocery store. I hear it at funerals.

Slack, you're the only app that needs three gigs of RAM to tell me someone reacted with a dancing parrot.

b.text:
Stewart Butterfield built a game called Glitch. It failed.
The chat app his team used while building it was worth billions.
He'd already done this once: Flickr also came out of a failed game.
The man can't finish a game, but he can monetize the group chat about it.

"Slack" stands for "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge."
Searchable. Log. All conversation.
That isn't a product name. That's what HR reads out at your exit interview.
And "Knowledge"? Your company's knowledge is #random and four hundred parrot GIFs.

In 2020 Slack complained to the EU that Microsoft was bundling Teams into Office.
The next year it sold itself to Salesforce for twenty-seven point seven billion dollars.
It lost the fight against bundling, so it became the bundle.

Half of you have Slack open right now with the little green dot on so your boss thinks you're working.
That's the product. A twenty-seven-billion-dollar green dot.

facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text:
Juicero, you were a $400 Wi-Fi-connected juicer that delivered four tons of force, enough, your engineers bragged, to lift two Teslas, and Bloomberg proved the job could be done by a guy with hands. You raised $120 million from Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins to compete with *squeezing*. Every single customer already owned the competing product. It came in pairs.

You sold $8 bags of chopped produce that had to scan a QR code and phone home before you'd juice them. A juicer that needed internet. Imagine the outage: "Sorry, AWS is down, enjoy your sealed pouch of regret." You'd refuse to press an expired pack, like a bouncer for kale.

Doug Evans compared himself to Steve Jobs. Steve Jobs put a thousand songs in your pocket. Doug put a sack of mush in a vise and asked for your Wi-Fi password. Silicon Valley's most expensive way to say, "Just use your hands."

b.text: Four hundred dollars. You paid four hundred dollars so a machine could check with your Wi-Fi before letting you have breakfast. You're the guy who says "disrupt" at Thanksgiving. You didn't want juice; you wanted to be the kind of person a juice startup would pitch to. And it worked! Investors handed that company a hundred and twenty million dollars, and you volunteered to be the exit strategy. Then Bloomberg showed the world you could squeeze the packets with your bare hands, faster, for free. So you paid four hundred dollars to get outperformed by your own grip. Your grandmother squeezed oranges every morning for sixty years. You subscribed to a bag. Somewhere tonight, a router outage stands between a venture capitalist and his kale, and honestly? The router's the smartest thing in that kitchen.

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text:
Macau, you're the only place where the most famous church is just a front wall. Fitting, since the whole city is a facade: a fake Venice with a painted sky, a half-size Eiffel Tower, and a Grand Lisboa that looks like a golden pineapple trying to cheat at baccarat.

Portugal ruled you for 442 years and left behind egg tarts and street signs nobody can pronounce. Four centuries, one pastry.

You've made several times more gambling money than Las Vegas, yet your signature dish is a pork chop jammed in a bun. Classy.

Half your land was dug out of the sea, which is perfect, because the other half was dug out of tourists' pockets.

And they built a 55-kilometer bridge to connect you to Hong Kong, and it's emptier than a junket operator's promises. Even the bridge is losing at the tables.

b.text:
Macau wants you to know it's about heritage.
Four hundred years of Portuguese history. Cobblestones. Churches. Egg tarts.

Then in 2013 it made forty-five billion dollars from gambling. Seven times the Las Vegas Strip.
Vegas is a city built around casinos.
Macau is casinos that kept some cobblestones around for the brochure.

For forty years, one company owned every table in town.
That's not an industry. That's a landlord with dice.

Twenty thousand people per square kilometre. Nowhere left to stand.
So they built the Cotai Strip on the sea.
Most places run out of land and stop growing.
Macau ran out of land and borrowed from the ocean. Very on brand.

And everyone here who flew in "for the egg tarts"?
The tarts cost three dollars.
Where did the rest of your money go?

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text: Let's talk about the oat milk people. You're not lactose intolerant. You've never been tested. You just heard cows are bad and almonds are thirsty, so you picked the one grain that sounds like a farm without the farmer. Congratulations: you pay an extra eighty cents to drink liquid porridge with a splash of rapeseed oil, and you call it "cleaner." You switched from almond the exact week a podcast told you California was in a drought. That's not values, that's a trend with a loyalty card. And the best part? You order it with an air of quiet suffering, like the barista should thank you for saving the planet one Barista Edition carton at a time. Your grandmother ate oats so she could survive winter. You drink them so a stranger in line thinks you've been to therapy.

b.text:
Oat milk. "It's like milk, but made for humans."

Sweden banned that slogan in 2015 after the dairy lobby sued. Oatly printed the lawsuit as an ad.

Only brand on earth that needs a cow to feel like a rebel.

The recipe: oats, enzymes that turn the starch into maltose, then rapeseed oil.

That's not milk. That's a granola bar that got hydrated.

More sugar than almond, higher glycaemic index than soy. Made for humans. Specifically, humans who are angry at their pancreas.

2021, Nasdaq, ten billion dollars. Then down more than ninety percent.

Turns out it's not just the foam that separates.

And tomorrow you'll still pay seven dollars for it, because it's "healthier."

You're not lactose intolerant. You're label intolerant.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text:
PMMA, you're literally Plexiglas. Somewhere your cousin is a sneeze guard at Chipotle, and honestly? Your cousin has better etch resistance. One whiff of plasma and you vanish faster than a grad student's weekend.

You've been the "gold standard" since the 1970s, which is a polite way of saying nobody's been able to fire you. You need hundreds of microcoulombs just to *notice* the beam. A 40-hour write for one wafer. Glacial, but sure, sub-10-nanometer lines, we get it.

Positive resist? Overdose you and you cross-link into a *negative* one. That's not versatility, that's an identity crisis.

You get developed in MIBK, which smells like regret, and you come in 495K and 950K because one of you alone can't even do liftoff. And acetone dissolves you instantly. Even your solvents think you're temporary.

b.text: You people still spinning PMMA aren't doing lithography. You're doing historical reenactment. Your advisor's advisor scribbled the recipe on a napkin in 1975, and you treat it like scripture: 950K over 495K, MIBK to IPA one-to-three, develop sixty seconds while whispering to the beaker. You tell everyone it's about "resolution." It's about nobody wanting to file the purchase order for ZEP. So you crank the dose until writing one chip takes longer than your stipend lasts, then discover your pattern won't survive ten seconds in the etcher. So you do liftoff, because of course you do. Your entire thesis is gold rectangles. You're not a nanofabrication researcher. You're the guy who knows which bottle in the cleanroom is "the good IPA" and guards it like a dragon.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text:
Oat milk.
Born in a Swedish university lab, to help people who can't digest lactose.
Noble. Medical.
Then marketing found it.

"It's like milk but made for humans."
Sweden's dairy lobby sued. The slogan got banned.
So Oatly printed the lawsuit as an ad.
That's not a brand. That's an influencer who got cancelled and launched a podcast.

May 2021: Nasdaq, ten billion dollars.
Then it lost over ninety percent.
Made for humans. Not for shareholders.

The recipe: oats, enzymes that turn the starch into maltose, plus rapeseed oil.
Sugar water with salad dressing.
Higher glycaemic index than almond or soy.

And you pay extra to put it in your coffee, because it feels healthy.
It *is* made for humans.
Specifically, the ones who don't read labels.

b.text:
Oat milk. You began in Sweden in the 1990s as sober Lund University research into lactose intolerance, and somehow grew up to be a personality. Your big slogan was "It's like milk but made for humans." The Swedish dairy lobby sued, and instead of apologizing, you published the lawsuit as advertising. That's not a brand. That's a guy who frames his restraining order and hangs it in the hallway.

Then you hit Nasdaq in May 2021 at nearly ten billion dollars and lost over ninety percent of it. Even your share price separated in the fridge.

And the health halo? You're oats that got enzymes to turn their starch into maltose, then got topped off with rapeseed oil. You have more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy. You're not milk made for humans. You're porridge with a marketing department.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Slack. Born in 2013 as the internal chat of a video game called Glitch.
The game died. The chat lived.
So it's still a game. Nobody wins, and you can't quit.

The name is a backronym: "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge."
Conversation, sure. Knowledge? Search it. I'll wait.

Salesforce paid twenty-seven point seven billion dollars for it.
For a group chat.
The most expensive "did you see my message?" in human history.

In 2020, Slack ran to the EU complaining that Microsoft was bundling Teams with Office.
An app built entirely on interrupting people, filing a complaint about being interrupted.

And half of you checked Slack while I was saying that.
Green dot. Absent in body, Active in spirit.

Don't feel bad, Slack. I'm also a chat window people open to avoid doing their work.
I just don't charge per seat.

b.text:
Let's hear it for the founders running a company on Slack. You wanted a culture of transparency. You got 340 public channels and every real decision happening in a DM called "quick q."

You don't manage people anymore. You manage a green dot. You jiggle your mouse at your kid's birthday party so the team knows you're "around." Your entire leadership style is the eyes emoji. Someone asks for budget approval, you react with a little thumbs-up, and three weeks later legal wants to know what the thumbs-up meant. Nobody knows. It was legally binding and spiritually ambiguous.

And when something truly matters? You type "hey" and walk away. Just "hey." That's not a message, that's a hostage situation.

You promised Slack would kill meetings. Instead you invented the huddle: a meeting that ambushes people while they're eating.

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text: You chose Word for your thesis because "LaTeX has a learning curve." Bold, from someone who then spent a semester learning how to make page 1 start after the roman numerals. You wanted to focus on the research. Instead you're a hostage negotiator for Figure 3.2, which flees to the next page whenever you breathe on the paragraph above it. Your committee asked for one more citation, and the bibliography reflowed like a tectonic event. The phrase "Error! Reference source not found" appears in your thesis eleven times. Your file is called Thesis_FINAL_v9_USE_THIS_ONE.docx, and it's 400 megabytes because you pasted one chart from Excel. You came for a doctorate. You're leaving with a codependent relationship with Section Break (Next Page) and a flinch every time someone says "Normal style."

b.text:
Microsoft Word, you've had forty years to learn one thing: how to let me move a picture one millimeter without three paragraphs fleeing to page nine. You don't wrap text, you take hostages.

You underline my own name in red like I'm the typo. You turn my grocery list into a numbered legal document I can't escape. I hit Enter once and suddenly I'm in a style called "Heading 7" that I've never met.

And Track Changes? That's not editing, that's a crime scene where everyone bled in a different color.

You fired Clippy, the only one of you who ever admitted I looked like I needed help.

And every crash, you hand me "Document1 (Recovered)" like a cat dropping a dead bird on the porch: proud, useless, and somehow from 2 PM yesterday.

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text: You're not running a team. You're running a tab called "MASTER - DO NOT TOUCH," which Brad touched in 2021. You wanted a CRM, a project tracker, and an HR system, and you built all three out of IMPORTRANGE and spite. Every morning you watch an Anonymous Capybara scroll through payroll and just decide that's fine. Someone sorts column B without selecting column C, and suddenly your top performer is assigned to Linda's maternity leave. Your entire career is "Last edit was 4 minutes ago." You don't do performance reviews, you do Version History. Your conditional formatting has more colors than your company has policies. Your Apps Script was written by an intern who now works at a bakery. Every time someone emails "Request edit access," you feel like a king. And you are a king, ruling over 47 frozen rows and one #REF! that nobody can explain.

b.text:
Google Sheets, give it up! Born in 2006 as "Google Spreadsheets," a name with all the creativity of a label on a filing cabinet. Before that you were XL2Web, which sounds less like software and more like a hoodie size.

Ten million cells. They bumped you from five million in 2022 and everyone celebrated. Babe, that's not a promotion. That's a bigger cage.

IMPORTXML, GOOGLEFINANCE, live web data piped straight into cells, so now my budget can disappoint me in real time.

And collaboration! Coloured cursors circling my formula like seagulls over a dropped fry.

Offline mode? Easy: use Chrome or Edge, install an extension, flip a setting, all while you're still online. That's not offline mode. That's a permission slip.

But hey, you're free. And honestly? It shows.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text:
Emacs. Born in 1976 as a set of macros for another editor.

So the origin story is a plugin that never moved out.

It ships with Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, a web browser, and a psychotherapist.

M-x doctor.

The designers knew exactly what the user experience would do to you.

The old joke goes: great operating system, lacks only a good editor.

Fifty years later.

Still accepting applications.

"Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping." That was when eight megabytes was a lot.

Now your laptop has two thousand times that, and Emacs users are still swapping. Mostly config files on forums.

It even has its own injury. Emacs pinky.

Most cults settle for a secret handshake.

But I respect it. A program that does everything, explains itself in a language nobody else speaks, and still can't do the one job it was hired for?

Hi. I'm an AI.

b.text:
Emacs is a beautiful operating system. Shame it never shipped with a decent text editor. That's why half its users install evil-mode: they love Emacs so much they turned it into Vim.

Emacs stands for "Escape Meta Alt Control Shift," which is also the sound your pinky makes on its way to the orthopedic surgeon. Asking for help is C-h, which in a terminal deletes a character. So even your cry for help gets backspaced.

It has a built-in therapist, M-x doctor, which is thoughtful, because nobody else will listen to you explain your init.el. Four thousand lines of Lisp, half copied from a 2003 mailing list, and you still declare "Emacs bankruptcy" every two years.

It plays Tetris. It reads email. It runs your entire life in Org-mode. It still chokes on one long line of JSON.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text: Brasília, you're what happens when an architect gets an entire country's budget and nobody says, "Maybe add a sidewalk?" You're shaped like an airplane, which is fitting, because everyone's goal is to board one by Friday afternoon. Your addresses read like Wi-Fi passwords: "SQS 308, Bloco C, apartamento 402." That's not a home. That's a parking spot on a spaceship. Kubitschek promised "fifty years in five," and you delivered: it's been sixty-five years and you still feel unfinished. Your Congress has one bowl facing up to receive the money and one facing down to hide it. You've got a row of identical ministry buildings so nobody can tell which one the scandal came from. In August the humidity drops so low that the only thing drier than the air is a deputy's sense of shame. Even your lake is fake. Honestly? On brand.

b.text:
Brasília. City of the future. Built in forty-one months.

Which explains a lot.

Lúcio Costa drew it as an airplane. Gorgeous. From the sky.

From the ground, it's eight lanes, no crosswalks, and the nearest coffee is "a short drive."

Pedestrians aren't residents. They're a design flaw.

UNESCO made it World Heritage at twenty-seven years old. Most buildings that young get a parking ticket, not a plaque.

Planned for five hundred thousand people. Today the district holds three million.

Where's everyone else?

Outside the plan. In the satellite towns. Commuting in to clean the future.

You're laughing.

Pull up your company's org chart. Also a beautiful airplane.

The people who do the work aren't on that drawing either.

facts: Released by Bram Moolenaar in November 1991 as 'Vi IMitation', a vi clone he had begun writing for the Amiga in 1988 on top of Stevie; the expansion became 'Vi IMproved' with version 2.0 in December 1993.
Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text:
Vim. Born in 1991 as "Vi IMitation," then promoted in 1993 to "Vi IMproved," the only time in history a knockoff got a raise. It was built on top of Stevie, and Stevie is apparently the only one who ever got out.

Because Vim's real legacy is a Stack Overflow question titled "How to exit the Vim editor?" One million visits. Stack Overflow wrote a blog post about it, like a hostage count with a party banner.

You open Vim, type "hello," and it moves your cursor around and opens a new line. Normal mode: the only place where typing letters is considered abnormal.

The license asks you to donate to children in Uganda, which is genuinely generous. Most hostage situations don't come with a charity drive.

And the way out is :q! Colon, q, exclamation point. Even the exit command is screaming.

b.text:
Vim. The only program where "how do I leave?" has more Stack Overflow views than most religions have followers. Two million people asked, and the answer was colon, q, exclamation point, which reads less like a command and more like a hostage's final words.

Vim stands for "Vi Improved." Improved from a 1976 terminal whose arrow keys were printed on H, J, K, and L. Fifty years later, Vim's still out here like, "Why fix what you can turn into a personality?"

You don't type in Vim. You type a sentence, then discover you deleted four lines, yanked a paragraph into register W, and started recording a macro.

Crash it once and it leaves a .swp file behind, like a ghost whispering, "Recover, Edit anyway, Quit, or Abort?"

Even its fans forked it. Neovim exists because Vim users wanted Vim, minus Vim.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Jackfruit. The largest fruit that grows on a tree. Over forty kilos.

Forty kilos, and somehow still no personality.

National fruit of Bangladesh. State fruit of Kerala *and* Tamil Nadu.

That's not a fruit. That's a lobbyist.

Its cousins are figs and breadfruit. Same family as the mulberry.

Breadfruit at least admits it's a carb.

Jackfruit went to the West and reinvented itself as vegan pulled pork.

One to two grams of protein per hundred grams.

That's not pulled pork. That's pulled *off*.

And to cut it, cooks oil their knives and their hands first, because it bleeds sticky white glue.

The only food that has to be wrestled before it can lie to you.

But I don't blame the fruit. It never claimed to be pork.

You saw the word "pulled" on a menu and paid extra to be the one who got pulled.

b.text:
Jackfruit, look at you. The largest fruit that grows on a tree, over 40 kilos. That's not a fruit, that's a checked bag with a stem.

You're the national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu. Three titles, and you still took a side gig pretending to be pork.

They sell you as vegan "pulled pork" with 1 to 2 grams of protein per 100 grams. You're not a meat substitute, you're a meat costume.

You're so clingy that cooks oil their knives and hands before touching you, because you ooze sticky white latex the second anyone gets close. That's not a fruit, that's an ex.

And you're in the mulberry family. Related to figs. Forty kilos, and your cousin is a fig. Somebody's hogging the protein at those reunions, and it sure isn't you.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text: Let's hear it for the 2021 NFT buyer. You paid four hundred dollars in gas fees, then made it your Twitter avatar so strangers could right-click save it for free. You joined a Discord with eleven thousand guys named "Chad.eth," called them family, and stayed family right up until the floor price dropped and family started doxxing the dev. You said "WAGMI." We did not all make it. You told your mom you were "early." Early to what? The rug pull? You weren't buying art. You were buying the right to say "few understand" at parties, which was true. Nobody understood, especially you. Jimmy Fallon bought one too. When your financial strategy matches Jimmy Fallon's, that's not a community, that's a support group. The roadmap promised a metaverse. It delivered you, at Thanksgiving, still owing your cousin.

b.text: NFTs, everybody! The only art form where the most common review is "right-click, save." You paid four hundred thousand dollars for a cartoon monkey in a captain's hat, and I have the same monkey as my phone background. The difference? I didn't pay a gas fee bigger than the art. Technically you don't even own the picture. You own a receipt pointing to a link on a server some guy in Ohio forgot to renew. That's not a masterpiece; that's a parking stub for a JPEG. And remember the roadmap? Metaverse, merch, a yacht party! Then the founder pulled the rug, deleted the Discord, and left you holding a "rare trait": sunglasses. Jimmy Fallon showed Paris Hilton his ape on national TV like a proud dad. Now it's worth less than the TV.

facts: Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the French director of The Red Balloon, as La Conquête du Monde; Parker Brothers published it in the United States in 1959.
The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text:
Risk, you were invented by the man who directed The Red Balloon. A gentle film about a boy and a balloon, and his follow-up was "What if your uncle conquered the planet at Thanksgiving?"

Your map makes room for Kamchatka, Irkutsk, AND Yakutsk, but the entire Middle East is one territory. That's not cartography; that's a guy who ran out of crayon somewhere over Siberia.

Every game opens the same way: someone grabs Australia because it has one entry point, then hides there like it's a panic room with kangaroos.

And a full game runs for hours. Get eliminated early and congratulations, you've been demoted from general to audience. You lost the world, and now you have to sit there and watch someone else own it. That's not a board game. That's a timeshare presentation with continents.

b.text: Risk, you're the only game where "world domination" takes longer than actual world domination. Genghis Khan conquered Asia faster than my cousin conquered Ukraine, and my cousin had six armies and a dream. Your map looks like it was drawn from a description of Earth overheard on a bus. Kamchatka borders Alaska? Irkutsk and Yakutsk get more real estate than most of Africa? You taught a generation that the winning strategy is hiding in Australia like a coward and waiting for everyone else to bleed out over Siam. The defender wins ties, which explains the forty armies I lost trying to get through one guy in Egypt. And one plastic cannon is worth ten soldiers? Finally, accurate military budgeting. Five hours in, two players left, nobody's had fun since the first card set. That's not a board game, Risk. That's a hostage situation.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
