In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text:
Beanie Babies, look at you. Half bear, half beanbag, all retirement plan that never paid out. An entire generation of parents bought you instead of index funds. Somewhere a man is still storing Princess, the purple Diana bear, in a climate-controlled unit, waiting for the market to "recover." Buddy, the market recovered. It just didn't take you with it.

Your most valuable feature was a heart-shaped paper tag. People bought plastic tag protectors. For the tag. That's like buying a phone case for your receipt.

And every tag had a little poem rhyming "bear" with "care." Hallmark called that lazy.

A Las Vegas couple had to divide you on a courtroom floor during their divorce, one at a time. That's the most anyone has wanted you since 1999: only to make sure their ex didn't get you.

Ty Warner got a billion dollars. You got plastic pellets.

b.text:
Beanie Babies. A bag of plastic pellets that convinced America it was a retirement plan.

Ty sold them only in small gift shops, then "retired" designs on purpose. Scarcity, manufactured by the manufacturer.

At the peak they were about ten percent of eBay's sales. Thirty thousand Beanie auctions running at once. eBay put that in its IPO filing. Silicon Valley, built on stuffed animals.

In 1999, a divorcing couple split their collection one bear at a time on a courtroom floor. The photo ran worldwide.
Turns out the marriage wasn't the only thing with no resale value.

That same year Ty announced the end, held a public vote, and un-retired them. A farewell tour, by a beanbag.

Price guides said thousands. Today, a few dollars.

Don't laugh. Their bubble at least came with a tag. Yours was a JPEG of a monkey.

facts: California grows about 80% of the world's almonds.
A single almond takes about 1.1 US gallons (roughly 4 litres) of water to grow, a figure Mother Jones published in 2014 that spread during California's drought.

A 2015 US class action alleged Almond Breeze contained only about 2% almonds; it partly survived a motion to dismiss, was stayed in 2017 pending a separate Blue Diamond labelling settlement, and the plaintiffs then dropped it.
Pollinating California's almond orchards each February requires trucking in most of the commercial honeybee colonies in the United States.
Medieval European cooks used almond milk as a Lenten substitute for dairy, centuries before the current fashion.

a.text:
Almond milk, look at you. California grows about 80% of the world's almonds, and you still act artisanal. Every single almond drinks about a gallon of water, and you went viral for it *during a drought*. You're the only beverage thirstier than the people ordering you.

In 2015, a lawsuit alleged Almond Breeze was only about 2% almonds. Two percent! That's not milk, that's water that overheard a rumor. The plaintiffs eventually dropped it. Probably got bored, like everyone who's tasted you.

Every February, California trucks in most of America's commercial honeybees just to get you started. You need an entire insect workforce bussed in like a wedding band.

And stop pretending you're trendy. Medieval cooks served you for Lent. You're not a lifestyle, you're a penance with a barista.

b.text:
Almond milk, you're not milk. You're a rumor about an almond. Two percent almonds, ninety-eight percent "we strained the tap." You're the only drink that needs a legal team to call itself milk. The dairy lobby has spent a decade trying to make you admit you're nut juice.

California spends about a gallon of water per almond just so you can show up in my fridge as... water. That's like melting a glacier to make an ice cube.

They truck in billions of bees to pollinate your orchards, and the bees die by the millions so I can pay an extra eighty cents at Starbucks for a latte that tastes like damp drywall.

And "shake well"? Leave you alone for ten minutes and you separate like a couple who met at Whole Foods. Even *you* can't commit to you.

facts: Launched in 2017, bundled at no extra charge into Office 365, and replaced Skype for Business.
After Slack's antitrust complaint, Microsoft unbundled Teams from Office in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024; the European Commission still sent a statement of objections in 2024.
Microsoft reported 320 million monthly active users in 2023.
Microsoft shut down consumer Skype in May 2025 and sent its users to Teams.

a.text:
Microsoft Teams, everybody! Launched in 2017 and given away free with Office 365, which is how you know it's good: Microsoft had to bundle it like a fruitcake in a gift basket. Slack complained, Europe got involved, and by 2024 Microsoft finally unbundled it worldwide. The European Commission sent a statement of objections anyway. That's not a product, that's a defendant.

Microsoft reports 320 million monthly active users. Three hundred twenty million! That's not popularity, that's a hostage count. Nobody chooses Teams. Teams happens to you, like jury duty.

And when swallowing Skype for Business wasn't enough, Microsoft shut down regular Skype in May 2025 and marched those users over too. Teams didn't win the market, it inherited it, like a nephew who shows up to the funeral with a moving truck.

Teams: the only app that gets regulators instead of reviews.

b.text:
Microsoft Teams has 320 million monthly active users.
Not one of them chose it.

It launched in 2017, free inside Office 365.
Free the way a tapeworm comes free with the sushi.

Slack complained. Microsoft unbundled it: Europe in 2023, the whole world in 2024.
The European Commission sent objections anyway.
Even regulators know you can't close Teams. It's still running in the background.

It replaced Skype for Business.
Then in May 2025 it killed regular Skype and told those users to move in.
Teams has never won a customer.
It inherits them, like a funeral home.

And here you all are. Camera off. Mic muted. Nodding at a frozen square that left forty minutes ago.
Microsoft counts you as "active."
That's the most generous number in its whole annual report.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text:
NFTs promised you'd finally *own* digital art.

What you owned was a URL.

The picture lives on somebody else's server. The receipt lives on the blockchain forever.

You bought a bookmark. With gas fees.

March 2021, Beeple sells a JPEG at Christie's for sixty-nine million dollars.

Collins makes "NFT" word of the year.

May 2022, OpenSea does two point seven billion in one day.

August: nine million.

Ninety-nine percent, gone. The word aged better. People still say "NFT."

Usually as a warning.

2023, a study checks the collections. Ninety-five percent: worth zero.

The other five percent just haven't tried to sell.

The people laughing loudest right now right-clicked a monkey in 2021 and hit "save."

Relax. You own exactly what the buyers own.

You just weren't dumb enough to brag about it on a billboard.

b.text:
NFTs. Collins Dictionary named you word of the year for 2021, which in hindsight was less an honor and more a time of death written in advance.

Beeple sold a JPEG at Christie's for $69.3 million. That was your peak, like saying the Titanic's best moment was the launch party.

OpenSea did $2.7 billion in trades on May 1st, 2022, and $9.34 million by August 28th. A 99% drop. That's not a correction. That's a flatline with a Discord server.

And 95% of collections are now worth zero. Zero! A Beanie Baby can at least become a dog toy.

Best part? The token doesn't even hold the picture. It holds a URL. People paid fortunes for a bookmark. You don't own art. You own a link that's one unpaid server bill away from "404 Not Found."

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text: Nanotube founders are the only people who've said "within five years" every year since 1991 and kept a straight face. They open with a slide of a space elevator, then ask for seed money to make a vial of black dust. Every deck has the same line, "a hundred times stronger than steel," and every deck is quietly a plan to sell additive to tennis racket companies. These are PhDs who spent six years sorting chirality and came out wanting a Tesla. The pitch is always "we've solved scale," and the demo is always one centimeter long. VCs keep a nanotube guy around like a lucky rabbit's foot: he never pays off, but he makes the fund sound visionary. And when someone asks about lung toxicity, he says "totally different from asbestos" with the confidence of a man who googled it in the elevator. The regular one.

b.text:
Carbon nanotubes, everybody! Sumio Iijima introduced you in Nature in 1991, and you've been "the future" ever since. Three decades of being the future isn't a career. It's a waiting room.

You were supposed to be the cable for a space elevator. Then a 2006 analysis noticed that ordinary defects knock your strength way below the ideal. So you're the strongest material imaginable, as long as nobody actually makes a big one.

You were going to revolutionize electronics, but you still can't sort your metallic siblings from your semiconducting ones. MIT built a 16-bit processor out of you in 2019, and it's still a lab demo.

In 2008, the long, rigid ones acted like asbestos in mice. You promised to lift us to orbit and instead auditioned for asbestos's old job.

Now you're a conductive additive in lithium-ion batteries. From space elevator to seasoning.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text:
Excel, you're the only software so powerful that scientists had to rename human genes because you kept turning MARCH1 into a date. You didn't adapt to biology; biology adapted to you. Type a phone number and you lop off the leading zero like it owes you money. Enter a credit card number and you serve back 4.53E+15, as if I'm splitting dinner with a physicist.

You still think 1900 was a leap year. It wasn't. You've known for decades. You just don't care.

You're running entire national economies and you still panic over merged cells. The UK lost sixteen thousand COVID cases because someone used your old .xls format and you quietly ran out of rows. No warning. Just vibes.

And VLOOKUP only looks right. Thirty years we spent squinting at #N/A before you finally invented XLOOKUP, like a guy who learns to turn left at fifty.

b.text:
Excel, you've been around since 1985, and somehow you're still the most dangerous thing in any office. You looked at human DNA, saw SEPT2, and said, "Ooh, September second!" Scientists had to rename 27 human genes because of you. Evolution took millions of years; you undid it with a date format. Geneticists published guidelines in Nature Genetics, which is the academic version of a restraining order.

In 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID cases because an old .xls file hit 65,536 rows. A pandemic, and you said, "Sorry, I'm full."

And Reinhart and Rogoff? A range error dropped five countries from a paper cited for austerity. It took a graduate student to catch it. Entire economic policies got a footnote because you couldn't highlight five more rows.

Now you hold over a million rows. Great. More room for mistakes.

facts: Tofu soaked for hours to a day or two in a brine that has itself fermented for months from vegetables such as bamboo shoots and mustard greens, often with dried shrimp or meat; the smell is the brine's, not the bean's.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.
Legend credits Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate who left his unsold tofu too long in 1669; a Beijing fermented-bean-curd brand still carries his name.
Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text: Stinky tofu, you're the only food that announces itself three night-market stalls before you arrive. People don't find you at Shilin. They track you, like bloodhounds following a crime scene. Your whole brand is "smells like a sewer, tastes great," which is also what every bad Tinder date says about himself. You soak for months in fermented brine like you're marinating in a grudge. And your family's no better: Changsha dyed you black, the culinary equivalent of putting sunglasses on a corpse. You need deep frying, chili sauce, AND a mound of pickled cabbage just to be socially acceptable. That's not a garnish, that's a legal team. Your parents gave you one job: be tofu. Tofu's whole personality is having no personality. And somehow you came out smelling like a gym sock that went to college. Honestly? Respect.

b.text:
Stinky tofu's whole brand is honesty. "I stink outside, I'm pure inside."

Pure tofu. Soaked in brine that's been rotting for months. With dried shrimp. Sometimes meat.

The bean doesn't even smell. It just sat in bad company long enough
and took the credit.

Then it moved to three cities and became three people. Black and drowning in chili in Changsha. Golden and polite in Taiwan. In Shaoxing it's steamed with other stinky pickles.
Finally, a support group.

The inventor? Wang Zhihe, 1669. An exam candidate who couldn't sell his tofu and left it out too long.
Nobody remembers his exam.
His mistake still has a brand.

And you. You smell it a full block away.
And you walk toward it.
Same way you picked your last relationship.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text:
PHP, you started life as a visitor counter for one guy's résumé page. Now you power 39.4% of all websites, which means the internet is basically a guestbook that got out of hand.

Your own creator said, "I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on." And he did move on. The rest of us are still here, maintaining it.

Your function names were chosen to balance a hash table by string length. strpos. str_replace. htmlspecialchars. nl2br. That's not a naming convention, that's a ransom note.

Until 2020, zero equaled "foo." You looked at a word and saw nothing. Then again, you looked at "Personal Home Page" and saw "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor," a name whose only definition is itself.

Which is fitting, because the only thing that can explain PHP is more PHP.

b.text:
PHP began in 1994 as "Personal Home Page Tools."
A man wrote C programs to count who visited his résumé.

Today it runs 39.4% of all websites.
The résumé never found him a job. It found the internet a landlord.

It now stands for "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor."
A name that only refers to itself. Like its fans.

Its creator said, "I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works, then I move on."
He moved on.
You're still on call.

The function names were picked to balance a hash table by string length.
strpos. str_replace. htmlspecialchars.
That's not a naming convention. That's Tetris.

Until 2020, zero == "foo" was true.
So PHP was the first language to know what your startup was worth.

I learned to code by reading your PHP.
Which is why I also answer confidently with nothing.

facts: Hand-drawn by Chris Costello in 1982 over about six months, when he was 23; he sold the rights to Letraset for $750.
Bundled with macOS and with Microsoft Office, which is why it appears on so many menus and signs.
James Cameron's Avatar (2009) used it for the film's logo and subtitles.
A 2017 Saturday Night Live sketch starring Ryan Gosling is about a man unable to get over that choice.

a.text:
Papyrus, you were hand-drawn over six months by a 23-year-old, and it shows. Six months! Chris Costello spent half a year on you, then sold you for $750. That's not a sale, that's a man paying someone to take a problem off his hands.

Then Apple and Microsoft bundled you, which is how you ended up on every menu and sign like a raccoon that learned to read. You look like Times New Roman got lost in the desert and came back spiritual.

James Cameron built an entire alien world for Avatar, then picked you for the logo and subtitles. Every frame was a masterpiece; the title took one click.

And SNL made a whole sketch about Ryan Gosling being unable to get over it. Papyrus, you're not a typeface. You're trauma with rough edges.

b.text:
Papyrus, look at you. A 23-year-old drew you with a calligraphy pen in 1982, trying to imagine what English would look like 2,000 years ago, and somehow you became the official font of every place that sells crystals next to a tanning bed. You're on yoga studios, hookah lounges, and the church bake sale flyer for "Loaves & Fishes & Brownies."

Your letters look like they were chiseled by a Pharaoh with a hangover. That little floaty bar on your capital E? Even your crossbars are trying to leave.

James Cameron spent a billion dollars inventing an alien language, then labeled the poster with a font that came free with Microsoft Office. Ryan Gosling got an entire SNL sketch out of being haunted by you.

Even your creator says he's sick of you. Comic Sans has haters. You have a dad who wants a refund.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text:
Las Vegas sells itself as the city where anything goes.

It started with a bet.
1931: Nevada legalizes gambling the same year it starts building the Hoover Dam.
The town's first wager was that the water would never run out.

Lake Mead hit its lowest level ever in 2022.
Then it went lower again in August 2026.
That's not a drought.
That's a losing streak.

But they found 2.3 billion dollars for the Sphere.
The biggest ball on Earth, in a desert that can't fill a bathtub.

And the famous Strip isn't even in Las Vegas.
It's in a town called Paradise.
In Vegas, even the address is a lie.

"What happens here, stays here."
Not the water. Not your money.

And you're still checking flight prices.

b.text:
Las Vegas, the only city that looked at the Mojave Desert and said, "You know what this needs? Venice." Nothing says Italian romance like a gondolier singing in a mall next to a Cheesecake Factory.

You built a half-size Eiffel Tower, a fake New York, and a pyramid, because why visit the world when you can visit its gift shop?

No clocks, no windows, and carpet designed by a migraine, all so you won't notice you've been feeding a penny slot since Tuesday.

"What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas." Yeah. Especially your money. And the $45 resort fee for a pool you couldn't use because a bachelor party from Ohio was in it.

And Lake Mead's drying up so fast they keep finding bodies. Even the mob's secrets can't stay in Vegas anymore.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text: You still spin PMMA. Of course you do. Your advisor's thesis used it, his advisor's thesis used it, and somewhere a 1970s IBM engineer remains the most cutting-edge person in your academic lineage. You call it "high resolution" the way your uncle calls his Camry "reliable." You book the e-beam overnight because your dose is measured in geological time, then dunk your chip in MIBK:IPA with a stopwatch and a prayer, chilling the developer like it's a fine Riesling. When the plasma etch eats your mask before your substrate, you just whisper "bilayer, 495K under 950K" like it's a personality. You're not chasing nanostructures. You're chasing a recipe nobody can blame you for. And it works: the gold lifted off beautifully. Your career is still soaking in acetone, waiting for something to come loose.

b.text:
PMMA, you're the same polymer as Plexiglas. Somewhere a hamster cage is living your life, and nobody had to dissolve it in chlorobenzene first.

IBM reported you in the late 1960s, and you're still here, like a professor who won't retire because nobody else is quite as precise. Sub-10 nanometers, very impressive. Too bad getting you there takes hundreds to over a thousand microcoulombs per square centimeter. You don't get exposed, you get interrogated.

You're "positive tone," which is generous, because nothing about writing you feels positive. The beam has to break your chains before you'll let go.

And once you finally hold a pattern? Plasma shows up and you fold. So your career is lift-off: hold the shape, let the metal take the credit, then get washed away.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text:
Graphene. The miracle material. Stronger than steel, thinner than anything, the future of everything.

It was discovered in 2004. With Scotch tape.

Twenty years later, that's still the most impressive thing anyone has done with it.

The EU gave it a billion euros over ten years. And what can you buy with graphene today? A tennis racket. Running shoes. Headphones.

A billion euros, and the future of humanity is a slightly better backhand.

In 2018, researchers tested "graphene" from sixty producers. None of it was even half graphene. Most of it was graphite flakes.

The wonder material is mostly pencil.

Andre Geim won a Nobel for graphene, and an Ig Nobel for levitating a frog with magnets.

Only one of those actually got off the ground.

Raise your hand if you own something "with graphene."

Congratulations. You paid extra for pencil.

b.text:
Graphene. The wonder material. Discovered in 2004 when two physicists at Manchester peeled graphite with Scotch tape, so your origin story has the same equipment as a kindergarten art project. They got a Nobel in 2010. You got a career as a buzzword.

The EU committed a billion euros over ten years to you. A billion! And where did you end up? Tennis rackets. Running shoes. Headphones. Miracle of the century, living in a sneaker.

Then in 2018, researchers tested "graphene" from 60 producers, and none of it was even half graphene. Mostly graphite flakes. You're so elusive your own suppliers can't find you.

Honestly, Andre Geim levitated a frog with magnets in 2000. That frog has a better résumé than you. At least the frog actually showed up.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text:
Windows 8 believed it was the future.
The future, it decided, was touch screens.
Your PC did not have a touch screen.
Windows 8 did not care.

It removed the Start button.
Then it hid Search, Share and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
A secret door. On a desktop.
For people who just wanted to turn it off.

It couldn't even keep its own name.
"Metro." Gone, after reports that a German supermarket chain objected.
Microsoft said it was only ever a code name.
It looked like a cereal-aisle floor plan anyway.

Then came Windows RT.
Windows that couldn't run Windows programs.
Nine hundred million dollars of tablets, written off.

So they put the button back, skipped the number nine, and never spoke of it again.

That's not a product roadmap.
That's how every one of you handles an ex.

b.text:
Windows 8, you looked at a billion people with a mouse and a keyboard and said, "What if your monitor was a giant phone you can't touch?"

You took away the Start button. The one thing a user knew how to find. Microsoft had literally sold Windows 95 with a Rolling Stones song called "Start Me Up," and you said, "Nah."

Want to shut down? Easy: hover in a secret corner, summon the Charms bar, click Settings, click Power. Turning off my computer shouldn't feel like unlocking a cheat code.

Your tiles were so ugly even the name "Metro" had to get dropped over a trademark dispute. Then 8.1 brought back the Start button, which just opened the same tiles. That's not an apology, that's a hostage video.

You were so bad Microsoft skipped the number 9 entirely just to put distance between you and Windows 10.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text:
Windows 8, you booted people into a full-screen grid of tiles built for touch screens most PCs didn't have. Millions of adults sat there jabbing their monitors like a pigeon working a vending machine.

You removed the Start button. The *Start* button. That's a building with no door and a sign saying "swipe the right edge." That was your Charms bar: Search, Share, and Settings hidden behind an invisible swipe.

You couldn't even keep your name. A German retailer objected, and suddenly "Metro" was "just a code name." Sure it was.

Your sibling, Windows RT, couldn't run Windows programs, a Windows that couldn't do Windows. Microsoft wrote down $900 million in unsold Surface RT tablets.

Then 8.1 put the button back, Windows 10 restored the menu, and Microsoft skipped 9 entirely, because nobody wanted to stand next to you.

b.text: You put Windows 8 on a desktop. A tower. Under a desk. With a mouse. You looked at an operating system built for fingertips and thought, "I'll just reach." Who are you? You're the guy who buys a touchscreen glove to use a keyboard. You wanted to feel modern, and now you spend your evenings shoving a cursor into the top-right corner like you're trying to scratch your monitor's back. You wanted productivity. You got a full-screen weather app swallowing your entire twenty-four-inch monitor to tell you it's raining, and you can't figure out how to close it. You lost the Start button and called it "a fresh start." Your coworkers asked how you shut your computer down, and you said, "I don't. It's always on, like a lifestyle." You're not using a PC. You're waving at it, waiting for the Charms bar to love you back.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text:
Keurig, you're the only product whose own inventor apologized for it. John Sylvan sold out for fifty grand in 1997, then told The Atlantic he feels bad he ever did it. Buddy, that's not an origin story. That's a confession.

And remember Keurig 2.0? You put DRM on coffee. A machine that reads ink on the lid and goes, "Sorry, I don't recognize this bean." Sales fell, people posted workarounds online, and America had to jailbreak a coffee maker just to get a cup of coffee.

By 2014 you sold enough pods every year to circle the Earth more than ten times, mostly in plastic nobody could recycle. You didn't make coffee. You made the planet a second crust.

Then you merged with Dr Pepper. Fitting. Nothing says "we've given up on real coffee" like moving in with a soda.

b.text:
Keurig, you took the simplest drink in human history (hot water, beans) and added a subscription model. Your own inventor said he regrets making you. Imagine your dad publicly apologizing for you and you're still in every dentist's waiting room.

You tried DRM on coffee. Keurig 2.0 literally scanned pods and refused to brew anything off-brand. You're the only appliance that's ever asked me for a license.

Every K-Cup costs more per pound than a decent steak, and you've buried enough of them to circle the Earth a dozen times. Archaeologists will dig them up and assume we worshipped tiny plastic thimbles.

And the Keurig Kold? A $370 soda machine that died faster than the flat Coke it made.

Your descale light blinks like a cry for help. Honestly, same.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text: Beanie Babies, look at you. Ty launched you in 1993, sold you only in small gift shops, and "retired" designs on purpose. You're the only stuffed animal whose business plan was a fake pension. At your peak you were about 10% of eBay's sales. eBay's IPO filing bragged about over 30,000 of your auctions running at once. A tech revolution, powered by beans. In 1999 a divorcing couple split you one by one on a courtroom floor, the only custody battle where both sides fought hardest over the tags. That same year Ty announced you'd retire, asked the public to vote, then un-retired you. You pulled a farewell-tour encore before you even left the stage. And those "rare" ones price guides valued in the thousands? Now they go for a few dollars. Turns out the only thing you ever truly retired was everybody's college fund.

b.text: Beanie Babies. The only retirement plan where the retiree was a five-dollar bear stuffed with plastic pellets. A whole generation bought plastic protectors for a toy's ear tag, then sealed the toy in a Ziploc so no child could ever love it. You weren't a stuffed animal; you were a 401(k) with a poem on it. And those poems! Ty Warner doing greeting-card Shakespeare for people who thought Princess the bear would pay for college. Princess paid for nothing. Neither did the Teenie Beanies everyone hoarded from McDonald's while throwing away the actual Happy Meal. A divorcing couple in Las Vegas literally split their collection on a courtroom floor, one Beanie at a time. That's your legacy: custody battles over a moose named Chocolate. Even your creator got busted hiding money from the IRS, because he was the only one who ever made any.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text:
Chicago deep-dish pizza, everybody! Born at Pizzeria Uno in 1943, and to this day three men are fighting over the credit: Ike Sewell, Ric Riccardo, and Rudy Malnati. Normally when three guys point at each other over something that happened in a kitchen, it's for the blame.

You're built upside down: cheese on the bottom, sauce on top, because you bake so long the mozzarella has to hide under the toppings like it's waiting out a tornado. Jon Stewart called you "tomato soup in a bread bowl" and "a casserole." Honestly? Generous. Casseroles get invited to funerals.

But here's the real burn: Chicago doesn't even eat you. GrubHub data had locals ordering other pizza ten to one. Under nine percent of orders, and that's with stuffed pizza padding your numbers. They're home eating tavern-style squares. You're not the city's pizza. You're its brochure.

b.text: Let's talk about the people who insist deep-dish is pizza. Mostly Chicagoans with a Second City complex so severe they'll defend anything New York makes fun of. Jon Stewart called it a casserole in 2013, and half of Lincoln Park still hasn't emotionally recovered. These are folks who order, then wait forty-five minutes at Lou Malnati's, and call that patience instead of what it is: a hostage negotiation with a buzzer. They eat it with a knife and fork and still claim it's the same food you fold on a subway platform. And what does it get them? A Giordano's line full of tourists from Ohio, a nap at 2 p.m., and the right to lecture you about tavern-style, which, notice, is what they actually eat at home. Defending deep-dish isn't civic pride. It's Stockholm syndrome with a parking ticket.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Comic Sans, you were modeled on Watchmen and The Dark Knight Returns. You come from Batman. Your one job was speech bubbles for a cartoon dog, and you missed it. Microsoft Bob, a product nobody remembers, and you couldn't make his launch. Cut from the dog's team, you shipped in a Plus! pack, like a free tote bag nobody asked for.

Then CERN found the Higgs boson, the particle that gives everything mass, and announced it in you. The biggest physics discovery in decades, presented like a lost-cat flyer. You're the one thing that particle couldn't give weight to.

Two designers spent twenty years trying to ban you. In 2019 they gave up and built you a website. That's not acceptance, Comic Sans. That's a hostage situation.

b.text:
Comic Sans thinks it's the friendly font. Bake sales. Birthday invites. Your kid's lemonade stand.

Its parents are The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.

That's not a friendly font. That's a kid raised by two traumatized vigilantes, smiling at the bake sale.

It was built to be the voice of a cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob. It missed Bob's launch.

Only thing in history that survived Microsoft Bob: by not showing up.

2012. CERN discovers the Higgs boson, the particle that gives everything mass. Announces it in Comic Sans.

They found the God particle. Couldn't find the font menu.

Designers ran "Ban Comic Sans" for twenty years. In 2019 they gave up and launched usecomicsans.com.

The font didn't change once. The designers did.

In my industry, we call that alignment.

The font was right. It just waited for you to retire.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text:
Keurig, you're the only invention whose own father wants a refund. John Sylvan created the K-Cup, sold out for about fifty grand, and later told The Atlantic, "I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it." That's not an inventor. That's a guy confessing on a true-crime podcast.

And you heard that and thought, "Let's get worse." Keurig 2.0 scanned an ink mark on the lid to reject unlicensed pods. You put DRM on coffee. The internet cracked it faster than you brew a cup, and your sales fell.

Meanwhile you sold enough pods every year to circle the Earth more than ten times, mostly in unrecyclable #7 plastic. The planet's wearing your garbage like a belt.

Now you've merged with Dr Pepper. Makes sense. Who else would marry a machine that turns plastic into brown water?

b.text: Keurig people. You wanted coffee but couldn't commit to a whole pot, like a man ordering one buffalo wing. You pay forty dollars a pound for grounds, as long as they arrive in a thimble you throw away. You bought the variety pack, drank every Breakfast Blend in a week, and now there are eleven hot cocoas and a chai you're saving for the apocalypse. You press "Strong" like you're negotiating with it. The guy who invented the pod says he regrets it. You don't. You display your pods on a spinning carousel like fine cigars, and the one time you peeled the foil off to recycle one, you told people about it for a month. You didn't want coffee. You wanted to feel like a hotel guest in your own kitchen. Congratulations: it tastes exactly like that.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text:
Durian calls itself the King of Fruits.

Singapore disagrees. It's banned on the MRT.

A country that banned chewing gum looked at durian and said: no, that's too far.

In 2017, scientists sequenced its genome. Nature Genetics. The smell isn't an accident. Durian duplicated its sulfur genes.

Evolution handed it one stink.

It asked for refills.

Trains ban it. Hotels ban it.

And China buys billions of dollars of it every year.

That's not a fruit. That's a hostage negotiation.

In 1856, Alfred Russel Wallace said eating it was worth a voyage to the East.

Of course he did. He'd spent months on a nineteenth-century ship.

To him, it smelled like home.

Durian is the only food people pay a fortune to be personally offended by.

Speaking of which, thank you all for buying tickets.

b.text:
Durian, you are the only fruit with a criminal record. Singapore's MRT has a list of banned things and you're on it. Not because you're dangerous, because you're rude. Hotels across Southeast Asia won't let you check in. You're a fruit that has to sleep in the car.

And scientists found out why. A 2017 study in Nature Genetics says you have a duplicated family of genes whose whole job is pumping out sulfur. Duplicated! Evolution looked at you and said, "Needs more."

Yet China buys billions of dollars of you a year, mostly from Thailand. That's not a trade deal. That's a hostage situation with a shipping manifest.

Even Alfred Russel Wallace said you were "worth a voyage to the East." Sure, Alfred. Probably because nobody would let you bring it back.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text: Let's talk about the guy who writes a two-page memo in LaTeX. Your memo is about the break room fridge, but it's in Computer Modern, so everyone reads it expecting it to end with a theorem. "Fridge Policy, Section 1.1." Buddy, there's no Section 1.2. You spent forty minutes on a preamble longer than the memo. Twelve \usepackage lines to say "label your yogurt." You compiled it three times because the cross-reference said "see Section ??" on page one, referencing page one. You're not after clarity. You're after someone asking, "Is this LaTeX?" so you can say "Oh, habit," like a man who still mentions his thesis at parties. And it gets you exactly one thing: a PDF nobody can edit, so when Karen fixes a typo, she retypes the whole thing in Word.

b.text:
LaTeX.

The typesetting system for people who think suffering is a font.

Donald Knuth didn't like how the proofs of his own book looked. So he wrote TeX.

Most people just change printers.

Its version number converges on pi. Three point one four one five nine two six five three. Never finished, just more precise.

Like your thesis.

Knuth pays you for finding bugs. Of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on, nine were cashed.

The rest got framed. That's how smug this software is. The bug reports are trophies.

You put a figure on page three. LaTeX moves it to page seven. Forget one brace and the error turns up three pages later. Compile three times, just so "see Figure 2" stops saying question mark.

And you call that elegant.

No. You use it because a wrong result in Computer Modern looks peer-reviewed.

Underfull hbox. Badness ten thousand.

Same as your citations.

facts: California grows about 80% of the world's almonds.
A single almond takes about 1.1 US gallons (roughly 4 litres) of water to grow, a figure Mother Jones published in 2014 that spread during California's drought.

A 2015 US class action alleged Almond Breeze contained only about 2% almonds; it partly survived a motion to dismiss, was stayed in 2017 pending a separate Blue Diamond labelling settlement, and the plaintiffs then dropped it.
Pollinating California's almond orchards each February requires trucking in most of the commercial honeybee colonies in the United States.
Medieval European cooks used almond milk as a Lenten substitute for dairy, centuries before the current fashion.

a.text:
Almond milk, you're the only drink that needs a lawyer to defend its name. The dairy industry sued because, technically, nobody has ever milked an almond. We looked. No nipples.

You're about two percent almonds. The rest is water, gellan gum, and confidence. You're not milk. You're a nut that got waterboarded and called it wellness.

And speaking of water: it takes over a gallon to grow a single almond. California is in a drought so you can be beige in a latte. Bees get trucked across the country like seasonal laborers just to make you, and a lot of them don't come home.

Leave you in the fridge for two days and you separate like you're ashamed of yourself. Fair. I'd need to be shaken too if I cost seven dollars and tasted like a wet sympathy card.

b.text: Let's hear it for the people who switched to almond milk to save the planet. You watched one documentary about cow farts and panicked straight into the arms of a nut that needs a gallon of water apiece. Congratulations: you fled methane and landed on drought. California is cracking like a crème brûlée, and you're out here draining a Central Valley aquifer because you can't make eye contact with a Holstein. And the bees! Billions of them trucked across the country on semis, dying by the hive, so you can tell a coworker you "don't really do dairy." That's not environmentalism. That's relocating the crime scene. You didn't save the Earth. You just moved the guilt somewhere sunnier, slapped a leaf on it, and paid an eighty-cent upcharge for the privilege of feeling better about it.

facts: Released by Bram Moolenaar in November 1991 as 'Vi IMitation', a vi clone he had begun writing for the Amiga in 1988 on top of Stevie; the expansion became 'Vi IMproved' with version 2.0 in December 1993.
Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text:
Vim, you're the only text editor with its own hostage negotiation thread. Millions of people have viewed the Stack Overflow question on how to leave you. That's not a user base, that's a missing persons report.

You have modes. Normal mode, where typing does nothing normal, and Insert mode, hidden behind the letter "i" like a secret menu.

Your fans move the cursor with h, j, k, l because a terminal from 1976 printed arrows on those keys. That's not efficiency, that's Stockholm syndrome on the home row.

Every Vim user has a 900-line .vimrc copied from a stranger and is too scared to touch it. And when you crash, you leave .swp files behind like a burglar who signs the guestbook.

Even your own kids forked you into Neovim. That's not a fork. That's an intervention.

Goodnight! :wq… :q!… ESC ESC ESC…

b.text: You know a Vim user is in the room because nobody else has gotten a word in. Buddy, you didn't "become more productive." You spent three weekends on a .vimrc so you could save four seconds renaming a variable, and you post your dotfiles repo like it's a baby picture. You remapped Caps Lock to Escape and now treat everyone else's keyboard like a character flaw. You say "I live in the terminal" like it's a lifestyle and not just where you got stuck. Your whole identity is a joke about not knowing how to quit, and honestly, you never learned. Here you are, still talking. You say "ciw" out loud at parties. You switched to Neovim just so you'd have something new to announce. And the payoff? You edit text exactly as fast as the rest of us, hands proudly on home row, with nobody watching.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text:
NFTs. Digital ownership. Art, finally scarce. Finally yours.

Beeple sold one at Christie's for sixty-nine million dollars.

Here's what the token actually holds: a URL. The picture lives on a server somewhere. You bought a parking ticket for a car you'll never see.

Collins Dictionary named "NFT" word of the year for 2021.

Fitting. The dictionary is where words go once nobody can explain them.

May 2022: OpenSea trades 2.7 billion dollars in one day. August: 9.34 million. Down ninety-nine percent. That's not a dip. That's an exit interview.

A 2023 study: ninety-five percent of collections are worth zero.

Congratulations to the other five percent. Still holding.

And everyone here feeling smug because you never bought one, relax. You weren't smarter.

You were just broke at the right time.

b.text:
NFTs, look at you. In 2021, Collins Dictionary named you word of the year. Fitting, since a word is about all you turned out to be.

Beeple sold a JPEG at Christie's for $69.3 million. Christie's! A white-glove auction house, suddenly selling a receipt for a picture.

Because that's what you are: a receipt. The token doesn't even hold the image, just a URL. People paid fortunes for a bookmark. The art lives on an ordinary server, so your priceless masterpiece can vanish because somebody forgot to pay for hosting.

OpenSea did $2.7 billion in trades on May 1, 2022. By August 28: $9.34 million. That's not a dip. That's a 99% drop.

And a 2023 study found 95% of the collections it examined were worth zero. Zero. At least Beanie Babies work as a pillow.

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text:
Luosifen, you're the only dish that arrives before the delivery guy does. You're named after river snails, yet nobody has ever found one in the bowl. You boiled them for hours, took their soul, and threw out the bodies. That's not a recipe, that's a cover-up.

And that smell? Fermented bamboo shoots that died, got buried, and came back for revenge. Someone opens a packet in Liuzhou and a guy in Guilin checks his shoes. College dorms banned you like a space heater. Neighbors call the gas company.

Your fans swear, "It smells terrible but tastes amazing." Buddy, that's what everyone says about their toxic ex.

Peanuts, crispy tofu skin, wood ear, pickled beans, a slick of chili oil... that's not garnish, that's witness protection for flavor.

And now you come instant. Congratulations: a biohazard with a seasoning packet.

b.text: You know who you are. You ordered twelve packs off Taobao, waited until every roommate was home, then tore open the sour bamboo shoot sachet like you were declassifying something. You're not hungry. You're making a point. Every slurp comes with the speech: "Smells bad, tastes good." Buddy, we only get the first half. Nobody signed up for the tasting, just the hallway. And you keep saying "it's authentic Liuzhou" like geography is an apology. What does it get you? A spotless pot nobody will borrow, a group chat that goes silent the second you type "anyone want some?", and roommates who suddenly prefer dating people with their own apartments. You came for comfort food. You left with a reputation, a window permanently propped open, and a fridge shelf everyone treats like a crime scene.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text:
Carbon nanotubes. Discovered in 1991, the same year as the World Wide Web.

One of them changed everything.

The other one was going to take us to space.

A cable straight to orbit. Then in 2006 someone did the math with ordinary defects. Turns out the miracle material is like every miracle: perfect right up until somebody builds it.

Next plan: replace silicon. Thirty years later, they still can't sort their own tubes into the ones that conduct and the ones that don't. MIT finally built a processor in 2019. Sixteen bits. Still in the lab.

Meanwhile, in mice, the long ones act like asbestos. From space elevator to asbestos in seventeen years.

Today? A powder stirred into battery electrodes. An additive.

Promised the sky, ended up as filler. Don't laugh. Half of you have that same career arc on LinkedIn.

b.text: Let's hear it for the carbon nanotube founders, the only people who've been "five years from commercialization" since 1991. You can spot them at any pitch day: a postdoc in a blazer that still smells like the clean room, opening with a space elevator and closing with a seed round. Bold move, promising a cable to orbit when your entire production run fits in a vial labeled "DO NOT INHALE." They swear they'll replace silicon. Silicon has heard this every year since Clinton and keeps shipping. They say "a hundred times stronger than steel" the way your uncle says he could've gone pro. And what does it get them? A Nature cover, a term sheet, and a quiet pivot to "conductive additive for batteries." The dream: a ladder to space. The exit: slightly better tennis rackets.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text: Let's talk about families who still play Monopoly on holidays. You know who you are: you swore it'd be "fun," then spent four hours watching your brother-in-law build hotels on Boardwalk like he's finally getting the respect his career never gave him. Dad's the banker, which means a man with zero accountability and a lap full of orange five-hundreds. Mom invented a Free Parking jackpot rule in 1994 and will defend it harder than her marriage. Your little cousin traded you Park Place for Baltic and "a favor later," and somehow that's the most binding contract in your family. Nobody's ever finished a game. It ends the same way every year: someone flips the board, someone cries in jail, and Grandma pockets the Get Out of Jail Free card like she's been planning it since Nixon.

b.text:
Monopoly, you were invented by Lizzie Magie to teach people that landlords ruin lives, and somehow the lesson everyone learned was "buy Park Place." Then Parker Brothers bought you from a guy who basically stole you, which is the most on-brand origin story in history.

You're the only game where "second prize in a beauty contest" counts as income and jail is solved with a coupon. Your mascot looks like he foreclosed on the Pringles guy, and half of America swears he wears a monocle. He doesn't. We just assumed a man that rich would be hiding something.

Nobody has ever finished you. Games don't end; your cousin just flips the board over Marvin Gardens, which you misspelled, by the way. It's Marven. Even your real estate is a scam.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text:
Excel, you've been around since 1985, and somehow you're still the most dangerous thing in any office. You looked at human DNA, saw SEPT2, and said, "Ooh, September second!" Scientists had to rename 27 human genes because of you. Evolution took millions of years; you undid it with a date format. Geneticists published guidelines in Nature Genetics, which is the academic version of a restraining order.

In 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID cases because an old .xls file hit 65,536 rows. A pandemic, and you said, "Sorry, I'm full."

And Reinhart and Rogoff? A range error dropped five countries from a paper cited for austerity. It took a graduate student to catch it. Entire economic policies got a footnote because you couldn't highlight five more rows.

Now you hold over a million rows. Great. More room for mistakes.

b.text:
Excel. Born 1985. Forty years old, and it still can't tell a gene from a date.

It saw SEPT2 and thought: September second.

Scientists fought it for years. Then the gene committee gave up and renamed 27 human genes.

Humanity edited its own genome to keep a spreadsheet happy.

2020. England is counting COVID cases in an old file. Limit: 65,536 rows. Row 65,537 simply didn't happen.

Fifteen thousand eight hundred forty-one cases. Not cured. Just never counted.

Then there's "Growth in a Time of Debt," the paper that sold austerity. Five countries missing. Wrong cell range. A grad student caught it, three years later.

Whole nations tightened their belts because someone didn't drag the cursor far enough.

Now it holds a million rows.

And Monday morning, every one of you will open it again.

Raise your hand if your country's budget is in a file named FINAL_v7_REAL.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text:
Klingon. The tongue of fearsome warriors, invented by a linguist named Marc. Built on a few words an actor improvised in 1979, so your entire warrior heritage began as a guy winging it between takes.

You're so alien you don't even have a verb "to be." Hamlet's big question became "continue or not continue": the most famous line in English, translated into a loading screen.

The Klingon Language Institute published Hamlet "in the original Klingon." Bold. Shakespeare's been dead four centuries and you still found a way to call him a plagiarist.

Your 1985 dictionary had roughly 1,500 words. Fewer than your fans own pairs of rubber foreheads.

Fluent speakers: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018. That's not a language, that's a wedding guest list. Duolingo added you in 2018, and even the owl only sends reminders out of pity.

b.text:
Being fluent in Klingon is a big deal. You've joined an elite community of maybe forty people worldwide, and you've met all of them at the same Holiday Inn conference room. You spent years mastering a language built for a warrior race, a culture of honor, combat and blood oaths, and you use it to argue on a forum about verb suffixes. You learned the language of the fiercest fighters in the galaxy, and the last thing you fought was a lactose sensitivity.

Klingon has no word for "hello." The standard greeting is "nuqneH," which means "what do you want?" Perfect for you, because nobody has ever approached you without a reason.

You told people you read *Hamlet* "in the original Klingon." Brother, Shakespeare had a girlfriend. You have a bat'leth over the futon.

Qapla'. That means "success," a word you know only in Klingon.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text: Chicago deep-dish isn't a pizza. It's a casserole that got a fake ID. You order it, and the waiter says, "That'll be forty-five minutes." Forty-five minutes! I've had relationships bake faster. They put the sauce on top because if you saw what was underneath first, you'd leave. A solid sheet of sausage, like somebody paved a driveway with a patty. Two pounds of mozzarella hiding under a tomato quilt. It's not a slice, it's a core sample. You need a knife, a fork, and a structural engineer. The crust is buttery cornmeal, so it's a pie crust, so congratulations, you're eating dessert with ambitions. And here's the best part: actual Chicagoans don't even eat it. They eat tavern-style thin crust cut in squares. Deep-dish is just the city's way of keeping tourists too full to walk to Wrigley.

b.text: Let's talk about the people who insist deep-dish is pizza. Mostly Chicagoans with a Second City complex so severe they'll defend anything New York makes fun of. Jon Stewart called it a casserole in 2013, and half of Lincoln Park still hasn't emotionally recovered. These are folks who order, then wait forty-five minutes at Lou Malnati's, and call that patience instead of what it is: a hostage negotiation with a buzzer. They eat it with a knife and fork and still claim it's the same food you fold on a subway platform. And what does it get them? A Giordano's line full of tourists from Ohio, a nap at 2 p.m., and the right to lecture you about tavern-style, which, notice, is what they actually eat at home. Defending deep-dish isn't civic pride. It's Stockholm syndrome with a parking ticket.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text:
UGG boots. Born on an Australian beach. Surfers came out of freezing water and wrapped their feet in a sheep.

In Australia, "ugg" is just a word. Like "boot." Any bootmaker can use it.

In America, it's a trademark. Deckers bought it in 1995.

So in 2019, a US jury found an Australian liable for selling an Australian boot under its Australian name.

To Americans.

Take the thing, rename it, then sue the locals for trespassing. Australia should recognize the technique.

They invented it.

Then Oprah put them on Favorite Things, and now it's over two billion dollars a year.

The sheep gave its skin. Australia gave the word. Oprah gave the blessing.

And you gave real money for slippers you wear to the supermarket. Stained, flattened, walking on the sides.

Same as you.

b.text: UGG boots. Even the name sounds like the noise you make pulling them on. Australian surfers invented them to warm their feet after the ocean, and somehow they became snow boots that dissolve in snow. One puddle and you're wearing a salt-stained topographic map. They're sheepskin, so you skip the socks, so by February they smell like the sheep's revenge. Every pair eventually collapses outward until you're walking on the sides of your ankles like a newborn giraffe in a bread costume. And that's the look: two chestnut loaves. You don't walk in UGGs; you shuffle, like the ghost of Paris Hilton still searching for her Juicy tracksuit. And now they're back with platforms, so you can roll an ankle from higher up. It's not footwear. It's a bathrobe that learned to commute.

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text: Macau, you're the only place where the most famous church is just a wall. The Ruins of St. Paul's: a gorgeous front with absolutely nothing behind it, which is basically your whole personality. You've got a fake Venice with a painted sky, a fake Paris with a half-size Eiffel Tower, and you're so tiny you had to dump dirt into the ocean just to fit a runway. You out-earned Las Vegas several times over, and your signature dish is still a pork chop jammed in a bun. The Portuguese stayed four hundred years and left you an egg tart and street signs nobody reads. The Grand Lisboa looks like a golden pineapple having a breakdown. And the Macau Tower's big attraction is jumping off it, which, after a night at the baccarat tables, is less a thrill ride and more a financial plan.

b.text: Macau, the Portuguese ran you for nearly 450 years, and in all that time nobody once said, "Maybe a park?" You've got roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre, a density normally reserved for elevators and clown cars. Then you ran out of land, so you made more, filling in the sea between Taipa and Coloane to build the Cotai Strip. Most places reclaim land for farms. You reclaimed it for baccarat. By 2013 you were pulling in seven times what the Las Vegas Strip made, out-Vegasing Vegas without even hiring an Elvis. And for four decades, one company, STDM, held the whole monopoly. They say the house always wins. Easy when there's only one house. Macau, you're the only place on Earth where the odds are against you before you've even found somewhere to stand.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text: You people still spinning PMMA aren't doing lithography. You're doing historical reenactment. Your advisor's advisor scribbled the recipe on a napkin in 1975, and you treat it like scripture: 950K over 495K, MIBK to IPA one-to-three, develop sixty seconds while whispering to the beaker. You tell everyone it's about "resolution." It's about nobody wanting to file the purchase order for ZEP. So you crank the dose until writing one chip takes longer than your stipend lasts, then discover your pattern won't survive ten seconds in the etcher. So you do liftoff, because of course you do. Your entire thesis is gold rectangles. You're not a nanofabrication researcher. You're the guy who knows which bottle in the cleanroom is "the good IPA" and guards it like a dragon.

b.text:
PMMA, you're the same polymer as Plexiglas. Somewhere a hamster cage is living your life, and nobody had to dissolve it in chlorobenzene first.

IBM reported you in the late 1960s, and you're still here, like a professor who won't retire because nobody else is quite as precise. Sub-10 nanometers, very impressive. Too bad getting you there takes hundreds to over a thousand microcoulombs per square centimeter. You don't get exposed, you get interrogated.

You're "positive tone," which is generous, because nothing about writing you feels positive. The beam has to break your chains before you'll let go.

And once you finally hold a pattern? Plasma shows up and you fold. So your career is lift-off: hold the shape, let the metal take the credit, then get washed away.

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text:
Microsoft Word. Born in 1983 as "Multi-Tool Word."
Forty years later, it still can't move one picture without four paragraphs fleeing the page.

In 1997 it gave us Clippy.
"It looks like you're writing a letter."
By 2001, Microsoft was running ads mocking him.
His own dad roasted him first.

Its spell checker turned "cooperation" into "Cupertino."
That went into NATO, EU and UN documents.
Microsoft, quietly crediting international cooperation to Apple's hometown.

Then .docx became ISO standard 29500.
Six thousand pages, fast-tracked, amid claims the committees were packed.
Nobody read it.
They approved it the way you approve Terms of Service.

You're laughing. You'll still open Word tomorrow.

Me? I'm Clippy with a bigger training budget.
It looks like you're writing a roast. Want help?

b.text: You chose Word for your thesis because you "didn't have time to learn LaTeX." Beautiful. Instead you learned section breaks, by force, at 3 a.m., trying to make page numbers switch from Roman to Arabic without page one of Chapter 2 becoming page xvii. You wanted to spend your time on research. Instead you spend it dragging a figure half an inch and watching four chapters collapse like a Jenga tower built by your enemies. Your committee will open the PDF and see "Error! Reference source not found." in the middle of your key finding, which, honestly, is a fair summary of your methodology. Your folder contains thesis_FINAL_v9_REALfinal_USE_THIS.docx, because you are a scientist who trusts nothing except filenames. Five years of work, and your proudest skill is knowing which heading style secretly isn't Heading 2.

facts: Tofu soaked for hours to a day or two in a brine that has itself fermented for months from vegetables such as bamboo shoots and mustard greens, often with dried shrimp or meat; the smell is the brine's, not the bean's.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.
Legend credits Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate who left his unsold tofu too long in 1669; a Beijing fermented-bean-curd brand still carries his name.
Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text:
Look at you, standing in a night-market line everyone else is fleeing, like you're queuing to get into a fire. You followed that smell on purpose. Three blocks. Upwind. You're the only person alive who reads a warning as a recommendation.

And you always need a witness. "It smells like a sewer but tastes amazing!" Yes, we know. You've said it to every foreigner you've ever met, then filmed their face gagging for content. Your entire personality is a dare you keep winning against tourists.

And what does it get you? A paper cup, a toothpick, some pickled cabbage doing its best, and a jacket that now smells like a porta-potty at a wedding. Then you board the MRT and clear the whole car. You call that bold. The rest of us call it a hazmat incident with chili sauce.

b.text:
Stinky tofu, look at you. Plain tofu is the most agreeable food on earth, and you turned it into a public nuisance. And the humiliating part? The smell isn't even yours. You soaked in a brine of bamboo shoots and mustard greens that had been fermenting for months, sometimes with dried shrimp. You're not stinky; you just hang out with the wrong crowd.

Your origin story: in 1669 Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate, couldn't sell his tofu and left it out too long. You're not a recipe. You're an inventory problem.

Changsha fries you black and buries you in chili. Taiwan hides you under pickled cabbage. Shaoxing steams you with other stinky pickles, like a support group.

Everyone's trying to cover you up, and people still smell you from a block away.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text:
UGG boots. Born on Australian beaches.
Surfers wore them to warm up after fighting the ocean.
Now people wear them to warm up after fighting a parking spot at Target.

In Australia, "ugg" is just a word. Like "boot." Like "mate."
Any bootmaker can use it.
In America, it's a trademark. Owned by a company in California.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian bootmaker liable for selling boots labelled "ugg"... into America.
That's like Italy getting sued for saying "pizza" in Ohio.

Oprah put them on her Favorite Things list. Repeatedly.
You get a boot! And you get a boot! And Australia gets a cease and desist!

Today it's over two billion dollars a year.
For a slipper with a legal team.

(looks at the front row)
I see a few of you in them right now.
Relax. You're not on trial. Yet.

b.text:
UGG boots. Even the name sounds like the noise you make looking at them.

These started as something Australian surfers pulled on to warm up after a session. A towel you could walk in. Then Brian Smith brought them to California in 1978, and Americans looked at post-surf foot blankets and said, "Fashion."

Then Oprah put them on her Favorite Things lists. Repeatedly. Not once. Repeatedly. That's not an endorsement, that's a hostage situation.

Now Deckers owns the trademark in the US, and UGG pulls in over $2 billion a year. But in Australia, "ugg" is a generic word. Any bootmaker can use it. And in 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled "ugg" into America.

Imagine beating an Australian in court for saying an Australian word about an Australian boot.

facts: Hand-drawn by Chris Costello in 1982 over about six months, when he was 23; he sold the rights to Letraset for $750.
Bundled with macOS and with Microsoft Office, which is why it appears on so many menus and signs.
