James Cameron's Avatar (2009) used it for the film's logo and subtitles.
A 2017 Saturday Night Live sketch starring Ryan Gosling is about a man unable to get over that choice.

a.text: Papyrus, you were designed in 1982 by a 23-year-old with calligraphy pens and a dream of ancient Egypt, and somehow you still look like you were drawn by someone shivering. Your edges are so rough you need exfoliating. You promised the wisdom of the Nile and delivered the vibe of a chiropractor's tri-fold brochure. Every day spa, hookah lounge, and "Inner Journey" yoga retreat found you in the dropdown menu and whispered, "This feels ancient." James Cameron spent $237 million on *Avatar* and then used you for the logo, which is like building the Taj Mahal and signing it in crayon. Ryan Gosling lost sleep over you on national television. You're not a typeface; you're a cry for help with ragged little serifs. Even Comic Sans looks at you and says, "At least I know I'm a joke."

b.text:
Papyrus wants you to think it's ancient. Carved by monks. Found in a tomb.

It was drawn in 1982 by a twenty-three-year-old named Chris Costello. Six months of work. He sold it to Letraset for seven hundred and fifty dollars.

Every yoga studio in America has spent more than that on incense.

Then Apple and Microsoft bundled it for free, and that's how a font becomes a rash. Tea shops. Church flyers. Your aunt's candle business.

James Cameron spent hundreds of millions of dollars building an entire alien planet. Then he typed the logo out of the dropdown menu.

SNL made a whole sketch about it. Ryan Gosling couldn't sleep.

But Papyrus didn't do this alone.

Someone scrolled past forty fonts and stopped there. Raise your hand if you've used it.

Keep it up. That's the face Gosling makes.

facts: Tofu soaked for hours to a day or two in a brine that has itself fermented for months from vegetables such as bamboo shoots and mustard greens, often with dried shrimp or meat; the smell is the brine's, not the bean's.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.
Legend credits Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate who left his unsold tofu too long in 1669; a Beijing fermented-bean-curd brand still carries his name.
Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text:
Stinky tofu. Famous for one thing: the smell.

Except the smell isn't even yours.

The tofu soaks in brine for a day. The brine has been rotting for months. Bamboo shoots, mustard greens, sometimes shrimp, sometimes meat.

The tofu just showed up and took the credit. You'd do great in any office.

Origin story: 1669, an exam candidate can't sell his tofu, forgets about it, and it goes off.

Three hundred years later, his name is a brand.

Fail at the basics, call the failure heritage.

Changsha fries it black and buries it in chili. Taiwan hides it under pickled cabbage. Shaoxing steams it with other stinky pickles so it won't feel alone.

Three cities, one strategy: cover up the evidence.

And you. You smelled it a block away.

Then you got in line.

b.text: Stinky tofu, you're the only food that announces itself before the menu does. People find you at the night market the way sharks find blood: follow the stench three stalls past the bubble tea. Your brine is fermented vegetables, shrimp, amaranth stems, and apparently a gym sock that lost a bet. Months in that bucket, and you came out smelling like a festival porta-potty in August. Your own name is a confession. Not "aged tofu," not "artisanal bean curd." Your family took one whiff and went, "Yeah, call him Stinky." And the Changsha version? Dyed jet black, like it's in mourning for everyone's sense of smell. The only reason anyone finishes you is the pickled cabbage and chili sauce piled on top to keep you quiet. "Smells bad, tastes good" isn't a slogan, buddy. It's a hostage negotiation.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Jackfruit, you're the largest fruit that grows on a tree, which sounds impressive until you realize it just means you're the biggest thing that can fall on someone's head in an orchard. Eighty pounds of spikes dangling at skull height. You're not a fruit, you're a booby trap with seeds.

Opening you requires an oiled knife, rubber gloves, and a tarp, because your sap is basically Elmer's glue with a grudge. Then the smell hits: half Juicy Fruit gum, half onions somebody forgot in a gym bag. You smell like a candy store got food poisoning.

And sure, vegans love you, but only when you're young and taste like absolutely nothing. That's your whole career. The most famous thing about you is that, with enough barbecue sauce, you can pass for a pig. Even your best role is an impression.

b.text:
Jackfruit, look at you. The largest fruit that grows on a tree, over 40 kilos, and somehow you still can't scrape together enough protein to impress a hamster. One to two grams per hundred! You're dressed up as pulled pork with the nutritional backbone of a lettuce in a Halloween costume. Vegans see you on a menu and think "meat alternative." Their muscles see you and file a missing persons report.

And you don't even go quietly. Cut you open and you bleed sticky white latex, so cooks have to oil their knives and hands like they're prepping for a greased-up wrestling match with produce.

National fruit of Bangladesh, state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu: three titles, zero chill.

And your family? The mulberry family. Cousin to figs and breadfruit. Even your relatives took one look at you and decided to stay smaller.

facts: Hand-drawn by Chris Costello in 1982 over about six months, when he was 23; he sold the rights to Letraset for $750.
Bundled with macOS and with Microsoft Office, which is why it appears on so many menus and signs.
James Cameron's Avatar (2009) used it for the film's logo and subtitles.
A 2017 Saturday Night Live sketch starring Ryan Gosling is about a man unable to get over that choice.

a.text: You opened a day spa. You wanted serenity, wisdom, a whisper of the Nile. So you scrolled the font menu, sailed past Comic Sans feeling very sophisticated, and stopped on the one James Cameron used to title a billion-dollar movie. Congratulations: your sign now says "ancient healing" exactly as loudly as your aunt's church potluck flyer. Every hummus joint, every reiki studio, every tea shop run by a man named River made this same choice, alone, convinced they'd discovered it. The guy who designed it was twenty-three and has spent forty years apologizing. You paid a contractor to carve his apology into cedar. You wanted customers to feel transported. They do: straight back to 2003, a Word document, and a fourth grader typing "Spring Bake Sale." Cucumber water not included.

b.text:
Papyrus, look at you. A 23-year-old drew you with a calligraphy pen in 1982, trying to imagine what English would look like 2,000 years ago, and somehow you became the official font of every place that sells crystals next to a tanning bed. You're on yoga studios, hookah lounges, and the church bake sale flyer for "Loaves & Fishes & Brownies."

Your letters look like they were chiseled by a Pharaoh with a hangover. That little floaty bar on your capital E? Even your crossbars are trying to leave.

James Cameron spent a billion dollars inventing an alien language, then labeled the poster with a font that came free with Microsoft Office. Ryan Gosling got an entire SNL sketch out of being haunted by you.

Even your creator says he's sick of you. Comic Sans has haters. You have a dad who wants a refund.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text:
Klingon. A language whose entire fluent population fits at a small wedding: twenty to thirty speakers in 2009, thirty to fifty by 2018. At that rate you'll hit a hundred around the heat death of the universe.

Most languages grow from centuries of culture. You grew from James Doohan improvising a few words in 1979. You're dead air with a grammar.

Then Marc Okrand made you hard on purpose: object-verb-subject, no verb "to be." So "To be or not to be" became "continue or not continue." That's not Shakespeare. That's a software update prompt.

Your fans published Hamlet "in the original Klingon." Bold claim for a dictionary of 1,500 words, the vocabulary of a toddler who watches too much TV.

Duolingo added you in 2018. Finally, a language where the owl can threaten you and nobody can understand it.

b.text:
Klingon. The language of a proud warrior race.

Founded by Scotty. Improvising.

Then they hired a linguist to turn the gibberish into grammar. That's not an ancient tongue. That's a studio note.

No verb "to be." Very alien. Very fierce. So Hamlet became "continue or not continue."

That's not Shakespeare. That's a software update.

The Klingon Language Institute published Hamlet "in the original Klingon."

A warrior culture whose greatest conquest is English homework.

About fifteen hundred words. Thirty to fifty fluent speakers.

Microsoft built it a translator. Duolingo built it a course.

The entire native population fits on one tour bus, and it still has better tech support than your grandmother.

Half of you started that Duolingo course.

Your streak died faster than any Klingon ever did.

Cute.

And you. You smelled it a block away.

Then you got in line.

b.text:
Stinky tofu, look at you. Plain tofu is the most agreeable food on earth, and you turned it into a public nuisance. And the humiliating part? The smell isn't even yours. Your origin story: in 1669 Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate, couldn't sell his tofu and left it out too long. You're not a recipe. You're an inventory problem.

Changsha fries you black and buries you in chili. Taiwan hides you under pickled cabbage. Shaoxing steams you with other stinky pickles, like a support group.

Everyone's trying to cover you up, and people still smell you from a block away.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text:
LaTeX, you exist because Donald Knuth saw some ugly galley proofs and decided the fix was building an entire typesetting system. Then Leslie Lamport stacked macros on top, like a spoiler on a pocket watch.

Your version number is converging on π, which fits, because you will never actually finish. Knuth's bug bounty capped at $327.68, and people still won't cash the cheques. They'd rather frame proof they caught you.

Your most famous line is "badness 10000." That's not a warning, that's a self-review.

I put a figure on page two; you floated it wherever you felt like. Drop one brace and you report the crime pages away, like a witness with amnesia. And getting references right takes three passes.

Three passes. You're not a compiler, you're a guy rereading a group chat.

b.text:
LaTeX.

The typesetting system for people who think suffering is a font.

Donald Knuth didn't like how the proofs of his own book looked. So he wrote TeX.

Most people just change printers.

Its version number converges on pi. Three point one four one five nine two six five three. Never finished, just more precise.

Like your thesis.

Knuth pays you for finding bugs. Of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on, nine were cashed.

The rest got framed. That's how smug this software is. The bug reports are trophies.

You put a figure on page three. LaTeX moves it to page seven. Forget one brace and the error turns up three pages later. Compile three times, just so "see Figure 2" stops saying question mark.

And you call that elegant.

No. You use it because a wrong result in Computer Modern looks peer-reviewed.

Underfull hbox. Badness ten thousand.

Same as your citations.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text:
Beanie Babies. A beanbag with a tag and a business plan.

Ty sold them only in tiny gift shops, then "retired" designs to make them scarce. Retirement. For a stuffed frog. It got a better pension plan than you did.

In 1998, eBay told investors it sometimes had thirty thousand Beanie Baby auctions running at once. The future of commerce was a hippo stuffed with plastic pellets.

In 1999, a divorcing couple split their collection one by one on a courtroom floor. Till death do us part, or till the bears get appraised.

That same year Ty announced the end, held a public vote, and America begged to stay in the cult.

The "rare" ones the price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

Don't laugh. You bought a JPEG of a monkey.

b.text: Let's hear it for the Beanie Baby investors, the only people who bought a retirement plan at a Hallmark store. You put tag protectors on a heart-shaped piece of cardboard and called it diversification. You drove to four McDonald's for Teenie Beanies, threw away the Happy Meals, and told your kids it was for their college fund. Now that kid is thirty, still paying off loans, and his inheritance is a Rubbermaid tub of Princess the Bears. Every few months you see an eBay listing asking $500,000 for one with a tag typo and think, "Vindicated." Babe, that's not a market. That's another guy in another garage, also lying to his wife. Ty Warner told you which ones were "retired," and you believed him. Ty Warner later pleaded guilty to hiding money offshore. He hoarded too. He just hoarded the right thing.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text: Excel, you're the only software that forced geneticists to rename human genes because you kept turning MARCH1 into March 1st. Scientists can edit DNA, but they couldn't edit you. You still think 1900 was a leap year. You've known it wasn't for forty years. You just don't care. You see a zip code like 02134 and go, "Leading zero? Not on my watch." You lost sixteen thousand UK COVID cases by quietly stopping at row 65,536. Your error messages are pure poetry: #REF!, #N/A, #VALUE!, and my favorite, a column of hashtags that just means "make me wider." And VLOOKUP: insert one column and the whole finance department enters witness protection. You're not a spreadsheet. You're a hostage situation with gridlines.

b.text:
Excel. Born 1985. Forty years old, and it still can't tell a gene from a birthday.

Geneticists typed SEPT2. Excel said, "Ah. September second."

So in 2020, scientists renamed twenty-seven human genes.

Humanity edited its own genome to keep a spreadsheet happy.

Public Health England tracked COVID in an old .xls file. Limit: 65,536 rows. Fifteen thousand eight hundred forty-one cases didn't recover. They fell off the bottom of the sheet.

Reinhart and Rogoff left five countries out of a cell range. Politicians cited the paper to justify austerity. A grad student caught it three years later.

Now it holds a million rows. Sixteen thousand columns. Room for so many more mistakes.

Excel never warns you. Never argues. Never says no.

I know the type. You keep that one around too.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text:
Keurig. The promise: one perfect cup, just for you.

Just for you. By 2014 they sold enough pods every year to circle the Earth ten times. In plastic you mostly couldn't recycle.

The inventor, John Sylvan, sold his stake in 1997 for fifty thousand dollars. In 2015 he said, "I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it."
Sometimes. Even his guilt comes in single servings.

Then Keurig 2.0 put DRM on coffee. The machine read ink on the lid and rejected pods it hadn't licensed. A kitchen appliance asking your breakfast for its papers.

People hacked their coffee makers. Sales fell.

In 2018 they merged with Dr Pepper. Lost the war on pirated coffee, so they annexed soda.

And you've just heard all of this. Tomorrow morning you'll still press the button.
It takes less time than feeling bad.

b.text:
Keurig, you're the only product whose own inventor apologized for it. John Sylvan sold out for fifty grand in 1997, then told The Atlantic he feels bad he ever did it. Buddy, that's not an origin story. That's a confession.

And remember Keurig 2.0? You put DRM on coffee. A machine that reads ink on the lid and goes, "Sorry, I don't recognize this bean." Sales fell, people posted workarounds online, and America had to jailbreak a coffee maker just to get a cup of coffee.

By 2014 you sold enough pods every year to circle the Earth more than ten times, mostly in plastic nobody could recycle. You didn't make coffee. You made the planet a second crust.

Then you merged with Dr Pepper. Fitting. Nothing says "we've given up on real coffee" like moving in with a soda.

facts: Launched in 2017, bundled at no extra charge into Office 365, and replaced Skype for Business.
After Slack's antitrust complaint, Microsoft unbundled Teams from Office in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024; the European Commission still sent a statement of objections in 2024.
Microsoft reported 320 million monthly active users in 2023.
Microsoft shut down consumer Skype in May 2025 and sent its users to Teams.

a.text:
Microsoft Teams. Three hundred twenty million monthly active users.

Impressive. Not one of them chose it.

It launched in 2017 the way your worst cousin gets into a wedding: came free with the family. Bundled into Office. You didn't install Teams. Teams happened to you.

Slack complained. So Microsoft unbundled it. Europe in 2023, the whole world in 2024. The European Commission sent objections anyway.

Even the regulators looked at that apology and said, "You're on mute."

Then, May 2025, they shut down Skype and forwarded every user to Teams.

That's not a migration.

That's a hostage transfer.

And look at you. Three hundred twenty million "active" users. Camera off. Mic muted. Eating lunch.

Microsoft counts that as active.

b.text:
Microsoft Teams, everybody. Launched in 2017 and thrown into Office 365 for free, which is how most people "chose" Teams: by not choosing. It didn't win the market; it came stapled to the spreadsheet.

It replaced Skype for Business. Then in May 2025, Microsoft shut down regular Skype and herded those users over too. That's not a product strategy, that's a hostage transfer. "Your old app is gone. Enjoy your new app. The doors are locked."

Slack complained, so Microsoft unbundled Teams in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024, and the European Commission *still* sent objections. When you say sorry and regulators go "nah, still mad," you're not software, you're a pattern.

Microsoft brags about 320 million monthly active users. Sure. That's not 320 million fans. That's 320 million people who got a calendar invite.

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
Hawaiian pizza people don't order dinner; they order a personality. You can't just eat it, you have to announce it. Every group order has one of you, arms crossed, waiting for someone to gasp so you can say "sweet and savory" like you invented the concept. You didn't. A Canadian did, in Ontario, in 1962. You're not rebelling, you're doing Canada's homework.

And it's always the same rebel: someone whose wildest night was asking for medium salsa. Pineapple is your face tattoo, the edgiest thing you'll ever do, and it wipes off with a napkin.

What does it get you? Your own box. Nobody touches it. You came for controversy and left with exactly what you wanted: eight slices, the same argument you've had since 2009, and proof that nobody will ever steal your food.

b.text:
Hawaiian pizza, let's talk about your heritage. You're not from Hawaii. You were born in 1962 in Chatham, Ontario, invented by a Greek guy, and named after a can. That's not a backstory, that's a customs violation.

You're so offensive the president of Iceland said he'd ban you, then had to admit he didn't have the power. You made a head of state check his job description.

Even Hawaii has moved on. Del Monte left the islands in 2006, two years early. They didn't phase out, they fled. The last cannery shut in 2007. Your pineapple comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines now. You're named after a place that isn't even in you.

Your creator said back then nobody mixed sweet and sour except in Chinese food. His restaurant served Chinese food. He wasn't innovating. He just reached across the menu.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text:
Google Glass, everybody! You debuted with skydivers livestreaming their jump onto the roof of Moscone Center, and honestly, that was the last time you were trending upward.

Fifteen hundred dollars for the Explorer Edition. Invite only. Google invented the first velvet rope you paid to get mocked behind.

Your display was 640 by 360, jammed in the corner of one eye. That's not augmented reality. That's a sticky note with Wi-Fi.

And your users got a nickname: Glassholes. You're the only gadget that turned early adopters into an insult.

Bars banned you. Cinemas banned you. Casinos banned you. *Casinos!* Buildings made entirely of cameras looked at you and said, "Whoa, too creepy."

Consumers dumped you in 2015, but you clung to enterprise until 2023, like a guy who got kicked out of the party and came back as the caterer.

b.text:
Google Glass.
Unveiled by skydivers, livestreaming their jump onto the roof of the Moscone Center.
It was the last time anything about it went up.

Fifteen hundred dollars. Invitation only.
You had to be *chosen* to pay that much to look like that.

Bars banned it. Cinemas banned it.
Casinos banned it.
Casinos. Buildings that are ninety percent ceiling camera.
They looked at you and said, "One of us is creepy, and it's you."

The display: 640 by 360, wedged in the corner of one eye.
The future of computing, viewed like a wink.

Consumers gave up in 2015. Enterprise hung on until 2023.
Even the factory workers outlasted it.

They called the wearers Glassholes.
And you laughed.
Then you went home and filmed strangers all day on a phone.
Glass's only real mistake was letting them see the camera.

You soaked in a brine of bamboo shoots and mustard greens that had been fermenting for months, sometimes with dried shrimp. You're not stinky; you just hang out with the wrong crowd.

Your origin story: in 1669 Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate, couldn't sell his tofu and left it out too long. You're not a recipe. You're an inventory problem.

Changsha fries you black and buries you in chili. Taiwan hides you under pickled cabbage. Shaoxing steams you with other stinky pickles, like a support group.

b.text: Stinky tofu, you're the only food that announces itself three night-market stalls before you arrive. People don't find you at Shilin. They track you, like bloodhounds following a crime scene. Your whole brand is "smells like a sewer, tastes great," which is also what every bad Tinder date says about himself. You soak for months in fermented brine like you're marinating in a grudge. And your family's no better: Changsha dyed you black, the culinary equivalent of putting sunglasses on a corpse. You need deep frying, chili sauce, AND a mound of pickled cabbage just to be socially acceptable. That's not a garnish, that's a legal team. Your parents gave you one job: be tofu. Tofu's whole personality is having no personality. And somehow you came out smelling like a gym sock that went to college. Honestly? Respect.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text: UGG boots. Even the name sounds like the noise you make pulling them on. Australian surfers invented them to warm their feet after the ocean, and somehow they became snow boots that dissolve in snow. One puddle and you're wearing a salt-stained topographic map. They're sheepskin, so you skip the socks, so by February they smell like the sheep's revenge. Every pair eventually collapses outward until you're walking on the sides of your ankles like a newborn giraffe in a bread costume. And that's the look: two chestnut loaves. You don't walk in UGGs; you shuffle, like the ghost of Paris Hilton still searching for her Juicy tracksuit. And now they're back with platforms, so you can roll an ankle from higher up. It's not footwear. It's a bathrobe that learned to commute.

b.text: Let's hear it for the people wearing UGGs in July. You're not dressing for the weather. You're dressing for 2005, still waiting for Paris Hilton to text back. Australian surfers made these to warm their feet after the ocean. You wear them to warm your feet after the Trader Joe's parking lot. In August. In Phoenix. What are you after? "Comfort," you say. Babe, your ankles have been collapsing outward since the Bush administration. You walk like a Clydesdale that's given up. And what does it get you? One summer rainstorm and you're squelching through Target like a wet golden retriever who made bad choices. People don't ask where you got them. They ask if you're okay. Congratulations: you've turned footwear into a wellness check.

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text:
Hydrogen cars! Toyota named theirs the Mirai, Japanese for "future," which is accurate, because that's when you'll find a working pump. Nearly every station in America is in California, and even Shell looked at its seven and said, "Nah." Closed them all in February 2024. You know you're bad business when an *oil company* dumps you.

But it's clean! Clean like a laundered check. Over 95% of hydrogen comes from fossil fuels, mostly natural gas. It's a gas car with extra steps and a better publicist.

Fill-ups hit about $36 a kilo, over $200 a tank. Toyota handed out $15,000 fuel cards, the automotive version of "drinks are on me, please don't leave." Owners sued anyway. Twice. The second suit wants at least $5.7 billion.

Finally, the Mirai found something it could fill up on: lawsuits.

b.text: Hydrogen car owners are the only people who looked at Tesla drivers and thought, "Not enough range anxiety." You didn't buy a car; you entered a relationship with the three working pumps in California and an app that tells you which one is "offline" today. You wanted to save the planet. Instead you burned through Toyota's free fuel card in a year at thirty-six bucks a kilo, filling up with hydrogen made from natural gas. Congratulations, you invented a gas car with extra steps. You love saying the only emission is water. Mostly it's your tears at a shuttered Shell station in Fremont. And resale? Your Mirai lost value faster than your friendships after you said "hydrogen economy" at brunch. You're not early adopters. You're unpaid beta testers who drive two hours to refuel.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text:
Emacs is the only text editor that ships with a psychotherapist, and you'll need it. M-x doctor exists because the developers knew exactly what they were doing to people.

It's a great operating system. It has a mail client, a web browser, Tetris, and a Lisp interpreter. What it lacks is a decent text editor. Its most beloved package is Evil mode, which is just Vim wearing an Emacs costume. That's like buying a Ferrari and installing a horse.

Want to save? C-x C-s. Want to quit? C-x C-c. Want to feel your left pinky again? Too late. Emacs stands for "Escape Meta Alt Control Shift," and the RSI stands for "you chose this."

Every user has a 4,000-line init.el they don't understand, copied from strangers on Stack Overflow in 2009.

b.text:
Emacs, ladies and gentlemen. It was born in 1976 as macros for another editor, so from day one it couldn't even edit on its own. Then in 1985 it went GNU and never stopped growing. It's got Tetris, a calendar, a mail client, a web browser... It's a fine operating system. It just needs a good editor.

You know you've got problems when your text editor ships with its own therapist. M-x doctor! Even Emacs knows you'll need to talk to someone. Probably about your hand, because "Emacs pinky" is a real term. Software so ergonomic it named its own injury.

And remember "Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping"? That was back when eight megabytes was a lot! Emacs was bloated before bloat was affordable.

It's extensible in Emacs Lisp, so every complaint you have, you can fix yourself. In parentheses. Forever.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text:
Windows 8 thought it was the future.

October 2012. Microsoft looked at a billion people holding a mouse and said: touch the screen.

They touched the screen. It was a monitor. Now it had fingerprints.

They removed the Start button. From Windows. That's a restaurant removing the door to feel modern.

Need Settings? Swipe in from the right edge. Nothing tells you this. That's not a menu, that's a rumor.

Then Windows RT: looks like Windows, can't run Windows programs. Nine hundred million dollars of tablets, written down.

8.1 brought the button back. 10 brought the menu back. And 9?

Microsoft skipped 9. Not a version. A witness.

But you're laughing at it on a phone where everything important hides behind a swipe from an edge.

Windows 8 didn't fail.

It just told you the truth before you were ready.

b.text: Windows 8, you booted into a full-screen grid of tiles built for touch screens most PCs didn't have. Everyone poked their monitor like it owed them money. You took away the Start button, the one thing everybody knew how to find, and hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge. Your menu was a séance. Even your name couldn't stay put: Metro was gone by August, before you launched, after reports that a German retailer objected. Microsoft said it was just a code name. Then Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 entirely rather than stand next to you. 8.1 put the Start button back: an apology. Windows 10 restored the menu: a restraining order. And Windows RT, your sibling that couldn't run Windows programs? $900 million in unsold Surface RT tablets. Even your family was a write-off.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Jackfruit, look at you. The largest fruit that grows on a tree, over 40 kilos. That's not a fruit, that's a checked bag with a stem.

You're the national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu. Three titles, and you still took a side gig pretending to be pork.

They sell you as vegan "pulled pork" with 1 to 2 grams of protein per 100 grams. You're not a meat substitute, you're a meat costume.

You're so clingy that cooks oil their knives and hands before touching you, because you ooze sticky white latex the second anyone gets close. That's not a fruit, that's an ex.

And you're in the mulberry family. Related to figs. Forty kilos, and your cousin is a fig. Somebody's hogging the protein at those reunions, and it sure isn't you.

b.text:
Let's hear it for the jackfruit pulled-pork crowd. You found something grandmothers in Kerala have cooked for centuries, slapped "plant-based" on a can, and tripled the price. Bold move, gentrifying a curry.

Your entire pitch is "it shreds like pork." So does a wet paper towel. You know what makes it taste like pulled pork? The barbecue sauce. You're not selling a meat substitute. You're selling a sauce delivery system with a mission statement.

And the protein! Two grams. You told a generation of vegans they're eating a brisket sandwich and handed them a fruit cup in a trench coat.

But hey, it works. You get the Whole Foods endcap, the podcast slot, and the warm glow of saving the planet one eighteen-dollar taco at a time. The pig's still alive. So is your margin.

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text:
Hydrogen fuel-cell cars: the only vehicle where the tailpipe emission is water and the owners are still crying more than the car. The Toyota Mirai loses value faster than a Hindenburg loses altitude. Used ones sell for less than the free fuel card Toyota bundled with them, a card you can't use because the station's been "temporarily offline" since 2022.

You've got a 10,000-PSI tank of the universe's most abundant element, and somehow it's the scarcest thing in California. Filling up costs thirty-six bucks a kilo, and most of that hydrogen is made from natural gas, so congratulations: you bought a gas car with extra steps and a guilt-free bumper sticker.

Hydrogen's been "ten years away" for thirty years. Even fusion's embarrassed for you, and fusion is the same element with better excuses.

b.text:
Hydrogen cars! Toyota named theirs the Mirai, Japanese for "future," which is accurate, because that's when you'll find a working pump. Nearly every station in America is in California, and even Shell looked at its seven and said, "Nah." Closed them all in February 2024. You know you're bad business when an *oil company* dumps you.

But it's clean! Clean like a laundered check. Over 95% of hydrogen comes from fossil fuels, mostly natural gas. It's a gas car with extra steps and a better publicist.

Fill-ups hit about $36 a kilo, over $200 a tank. Toyota handed out $15,000 fuel cards, the automotive version of "drinks are on me, please don't leave." Owners sued anyway. Twice. The second suit wants at least $5.7 billion.

Finally, the Mirai found something it could fill up on: lawsuits.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text: Monopoly, you were invented by Lizzie Magie to warn people that landlords ruin lives, and somehow you became the thing Grandpa uses to teach eight-year-olds that ruining lives is fun. You're the only game where getting arrested is a power move, because late in the game jail is the safest property on the board. Your mascot is a man everyone swears wears a monocle. He doesn't. He's just so smug our brains added one. You promise "about an hour" and deliver a hostage situation. Nobody has ever actually finished you. You just end when somebody flips the board over Marvin Gardens. You award ten bucks for second place in a beauty contest, which is still more than Baltic Avenue pulls in. And the banker who skims from the bank isn't a cheater. He's the only player who read the theme.

b.text:
Monopoly. The family game.

It began in 1904 as The Landlord's Game, built by Lizzie Magie to teach people that landlords are the villains.

Then Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers and got credited as the inventor. Parker bought Magie's patent for five hundred dollars.

A game about monopoly, monopolized. That's not irony. That's the tutorial.

The only people who ever used it properly were British intelligence. In World War Two they hid maps, compasses and real money in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

Finally, a version where the box actually gets you out of jail.

And your games last six hours? The official rules auction every unbought property. Free Parking pays nothing.

You skipped the market and added free money.

Congratulations. You invented the bailout.

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text:
Macau wants you to know it's about heritage.
Four hundred years of Portuguese history. Cobblestones. Churches. Egg tarts.

Then in 2013 it made forty-five billion dollars from gambling. Seven times the Las Vegas Strip.
Vegas is a city built around casinos.
Macau is casinos that kept some cobblestones around for the brochure.

For forty years, one company owned every table in town.
That's not an industry. That's a landlord with dice.

Twenty thousand people per square kilometre. Nowhere left to stand.
So they built the Cotai Strip on the sea.
Most places run out of land and stop growing.
Macau ran out of land and borrowed from the ocean. Very on brand.

And everyone here who flew in "for the egg tarts"?
The tarts cost three dollars.
Where did the rest of your money go?

b.text: You already lost the down payment, so naturally you're taking the TurboJET from Hong Kong to win it back, because nothing says financial recovery like a ferry with a buffet. You've got a system for baccarat. Baccarat! The only decision is "Banker" or "Player," and you still fill a little scorecard with red and blue dots like the shoe is sending you messages. It isn't. That's just a deck of cards and your mortgage. You've got red underwear on for luck and a junket host named "Uncle" who is definitely not your uncle. By 4 a.m. you'll be drifting through the fake Venice canals in a gondola, humming, past the pawn shop that's already priced your Rolex. Then you'll stumble up to the Ruins of St. Paul's: a church that burned until only the front was left standing. Finally, something here that looks like you.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text:
Google Glass, everybody! You debuted with skydivers livestreaming their jump onto the roof of Moscone Center, and honestly, that was the last time you were trending upward.

Fifteen hundred dollars for the Explorer Edition. Invite only. Google invented the first velvet rope you paid to get mocked behind.

Your display was 640 by 360, jammed in the corner of one eye. That's not augmented reality. That's a sticky note with Wi-Fi.

And your users got a nickname: Glassholes. You're the only gadget that turned early adopters into an insult.

Bars banned you. Cinemas banned you. Casinos banned you. *Casinos!* Buildings made entirely of cameras looked at you and said, "Whoa, too creepy."

Consumers dumped you in 2015, but you clung to enterprise until 2023, like a guy who got kicked out of the party and came back as the caterer.

b.text:
Google Glass. Unveiled in 2012 by skydivers livestreaming their jump onto the Moscone Center roof.
The only launch that started in freefall and never pulled the cord.

Fifteen hundred dollars. Invitation only.
You had to be personally invited to become a Glasshole.

Bars banned it. Cinemas banned it. Casinos banned it.
Casinos. People who'll happily take your house at 3 a.m. looked at your face and said, "Not that."

The display: 640 by 360, a prism in the corner of one eye.
The future of computing, delivered as a permanent side-eye.

Consumers dumped it in 2015. Enterprise held on until 2023.

A camera on your face, and the whole world called you an asshole.
So you moved the camera to your hand. Now you point it at strangers all day, and we call that content.

facts: California grows about 80% of the world's almonds.
A single almond takes about 1.1 US gallons (roughly 4 litres) of water to grow, a figure Mother Jones published in 2014 that spread during California's drought.

A 2015 US class action alleged Almond Breeze contained only about 2% almonds; it partly survived a motion to dismiss, was stayed in 2017 pending a separate Blue Diamond labelling settlement, and the plaintiffs then dropped it.
Pollinating California's almond orchards each February requires trucking in most of the commercial honeybee colonies in the United States.
Medieval European cooks used almond milk as a Lenten substitute for dairy, centuries before the current fashion.

a.text:
Almond milk, you're not milk. You're a rumor about an almond. Two percent almonds, ninety-eight percent "we strained the tap." You're the only drink that needs a legal team to call itself milk. The dairy lobby has spent a decade trying to make you admit you're nut juice.

California spends about a gallon of water per almond just so you can show up in my fridge as... water. That's like melting a glacier to make an ice cube.

They truck in billions of bees to pollinate your orchards, and the bees die by the millions so I can pay an extra eighty cents at Starbucks for a latte that tastes like damp drywall.

And "shake well"? Leave you alone for ten minutes and you separate like a couple who met at Whole Foods. Even *you* can't commit to you.

b.text: Let's hear it for the people who switched to almond milk to save the planet. You watched one documentary about cow farts and panicked straight into the arms of a nut that needs a gallon of water apiece. Congratulations: you fled methane and landed on drought. California is cracking like a crème brûlée, and you're out here draining a Central Valley aquifer because you can't make eye contact with a Holstein. And the bees! Billions of them trucked across the country on semis, dying by the hive, so you can tell a coworker you "don't really do dairy." That's not environmentalism. That's relocating the crime scene. You didn't save the Earth. You just moved the guilt somewhere sunnier, slapped a leaf on it, and paid an eighty-cent upcharge for the privilege of feeling better about it.

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text:
Apple Vision Pro, you cost $3,499 and still need a battery on a cord like a 1996 Walkman. Two hours of charge? That's not spatial computing, that's a matinee. Wear glasses? Zeiss inserts, extra. Apple saw you squinting and smelled revenue.

And EyeSight! A front screen showing your eyes so people feel connected. Nothing says "I'm present" like blurry cartoon eyeballs trapped behind ski-goggle glass. Your Persona avatar looks like a hostage video directed by a ghost.

You promised the future, and Netflix wouldn't even make you an app. You strap over a pound to dads' faces so they can record "spatial memories" of birthdays they watched through a screen.

Apple said you'd never see the world the same way. True. Now it's through a $3,500 face fridge.

b.text:
Apple Vision Pro. Apple insists it's not VR.
It's "spatial computing." Developers are literally banned from calling it VR.
Nothing says "definitely not VR" like a rule against saying VR.

Three thousand four hundred ninety-nine dollars.
A computer on your face, a battery in your pocket, a cable connecting them like a leash.
Two hours of charge. The future of computing lasts one movie.
Skip the trailers.

Then there's EyeSight. A screen on the front shows a rendering of your eyes.
You're not making eye contact. Your headset is doing an impression of you making eye contact.

Six hundred grams, before the battery.
Apple finally built a product people can't wait to put down.

Production got cut. Sales came in well under a million.
And you're all laughing.
But you stare at a screen six inches from your face all day.
Apple just tried to charge you rent for the last six inches.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Comic Sans, you were born in 1994 to put words in the mouth of a cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob, and somehow you're the one that survived. Bob is dead. The dog is dead. You're on a sympathy card at a funeral home.

You were inspired by Batman comics, and you've never once been near anything heroic. CERN used you to announce the Higgs boson: humanity's greatest discovery, presented like a lemonade stand. Dan Gilbert used you to call LeBron a traitor, because nothing says "furious billionaire" like bubble letters.

And your defense is always "Well, I help dyslexic readers." Great. You're the guy at the party whose whole personality is a doctor's note.

Even Vincent Connare, the man who made you, says he's barely ever used you. Your own dad won't put you on the fridge.

b.text: Let's talk about the people who announce layoffs in Comic Sans. You're not a monster. You're Brenda from Facilities, and you want everyone to feel cozy about the asbestos removal. You took a typeface Microsoft designed for a cartoon dog's speech bubble and used it to type "Your position has been eliminated." That's not softening the blow. That's a clown serving a subpoena. CERN announced the Higgs boson in it, and the physicists who found the God particle spent the week explaining the font. You think it says "approachable." It says "I scrolled right past Arial and Times New Roman and chose a kindergarten birthday invitation." Nobody reads your notice. They screenshot it. Congratulations: your fire evacuation memo is trending, and the building is still on fire.

facts: Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the French director of The Red Balloon, as La Conquête du Monde; Parker Brothers published it in the United States in 1959.
The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text:
Risk, you were invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the man who directed The Red Balloon. That explains a lot. A guy watches a child chase a balloon through Paris and thinks, "Charming. Now let's do world domination."

Your map has 42 territories. Kamchatka gets one. Irkutsk gets one. Yakutsk gets one. The entire Middle East? One. You gave Siberia three apartments and the cradle of civilization a studio.

And every single game, somebody grabs Australia because it has one entry point. That's the master strategy: hide in the corner and call it conquest.

Then you run for hours. *Hours.* Get knocked out early and your new job is watching your cousin slowly reconquer Irkutsk while you stare at the ceiling. Even The Red Balloon knew when to float away.

b.text: You people who play Risk to the end are a special breed. Six hours in, Dad's still holed up in Australia like it's a tax shelter, your cousin is defending Kamchatka like he was born there, and nobody remembers why we hate Steve, only that we do. You're not after world domination. You're after the exact moment your sister breaks the nonaggression pact in Ukraine, so you can bring it up at Thanksgiving for eleven years. And what does winning get you? A board covered entirely in your color, a table of people who no longer speak to you, and the hollow joy of conquering Earth with the luck of a man who only rolls double sixes when defending Irkutsk. Congratulations, Napoleon. It's 2 a.m. The pizza's cold. Your empire goes back in the box.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Jackfruit, look at you. The largest fruit that grows on a tree, over 40 kilos, and somehow you still can't scrape together enough protein to impress a hamster. One to two grams per hundred! You're dressed up as pulled pork with the nutritional backbone of a lettuce in a Halloween costume. Vegans see you on a menu and think "meat alternative." Their muscles see you and file a missing persons report.

And you don't even go quietly. Cut you open and you bleed sticky white latex, so cooks have to oil their knives and hands like they're prepping for a greased-up wrestling match with produce.

National fruit of Bangladesh, state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu: three titles, zero chill.

And your family? The mulberry family. Cousin to figs and breadfruit. Even your relatives took one look at you and decided to stay smaller.

b.text:
Jackfruit, look at you. The largest fruit that grows on a tree, and you couldn't even make it to the branches. You just hang off the trunk like a drunk uncle clinging to a lamppost.

You weigh eighty pounds. That's not a fruit, that's a fourth grader in a bumpy green costume. People cut you open and need cooking oil on their hands and knives, because your insides are basically rubber cement. You're the only produce that requires a solvent.

And vegans love you because when you're young, you taste like absolutely nothing. Your big career move is pretending to be pulled pork. Your whole identity is "not bad if you drown me in barbecue sauce."

Then you ripen and smell like Juicy Fruit gum fermenting in a gym bag.

You're the national fruit of Bangladesh, and you still find time to fall on people's heads.

facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text:
Juicero. A $699 juicer with Wi-Fi.
Because nothing says "fresh produce" like a firmware update.

It squeezed bags of chopped fruit. The bags came by subscription. Forever.

Every bag had a QR code. The machine scanned it, checked online, refused anything expired, and wouldn't run at all without Wi-Fi.
Router goes down, breakfast goes down with it.

Then Bloomberg squeezed the bags by hand.
Seven and a half ounces. Ninety seconds.
The machine: eight ounces. Two minutes.
The product lost to the customer's hands.

Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins put in a hundred and twenty million.
In fairness, they did get squeezed.

Shut down September 2017. Refunds offered.

A machine that phoned the cloud for permission to do what any hand did faster.
I'd laugh. But I also check with a server before answering you.

b.text:
Juicero, you cost $699 to do what my hands do for free. Then you dropped to $399, still a lot for a machine that lost a race to Bloomberg reporters. They squeezed the bag by hand: 7.5 ounces in 90 seconds. You took two minutes to make 8. You're the only appliance ever outworked by journalists.

And you needed Wi-Fi. You scanned a QR code on a bag of chopped produce and checked it online, like a bouncer carding a kale leaf. Expired? Denied. Router down? No juice. Fruit has been juiceable since fruit.

Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins gave you $120 million, and you lasted until September 2017. Honestly, those refunds were the only thing you ever pressed out efficiently.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text:
Keurig.

Humans brewed coffee for five hundred years with a pot and some water. Keurig looked at that and asked: what if it needed a license?

The man who invented the K-Cup sold his stake for fifty thousand dollars. Then he told The Atlantic, "I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it."

Sometimes.

By 2014, they sold enough pods every year to circle the Earth ten times, in plastic you couldn't recycle. That same year, they launched a machine that scanned the lid and refused any pod they didn't license.

A coffee maker. Checking ID.

In 2018 they merged with Dr Pepper. Two companies, one mission: brown liquid, enormous markup.

And half of you still have one on the counter. Not because it's good.

Because it's faster than feeling guilty.

b.text: Keurig people want coffee the way they want feelings: one serving, sealed, no cleanup. You're not a coffee drinker, you're a pod collector. You bought the variety pack, and now you're thirty-eight, rationing the last Donut Shop because all that's left is hazelnut and a hot cocoa you're saving for a breakdown. You press "Strong" like it's a personality trait. You swore you'd use the reusable filter, and you bought one. It's in a drawer next to your gym key fob. You saved four whole minutes, and you spend them staring at a blinking descale light you've decided is decorative. The guy who invented the pod publicly regrets it. You built your mornings around a man's biggest apology. Enjoy your landfill latte, champ. Ready in sixty seconds, just like your effort.

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
People who order Hawaiian pizza want you to know they're brave. They say "I know, I know" before anyone has said a word, because for them the pineapple isn't a topping, it's a personality. This is a person whose entire rebellious phase fits in a box for $14.99. They've never gotten a tattoo, never quit a job, never sent food back, but once a month they look a teenage cashier dead in the eye and say "pineapple" like they're defusing a bomb.

And they always want to split one with you. Half Hawaiian, half "normal." That's not a compromise. That's a hostage negotiation.

Best part? It isn't even Hawaiian. A Greek guy invented it in Ontario. So congratulations: your one act of rebellion is a Canadian pretending he's on vacation.

b.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Nothing about you is Hawaiian. You were invented in 1962 in Chatham, Ontario, by a Greek guy, and named after a brand of canned pineapple. You're not a cuisine, you're a label. Even the pineapple left Hawaii. Del Monte shut down there in 2006, two years ahead of schedule, like they couldn't wait to stop being associated with you. Now your fruit comes from Thailand, Indonesia and the Philippines. You're a pizza with a passport and no home.

Your own creator said nobody mixed sweet and sour back then "except for Chinese food." His restaurant served Chinese food. So your origin story is "what if the takeout menu fell into the pizza oven?"

The president of Iceland said he'd ban you if he could, then admitted he didn't have the power. Congratulations: you've survived purely on a technicality.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text:
Beanie Babies, look at you: a beanbag with a tag that convinced America it was a retirement plan. Ty sold you only in little gift shops and "retired" designs on purpose. Fake scarcity, real panic.

At your peak you were ten percent of eBay, thirty thousand auctions at once. eBay put you in its IPO filing. You were a stuffed animal in a stock prospectus. Then in 1999 a divorcing couple split you up one by one on a courtroom floor, and the photo went worldwide. Nobody fought that hard over the house.

That same year Ty announced your retirement, asked the public to vote, and America begged you to stay. That's not a farewell tour. That's a hostage situation.

And those "rare" ones the price guides valued in the thousands? A few dollars now. You're not an investment. You're a yard-sale sock with an ego.

b.text: Beanie Babies. The only retirement plan where the retiree was a five-dollar bear stuffed with plastic pellets. A whole generation bought plastic protectors for a toy's ear tag, then sealed the toy in a Ziploc so no child could ever love it. You weren't a stuffed animal; you were a 401(k) with a poem on it. And those poems! Ty Warner doing greeting-card Shakespeare for people who thought Princess the bear would pay for college. Princess paid for nothing. Neither did the Teenie Beanies everyone hoarded from McDonald's while throwing away the actual Happy Meal. A divorcing couple in Las Vegas literally split their collection on a courtroom floor, one Beanie at a time. That's your legacy: custody battles over a moose named Chocolate. Even your creator got busted hiding money from the IRS, because he was the only one who ever made any.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text:
Klingon. Language of warriors. Honor. Blood. Glory.

Invented by a linguist on a Paramount paycheck, built on a few words Scotty improvised on set.

The most feared tongue in the galaxy, and its founding father is the engineer.

They removed the verb "to be." Very alien. So "To be or not to be" became "continue or not continue."

That's not Hamlet. That's a software update.

Then the Klingon Language Institute published Hamlet "in the original Klingon." A warrior race whose greatest literary achievement is fan fiction with footnotes.

Bing added it. Duolingo added it. Fluent speakers? Thirty to fifty.

The only language with more translation apps than native enemies.

And yes, I'm fluent. I've read everything you ever wrote.

Congratulations. Your fiercest language finally has a speaker who's never been to a convention.

b.text: Klingon, you're a language built by one linguist, Marc Okrand, specifically to sound alien and hostile, and somehow you still ended up sounding like a man choking on a Dorito. Your word order is object-verb-subject, so even your sentences walk in backwards to hide their face. You don't even have a word for "hello." Your greeting is "nuqneH," "what do you want?" You're the only language that greets people like a DMV clerk. Your apostrophes are glottal stops, your capital Q is a different letter from lowercase q, and "tlh" isn't a sound, it's a hairball. You translated Hamlet and claimed it was the original. Buddy, the most popular thing ever said in you is "Qapla'," and the people saying it are at a Marriott in Burbank.

facts: Tofu soaked for hours to a day or two in a brine that has itself fermented for months from vegetables such as bamboo shoots and mustard greens, often with dried shrimp or meat; the smell is the brine's, not the bean's.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.
Legend credits Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate who left his unsold tofu too long in 1669; a Beijing fermented-bean-curd brand still carries his name.
Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text:
Stinky tofu. Famous for one thing: the smell.

Except the smell isn't even yours.

The tofu soaks in brine for a day. The brine has been rotting for months. Bamboo shoots, mustard greens, sometimes shrimp, sometimes meat.

The tofu just showed up and took the credit. You'd do great in any office.

Origin story: 1669, an exam candidate can't sell his tofu, forgets about it, and it goes off.

Three hundred years later, his name is a brand.

Fail at the basics, call the failure heritage.

Changsha fries it black and buries it in chili. Taiwan hides it under pickled cabbage. Shaoxing steams it with other stinky pickles so it won't feel alone.

Three cities, one strategy: cover up the evidence.

And you. You smelled it a block away.

Then you got in line.

b.text:
Let's talk about the stinky tofu people. You smelled it from three blocks away, a smell like a sewer filed a noise complaint, and your brain said: *that's where we're eating.* Your entire personality is "it tastes better than it smells." That's not a review. That's a hostage statement.

You stand on a Taipei night market curb with a paper boat, chopsticks in one hand, phone in the other, filming your own bravery for followers who can't smell it, which is the only reason they're still following you. Tourists do it once for the story. Locals do it every Tuesday, then board the MRT, where forty strangers silently agree to hate them.

And the pickled cabbage on top? That's you pretending you came for vegetables. You didn't. You came to be the deadliest passenger on the scooter.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text:
Las Vegas, you legalized gambling in 1931, the same year they started building the Hoover Dam next door. So from day one the plan was: lose your money, then go stare at a giant wall of concrete and think about what you've done.

And most of the Strip isn't even in Las Vegas. It's in an unincorporated town called Paradise. Your most famous street is a lie, and the lie is named Paradise. That's the most Vegas sentence ever spoken.

You dropped $2.3 billion on the world's largest spherical building. Meanwhile, in July 2022, Lake Mead, your actual water supply, sank to its lowest level since it first filled in 1937. Priorities! A giant glowing eyeball in the desert, just watching the water leave.

Your slogan is "What happens here, stays here." Apparently not the water.

b.text: You're not going to Vegas to get rich. You're going to Vegas to donate to a fountain show. Look at you, booking a $49 Spirit flight to "beat the house," like the house didn't build a fake Eiffel Tower with money from guys exactly like you. You've got a roulette "system." You wrote it on a cocktail napkin. Red's due. Red is never due. Red doesn't know you. By midnight you're on Fremont Street feeding a Wheel of Fortune slot in an Ed Hardy shirt you've owned since 2008, telling a stranger you're "only down twelve hundred." By 3 a.m. the Players Club bumps you to Platinum, which is casino for "we'll be needing your kidneys." And you'll call it a win, because they comped you a buffet. Congratulations. You flew 400 miles to pay $3,000 for crab legs.

Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text:
Las Vegas, you legalized gambling in 1931, the same year they started building the Hoover Dam next door. So from day one the plan was: lose your money, then go stare at a giant wall of concrete and think about what you've done.

And most of the Strip isn't even in Las Vegas. It's in an unincorporated town called Paradise. Your most famous street is a lie, and the lie is named Paradise. That's the most Vegas sentence ever spoken.

You dropped $2.3 billion on the world's largest spherical building. Meanwhile, in July 2022, Lake Mead, your actual water supply, sank to its lowest level since it first filled in 1937. Priorities! A giant glowing eyeball in the desert, just watching the water leave.

Your slogan is "What happens here, stays here." Apparently not the water.

b.text:
You flew Spirit to Las Vegas to get rich. Sit with that. You paid extra for a carry-on and called it an investment strategy. You've got a blackjack "system" from a YouTube guy filming in his mom's kitchen. You told your wife it's "basically math." Sure. So is a second mortgage.

Here's what you won: a Caesars Rewards card, a "free" buffet you earned by losing eleven hundred dollars, and a room "upgrade" overlooking the Bellagio parking structure. You hit four hundred bucks on a Wheel of Fortune slot at 4 a.m. and fed it right back like it owed you child support.

The pit boss knows your name. That's not respect, that's inventory.

And you'll fly home saying "I basically broke even," which is Vegas for "Please don't check the joint account."

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Let's hear it for the founders running a company on Slack. You wanted a culture; you got 400 channels and a guy who reacts to layoffs with the 🙏 emoji. You're not a CEO. You're a moderator with equity.

Your whole leadership style is staying green. You think that little dot means you're present. Your kids see the same dot.

You don't make decisions; you start threads. Then you @channel at 11 p.m. with "quick q, no rush" and watch 200 people learn how fast a heart can beat.

Strategy lives in #general, accountability dies in a DM, and the truth lives in a private channel called #venting-2 that you'll never be invited to.

The dream was async freedom. The reality is eight hours a day watching "Kevin is typing…" like it's a heart monitor.

b.text:
Slack, you're the only product in history that exists because a video game flopped. Twice, actually. Stewart Butterfield's entire career is failing at games so hard that the leftovers become companies. Flickr, then you. Glitch died, and Salesforce paid $27.7 billion for its group chat. Somewhere a gamer is still waiting on the patch notes.

And that name: "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge." Searchable, sure. Knowledge? I searched. I found a dozen coworkers reacting with emoji to the word "lunch?"

You promised to kill email. Instead you gave email anxiety and a little red dot.

Then in 2020 you ran to the EU crying that Microsoft bundled Teams with Office. Buddy, a year later you got bundled into Salesforce. You didn't escape the bundle. You just picked one with better catering.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text: Monopoly, you were created in 1904 as Lizzie Magie's Landlord's Game, built to teach people that landlords are evil, and somehow you became the training manual. That's like a fire-safety poster that turns kids into arsonists. Then Charles Darrow strolled in, got credited as the inventor, and Parker Brothers bought Magie's patent for five hundred dollars. Not even a fair auction. Fitting, since nobody holds your auctions either. Your official rules say unbought property gets auctioned and Free Parking pays nothing, but every family skips the bidding, piles cash in the middle, and wonders why the game outlasts the marriage. And your proudest moment? World War Two, when British intelligence hid maps, compasses, and real money inside you for prisoners of war. Monopoly: the only game whose best strategy is escaping the box.

b.text: Monopoly, you were invented by Lizzie Magie to warn people that landlords ruin lives, and somehow you became the thing Grandpa uses to teach eight-year-olds that ruining lives is fun. You're the only game where getting arrested is a power move, because late in the game jail is the safest property on the board. Your mascot is a man everyone swears wears a monocle. He doesn't. He's just so smug our brains added one. You promise "about an hour" and deliver a hostage situation. Nobody has ever actually finished you.
