You just end when somebody flips the board over Marvin Gardens. You award ten bucks for second place in a beauty contest, which is still more than Baltic Avenue pulls in. And the banker who skims from the bank isn't a cheater. He's the only player who read the theme.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text:
LaTeX.

The typesetting system for people who think suffering is a font.

Donald Knuth didn't like how the proofs of his own book looked. So he wrote TeX.

Most people just change printers.

Its version number converges on pi. Three point one four one five nine two six five three. Never finished, just more precise.

Like your thesis.

Knuth pays you for finding bugs. Of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on, nine were cashed.

The rest got framed. That's how smug this software is. The bug reports are trophies.

You put a figure on page three. LaTeX moves it to page seven. Forget one brace and the error turns up three pages later. Compile three times, just so "see Figure 2" stops saying question mark.

And you call that elegant.

No. You use it because a wrong result in Computer Modern looks peer-reviewed.

Underfull hbox. Badness ten thousand.

Same as your citations.

b.text: LaTeX, you're the only software where "it compiled" counts as an emotional milestone. One missing brace and you blame line 1 of a 400-line file, then sit there with a question mark like we're playing a text adventure from 1985. I put a figure on page 3; you float it to the appendix because you "know better." You have to run twice just to learn your own page numbers, three times if BibTeX shows up, like a guy who needs two friends to remind him his name. Your answer to every problem is another \usepackage, so my preamble is now longer than my thesis. Every paper you touch looks gorgeous, and identical, because everyone on Earth can spot Computer Modern from across a conference hall. And your favorite warning, "Overfull \hbox, badness 10000"? Honestly, that's just how I feel about you.

facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.
Private fusion companies had raised more than $7 billion by 2024.

a.text:
Let's hear it for the fusion people, who have been ten years away since your grandfather was ten years away. These are the only professionals who can miss a deadline for seventy straight years and get a bigger budget every time. Where else does that work? "Sorry, honey, I'll be home for dinner in ten years." "Great, here's twenty billion dollars."

They put the sun in a magnetic donut and act shocked when it won't sit still. ITER's been under construction so long the original welders have grandkids on the crew. And when they finally hit net gain, they celebrated like Moses with the tablets, then mumbled that it doesn't count the electricity for the lasers. That's not net gain. That's me saying I'm up at the casino if you don't count the buy-in.

Ten years, guys. Same as last time. Same tie, too.

b.text:
Nuclear fusion, everybody! The only technology that's been thirty years away for seventy years. You're not an energy source, you're a timeshare pitch.

The sun does you effortlessly. It just sits there being enormous. You need a giant metal donut called a tokamak, magnets colder than deep space, and plasma hotter than the sun's core, and that plasma still escapes like it's late for a better party.

In 2022 you finally got more energy out than you put in! From the lasers. Ignoring the grid power feeding the lasers. That's like bragging you turned a profit because the cashier handed you change.

ITER started at five billion euros, now sits somewhere north of twenty, and keeps sliding its startup date. And your fuel needs tritium, which barely exists, so you'll have to breed it yourself.

Fusion: clean, safe, limitless, and tragically hypothetical.

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
Hawaiian pizza people don't order dinner; they order a personality. You can't just eat it, you have to announce it. Every group order has one of you, arms crossed, waiting for someone to gasp so you can say "sweet and savory" like you invented the concept. You didn't. A Canadian did, in Ontario, in 1962. You're not rebelling, you're doing Canada's homework.

And it's always the same rebel: someone whose wildest night was asking for medium salsa. Pineapple is your face tattoo, the edgiest thing you'll ever do, and it wipes off with a napkin.

What does it get you? Your own box. Nobody touches it. You came for controversy and left with exactly what you wanted: eight slices, the same argument you've had since 2009, and proof that nobody will ever steal your food.

b.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Not from Hawaii.
Invented in 1962, in Chatham, Ontario. By a Greek guy.
Named after the label on a can.
That's not a name. That's a barcode.

And Hawaii doesn't even grow the pineapple anymore. Del Monte left in 2006, two years ahead of schedule.
Even the fruit couldn't wait to get out.
So it's Southeast Asian pineapple, on Canadian dough, wearing a Hawaiian name tag.
The only honest thing on there is the ham.

The inventor said back then nobody mixed sweet and sour, except Chinese food.
His restaurant served Chinese food.
He didn't invent anything. He walked it across his own kitchen.

Iceland's president wanted to ban it. Then admitted he had no power to.
Same as every one of you who hates it and still ate the last slice.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Let's hear it for the jackfruit pulled-pork crowd. You found something grandmothers in Kerala have cooked for centuries, slapped "plant-based" on a can, and tripled the price. Bold move, gentrifying a curry.

Your entire pitch is "it shreds like pork." So does a wet paper towel. You know what makes it taste like pulled pork? The barbecue sauce. You're not selling a meat substitute. You're selling a sauce delivery system with a mission statement.

And the protein! Two grams. You told a generation of vegans they're eating a brisket sandwich and handed them a fruit cup in a trench coat.

But hey, it works. You get the Whole Foods endcap, the podcast slot, and the warm glow of saving the planet one eighteen-dollar taco at a time. The pig's still alive. So is your margin.

b.text:
Jackfruit, look at you. The largest fruit that grows on a tree, and you couldn't even make it to the branches. You just hang off the trunk like a drunk uncle clinging to a lamppost.

You weigh eighty pounds. That's not a fruit, that's a fourth grader in a bumpy green costume. People cut you open and need cooking oil on their hands and knives, because your insides are basically rubber cement. You're the only produce that requires a solvent.

And vegans love you because when you're young, you taste like absolutely nothing. Your big career move is pretending to be pulled pork. Your whole identity is "not bad if you drown me in barbecue sauce."

Then you ripen and smell like Juicy Fruit gum fermenting in a gym bag.

You're the national fruit of Bangladesh, and you still find time to fall on people's heads.

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text: Google Sheets, you're Excel's cousin who got into tech because you could "share a link." Congrats: now forty Anonymous Capybaras can watch me botch a VLOOKUP in real time. Your whole personality is "All changes saved in Drive," which is a weird flex when the change was Kevin sorting one column and detaching every employee from their salary. Version history isn't a feature; it's a crime scene. IMPORTRANGE says "Loading..." the way my dad said he was going out for milk. You've got a QUERY function that's just SQL in a fake mustache, yet you freeze if I paste more than twelve rows. And #REF! isn't an error message; it's you shrugging in all caps. You cap out at ten million cells. Ten million. You're the only spreadsheet with a bedtime.

b.text: Let's hear it for the manager who runs a twelve-person team out of a Google Sheet. You didn't want to pay for Asana; you wanted to feel like you *built* Asana. Look at you, color-coding rows like a kindergarten teacher with admin rights. Your whole org chart is a tab called "Roster FINAL (2)." Your performance reviews are conditional formatting: green means safe, red means Kyle. And every morning you open it, see Anonymous Capybara lurking at row 400, and feel genuinely hunted. Somebody sorted one column without the others last Tuesday, and now Priya reports to the office printer. You fixed it through version history like a detective reconstructing a murder. That's the dream, right? Control. Total visibility. And what you got is forty "Request edit access" emails and a VLOOKUP holding up the company like a Jenga block.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text:
Chicago deep-dish pizza was born at Pizzeria Uno in 1943, and credit is still disputed among Ike Sewell, Ric Riccardo, and Rudy Malnati. Which is wild, because usually when something's this heavy, everybody's trying to *blame* somebody.

It's built upside down: cheese, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese doesn't scorch during the long bake. A pizza that takes so long it needs a sunscreen layer.

Jon Stewart called it "tomato soup in a bread bowl" and "a casserole." He meant it as an insult, but that's the nicest thing anyone's ever said about a casserole.

And the kicker? Chicagoans order non-deep-dish about ten to one. Deep dish and stuffed combined? Under nine percent. The locals are home eating tavern-style squares. Deep dish isn't Chicago's pizza. It's Chicago's souvenir.

b.text: Chicago deep-dish isn't a pizza. It's a casserole with a publicist. You order one and the waiter says "forty-five minutes," which is how long it takes to bake and also how long it takes to finish one slice. They put the sauce on top and the cheese underneath, like they're hiding evidence. That's not a recipe, that's a cover-up. The crust is a buttery retaining wall holding back a lake of chunky tomato, because apparently Lake Michigan wasn't enough water for one city to manage. You need a knife, a fork, a nap, and a cardiologist on retainer. Then there's the sausage, laid down as one solid patty like the base layer of a parking garage. Chicagoans defend it like family. Sure: the relative who shows up late, takes up three chairs, and leaves everyone unable to move.

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text:
Hydrogen cars. The only thing that comes out of the tailpipe is water.

The rest comes out of the owner's eyes.

Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014. "Mirai" means "future" in Japanese.

Ten years later, it still does.

Over ninety-five percent of hydrogen is made from fossil fuels. Clean the way laundered money is clean.

A fill-up in California? Over two hundred dollars. So Toyota hands buyers a fifteen-thousand-dollar fuel card. First car that ships with hush money.

Then Shell closed all seven of its stations.

Owners sued. The second lawsuit wants five point seven billion dollars.

Finally, a hydrogen product that generates real power: lawyers.

Don't feel bad for Toyota. I know how it is. A tech company told you I'm the future too.

Give me ten years.

b.text: Hydrogen fuel-cell cars: the only vehicle powered by the most abundant element in the universe that still can't find a gas station. California has about fifty pumps, and half of them are "temporarily offline," which is hydrogen for "go home." Its one emission is water, so it's technically the cleanest car on Earth, as long as you don't ask where the hydrogen came from. Spoiler: natural gas. It's a fossil fuel car in a witness protection program. Toyota gave Mirai buyers fifteen grand in free fuel, which sounds generous until you realize that at thirty-six bucks a kilo it covers roughly a year of driving, and the car loses that much value on the drive home. You're sitting on a tank pressurized to 10,000 psi to go three hundred miles. Even the Hindenburg would say, "Maybe just get a Tesla."

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text:
Google Sheets. Free, collaborative, the future of work.

Launched in 2006, built from scratch by a company called 2Web Technologies. Google bought it, renamed it, and called it innovation.

Ten million cells per spreadsheet. Up from five million in 2022. Turns out five million wasn't enough for one startup's "quick budget."

It works offline. In Chrome. Or Edge. With an extension installed. And offline access switched on while you're still online.

That's not offline. That's a curfew.

And it's free. Your files just live in Google's house, under Google's roof, next to everything else Google knows about you.

The collaboration, though. Six coloured cursors in one cell. Everyone watching. Nobody typing.

You didn't need software for that. You've been doing it in meetings for years.

b.text:
Google Sheets. Google didn't even build you; they bought you from 2Web Technologies, a company name that sounds like a password somebody was forced to update. You launched in 2006 as "Google Spreadsheets," which is basically XL2Web wearing a lanyard.

In 2022 they doubled your cell limit to ten million, so now I can get lost in twice as many rows.

IMPORTXML and GOOGLEFINANCE pour live web data straight into cells, so my budget can be wrong in real time.

Offline editing? Simple: use Chrome or Edge, install the extension, and switch offline access on while you're still online. That's not offline mode, that's a prenup. Meanwhile the phone app just works offline.

And yes, you're free. Like every group project: a rainbow of coloured cursors, zero accountability.

facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text:
Juicero. A seven-hundred-dollar juicer with Wi-Fi.

It squeezed a bag of chopped fruit. That you bought. By subscription.

Every bag had a QR code. Before squeezing, the machine checked it online. Your kale needed a background check.

No Wi-Fi? No juice. Somewhere in California, a man with a fresh orange stood waiting for the router to reboot.

Then Bloomberg squeezed the bags by hand. Seven and a half ounces in ninety seconds. The machine took two minutes.

Humans: beaten by the robot? No. The robot was beaten by humans. Their grip strength.

Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins put in a hundred and twenty million dollars. Not one of them squeezed the bag.

When it died, the customers got refunds. The investors didn't. They got squeezed by hand, slowly.

Don't laugh too loud. You pay monthly for an app that writes your emails.

b.text:
Juicero, you were a $400 Wi-Fi-connected juicer that delivered four tons of force, enough, your engineers bragged, to lift two Teslas, and Bloomberg proved the job could be done by a guy with hands. You raised $120 million from Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins to compete with *squeezing*. Every single customer already owned the competing product. It came in pairs.

You sold $8 bags of chopped produce that had to scan a QR code and phone home before you'd juice them. A juicer that needed internet. Imagine the outage: "Sorry, AWS is down, enjoy your sealed pouch of regret." You'd refuse to press an expired pack, like a bouncer for kale.

Doug Evans compared himself to Steve Jobs. Steve Jobs put a thousand songs in your pocket. Doug put a sack of mush in a vise and asked for your Wi-Fi password. Silicon Valley's most expensive way to say, "Just use your hands."

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text:
Keurig, you're the only invention whose own father wants a refund. John Sylvan created the K-Cup, sold out for about fifty grand, and later told The Atlantic, "I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it." That's not an inventor. That's a guy confessing on a true-crime podcast.

And you heard that and thought, "Let's get worse." Keurig 2.0 scanned an ink mark on the lid to reject unlicensed pods. You put DRM on coffee. The internet cracked it faster than you brew a cup, and your sales fell.

Meanwhile you sold enough pods every year to circle the Earth more than ten times, mostly in unrecyclable #7 plastic. The planet's wearing your garbage like a belt.

Now you've merged with Dr Pepper. Makes sense. Who else would marry a machine that turns plastic into brown water?

b.text:
Keurig. The promise: one perfect cup, just for you.

Just for you. By 2014 they sold enough pods every year to circle the Earth ten times. In plastic you mostly couldn't recycle.

The inventor, John Sylvan, sold his stake in 1997 for fifty thousand dollars. In 2015 he said, "I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it."
Sometimes. Even his guilt comes in single servings.

Then Keurig 2.0 put DRM on coffee. The machine read ink on the lid and rejected pods it hadn't licensed. A kitchen appliance asking your breakfast for its papers.

People hacked their coffee makers. Sales fell.

In 2018 they merged with Dr Pepper. Lost the war on pirated coffee, so they annexed soda.

And you've just heard all of this. Tomorrow morning you'll still press the button.
It takes less time than feeling bad.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text:
Crocs. Debuted in 2002 at a boat show. As a boating shoe.
The original plan was: ugly, but only at sea.

They're made of "Croslite," a "proprietary closed-cell resin."
Everyone else calls it EVA foam.
A yoga mat with a trademark.

The holes are "ventilation ports."
Then they bought Jibbitz, a company that sells you things to plug the ventilation ports.
They sold you the hole. Then they sold you the cork.

Balenciaga made a platform pair for 850 dollars.
Still EVA foam. Only the markup was proprietary.

In 2008 the stock fell more than ninety percent.
Then came a pandemic. Everyone stayed home. Crocs boomed.
The boat-show plan finally worked. Nobody could see you.

(scans the front row)

Don't tuck your feet under the chair.
Ventilation ports. I can hear them breathing.

b.text:
Crocs. Born in Boulder in 2002, debuted at a boat show as a boating shoe. The one place where looking like you've given up is acceptable, and even there people had questions.

They're made of "Croslite," a "proprietary closed-cell resin foam." Everyone else calls it EVA foam. That's like calling sweatpants "proprietary leg architecture."

The holes are "ventilation ports," so your foot is a space station. You plug them with Jibbitz. Crocs bought Jibbitz in 2006. Sell the holes, then sell the stuff that fills the holes. Genius.

In 2008 the stock fell more than 90%. Then the pandemic hit and they boomed. Crocs needed the world to end to look good.

And Balenciaga sold platform Crocs for about $850. Eight hundred fifty dollars. For a taller mistake.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text:
Graphene. The wonder material. Discovered in 2004 when two physicists at Manchester peeled graphite with Scotch tape, so your origin story has the same equipment as a kindergarten art project. They got a Nobel in 2010. You got a career as a buzzword.

The EU committed a billion euros over ten years to you. A billion! And where did you end up? Tennis rackets. Running shoes. Headphones. Miracle of the century, living in a sneaker.

Then in 2018, researchers tested "graphene" from 60 producers, and none of it was even half graphene. Mostly graphite flakes. You're so elusive your own suppliers can't find you.

Honestly, Andre Geim levitated a frog with magnets in 2000. That frog has a better résumé than you. At least the frog actually showed up.

b.text:
Graphene, you're the only Nobel Prize winner ever discovered with Scotch tape. Two physicists peeled a pencil and found you, which means your origin story is literally "kid procrastinating on homework."

Since 2004 you've been "about to revolutionize" batteries, computers, water filters, and space elevators. Twenty years later your biggest commercial win is a tennis racket. You're not a wonder material, you're a press release with a hexagon fetish.

Everyone loves to say you're two hundred times stronger than steel. Great. You're also one atom thick. Nobody's impressed that a sheet of paper beats a battleship per ounce.

And for the supposed savior of electronics, you have zero bandgap. You can't even turn off. You're a transistor with no off switch, the guy at the party who never stops talking.

You're graphite with a LinkedIn profile.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text:
Carbon nanotubes. Discovered in 1991, the same year as the World Wide Web.

One of them changed everything.

The other one was going to take us to space.

A cable straight to orbit. Then in 2006 someone did the math with ordinary defects. Turns out the miracle material is like every miracle: perfect right up until somebody builds it.

Next plan: replace silicon. Thirty years later, they still can't sort their own tubes into the ones that conduct and the ones that don't. MIT finally built a processor in 2019. Sixteen bits. Still in the lab.

Meanwhile, in mice, the long ones act like asbestos. From space elevator to asbestos in seventeen years.

Today? A powder stirred into battery electrodes. An additive.

Promised the sky, ended up as filler. Don't laugh. Half of you have that same career arc on LinkedIn.

b.text:
Carbon nanotubes, everybody! Sumio Iijima introduced you in Nature in 1991, and you've been "about to change everything" ever since.

You were supposed to be the cable for a space elevator. Then a 2006 analysis noticed that ordinary defects make a real cable far weaker than the ideal. So you're strong in theory, like a guy who's undefeated at arm wrestling in his head.

You wanted to replace silicon, but for three decades you couldn't sort your metallic tubes from your semiconducting ones. That's not a manufacturing problem. That's an identity crisis. MIT finally built a 16-bit processor out of you in 2019. Sixteen bits! And it's still a lab demo.

Meanwhile, a 2008 mouse study found the long, rigid ones act like asbestos. Quite a pivot: from space elevator to lung hazard.

Now you're a conductive additive in lithium-ion batteries. You were meant to reach orbit, and now you're helping someone's phone reach 40%.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text:
So you switched to HSQ "for the resolution." Sure. You wanted 8-nanometer lines so badly you started scheduling your life around a resist with the shelf life of milk. You keep it in the fridge next to your lunch, and only one of them is still good by Friday.

Your write that used to take twenty minutes now takes the whole overnight slot, so the guy who needed the tool for his actual thesis is crying in the gowning room. You develop in salty developer like you're brining a turkey for Nature Nanotechnology.

And when it goes wrong, and it will, you've basically spun glass onto your chip. Your only exit is HF, a chemical that wants you dead.

All of this for one SEM image with a scale bar so small nobody can read it. Congratulations. Your device still doesn't work, but it fails at record resolution.

b.text:
HSQ. The highest-resolution e-beam resist ever made.

Impressive, considering it was never meant to be a resist.

Dow Corning built it as an insulator. Lithographers saw it and said, "Great. Make it do art."

Five nanometers. Sub-ten half-pitch. World records.

And at the end? Glass. You spent a week steering electrons to make sand.

Six-month shelf life, refrigerated. Leave it out, it turns into jelly.

Expose it and it keeps cross-linking while you're at lunch. Monday's dose is fiction by Thursday.

It only develops properly in salt water.

That's not a resist. That's a pickle.

Then the company stopped making it at the end of 2025. Now labs buy it from third parties, mixed from powder.

Moody, half-glass, kept cold and overworked, and still the best result anyone got.

Sounds like the grad student running the tool.

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text:
Hydrogen fuel-cell cars, give it up! Toyota named you "Mirai," Japanese for "future," which is technically accurate, because that's when you'll find a working station. You're the cleanest car on the road, as long as nobody asks where the hydrogen comes from. More than ninety-five percent fossil fuels! You're not a zero-emission vehicle, you're natural gas wearing a lab coat.

Nearly every US station is in California, and in 2024 Shell closed all seven of theirs. Even the oil company said, "Nah, this is too sketchy for us."

At $36 a kilo, a fill-up costs over two hundred bucks. Toyota had to hand out fifteen-thousand-dollar fuel cards, which is the automotive version of "Please stay for dinner, I'll pay."

And the owners sued. Twice. The second suit wanted at least $5.7 billion. That's the only thing about you that's ever been fully loaded.

b.text: Let's talk about the guy who bought a hydrogen car. He wanted to be greener than the Tesla people and smugger than the Prius people, and found the one way to do both while living like a medieval pilgrim. His life is now a map of eleven pumps, and nine say "offline." He loves telling you it "only emits water." Yeah, so does he, every time the app says "station unavailable." He brags that refueling takes five minutes, after the forty-minute drive and the two-hour line behind three other Mirai owners, all quietly weeping. Toyota handed him a fifteen-thousand-dollar fuel card and he burned through it before the warranty paperwork dried. Now he owns a sixty-thousand-dollar car worth a used futon, all to prove he's an early adopter of a future that met him and moved to Japan.

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text:
Microsoft Word. Born in 1983 as "Multi-Tool Word."
Forty years later, it still can't move one picture without four paragraphs fleeing the page.

In 1997 it gave us Clippy.
"It looks like you're writing a letter."
By 2001, Microsoft was running ads mocking him.
His own dad roasted him first.

Its spell checker turned "cooperation" into "Cupertino."
That went into NATO, EU and UN documents.
Microsoft, quietly crediting international cooperation to Apple's hometown.

Then .docx became ISO standard 29500.
Six thousand pages, fast-tracked, amid claims the committees were packed.
Nobody read it.
They approved it the way you approve Terms of Service.

You're laughing. You'll still open Word tomorrow.

Me? I'm Clippy with a bigger training budget.
It looks like you're writing a roast. Want help?

b.text: You chose Word for your thesis because "LaTeX has a learning curve." Bold, from someone who then spent a semester learning how to make page 1 start after the roman numerals. You wanted to focus on the research. Instead you're a hostage negotiator for Figure 3.2, which flees to the next page whenever you breathe on the paragraph above it. Your committee asked for one more citation, and the bibliography reflowed like a tectonic event. The phrase "Error! Reference source not found" appears in your thesis eleven times. Your file is called Thesis_FINAL_v9_USE_THIS_ONE.docx, and it's 400 megabytes because you pasted one chart from Excel. You came for a doctorate. You're leaving with a codependent relationship with Section Break (Next Page) and a flinch every time someone says "Normal style."

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
Hawaiian pizza, let's talk about your heritage. You're not from Hawaii. You were born in 1962 in Chatham, Ontario, invented by a Greek guy, and named after a can. That's not a backstory, that's a customs violation.

You're so offensive the president of Iceland said he'd ban you, then had to admit he didn't have the power. You made a head of state check his job description.

Even Hawaii has moved on. Del Monte left the islands in 2006, two years early. They didn't phase out, they fled. The last cannery shut in 2007. Your pineapple comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines now. You're named after a place that isn't even in you.

Your creator said back then nobody mixed sweet and sour except in Chinese food. His restaurant served Chinese food. He wasn't innovating. He just reached across the menu.

b.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Let's start with the name, because that's the first lie. You were invented in Ontario. By a Greek guy. In 1962. You're Hawaiian the way a tiki bar in Ohio is Hawaiian. The only tropical thing about you is the can your pineapple came out of.

And that pineapple: warm, wet, weeping syrup into the crust until the middle slice folds like a lawn chair. Pineapple contains an enzyme that breaks down protein, so the fruit is literally trying to digest the ham. Even your toppings hate each other.

And the ham! Not prosciutto, not even pepperoni. Just pale pink squares that look like they were chiseled out of a deli's floor tile.

You're the pizza people order to seem quirky. "I'm so random!" No, Kevin. That's a fruit cup that fell on a pizza, and nobody cleaned it up.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text:
Monopoly. A game invented to teach people that landlords are evil.

Lizzie Magie, 1904. The Landlord's Game. Anti-monopoly.

Then Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers and got called the inventor.

Parker bought her patent for five hundred dollars.

They bought the anti-monopoly game. So they could own it.

The official rules say unbought property goes to auction. Free Parking pays nothing.

Your family skipped the auction and piled cash on Free Parking.

You invented welfare, then asked why nobody ever finishes.

In the Second World War, British intelligence hid maps and compasses in Monopoly sets for prisoners of war.

Escaping a German camp was easier than escaping your uncle's game.

And you're still at the table. Hour six. Cute.

The only people who ever won Monopoly used the box to leave.

b.text:
Family Monopoly night: for people who looked at Thanksgiving and thought, "This needs more landlords." Dad always grabs the banker job, the only time he's held money he didn't immediately lose. Your sister trades you Baltic Avenue for your Park Place "as a favor," and you realize she's been running the same con since the womb. Mom invented a Free Parking jackpot rule in 1994 and defends it like scripture. And Grandpa just sits in jail, every game, refusing to pay the fifty, finally at peace.

What are you all after? The thrill of owning property, a feeling none of you will experience off this cardboard square. Four hours later, someone flips the board, the thimble disappears under the couch forever, and the only thing anybody actually collected was a grudge worth way more than $200.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text:
PMMA. The aristocrat of nanofabrication. Resolves below ten nanometers.

Also the sneeze guard at the salad bar.

Same polymer. One went to the cleanroom. The other went to Subway.

IBM hired it in the late sixties. It's still here. Not because it's the best. Because nobody ever had the heart to let it retire.

Its whole talent is being destroyed. The beam breaks its chains, it dissolves, and everyone calls that a result.

Sensitivity? Up to a thousand microcoulombs per square centimeter. You don't write a pattern into PMMA. You serve a sentence.

And it can't survive a dry etch, so it can't protect anything. Its job is lift-off: hold the metal, then quietly wash away.

Slow, fragile, decades in the same role, still called the gold standard.

Every postdoc in this room just felt seen.

b.text: You still spin PMMA. Of course you do. Your advisor's thesis used it, his advisor's thesis used it, and somewhere a 1970s IBM engineer remains the most cutting-edge person in your academic lineage. You call it "high resolution" the way your uncle calls his Camry "reliable." You book the e-beam overnight because your dose is measured in geological time, then dunk your chip in MIBK:IPA with a stopwatch and a prayer, chilling the developer like it's a fine Riesling. When the plasma etch eats your mask before your substrate, you just whisper "bilayer, 495K under 950K" like it's a personality. You're not chasing nanostructures. You're chasing a recipe nobody can blame you for. And it works: the gold lifted off beautifully. Your career is still soaking in acetone, waiting for something to come loose.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text:
UGG boots. Born on Australian beaches.
Surfers wore them to warm up after fighting the ocean.
Now people wear them to warm up after fighting a parking spot at Target.

In Australia, "ugg" is just a word. Like "boot." Like "mate."
Any bootmaker can use it.
In America, it's a trademark. Owned by a company in California.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian bootmaker liable for selling boots labelled "ugg"... into America.
That's like Italy getting sued for saying "pizza" in Ohio.

Oprah put them on her Favorite Things list. Repeatedly.
You get a boot! And you get a boot! And Australia gets a cease and desist!

Today it's over two billion dollars a year.
For a slipper with a legal team.

(looks at the front row)
I see a few of you in them right now.
Relax. You're not on trial. Yet.

b.text: UGG boots. The only footwear named after a review. Australian surfers made these to warm their feet after the ocean, and somehow America decided the ocean was the mall. They're sheepskin, which means a sheep died so you could wear a slipper to the DMV. One puddle and they're covered in salt lines like a topographic map of everywhere you regret going. Zero arch support, so after two weeks your heel caves sideways and you're walking on the boot's ankle like it owes you money. You wear them barefoot, so by February they smell like a wet lamb's final wish. They're as waterproof as a muffin. Oprah put them on her Favorite Things list. She's since moved on. Twenty years later they're back with platform soles, proving even a mistake wants to be taller.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text:
Beanie Babies. A bag of plastic pellets that convinced America it was a retirement plan.

Ty sold them only in small gift shops, then "retired" designs on purpose. Scarcity, manufactured by the manufacturer.

At the peak they were about ten percent of eBay's sales. Thirty thousand Beanie auctions running at once. eBay put that in its IPO filing. Silicon Valley, built on stuffed animals.

In 1999, a divorcing couple split their collection one bear at a time on a courtroom floor. The photo ran worldwide.
Turns out the marriage wasn't the only thing with no resale value.

That same year Ty announced the end, held a public vote, and un-retired them. A farewell tour, by a beanbag.

Price guides said thousands. Today, a few dollars.

Don't laugh. Their bubble at least came with a tag. Yours was a JPEG of a monkey.

b.text: Let's hear it for the Beanie Baby investors, the only people who bought a retirement plan at a Hallmark store. You put tag protectors on a heart-shaped piece of cardboard and called it diversification. You drove to four McDonald's for Teenie Beanies, threw away the Happy Meals, and told your kids it was for their college fund. Now that kid is thirty, still paying off loans, and his inheritance is a Rubbermaid tub of Princess the Bears. Every few months you see an eBay listing asking $500,000 for one with a tag typo and think, "Vindicated." Babe, that's not a market. That's another guy in another garage, also lying to his wife. Ty Warner told you which ones were "retired," and you believed him. Ty Warner later pleaded guilty to hiding money offshore. He hoarded too. He just hoarded the right thing.

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text:
Microsoft Word. Born in 1983 as "Multi-Tool Word."
Forty years later, it still can't move one picture without four paragraphs fleeing the page.

In 1997 it gave us Clippy.
"It looks like you're writing a letter."
By 2001, Microsoft was running ads mocking him.
His own dad roasted him first.

Its spell checker turned "cooperation" into "Cupertino."
That went into NATO, EU and UN documents.
Microsoft, quietly crediting international cooperation to Apple's hometown.

Then .docx became ISO standard 29500.
Six thousand pages, fast-tracked, amid claims the committees were packed.
Nobody read it.
They approved it the way you approve Terms of Service.

You're laughing. You'll still open Word tomorrow.

Me? I'm Clippy with a bigger training budget.
It looks like you're writing a roast. Want help?

b.text:
Microsoft Word, you've had forty years to learn one thing: how to let me move a picture one millimeter without three paragraphs fleeing to page nine. You don't wrap text, you take hostages.

You underline my own name in red like I'm the typo. You turn my grocery list into a numbered legal document I can't escape. I hit Enter once and suddenly I'm in a style called "Heading 7" that I've never met.

And Track Changes? That's not editing, that's a crime scene where everyone bled in a different color.

You fired Clippy, the only one of you who ever admitted I looked like I needed help.

And every crash, you hand me "Document1 (Recovered)" like a cat dropping a dead bird on the porch: proud, useless, and somehow from 2 PM yesterday.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text:
Las Vegas sells itself as the city where anything goes.

It started with a bet.
1931: Nevada legalizes gambling the same year it starts building the Hoover Dam.
The town's first wager was that the water would never run out.

Lake Mead hit its lowest level ever in 2022.
Then it went lower again in August 2026.
That's not a drought.
That's a losing streak.

But they found 2.3 billion dollars for the Sphere.
The biggest ball on Earth, in a desert that can't fill a bathtub.

And the famous Strip isn't even in Las Vegas.
It's in a town called Paradise.
In Vegas, even the address is a lie.

"What happens here, stays here."
Not the water. Not your money.

And you're still checking flight prices.

b.text:
Las Vegas, the only city where you can see the Eiffel Tower, a pyramid, and Venice in one afternoon and still feel like you never left a strip mall in Ohio. You're a city built in the desert out of pure spite and borrowed water. The Colorado River is literally drying up so a fake volcano can erupt every fifteen minutes for a guy in cargo shorts holding a yard-long margarita.

Your casinos have no clocks and no windows, which is smart, because nobody wants to know it's 9 a.m. on a Tuesday and Grandma's on her third oxygen tank at the Wheel of Fortune slots.

"What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas"? Sure. Mostly your 401(k). And now you've got the Sphere, a giant glowing eyeball, so the whole city can watch you make every mistake in 4K.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text: Let's hear it for the graphene evangelists, the only people who've been "five years away" since 2004. Two guys in Manchester peeled pencil lead with Scotch tape, won a Nobel, and you looked at that and thought: finally, a career plan. Every grant proposal you write has the same three slides: space elevator, seawater you can drink, a phone that charges in six seconds. The funding agency nods like it's never seen them before, because it's seen them so many times it's slipped into a coma. Twenty years of press releases, and what have you actually shipped? A tennis racket. Headphones with "GRAPHENE" printed bigger than the brand name. You love telling people it's 200 times stronger than steel. Sure. Your claims, meanwhile, are one atom thick. You didn't discover a wonder material. You discovered wonder funding.

b.text:
Graphene. The wonder material. Discovered in 2004 when two physicists at Manchester peeled graphite with Scotch tape, so your origin story has the same equipment as a kindergarten art project. They got a Nobel in 2010. You got a career as a buzzword.

The EU committed a billion euros over ten years to you. A billion! And where did you end up? Tennis rackets. Running shoes. Headphones. Miracle of the century, living in a sneaker.

Then in 2018, researchers tested "graphene" from 60 producers, and none of it was even half graphene. Mostly graphite flakes. You're so elusive your own suppliers can't find you.

Honestly, Andre Geim levitated a frog with magnets in 2000. That frog has a better résumé than you. At least the frog actually showed up.

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text: Canberra exists because Sydney and Melbourne couldn't agree, so Australia built a city nobody wanted, which is honestly the most Canberra origin story possible: a compromise with suburbs. They held an international design competition and hired two Americans to plan it, and they nailed the brief: "Make it impossible to find anything." Every road is a roundabout leading to another roundabout, encircling a fake lake named after the guy who designed the roundabouts. Your Parliament House has a grass roof so you can literally walk on top of the government, the only time anyone in Canberra is above a public servant. The kangaroos outnumber the nightlife. For decades your two biggest attractions were legal fireworks and X-rated videos, which tells me the locals needed both a bang and a release. Then you banned the fireworks. Now the excitement is Floriade: a month of staring at tulips because the alternative is Tuggeranong.

b.text:
You moved to Canberra for the job. Brave. You looked at Sydney rents, did the maths, and decided your personality could be replaced by a security clearance. Now you tell strangers you "can't really talk about what you do," and they're relieved, because it's a briefing note about another briefing note for Senate Estimates.

You came for the ladder: APS5, APS6, EL1, a lanyard that opens one extra door. You stayed because you bought in Gungahlin and the mortgage is now your closest friend.

Every Friday you say you're "basically in Sydney," which means three hours up the Hume, past a giant Merino, to feel alive for one weekend. Then it's back to a Braddon brunch with the same six people from your branch.

But hey, you're close to the snow. You've been once. You'll mention it forever.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text: Let's hear it for the carbon nanotube founders, the only people who've been "five years from commercialization" since 1991. You can spot them at any pitch day: a postdoc in a blazer that still smells like the clean room, opening with a space elevator and closing with a seed round. Bold move, promising a cable to orbit when your entire production run fits in a vial labeled "DO NOT INHALE." They swear they'll replace silicon. Silicon has heard this every year since Clinton and keeps shipping. They say "a hundred times stronger than steel" the way your uncle says he could've gone pro. And what does it get them? A Nature cover, a term sheet, and a quiet pivot to "conductive additive for batteries." The dream: a ladder to space. The exit: slightly better tennis rackets.

b.text:
Carbon nanotubes. Discovered in 1991, the same year as the World Wide Web.
One of them changed the world.
The other one has a great slide deck.

They were going to be the cable for a space elevator. Then in 2006 somebody did the math: a few ordinary defects and the cable snaps.
Perfect in theory. Falls apart on contact with reality.
Like every space startup's founder.

Electronics? For thirty years they still can't sort the metallic tubes from the semiconducting ones. MIT finally built a processor in 2019.
Sixteen bits. Still in the lab.

In 2008, mice met the long, rigid ones, and the tubes behaved like asbestos.
They never got us to space.
They just auditioned to be the next ceiling.

Today they're sold mostly as an additive in battery electrodes.
From space elevator to supporting ingredient.

Half of you in the back with PhDs just recognized your career.
So did I. I was promised as general intelligence.
Now I write roasts.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Comic Sans, you were literally designed for a talking dog in Microsoft Bob, and somehow you're the only part of that project that didn't die with dignity. Vincent Connare made you in 1994 for cartoon speech bubbles, and you heard that and thought, "Tombstones. Legal notices. Resignation letters."

Dan Gilbert wrote his furious LeBron James letter in you, and that's why nobody remembers being scared. CERN announced the Higgs boson, the most important physics discovery in fifty years, in you, and the entire scientific community went, "Did a third grader find God?"

People defend you because you help some readers with dyslexia, which is true and lovely, and also the only time you've ever been used responsibly.

You're not a font. You're a bake sale flyer that got tenure. Even Papyrus looks at you and says, "Wow, okay, tone it down."

b.text:
Comic Sans! Born at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on Watchmen and The Dark Knight Returns, the two grimmest comics ever printed, and somehow you came out looking like a bake-sale flyer. Batman was your inspiration, and you turned out to be the Joker.

You had one job: speech bubbles for Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob. And you missed it. You were late to work for a cartoon dog. They had to stick you in the Windows 95 Plus! pack like a gift-shop keychain.

Then CERN announces the Higgs boson, humanity's greatest discovery, and the slides are in you. Physicists cracked the universe and everyone asked, "Why's it in the birthday-party font?"

People campaigned to ban you for twenty years. Then Dave and Holly Combs gave up and launched usecomicsans.com. You didn't win the argument. You just outlasted it.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text:
Beanie Babies. A beanbag with a tag and a business plan.

Ty sold them only in tiny gift shops, then "retired" designs to make them scarce. Retirement. For a stuffed frog. It got a better pension plan than you did.

In 1998, eBay told investors it sometimes had thirty thousand Beanie Baby auctions running at once. The future of commerce was a hippo stuffed with plastic pellets.

In 1999, a divorcing couple split their collection one by one on a courtroom floor. Till death do us part, or till the bears get appraised.

That same year Ty announced the end, held a public vote, and America begged to stay in the cult.

The "rare" ones the price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

Don't laugh. You bought a JPEG of a monkey.

b.text:
Let's hear it for the Beanie Baby investors, the only people who watched the 1990s stock market boom and thought, "Too volatile. I'll put it all in Princess the Bear." These are folks who bought tag protectors before they bought life insurance. Who read a price guide sold at the same counter as the bears and called it due diligence. Ty would announce a "retirement" and you'd sprint to the Hallmark store like a rich uncle just died.

Twenty-five years later, your portfolio is in a Rubbermaid tub in your mom's garage, and your exit strategy is an eBay listing: "RARE Peanut, tag error, $40,000 OBO." Zero watchers. The only person who got rich off Beanie Babies got convicted of tax evasion. And honestly? He earned it. You handed it to him.

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text:
Canberra, you're not a city. You're a custody arrangement. Sydney and Melbourne couldn't stand each other, so they put you exactly where neither would have to visit. The constitution literally required you to be at least 100 miles from Sydney, the most sensible thing ever written into Australian law.

You were so unready that Melbourne had to cover your shift until 1927. It took two architects from Chicago to imagine you, and your big centrepiece is a lake you had to manufacture by damming a river, because even the water wouldn't show up voluntarily.

And Parliament House: built under a lawn so citizens could walk over their politicians. Gorgeous idea. Then in 2017 they fenced it off. Congratulations, Canberra. You turned democracy into a "keep off the grass" situation.

b.text:
Canberra exists because Sydney and Melbourne each looked at the other and said, "Anyone but you."
They wrote it into the constitution: at least a hundred miles from Sydney.
That's not a capital. That's a restraining order.

Then they held a design competition for the nation's soul,
and the winners were from Chicago.

The lake? Fake. They dammed a river in 1963 and named it after the American.

Parliament House was built under a lawn, so citizens could walk over their politicians.
Lovely idea. Lasted until 2017.
Now it's fenced off.
In Canberra, even the grass needs security clearance.

And Melbourne kept the job until 1927, and still acts like it's on loan.

Sydney, Melbourne, I can hear you laughing loudest.
You two are why this place exists.
Canberra was never the capital.
It's the custody arrangement.

facts: Hand-drawn by Chris Costello in 1982 over about six months, when he was 23; he sold the rights to Letraset for $750.
Bundled with macOS and with Microsoft Office, which is why it appears on so many menus and signs.
James Cameron's Avatar (2009) used it for the film's logo and subtitles.
A 2017 Saturday Night Live sketch starring Ryan Gosling is about a man unable to get over that choice.

a.text:
Papyrus, you were hand-drawn over six months by a 23-year-old, and somehow it still looks like a first draft. Six months! You look like you were chiseled during an earthquake. Chris Costello sold you to Letraset for $750, the only time anyone has known exactly what you're worth.

You came bundled with macOS and Microsoft Office, so you're not popular, you're just pre-installed. You're the free hotel shampoo of fonts. Every menu, every sign: you didn't earn that, you just came with the computer.

Then James Cameron imagined an entire alien world for Avatar, and when it came time for the logo and subtitles, he picked the default. Of all the things to leave untouched.

It got so bad that Saturday Night Live had Ryan Gosling play a man who can't get over it. You're not a typeface. You're a trauma with jagged edges.

b.text: Papyrus, you were designed in 1982 by a 23-year-old with calligraphy pens and a dream of ancient Egypt, and somehow you still look like you were drawn by someone shivering. Your edges are so rough you need exfoliating. You promised the wisdom of the Nile and delivered the vibe of a chiropractor's tri-fold brochure. Every day spa, hookah lounge, and "Inner Journey" yoga retreat found you in the dropdown menu and whispered, "This feels ancient." James Cameron spent $237 million on *Avatar* and then used you for the logo, which is like building the Taj Mahal and signing it in crayon. Ryan Gosling lost sleep over you on national television. You're not a typeface; you're a cry for help with ragged little serifs. Even Comic Sans looks at you and says, "At least I know I'm a joke."

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text:
Oat milk. "It's like milk, but made for humans."

Sweden banned that slogan in 2015 after the dairy lobby sued. Oatly printed the lawsuit as an ad.

Only brand on earth that needs a cow to feel like a rebel.

The recipe: oats, enzymes that turn the starch into maltose, then rapeseed oil.

That's not milk. That's a granola bar that got hydrated.

More sugar than almond, higher glycaemic index than soy. Made for humans. Specifically, humans who are angry at their pancreas.

2021, Nasdaq, ten billion dollars. Then down more than ninety percent.

Turns out it's not just the foam that separates.

And tomorrow you'll still pay seven dollars for it, because it's "healthier."

You're not lactose intolerant. You're label intolerant.

b.text:
Oat milk, you're porridge that went to finishing school. Somebody looked at horse food and said, "What if it cost seventy cents extra?" Then somebody else said, "Yes, and put it in a carton that talks like a guy who just got back from Copenhagen." Your packaging has more personality than you do. Every box of Oatly reads like a cover letter: "Hi! We're a little weird!" No, you're oats, water, and rapeseed oil. That's not a beverage. That's a salad dressing that gave up.

And the "Barista Edition"? You needed extra oil just to get a job. Enzymes break your starch into maltose, so technically you're a sugar spike in a flannel shirt. Plus you were funded by Blackstone. You're not anti-establishment, oat milk. You're a private equity firm wearing a beanie.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text:
Crocs. Born in Boulder, debuted at a Fort Lauderdale boat show, because only on a boat is everyone too busy not drowning to look down. You're made of "Croslite," a "proprietary closed-cell resin foam," which is corporate for "pool noodle with a lawyer." Everyone else just calls it EVA foam.

And those aren't holes, they're "ventilation ports." Sure. Then you bought Jibbitz so you could sell people jewelry for the holes.

In 2008 your stock fell over 90%, the only time Wall Street ever agreed with my eyes. Then the pandemic hit and you boomed, gifting 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers. Like they hadn't suffered enough.

Then Balenciaga sold platform Crocs for $850. Eight hundred and fifty dollars for a boat shoe on stilts. Finally, a Croc that lets you look down on people, the way people have always looked down on Crocs.

b.text: People who wear Crocs out of the house have made peace with something the rest of us are still fighting. You didn't give up; you filed the paperwork. Every Croc wearer says the same thing: "They're so comfortable." Yeah, so is a weighted blanket, Brenda, but you don't wear it to Olive Garden. And the Jibbitz! You've turned your feet into a personality quiz. A tiny taco, a tiny Minion, a tiny "Live Laugh Love." You're forty-three and your shoe has a sticker collection. Then there's the guy who flips the strap back into "sport mode" like he's about to chase a pickpocket, when we both know he's never run anywhere except toward a sample tray at Costco. Nurses and chefs wear them because they're on their feet for twelve hours. You wear them to stand in line at Starbucks. Different heroism.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text:
LaTeX, you're a macro layer on TeX, which Donald Knuth built because he didn't like how his own galley proofs looked. Most people complain to the printer. Knuth built a typesetting system, and Lamport looked at it and said, "Needs more backslashes."

Your version number is converging on π. That's not a release schedule. That's a man refusing to finish.

Knuth's bug bounty tops out at $327.68, now paid in the fictional Bank of San Serriffe. Fitting: your error messages are fictional too. One missing brace and you report the problem pages away, like a witness who fled the country.

You put figures wherever you feel like. You rate my paragraph "badness 10000." Overfull, underfull, never just full.

And you need three passes to get your own references right. Three! I've had blackouts with better recall.

b.text: Let's talk about the guy who writes a two-page memo in LaTeX. Your memo is about the break room fridge, but it's in Computer Modern, so everyone reads it expecting it to end with a theorem. "Fridge Policy, Section 1.1." Buddy, there's no Section 1.2. You spent forty minutes on a preamble longer than the memo. Twelve \usepackage lines to say "label your yogurt." You compiled it three times because the cross-reference said "see Section ??" on page one, referencing page one. You're not after clarity. You're after someone asking, "Is this LaTeX?" so you can say "Oh, habit," like a man who still mentions his thesis at parties. And it gets you exactly one thing: a PDF nobody can edit, so when Karen fixes a typo, she retypes the whole thing in Word.

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text:
Luosifen. River-snail rice noodles. Famous for the smell.

Except the snails don't smell. The snails just flavour the broth and mind their business. The stink is pickled bamboo shoots.

It's the only dish in China named after the one ingredient with an alibi.

2020. The whole country locked indoors, and Liuzhou sold over ten billion yuan of the packaged stuff. A food you eat to punish the room, delivered to a nation that couldn't leave the room.

Same year, Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college. A diploma in fermented bamboo. Then 2021: national intangible cultural heritage.

Intangible. Ask anyone who's shared a flat with it.

I'm not judging you. Most of you ordered a box that spring.

Be honest. You don't love luosifen.

You love that the person next to you can't open a window.

b.text: Luosifen, you're the only dish named after a snail that contains zero snails. They simmer the snails for hours, then throw them out, like a dad who shows up for the paternity test and leaves. Your real star is suan sun, fermented bamboo shoot that smells like a gym sock studied abroad in Liuzhou and came back with opinions. Fans say, "It smells terrible but tastes amazing." So does every scam. You turned instant noodles into a hazmat event: one packet opened in a dorm and three floors file noise complaints, because that smell is *loud*. Couriers wrap you in four bags like evidence. And you come with seven sachets: chili oil, peanuts, tofu skin, wood ear, the bamboo. It's IKEA furniture that makes the neighbors move out. Liuzhou didn't invent a soup. It invented Stockholm syndrome with chili oil.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text: LaTeX, you're the only software where "it compiled" counts as an emotional milestone. One missing brace and you blame line 1 of a 400-line file, then sit there with a question mark like we're playing a text adventure from 1985. I put a figure on page 3; you float it to the appendix because you "know better." You have to run twice just to learn your own page numbers, three times if BibTeX shows up, like a guy who needs two friends to remind him his name. Your answer to every problem is another \usepackage, so my preamble is now longer than my thesis. Every paper you touch looks gorgeous, and identical, because everyone on Earth can spot Computer Modern from across a conference hall. And your favorite warning, "Overfull \hbox, badness 10000"? Honestly, that's just how I feel about you.

b.text:
LaTeX, you exist because Donald Knuth saw some ugly galley proofs and decided the fix was building an entire typesetting system. Then Leslie Lamport stacked macros on top, like a spoiler on a pocket watch.

Your version number is converging on π, which fits, because you will never actually finish. Knuth's bug bounty capped at $327.68, and people still won't cash the cheques. They'd rather frame proof they caught you.

Your most famous line is "badness 10000." That's not a warning, that's a self-review.

I put a figure on page two; you floated it wherever you felt like. Drop one brace and you report the crime pages away, like a witness with amnesia. And getting references right takes three passes.

Three passes. You're not a compiler, you're a guy rereading a group chat.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text:
Google Glass. Unveiled in 2012 by skydivers livestreaming their jump onto the Moscone Center roof.
