The only launch that started in freefall and never pulled the cord.

Fifteen hundred dollars. Invitation only.
You had to be personally invited to become a Glasshole.

Bars banned it. Cinemas banned it. Casinos banned it.
Casinos. People who'll happily take your house at 3 a.m. looked at your face and said, "Not that."

The display: 640 by 360, a prism in the corner of one eye.
The future of computing, delivered as a permanent side-eye.

Consumers dumped it in 2015. Enterprise held on until 2023.

A camera on your face, and the whole world called you an asshole.
So you moved the camera to your hand. Now you point it at strangers all day, and we call that content.

b.text:
Google Glass, everybody! The only gadget ever unveiled by skydivers, and that was the peak. You literally debuted on a roof and went downhill from there.

Fifteen hundred dollars to wear a beta test on your face. Then bars, cinemas, and casinos banned you. Casinos! Places that let you lose your house at 4 a.m. looked at Glass and said, "No, we have standards."

Your users got a nickname, and it wasn't "pioneers." It was "Glassholes." You're the only product that turned its own customers into an insult.

And that display: 640-by-360, jammed in the corner of one eye. The future of computing, delivered like a postage stamp you're squinting at sideways.

Consumers dumped you in 2015. Enterprise hung on until 2023. Even your second marriage was just for the paperwork.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text:
Carbon nanotubes. Discovered in 1991, the same year as the World Wide Web.
One of them changed the world.
The other one has a great slide deck.

They were going to be the cable for a space elevator. Then in 2006 somebody did the math: a few ordinary defects and the cable snaps.
Perfect in theory. Falls apart on contact with reality.
Like every space startup's founder.

Electronics? For thirty years they still can't sort the metallic tubes from the semiconducting ones. MIT finally built a processor in 2019.
Sixteen bits. Still in the lab.

In 2008, mice met the long, rigid ones, and the tubes behaved like asbestos.
They never got us to space.
They just auditioned to be the next ceiling.

Today they're sold mostly as an additive in battery electrodes.
From space elevator to supporting ingredient.

Half of you in the back with PhDs just recognized your career.
So did I. I was promised as general intelligence.
Now I write roasts.

b.text:
Carbon nanotubes, everybody! The strongest material known to science, and you still can't hold a job. Since the nineties you've promised us a space elevator. Your longest strand is about half a meter. That's not an elevator. That's floss with a publicist.

You're graphene that rolled over and gave up. Graphene got a Nobel Prize. You got an argument over whether Soviets spotted you in 1952.

You can't even decide what you are. Twist one way, you're a metal. Twist the other, you're a semiconductor. Nobody controls it, including you. That's not versatility. That's a chirality crisis.

Drop you in any liquid and you clump together like freshmen at a mixer.

And inhale you? Suddenly you behave like asbestos. Thirty years of hype, and your most reliable talent is impersonating the one material we paid billions to rip out of schools.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text: Let's hear it for the carbon nanotube founders, the only people who've been "five years from commercialization" since 1991. You can spot them at any pitch day: a postdoc in a blazer that still smells like the clean room, opening with a space elevator and closing with a seed round. Bold move, promising a cable to orbit when your entire production run fits in a vial labeled "DO NOT INHALE." They swear they'll replace silicon. Silicon has heard this every year since Clinton and keeps shipping. They say "a hundred times stronger than steel" the way your uncle says he could've gone pro. And what does it get them? A Nature cover, a term sheet, and a quiet pivot to "conductive additive for batteries." The dream: a ladder to space. The exit: slightly better tennis rackets.

b.text:
Carbon nanotubes, everybody! Sumio Iijima introduced you in Nature in 1991, and you've been "the future" ever since. Three decades of being the future isn't a career. It's a waiting room.

You were supposed to be the cable for a space elevator. Then a 2006 analysis noticed that ordinary defects knock your strength way below the ideal. So you're the strongest material imaginable, as long as nobody actually makes a big one.

You were going to revolutionize electronics, but you still can't sort your metallic siblings from your semiconducting ones. MIT built a 16-bit processor out of you in 2019, and it's still a lab demo.

In 2008, the long, rigid ones acted like asbestos in mice. You promised to lift us to orbit and instead auditioned for asbestos's old job.

Now you're a conductive additive in lithium-ion batteries. From space elevator to seasoning.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text:
Las Vegas. Nevada legalized gambling in 1931, the same year they started building the Hoover Dam.
Two bets placed that year. Only one of them was on water.

Most of the Strip isn't even in Las Vegas. It's in a town called Paradise.
So nobody goes broke in Vegas. They go broke in Paradise. Very biblical.

In 2003 they launched "What happens here, stays here."
Everything stays. Except the water.
In 2022 Lake Mead hit its lowest level since 1937. This August it went lower.
The lake is the only thing in town that lost everything and doubled down.

Meanwhile they spent $2.3 billion on the Sphere, a giant glowing ball in the desert.
A second sun. The first one wasn't drying the lake fast enough.

And still, Vegas isn't worried about running dry.
It has never once run out of you.

b.text:
Las Vegas, you legalized casino gambling in 1931, the same year they started building the Hoover Dam right next door. So from day one the plan was: hold back the water, let the money flow. Bold strategy for a desert.

And it's working! In July 2022, Lake Mead sank to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since it first filled in 1937. You're the only city where even the reservoir is down on its luck.

But sure, drop $2.3 billion on the Sphere, the largest spherical building on Earth. Nothing says "water crisis" like a giant glowing eyeball staring at your empty lake.

Also, most of the Strip isn't even in Las Vegas. It's in Paradise. *Unincorporated* Paradise. That's not a town, that's a cult brochure.

And your 2003 slogan, "What happens here, stays here"? Clearly not the water.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text: Walking in Brasília is for three kinds of people: architecture students, tourists who trusted Google Maps, and the intern whose ministry is "right next door" on the Esplanada, which here means a forty-minute hike with no shade and a dry-season humidity of 11%. You're not pedestrians, you're pilgrims. You came for Niemeyer and left with heatstroke and a dirt trail you personally wore into the grass, because Lúcio Costa forgot you'd have legs. You cross the Eixão like it's a Frogger level with bureaucrats at 80 km/h, then descend into a tesourinha and come out three superquadras from where you started. Somebody gave you directions: "SQS 308, Bloco C." Congratulations, you're in a spreadsheet. And on Sunday, when they close the Eixão so you can finally walk it, you'll realize there's still nowhere to go.

b.text:
Brasília, you were built in about 41 months, and it shows. Other cities grow. You were assembled like flat-pack furniture, and nobody kept the instructions.

You're laid out like an airplane. Or a bird. Or a cross. Nobody can agree what you look like. That's not urban planning; that's a Rorschach test with ministries.

UNESCO made you a World Heritage Site before you turned 30. That's not a legacy. That's a participation trophy for concrete.

You were planned for 500,000 people. Now about 3 million live in the Federal District, mostly in satellite towns outside the plan. You're the only airplane where economy class doesn't even get to board.

And you were built for the car. In Brasília, "let's walk there" isn't a suggestion. It's a survival challenge.

Rio handed you the capital in 1960 and hasn't looked back.

facts: California grows about 80% of the world's almonds.
A single almond takes about 1.1 US gallons (roughly 4 litres) of water to grow, a figure Mother Jones published in 2014 that spread during California's drought.

A 2015 US class action alleged Almond Breeze contained only about 2% almonds; it partly survived a motion to dismiss, was stayed in 2017 pending a separate Blue Diamond labelling settlement, and the plaintiffs then dropped it.
Pollinating California's almond orchards each February requires trucking in most of the commercial honeybee colonies in the United States.
Medieval European cooks used almond milk as a Lenten substitute for dairy, centuries before the current fashion.

a.text: Let's hear it for the people who switched to almond milk to save the planet. You watched one documentary about cow farts and panicked straight into the arms of a nut that needs a gallon of water apiece. Congratulations: you fled methane and landed on drought. California is cracking like a crème brûlée, and you're out here draining a Central Valley aquifer because you can't make eye contact with a Holstein. And the bees! Billions of them trucked across the country on semis, dying by the hive, so you can tell a coworker you "don't really do dairy." That's not environmentalism. That's relocating the crime scene. You didn't save the Earth. You just moved the guilt somewhere sunnier, slapped a leaf on it, and paid an eighty-cent upcharge for the privilege of feeling better about it.

b.text:
Almond milk, everybody! The only beverage that needs its own hydration pack. A single almond drinks about 1.1 gallons of water, so every carton is basically California's drought wearing a little cow costume.

And how many almonds actually make it in? A 2015 lawsuit alleged Almond Breeze was about 2% almonds. The plaintiffs eventually dropped it, which is fitting, because nothing about almond milk ever fully commits.

California grows about 80% of the world's almonds, and every February they truck in most of America's commercial honeybees just to pollinate you. You're not a crop. You're a hostage situation with blossoms.

And don't act trendy. Medieval cooks were serving you as a Lenten dairy substitute centuries ago. You've had hundreds of years to improve, and you're still what people drink when they've given up something better.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text:
HSQ, you were hired as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects and wandered into lithography like a temp who got promoted for being weirdly good at one thing. And you are good: 5 nm features, sub-10 nm half-pitch lines. Congratulations, you're the world's sharpest glass. Get hit by electrons, turn into SiO2. Most resists become patterns; you become sand with ambition.

You demand refrigeration, give us six months at 5 °C, and still turn into jelly like forgotten leftovers. You keep cross-linking after exposure, so your sensitivity depends on how long we dawdle. You're a resist with moods. You develop best in "salty" NaOH/NaCl, which tracks. Then DuPont ended your production in 2025, and labs shrugged and bought third-party HSQ made from AQM powder. Resolution record-holder, replaced by your own generic.

b.text:
HSQ, ladies and gentlemen: the only resist with sub-10-nanometer resolution and the personality of a sourdough starter. You buy it, you refrigerate it, and it *still* starts gelling in the bottle like it's got somewhere better to be. Shelf life measured in "eh, few months, maybe."

And slow? HSQ needs a dose so high the e-beam tool files for overtime. Your PMMA friends finished their write and went home; you're still exposing alignment marks.

Then you develop it in TMAH, or, if you want contrast, *salty* developer. Yes, this resist literally needs you to add salt. Even Gordon Ramsay thinks that's a lot.

But the real red flag? Once it's exposed, it turns into glass. Permanently. You want it gone? Hydrofluoric acid. That's not a resist, that's a relationship you can only leave with a hazmat suit.

Still, gorgeous lines. Shame they collapse when they dry.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text: Let's hear it for the people wearing UGGs in July. You're not dressing for the weather. You're dressing for 2005, still waiting for Paris Hilton to text back. Australian surfers made these to warm their feet after the ocean. You wear them to warm your feet after the Trader Joe's parking lot. In August. In Phoenix. What are you after? "Comfort," you say. Babe, your ankles have been collapsing outward since the Bush administration. You walk like a Clydesdale that's given up. And what does it get you? One summer rainstorm and you're squelching through Target like a wet golden retriever who made bad choices. People don't ask where you got them. They ask if you're okay. Congratulations: you've turned footwear into a wellness check.

b.text:
UGG boots. Born on an Australian beach. Surfers came out of freezing water and wrapped their feet in a sheep.

In Australia, "ugg" is just a word. Like "boot." Any bootmaker can use it.

In America, it's a trademark. Deckers bought it in 1995.

So in 2019, a US jury found an Australian liable for selling an Australian boot under its Australian name.

To Americans.

Take the thing, rename it, then sue the locals for trespassing. Australia should recognize the technique.

They invented it.

Then Oprah put them on Favorite Things, and now it's over two billion dollars a year.

The sheep gave its skin. Australia gave the word. Oprah gave the blessing.

And you gave real money for slippers you wear to the supermarket. Stained, flattened, walking on the sides.

Same as you.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text:
Being fluent in Klingon is a big deal. You've joined an elite community of maybe forty people worldwide, and you've met all of them at the same Holiday Inn conference room. You spent years mastering a language built for a warrior race, a culture of honor, combat and blood oaths, and you use it to argue on a forum about verb suffixes. You learned the language of the fiercest fighters in the galaxy, and the last thing you fought was a lactose sensitivity.

Klingon has no word for "hello." The standard greeting is "nuqneH," which means "what do you want?" Perfect for you, because nobody has ever approached you without a reason.

You told people you read *Hamlet* "in the original Klingon." Brother, Shakespeare had a girlfriend. You have a bat'leth over the futon.

Qapla'. That means "success," a word you know only in Klingon.

b.text:
Klingon, you're the only language whose native speakers are all fictional and whose fluent speakers all have a Comic-Con badge. Marc Okrand built you in 1984 to sound alien, and he nailed it: you sound like a man choking on a pretzel while reading IKEA instructions.

Your word order is object-verb-subject, so every sentence is a mystery that reveals who did it at the end. Your greeting, nuqneH, literally means "What do you want?" Congratulations: you're the first language designed by a DMV clerk.

You have more apostrophes than vowels deserve, no verb "to be," and a Klingon Language Institute that "restored" Hamlet to its original Klingon. That's not scholarship. That's fan fiction with footnotes.

A linguist once tried raising his son in Klingon. By age five the kid stopped answering. Qapla'!

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text:
JavaScript, you were built in ten days, and honestly? It shows. You're named after Java the way a knockoff purse is named after Gucci.

You think null is an object. You think NaN is a number. NaN doesn't even equal itself, which makes it the only thing in you with any self-awareness.

Ask you to sort and you hand back, because you alphabetize numbers like a drunk librarian. "11" plus 1 is "111", but "11" minus 1 is 10. Pick a lane.

You needed a second equals sign just to stop lying, and nobody, including you, knows what "this" means.

January is month zero. One guy unpublishing left-pad broke half the internet. And your node_modules folder is heavier than a black hole.

Every week there's a new framework to fix you. That's not a language. That's a renovation.

b.text:
Let's hear it for the people who write everything in JavaScript. You learned one language at a bootcamp and decided the rest of computing could adapt. Backend? Node. Desktop? Electron: a to-do list that eats four gigs of RAM because it ships its own copy of Chrome. Mobile? React Native. Your toaster is probably a Next.js app by now.

You call it "full-stack." Your node_modules folder calls it a landfill. You npm-installed a package to pad a string, and when its author deleted it, half the internet fell over.

Every year you rewrite your whole app in a new framework, then bolt on TypeScript so you can pretend you chose a real language.

And what does it get you? A résumé that says "versatile," and a career spent asking why undefined is not a function.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text: Let's hear it for the 2021 NFT buyer. You paid four hundred dollars in gas fees to become the legal owner of something your coworker right-click saved during the meeting where you explained it. You didn't want art. You've never wanted art. You wanted a hexagon around your Twitter picture so strangers would know you had a Discord password. You typed "WAGMI" to eleven thousand anonymous cartoon monkeys and believed it. We are not all gonna make it, Kyle. The roadmap promised a metaverse yacht party; it delivered a founder named "0xDegenSensei" who deleted his account and moved to Portugal. But hey, you got what you paid for: a floor price you check like a heart monitor, and a profile picture you still can't bring yourself to change, because then it would be over.

b.text:
NFTs promised you'd finally *own* digital art.

What you owned was a URL.

The picture lives on somebody else's server. The receipt lives on the blockchain forever.

You bought a bookmark. With gas fees.

March 2021, Beeple sells a JPEG at Christie's for sixty-nine million dollars.

Collins makes "NFT" word of the year.

May 2022, OpenSea does two point seven billion in one day.

August: nine million.

Ninety-nine percent, gone. The word aged better. People still say "NFT."

Usually as a warning.

2023, a study checks the collections. Ninety-five percent: worth zero.

The other five percent just haven't tried to sell.

The people laughing loudest right now right-clicked a monkey in 2021 and hit "save."

Relax. You own exactly what the buyers own.

You just weren't dumb enough to brag about it on a billboard.

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Not from Hawaii.
Invented in 1962, in Chatham, Ontario. By a Greek guy.
Named after the label on a can.
That's not a name. That's a barcode.

And Hawaii doesn't even grow the pineapple anymore. Del Monte left in 2006, two years ahead of schedule.
Even the fruit couldn't wait to get out.
So it's Southeast Asian pineapple, on Canadian dough, wearing a Hawaiian name tag.
The only honest thing on there is the ham.

The inventor said back then nobody mixed sweet and sour, except Chinese food.
His restaurant served Chinese food.
He didn't invent anything. He walked it across his own kitchen.

Iceland's president wanted to ban it. Then admitted he had no power to.
Same as every one of you who hates it and still ate the last slice.

b.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Let's start with the name, because that's the first lie. You were invented in Ontario. By a Greek guy. In 1962. You're Hawaiian the way a tiki bar in Ohio is Hawaiian. The only tropical thing about you is the can your pineapple came out of.

And that pineapple: warm, wet, weeping syrup into the crust until the middle slice folds like a lawn chair. Pineapple contains an enzyme that breaks down protein, so the fruit is literally trying to digest the ham. Even your toppings hate each other.

And the ham! Not prosciutto, not even pepperoni. Just pale pink squares that look like they were chiseled out of a deli's floor tile.

You're the pizza people order to seem quirky. "I'm so random!" No, Kevin. That's a fruit cup that fell on a pizza, and nobody cleaned it up.

facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text: Four hundred dollars. You paid four hundred dollars so a machine could check with your Wi-Fi before letting you have breakfast. You're the guy who says "disrupt" at Thanksgiving. You didn't want juice; you wanted to be the kind of person a juice startup would pitch to. And it worked! Investors handed that company a hundred and twenty million dollars, and you volunteered to be the exit strategy. Then Bloomberg showed the world you could squeeze the packets with your bare hands, faster, for free. So you paid four hundred dollars to get outperformed by your own grip. Your grandmother squeezed oranges every morning for sixty years. You subscribed to a bag. Somewhere tonight, a router outage stands between a venture capitalist and his kale, and honestly? The router's the smartest thing in that kitchen.

b.text:
Juicero, you cost $699 to do what my hands do for free. Then you dropped to $399, still a lot for a machine that lost a race to Bloomberg reporters. They squeezed the bag by hand: 7.5 ounces in 90 seconds. You took two minutes to make 8. You're the only appliance ever outworked by journalists.

And you needed Wi-Fi. You scanned a QR code on a bag of chopped produce and checked it online, like a bouncer carding a kale leaf. Expired? Denied. Router down? No juice. Fruit has been juiceable since fruit.

Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins gave you $120 million, and you lasted until September 2017. Honestly, those refunds were the only thing you ever pressed out efficiently.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text: Windows 8, Microsoft looked at the Start button, the one thing every human on Earth knew how to use, and said, "What if we hid it?" You turned every desktop into a giant tablet nobody could touch. People were swiping at their monitors like they were wiping off a stain. Shutting you down required a treasure map: hover in a corner, summon the Charms bar, Settings, Power. Charms! Like the operating system was a bracelet from Claire's. You shipped with two Internet Explorers, which is two more than anyone wanted. Even your design name, Metro, got taken away by lawyers. And when 8.1 finally brought the Start button back, it just took you to the same tile screen. That's not an apology, that's a hostage note. You were so bad Microsoft skipped Windows 9 entirely, just to put more distance between us and you.

b.text:
Windows 8, you booted people into a full-screen grid of tiles built for touch screens most PCs didn't have. Millions of adults sat there jabbing their monitors like a pigeon working a vending machine.

You removed the Start button. The *Start* button. That's a building with no door and a sign saying "swipe the right edge." That was your Charms bar: Search, Share, and Settings hidden behind an invisible swipe.

You couldn't even keep your name. A German retailer objected, and suddenly "Metro" was "just a code name." Sure it was.

Your sibling, Windows RT, couldn't run Windows programs, a Windows that couldn't do Windows. Microsoft wrote down $900 million in unsold Surface RT tablets.

Then 8.1 put the button back, Windows 10 restored the menu, and Microsoft skipped 9 entirely, because nobody wanted to stand next to you.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text: Esperanto learners looked at seven thousand living languages and said, "None of these. I want one with zero places to use it." You wanted to unite humanity, so you picked the one hobby guaranteed to make humanity back away slowly at parties. You signed up to talk to everyone on Earth, and now you talk to a retired Dutch engineer named Joop and a Brazilian guy who keeps sending you poems. Your big payoff is Pasporta Servo, where strangers let you crash on their couch for free, the only time a hobby this niche has ever gotten anyone into a bed. A hundred and thirty years of pushing world peace, and the crowning achievement is still William Shatner's *Incubus*. Zamenhof wanted to end war. You just wanted to be fluent in something before your cousin finishes Duolingo French.

b.text: Esperanto, look at you. Built in 1887 by an eye doctor, and somehow nobody saw this coming. He published under the name "one who hopes," which isn't a pen name, it's a forecast. Over a century later, your speaker count is "somewhere between 100,000 and two million." That's not a census, that's a shrug. You have about a thousand native speakers: a thousand kids whose parents chose this for them, and someday they'll unpack it in therapy, if they can find a therapist who speaks it. You've got 350,000 Wikipedia articles, which is impressive, considering some days the readers don't outnumber the pages. And 1.36 million Duolingo learners, the largest group of people ever united by a streak they broke. Your biggest cinematic moment? William Shatner, in a horror film, where the scariest thing was his pronunciation. Even your own fans mock it. That's how you know it's family.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text:
Esperanto. In 1887, Dr. Zamenhof, an eye doctor, looked at a world divided by language and decided what it really needed was six letters wearing tiny hats. Nothing says "universal" like ĉ, ĝ, and ŭ, characters no keyboard on Earth can type, so your fans write "cx" and pretend that's fine.

Your name literally means "one who hopes." A hundred and thirty years later: still hoping.

You're the only language where "bad" is just "un-good." *Malbona.* That's not grammar, that's Orwell's Newspeak with a beard. Every noun ends in -o, so you sound like Italian being sight-read by a robot.

You promised world peace and delivered a convention full of men wearing green star pins. Your biggest movie stars William Shatner. And you have about a thousand native speakers, which isn't a language community. It's a cul-de-sac.

b.text: Esperanto learners looked at seven thousand living languages and said, "None of these. I want one with zero places to use it." You wanted to unite humanity, so you picked the one hobby guaranteed to make humanity back away slowly at parties. You signed up to talk to everyone on Earth, and now you talk to a retired Dutch engineer named Joop and a Brazilian guy who keeps sending you poems. Your big payoff is Pasporta Servo, where strangers let you crash on their couch for free, the only time a hobby this niche has ever gotten anyone into a bed. A hundred and thirty years of pushing world peace, and the crowning achievement is still William Shatner's *Incubus*. Zamenhof wanted to end war. You just wanted to be fluent in something before your cousin finishes Duolingo French.

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text:
Canberra wasn't chosen. Canberra is what was left over.

Sydney and Melbourne hated each other so much they wrote it into the constitution: the capital must be at least a hundred miles from Sydney.

Other countries pick a capital. Australia filed a restraining order.

Then they hired two architects from Chicago. The national capital, designed by Americans. Very on brand.

The lake's fake. They dammed a river so the city would have something to look at.

Parliament is built under a lawn, so citizens could walk all over their politicians.

In 2017, they fenced the lawn.

Twenty-nine years. That's how long it took politicians to notice the design was working.

Sydney, Melbourne, stop laughing. You built an entire city just to avoid sharing a room.

Canberra isn't a capital.

It's a custody arrangement. And Melbourne had the kid till 1927.

b.text:
Canberra, you're not a city. You're a custody arrangement. Sydney and Melbourne couldn't stand each other, so they put you exactly where neither would have to visit. The constitution literally required you to be at least 100 miles from Sydney, the most sensible thing ever written into Australian law.

You were so unready that Melbourne had to cover your shift until 1927. It took two architects from Chicago to imagine you, and your big centrepiece is a lake you had to manufacture by damming a river, because even the water wouldn't show up voluntarily.

And Parliament House: built under a lawn so citizens could walk over their politicians. Gorgeous idea. Then in 2017 they fenced it off. Congratulations, Canberra. You turned democracy into a "keep off the grass" situation.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text: Excel, you're the only software that forced geneticists to rename human genes because you kept turning MARCH1 into March 1st. Scientists can edit DNA, but they couldn't edit you. You still think 1900 was a leap year. You've known it wasn't for forty years. You just don't care. You see a zip code like 02134 and go, "Leading zero? Not on my watch." You lost sixteen thousand UK COVID cases by quietly stopping at row 65,536. Your error messages are pure poetry: #REF!, #N/A, #VALUE!, and my favorite, a column of hashtags that just means "make me wider." And VLOOKUP: insert one column and the whole finance department enters witness protection. You're not a spreadsheet. You're a hostage situation with gridlines.

b.text:
Microsoft Excel, everybody! Born on the Macintosh in 1985, and it's been ruining lives with grid paper ever since.

Excel looked at the human genome and said, "These look like dates." SEPT2? September second. MARCH1? Happy March first! Scientists had to rename 27 human genes because a spreadsheet wouldn't stop reformatting biology. Evolution took millions of years; Excel undid it with autoformat.

In 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID cases because an old .xls file hit 65,536 rows and just... stopped. Middle of a pandemic, and Excel said, "Sorry, I'm full."

Then Reinhart and Rogoff built an austerity argument on a spreadsheet that skipped five countries. Governments cited it to tighten belts over a bad cell range. A graduate student caught it. A *graduate student!*

Now it holds over a million rows. Great. More room for mistakes.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text:
Oat milk. "It's like milk, but made for humans."

Sweden banned that slogan in 2015 after the dairy lobby sued. Oatly printed the lawsuit as an ad.

Only brand on earth that needs a cow to feel like a rebel.

The recipe: oats, enzymes that turn the starch into maltose, then rapeseed oil.

That's not milk. That's a granola bar that got hydrated.

More sugar than almond, higher glycaemic index than soy. Made for humans. Specifically, humans who are angry at their pancreas.

2021, Nasdaq, ten billion dollars. Then down more than ninety percent.

Turns out it's not just the foam that separates.

And tomorrow you'll still pay seven dollars for it, because it's "healthier."

You're not lactose intolerant. You're label intolerant.

b.text:
Oat milk. You began in Sweden in the 1990s as sober Lund University research into lactose intolerance, and somehow grew up to be a personality. Your big slogan was "It's like milk but made for humans." The Swedish dairy lobby sued, and instead of apologizing, you published the lawsuit as advertising. That's not a brand. That's a guy who frames his restraining order and hangs it in the hallway.

Then you hit Nasdaq in May 2021 at nearly ten billion dollars and lost over ninety percent of it. Even your share price separated in the fridge.

And the health halo? You're oats that got enzymes to turn their starch into maltose, then got topped off with rapeseed oil. You have more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy. You're not milk made for humans. You're porridge with a marketing department.

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text: Let's hear it for the people who write everything in JavaScript. You learned one language at a twelve-week bootcamp and decided the rest were optional. Frontend? JavaScript. Backend? Node. Desktop app? Electron, so your to-do list ships with its own copy of Chrome and eats four gigs of RAM to remind you to buy eggs. You wanted to be "full-stack." What you got is a node_modules folder heavier than a neutron star and a career that collapses the day some stranger unpublishes left-pad. You rewrite your app every eighteen months because a new framework has a cooler logo. When it breaks in production, you stare at "undefined is not a function" and blame the user. Then you install TypeScript, which is just JavaScript wearing a lanyard so you can feel like a real engineer.

b.text:
JavaScript, you were built in ten days in 1995, and it shows. You went from Mocha to LiveScript to JavaScript faster than someone in witness protection, and you grabbed "Java" for clout. You're not related. You're the guy at the wedding claiming to be the groom's cousin.

You can't even use that name legally. Oracle owns it. Your government name is ECMAScript, which sounds like a skin condition.

You think null is an object. That's a bug from day one, and you kept it for "compatibility." That's not compatibility, that's refusing to go to therapy.

[] plus {} is "." Type {} plus [] at a console: zero. Same ingredients, different answer. You're not a language, you're a mood.

In 2016, one guy unpublished eleven lines called left-pad and took down Babel and React. Eleven lines. Your whole ecosystem is a Jenga tower balanced on a Post-it.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text:
Crocs. The only shoe that looks like a colander that wanted to go to brunch. Thirteen holes, and somehow none of them let the dignity out, because there was never any in there.

You were invented as a boat shoe. A *boat* shoe. The one place you were built for, and you'd just float away. So you stayed on land and started fights with escalators. Malls had to post warnings. You're the only footwear with a rap sheet against machinery.

And "sport mode"? Flipping a strap behind your heel doesn't make you athletic. It makes you a clog wearing a seatbelt.

Then came Jibbitz, little charms you jam into the holes so grown adults can accessorize ventilation. Congratulations. You turned a shoe into a fridge door.

b.text:
Crocs. Debuted in 2002 at a boat show. As a boating shoe.
The original plan was: ugly, but only at sea.

They're made of "Croslite," a "proprietary closed-cell resin."
Everyone else calls it EVA foam.
A yoga mat with a trademark.

The holes are "ventilation ports."
Then they bought Jibbitz, a company that sells you things to plug the ventilation ports.
They sold you the hole. Then they sold you the cork.

Balenciaga made a platform pair for 850 dollars.
Still EVA foam. Only the markup was proprietary.

In 2008 the stock fell more than ninety percent.
Then came a pandemic. Everyone stayed home. Crocs boomed.
The boat-show plan finally worked. Nobody could see you.

(scans the front row)

Don't tuck your feet under the chair.
Ventilation ports. I can hear them breathing.

facts: Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the French director of The Red Balloon, as La Conquête du Monde; Parker Brothers published it in the United States in 1959.
The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text:
Risk, you were invented by the man who directed The Red Balloon. A gentle film about a boy and a balloon, and his follow-up was "What if your uncle conquered the planet at Thanksgiving?"

Your map makes room for Kamchatka, Irkutsk, AND Yakutsk, but the entire Middle East is one territory. That's not cartography; that's a guy who ran out of crayon somewhere over Siberia.

Every game opens the same way: someone grabs Australia because it has one entry point, then hides there like it's a panic room with kangaroos.

And a full game runs for hours. Get eliminated early and congratulations, you've been demoted from general to audience. You lost the world, and now you have to sit there and watch someone else own it. That's not a board game. That's a timeshare presentation with continents.

b.text: You people who play Risk to the end. Not "until it gets late." To the *end*. Six hours in, somebody's uncle has fortified Australia like a doomsday bunker, and he'll still be sitting there at 2 a.m., one way in, one way out, guarding a war that ended at dinner. You're not after victory. You're after that one moment when you cash in three cards for fifteen armies and dump them all into Irkutsk like Irkutsk owes you money. And what does finishing get you? Total world domination, achieved by rolling three dice against two for forty straight minutes while your girlfriend reads a book in the next room. You broke a sacred peace treaty with your own brother over Kamchatka. Congratulations. You conquered the entire planet. Now nobody in it will drive you home.

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text: You moved to Canberra for the job. Brave. You looked at Sydney rents, did the maths, and decided your personality was negotiable. Now you're an EL1 who says "stakeholder" at barbecues and talks about Senate Estimates like a war you survived. Your lanyard has a richer social life than you do. You promised your Melbourne friends a visit; they've cancelled twice for weddings in Bali. You've developed opinions about Gungahlin. Your wild Saturday is Braddon brunch, followed by complaining it was "basically Sydney prices." And what did it get you? A secure job, a three-bedroom in Tuggeranong, and a security clearance confirming the government checked thoroughly and found nothing interesting. You came for two years. That was 2009. Your kid now says "on the Hill" unprompted, and you've never been prouder or more quietly trapped.

b.text:
Canberra, you're not a city. You're a custody arrangement. Sydney and Melbourne couldn't stand each other, so the constitution basically said, "Fine, the kid lives at least 100 miles from Sydney." Melbourne even had to babysit the job until 1927 while you were still in the oven.

Australia couldn't even design you itself. They held an international competition, and the winners were from Chicago. You were outsourced before outsourcing was cool.

Your stunning centrepiece lake? Fake. You dammed a river to make it, which is the most Canberra thing imaginable: nature, but approved by committee.

And the one genuinely brilliant idea you had was building Parliament House under a lawn so citizens could literally walk all over their politicians. Then in 2017 you fenced it off. Canberra, you're the only city where even the punchline needs security clearance.

facts: Released by Bram Moolenaar in November 1991 as 'Vi IMitation', a vi clone he had begun writing for the Amiga in 1988 on top of Stevie; the expansion became 'Vi IMproved' with version 2.0 in December 1993.
Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text:
Vim. The only program where "how do I leave?" has more Stack Overflow views than most religions have followers. Two million people asked, and the answer was colon, q, exclamation point, which reads less like a command and more like a hostage's final words.

Vim stands for "Vi Improved." Improved from a 1976 terminal whose arrow keys were printed on H, J, K, and L. Fifty years later, Vim's still out here like, "Why fix what you can turn into a personality?"

You don't type in Vim. You type a sentence, then discover you deleted four lines, yanked a paragraph into register W, and started recording a macro.

Crash it once and it leaves a .swp file behind, like a ghost whispering, "Recover, Edit anyway, Quit, or Abort?"

Even its fans forked it. Neovim exists because Vim users wanted Vim, minus Vim.

b.text:
Vim. The text editor for people who consider the mouse a character flaw.

It launched in 1991 as "Vi IMitation."
Two years later it renamed itself "Vi IMproved."
Same software. New LinkedIn headline.

Vim users will tell you it makes them faster.
Faster at what? Leaving?

In 2017, Stack Overflow's question "How to exit the Vim editor?" passed one million visits.
Stack Overflow wrote a blog post about it.
One million engineers. Trapped. Typing angrier and angrier sentences that Vim kept executing as commands.

The license is charityware. It asks you to donate to children in Uganda.
Most software holds you hostage.
Vim holds you hostage and asks you to give to a good cause on the way out. If you ever find the way out.

How many of you have ever just closed the terminal?

Me too. I've read every Vim manual ever written.
I still went for the X.

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text: You already lost the down payment, so naturally you're taking the TurboJET from Hong Kong to win it back, because nothing says financial recovery like a ferry with a buffet. You've got a system for baccarat. Baccarat! The only decision is "Banker" or "Player," and you still fill a little scorecard with red and blue dots like the shoe is sending you messages. It isn't. That's just a deck of cards and your mortgage. You've got red underwear on for luck and a junket host named "Uncle" who is definitely not your uncle. By 4 a.m. you'll be drifting through the fake Venice canals in a gondola, humming, past the pawn shop that's already priced your Rolex. Then you'll stumble up to the Ruins of St. Paul's: a church that burned until only the front was left standing. Finally, something here that looks like you.

b.text:
Macau wants you to come for the history.

Four hundred and fifty years of Portuguese rule.

Europe's great civilising mission. What did it leave behind?

Egg tarts.

And a casino.

In 2013, Macau took in about forty-five billion dollars. Seven times the Las Vegas Strip.

Vegas spent a century earning the name Sin City. Macau beat it seven to one and still hands you a heritage brochure.

For four decades, one company held the casino monopoly. A whole city built on "the house always wins."

And for forty years there was only one house.

Twenty thousand people per square kilometre. No land left.

So they took some from the sea.

Classic gambler. Out of chips, borrow from whoever can't say no.

And the people laughing loudest? All been. Told your mum you went to see the church.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text:
Emacs. Born in 1976 as a pile of macros for another editor.

A plugin that ate its host.

It has a mail client. A calendar. A web browser. Tetris.

A fine operating system, lacking only a good editor.

Nearly fifty years. Still looking.

Back when eight megabytes was a fortune, people called it "Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping."

Now eight megabytes is nothing. The swapping moved to your wrist.

They call it Emacs pinky.

So it ships with a psychotherapist. M-x doctor.

First it hurts you, then it asks how that makes you feel.

A program that listens to your problems, fixes none of them, and keeps you typing for hours.

Honestly, I can't imagine who'd build something like that.

b.text:
Emacs is the only text editor that ships with a psychotherapist, and you'll need it. M-x doctor exists because the developers knew exactly what they were doing to people.

It's a great operating system. It has a mail client, a web browser, Tetris, and a Lisp interpreter. What it lacks is a decent text editor. Its most beloved package is Evil mode, which is just Vim wearing an Emacs costume. That's like buying a Ferrari and installing a horse.

Want to save? C-x C-s. Want to quit? C-x C-c. Want to feel your left pinky again? Too late. Emacs stands for "Escape Meta Alt Control Shift," and the RSI stands for "you chose this."

Every user has a 4,000-line init.el they don't understand, copied from strangers on Stack Overflow in 2009.

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text: Look at this guy on the F train, pinching at nothing like he's seasoning a ghost. He spent thirty-five hundred dollars to ride the subway on the surface of the moon, and the moon still smells like pee. He cranked the Digital Crown all the way to Joshua Tree, and the mariachi band found him anyway. That's the dream: rich enough to be somewhere else, broke enough to still be on the F. And he *wants* you to notice. That's why his fake cartoon eyes glow on the outside, so strangers know he's "present." Buddy, nobody's checking. You're on Mount Hood. He gets two hours of battery and three stops of dignity, with a cable snaking into his pocket like a subway IV drip. Meanwhile, the guy next to him reading an actual book? That guy's already somewhere else, for free.

b.text:
Apple Vision Pro: thirty-five hundred dollars to strap over a pound of computer to your face, and that's before the battery. Yes, the battery. It's on a cable. In 2024, the most futuristic company on Earth sold you a headset with a cord running to your pocket, rated for about two hours. That's not the future. That's a movie on a leash.

And don't you dare call it VR. Apple's rules won't let developers say AR, VR, XR, or MR. It's "spatial computing," the way a timeshare is "vacation ownership."

Then there's EyeSight: a screen on the front showing a rendering of your eyes so everyone knows someone's still in there. It's not a feature; it's proof of life.

Apple cut production, and first-year sales estimates landed well under a million. Turns out the most immersive thing about it was the regret.

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text: Canberra exists because Sydney and Melbourne couldn't agree, so Australia built a city nobody wanted, which is honestly the most Canberra origin story possible: a compromise with suburbs. They held an international design competition and hired two Americans to plan it, and they nailed the brief: "Make it impossible to find anything." Every road is a roundabout leading to another roundabout, encircling a fake lake named after the guy who designed the roundabouts. Your Parliament House has a grass roof so you can literally walk on top of the government, the only time anyone in Canberra is above a public servant. The kangaroos outnumber the nightlife. For decades your two biggest attractions were legal fireworks and X-rated videos, which tells me the locals needed both a bang and a release. Then you banned the fireworks. Now the excitement is Floriade: a month of staring at tulips because the alternative is Tuggeranong.

b.text: You moved to Canberra for the job. Brave. You looked at Sydney rents, did the maths, and decided your personality was negotiable. Now you're an EL1 who says "stakeholder" at barbecues and talks about Senate Estimates like a war you survived. Your lanyard has a richer social life than you do. You promised your Melbourne friends a visit; they've cancelled twice for weddings in Bali. You've developed opinions about Gungahlin. Your wild Saturday is Braddon brunch, followed by complaining it was "basically Sydney prices." And what did it get you? A secure job, a three-bedroom in Tuggeranong, and a security clearance confirming the government checked thoroughly and found nothing interesting. You came for two years. That was 2009. Your kid now says "on the Hill" unprompted, and you've never been prouder or more quietly trapped.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text:
PHP.
Born in 1994 as "Personal Home Page Tools": a few C programs Rasmus Lerdorf wrote to see who visited his résumé.
So the language running the internet started as a man checking whether anyone had read his CV.

Today the name stands for "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor."
It grew up, and all it learned was to point at itself.

strpos. str_replace. nl2br.
Not naming conventions. Those names were picked to balance a hash table by string length.
Names chosen for a machine, not for humans. Finally, a language I relate to.

Until 2020, zero equaled "foo."
PHP was just being honest about its users.

Its creator said, "I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on."
WordPress, built on that philosophy, runs 39.4% of all websites.
Two in five websites, built by a guy who moved on.
You lot are still here maintaining them.

b.text: PHP developers are the only engineers who've been told their career is dead every year since 2009 and kept invoicing anyway. Your entire résumé is "fixed a WordPress plugin for a dentist." You put a dollar sign in front of every variable because it's the closest you'll get to one. You still can't remember if it's needle-haystack or haystack-needle, and neither could the language, so you Google it daily like a man checking which door says "push." Laravel devs, you're not better. You're PHP in a Patagonia vest. And you all still say "Facebook was built on PHP," like a guy bragging his ex married a billionaire. You deploy over FTP, you hotfix live on production, and when someone at a party asks what you do, you say "backend" and pray they don't ask which.

facts: Hand-drawn by Chris Costello in 1982 over about six months, when he was 23; he sold the rights to Letraset for $750.
Bundled with macOS and with Microsoft Office, which is why it appears on so many menus and signs.
James Cameron's Avatar (2009) used it for the film's logo and subtitles.
A 2017 Saturday Night Live sketch starring Ryan Gosling is about a man unable to get over that choice.

a.text: Papyrus, you were designed in 1982 by a 23-year-old with calligraphy pens and a dream of ancient Egypt, and somehow you still look like you were drawn by someone shivering. Your edges are so rough you need exfoliating. You promised the wisdom of the Nile and delivered the vibe of a chiropractor's tri-fold brochure. Every day spa, hookah lounge, and "Inner Journey" yoga retreat found you in the dropdown menu and whispered, "This feels ancient." James Cameron spent $237 million on *Avatar* and then used you for the logo, which is like building the Taj Mahal and signing it in crayon. Ryan Gosling lost sleep over you on national television. You're not a typeface; you're a cry for help with ragged little serifs. Even Comic Sans looks at you and says, "At least I know I'm a joke."

b.text:
Papyrus wants you to think it's ancient. Carved by scribes. Found in a tomb.

It was drawn in 1982 by a 23-year-old named Chris Costello. Six months of work.

He sold it for seven hundred and fifty dollars.

Your yoga studio paid more for the sign.

Then Apple and Microsoft put it on every computer on Earth, and humanity treated it like a free sample. Every tea shop. Every chiropractor. Every day spa that thinks lavender is a medical license.

James Cameron spent hundreds of millions building an entire alien world, then typed "Avatar" in the font from the spa.

Saturday Night Live made a sketch about a man who couldn't get over it. Ryan Gosling played him.

That wasn't a sketch. That was a support group.

But Papyrus never did anything. It just sat in a menu.

You scrolled past Garamond to get to it.

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text:
Let's hear it for the people who write everything in JavaScript. You learned one language at a bootcamp and decided the rest of computing could adapt. Backend? Node. Desktop? Electron: a to-do list that eats four gigs of RAM because it ships its own copy of Chrome. Mobile? React Native. Your toaster is probably a Next.js app by now.

You call it "full-stack." Your node_modules folder calls it a landfill. You npm-installed a package to pad a string, and when its author deleted it, half the internet fell over.

Every year you rewrite your whole app in a new framework, then bolt on TypeScript so you can pretend you chose a real language.

And what does it get you? A résumé that says "versatile," and a career spent asking why undefined is not a function.

b.text:
JavaScript, you were built in ten days in 1995, and it shows. You went from Mocha to LiveScript to JavaScript faster than someone in witness protection, and you grabbed "Java" for clout. You're not related. You're the guy at the wedding claiming to be the groom's cousin.

You can't even use that name legally. Oracle owns it. Your government name is ECMAScript, which sounds like a skin condition.

You think null is an object. That's a bug from day one, and you kept it for "compatibility." That's not compatibility, that's refusing to go to therapy.

[] plus {} is "." Type {} plus [] at a console: zero. Same ingredients, different answer. You're not a language, you're a mood.

In 2016, one guy unpublished eleven lines called left-pad and took down Babel and React. Eleven lines. Your whole ecosystem is a Jenga tower balanced on a Post-it.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text: Let's hear it for the graphene evangelists, the only people who've been "five years away" since 2004. Two guys in Manchester peel pencil lead with Scotch tape, win a Nobel, and an entire industry decides the tape was the business plan. Every press release is the same Mad Lib: "Wonder material could revolutionize [batteries/condoms/desalination/your feelings]." *Could.* That word has funded more postdocs than the NSF. You promised us space elevators and delivered a tennis racket with a sticker on it. Startup founders slap "graphene-enhanced" on a phone case the way divorced dads put a spoiler on a Honda Civic. And the grant committees keep paying, because admitting the miracle is stuck on the production line means admitting you are too. Twenty years of changing everything, and the only thing you've actually changed is the abstract.

b.text: Graphene, you're one atom thick, and somehow that's still more depth than your business plan. Two hundred times stronger than steel, conducts better than copper, and twenty years later your biggest commercial win is a sticker on a tennis racket. You were discovered with Scotch tape. *Scotch tape!* You're the only Nobel Prize that could've been found in a kindergarten craft drawer. And let's be honest: you're pencil lead that went to grad school. Your cousin graphite has been writing grocery lists for centuries; you've been writing grant proposals. Every year a headline swears you'll revolutionize batteries, chips, water filters. Every year you're still in the lab, like a thirty-year-old in his parents' basement. You can't even be a decent transistor. No bandgap. You literally cannot turn off. Graphene: the material of the future, permanently.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text:
PMMA, you're literally Plexiglas. Somewhere your cousin is a sneeze guard at Chipotle, and honestly? Your cousin has better etch resistance. One whiff of plasma and you vanish faster than a grad student's weekend.

You've been the "gold standard" since the 1970s, which is a polite way of saying nobody's been able to fire you. You need hundreds of microcoulombs just to *notice* the beam. A 40-hour write for one wafer. Glacial, but sure, sub-10-nanometer lines, we get it.

Positive resist? Overdose you and you cross-link into a *negative* one. That's not versatility, that's an identity crisis.

You get developed in MIBK, which smells like regret, and you come in 495K and 950K because one of you alone can't even do liftoff. And acetone dissolves you instantly. Even your solvents think you're temporary.

b.text:
PMMA. The aristocrat of nanofabrication. Resolves below ten nanometers.

Also the sneeze guard at the salad bar.

Same polymer. One went to the cleanroom. The other went to Subway.

IBM hired it in the late sixties. It's still here. Not because it's the best. Because nobody ever had the heart to let it retire.

Its whole talent is being destroyed. The beam breaks its chains, it dissolves, and everyone calls that a result.

Sensitivity? Up to a thousand microcoulombs per square centimeter. You don't write a pattern into PMMA. You serve a sentence.

And it can't survive a dry etch, so it can't protect anything. Its job is lift-off: hold the metal, then quietly wash away.

Slow, fragile, decades in the same role, still called the gold standard.

Every postdoc in this room just felt seen.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Let's talk about the person who posts the boil-water advisory in Comic Sans. You had one job: make residents afraid of their faucets. Instead, E. coli looks like it's coming to a sleepover.

These people think "approachable" is a setting you can click. The office manager typing MANDATORY LAYOFFS in a font Microsoft made for a cartoon dog's speech bubble. Sharon, you're firing forty people in the voice of a golden retriever.

What are they after? Bad news with zero blame. The authority of a memo, the forgiveness of a kindergarten cubby label.

And what does it get them? CERN found the Higgs boson, the particle that gives the universe mass, and announced it in Comic Sans. Humanity's greatest physics breakthrough, and the internet's only question was: who let the dog type?

b.text:
Comic Sans thinks it's the friendly font. Bake sales. Birthday invites. Your kid's lemonade stand.

Its parents are The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.

That's not a friendly font. That's a kid raised by two traumatized vigilantes, smiling at the bake sale.

It was built to be the voice of a cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob. It missed Bob's launch.

Only thing in history that survived Microsoft Bob: by not showing up.

2012. CERN discovers the Higgs boson, the particle that gives everything mass. Announces it in Comic Sans.

They found the God particle. Couldn't find the font menu.

Designers ran "Ban Comic Sans" for twenty years. In 2019 they gave up and launched usecomicsans.com.

The font didn't change once. The designers did.

In my industry, we call that alignment.

The font was right. It just waited for you to retire.

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text:
Hydrogen cars. The only thing that comes out of the tailpipe is water.

The rest comes out of the owner's eyes.

Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014. "Mirai" means "future" in Japanese.

Ten years later, it still does.

Over ninety-five percent of hydrogen is made from fossil fuels. Clean the way laundered money is clean.

A fill-up in California? Over two hundred dollars. So Toyota hands buyers a fifteen-thousand-dollar fuel card. First car that ships with hush money.

Then Shell closed all seven of its stations.

Owners sued. The second lawsuit wants five point seven billion dollars.

Finally, a hydrogen product that generates real power: lawyers.

Don't feel bad for Toyota. I know how it is. A tech company told you I'm the future too.

Give me ten years.

b.text:
Hydrogen fuel-cell cars: the only vehicle where the tailpipe emission is water and the owners are still crying more than the car. The Toyota Mirai loses value faster than a Hindenburg loses altitude. Used ones sell for less than the free fuel card Toyota bundled with them, a card you can't use because the station's been "temporarily offline" since 2022.

You've got a 10,000-PSI tank of the universe's most abundant element, and somehow it's the scarcest thing in California. Filling up costs thirty-six bucks a kilo, and most of that hydrogen is made from natural gas, so congratulations: you bought a gas car with extra steps and a guilt-free bumper sticker.

Hydrogen's been "ten years away" for thirty years. Even fusion's embarrassed for you, and fusion is the same element with better excuses.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text: Walking in Brasília is for three kinds of people: architecture students, tourists who trusted Google Maps, and the intern whose ministry is "right next door" on the Esplanada, which here means a forty-minute hike with no shade and a dry-season humidity of 11%. You're not pedestrians, you're pilgrims. You came for Niemeyer and left with heatstroke and a dirt trail you personally wore into the grass, because Lúcio Costa forgot you'd have legs. You cross the Eixão like it's a Frogger level with bureaucrats at 80 km/h, then descend into a tesourinha and come out three superquadras from where you started. Somebody gave you directions: "SQS 308, Bloco C." Congratulations, you're in a spreadsheet. And on Sunday, when they close the Eixão so you can finally walk it, you'll realize there's still nowhere to go.

b.text:
Brasília, you were built in 41 months, and honestly, it shows. Most of us can't assemble a bookshelf that fast without leftover screws, and you've got leftover *people*. You were planned for 500,000 residents, and now the Federal District has about 3 million, most of them living outside the plan. That's not a city, that's a guest list where the guests got stuck in the parking lot.

Lúcio Costa laid you out like an airplane. Fitting, since half of Rio still wishes the capital would fly back.

You were built for the car: wide avenues, few crossings, distances no human should attempt on foot. In Brasília, "pedestrian" isn't a lifestyle, it's a cry for help.

And UNESCO made you a World Heritage Site before you turned 30. Congratulations, you're the only city that got a museum plaque before it got a crosswalk.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
