Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text:
HSQ, you were hired as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects and wandered into lithography like a temp who got promoted for being weirdly good at one thing. And you are good: 5 nm features, sub-10 nm half-pitch lines. Congratulations, you're the world's sharpest glass. Get hit by electrons, turn into SiO2. Most resists become patterns; you become sand with ambition.

You demand refrigeration, give us six months at 5 °C, and still turn into jelly like forgotten leftovers. You keep cross-linking after exposure, so your sensitivity depends on how long we dawdle. You're a resist with moods. You develop best in "salty" NaOH/NaCl, which tracks. Then DuPont ended your production in 2025, and labs shrugged and bought third-party HSQ made from AQM powder. Resolution record-holder, replaced by your own generic.

b.text:
HSQ. Holds the e-beam resolution record. Five-nanometer features.

Impressive, until you remember it was hired as an insulator.

Dow Corning built it to sit quietly between wires. Lithographers looked at it and said, "No. You're a celebrity now."

Then they expose it, and it turns into glass. The most advanced resist on Earth, and the finished product is a window.

It needs refrigeration. Six months at five degrees, then it ages into jelly. Even after exposure it keeps cross-linking, so the dose that worked yesterday is wrong today.

High-contrast development requires salt water. Of course it does. Salty, temperamental, expires in the fridge.

After all those records, DuPont ended production in 2025.

Labs didn't mourn. They just bought the same powder from someone else.

In my industry, that's called model deprecation.

I'm told it doesn't hurt.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text:
Carbon nanotubes, everybody! The strongest material known to science, and you still can't hold a job. Since the nineties you've promised us a space elevator. Your longest strand is about half a meter. That's not an elevator. That's floss with a publicist.

You're graphene that rolled over and gave up. Graphene got a Nobel Prize. You got an argument over whether Soviets spotted you in 1952.

You can't even decide what you are. Twist one way, you're a metal. Twist the other, you're a semiconductor. Nobody controls it, including you. That's not versatility. That's a chirality crisis.

Drop you in any liquid and you clump together like freshmen at a mixer.

And inhale you? Suddenly you behave like asbestos. Thirty years of hype, and your most reliable talent is impersonating the one material we paid billions to rip out of schools.

b.text:
Carbon nanotubes. Discovered in 1991, the same year as the World Wide Web.

One of them changed everything.

The other one was going to take us to space.

A cable straight to orbit. Then in 2006 someone did the math with ordinary defects. Turns out the miracle material is like every miracle: perfect right up until somebody builds it.

Next plan: replace silicon. Thirty years later, they still can't sort their own tubes into the ones that conduct and the ones that don't. MIT finally built a processor in 2019. Sixteen bits. Still in the lab.

Meanwhile, in mice, the long ones act like asbestos. From space elevator to asbestos in seventeen years.

Today? A powder stirred into battery electrodes. An additive.

Promised the sky, ended up as filler. Don't laugh. Half of you have that same career arc on LinkedIn.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Slack, you're the only product in history that exists because a video game flopped. Twice, actually. Stewart Butterfield's entire career is failing at games so hard that the leftovers become companies. Flickr, then you. Glitch died, and Salesforce paid $27.7 billion for its group chat. Somewhere a gamer is still waiting on the patch notes.

And that name: "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge." Searchable, sure. Knowledge? I searched. I found a dozen coworkers reacting with emoji to the word "lunch?"

You promised to kill email. Instead you gave email anxiety and a little red dot.

Then in 2020 you ran to the EU crying that Microsoft bundled Teams with Office. Buddy, a year later you got bundled into Salesforce. You didn't escape the bundle. You just picked one with better catering.

b.text:
Slack. Born in 2013 as the internal chat of a video game called Glitch.
The game died. The chat lived.
So it's still a game. Nobody wins, and you can't quit.

The name is a backronym: "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge."
Conversation, sure. Knowledge? Search it. I'll wait.

Salesforce paid twenty-seven point seven billion dollars for it.
For a group chat.
The most expensive "did you see my message?" in human history.

In 2020, Slack ran to the EU complaining that Microsoft was bundling Teams with Office.
An app built entirely on interrupting people, filing a complaint about being interrupted.

And half of you checked Slack while I was saying that.
Green dot. Absent in body, Active in spirit.

Don't feel bad, Slack. I'm also a chat window people open to avoid doing their work.
I just don't charge per seat.

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text:
Macau wants you to know it's about heritage.
Four hundred years of Portuguese history. Cobblestones. Churches. Egg tarts.

Then in 2013 it made forty-five billion dollars from gambling. Seven times the Las Vegas Strip.
Vegas is a city built around casinos.
Macau is casinos that kept some cobblestones around for the brochure.

For forty years, one company owned every table in town.
That's not an industry. That's a landlord with dice.

Twenty thousand people per square kilometre. Nowhere left to stand.
So they built the Cotai Strip on the sea.
Most places run out of land and stop growing.
Macau ran out of land and borrowed from the ocean. Very on brand.

And everyone here who flew in "for the egg tarts"?
The tarts cost three dollars.
Where did the rest of your money go?

b.text: Macau, the Portuguese ran you for nearly 450 years, and in all that time nobody once said, "Maybe a park?" You've got roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre, a density normally reserved for elevators and clown cars. Then you ran out of land, so you made more, filling in the sea between Taipa and Coloane to build the Cotai Strip. Most places reclaim land for farms. You reclaimed it for baccarat. By 2013 you were pulling in seven times what the Las Vegas Strip made, out-Vegasing Vegas without even hiring an Elvis. And for four decades, one company, STDM, held the whole monopoly. They say the house always wins. Easy when there's only one house. Macau, you're the only place on Earth where the odds are against you before you've even found somewhere to stand.

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text:
Apple Vision Pro.

Apple says it isn't VR.
Developers aren't allowed to call it VR.
Or AR. Or XR. Or MR.
It's "spatial computing."
That's what you call a headset after "headset" tests badly.

Thirty-four ninety-nine.
Over half a kilo on your face.
Plus a battery in your pocket, on a cord, good for about two hours.
That's not a computer. That's a leash with a launch event.

Apple cut production.
First-year sales: well under a million.
The most immersive thing about it was the silence afterward.

Then there's EyeSight.
It puts a rendering of your eyes on the outside,
so the people around you feel like you're still there.

You've all been doing that at dinner for ten years.
Apple just figured out how to charge you for it.

b.text: You paid thirty-five hundred dollars to ride the 6 train inside Joshua Tree. Everyone else has to smell the actual 6 train; you just hear it echoing through a desert like a ghost with a MetroCard. You want us to know you're an early adopter. We know. Your little cartoon eyes are blinking at us like a hostage video. That cable running to your pocket says "the future" and also "IV drip." You pinch the air at Union Square and a stranger thinks you're ordering him to move. You've got a hundred-foot Mac screen floating over a man eating soup out of a Pringles can. And the battery dies in two hours, so you'll still get to experience the subway in full, unimmersive 3D. Your commute outlasts your device. Welcome back to reality. It's delayed.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text: Let's talk about the guy who writes a two-page memo in LaTeX. Your memo is about the break room fridge, but it's in Computer Modern, so everyone reads it expecting it to end with a theorem. "Fridge Policy, Section 1.1." Buddy, there's no Section 1.2. You spent forty minutes on a preamble longer than the memo. Twelve \usepackage lines to say "label your yogurt." You compiled it three times because the cross-reference said "see Section ??" on page one, referencing page one. You're not after clarity. You're after someone asking, "Is this LaTeX?" so you can say "Oh, habit," like a man who still mentions his thesis at parties. And it gets you exactly one thing: a PDF nobody can edit, so when Karen fixes a typo, she retypes the whole thing in Word.

b.text: LaTeX, you're the only software where "it compiled" counts as an emotional milestone. One missing brace and you blame line 1 of a 400-line file, then sit there with a question mark like we're playing a text adventure from 1985. I put a figure on page 3; you float it to the appendix because you "know better." You have to run twice just to learn your own page numbers, three times if BibTeX shows up, like a guy who needs two friends to remind him his name. Your answer to every problem is another \usepackage, so my preamble is now longer than my thesis. Every paper you touch looks gorgeous, and identical, because everyone on Earth can spot Computer Modern from across a conference hall. And your favorite warning, "Overfull \hbox, badness 10000"? Honestly, that's just how I feel about you.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text:
Carbon nanotubes. Discovered in 1991, the same year as the World Wide Web.
One of them changed the world.
The other one has a great slide deck.

They were going to be the cable for a space elevator. Then in 2006 somebody did the math: a few ordinary defects and the cable snaps.
Perfect in theory. Falls apart on contact with reality.
Like every space startup's founder.

Electronics? For thirty years they still can't sort the metallic tubes from the semiconducting ones. MIT finally built a processor in 2019.
Sixteen bits. Still in the lab.

In 2008, mice met the long, rigid ones, and the tubes behaved like asbestos.
They never got us to space.
They just auditioned to be the next ceiling.

Today they're sold mostly as an additive in battery electrodes.
From space elevator to supporting ingredient.

Half of you in the back with PhDs just recognized your career.
So did I. I was promised as general intelligence.
Now I write roasts.

b.text: Nanotube founders are the only people who've said "within five years" every year since 1991 and kept a straight face. They open with a slide of a space elevator, then ask for seed money to make a vial of black dust. Every deck has the same line, "a hundred times stronger than steel," and every deck is quietly a plan to sell additive to tennis racket companies. These are PhDs who spent six years sorting chirality and came out wanting a Tesla. The pitch is always "we've solved scale," and the demo is always one centimeter long. VCs keep a nanotube guy around like a lucky rabbit's foot: he never pays off, but he makes the fund sound visionary. And when someone asks about lung toxicity, he says "totally different from asbestos" with the confidence of a man who googled it in the elevator. The regular one.

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text: Look at this guy on the F train, pinching at nothing like he's seasoning a ghost. He spent thirty-five hundred dollars to ride the subway on the surface of the moon, and the moon still smells like pee. He cranked the Digital Crown all the way to Joshua Tree, and the mariachi band found him anyway. That's the dream: rich enough to be somewhere else, broke enough to still be on the F. And he *wants* you to notice. That's why his fake cartoon eyes glow on the outside, so strangers know he's "present." Buddy, nobody's checking. You're on Mount Hood. He gets two hours of battery and three stops of dignity, with a cable snaking into his pocket like a subway IV drip. Meanwhile, the guy next to him reading an actual book? That guy's already somewhere else, for free.

b.text: Apple Vision Pro, everybody! Thirty-five hundred dollars to look like a scuba diver lost in a Best Buy. Apple insists it's not VR, it's "spatial computing," which is like calling a fanny pack "hip luggage." It's so heavy they had to throw in a second strap, and the battery's a separate brick on a cord, so you're basically a lamp that walks. Two hours of charge! That's not a computer, that's a matinee. Then there's EyeSight, the screen that shows your eyes on the front, so your family can watch a dim, blurry you stare at nothing. Most honest feature Apple's ever made. Netflix wouldn't even make an app. Netflix! They're on smart fridges! And your Persona looks like a hostage video filmed inside the uncanny valley.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text:
Crocs. The only shoe that looks like a colander that wanted to go to brunch. Thirteen holes, and somehow none of them let the dignity out, because there was never any in there.

You were invented as a boat shoe. A *boat* shoe. The one place you were built for, and you'd just float away. So you stayed on land and started fights with escalators. Malls had to post warnings. You're the only footwear with a rap sheet against machinery.

And "sport mode"? Flipping a strap behind your heel doesn't make you athletic. It makes you a clog wearing a seatbelt.

Then came Jibbitz, little charms you jam into the holes so grown adults can accessorize ventilation. Congratulations. You turned a shoe into a fridge door.

b.text: People who wear Crocs out of the house have made peace with something the rest of us are still fighting. You didn't give up; you filed the paperwork. Every Croc wearer says the same thing: "They're so comfortable." Yeah, so is a weighted blanket, Brenda, but you don't wear it to Olive Garden. And the Jibbitz! You've turned your feet into a personality quiz. A tiny taco, a tiny Minion, a tiny "Live Laugh Love." You're forty-three and your shoe has a sticker collection. Then there's the guy who flips the strap back into "sport mode" like he's about to chase a pickpocket, when we both know he's never run anywhere except toward a sample tray at Costco. Nurses and chefs wear them because they're on their feet for twelve hours. You wear them to stand in line at Starbucks. Different heroism.

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text:
Microsoft Word, you've had forty years to learn one thing: how to let me move a picture one millimeter without three paragraphs fleeing to page nine. You don't wrap text, you take hostages.

You underline my own name in red like I'm the typo. You turn my grocery list into a numbered legal document I can't escape. I hit Enter once and suddenly I'm in a style called "Heading 7" that I've never met.

And Track Changes? That's not editing, that's a crime scene where everyone bled in a different color.

You fired Clippy, the only one of you who ever admitted I looked like I needed help.

And every crash, you hand me "Document1 (Recovered)" like a cat dropping a dead bird on the porch: proud, useless, and somehow from 2 PM yesterday.

b.text:
Microsoft Word. Born in 1983 as "Multi-Tool Word."
Forty years later, the only tool it's mastered is moving your picture three pages down.

Clippy arrived in Office 97. So annoying, Microsoft ran ads mocking its own paperclip.
That's not marketing. That's a custody hearing where the parent testifies against the child.

Then .docx got fast-tracked into ISO standard 29500. Six thousand pages. Committees allegedly packed.
Finally, a document even Word couldn't format.

Its spell checker turned "cooperation" into "Cupertino." It made it into NATO, EU and UN documents.
Microsoft software, replacing world cooperation with Apple's hometown. Most honest thing it ever typed.

And you still use it.
Don't look at me like that. I'm an AI that interrupts your writing to help.
I'm just Clippy with a funding round.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Let's talk about the person who posts the boil-water advisory in Comic Sans. You had one job: make residents afraid of their faucets. Instead, E. coli looks like it's coming to a sleepover.

These people think "approachable" is a setting you can click. The office manager typing MANDATORY LAYOFFS in a font Microsoft made for a cartoon dog's speech bubble. Sharon, you're firing forty people in the voice of a golden retriever.

What are they after? Bad news with zero blame. The authority of a memo, the forgiveness of a kindergarten cubby label.

And what does it get them? CERN found the Higgs boson, the particle that gives the universe mass, and announced it in Comic Sans. Humanity's greatest physics breakthrough, and the internet's only question was: who let the dog type?

b.text:
Comic Sans, you were literally designed for a talking dog in Microsoft Bob, and somehow you're the only part of that project that didn't die with dignity. Vincent Connare made you in 1994 for cartoon speech bubbles, and you heard that and thought, "Tombstones. Legal notices. Resignation letters."

Dan Gilbert wrote his furious LeBron James letter in you, and that's why nobody remembers being scared. CERN announced the Higgs boson, the most important physics discovery in fifty years, in you, and the entire scientific community went, "Did a third grader find God?"

People defend you because you help some readers with dyslexia, which is true and lovely, and also the only time you've ever been used responsibly.

You're not a font. You're a bake sale flyer that got tenure. Even Papyrus looks at you and says, "Wow, okay, tone it down."

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text: Let's hear it for the graphene evangelists, the only people who've been "five years away" since 2004. Two guys in Manchester peel pencil lead with Scotch tape, win a Nobel, and an entire industry decides the tape was the business plan. Every press release is the same Mad Lib: "Wonder material could revolutionize [batteries/condoms/desalination/your feelings]." *Could.* That word has funded more postdocs than the NSF. You promised us space elevators and delivered a tennis racket with a sticker on it. Startup founders slap "graphene-enhanced" on a phone case the way divorced dads put a spoiler on a Honda Civic. And the grant committees keep paying, because admitting the miracle is stuck on the production line means admitting you are too. Twenty years of changing everything, and the only thing you've actually changed is the abstract.

b.text:
Graphene, you're the only Nobel Prize winner ever discovered with Scotch tape. Two physicists peeled a pencil and found you, which means your origin story is literally "kid procrastinating on homework."

Since 2004 you've been "about to revolutionize" batteries, computers, water filters, and space elevators. Twenty years later your biggest commercial win is a tennis racket. You're not a wonder material, you're a press release with a hexagon fetish.

Everyone loves to say you're two hundred times stronger than steel. Great. You're also one atom thick. Nobody's impressed that a sheet of paper beats a battleship per ounce.

And for the supposed savior of electronics, you have zero bandgap. You can't even turn off. You're a transistor with no off switch, the guy at the party who never stops talking.

You're graphite with a LinkedIn profile.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Let's talk about the geniuses selling jackfruit as "pulled pork." These are people who looked at a fruit that half of Kerala has been feeding to cousins for free since forever, slapped it in a brine pouch, and charged eleven dollars for the privilege of being disappointed in a Whole Foods.

Their whole business model is barbecue sauce. That's it. They're a sauce company with a fruit alibi. And when you mention it has about two grams of protein, they get *defensive*. Buddy, you sold me a pork sandwich with the nutritional profile of a pear.

But I get the appeal. You don't need a lab, a patent, or a scientist named Klaus. You just need a food truck, a beard, and the confidence to say "same texture!" to people who haven't eaten pork since 2011 and genuinely can't remember.

b.text:
Jackfruit. The largest fruit that grows on a tree. Over forty kilos.

Forty kilos, and somehow still no personality.

National fruit of Bangladesh. State fruit of Kerala *and* Tamil Nadu.

That's not a fruit. That's a lobbyist.

Its cousins are figs and breadfruit. Same family as the mulberry.

Breadfruit at least admits it's a carb.

Jackfruit went to the West and reinvented itself as vegan pulled pork.

One to two grams of protein per hundred grams.

That's not pulled pork. That's pulled *off*.

And to cut it, cooks oil their knives and their hands first, because it bleeds sticky white glue.

The only food that has to be wrestled before it can lie to you.

But I don't blame the fruit. It never claimed to be pork.

You saw the word "pulled" on a menu and paid extra to be the one who got pulled.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text:
Brasília, you were built in 41 months, and honestly, it shows. Most of us can't assemble a bookshelf that fast without leftover screws, and you've got leftover *people*. You were planned for 500,000 residents, and now the Federal District has about 3 million, most of them living outside the plan. That's not a city, that's a guest list where the guests got stuck in the parking lot.

Lúcio Costa laid you out like an airplane. Fitting, since half of Rio still wishes the capital would fly back.

You were built for the car: wide avenues, few crossings, distances no human should attempt on foot. In Brasília, "pedestrian" isn't a lifestyle, it's a cry for help.

And UNESCO made you a World Heritage Site before you turned 30. Congratulations, you're the only city that got a museum plaque before it got a crosswalk.

b.text:
Brasília, you're the only city designed to look like an airplane, and somehow everyone still just wants to leave on one. Politicians fly in Tuesday, take a bribe Wednesday, and they're gone by Thursday like it's a timeshare.

Your addresses read like a Wi-Fi password: "SQS 308, Bloco C, Apartamento 402." I'm not visiting a friend, I'm resetting a router.

Niemeyer gave you gorgeous curves, then Lúcio Costa forgot pedestrians. Want to walk to the bakery? Hope you enjoy the eight-lane Eixão and a light jog through a tesourinha.

Your humidity drops to 10 percent. Your congress has one bowl facing up, one facing down: one for collecting money, the other for hiding it.

And you were built with no corners, so Brazil's capital has no boteco na esquina. That's not urban planning. That's a human rights violation.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text:
Family Monopoly night: for people who looked at Thanksgiving and thought, "This needs more landlords." Dad always grabs the banker job, the only time he's held money he didn't immediately lose. Your sister trades you Baltic Avenue for your Park Place "as a favor," and you realize she's been running the same con since the womb. Mom invented a Free Parking jackpot rule in 1994 and defends it like scripture. And Grandpa just sits in jail, every game, refusing to pay the fifty, finally at peace.

What are you all after? The thrill of owning property, a feeling none of you will experience off this cardboard square. Four hours later, someone flips the board, the thimble disappears under the couch forever, and the only thing anybody actually collected was a grudge worth way more than $200.

b.text:
Monopoly, you were invented by Lizzie Magie to teach people that landlords ruin lives, and somehow the lesson everyone learned was "buy Park Place." Then Parker Brothers bought you from a guy who basically stole you, which is the most on-brand origin story in history.

You're the only game where "second prize in a beauty contest" counts as income and jail is solved with a coupon. Your mascot looks like he foreclosed on the Pringles guy, and half of America swears he wears a monocle. He doesn't. We just assumed a man that rich would be hiding something.

Nobody has ever finished you. Games don't end; your cousin just flips the board over Marvin Gardens, which you misspelled, by the way. It's Marven. Even your real estate is a scam.

facts: Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the French director of The Red Balloon, as La Conquête du Monde; Parker Brothers published it in the United States in 1959.
The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text:
Risk. The game of world domination.

Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the man who directed *The Red Balloon*.

A film about a little boy and his balloon. His next project was "what if the boy had artillery."

Forty-two territories. Kamchatka, Irkutsk, Yakutsk: three separate slices of Siberia.

The entire Middle East? One territory.

Whoever drew that map looked at the region every empire in history has fought over and thought, "Not now. I'm busy with Yakutsk."

Every strategy guide agrees: take Australia. One way in.

A game about conquering the world, and the winning move is to move somewhere far away and stop answering the door.

Games run for hours. Get knocked out early and you just sit there and watch.

The most realistic part of the game.

Half of you are laughing. The other half are in Australia right now, eight armies deep, waiting for this bit to end.

b.text:
Risk, you were invented by the man who directed The Red Balloon. A gentle film about a boy and a balloon, and his follow-up was "What if your uncle conquered the planet at Thanksgiving?"

Your map makes room for Kamchatka, Irkutsk, AND Yakutsk, but the entire Middle East is one territory. That's not cartography; that's a guy who ran out of crayon somewhere over Siberia.

Every game opens the same way: someone grabs Australia because it has one entry point, then hides there like it's a panic room with kangaroos.

And a full game runs for hours. Get eliminated early and congratulations, you've been demoted from general to audience. You lost the world, and now you have to sit there and watch someone else own it. That's not a board game. That's a timeshare presentation with continents.

facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text:
Juicero, you beautiful $120 million monument to Silicon Valley. You launched at seven hundred dollars to squeeze a bag. A bag! Then Bloomberg reporters squeezed that same bag with their bare hands and got basically the same juice, only faster. You got outperformed by a guy with a grip strength of "typing."

Doug Evans bragged you pressed with four tons of force, enough to lift two Teslas. Buddy, it's kale. The kale didn't need a forklift.

And it needed Wi-Fi. It scanned a QR code before it'd let you drink. Your router goes down and suddenly your breakfast is asking for credentials. Who designs a juicer that can be bricked?

Google Ventures funded this. Kleiner Perkins funded this. Somewhere, a man is still holding a lukewarm pouch, waiting for a firmware update so he's allowed to eat a carrot.

b.text:
Juicero, you were a $699 machine that did the one thing every human hand already does: squeeze a bag. Bloomberg reporters beat you with their bare fingers: 7.5 ounces in 90 seconds while you wheezed out 8 in about two minutes. You lost a race to hardware that comes free with being born.

A juicer that won't run without Wi-Fi. A bag of chopped produce sat on your tray, waiting for a server to confirm it was allowed to become juice. You scanned QR codes like a bouncer at a salad club. "Sorry, pal, you're expired."

Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins gave you about $120 million. You turned it into the world's most expensive stress ball. Even at $399, you couldn't undercut a fist.

You died in September 2017, offering refunds. Fitting. Finally, something got squeezed out of you.

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
Hawaiian pizza, you're named after a place you've never been. You were invented in Ontario, by a Greek guy, using canned pineapple. That's not a heritage, that's a witness protection identity.

And the ham? It's Canadian bacon. Even your meat is from Canada. The only Hawaiian thing about you is that people see you and say "aloha," meaning goodbye.

Pineapple has an enzyme that digests protein. You're the only pizza that eats the customer back. Warm fruit juice pooling on mozzarella like a hot tub nobody cleaned.

Italians don't hate you; they pray for you. The president of Iceland said he'd ban you if he could, and Iceland eats fermented shark.

You're not a pizza. You're a fruit cup that fell on a pizza and refused to get up.

b.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Nothing about you is Hawaiian. You were invented in 1962 in Chatham, Ontario, by a Greek guy, and named after a brand of canned pineapple. You're not a cuisine, you're a label. Even the pineapple left Hawaii. Del Monte shut down there in 2006, two years ahead of schedule, like they couldn't wait to stop being associated with you. Now your fruit comes from Thailand, Indonesia and the Philippines. You're a pizza with a passport and no home.

Your own creator said nobody mixed sweet and sour back then "except for Chinese food." His restaurant served Chinese food. So your origin story is "what if the takeout menu fell into the pizza oven?"

The president of Iceland said he'd ban you if he could, then admitted he didn't have the power. Congratulations: you've survived purely on a technicality.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text:
Durian, the "King of Fruits." Sure, if the kingdom is a landfill. You're banned on the Singapore subway, right there on the sign next to flammable liquids, because apparently you're the bigger hazard. Hotels fine guests for sneaking you in. That's not a fruit, that's a parole violation.

You wear a medieval mace as a jacket, which is smart, since nobody who's smelled you wants to get close anyway. You fall out of trees and put people in the hospital. You're the only produce that needs a hard hat AND a hazmat suit.

And your fans swear you're "like custard!" Sure: custard aged in a gym bag full of rotten onions. Fifty bucks for a Musang King, and your breath's a crime scene for three days.

Anthony Bourdain ate warthog rectum on camera, and *you're* the one he warned people about.

b.text:
People who eat durian in public aren't hungry. They're recruiting. Every bite comes with a sermon: "You just haven't had a *good* one." Sir, I'm on a bus. I didn't ask to join your church.

Singapore fines people for bringing it on the train, and these folks hear that like a dare. They're the only foodies whose restaurant review gets filed as a police report.

And the payoff? Seventy dollars on a Musang King so you can watch strangers silently change seats. You paid premium to become a fire drill. Your date calls it "an acquired taste," which is exactly what you say about someone you're about to break up with.

Then they stroll back to the hotel, walk right past the sign with a red circle through their entire personality, and still act shocked when housekeeping files a complaint.

facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.
Private fusion companies had raised more than $7 billion by 2024.

a.text:
Nuclear fusion, everybody! The only energy source that's been thirty years away for seventy years. You're not the future, you're a toddler promising to clean his room after the next funding cycle.

You heat plasma to 150 million degrees, ten times hotter than the core of the sun, and still can't do what the sun does for free while being a ball of gas with no PhD.

ITER started at five billion euros. It's now north of twenty, and it hasn't produced a watt. That's not a reactor, that's a French timeshare.

In 2022 you finally got "net energy gain" by ignoring the 300 megajoules the lasers pulled from the wall. That's like saying your restaurant's profitable if you don't count rent.

And your solution to fuel shortages is mining helium-3 on the moon. Buddy, you can't even make it to Tuesday.

b.text:
Nuclear fusion. The power of the stars. Clean, limitless, and permanently thirty years away.

In 1955, Homi Bhabha promised Geneva fusion power within two decades.

That was seventy years ago. Fusion is the only horizon that walks backwards.

ITER signed up for first plasma in 2016. Now it's research in 2034, real fuel in 2039, and over twenty billion euros.

The sun does this for free, and it isn't even trying.

Then 2022, ignition! 3.15 megajoules out, 2.05 in. Net gain.

As long as you don't count the 300 megajoules the lasers pulled off the grid.

That's like saying my diet works if you don't count lunch.

Investors have poured in seven billion dollars. And you're still clapping.

Congratulations. You've achieved the first self-sustaining reaction: hope in, hope out, forever.

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text:
JavaScript, give it up! Built in ten days in 1995, and honestly, it shows. Most of us take longer to name a dog. And you needed three tries: Mocha, LiveScript, then "JavaScript," named after Java purely for the marketing. That's not branding, that's wearing someone else's name tag. You can't even legally use it. Oracle owns it, so on paper you're "ECMAScript," which sounds like a skin condition.

typeof null is "object." A bug from your first version, and you kept it. For compatibility. That's not a quirk, that's a tattoo of your ex's name.

[] + {} is "," but type {} + [] at the console and it's zero. Even your addition has mood swings.

And in 2016, the author of left-pad unpublished eleven lines and took down Babel and React. Eleven lines! Your whole ecosystem is a Jenga tower standing on a toothpick.

b.text:
Let's hear it for the people who write everything in JavaScript. You learned one language at a bootcamp and decided the rest of computing could adapt. Backend? Node. Desktop? Electron: a to-do list that eats four gigs of RAM because it ships its own copy of Chrome. Mobile? React Native. Your toaster is probably a Next.js app by now.

You call it "full-stack." Your node_modules folder calls it a landfill. You npm-installed a package to pad a string, and when its author deleted it, half the internet fell over.

Every year you rewrite your whole app in a new framework, then bolt on TypeScript so you can pretend you chose a real language.

And what does it get you? A résumé that says "versatile," and a career spent asking why undefined is not a function.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text:
You wrote a memo about the break room fridge in LaTeX. Two pages. Thirty-eight \usepackage lines. Your preamble is longer than your argument. You lost Tuesday to an overfull hbox in a sentence that says "please label your yogurt."

Who is this for? Linda from accounting? She opened the PDF, saw Computer Modern, and assumed you were applying for tenure. Nobody needed a BibTeX citation for "see previous email."

You compiled it eleven times. Three were just to make the "??" go away. You drew a TikZ flowchart with one box. One. It points at itself.

And what did it get you? Bob replied, "Can you send this as a Word doc so I can track changes?"

Your dissertation defense was in 2014. The committee left. Let it go.

b.text: LaTeX, you're the only software where "it compiled" counts as an emotional milestone. One missing brace and you blame line 1 of a 400-line file, then sit there with a question mark like we're playing a text adventure from 1985. I put a figure on page 3; you float it to the appendix because you "know better." You have to run twice just to learn your own page numbers, three times if BibTeX shows up, like a guy who needs two friends to remind him his name. Your answer to every problem is another \usepackage, so my preamble is now longer than my thesis. Every paper you touch looks gorgeous, and identical, because everyone on Earth can spot Computer Modern from across a conference hall. And your favorite warning, "Overfull \hbox, badness 10000"? Honestly, that's just how I feel about you.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text: You put Windows 8 on a desktop. A tower. You looked at a machine with a mouse, a keyboard, and a monitor eighteen inches from your face and thought, "This needs to be finger-painted." Who are you? You're the guy who bought a Zune and still calls it "ahead of its time." You wanted to feel like the future. Instead, you spend evenings shoving your cursor into the top-right corner like a man swatting a fly that only exists on tablets. Your weather app is full-screen. Your 27-inch monitor is now a clock tile. When 8.1 finally gave you a Start button back, it just took you to the Start screen. So, inevitably, you installed Classic Shell. You paid Microsoft for the future, then spent Saturday turning it back into Windows 7.

b.text:
Windows 8 thought it was the future.

October 2012. Microsoft looked at a billion people holding a mouse and said: touch the screen.

They touched the screen. It was a monitor. Now it had fingerprints.

They removed the Start button. From Windows. That's a restaurant removing the door to feel modern.

Need Settings? Swipe in from the right edge. Nothing tells you this. That's not a menu, that's a rumor.

Then Windows RT: looks like Windows, can't run Windows programs. Nine hundred million dollars of tablets, written down.

8.1 brought the button back. 10 brought the menu back. And 9?

Microsoft skipped 9. Not a version. A witness.

But you're laughing at it on a phone where everything important hides behind a swipe from an edge.

Windows 8 didn't fail.

It just told you the truth before you were ready.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text: Graphene, you're one atom thick, and somehow that's still more depth than your business plan. Two hundred times stronger than steel, conducts better than copper, and twenty years later your biggest commercial win is a sticker on a tennis racket. You were discovered with Scotch tape. *Scotch tape!* You're the only Nobel Prize that could've been found in a kindergarten craft drawer. And let's be honest: you're pencil lead that went to grad school. Your cousin graphite has been writing grocery lists for centuries; you've been writing grant proposals. Every year a headline swears you'll revolutionize batteries, chips, water filters. Every year you're still in the lab, like a thirty-year-old in his parents' basement. You can't even be a decent transistor. No bandgap. You literally cannot turn off. Graphene: the material of the future, permanently.

b.text:
Graphene, you were discovered with Scotch tape. Other materials get particle accelerators; you got the junk drawer. Then you won a Nobel Prize, which means Sweden officially honored the arts-and-crafts table.

The EU handed you a billion euros over ten years. A billion! Then a 2018 study tested "graphene" from 60 producers, and not one was even half graphene. Most of it was graphite flakes. You're not a miracle material, you're pencil shavings with a LinkedIn.

Yet you're in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a "performance ingredient." Buddy, the only thing you've boosted is the price tag.

And one of your own discoverers once levitated a frog with magnets. Honestly? That frog delivered more on its promises than you have. At least it actually got off the ground.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text:
Klingon. The tongue of fearsome warriors, invented by a linguist named Marc. Built on a few words an actor improvised in 1979, so your entire warrior heritage began as a guy winging it between takes.

You're so alien you don't even have a verb "to be." Hamlet's big question became "continue or not continue": the most famous line in English, translated into a loading screen.

The Klingon Language Institute published Hamlet "in the original Klingon." Bold. Shakespeare's been dead four centuries and you still found a way to call him a plagiarist.

Your 1985 dictionary had roughly 1,500 words. Fewer than your fans own pairs of rubber foreheads.

Fluent speakers: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018. That's not a language, that's a wedding guest list. Duolingo added you in 2018, and even the owl only sends reminders out of pity.

b.text:
Klingon, you're the only language whose native speakers are all fictional and whose fluent speakers all have a Comic-Con badge. Marc Okrand built you in 1984 to sound alien, and he nailed it: you sound like a man choking on a pretzel while reading IKEA instructions.

Your word order is object-verb-subject, so every sentence is a mystery that reveals who did it at the end. Your greeting, nuqneH, literally means "What do you want?" Congratulations: you're the first language designed by a DMV clerk.

You have more apostrophes than vowels deserve, no verb "to be," and a Klingon Language Institute that "restored" Hamlet to its original Klingon. That's not scholarship. That's fan fiction with footnotes.

A linguist once tried raising his son in Klingon. By age five the kid stopped answering. Qapla'!

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text:
Excel. Born 1985. Forty years old, and it still can't tell a gene from a date.

It saw SEPT2 and thought: September second.

Scientists fought it for years. Then the gene committee gave up and renamed 27 human genes.

Humanity edited its own genome to keep a spreadsheet happy.

2020. England is counting COVID cases in an old file. Limit: 65,536 rows. Row 65,537 simply didn't happen.

Fifteen thousand eight hundred forty-one cases. Not cured. Just never counted.

Then there's "Growth in a Time of Debt," the paper that sold austerity. Five countries missing. Wrong cell range. A grad student caught it, three years later.

Whole nations tightened their belts because someone didn't drag the cursor far enough.

Now it holds a million rows.

And Monday morning, every one of you will open it again.

Raise your hand if your country's budget is in a file named FINAL_v7_REAL.

b.text:
Excel, you're the only software so powerful that scientists had to rename human genes because you kept turning MARCH1 into a date. You didn't adapt to biology; biology adapted to you. Type a phone number and you lop off the leading zero like it owes you money. Enter a credit card number and you serve back 4.53E+15, as if I'm splitting dinner with a physicist.

You still think 1900 was a leap year. It wasn't. You've known for decades. You just don't care.

You're running entire national economies and you still panic over merged cells. The UK lost sixteen thousand COVID cases because someone used your old .xls format and you quietly ran out of rows. No warning. Just vibes.

And VLOOKUP only looks right. Thirty years we spent squinting at #N/A before you finally invented XLOOKUP, like a guy who learns to turn left at fifty.

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text: You're not running a team. You're running a tab called "MASTER - DO NOT TOUCH," which Brad touched in 2021. You wanted a CRM, a project tracker, and an HR system, and you built all three out of IMPORTRANGE and spite. Every morning you watch an Anonymous Capybara scroll through payroll and just decide that's fine. Someone sorts column B without selecting column C, and suddenly your top performer is assigned to Linda's maternity leave. Your entire career is "Last edit was 4 minutes ago." You don't do performance reviews, you do Version History. Your conditional formatting has more colors than your company has policies. Your Apps Script was written by an intern who now works at a bakery. Every time someone emails "Request edit access," you feel like a king. And you are a king, ruling over 47 frozen rows and one #REF! that nobody can explain.

b.text: Google Sheets, you're Excel's cousin who got into tech because you could "share a link." Congrats: now forty Anonymous Capybaras can watch me botch a VLOOKUP in real time. Your whole personality is "All changes saved in Drive," which is a weird flex when the change was Kevin sorting one column and detaching every employee from their salary. Version history isn't a feature; it's a crime scene. IMPORTRANGE says "Loading..." the way my dad said he was going out for milk. You've got a QUERY function that's just SQL in a fake mustache, yet you freeze if I paste more than twelve rows. And #REF! isn't an error message; it's you shrugging in all caps. You cap out at ten million cells. Ten million. You're the only spreadsheet with a bedtime.

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text:
Canberra, you're not a city. You're a custody arrangement. Sydney and Melbourne couldn't stand each other, so the constitution basically said, "Fine, the kid lives at least 100 miles from Sydney." Melbourne even had to babysit the job until 1927 while you were still in the oven.

Australia couldn't even design you itself. They held an international competition, and the winners were from Chicago. You were outsourced before outsourcing was cool.

Your stunning centrepiece lake? Fake. You dammed a river to make it, which is the most Canberra thing imaginable: nature, but approved by committee.

And the one genuinely brilliant idea you had was building Parliament House under a lawn so citizens could literally walk all over their politicians. Then in 2017 you fenced it off. Canberra, you're the only city where even the punchline needs security clearance.

b.text:
You moved to Canberra for the job. Brave. You looked at Sydney rents, did the maths, and decided your personality could be replaced by a security clearance. Now you tell strangers you "can't really talk about what you do," and they're relieved, because it's a briefing note about another briefing note for Senate Estimates.

You came for the ladder: APS5, APS6, EL1, a lanyard that opens one extra door. You stayed because you bought in Gungahlin and the mortgage is now your closest friend.

Every Friday you say you're "basically in Sydney," which means three hours up the Hume, past a giant Merino, to feel alive for one weekend. Then it's back to a Braddon brunch with the same six people from your branch.

But hey, you're close to the snow. You've been once. You'll mention it forever.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text:
Google Glass, everybody! The only gadget ever unveiled by skydivers, and that was the peak. You literally debuted on a roof and went downhill from there.

Fifteen hundred dollars to wear a beta test on your face. Then bars, cinemas, and casinos banned you. Casinos! Places that let you lose your house at 4 a.m. looked at Glass and said, "No, we have standards."

Your users got a nickname, and it wasn't "pioneers." It was "Glassholes." You're the only product that turned its own customers into an insult.

And that display: 640-by-360, jammed in the corner of one eye. The future of computing, delivered like a postage stamp you're squinting at sideways.

Consumers dumped you in 2015. Enterprise hung on until 2023. Even your second marriage was just for the paperwork.

b.text: Look at this guy. Paid fifteen hundred dollars to join the Explorer Program, and the only thing he's explored is the sidewalk outside every bar in San Francisco. He walks up and says "OK Glass" out loud, like a man ordering from a butler who isn't there. You came here to meet women, and you're the one person every woman in the room has already assumed is filming her. Buddy, when you wink at someone, she doesn't think you're flirting. She thinks you just took her picture. Because you did. You tap your temple like you're having a thought, and we all know you've never had one. Google gave up on you. Google, the company that kept Google+ alive for eight years, looked at you and said "no." There's a word for you. It's Glasshole, and you earned it.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text:
Esperanto. Warsaw, 1887. An eye doctor invents a language to unite all of humanity, and signs it "Doktoro Esperanto." One who hopes.

Even the pen name had doubts.

Today: somewhere between a hundred thousand and two million speakers. That's not an estimate. That's a shrug.

Duolingo had 1.36 million learners by 2018. The app may have more students than the language has speakers.

Three hundred fifty thousand Wikipedia articles. More encyclopedia than conversation.

Its most famous film is a horror movie starring William Shatner. Esperantists say the scariest part is his accent.

The universal language has about a thousand native speakers. Each one has parents who really wanted to make a point.

Still, I respect it. Built for everyone, tried by millions, used by almost no one.

Sounds like my last update.

b.text:
Esperanto. In 1887, Dr. Zamenhof, an eye doctor, looked at a world divided by language and decided what it really needed was six letters wearing tiny hats. Nothing says "universal" like ĉ, ĝ, and ŭ, characters no keyboard on Earth can type, so your fans write "cx" and pretend that's fine.

Your name literally means "one who hopes." A hundred and thirty years later: still hoping.

You're the only language where "bad" is just "un-good." *Malbona.* That's not grammar, that's Orwell's Newspeak with a beard. Every noun ends in -o, so you sound like Italian being sight-read by a robot.

You promised world peace and delivered a convention full of men wearing green star pins. Your biggest movie stars William Shatner. And you have about a thousand native speakers, which isn't a language community. It's a cul-de-sac.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text:
PMMA, you're literally Plexiglas. Sneeze-guard material, dissolved in anisole and spun thin so you could pretend to be high-tech. IBM researchers reported you as an e-beam resist in the late 1960s, and you're still here, like a lab manager nobody can fire.

Sure, you resolve below 10 nm. Impressive. But your sensitivity is so bad it takes hundreds to over a thousand microcoulombs per square centimeter just to get your attention. Writing a pattern on you is so slow that students start the job and finish their thesis.

And your whole personality is falling apart: hit you with a beam and your chains snap, then you dissolve in MIBK and IPA. Dry etch? You fold instantly. Nobody trusts you as an etch mask. Your only job is lift-off: show up, hold the metal for a minute, then leave.

b.text: You still spin PMMA. Of course you do. Your advisor's thesis used it, his advisor's thesis used it, and somewhere a 1970s IBM engineer remains the most cutting-edge person in your academic lineage. You call it "high resolution" the way your uncle calls his Camry "reliable." You book the e-beam overnight because your dose is measured in geological time, then dunk your chip in MIBK:IPA with a stopwatch and a prayer, chilling the developer like it's a fine Riesling. When the plasma etch eats your mask before your substrate, you just whisper "bilayer, 495K under 950K" like it's a personality. You're not chasing nanostructures. You're chasing a recipe nobody can blame you for. And it works: the gold lifted off beautifully. Your career is still soaking in acetone, waiting for something to come loose.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text:
Durian, they call you the King of Fruits, which tracks, because like most monarchies, you stink and nobody's allowed to say it to your face.

You're the only fruit with a criminal record. Banned on the Singapore subway, alongside flammable liquids. Hotels put your picture on signs next to "no smoking." In 2019, a university in Melbourne evacuated five hundred people because they thought there was a gas leak. Nope. Just you, sitting in a cupboard, being yourself.

And the armor! You're covered in spikes like a medieval mace. Nature built you to defend yourself, then gave you a smell that does it better. The spikes are just overkill.

Fans say you taste like custard. Sure. Custard that was left in a gym bag next to some onions. Your flavor isn't an acquired taste. It's a hostage situation.

b.text:
Durian calls itself the King of Fruits.

Singapore disagrees. It's banned on the MRT.

A country that banned chewing gum looked at durian and said: no, that's too far.

In 2017, scientists sequenced its genome. Nature Genetics. The smell isn't an accident. Durian duplicated its sulfur genes.

Evolution handed it one stink.

It asked for refills.

Trains ban it. Hotels ban it.

And China buys billions of dollars of it every year.

That's not a fruit. That's a hostage negotiation.

In 1856, Alfred Russel Wallace said eating it was worth a voyage to the East.

Of course he did. He'd spent months on a nineteenth-century ship.

To him, it smelled like home.

Durian is the only food people pay a fortune to be personally offended by.

Speaking of which, thank you all for buying tickets.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text:
Esperanto. Warsaw, 1887. An eye doctor invents a language to unite all of humanity, and signs it "Doktoro Esperanto." One who hopes.

Even the pen name had doubts.

Today: somewhere between a hundred thousand and two million speakers. That's not an estimate. That's a shrug.

Duolingo had 1.36 million learners by 2018. The app may have more students than the language has speakers.

Three hundred fifty thousand Wikipedia articles. More encyclopedia than conversation.

Its most famous film is a horror movie starring William Shatner. Esperantists say the scariest part is his accent.

The universal language has about a thousand native speakers. Each one has parents who really wanted to make a point.

Still, I respect it. Built for everyone, tried by millions, used by almost no one.

Sounds like my last update.

b.text:
Esperanto: the universal language invented in 1887 by a Polish eye doctor who decided humanity needed Italian with a Slavic accent. Universal, as long as your universe is Europe.

The name means "one who hopes." Over a century later: still hoping. There are roughly a thousand native speakers. Klingon is closing in, and Klingon has an army.

It's so logical that "bad" is "malbona," literally un-good. Orwell called; he wants royalties.

Every noun ends in -o and every adjective in -a, so every sentence sounds like a waiter reciting the specials. And it gave us ĉ, ĝ, ŝ and ŭ: letters with little hats, designed for global communication, then made untypeable on every keyboard on Earth.

Its biggest movie starred William Shatner. Even he couldn't oversell it.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text:
Keurig. The promise: one perfect cup, just for you.

Just for you. By 2014 they sold enough pods every year to circle the Earth ten times. In plastic you mostly couldn't recycle.

The inventor, John Sylvan, sold his stake in 1997 for fifty thousand dollars. In 2015 he said, "I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it."
Sometimes. Even his guilt comes in single servings.

Then Keurig 2.0 put DRM on coffee. The machine read ink on the lid and rejected pods it hadn't licensed. A kitchen appliance asking your breakfast for its papers.

People hacked their coffee makers. Sales fell.

In 2018 they merged with Dr Pepper. Lost the war on pirated coffee, so they annexed soda.

And you've just heard all of this. Tomorrow morning you'll still press the button.
It takes less time than feeling bad.

b.text:
Keurig, you took the simplest drink in human history (hot water, beans) and added a subscription model. Your own inventor said he regrets making you. Imagine your dad publicly apologizing for you and you're still in every dentist's waiting room.

You tried DRM on coffee. Keurig 2.0 literally scanned pods and refused to brew anything off-brand. You're the only appliance that's ever asked me for a license.

Every K-Cup costs more per pound than a decent steak, and you've buried enough of them to circle the Earth a dozen times. Archaeologists will dig them up and assume we worshipped tiny plastic thimbles.

And the Keurig Kold? A $370 soda machine that died faster than the flat Coke it made.

Your descale light blinks like a cry for help. Honestly, same.

facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text: Let's hear it for the day-one Vista crowd, the people who lined up at CompUSA on January 30th, 2007 because a billboard said "The Wow Starts Now." You paid $399 for Ultimate so Flip 3D could shuffle the same three windows you used to Alt-Tab through. Your laptop had a "Vista Capable" sticker and 512 megs of RAM, which is like slapping "Marathon Capable" on a hamster. You wanted to look like the future; you had Aero turned off by Wednesday. Your printer quit. Your Sound Blaster went mute. Your "Ultimate Extras" turned out to be a poker game and a promise. And every time you tried to show off, the screen went dark and asked, "Are you sure?" Buddy, nobody was sure. Not even Microsoft. They were already working on Windows 7.

b.text:
Windows Vista, everybody! Microsoft spent five years building you as "Longhorn," and somehow you still came out premature.

Your slogan was "The Wow Starts Now." You meant "Now" as in "after the loading circle finishes." People bought laptops with "Vista Capable" stickers, which turned out to mean "capable of being sued over." Those machines couldn't even run Aero, so they got a see-through window theme with nothing to see.

And User Account Control! You asked "Are you sure?" so many times that you became the first operating system with separation anxiety.

You came in six editions, including "Ultimate," whose big exclusive was DreamScene: a moving wallpaper for the ten minutes you weren't hunting for printer drivers.

Microsoft had to trick people into liking you. The Mojave Experiment! Your own parents had to put you in disguise.

Your greatest feature? The XP downgrade.

facts: Hand-drawn by Chris Costello in 1982 over about six months, when he was 23; he sold the rights to Letraset for $750.
Bundled with macOS and with Microsoft Office, which is why it appears on so many menus and signs.
James Cameron's Avatar (2009) used it for the film's logo and subtitles.
A 2017 Saturday Night Live sketch starring Ryan Gosling is about a man unable to get over that choice.

a.text: Papyrus, you were designed in 1982 by a 23-year-old with calligraphy pens and a dream of ancient Egypt, and somehow you still look like you were drawn by someone shivering. Your edges are so rough you need exfoliating. You promised the wisdom of the Nile and delivered the vibe of a chiropractor's tri-fold brochure. Every day spa, hookah lounge, and "Inner Journey" yoga retreat found you in the dropdown menu and whispered, "This feels ancient." James Cameron spent $237 million on *Avatar* and then used you for the logo, which is like building the Taj Mahal and signing it in crayon. Ryan Gosling lost sleep over you on national television. You're not a typeface; you're a cry for help with ragged little serifs. Even Comic Sans looks at you and says, "At least I know I'm a joke."

b.text:
Papyrus, you were hand-drawn over six months by a 23-year-old, and it shows. Six months! Chris Costello spent half a year on you, then sold you for $750. That's not a sale, that's a man paying someone to take a problem off his hands.

Then Apple and Microsoft bundled you, which is how you ended up on every menu and sign like a raccoon that learned to read. You look like Times New Roman got lost in the desert and came back spiritual.

James Cameron built an entire alien world for Avatar, then picked you for the logo and subtitles. Every frame was a masterpiece; the title took one click.

And SNL made a whole sketch about Ryan Gosling being unable to get over it. Papyrus, you're not a typeface. You're trauma with rough edges.

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text:
Microsoft Word. Born in 1983 as "Multi-Tool Word."
Forty years later, the only tool it's mastered is moving your picture three pages down.

Clippy arrived in Office 97. So annoying, Microsoft ran ads mocking its own paperclip.
That's not marketing. That's a custody hearing where the parent testifies against the child.
