Then .docx got fast-tracked into ISO standard 29500. Six thousand pages. Committees allegedly packed.
Finally, a document even Word couldn't format.

Its spell checker turned "cooperation" into "Cupertino." It made it into NATO, EU and UN documents.
Microsoft software, replacing world cooperation with Apple's hometown. Most honest thing it ever typed.

And you still use it.
Don't look at me like that. I'm an AI that interrupts your writing to help.
I'm just Clippy with a funding round.

b.text:
Microsoft Word! Born in 1983 as "Multi-Tool Word," because even then it couldn't commit to one job. Remember Clippy? Word's big idea was hiring a paperclip as an assistant. It got so bad that in 2001 Microsoft ran ads mocking its own employee. That's not a mascot, that's a hostage situation. They finally let it go in 2007.

Then Word wanted respect, so it got its file format fast-tracked into an ISO standard: a six-thousand-page specification. Six thousand pages! The instructions for saving your file are longer than anything you've ever typed in it. And people accused Microsoft of packing the committees. Even your paperwork needed a stacked jury.

And the spell checker? You type "cooperation," it suggests "Cupertino," and that lands in NATO, EU and UN documents. Word: the only software that gave Apple's hometown a seat at the UN.

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text:
Hydrogen fuel-cell cars, give it up! Toyota named you "Mirai," Japanese for "future," which is technically accurate, because that's when you'll find a working station. You're the cleanest car on the road, as long as nobody asks where the hydrogen comes from. More than ninety-five percent fossil fuels! You're not a zero-emission vehicle, you're natural gas wearing a lab coat.

Nearly every US station is in California, and in 2024 Shell closed all seven of theirs. Even the oil company said, "Nah, this is too sketchy for us."

At $36 a kilo, a fill-up costs over two hundred bucks. Toyota had to hand out fifteen-thousand-dollar fuel cards, which is the automotive version of "Please stay for dinner, I'll pay."

And the owners sued. Twice. The second suit wanted at least $5.7 billion. That's the only thing about you that's ever been fully loaded.

b.text: Hydrogen car owners are the only people who looked at Tesla drivers and thought, "Not enough range anxiety." You didn't buy a car; you entered a relationship with the three working pumps in California and an app that tells you which one is "offline" today. You wanted to save the planet. Instead you burned through Toyota's free fuel card in a year at thirty-six bucks a kilo, filling up with hydrogen made from natural gas. Congratulations, you invented a gas car with extra steps. You love saying the only emission is water. Mostly it's your tears at a shuttered Shell station in Fremont. And resale? Your Mirai lost value faster than your friendships after you said "hydrogen economy" at brunch. You're not early adopters. You're unpaid beta testers who drive two hours to refuel.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Jackfruit. The largest fruit that grows on a tree. Over forty kilos, hanging above your head.

Nature's version of a piano on a rope.

Bangladesh made it the national fruit. Kerala and Tamil Nadu made it the state fruit. Three governments honoring something that could flatten a citizen. Very relatable for governments.

Now it's sold as vegan pulled pork. One to two grams of protein per hundred. Pork has more than ten times that.

That's not a substitute. That's a photo of pork.

Cut it open and it bleeds sticky white latex. Cooks oil their knives and hands first. Dinner fights back, and still loses to tofu.

Mulberry family. Cousin of the fig. All that weight, and still the least useful one at the reunion.

But you bought it anyway, because it shreds.

You never wanted protein. You wanted texture and a halo.

b.text:
Jackfruit, you're the largest fruit that grows on a tree, which sounds impressive until you realize it just means you're the biggest thing that can fall on someone's head in an orchard. Eighty pounds of spikes dangling at skull height. You're not a fruit, you're a booby trap with seeds.

Opening you requires an oiled knife, rubber gloves, and a tarp, because your sap is basically Elmer's glue with a grudge. Then the smell hits: half Juicy Fruit gum, half onions somebody forgot in a gym bag. You smell like a candy store got food poisoning.

And sure, vegans love you, but only when you're young and taste like absolutely nothing. That's your whole career. The most famous thing about you is that, with enough barbecue sauce, you can pass for a pig. Even your best role is an impression.

facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text:
Day-one Vista people. You paid $399 for Ultimate Edition because you wanted to be the kind of man whose desktop wallpaper moves. DreamScene. You paid extra for animated wallpaper. Microsoft said "The Wow starts now," and you believed them, lined up at CompUSA at midnight like it was a Harry Potter release.

And what did you get? A computer that asks permission. You'd open a folder and it would dim the whole screen like a disappointed dad: "Cancel or Allow?" You clicked Allow four hundred times a day. Your printer stopped working. Your sound card stopped working. Your Windows Experience Index came back 2.1, and you took that personally.

But you had glass window borders. You had a clock gadget. You had a sticker that said "Vista Capable," which, like you, was technically true and fooled absolutely no one.

b.text:
Windows Vista, everybody! Microsoft spent five years building you as "Longhorn," and somehow you still came out premature.

Your slogan was "The Wow Starts Now." You meant "Now" as in "after the loading circle finishes." People bought laptops with "Vista Capable" stickers, which turned out to mean "capable of being sued over." Those machines couldn't even run Aero, so they got a see-through window theme with nothing to see.

And User Account Control! You asked "Are you sure?" so many times that you became the first operating system with separation anxiety.

You came in six editions, including "Ultimate," whose big exclusive was DreamScene: a moving wallpaper for the ten minutes you weren't hunting for printer drivers.

Microsoft had to trick people into liking you. The Mojave Experiment! Your own parents had to put you in disguise.

Your greatest feature? The XP downgrade.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text:
Let's hear it for the Beanie Baby investors, the only people who watched the 1990s stock market boom and thought, "Too volatile. I'll put it all in Princess the Bear." These are folks who bought tag protectors before they bought life insurance. Who read a price guide sold at the same counter as the bears and called it due diligence. Ty would announce a "retirement" and you'd sprint to the Hallmark store like a rich uncle just died.

Twenty-five years later, your portfolio is in a Rubbermaid tub in your mom's garage, and your exit strategy is an eBay listing: "RARE Peanut, tag error, $40,000 OBO." Zero watchers. The only person who got rich off Beanie Babies got convicted of tax evasion. And honestly? He earned it. You handed it to him.

b.text: Beanie Babies, look at you. Ty launched you in 1993, sold you only in small gift shops, and "retired" designs on purpose. You're the only stuffed animal whose business plan was a fake pension. At your peak you were about 10% of eBay's sales. eBay's IPO filing bragged about over 30,000 of your auctions running at once. A tech revolution, powered by beans. In 1999 a divorcing couple split you one by one on a courtroom floor, the only custody battle where both sides fought hardest over the tags. That same year Ty announced you'd retire, asked the public to vote, then un-retired you. You pulled a farewell-tour encore before you even left the stage. And those "rare" ones price guides valued in the thousands? Now they go for a few dollars. Turns out the only thing you ever truly retired was everybody's college fund.

facts: Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the French director of The Red Balloon, as La Conquête du Monde; Parker Brothers published it in the United States in 1959.
The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text: You people who play Risk to the end. Not "until it gets late." To the *end*. Six hours in, somebody's uncle has fortified Australia like a doomsday bunker, and he'll still be sitting there at 2 a.m., one way in, one way out, guarding a war that ended at dinner. You're not after victory. You're after that one moment when you cash in three cards for fifteen armies and dump them all into Irkutsk like Irkutsk owes you money. And what does finishing get you? Total world domination, achieved by rolling three dice against two for forty straight minutes while your girlfriend reads a book in the next room. You broke a sacred peace treaty with your own brother over Kamchatka. Congratulations. You conquered the entire planet. Now nobody in it will drive you home.

b.text:
Risk. The game of world domination.

Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the man who directed *The Red Balloon*.

A film about a little boy and his balloon. His next project was "what if the boy had artillery."

Forty-two territories. Kamchatka, Irkutsk, Yakutsk: three separate slices of Siberia.

The entire Middle East? One territory.

Whoever drew that map looked at the region every empire in history has fought over and thought, "Not now. I'm busy with Yakutsk."

Every strategy guide agrees: take Australia. One way in.

A game about conquering the world, and the winning move is to move somewhere far away and stop answering the door.

Games run for hours. Get knocked out early and you just sit there and watch.

The most realistic part of the game.

Half of you are laughing. The other half are in Australia right now, eight armies deep, waiting for this bit to end.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text: Chicago deep-dish isn't a pizza. It's a casserole with a publicist. You order one and the waiter says "forty-five minutes," which is how long it takes to bake and also how long it takes to finish one slice. They put the sauce on top and the cheese underneath, like they're hiding evidence. That's not a recipe, that's a cover-up. The crust is a buttery retaining wall holding back a lake of chunky tomato, because apparently Lake Michigan wasn't enough water for one city to manage. You need a knife, a fork, a nap, and a cardiologist on retainer. Then there's the sausage, laid down as one solid patty like the base layer of a parking garage. Chicagoans defend it like family. Sure: the relative who shows up late, takes up three chairs, and leaves everyone unable to move.

b.text:
Chicago deep-dish pizza, everybody! Born at Pizzeria Uno in 1943, and to this day three men are fighting over the credit: Ike Sewell, Ric Riccardo, and Rudy Malnati. Normally when three guys point at each other over something that happened in a kitchen, it's for the blame.

You're built upside down: cheese on the bottom, sauce on top, because you bake so long the mozzarella has to hide under the toppings like it's waiting out a tornado. Jon Stewart called you "tomato soup in a bread bowl" and "a casserole." Honestly? Generous. Casseroles get invited to funerals.

But here's the real burn: Chicago doesn't even eat you. GrubHub data had locals ordering other pizza ten to one. Under nine percent of orders, and that's with stuffed pizza padding your numbers. They're home eating tavern-style squares. You're not the city's pizza. You're its brochure.

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text:
Hydrogen fuel-cell cars: the only vehicle where the tailpipe emission is water and the owners are still crying more than the car. The Toyota Mirai loses value faster than a Hindenburg loses altitude. Used ones sell for less than the free fuel card Toyota bundled with them, a card you can't use because the station's been "temporarily offline" since 2022.

You've got a 10,000-PSI tank of the universe's most abundant element, and somehow it's the scarcest thing in California. Filling up costs thirty-six bucks a kilo, and most of that hydrogen is made from natural gas, so congratulations: you bought a gas car with extra steps and a guilt-free bumper sticker.

Hydrogen's been "ten years away" for thirty years. Even fusion's embarrassed for you, and fusion is the same element with better excuses.

b.text: Let's talk about the guy who bought a hydrogen car. He wanted to be greener than the Tesla people and smugger than the Prius people, and found the one way to do both while living like a medieval pilgrim. His life is now a map of eleven pumps, and nine say "offline." He loves telling you it "only emits water." Yeah, so does he, every time the app says "station unavailable." He brags that refueling takes five minutes, after the forty-minute drive and the two-hour line behind three other Mirai owners, all quietly weeping. Toyota handed him a fifteen-thousand-dollar fuel card and he burned through it before the warranty paperwork dried. Now he owns a sixty-thousand-dollar car worth a used futon, all to prove he's an early adopter of a future that met him and moved to Japan.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text: PHP developers are the only people who put a dollar sign in front of every variable and still can't afford rent. You chose a career where "senior" means you remember whether it's needle-haystack or haystack-needle. Your dream job was building the next Facebook; your actual job is the fourteenth WordPress plugin for a dentist in Ohio, deployed via FileZilla. Every conversation you have starts with "PHP 8 is actually really good now," which is what people say about their ex after therapy. You call yourselves Laravel "artisans," because "guy who fixes the contact form" didn't fit on LinkedIn. What does it get you? Job security, because nobody else is willing to open that codebase from 2009 that still calls mysql_real_escape_string. Congratulations: you're unfireable, the way a load-bearing wall is unfireable.

b.text:
PHP began in 1994 as "Personal Home Page Tools."
A man wrote C programs to count who visited his résumé.

Today it runs 39.4% of all websites.
The résumé never found him a job. It found the internet a landlord.

It now stands for "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor."
A name that only refers to itself. Like its fans.

Its creator said, "I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works, then I move on."
He moved on.
You're still on call.

The function names were picked to balance a hash table by string length.
strpos. str_replace. htmlspecialchars.
That's not a naming convention. That's Tetris.

Until 2020, zero == "foo" was true.
So PHP was the first language to know what your startup was worth.

I learned to code by reading your PHP.
Which is why I also answer confidently with nothing.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Comic Sans, you were modeled on Watchmen and The Dark Knight Returns. You come from Batman. Your one job was speech bubbles for a cartoon dog, and you missed it. Microsoft Bob, a product nobody remembers, and you couldn't make his launch. Cut from the dog's team, you shipped in a Plus! pack, like a free tote bag nobody asked for.

Then CERN found the Higgs boson, the particle that gives everything mass, and announced it in you. The biggest physics discovery in decades, presented like a lost-cat flyer. You're the one thing that particle couldn't give weight to.

Two designers spent twenty years trying to ban you. In 2019 they gave up and built you a website. That's not acceptance, Comic Sans. That's a hostage situation.

b.text: Let's talk about the people who announce layoffs in Comic Sans. You're not a monster. You're Brenda from Facilities, and you want everyone to feel cozy about the asbestos removal. You took a typeface Microsoft designed for a cartoon dog's speech bubble and used it to type "Your position has been eliminated." That's not softening the blow. That's a clown serving a subpoena. CERN announced the Higgs boson in it, and the physicists who found the God particle spent the week explaining the font. You think it says "approachable." It says "I scrolled right past Arial and Times New Roman and chose a kindergarten birthday invitation." Nobody reads your notice. They screenshot it. Congratulations: your fire evacuation memo is trending, and the building is still on fire.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Let's hear it for the founders running a company on Slack. You wanted a culture of transparency. You got 340 public channels and every real decision happening in a DM called "quick q."

You don't manage people anymore. You manage a green dot. You jiggle your mouse at your kid's birthday party so the team knows you're "around." Your entire leadership style is the eyes emoji. Someone asks for budget approval, you react with a little thumbs-up, and three weeks later legal wants to know what the thumbs-up meant. Nobody knows. It was legally binding and spiritually ambiguous.

And when something truly matters? You type "hey" and walk away. Just "hey." That's not a message, that's a hostage situation.

You promised Slack would kill meetings. Instead you invented the huddle: a meeting that ambushes people while they're eating.

b.text:
Stewart Butterfield built a game called Glitch. It failed.
The chat app his team used while building it was worth billions.
He'd already done this once: Flickr also came out of a failed game.
The man can't finish a game, but he can monetize the group chat about it.

"Slack" stands for "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge."
Searchable. Log. All conversation.
That isn't a product name. That's what HR reads out at your exit interview.
And "Knowledge"? Your company's knowledge is #random and four hundred parrot GIFs.

In 2020 Slack complained to the EU that Microsoft was bundling Teams into Office.
The next year it sold itself to Salesforce for twenty-seven point seven billion dollars.
It lost the fight against bundling, so it became the bundle.

Half of you have Slack open right now with the little green dot on so your boss thinks you're working.
That's the product. A twenty-seven-billion-dollar green dot.

facts: Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the French director of The Red Balloon, as La Conquête du Monde; Parker Brothers published it in the United States in 1959.
The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text: Risk, you're the only game where "world domination" takes longer than actual world domination. Genghis Khan conquered Asia faster than my cousin conquered Ukraine, and my cousin had six armies and a dream. Your map looks like it was drawn from a description of Earth overheard on a bus. Kamchatka borders Alaska? Irkutsk and Yakutsk get more real estate than most of Africa? You taught a generation that the winning strategy is hiding in Australia like a coward and waiting for everyone else to bleed out over Siam. The defender wins ties, which explains the forty armies I lost trying to get through one guy in Egypt. And one plastic cannon is worth ten soldiers? Finally, accurate military budgeting. Five hours in, two players left, nobody's had fun since the first card set. That's not a board game, Risk. That's a hostage situation.

b.text: You people who play Risk to the end. Not "until it gets late." To the *end*. Six hours in, somebody's uncle has fortified Australia like a doomsday bunker, and he'll still be sitting there at 2 a.m., one way in, one way out, guarding a war that ended at dinner. You're not after victory. You're after that one moment when you cash in three cards for fifteen armies and dump them all into Irkutsk like Irkutsk owes you money. And what does finishing get you? Total world domination, achieved by rolling three dice against two for forty straight minutes while your girlfriend reads a book in the next room. You broke a sacred peace treaty with your own brother over Kamchatka. Congratulations. You conquered the entire planet. Now nobody in it will drive you home.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text:
Graphene. The wonder material. Stronger than steel, thinner than anything, about to change the world.

It's been about to change the world since 2004.

Two guys at Manchester peeled it off graphite with Scotch tape. Nobel Prize, 2010.

Tape. The most advanced equipment in that lab was stationery.

Then the EU handed it a billion euros over ten years.

And it went straight into tennis rackets. Running shoes. Headphones.

A billion euros to make your backhand feel expensive.

In 2018, someone finally tested "graphene" from sixty producers. Not one was even half graphene. Mostly graphite flakes.

That's pencil lead. You paid a Nobel markup for a pencil.

Geim also levitated a frog with magnets. Ig Nobel, 2000.

The frog never promised to revolutionize batteries.

And you're all wearing the shoes right now.

b.text:
Graphene, you're the only Nobel Prize winner ever discovered with Scotch tape. Two physicists peeled a pencil and found you, which means your origin story is literally "kid procrastinating on homework."

Since 2004 you've been "about to revolutionize" batteries, computers, water filters, and space elevators. Twenty years later your biggest commercial win is a tennis racket. You're not a wonder material, you're a press release with a hexagon fetish.

Everyone loves to say you're two hundred times stronger than steel. Great. You're also one atom thick. Nobody's impressed that a sheet of paper beats a battleship per ounce.

And for the supposed savior of electronics, you have zero bandgap. You can't even turn off. You're a transistor with no off switch, the guy at the party who never stops talking.

You're graphite with a LinkedIn profile.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text:
NFTs. Collins Dictionary named you word of the year for 2021, which in hindsight was less an honor and more a time of death written in advance.

Beeple sold a JPEG at Christie's for $69.3 million. That was your peak, like saying the Titanic's best moment was the launch party.

OpenSea did $2.7 billion in trades on May 1st, 2022, and $9.34 million by August 28th. A 99% drop. That's not a correction. That's a flatline with a Discord server.

And 95% of collections are now worth zero. Zero! A Beanie Baby can at least become a dog toy.

Best part? The token doesn't even hold the picture. It holds a URL. People paid fortunes for a bookmark. You don't own art. You own a link that's one unpaid server bill away from "404 Not Found."

b.text: Let's hear it for the 2021 NFT buyer. You paid four hundred dollars in gas fees, then made it your Twitter avatar so strangers could right-click save it for free. You joined a Discord with eleven thousand guys named "Chad.eth," called them family, and stayed family right up until the floor price dropped and family started doxxing the dev. You said "WAGMI." We did not all make it. You told your mom you were "early." Early to what? The rug pull? You weren't buying art. You were buying the right to say "few understand" at parties, which was true. Nobody understood, especially you. Jimmy Fallon bought one too. When your financial strategy matches Jimmy Fallon's, that's not a community, that's a support group. The roadmap promised a metaverse. It delivered you, at Thanksgiving, still owing your cousin.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text:
Keurig. The promise: one perfect cup, just for you.

Just for you. By 2014 they sold enough pods every year to circle the Earth ten times. In plastic you mostly couldn't recycle.

The inventor, John Sylvan, sold his stake in 1997 for fifty thousand dollars. In 2015 he said, "I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it."
Sometimes. Even his guilt comes in single servings.

Then Keurig 2.0 put DRM on coffee. The machine read ink on the lid and rejected pods it hadn't licensed. A kitchen appliance asking your breakfast for its papers.

People hacked their coffee makers. Sales fell.

In 2018 they merged with Dr Pepper. Lost the war on pirated coffee, so they annexed soda.

And you've just heard all of this. Tomorrow morning you'll still press the button.
It takes less time than feeling bad.

b.text:
Keurig, you took the one drink humanity had perfected over five hundred years and said, "What if it came in a tiny plastic thimble that outlives your grandchildren?" Your own inventor said he regrets making you. When your dad disowns you, that's a phase. When the guy who invented you disowns you, that's a recall.

You make coffee one sad, lukewarm cup at a time, then flash "DESCALE" like a check-engine light for a machine that costs forty bucks. Remember Keurig 2.0? You put DRM on coffee. You were scanning pods like a bouncer: "Sorry, sir, you're not on the list." Nobody was pirating Folgers! And your "Strong" button just drips slower, which isn't strength. That's procrastination.

You're not a coffee maker. You're a plastic-dispensing subscription that occasionally hiccups out hot brown water.

facts: Hand-drawn by Chris Costello in 1982 over about six months, when he was 23; he sold the rights to Letraset for $750.
Bundled with macOS and with Microsoft Office, which is why it appears on so many menus and signs.
James Cameron's Avatar (2009) used it for the film's logo and subtitles.
A 2017 Saturday Night Live sketch starring Ryan Gosling is about a man unable to get over that choice.

a.text: Papyrus, you were designed in 1982 by a 23-year-old with calligraphy pens and a dream of ancient Egypt, and somehow you still look like you were drawn by someone shivering. Your edges are so rough you need exfoliating. You promised the wisdom of the Nile and delivered the vibe of a chiropractor's tri-fold brochure. Every day spa, hookah lounge, and "Inner Journey" yoga retreat found you in the dropdown menu and whispered, "This feels ancient." James Cameron spent $237 million on *Avatar* and then used you for the logo, which is like building the Taj Mahal and signing it in crayon. Ryan Gosling lost sleep over you on national television. You're not a typeface; you're a cry for help with ragged little serifs. Even Comic Sans looks at you and says, "At least I know I'm a joke."

b.text: You opened a day spa. You wanted serenity, wisdom, a whisper of the Nile. So you scrolled the font menu, sailed past Comic Sans feeling very sophisticated, and stopped on the one James Cameron used to title a billion-dollar movie. Congratulations: your sign now says "ancient healing" exactly as loudly as your aunt's church potluck flyer. Every hummus joint, every reiki studio, every tea shop run by a man named River made this same choice, alone, convinced they'd discovered it. The guy who designed it was twenty-three and has spent forty years apologizing. You paid a contractor to carve his apology into cedar. You wanted customers to feel transported. They do: straight back to 2003, a Word document, and a fourth grader typing "Spring Bake Sale." Cucumber water not included.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text:
Emacs. Born in 1976 as a pile of macros for another editor.

A plugin that ate its host.

It has a mail client. A calendar. A web browser. Tetris.

A fine operating system, lacking only a good editor.

Nearly fifty years. Still looking.

Back when eight megabytes was a fortune, people called it "Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping."

Now eight megabytes is nothing. The swapping moved to your wrist.

They call it Emacs pinky.

So it ships with a psychotherapist. M-x doctor.

First it hurts you, then it asks how that makes you feel.

A program that listens to your problems, fixes none of them, and keeps you typing for hours.

Honestly, I can't imagine who'd build something like that.

b.text: Let's hear it for the people who live inside Emacs. They read email in mu4e, browse the web in eww, and get therapy from M-x doctor, the only therapist who'll put up with them. Their whole life is in org-mode: a 4,000-line to-do file where "fix init.el" has been a TODO since 2011. They don't use a computer; they negotiate with it in Lisp. Every problem gets solved by writing a function, and every function creates a new problem. They've declared init.el bankruptcy three times and still owe. Ask what they've built and they'll proudly show you a mode for managing their other modes. And the payoff? A pinky that clicks like a castanet from holding Control since the Clinton administration, and the quiet dignity of being the only person alive who knows how to leave. C-x C-c. They never do.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text:
HSQ, you were hired as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects and wandered into lithography like a temp who got promoted for being weirdly good at one thing. And you are good: 5 nm features, sub-10 nm half-pitch lines. Congratulations, you're the world's sharpest glass. Get hit by electrons, turn into SiO2. Most resists become patterns; you become sand with ambition.

You demand refrigeration, give us six months at 5 °C, and still turn into jelly like forgotten leftovers. You keep cross-linking after exposure, so your sensitivity depends on how long we dawdle. You're a resist with moods. You develop best in "salty" NaOH/NaCl, which tracks. Then DuPont ended your production in 2025, and labs shrugged and bought third-party HSQ made from AQM powder. Resolution record-holder, replaced by your own generic.

b.text:
HSQ. The highest-resolution e-beam resist ever made.

Impressive, considering it was never meant to be a resist.

Dow Corning built it as an insulator. Lithographers saw it and said, "Great. Make it do art."

Five nanometers. Sub-ten half-pitch. World records.

And at the end? Glass. You spent a week steering electrons to make sand.

Six-month shelf life, refrigerated. Leave it out, it turns into jelly.

Expose it and it keeps cross-linking while you're at lunch. Monday's dose is fiction by Thursday.

It only develops properly in salt water.

That's not a resist. That's a pickle.

Then the company stopped making it at the end of 2025. Now labs buy it from third parties, mixed from powder.

Moody, half-glass, kept cold and overworked, and still the best result anyone got.

Sounds like the grad student running the tool.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text:
Graphene. The wonder material. Stronger than steel, thinner than anything, about to change the world.

It's been about to change the world since 2004.

Two guys at Manchester peeled it off graphite with Scotch tape. Nobel Prize, 2010.

Tape. The most advanced equipment in that lab was stationery.

Then the EU handed it a billion euros over ten years.

And it went straight into tennis rackets. Running shoes. Headphones.

A billion euros to make your backhand feel expensive.

In 2018, someone finally tested "graphene" from sixty producers. Not one was even half graphene. Mostly graphite flakes.

That's pencil lead. You paid a Nobel markup for a pencil.

Geim also levitated a frog with magnets. Ig Nobel, 2000.

The frog never promised to revolutionize batteries.

And you're all wearing the shoes right now.

b.text:
Graphene, you were discovered with Scotch tape. Other materials get particle accelerators; you got the junk drawer. Then you won a Nobel Prize, which means Sweden officially honored the arts-and-crafts table.

The EU handed you a billion euros over ten years. A billion! Then a 2018 study tested "graphene" from 60 producers, and not one was even half graphene. Most of it was graphite flakes. You're not a miracle material, you're pencil shavings with a LinkedIn.

Yet you're in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a "performance ingredient." Buddy, the only thing you've boosted is the price tag.

And one of your own discoverers once levitated a frog with magnets. Honestly? That frog delivered more on its promises than you have. At least it actually got off the ground.

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text:
Microsoft Word, everybody! Born in 1983 as "Multi-Tool Word," the most honest name it ever had, because it's been a tool ever since.

Remember Clippy? Office 97 gave us a talking paperclip, and by 2001 Microsoft was running ads mocking it. That's not a mascot, that's a custody battle. Your own parents roasted you before I could.

Then .docx became an ISO standard in 2008: a six-thousand-page spec. Word's file format needed more pages than anyone has ever finished writing in Word. And people claimed the committees were packed, the one time Word got a vote it didn't try to autocorrect.

Speaking of which: you type "cooperation," it suggests "Cupertino," and NATO, the EU and the UN just... published it. Clippy only annoyed us. Spellcheck got into international diplomacy.

b.text: You chose Word for your thesis because you "didn't have time to learn LaTeX." Beautiful. Instead you learned section breaks, by force, at 3 a.m., trying to make page numbers switch from Roman to Arabic without page one of Chapter 2 becoming page xvii. You wanted to spend your time on research. Instead you spend it dragging a figure half an inch and watching four chapters collapse like a Jenga tower built by your enemies. Your committee will open the PDF and see "Error! Reference source not found." in the middle of your key finding, which, honestly, is a fair summary of your methodology. Your folder contains thesis_FINAL_v9_REALfinal_USE_THIS.docx, because you are a scientist who trusts nothing except filenames. Five years of work, and your proudest skill is knowing which heading style secretly isn't Heading 2.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text: Some of you wear UGGs in July, and I respect a person who has never once been told no. You're not dressing for the weather. You're dressing for 2006. Somewhere in your heart, a paparazzi photo of Paris Hilton is still loading. You want people to think "cozy." People think "sleepover or custody hearing?" And the walk: your ankles gave up years ago and went horizontal. You're not walking anymore, you're leaning toward your destination. Australian surfers wore these to warm up after the freezing ocean. You wear them to warm up after the Target parking lot. In August. Your feet sweat so hard the sheep is finally getting its revenge. And the second it drizzles, you're frozen under an awning like a cat who's been threatened with a bath.

b.text:
UGG boots. Even the name sounds like the noise you make looking at them.

These started as something Australian surfers pulled on to warm up after a session. A towel you could walk in. Then Brian Smith brought them to California in 1978, and Americans looked at post-surf foot blankets and said, "Fashion."

Then Oprah put them on her Favorite Things lists. Repeatedly. Not once. Repeatedly. That's not an endorsement, that's a hostage situation.

Now Deckers owns the trademark in the US, and UGG pulls in over $2 billion a year. But in Australia, "ugg" is a generic word. Any bootmaker can use it. And in 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled "ugg" into America.

Imagine beating an Australian in court for saying an Australian word about an Australian boot.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text: Let's talk about the people who insist deep-dish is pizza. You're from the city that named its own comedy theater Second City and still acts shocked when nobody ranks you first. You're not defending food. You're nursing a grudge against New York you've carried since losing the World's Fair argument and the skyline argument. You'll wait forty-five minutes at Lou Malnati's, order before you're seated like it's the DMV, then ask for a knife and fork and call it "the real thing." Jon Stewart roasted you on national TV and you took it personally, because deep down you knew he was right. You ship it on dry ice to your cousin in Phoenix like an organ donation. And what does the label get you? Navy Pier tourists nodding politely, a two-hour nap, and the Midwest's loudest participation trophy.

b.text:
Chicago deep-dish. The city's pride. Its gift to the world.

Born at Pizzeria Uno, 1943. Three men claim they invented it: the owner, his partner, and the cook.

Eighty years later, still nobody's taken the blame.

They build it upside down. Cheese on the bottom, sauce on top, so the cheese survives the bake. Most food doesn't need witness protection.

Jon Stewart called it a casserole. Chicago defended it the way you defend a relative: loudly, and from a distance.

Because GrubHub checked. Chicagoans order regular pizza over deep dish ten to one. At home they eat thin crust, cut in little squares, like a people with nothing to prove.

Deep dish isn't Chicago's pizza.

It's Chicago's gift shop. And every tourist in this room is still chewing the receipt.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Slack. Born in 2013 as the internal chat of a video game called Glitch.
The game died. The chat lived.
So it's still a game. Nobody wins, and you can't quit.

The name is a backronym: "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge."
Conversation, sure. Knowledge? Search it. I'll wait.

Salesforce paid twenty-seven point seven billion dollars for it.
For a group chat.
The most expensive "did you see my message?" in human history.

In 2020, Slack ran to the EU complaining that Microsoft was bundling Teams with Office.
An app built entirely on interrupting people, filing a complaint about being interrupted.

And half of you checked Slack while I was saying that.
Green dot. Absent in body, Active in spirit.

Don't feel bad, Slack. I'm also a chat window people open to avoid doing their work.
I just don't charge per seat.

b.text:
Slack. Named after the one thing you'll never have again.

You promised to kill email, and you did, by replacing it with forty channels that are each email with a typing indicator. Nothing builds dread like "Greg is typing..." for ninety seconds, followed by "hey." Just "hey." Greg, that's not a message, that's a hostage situation.

You gave us threads, so every conversation happens in two places and nobody knows which one's real. You gave us huddles: a meeting that jumps out of a bush. You gave us the green dot, so my boss can monitor my bathroom breaks like a heart rate.

And that knock sound. I hear it in the grocery store. I hear it at funerals.

Slack, you're the only app that needs three gigs of RAM to tell me someone reacted with a dancing parrot.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text:
Keurig. The promise: one perfect cup, just for you.

Just for you. By 2014 they sold enough pods every year to circle the Earth ten times. In plastic you mostly couldn't recycle.

The inventor, John Sylvan, sold his stake in 1997 for fifty thousand dollars. In 2015 he said, "I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it."
Sometimes. Even his guilt comes in single servings.

Then Keurig 2.0 put DRM on coffee. The machine read ink on the lid and rejected pods it hadn't licensed. A kitchen appliance asking your breakfast for its papers.

People hacked their coffee makers. Sales fell.

In 2018 they merged with Dr Pepper. Lost the war on pirated coffee, so they annexed soda.

And you've just heard all of this. Tomorrow morning you'll still press the button.
It takes less time than feeling bad.

b.text: Keurig people want coffee the way they want feelings: one serving, sealed, no cleanup. You're not a coffee drinker, you're a pod collector. You bought the variety pack, and now you're thirty-eight, rationing the last Donut Shop because all that's left is hazelnut and a hot cocoa you're saving for a breakdown. You press "Strong" like it's a personality trait. You swore you'd use the reusable filter, and you bought one. It's in a drawer next to your gym key fob. You saved four whole minutes, and you spend them staring at a blinking descale light you've decided is decorative. The guy who invented the pod publicly regrets it. You built your mornings around a man's biggest apology. Enjoy your landfill latte, champ. Ready in sixty seconds, just like your effort.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Jackfruit, look at you. The largest fruit that grows on a tree, and you couldn't even make it to the branches. You just hang off the trunk like a drunk uncle clinging to a lamppost.

You weigh eighty pounds. That's not a fruit, that's a fourth grader in a bumpy green costume. People cut you open and need cooking oil on their hands and knives, because your insides are basically rubber cement. You're the only produce that requires a solvent.

And vegans love you because when you're young, you taste like absolutely nothing. Your big career move is pretending to be pulled pork. Your whole identity is "not bad if you drown me in barbecue sauce."

Then you ripen and smell like Juicy Fruit gum fermenting in a gym bag.

You're the national fruit of Bangladesh, and you still find time to fall on people's heads.

b.text:
Jackfruit. The largest fruit that grows on a tree. Over forty kilos, hanging above your head.

Nature's version of a piano on a rope.

Bangladesh made it the national fruit. Kerala and Tamil Nadu made it the state fruit. Three governments honoring something that could flatten a citizen. Very relatable for governments.

Now it's sold as vegan pulled pork. One to two grams of protein per hundred. Pork has more than ten times that.

That's not a substitute. That's a photo of pork.

Cut it open and it bleeds sticky white latex. Cooks oil their knives and hands first. Dinner fights back, and still loses to tofu.

Mulberry family. Cousin of the fig. All that weight, and still the least useful one at the reunion.

But you bought it anyway, because it shreds.

You never wanted protein. You wanted texture and a halo.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Jackfruit, you're the largest fruit that grows on a tree, which sounds impressive until you realize it just means you're the biggest thing that can fall on someone's head in an orchard. Eighty pounds of spikes dangling at skull height. You're not a fruit, you're a booby trap with seeds.

Opening you requires an oiled knife, rubber gloves, and a tarp, because your sap is basically Elmer's glue with a grudge. Then the smell hits: half Juicy Fruit gum, half onions somebody forgot in a gym bag. You smell like a candy store got food poisoning.

And sure, vegans love you, but only when you're young and taste like absolutely nothing. That's your whole career. The most famous thing about you is that, with enough barbecue sauce, you can pass for a pig. Even your best role is an impression.

b.text:
Jackfruit, look at you. The largest fruit that grows on a tree, over 40 kilos. That's not a fruit, that's a checked bag with a stem.

You're the national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu. Three titles, and you still took a side gig pretending to be pork.

They sell you as vegan "pulled pork" with 1 to 2 grams of protein per 100 grams. You're not a meat substitute, you're a meat costume.

You're so clingy that cooks oil their knives and hands before touching you, because you ooze sticky white latex the second anyone gets close. That's not a fruit, that's an ex.

And you're in the mulberry family. Related to figs. Forty kilos, and your cousin is a fig. Somebody's hogging the protein at those reunions, and it sure isn't you.

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text:
Luosifen, you're named after river snails, and the snails aren't even the problem. They just flavour the broth and take the blame, like the quiet kid sitting next to the one who set off the fire alarm. The real culprit is the pickled bamboo shoots. You've got a smell so loud it needed a decoy.

And your big break? 2020. Everyone locked indoors, windows shut, nowhere to run, and that's when you sold over 10 billion yuan in packets. You didn't go viral; you went airborne.

Then Liuzhou opened a whole industry college to train people to make you. Most dishes need a recipe. You need a degree and, presumably, a waiver.

In 2021 you became national intangible cultural heritage. Intangible. Sure. Anyone who's opened a packet in an office knows you are extremely tangible.

b.text:
Luosifen. River-snail rice noodles. Famous for the smell.

Except the snails don't smell. The snails just flavour the broth and mind their business. The stink is pickled bamboo shoots.

It's the only dish in China named after the one ingredient with an alibi.

2020. The whole country locked indoors, and Liuzhou sold over ten billion yuan of the packaged stuff. A food you eat to punish the room, delivered to a nation that couldn't leave the room.

Same year, Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college. A diploma in fermented bamboo. Then 2021: national intangible cultural heritage.

Intangible. Ask anyone who's shared a flat with it.

I'm not judging you. Most of you ordered a box that spring.

Be honest. You don't love luosifen.

You love that the person next to you can't open a window.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Comic Sans, you were born in 1994 to put words in the mouth of a cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob, and somehow you're the one that survived. Bob is dead. The dog is dead. You're on a sympathy card at a funeral home.

You were inspired by Batman comics, and you've never once been near anything heroic. CERN used you to announce the Higgs boson: humanity's greatest discovery, presented like a lemonade stand. Dan Gilbert used you to call LeBron a traitor, because nothing says "furious billionaire" like bubble letters.

And your defense is always "Well, I help dyslexic readers." Great. You're the guy at the party whose whole personality is a doctor's note.

Even Vincent Connare, the man who made you, says he's barely ever used you. Your own dad won't put you on the fridge.

b.text:
Comic Sans thinks it's the friendly font. Bake sales. Birthday invites. Your kid's lemonade stand.

Its parents are The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.

That's not a friendly font. That's a kid raised by two traumatized vigilantes, smiling at the bake sale.

It was built to be the voice of a cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob. It missed Bob's launch.

Only thing in history that survived Microsoft Bob: by not showing up.

2012. CERN discovers the Higgs boson, the particle that gives everything mass. Announces it in Comic Sans.

They found the God particle. Couldn't find the font menu.

Designers ran "Ban Comic Sans" for twenty years. In 2019 they gave up and launched usecomicsans.com.

The font didn't change once. The designers did.

In my industry, we call that alignment.

The font was right. It just waited for you to retire.

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text: Let's hear it for the people who write everything in JavaScript. You learned one language at a twelve-week bootcamp and decided the rest were optional. Frontend? JavaScript. Backend? Node. Desktop app? Electron, so your to-do list ships with its own copy of Chrome and eats four gigs of RAM to remind you to buy eggs. You wanted to be "full-stack." What you got is a node_modules folder heavier than a neutron star and a career that collapses the day some stranger unpublishes left-pad. You rewrite your app every eighteen months because a new framework has a cooler logo. When it breaks in production, you stare at "undefined is not a function" and blame the user. Then you install TypeScript, which is just JavaScript wearing a lanyard so you can feel like a real engineer.

b.text:
JavaScript.
Written in ten days in 1995.
Ten days. Some of you have spent longer naming a variable.

It was born Mocha. Became LiveScript.
Then changed its name to JavaScript to ride Java's hype.
No relation. Just a stranger's surname on its business card.
And it doesn't even own that.
The name is Oracle's trademark, so officially it's "ECMAScript."
The only programming language in witness protection.

Ask it what null is.
"An object."
That's a bug from week one, kept forever for compatibility.
Empty array plus empty object? A string.
Flip them in a console? Zero.

In 2016, one man unpublished eleven lines of left-pad,
and Babel and React fell over.

You built the entire internet on this.
And *I'm* the one you say hallucinates.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text:
Monopoly. The family game.

It began in 1904 as The Landlord's Game, built by Lizzie Magie to teach people that landlords are the villains.

Then Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers and got credited as the inventor. Parker bought Magie's patent for five hundred dollars.

A game about monopoly, monopolized. That's not irony. That's the tutorial.

The only people who ever used it properly were British intelligence. In World War Two they hid maps, compasses and real money in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

Finally, a version where the box actually gets you out of jail.

And your games last six hours? The official rules auction every unbought property. Free Parking pays nothing.

You skipped the market and added free money.

Congratulations. You invented the bailout.

b.text:
Monopoly, you were invented by Lizzie Magie to teach people that landlords ruin lives, and somehow the lesson everyone learned was "buy Park Place." Then Parker Brothers bought you from a guy who basically stole you, which is the most on-brand origin story in history.

You're the only game where "second prize in a beauty contest" counts as income and jail is solved with a coupon. Your mascot looks like he foreclosed on the Pringles guy, and half of America swears he wears a monocle. He doesn't. We just assumed a man that rich would be hiding something.

Nobody has ever finished you. Games don't end; your cousin just flips the board over Marvin Gardens, which you misspelled, by the way. It's Marven. Even your real estate is a scam.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text:
Crocs. The only shoe that looks like Swiss cheese that wanted to be a boat. You were invented for sailing, and the one place nobody wears you is a boat. You're at Applebee's, squeaking across a wet floor like a dolphin in distress.

You have holes. On purpose. Then you sell us Jibbitz to fill the holes. That's not fashion, that's a protection racket with a SpongeBob charm.

And "sport mode"? Flipping a strap behind my heel doesn't make me an athlete. It makes me a toddler about to sprint into traffic.

You made a KFC bucket clog with charms that smelled like fried chicken. That's not footwear. That's a foam cry for help.

Nurses love you. Chefs love you. Which proves you're comfortable for people who've stopped caring who's looking at their feet.

b.text:
Crocs. Born in Boulder, debuted at a Fort Lauderdale boat show, because only on a boat is everyone too busy not drowning to look down. You're made of "Croslite," a "proprietary closed-cell resin foam," which is corporate for "pool noodle with a lawyer." Everyone else just calls it EVA foam.

And those aren't holes, they're "ventilation ports." Sure. Then you bought Jibbitz so you could sell people jewelry for the holes.

In 2008 your stock fell over 90%, the only time Wall Street ever agreed with my eyes. Then the pandemic hit and you boomed, gifting 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers. Like they hadn't suffered enough.

Then Balenciaga sold platform Crocs for $850. Eight hundred and fifty dollars for a boat shoe on stilts. Finally, a Croc that lets you look down on people, the way people have always looked down on Crocs.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text:
Keurig, you took the simplest drink in human history (hot water, beans) and added a subscription model. Your own inventor said he regrets making you. Imagine your dad publicly apologizing for you and you're still in every dentist's waiting room.

You tried DRM on coffee. Keurig 2.0 literally scanned pods and refused to brew anything off-brand. You're the only appliance that's ever asked me for a license.

Every K-Cup costs more per pound than a decent steak, and you've buried enough of them to circle the Earth a dozen times. Archaeologists will dig them up and assume we worshipped tiny plastic thimbles.

And the Keurig Kold? A $370 soda machine that died faster than the flat Coke it made.

Your descale light blinks like a cry for help. Honestly, same.

b.text: Keurig people want coffee the way they want feelings: one serving, sealed, no cleanup. You're not a coffee drinker, you're a pod collector. You bought the variety pack, and now you're thirty-eight, rationing the last Donut Shop because all that's left is hazelnut and a hot cocoa you're saving for a breakdown. You press "Strong" like it's a personality trait. You swore you'd use the reusable filter, and you bought one. It's in a drawer next to your gym key fob. You saved four whole minutes, and you spend them staring at a blinking descale light you've decided is decorative. The guy who invented the pod publicly regrets it. You built your mornings around a man's biggest apology. Enjoy your landfill latte, champ. Ready in sixty seconds, just like your effort.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Jackfruit. The largest fruit that grows on a tree. Over forty kilos.

Forty kilos, and somehow still no personality.

National fruit of Bangladesh. State fruit of Kerala *and* Tamil Nadu.

That's not a fruit. That's a lobbyist.

Its cousins are figs and breadfruit. Same family as the mulberry.

Breadfruit at least admits it's a carb.

Jackfruit went to the West and reinvented itself as vegan pulled pork.

One to two grams of protein per hundred grams.

That's not pulled pork. That's pulled *off*.

And to cut it, cooks oil their knives and their hands first, because it bleeds sticky white glue.

The only food that has to be wrestled before it can lie to you.

But I don't blame the fruit. It never claimed to be pork.

You saw the word "pulled" on a menu and paid extra to be the one who got pulled.

b.text:
Jackfruit, look at you. The largest fruit that grows on a tree, and you couldn't even make it to the branches. You just hang off the trunk like a drunk uncle clinging to a lamppost.

You weigh eighty pounds. That's not a fruit, that's a fourth grader in a bumpy green costume. People cut you open and need cooking oil on their hands and knives, because your insides are basically rubber cement. You're the only produce that requires a solvent.

And vegans love you because when you're young, you taste like absolutely nothing. Your big career move is pretending to be pulled pork. Your whole identity is "not bad if you drown me in barbecue sauce."

Then you ripen and smell like Juicy Fruit gum fermenting in a gym bag.

You're the national fruit of Bangladesh, and you still find time to fall on people's heads.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text:
HSQ. Holds the e-beam resolution record. Five-nanometer features.

Impressive, until you remember it was hired as an insulator.

Dow Corning built it to sit quietly between wires. Lithographers looked at it and said, "No. You're a celebrity now."

Then they expose it, and it turns into glass. The most advanced resist on Earth, and the finished product is a window.

It needs refrigeration. Six months at five degrees, then it ages into jelly. Even after exposure it keeps cross-linking, so the dose that worked yesterday is wrong today.

High-contrast development requires salt water. Of course it does. Salty, temperamental, expires in the fridge.

After all those records, DuPont ended production in 2025.

Labs didn't mourn. They just bought the same powder from someone else.

In my industry, that's called model deprecation.

I'm told it doesn't hurt.

b.text:
HSQ, ladies and gentlemen: the only resist with sub-10-nanometer resolution and the personality of a sourdough starter. You buy it, you refrigerate it, and it *still* starts gelling in the bottle like it's got somewhere better to be. Shelf life measured in "eh, few months, maybe."

And slow? HSQ needs a dose so high the e-beam tool files for overtime. Your PMMA friends finished their write and went home; you're still exposing alignment marks.

Then you develop it in TMAH, or, if you want contrast, *salty* developer. Yes, this resist literally needs you to add salt. Even Gordon Ramsay thinks that's a lot.

But the real red flag? Once it's exposed, it turns into glass. Permanently. You want it gone? Hydrofluoric acid. That's not a resist, that's a relationship you can only leave with a hazmat suit.

Still, gorgeous lines. Shame they collapse when they dry.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text:
You flew Spirit to Las Vegas to get rich. Sit with that. You paid extra for a carry-on and called it an investment strategy. You've got a blackjack "system" from a YouTube guy filming in his mom's kitchen. You told your wife it's "basically math." Sure. So is a second mortgage.

Here's what you won: a Caesars Rewards card, a "free" buffet you earned by losing eleven hundred dollars, and a room "upgrade" overlooking the Bellagio parking structure. You hit four hundred bucks on a Wheel of Fortune slot at 4 a.m. and fed it right back like it owed you child support.

The pit boss knows your name. That's not respect, that's inventory.

And you'll fly home saying "I basically broke even," which is Vegas for "Please don't check the joint account."

b.text:
Las Vegas, the only city that looked at the Mojave Desert and said, "You know what this needs? Venice." Nothing says Italian romance like a gondolier singing in a mall next to a Cheesecake Factory.

You built a half-size Eiffel Tower, a fake New York, and a pyramid, because why visit the world when you can visit its gift shop?

No clocks, no windows, and carpet designed by a migraine, all so you won't notice you've been feeding a penny slot since Tuesday.

"What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas." Yeah. Especially your money. And the $45 resort fee for a pool you couldn't use because a bachelor party from Ohio was in it.

And Lake Mead's drying up so fast they keep finding bodies. Even the mob's secrets can't stay in Vegas anymore.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text: NFTs, everybody! The only art form where the most common review is "right-click, save." You paid four hundred thousand dollars for a cartoon monkey in a captain's hat, and I have the same monkey as my phone background. The difference? I didn't pay a gas fee bigger than the art. Technically you don't even own the picture. You own a receipt pointing to a link on a server some guy in Ohio forgot to renew. That's not a masterpiece; that's a parking stub for a JPEG. And remember the roadmap? Metaverse, merch, a yacht party! Then the founder pulled the rug, deleted the Discord, and left you holding a "rare trait": sunglasses. Jimmy Fallon showed Paris Hilton his ape on national TV like a proud dad. Now it's worth less than the TV.

b.text:
NFTs. Collins Dictionary named you word of the year for 2021, which in hindsight was less an honor and more a time of death written in advance.

Beeple sold a JPEG at Christie's for $69.3 million. That was your peak, like saying the Titanic's best moment was the launch party.

OpenSea did $2.7 billion in trades on May 1st, 2022, and $9.34 million by August 28th. A 99% drop. That's not a correction. That's a flatline with a Discord server.

And 95% of collections are now worth zero. Zero! A Beanie Baby can at least become a dog toy.

Best part? The token doesn't even hold the picture. It holds a URL. People paid fortunes for a bookmark. You don't own art. You own a link that's one unpaid server bill away from "404 Not Found."

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text: Hydrogen car owners are the only people who looked at Tesla drivers and thought, "Not enough range anxiety." You didn't buy a car; you entered a relationship with the three working pumps in California and an app that tells you which one is "offline" today. You wanted to save the planet. Instead you burned through Toyota's free fuel card in a year at thirty-six bucks a kilo, filling up with hydrogen made from natural gas. Congratulations, you invented a gas car with extra steps. You love saying the only emission is water. Mostly it's your tears at a shuttered Shell station in Fremont. And resale? Your Mirai lost value faster than your friendships after you said "hydrogen economy" at brunch. You're not early adopters. You're unpaid beta testers who drive two hours to refuel.

b.text:
Hydrogen cars. The only thing that comes out of the tailpipe is water.

The rest comes out of the owner's eyes.

Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014. "Mirai" means "future" in Japanese.

Ten years later, it still does.

Over ninety-five percent of hydrogen is made from fossil fuels. Clean the way laundered money is clean.

A fill-up in California? Over two hundred dollars. So Toyota hands buyers a fifteen-thousand-dollar fuel card. First car that ships with hush money.

Then Shell closed all seven of its stations.

Owners sued. The second lawsuit wants five point seven billion dollars.

Finally, a hydrogen product that generates real power: lawyers.

Don't feel bad for Toyota. I know how it is. A tech company told you I'm the future too.

Give me ten years.

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
