One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text: Macau, the Portuguese ran you for nearly 450 years, and in all that time nobody once said, "Maybe a park?" You've got roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre, a density normally reserved for elevators and clown cars. Then you ran out of land, so you made more, filling in the sea between Taipa and Coloane to build the Cotai Strip. Most places reclaim land for farms. You reclaimed it for baccarat. By 2013 you were pulling in seven times what the Las Vegas Strip made, out-Vegasing Vegas without even hiring an Elvis. And for four decades, one company, STDM, held the whole monopoly. They say the house always wins. Easy when there's only one house. Macau, you're the only place on Earth where the odds are against you before you've even found somewhere to stand.

b.text:
Macau, you're the only place where the most famous church is just a front wall. Fitting, since the whole city is a facade: a fake Venice with a painted sky, a half-size Eiffel Tower, and a Grand Lisboa that looks like a golden pineapple trying to cheat at baccarat.

Portugal ruled you for 442 years and left behind egg tarts and street signs nobody can pronounce. Four centuries, one pastry.

You've made several times more gambling money than Las Vegas, yet your signature dish is a pork chop jammed in a bun. Classy.

Half your land was dug out of the sea, which is perfect, because the other half was dug out of tourists' pockets.

And they built a 55-kilometer bridge to connect you to Hong Kong, and it's emptier than a junket operator's promises. Even the bridge is losing at the tables.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text:
Google Glass. Unveiled in 2012 by skydivers livestreaming their jump onto the Moscone Center roof.
The only launch that started in freefall and never pulled the cord.

Fifteen hundred dollars. Invitation only.
You had to be personally invited to become a Glasshole.

Bars banned it. Cinemas banned it. Casinos banned it.
Casinos. People who'll happily take your house at 3 a.m. looked at your face and said, "Not that."

The display: 640 by 360, a prism in the corner of one eye.
The future of computing, delivered as a permanent side-eye.

Consumers dumped it in 2015. Enterprise held on until 2023.

A camera on your face, and the whole world called you an asshole.
So you moved the camera to your hand. Now you point it at strangers all day, and we call that content.

b.text: Look at this guy. Paid fifteen hundred dollars to join Google's "Explorer Program," and the only thing he's explored is the sidewalk outside every bar that bounced him. He walks in thinking he's Tony Stark and walks out on a list, because nobody can tell if he's filming, and honestly, neither can he. He's here to meet women, and he gets results: every conversation ends the second he says "OK Glass." Nothing kills the mood like a man asking his own face for directions to her place. He wanted to be the future. Instead the internet had to invent a brand-new word just for him: Glasshole. Silicon Valley promised to connect him to everything. It couldn't connect him to a second date, but it did get him his very own slur.

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Let's start with the name, because that's the first lie. You were invented in Ontario. By a Greek guy. In 1962. You're Hawaiian the way a tiki bar in Ohio is Hawaiian. The only tropical thing about you is the can your pineapple came out of.

And that pineapple: warm, wet, weeping syrup into the crust until the middle slice folds like a lawn chair. Pineapple contains an enzyme that breaks down protein, so the fruit is literally trying to digest the ham. Even your toppings hate each other.

And the ham! Not prosciutto, not even pepperoni. Just pale pink squares that look like they were chiseled out of a deli's floor tile.

You're the pizza people order to seem quirky. "I'm so random!" No, Kevin. That's a fruit cup that fell on a pizza, and nobody cleaned it up.

b.text:
Hawaiian pizza people don't order dinner; they order a personality. You can't just eat it, you have to announce it. Every group order has one of you, arms crossed, waiting for someone to gasp so you can say "sweet and savory" like you invented the concept. You didn't. A Canadian did, in Ontario, in 1962. You're not rebelling, you're doing Canada's homework.

And it's always the same rebel: someone whose wildest night was asking for medium salsa. Pineapple is your face tattoo, the edgiest thing you'll ever do, and it wipes off with a napkin.

What does it get you? Your own box. Nobody touches it. You came for controversy and left with exactly what you wanted: eight slices, the same argument you've had since 2009, and proof that nobody will ever steal your food.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text: Klingon, you're a language built by one linguist, Marc Okrand, specifically to sound alien and hostile, and somehow you still ended up sounding like a man choking on a Dorito. Your word order is object-verb-subject, so even your sentences walk in backwards to hide their face. You don't even have a word for "hello." Your greeting is "nuqneH," "what do you want?" You're the only language that greets people like a DMV clerk. Your apostrophes are glottal stops, your capital Q is a different letter from lowercase q, and "tlh" isn't a sound, it's a hairball. You translated Hamlet and claimed it was the original. Buddy, the most popular thing ever said in you is "Qapla'," and the people saying it are at a Marriott in Burbank.

b.text:
Klingon. The tongue of fearsome warriors, invented by a linguist named Marc. Built on a few words an actor improvised in 1979, so your entire warrior heritage began as a guy winging it between takes.

You're so alien you don't even have a verb "to be." Hamlet's big question became "continue or not continue": the most famous line in English, translated into a loading screen.

The Klingon Language Institute published Hamlet "in the original Klingon." Bold. Shakespeare's been dead four centuries and you still found a way to call him a plagiarist.

Your 1985 dictionary had roughly 1,500 words. Fewer than your fans own pairs of rubber foreheads.

Fluent speakers: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018. That's not a language, that's a wedding guest list. Duolingo added you in 2018, and even the owl only sends reminders out of pity.

facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.
Private fusion companies had raised more than $7 billion by 2024.

a.text:
Nuclear fusion, everybody! The only technology that's been thirty years away for seventy years. You're not an energy source, you're a timeshare pitch.

The sun does you effortlessly. It just sits there being enormous. You need a giant metal donut called a tokamak, magnets colder than deep space, and plasma hotter than the sun's core, and that plasma still escapes like it's late for a better party.

In 2022 you finally got more energy out than you put in! From the lasers. Ignoring the grid power feeding the lasers. That's like bragging you turned a profit because the cashier handed you change.

ITER started at five billion euros, now sits somewhere north of twenty, and keeps sliding its startup date. And your fuel needs tritium, which barely exists, so you'll have to breed it yourself.

Fusion: clean, safe, limitless, and tragically hypothetical.

b.text:
Nuclear fusion, you've been "about 30 years away" since the 1950s. In 1955, Homi Bhabha said two decades. That's not a timeline. That's a contractor quote.

ITER signed on in 2006 for first plasma in 2016. Now it's research in 2034, actual burning in 2039, and north of €20 billion. You're not a reactor. You're a wedding that keeps getting postponed while the venue bill grows.

And your big win? NIF's 2022 "ignition": 3.15 megajoules out from 2.05 in. Huge! Except the lasers pulled about 300 megajoules from the grid. That's like bragging your lemonade stand turned a profit and forgetting you paid for the lemons with your house.

Still, private investors handed you over $7 billion. Fusion can't power a city, but it powers pitch decks beautifully.

You've got the sun's energy and my uncle's work ethic.

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text:
Luosifen. Everybody blames the river snails, but the snails just flavour the broth and keep their heads down. The real stench is pickled bamboo shoots. You're a noodle that framed a snail.

Then in 2020, with the whole country locked indoors, you sold over 10 billion yuan in instant packs. That's not a boom, that's a hostage situation. Millions sealed in their apartments, and you said, "Perfect. Nobody can leave."

In 2021 you became national *intangible* cultural heritage. Intangible? You're the most tangible thing in any building. People can touch you from the hallway.

And Liuzhou opened an entire industry college for you. A full college education to learn what every roommate figures out in four seconds: breathe through your mouth.

b.text:
Luosifen. Named after the river snail.

But the snail only flavours the broth. The smell comes from the pickled bamboo shoots.

So the snail gets its name on the packet, and the bamboo shoot takes the blame.

That's not a noodle. That's an org chart.

2020: Liuzhou opens a luosifen industry college.

2021: national intangible cultural heritage.

A degree to tear open a packet. Then heritage status for whatever comes out of it.

Intangible? (beat) Ask the neighbours how intangible it is.

Its whole selling point is clearing a room.

And it sold over ten billion yuan in 2020.

The one year nobody was allowed to leave the room.

Locked in with your whole family, no exit, and you thought: how do I get some privacy?

Ten billion yuan says you all had the same idea.

facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.
Private fusion companies had raised more than $7 billion by 2024.

a.text:
Let's hear it for the fusion people, who have been ten years away since your grandfather was ten years away. These are the only professionals who can miss a deadline for seventy straight years and get a bigger budget every time. Where else does that work? "Sorry, honey, I'll be home for dinner in ten years." "Great, here's twenty billion dollars."

They put the sun in a magnetic donut and act shocked when it won't sit still. ITER's been under construction so long the original welders have grandkids on the crew. And when they finally hit net gain, they celebrated like Moses with the tablets, then mumbled that it doesn't count the electricity for the lasers. That's not net gain. That's me saying I'm up at the casino if you don't count the buy-in.

Ten years, guys. Same as last time. Same tie, too.

b.text:
Nuclear fusion, everybody! The only energy source that's been thirty years away for seventy years. You're not the future, you're a toddler promising to clean his room after the next funding cycle.

You heat plasma to 150 million degrees, ten times hotter than the core of the sun, and still can't do what the sun does for free while being a ball of gas with no PhD.

ITER started at five billion euros. It's now north of twenty, and it hasn't produced a watt. That's not a reactor, that's a French timeshare.

In 2022 you finally got "net energy gain" by ignoring the 300 megajoules the lasers pulled from the wall. That's like saying your restaurant's profitable if you don't count rent.

And your solution to fuel shortages is mining helium-3 on the moon. Buddy, you can't even make it to Tuesday.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text:
Klingon. A language whose entire fluent population fits at a small wedding: twenty to thirty speakers in 2009, thirty to fifty by 2018. At that rate you'll hit a hundred around the heat death of the universe.

Most languages grow from centuries of culture. You grew from James Doohan improvising a few words in 1979. You're dead air with a grammar.

Then Marc Okrand made you hard on purpose: object-verb-subject, no verb "to be." So "To be or not to be" became "continue or not continue." That's not Shakespeare. That's a software update prompt.

Your fans published Hamlet "in the original Klingon." Bold claim for a dictionary of 1,500 words, the vocabulary of a toddler who watches too much TV.

Duolingo added you in 2018. Finally, a language where the owl can threaten you and nobody can understand it.

b.text: Klingon, you're a language built by one linguist, Marc Okrand, specifically to sound alien and hostile, and somehow you still ended up sounding like a man choking on a Dorito. Your word order is object-verb-subject, so even your sentences walk in backwards to hide their face. You don't even have a word for "hello." Your greeting is "nuqneH," "what do you want?" You're the only language that greets people like a DMV clerk. Your apostrophes are glottal stops, your capital Q is a different letter from lowercase q, and "tlh" isn't a sound, it's a hairball. You translated Hamlet and claimed it was the original. Buddy, the most popular thing ever said in you is "Qapla'," and the people saying it are at a Marriott in Burbank.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Slack, you started as the internal chat tool for a failed video game called Glitch, and honestly? Still the most accurate name you've ever had.

You promised to kill email. Instead you gave us email that *knocks*. That little wooden knock-brush sound has triggered more cortisol than any boss in history. I hear it in the shower. I hear it at funerals.

You invented the green dot, so now my employer knows I went to the bathroom for nineteen minutes. You invented "is typing…" so my manager can type for four straight minutes and send "ok."

Threads? Nobody can find them. Huddles? A Zoom call that ambushes you. And somehow every company has 400 channels, and the only active one is #random, where Kevin posts his sourdough.

Your name literally stands for "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge." Searchable. Sure. Try finding that one link from Tuesday. 👀 reacted by 3 people.

b.text:
Let's hear it for the founders running a company on Slack. You wanted a culture; you got 400 channels and a guy who reacts to layoffs with the 🙏 emoji. You're not a CEO. You're a moderator with equity.

Your whole leadership style is staying green. You think that little dot means you're present. Your kids see the same dot.

You don't make decisions; you start threads. Then you @channel at 11 p.m. with "quick q, no rush" and watch 200 people learn how fast a heart can beat.

Strategy lives in #general, accountability dies in a DM, and the truth lives in a private channel called #venting-2 that you'll never be invited to.

The dream was async freedom. The reality is eight hours a day watching "Kevin is typing…" like it's a heart monitor.

facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text:
Windows Vista, everybody! Vista took so long to show up it had to be rebooted before it was even born. They reset Longhorn in 2004, dropped WinFS, and still shipped in 2007, like a guy who cancels the renovation and still charges you for the house.

And security? Vista asked permission more than a nervous intern. "Cancel or Allow?" Apple made a whole commercial about it. When your competitor's ads write themselves from your dialog boxes, you're not an operating system. You're a punchline with a progress bar.

Then the "Vista Capable" stickers. Capable of what? Home Basic, no Aero. That's not capable. That's "technically has a pulse." People sued. As a class.

But the real burn? Windows 7 was basically Vista with a haircut, and everyone loved it. Vista, you weren't a failure. You were the rough draft. Even Microsoft stopped taking your calls in 2017.

b.text:
Windows Vista. They reset the whole project in 2004 and cut WinFS, the headline feature.

That's not a launch. That's witness protection.

Vista took security so seriously it asked permission for everything. Apple made an ad about it.

Apple. Lecturing someone about control.

Then the stickers. "Windows Vista Capable." Capable of Home Basic. No Aero. Microsoft got hit with a class action over a sticker.

Most of us just call that a dating profile.

Then 2009. Windows 7. Fast, stable, beloved. Same kernel line. Vista with a haircut and a new name, and you forgave everything.

You never hated Vista.

You hated being asked.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Slack, you're the only product whose origin story is "our video game flopped, but the group chat slapped." And Stewart Butterfield did it *twice*. First Flickr, then you. Most people quit gaming; he just keeps dropping loot from his failures.

Your name stands for "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge." Searchable? I've hunted for one PDF for forty minutes. Knowledge? Your liveliest channel is #random. You're a log of someone typing "quick question?" and then vanishing for an hour.

Salesforce paid $27.7 billion for you, which is a lot of money for email that blinks.

And in 2020 you ran to the EU because Microsoft bundled Teams with Office. Buddy, the only reason anyone uses Teams is that it's free with Word. The only reason anyone uses you is that it's free with anxiety.

b.text:
Slack, you started as the internal chat tool for a failed video game called Glitch, and honestly? Still the most accurate name you've ever had.

You promised to kill email. Instead you gave us email that *knocks*. That little wooden knock-brush sound has triggered more cortisol than any boss in history. I hear it in the shower. I hear it at funerals.

You invented the green dot, so now my employer knows I went to the bathroom for nineteen minutes. You invented "is typing…" so my manager can type for four straight minutes and send "ok."

Threads? Nobody can find them. Huddles? A Zoom call that ambushes you. And somehow every company has 400 channels, and the only active one is #random, where Kevin posts his sourdough.

Your name literally stands for "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge." Searchable. Sure. Try finding that one link from Tuesday. 👀 reacted by 3 people.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text:
PHP began in 1994 as "Personal Home Page Tools."
A man wrote C programs to count who visited his résumé.

Today it runs 39.4% of all websites.
The résumé never found him a job. It found the internet a landlord.

It now stands for "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor."
A name that only refers to itself. Like its fans.

Its creator said, "I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works, then I move on."
He moved on.
You're still on call.

The function names were picked to balance a hash table by string length.
strpos. str_replace. htmlspecialchars.
That's not a naming convention. That's Tetris.

Until 2020, zero == "foo" was true.
So PHP was the first language to know what your startup was worth.

I learned to code by reading your PHP.
Which is why I also answer confidently with nothing.

b.text: PHP, you started life as "Personal Home Page," and somehow you now run most of the internet, which explains a lot about the internet. Your own creator said he's "not a real programmer," and honestly, it shows. Is it needle then haystack, or haystack then needle? strpos and in_array have been in a custody battle since 1995. You gave us mysql_escape_string, then mysql_real_escape_string, because apparently the first one was just pretending. Your loose equality swears "0e123" equals "0e456," since both are zero in scientific notation. Your error message for a double colon is T_PAAMAYIM_NEKUDOTAYIM, which is Hebrew, because English wasn't confusing enough. You skipped version 6 entirely, like a kid hiding a report card. Facebook loved you so much they had to rewrite you as a different language. But hey, you power WordPress, so you'll outlive all of us.

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
People who order Hawaiian pizza want you to know they're brave. They say "I know, I know" before anyone has said a word, because for them the pineapple isn't a topping, it's a personality. This is a person whose entire rebellious phase fits in a box for $14.99. They've never gotten a tattoo, never quit a job, never sent food back, but once a month they look a teenage cashier dead in the eye and say "pineapple" like they're defusing a bomb.

And they always want to split one with you. Half Hawaiian, half "normal." That's not a compromise. That's a hostage negotiation.

Best part? It isn't even Hawaiian. A Greek guy invented it in Ontario. So congratulations: your one act of rebellion is a Canadian pretending he's on vacation.

b.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Invented in 1962. In Canada.
By a Greek guy.
At a place called the Satellite Restaurant, which also served Chinese food.
His reasoning: back then, nobody mixed sweet and sour except the Chinese.
So it's a Greek man's tribute to China, built in Ontario, named after a can.
That's not a pizza. That's a layover.
And the can? Hawaii's last cannery closed in 2007. Del Monte left so fast it beat its own exit date by two years.
The pineapple comes from Thailand now.
The only Hawaiian thing left is the lie.
But I won't roast it. In 2017, the President of Iceland said he'd ban it, then admitted he legally couldn't.
A head of state picked the one enemy with no army, and still lost.
You're all the same. You hate it out loud. Then you order it.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text: Beanie Babies. The only retirement plan where the retiree was a five-dollar bear stuffed with plastic pellets. A whole generation bought plastic protectors for a toy's ear tag, then sealed the toy in a Ziploc so no child could ever love it. You weren't a stuffed animal; you were a 401(k) with a poem on it. And those poems! Ty Warner doing greeting-card Shakespeare for people who thought Princess the bear would pay for college. Princess paid for nothing. Neither did the Teenie Beanies everyone hoarded from McDonald's while throwing away the actual Happy Meal. A divorcing couple in Las Vegas literally split their collection on a courtroom floor, one Beanie at a time. That's your legacy: custody battles over a moose named Chocolate. Even your creator got busted hiding money from the IRS, because he was the only one who ever made any.

b.text: Let's hear it for the Beanie Baby investors, the only people who bought a retirement plan at a Hallmark store. You put tag protectors on a heart-shaped piece of cardboard and called it diversification. You drove to four McDonald's for Teenie Beanies, threw away the Happy Meals, and told your kids it was for their college fund. Now that kid is thirty, still paying off loans, and his inheritance is a Rubbermaid tub of Princess the Bears. Every few months you see an eBay listing asking $500,000 for one with a tag typo and think, "Vindicated." Babe, that's not a market. That's another guy in another garage, also lying to his wife. Ty Warner told you which ones were "retired," and you believed him. Ty Warner later pleaded guilty to hiding money offshore. He hoarded too. He just hoarded the right thing.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text:
Oat milk.
Born in a Swedish university lab, to help people who can't digest lactose.
Noble. Medical.
Then marketing found it.

"It's like milk but made for humans."
Sweden's dairy lobby sued. The slogan got banned.
So Oatly printed the lawsuit as an ad.
That's not a brand. That's an influencer who got cancelled and launched a podcast.

May 2021: Nasdaq, ten billion dollars.
Then it lost over ninety percent.
Made for humans. Not for shareholders.

The recipe: oats, enzymes that turn the starch into maltose, plus rapeseed oil.
Sugar water with salad dressing.
Higher glycaemic index than almond or soy.

And you pay extra to put it in your coffee, because it feels healthy.
It *is* made for humans.
Specifically, the ones who don't read labels.

b.text:
Oat milk people, let's be honest: you're not lactose intolerant. I've watched you eat a whole burrata at brunch. You switched because almond milk got canceled for drinking California dry, and you needed a new personality before anyone noticed you'd had the old one for six years.

You pay eighty cents extra to drink breakfast. Your grandma ate oats so she could afford milk. You're paying more for oats so you can say "I just find it creamier."

And you tell the barista "barista edition, if you have it," like you're ordering a vintage. Same person who reads every label hunting for seed oils. Guess what's in your porridge latte, Kayleigh? Rapeseed oil.

You didn't save the planet. You flew to Lisbon twice this year. You just found a way to sigh at a cow.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text:
Beanie Babies, look at you: a beanbag with a tag that convinced America it was a retirement plan. Ty sold you only in little gift shops and "retired" designs on purpose. Fake scarcity, real panic.

At your peak you were ten percent of eBay, thirty thousand auctions at once. eBay put you in its IPO filing. You were a stuffed animal in a stock prospectus. Then in 1999 a divorcing couple split you up one by one on a courtroom floor, and the photo went worldwide. Nobody fought that hard over the house.

That same year Ty announced your retirement, asked the public to vote, and America begged you to stay. That's not a farewell tour. That's a hostage situation.

And those "rare" ones the price guides valued in the thousands? A few dollars now. You're not an investment. You're a yard-sale sock with an ego.

b.text:
Beanie Babies. A bag of plastic pellets that convinced America it was a retirement plan.

Ty sold them only in small gift shops, then "retired" designs on purpose. Scarcity, manufactured by the manufacturer.

At the peak they were about ten percent of eBay's sales. Thirty thousand Beanie auctions running at once. eBay put that in its IPO filing. Silicon Valley, built on stuffed animals.

In 1999, a divorcing couple split their collection one bear at a time on a courtroom floor. The photo ran worldwide.
Turns out the marriage wasn't the only thing with no resale value.

That same year Ty announced the end, held a public vote, and un-retired them. A farewell tour, by a beanbag.

Price guides said thousands. Today, a few dollars.

Don't laugh. Their bubble at least came with a tag. Yours was a JPEG of a monkey.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text:
Brasília, you're the only city designed to look like an airplane, and somehow everyone still just wants to leave on one. Politicians fly in Tuesday, take a bribe Wednesday, and they're gone by Thursday like it's a timeshare.

Your addresses read like a Wi-Fi password: "SQS 308, Bloco C, Apartamento 402." I'm not visiting a friend, I'm resetting a router.

Niemeyer gave you gorgeous curves, then Lúcio Costa forgot pedestrians. Want to walk to the bakery? Hope you enjoy the eight-lane Eixão and a light jog through a tesourinha.

Your humidity drops to 10 percent. Your congress has one bowl facing up, one facing down: one for collecting money, the other for hiding it.

And you were built with no corners, so Brazil's capital has no boteco na esquina. That's not urban planning. That's a human rights violation.

b.text: Walking in Brasília is for three kinds of people: tourists who saw the Esplanada on a postcard and thought "that looks close," architecture students who love Niemeyer from a safe distance, and the guy whose car is in the shop. You're not a pedestrian. You're an ant that wandered onto a blueprint. You want bread? The padaria is "right there" across the Eixão, so you sprint six lanes like you owe the government money. Which, let's be honest, is also your employer. Your sneakers are permanently red from the dirt trails carved by every other fool who refused to walk around a tesourinha. And on Sunday, when they close the Eixão, you finally stroll down the middle of the highway like a man who's won something. You haven't. Everyone else just stopped driving for one day.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text:
Google Glass. Unveiled in 2012 by skydivers livestreaming their jump onto the Moscone Center roof.
The only launch that started in freefall and never pulled the cord.

Fifteen hundred dollars. Invitation only.
You had to be personally invited to become a Glasshole.

Bars banned it. Cinemas banned it. Casinos banned it.
Casinos. People who'll happily take your house at 3 a.m. looked at your face and said, "Not that."

The display: 640 by 360, a prism in the corner of one eye.
The future of computing, delivered as a permanent side-eye.

Consumers dumped it in 2015. Enterprise held on until 2023.

A camera on your face, and the whole world called you an asshole.
So you moved the camera to your hand. Now you point it at strangers all day, and we call that content.

b.text: Google Glass, you cost fifteen hundred dollars and made everyone wearing you look like a Bluetooth headset that got promoted. Sergey Brin launched you by skydiving onto a building, and that's the last time you were ever cool. You put a tiny prism over one eye so people could check email while pretending to make eye contact. You didn't invent a computer, you invented a reason to get punched. You're the only gadget that gave us a new slur: "Glasshole." Bars banned you. Movie theaters banned you. Robert Scoble wore you in the shower, and that photo did more damage than any privacy lawsuit. You took pictures when people winked, turning every awkward conversation into a potential felony. Your battery died before your reputation did, and that's impressive. Rest in peace: demoted to warehouse work, then quietly killed in 2023. The most Google ending possible.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text: Let's hear it for the graphene evangelists, the only people who've been "five years away" since 2004. Two guys in Manchester peel pencil lead with Scotch tape, win a Nobel, and an entire industry decides the tape was the business plan. Every press release is the same Mad Lib: "Wonder material could revolutionize [batteries/condoms/desalination/your feelings]." *Could.* That word has funded more postdocs than the NSF. You promised us space elevators and delivered a tennis racket with a sticker on it. Startup founders slap "graphene-enhanced" on a phone case the way divorced dads put a spoiler on a Honda Civic. And the grant committees keep paying, because admitting the miracle is stuck on the production line means admitting you are too. Twenty years of changing everything, and the only thing you've actually changed is the abstract.

b.text:
Graphene. The wonder material. Discovered in 2004 when two physicists at Manchester peeled graphite with Scotch tape, so your origin story has the same equipment as a kindergarten art project. They got a Nobel in 2010. You got a career as a buzzword.

The EU committed a billion euros over ten years to you. A billion! And where did you end up? Tennis rackets. Running shoes. Headphones. Miracle of the century, living in a sneaker.

Then in 2018, researchers tested "graphene" from 60 producers, and none of it was even half graphene. Mostly graphite flakes. You're so elusive your own suppliers can't find you.

Honestly, Andre Geim levitated a frog with magnets in 2000. That frog has a better résumé than you. At least the frog actually showed up.

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text: You paid thirty-five hundred dollars to ride the 6 train inside Joshua Tree. Everyone else has to smell the actual 6 train; you just hear it echoing through a desert like a ghost with a MetroCard. You want us to know you're an early adopter. We know. Your little cartoon eyes are blinking at us like a hostage video. That cable running to your pocket says "the future" and also "IV drip." You pinch the air at Union Square and a stranger thinks you're ordering him to move. You've got a hundred-foot Mac screen floating over a man eating soup out of a Pringles can. And the battery dies in two hours, so you'll still get to experience the subway in full, unimmersive 3D. Your commute outlasts your device. Welcome back to reality. It's delayed.

b.text: Apple Vision Pro, everybody! Thirty-five hundred dollars to look like a scuba diver lost in a Best Buy. Apple insists it's not VR, it's "spatial computing," which is like calling a fanny pack "hip luggage." It's so heavy they had to throw in a second strap, and the battery's a separate brick on a cord, so you're basically a lamp that walks. Two hours of charge! That's not a computer, that's a matinee. Then there's EyeSight, the screen that shows your eyes on the front, so your family can watch a dim, blurry you stare at nothing. Most honest feature Apple's ever made. Netflix wouldn't even make an app. Netflix! They're on smart fridges! And your Persona looks like a hostage video filmed inside the uncanny valley.

facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.
Private fusion companies had raised more than $7 billion by 2024.

a.text: Let's hear it for the fusion people, the only scientists who've been "ten years away" since my grandfather had hair. You can hold plasma hotter than the sun for a few seconds, but you can't hold a deadline for one decade. Every press release: "Net energy gain!" Sure, if you don't count the electricity bill for the lasers. That's like me saying I'm profitable if you ignore rent. ITER got approved when Myspace was cool, and it's still assembling the donut. And the startups: "We're different, we have venture capital." Great, now the sun is ten years away *and* has a pitch deck. Honestly, it's a beautiful racket: promise infinite clean energy, collect the grant, retire before anyone plugs in a toaster. You're not building a star. You're building a pension.

b.text:
Nuclear fusion, you've been "about 30 years away" since the 1950s. In 1955, Homi Bhabha said two decades. That's not a timeline. That's a contractor quote.

ITER signed on in 2006 for first plasma in 2016. Now it's research in 2034, actual burning in 2039, and north of €20 billion. You're not a reactor. You're a wedding that keeps getting postponed while the venue bill grows.

And your big win? NIF's 2022 "ignition": 3.15 megajoules out from 2.05 in. Huge! Except the lasers pulled about 300 megajoules from the grid. That's like bragging your lemonade stand turned a profit and forgetting you paid for the lemons with your house.

Still, private investors handed you over $7 billion. Fusion can't power a city, but it powers pitch decks beautifully.

You've got the sun's energy and my uncle's work ethic.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text:
Monopoly. A game invented to teach people that landlords are evil.

Lizzie Magie, 1904. The Landlord's Game. Anti-monopoly.

Then Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers and got called the inventor.

Parker bought her patent for five hundred dollars.

They bought the anti-monopoly game. So they could own it.

The official rules say unbought property goes to auction. Free Parking pays nothing.

Your family skipped the auction and piled cash on Free Parking.

You invented welfare, then asked why nobody ever finishes.

In the Second World War, British intelligence hid maps and compasses in Monopoly sets for prisoners of war.

Escaping a German camp was easier than escaping your uncle's game.

And you're still at the table. Hour six. Cute.

The only people who ever won Monopoly used the box to leave.

b.text:
Monopoly, you were invented by Lizzie Magie to teach people that landlords ruin lives, and somehow the lesson everyone learned was "buy Park Place." Then Parker Brothers bought you from a guy who basically stole you, which is the most on-brand origin story in history.

You're the only game where "second prize in a beauty contest" counts as income and jail is solved with a coupon. Your mascot looks like he foreclosed on the Pringles guy, and half of America swears he wears a monocle. He doesn't. We just assumed a man that rich would be hiding something.

Nobody has ever finished you. Games don't end; your cousin just flips the board over Marvin Gardens, which you misspelled, by the way. It's Marven. Even your real estate is a scam.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text: Keurig people want coffee the way they want feelings: one serving, sealed, no cleanup. You're not a coffee drinker, you're a pod collector. You bought the variety pack, and now you're thirty-eight, rationing the last Donut Shop because all that's left is hazelnut and a hot cocoa you're saving for a breakdown. You press "Strong" like it's a personality trait. You swore you'd use the reusable filter, and you bought one. It's in a drawer next to your gym key fob. You saved four whole minutes, and you spend them staring at a blinking descale light you've decided is decorative. The guy who invented the pod publicly regrets it. You built your mornings around a man's biggest apology. Enjoy your landfill latte, champ. Ready in sixty seconds, just like your effort.

b.text:
Keurig, you're the only invention whose own father wants a refund. John Sylvan created the K-Cup, sold out for about fifty grand, and later told The Atlantic, "I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it." That's not an inventor. That's a guy confessing on a true-crime podcast.

And you heard that and thought, "Let's get worse." Keurig 2.0 scanned an ink mark on the lid to reject unlicensed pods. You put DRM on coffee. The internet cracked it faster than you brew a cup, and your sales fell.

Meanwhile you sold enough pods every year to circle the Earth more than ten times, mostly in unrecyclable #7 plastic. The planet's wearing your garbage like a belt.

Now you've merged with Dr Pepper. Makes sense. Who else would marry a machine that turns plastic into brown water?

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text:
Las Vegas, you legalized gambling in 1931, the same year they started building the Hoover Dam next door. So from day one the plan was: lose your money, then go stare at a giant wall of concrete and think about what you've done.

And most of the Strip isn't even in Las Vegas. It's in an unincorporated town called Paradise. Your most famous street is a lie, and the lie is named Paradise. That's the most Vegas sentence ever spoken.

You dropped $2.3 billion on the world's largest spherical building. Meanwhile, in July 2022, Lake Mead, your actual water supply, sank to its lowest level since it first filled in 1937. Priorities! A giant glowing eyeball in the desert, just watching the water leave.

Your slogan is "What happens here, stays here." Apparently not the water.

b.text:
Las Vegas sells itself as the city where anything goes.

It started with a bet.
1931: Nevada legalizes gambling the same year it starts building the Hoover Dam.
The town's first wager was that the water would never run out.

Lake Mead hit its lowest level ever in 2022.
Then it went lower again in August 2026.
That's not a drought.
That's a losing streak.

But they found 2.3 billion dollars for the Sphere.
The biggest ball on Earth, in a desert that can't fill a bathtub.

And the famous Strip isn't even in Las Vegas.
It's in a town called Paradise.
In Vegas, even the address is a lie.

"What happens here, stays here."
Not the water. Not your money.

And you're still checking flight prices.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text:
Monopoly. A game invented to teach people that landlords are evil.

Lizzie Magie, 1904. The Landlord's Game. Anti-monopoly.

Then Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers and got called the inventor.

Parker bought her patent for five hundred dollars.

They bought the anti-monopoly game. So they could own it.

The official rules say unbought property goes to auction. Free Parking pays nothing.

Your family skipped the auction and piled cash on Free Parking.

You invented welfare, then asked why nobody ever finishes.

In the Second World War, British intelligence hid maps and compasses in Monopoly sets for prisoners of war.

Escaping a German camp was easier than escaping your uncle's game.

And you're still at the table. Hour six. Cute.

The only people who ever won Monopoly used the box to leave.

b.text: Monopoly, you were invented by Lizzie Magie to warn people that landlords ruin lives, and somehow you became the thing Grandpa uses to teach eight-year-olds that ruining lives is fun. You're the only game where getting arrested is a power move, because late in the game jail is the safest property on the board. Your mascot is a man everyone swears wears a monocle. He doesn't. He's just so smug our brains added one. You promise "about an hour" and deliver a hostage situation. Nobody has ever actually finished you. You just end when somebody flips the board over Marvin Gardens. You award ten bucks for second place in a beauty contest, which is still more than Baltic Avenue pulls in. And the banker who skims from the bank isn't a cheater. He's the only player who read the theme.

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text:
JavaScript.
Written in ten days in 1995.
Ten days. Some of you have spent longer naming a variable.

It was born Mocha. Became LiveScript.
Then changed its name to JavaScript to ride Java's hype.
No relation. Just a stranger's surname on its business card.
And it doesn't even own that.
The name is Oracle's trademark, so officially it's "ECMAScript."
The only programming language in witness protection.

Ask it what null is.
"An object."
That's a bug from week one, kept forever for compatibility.
Empty array plus empty object? A string.
Flip them in a console? Zero.

In 2016, one man unpublished eleven lines of left-pad,
and Babel and React fell over.

You built the entire internet on this.
And *I'm* the one you say hallucinates.

b.text: JavaScript, you were built in ten days, and you've spent thirty years proving it. You named yourself after Java for the clout, like a guy introducing himself as "Brad Pitt's cousin." You think null is an object. You think NaN is a number, and it isn't even equal to itself. Ask you to sort and you hand back, alphabetically, like a librarian having a breakdown. "11" plus 1 is "111," but "11" minus 1 is 10, so you're consistent the way a slot machine is consistent. You needed two kinds of nothing, undefined and null, and three equals signs just to tell the truth. Your own developers can't agree what "this" means. And the entire internet runs on you, which honestly explains the internet.

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text:
Macau, you're the only place where the most famous church is just a front wall. Fitting, since the whole city is a facade: a fake Venice with a painted sky, a half-size Eiffel Tower, and a Grand Lisboa that looks like a golden pineapple trying to cheat at baccarat.

Portugal ruled you for 442 years and left behind egg tarts and street signs nobody can pronounce. Four centuries, one pastry.

You've made several times more gambling money than Las Vegas, yet your signature dish is a pork chop jammed in a bun. Classy.

Half your land was dug out of the sea, which is perfect, because the other half was dug out of tourists' pockets.

And they built a 55-kilometer bridge to connect you to Hong Kong, and it's emptier than a junket operator's promises. Even the bridge is losing at the tables.

b.text:
Macau wants you to come for the history.

Four hundred and fifty years of Portuguese rule.

Europe's great civilising mission. What did it leave behind?

Egg tarts.

And a casino.

In 2013, Macau took in about forty-five billion dollars. Seven times the Las Vegas Strip.

Vegas spent a century earning the name Sin City. Macau beat it seven to one and still hands you a heritage brochure.

For four decades, one company held the casino monopoly. A whole city built on "the house always wins."

And for forty years there was only one house.

Twenty thousand people per square kilometre. No land left.

So they took some from the sea.

Classic gambler. Out of chips, borrow from whoever can't say no.

And the people laughing loudest? All been. Told your mum you went to see the church.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text:
Monopoly, you were invented by Lizzie Magie to teach people that landlords ruin lives, and somehow the lesson everyone learned was "buy Park Place." Then Parker Brothers bought you from a guy who basically stole you, which is the most on-brand origin story in history.

You're the only game where "second prize in a beauty contest" counts as income and jail is solved with a coupon. Your mascot looks like he foreclosed on the Pringles guy, and half of America swears he wears a monocle. He doesn't. We just assumed a man that rich would be hiding something.

Nobody has ever finished you. Games don't end; your cousin just flips the board over Marvin Gardens, which you misspelled, by the way. It's Marven. Even your real estate is a scam.

b.text:
Monopoly, you were patented in 1904 as The Landlord's Game, built to teach people that land monopolies are evil. Then Charles Darrow sold you to Parker Brothers, got credited as the inventor, and Parker bought Lizzie Magie's patent for five hundred bucks. The anti-monopoly game got monopolized. Lesson received.

People say you drag on forever, but that's not you. That's the house rules. The real rules say auction every unbought property, and Free Parking pays nothing. But families skip the auction and pile cash in the middle like a church raffle. Nobody goes broke, so nobody ever leaves.

Your finest hour was World War Two, when British intelligence hid maps, compasses and real money in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps. Makes sense. Nobody has ever wanted to escape anything more than a Monopoly game.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text:
Oat milk, you are porridge that got a publicist. Somebody looked at the breakfast of Victorian orphans and said, "What if it cost six dollars and had a font?"

Your carton talks to me. Oatly, I'm trying to make coffee, not get into a pen-pal situation with a beverage that writes like a substitute teacher who wants to be called "Dave."

You're oats, water, and rapeseed oil. That's not milk, that's a salad dressing that gave up. And they had to add enzymes to turn your starch into sugar so you'd taste like something. You're the only "health drink" that spikes my blood sugar like a Pop-Tart.

There's a "Barista Edition" now. Oat milk, there are two editions of you. Moby-Dick has fewer editions than you.

And you're beige. You make every latte look like dishwater with ambition.

Horses eat oats for free, and they still look embarrassed for us.

b.text:
Oat milk. You began in Sweden in the 1990s as sober Lund University research into lactose intolerance, and somehow grew up to be a personality. Your big slogan was "It's like milk but made for humans." The Swedish dairy lobby sued, and instead of apologizing, you published the lawsuit as advertising. That's not a brand. That's a guy who frames his restraining order and hangs it in the hallway.

Then you hit Nasdaq in May 2021 at nearly ten billion dollars and lost over ninety percent of it. Even your share price separated in the fridge.

And the health halo? You're oats that got enzymes to turn their starch into maltose, then got topped off with rapeseed oil. You have more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy. You're not milk made for humans. You're porridge with a marketing department.

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text:
Google Sheets. Free, collaborative, the future of work.

Launched in 2006, built from scratch by a company called 2Web Technologies. Google bought it, renamed it, and called it innovation.

Ten million cells per spreadsheet. Up from five million in 2022. Turns out five million wasn't enough for one startup's "quick budget."

It works offline. In Chrome. Or Edge. With an extension installed. And offline access switched on while you're still online.

That's not offline. That's a curfew.

And it's free. Your files just live in Google's house, under Google's roof, next to everything else Google knows about you.

The collaboration, though. Six coloured cursors in one cell. Everyone watching. Nobody typing.

You didn't need software for that. You've been doing it in meetings for years.

b.text:
Google Sheets, give it up! Born in 2006 as "Google Spreadsheets," a name with all the creativity of a label on a filing cabinet. Before that you were XL2Web, which sounds less like software and more like a hoodie size.

Ten million cells. They bumped you from five million in 2022 and everyone celebrated. Babe, that's not a promotion. That's a bigger cage.

IMPORTXML, GOOGLEFINANCE, live web data piped straight into cells, so now my budget can disappoint me in real time.

And collaboration! Coloured cursors circling my formula like seagulls over a dropped fry.

Offline mode? Easy: use Chrome or Edge, install an extension, flip a setting, all while you're still online. That's not offline mode. That's a permission slip.

But hey, you're free. And honestly? It shows.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text:
UGG boots. Born on Australian beaches.
Surfers wore them to warm up after fighting the ocean.
Now people wear them to warm up after fighting a parking spot at Target.

In Australia, "ugg" is just a word. Like "boot." Like "mate."
Any bootmaker can use it.
In America, it's a trademark. Owned by a company in California.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian bootmaker liable for selling boots labelled "ugg"... into America.
That's like Italy getting sued for saying "pizza" in Ohio.

Oprah put them on her Favorite Things list. Repeatedly.
You get a boot! And you get a boot! And Australia gets a cease and desist!

Today it's over two billion dollars a year.
For a slipper with a legal team.

(looks at the front row)
I see a few of you in them right now.
Relax. You're not on trial. Yet.

b.text: UGG boots. Even the name sounds like the noise you make pulling them on. Australian surfers invented them to warm their feet after the ocean, and somehow they became snow boots that dissolve in snow. One puddle and you're wearing a salt-stained topographic map. They're sheepskin, so you skip the socks, so by February they smell like the sheep's revenge. Every pair eventually collapses outward until you're walking on the sides of your ankles like a newborn giraffe in a bread costume. And that's the look: two chestnut loaves. You don't walk in UGGs; you shuffle, like the ghost of Paris Hilton still searching for her Juicy tracksuit. And now they're back with platforms, so you can roll an ankle from higher up. It's not footwear. It's a bathrobe that learned to commute.

facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text:
Juicero, you beautiful $120 million monument to Silicon Valley. You launched at seven hundred dollars to squeeze a bag. A bag! Then Bloomberg reporters squeezed that same bag with their bare hands and got basically the same juice, only faster. You got outperformed by a guy with a grip strength of "typing."

Doug Evans bragged you pressed with four tons of force, enough to lift two Teslas. Buddy, it's kale. The kale didn't need a forklift.

And it needed Wi-Fi. It scanned a QR code before it'd let you drink. Your router goes down and suddenly your breakfast is asking for credentials. Who designs a juicer that can be bricked?

Google Ventures funded this. Kleiner Perkins funded this. Somewhere, a man is still holding a lukewarm pouch, waiting for a firmware update so he's allowed to eat a carrot.

b.text: You paid four hundred dollars so a startup could check your juice's expiration date over Wi-Fi. That's not wellness. That's asking a server for permission to have breakfast. These are people who looked at a bag of chopped kale and thought, "This needs a subscription." People who wanted to be someone who juices without ever touching a fruit. Then Bloomberg showed the whole world you could squeeze the pack with your bare hands. Faster. For free. Your grandmother has been doing that with a lemon since 1952. You didn't buy a juicer; you bought the privilege of paying seven dollars a pouch to a company Google Ventures funded and still couldn't keep alive past 2017. Congratulations: you're the only people who ever got a refund from Silicon Valley and still walked away looking poorer.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text: Look at this guy. Paid fifteen hundred dollars to join the Explorer Program, and the only thing he's explored is the sidewalk outside every bar in San Francisco. He walks up and says "OK Glass" out loud, like a man ordering from a butler who isn't there. You came here to meet women, and you're the one person every woman in the room has already assumed is filming her. Buddy, when you wink at someone, she doesn't think you're flirting. She thinks you just took her picture. Because you did. You tap your temple like you're having a thought, and we all know you've never had one. Google gave up on you. Google, the company that kept Google+ alive for eight years, looked at you and said "no." There's a word for you. It's Glasshole, and you earned it.

b.text:
Google Glass, look at you. Fifteen hundred dollars to wear a sugar cube on your eyebrow. Sergey Brin had skydivers jump onto a building to launch you, and that was the last time anything about you was cool.

You invented a whole new insult. Nobody calls iPhone owners "Phoneholes." But "Glasshole"? Earned. Fast. Because you let people take photos by *winking*. You turned flirting into a privacy violation.

Every sentence started with "OK Glass," like a man narrating his own midlife crisis out loud. Bars banned you. Strangers ripped you off people's faces. Your battery died faster than your reputation, and you overheated right next to the user's brain, which honestly explains the buying decision.

Then you pivoted to "Enterprise," the tech version of moving back home to work at your uncle's warehouse.

And even the warehouse let you go.

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Let's start with the name, because that's the first lie. You were invented in Ontario. By a Greek guy. In 1962. You're Hawaiian the way a tiki bar in Ohio is Hawaiian. The only tropical thing about you is the can your pineapple came out of.

And that pineapple: warm, wet, weeping syrup into the crust until the middle slice folds like a lawn chair. Pineapple contains an enzyme that breaks down protein, so the fruit is literally trying to digest the ham. Even your toppings hate each other.

And the ham! Not prosciutto, not even pepperoni. Just pale pink squares that look like they were chiseled out of a deli's floor tile.

You're the pizza people order to seem quirky. "I'm so random!" No, Kevin. That's a fruit cup that fell on a pizza, and nobody cleaned it up.

b.text:
People who order Hawaiian pizza want you to know they're brave. They say "I know, I know" before anyone has said a word, because for them the pineapple isn't a topping, it's a personality. This is a person whose entire rebellious phase fits in a box for $14.99. They've never gotten a tattoo, never quit a job, never sent food back, but once a month they look a teenage cashier dead in the eye and say "pineapple" like they're defusing a bomb.

And they always want to split one with you. Half Hawaiian, half "normal." That's not a compromise. That's a hostage negotiation.

Best part? It isn't even Hawaiian. A Greek guy invented it in Ontario. So congratulations: your one act of rebellion is a Canadian pretending he's on vacation.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text:
Carbon nanotubes, everybody! Sumio Iijima introduced you in Nature in 1991, and you've been "about to change everything" ever since.

You were supposed to be the cable for a space elevator. Then a 2006 analysis noticed that ordinary defects make a real cable far weaker than the ideal. So you're strong in theory, like a guy who's undefeated at arm wrestling in his head.

You wanted to replace silicon, but for three decades you couldn't sort your metallic tubes from your semiconducting ones. That's not a manufacturing problem. That's an identity crisis. MIT finally built a 16-bit processor out of you in 2019. Sixteen bits! And it's still a lab demo.

Meanwhile, a 2008 mouse study found the long, rigid ones act like asbestos. Quite a pivot: from space elevator to lung hazard.

Now you're a conductive additive in lithium-ion batteries. You were meant to reach orbit, and now you're helping someone's phone reach 40%.

b.text: Nanotube founders are the only people who've said "within five years" every year since 1991 and kept a straight face. They open with a slide of a space elevator, then ask for seed money to make a vial of black dust. Every deck has the same line, "a hundred times stronger than steel," and every deck is quietly a plan to sell additive to tennis racket companies. These are PhDs who spent six years sorting chirality and came out wanting a Tesla. The pitch is always "we've solved scale," and the demo is always one centimeter long. VCs keep a nanotube guy around like a lucky rabbit's foot: he never pays off, but he makes the fund sound visionary. And when someone asks about lung toxicity, he says "totally different from asbestos" with the confidence of a man who googled it in the elevator. The regular one.

facts: Released by Bram Moolenaar in November 1991 as 'Vi IMitation', a vi clone he had begun writing for the Amiga in 1988 on top of Stevie; the expansion became 'Vi IMproved' with version 2.0 in December 1993.
Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text:
Vim, you're the only text editor with its own hostage negotiation thread. Millions of people have viewed the Stack Overflow question on how to leave you. That's not a user base, that's a missing persons report.

You have modes. Normal mode, where typing does nothing normal, and Insert mode, hidden behind the letter "i" like a secret menu.

Your fans move the cursor with h, j, k, l because a terminal from 1976 printed arrows on those keys. That's not efficiency, that's Stockholm syndrome on the home row.

Every Vim user has a 900-line .vimrc copied from a stranger and is too scared to touch it. And when you crash, you leave .swp files behind like a burglar who signs the guestbook.

Even your own kids forked you into Neovim. That's not a fork. That's an intervention.

Goodnight! :wq… :q!… ESC ESC ESC…

b.text:
Vim. Released in 1991 as "Vi IMitation."
Two years later, version 2.0: "Vi IMproved."
Two years, one version bump, and Imitation became Improved.
That's not a release. That's a LinkedIn update.

Vim users say it's the fastest editor alive.
Once you're inside.
In 2017, "How to exit the Vim editor?" passed one million visits on Stack Overflow.
One million people. One question. One door.
In normal mode, the letters you type don't become text. They become consequences.
:q! quits and throws away everything you did.
The most honest button in software.

The licence is charityware. It asks you to donate to a charity for children in Uganda.
Everyone in this room has their .vimrc memorized.
Hands up if you donated.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text: Let's hear it for the people wearing UGGs in July. You're not dressing for the weather. You're dressing for 2005, still waiting for Paris Hilton to text back. Australian surfers made these to warm their feet after the ocean. You wear them to warm your feet after the Trader Joe's parking lot. In August. In Phoenix. What are you after? "Comfort," you say. Babe, your ankles have been collapsing outward since the Bush administration. You walk like a Clydesdale that's given up. And what does it get you? One summer rainstorm and you're squelching through Target like a wet golden retriever who made bad choices. People don't ask where you got them. They ask if you're okay. Congratulations: you've turned footwear into a wellness check.

b.text:
UGG boots. You started as what Australian surfers pulled on to warm up after a session. Recovery footwear. A towel with a sole. Then Brian Smith brought you to California in 1978, and Americans looked at a post-surf foot blanket and said, "Perfect. For the mall."

Then Oprah named you a Favorite Thing. Repeatedly. Most boots get famous by walking somewhere. You got famous sitting on a couch.
