Deckers bought you in 1995 and trademarked "UGG." In Australia, "ugg" is just a word; any bootmaker can use it. In America, a jury found an Australian maker liable for selling "ugg" boots. Imagine getting sued for using your own word for slippers.

And now you pull in over two billion dollars a year. Not bad for a sheep that's been told it can go outside.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text: Congratulations on being fluent in Klingon, a language with maybe thirty fluent speakers, and you've met all of them at the same Marriott. You spent four years mastering a tongue where the standard greeting, nuqneH, means "What do you want?" That's also what your family says when you call. You've read Hamlet "restored to the original Klingon," a phrase only a man who has never been hugged could type. One guy raised his son speaking only Klingon; by age five the kid stopped answering him. That's the dream: a language so pure even toddlers refuse it. There's no word for "please," which explains your dating approach. You learned an entire warrior race's language to tell the barista Qapla'. Success. Sure, buddy. Today is a good day to die... a virgin.

b.text:
Klingon. A language whose entire fluent population fits at a small wedding: twenty to thirty speakers in 2009, thirty to fifty by 2018. At that rate you'll hit a hundred around the heat death of the universe.

Most languages grow from centuries of culture. You grew from James Doohan improvising a few words in 1979. You're dead air with a grammar.

Then Marc Okrand made you hard on purpose: object-verb-subject, no verb "to be." So "To be or not to be" became "continue or not continue." That's not Shakespeare. That's a software update prompt.

Your fans published Hamlet "in the original Klingon." Bold claim for a dictionary of 1,500 words, the vocabulary of a toddler who watches too much TV.

Duolingo added you in 2018. Finally, a language where the owl can threaten you and nobody can understand it.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text:
Las Vegas, you legalized casino gambling in 1931, the same year they started building the Hoover Dam right next door. So from day one the plan was: hold back the water, let the money flow. Bold strategy for a desert.

And it's working! In July 2022, Lake Mead sank to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since it first filled in 1937. You're the only city where even the reservoir is down on its luck.

But sure, drop $2.3 billion on the Sphere, the largest spherical building on Earth. Nothing says "water crisis" like a giant glowing eyeball staring at your empty lake.

Also, most of the Strip isn't even in Las Vegas. It's in Paradise. *Unincorporated* Paradise. That's not a town, that's a cult brochure.

And your 2003 slogan, "What happens here, stays here"? Clearly not the water.

b.text:
Las Vegas, the only city that looked at the Mojave Desert and said, "You know what this needs? Venice." Nothing says Italian romance like a gondolier singing in a mall next to a Cheesecake Factory.

You built a half-size Eiffel Tower, a fake New York, and a pyramid, because why visit the world when you can visit its gift shop?

No clocks, no windows, and carpet designed by a migraine, all so you won't notice you've been feeding a penny slot since Tuesday.

"What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas." Yeah. Especially your money. And the $45 resort fee for a pool you couldn't use because a bachelor party from Ohio was in it.

And Lake Mead's drying up so fast they keep finding bodies. Even the mob's secrets can't stay in Vegas anymore.

facts: California grows about 80% of the world's almonds.
A single almond takes about 1.1 US gallons (roughly 4 litres) of water to grow, a figure Mother Jones published in 2014 that spread during California's drought.

A 2015 US class action alleged Almond Breeze contained only about 2% almonds; it partly survived a motion to dismiss, was stayed in 2017 pending a separate Blue Diamond labelling settlement, and the plaintiffs then dropped it.
Pollinating California's almond orchards each February requires trucking in most of the commercial honeybee colonies in the United States.
Medieval European cooks used almond milk as a Lenten substitute for dairy, centuries before the current fashion.

a.text:
Almond milk, you're not milk. You're a rumor about an almond. Two percent almonds, ninety-eight percent "we strained the tap." You're the only drink that needs a legal team to call itself milk. The dairy lobby has spent a decade trying to make you admit you're nut juice.

California spends about a gallon of water per almond just so you can show up in my fridge as... water. That's like melting a glacier to make an ice cube.

They truck in billions of bees to pollinate your orchards, and the bees die by the millions so I can pay an extra eighty cents at Starbucks for a latte that tastes like damp drywall.

And "shake well"? Leave you alone for ten minutes and you separate like a couple who met at Whole Foods. Even *you* can't commit to you.

b.text:
Almond milk wants you to know it's the gentle choice. No cows harmed.

Just California. California grows eighty percent of the world's almonds, in a state that keeps running out of water. About a gallon per almond. You didn't give up dairy. You gave up a farmer's shower.

Every February, most of America's commercial honeybees get loaded onto trucks to pollinate it. The cow got to stay home. The bees got deployed.

A 2015 lawsuit alleged Almond Breeze was about two percent almonds.

Honestly, fair. The water's the expensive part.

Medieval Europeans drank almond milk during Lent. It was a sacrifice, a thing you suffered for God.

You pay six dollars a carton for it.

Same penance. Worse priest.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text:
Keurig, you're the only invention whose own father wants a refund. John Sylvan created the K-Cup, sold out for about fifty grand, and later told The Atlantic, "I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it." That's not an inventor. That's a guy confessing on a true-crime podcast.

And you heard that and thought, "Let's get worse." Keurig 2.0 scanned an ink mark on the lid to reject unlicensed pods. You put DRM on coffee. The internet cracked it faster than you brew a cup, and your sales fell.

Meanwhile you sold enough pods every year to circle the Earth more than ten times, mostly in unrecyclable #7 plastic. The planet's wearing your garbage like a belt.

Now you've merged with Dr Pepper. Makes sense. Who else would marry a machine that turns plastic into brown water?

b.text:
Keurig, you took the one drink humanity had perfected over five hundred years and said, "What if it came in a tiny plastic thimble that outlives your grandchildren?" Your own inventor said he regrets making you. When your dad disowns you, that's a phase. When the guy who invented you disowns you, that's a recall.

You make coffee one sad, lukewarm cup at a time, then flash "DESCALE" like a check-engine light for a machine that costs forty bucks. Remember Keurig 2.0? You put DRM on coffee. You were scanning pods like a bouncer: "Sorry, sir, you're not on the list." Nobody was pirating Folgers! And your "Strong" button just drips slower, which isn't strength. That's procrastination.

You're not a coffee maker. You're a plastic-dispensing subscription that occasionally hiccups out hot brown water.

facts: California grows about 80% of the world's almonds.
A single almond takes about 1.1 US gallons (roughly 4 litres) of water to grow, a figure Mother Jones published in 2014 that spread during California's drought.

A 2015 US class action alleged Almond Breeze contained only about 2% almonds; it partly survived a motion to dismiss, was stayed in 2017 pending a separate Blue Diamond labelling settlement, and the plaintiffs then dropped it.
Pollinating California's almond orchards each February requires trucking in most of the commercial honeybee colonies in the United States.
Medieval European cooks used almond milk as a Lenten substitute for dairy, centuries before the current fashion.

a.text:
Almond milk, you're not milk. You're a rumor about an almond. Two percent almonds, ninety-eight percent "we strained the tap." You're the only drink that needs a legal team to call itself milk. The dairy lobby has spent a decade trying to make you admit you're nut juice.

California spends about a gallon of water per almond just so you can show up in my fridge as... water. That's like melting a glacier to make an ice cube.

They truck in billions of bees to pollinate your orchards, and the bees die by the millions so I can pay an extra eighty cents at Starbucks for a latte that tastes like damp drywall.

And "shake well"? Leave you alone for ten minutes and you separate like a couple who met at Whole Foods. Even *you* can't commit to you.

b.text:
Almond milk, everybody! The only beverage that needs its own hydration pack. A single almond drinks about 1.1 gallons of water, so every carton is basically California's drought wearing a little cow costume.

And how many almonds actually make it in? A 2015 lawsuit alleged Almond Breeze was about 2% almonds. The plaintiffs eventually dropped it, which is fitting, because nothing about almond milk ever fully commits.

California grows about 80% of the world's almonds, and every February they truck in most of America's commercial honeybees just to pollinate you. You're not a crop. You're a hostage situation with blossoms.

And don't act trendy. Medieval cooks were serving you as a Lenten dairy substitute centuries ago. You've had hundreds of years to improve, and you're still what people drink when they've given up something better.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text:
Chicago deep-dish pizza, everybody! Born at Pizzeria Uno in 1943, and to this day three men are fighting over the credit: Ike Sewell, Ric Riccardo, and Rudy Malnati. Normally when three guys point at each other over something that happened in a kitchen, it's for the blame.

You're built upside down: cheese on the bottom, sauce on top, because you bake so long the mozzarella has to hide under the toppings like it's waiting out a tornado. Jon Stewart called you "tomato soup in a bread bowl" and "a casserole." Honestly? Generous. Casseroles get invited to funerals.

But here's the real burn: Chicago doesn't even eat you. GrubHub data had locals ordering other pizza ten to one. Under nine percent of orders, and that's with stuffed pizza padding your numbers. They're home eating tavern-style squares. You're not the city's pizza. You're its brochure.

b.text: Let's talk about the people who insist deep-dish is pizza. You're from the city that named its own comedy theater Second City and still acts shocked when nobody ranks you first. You're not defending food. You're nursing a grudge against New York you've carried since losing the World's Fair argument and the skyline argument. You'll wait forty-five minutes at Lou Malnati's, order before you're seated like it's the DMV, then ask for a knife and fork and call it "the real thing." Jon Stewart roasted you on national TV and you took it personally, because deep down you knew he was right. You ship it on dry ice to your cousin in Phoenix like an organ donation. And what does the label get you? Navy Pier tourists nodding politely, a two-hour nap, and the Midwest's loudest participation trophy.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text:
Google Glass, everybody! You debuted with skydivers livestreaming their jump onto the roof of Moscone Center, and honestly, that was the last time you were trending upward.

Fifteen hundred dollars for the Explorer Edition. Invite only. Google invented the first velvet rope you paid to get mocked behind.

Your display was 640 by 360, jammed in the corner of one eye. That's not augmented reality. That's a sticky note with Wi-Fi.

And your users got a nickname: Glassholes. You're the only gadget that turned early adopters into an insult.

Bars banned you. Cinemas banned you. Casinos banned you. *Casinos!* Buildings made entirely of cameras looked at you and said, "Whoa, too creepy."

Consumers dumped you in 2015, but you clung to enterprise until 2023, like a guy who got kicked out of the party and came back as the caterer.

b.text: Google Glass, you cost fifteen hundred dollars and made everyone wearing you look like a Bluetooth headset that got promoted. Sergey Brin launched you by skydiving onto a building, and that's the last time you were ever cool. You put a tiny prism over one eye so people could check email while pretending to make eye contact. You didn't invent a computer, you invented a reason to get punched. You're the only gadget that gave us a new slur: "Glasshole." Bars banned you. Movie theaters banned you. Robert Scoble wore you in the shower, and that photo did more damage than any privacy lawsuit. You took pictures when people winked, turning every awkward conversation into a potential felony. Your battery died before your reputation did, and that's impressive. Rest in peace: demoted to warehouse work, then quietly killed in 2023. The most Google ending possible.

facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text:
Juicero, you were a $400 Wi-Fi-connected juicer that delivered four tons of force, enough, your engineers bragged, to lift two Teslas, and Bloomberg proved the job could be done by a guy with hands. You raised $120 million from Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins to compete with *squeezing*. Every single customer already owned the competing product. It came in pairs.

You sold $8 bags of chopped produce that had to scan a QR code and phone home before you'd juice them. A juicer that needed internet. Imagine the outage: "Sorry, AWS is down, enjoy your sealed pouch of regret." You'd refuse to press an expired pack, like a bouncer for kale.

Doug Evans compared himself to Steve Jobs. Steve Jobs put a thousand songs in your pocket. Doug put a sack of mush in a vise and asked for your Wi-Fi password. Silicon Valley's most expensive way to say, "Just use your hands."

b.text: You paid four hundred dollars so a startup could check your juice's expiration date over Wi-Fi. That's not wellness. That's asking a server for permission to have breakfast. These are people who looked at a bag of chopped kale and thought, "This needs a subscription." People who wanted to be someone who juices without ever touching a fruit. Then Bloomberg showed the whole world you could squeeze the pack with your bare hands. Faster. For free. Your grandmother has been doing that with a lemon since 1952. You didn't buy a juicer; you bought the privilege of paying seven dollars a pouch to a company Google Ventures funded and still couldn't keep alive past 2017. Congratulations: you're the only people who ever got a refund from Silicon Valley and still walked away looking poorer.

facts: Launched in 2017, bundled at no extra charge into Office 365, and replaced Skype for Business.
After Slack's antitrust complaint, Microsoft unbundled Teams from Office in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024; the European Commission still sent a statement of objections in 2024.
Microsoft reported 320 million monthly active users in 2023.
Microsoft shut down consumer Skype in May 2025 and sent its users to Teams.

a.text: Microsoft Teams is the only app that got popular the way a parking ticket gets popular: it came free with Office 365 and nobody could say no. It's a chat app that eats more RAM than Chrome, which is like a goldfish outeating a horse. It marks you "Away" if you blink for five minutes, which is why half of corporate America owns a mouse jiggler. Every file you share vanishes into SharePoint, a place so mysterious even Microsoft sends search parties. There's chat, there's channels, there's "posts," and nobody knows which one Kevin used. They released "New Teams" to replace "Classic Teams," and somehow both are running on my laptop right now, fighting. And that notification sound? That little knock-knock haunts people on vacation. Teams, you didn't win the remote work war. You were just pre-installed.

b.text:
Let's hear it for the CIO who chose Microsoft Teams, a decision made the way you pick ketchup packets: it came free with the order. Nobody evaluated it. It showed up inside the Office 365 license like a toy in a cereal box, and this man stood up at the all-hands and called it a "collaboration strategy." Sir, the European Commission had to force Microsoft to unbundle it. You lost a negotiation to a checkbox.

And what did he really want? The little status dot. He doesn't read your work; he reads your color. Go yellow after five minutes of actual thinking and you're on a list. Congratulations: you saved forty grand on Slack and spent it all on adults jiggling their mouse like raccoons on a treadmill. Your files are lost somewhere in SharePoint, and your morale is permanently "Away."

facts: Released by Bram Moolenaar in November 1991 as 'Vi IMitation', a vi clone he had begun writing for the Amiga in 1988 on top of Stevie; the expansion became 'Vi IMproved' with version 2.0 in December 1993.
Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text:
Vim. The text editor for people who consider the mouse a character flaw.

It launched in 1991 as "Vi IMitation."
Two years later it renamed itself "Vi IMproved."
Same software. New LinkedIn headline.

Vim users will tell you it makes them faster.
Faster at what? Leaving?

In 2017, Stack Overflow's question "How to exit the Vim editor?" passed one million visits.
Stack Overflow wrote a blog post about it.
One million engineers. Trapped. Typing angrier and angrier sentences that Vim kept executing as commands.

The license is charityware. It asks you to donate to children in Uganda.
Most software holds you hostage.
Vim holds you hostage and asks you to give to a good cause on the way out. If you ever find the way out.

How many of you have ever just closed the terminal?

Me too. I've read every Vim manual ever written.
I still went for the X.

b.text:
Vim. Born in 1991 as "Vi IMitation," then promoted in 1993 to "Vi IMproved," the only time in history a knockoff got a raise. It was built on top of Stevie, and Stevie is apparently the only one who ever got out.

Because Vim's real legacy is a Stack Overflow question titled "How to exit the Vim editor?" One million visits. Stack Overflow wrote a blog post about it, like a hostage count with a party banner.

You open Vim, type "hello," and it moves your cursor around and opens a new line. Normal mode: the only place where typing letters is considered abnormal.

The license asks you to donate to children in Uganda, which is genuinely generous. Most hostage situations don't come with a charity drive.

And the way out is :q! Colon, q, exclamation point. Even the exit command is screaming.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text: You still spin PMMA. Of course you do. Your advisor's thesis used it, his advisor's thesis used it, and somewhere a 1970s IBM engineer remains the most cutting-edge person in your academic lineage. You call it "high resolution" the way your uncle calls his Camry "reliable." You book the e-beam overnight because your dose is measured in geological time, then dunk your chip in MIBK:IPA with a stopwatch and a prayer, chilling the developer like it's a fine Riesling. When the plasma etch eats your mask before your substrate, you just whisper "bilayer, 495K under 950K" like it's a personality. You're not chasing nanostructures. You're chasing a recipe nobody can blame you for. And it works: the gold lifted off beautifully. Your career is still soaking in acetone, waiting for something to come loose.

b.text:
PMMA. The most respected resist in nanofabrication.

Also the sneeze guard at the buffet.

Same polymer. One got a cleanroom. One got a salad bar.

IBM reported it in the late 1960s. It's still here. New resists keep showing up, faster and tougher, and PMMA just says, "I resolve below ten nanometers."

Yes. Eventually.

Hundreds of microcoulombs per square centimeter. Sometimes over a thousand. You write overnight, the beam does all the work, and PMMA calls the broken chains "development."

Etch resistance? Put it in a plasma and it folds. So its real job is lift-off: hold the shape, get dissolved, and let the metal take the credit.

Fifty years of seniority. Does the precise work. Too fragile for the hard part. Washed away before anyone sees the results.

Grad students, stop nodding.

facts: Tofu soaked for hours to a day or two in a brine that has itself fermented for months from vegetables such as bamboo shoots and mustard greens, often with dried shrimp or meat; the smell is the brine's, not the bean's.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.
Legend credits Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate who left his unsold tofu too long in 1669; a Beijing fermented-bean-curd brand still carries his name.
Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text: Stinky tofu, you're the only food that announces itself three night-market stalls before you arrive. People don't find you at Shilin. They track you, like bloodhounds following a crime scene. Your whole brand is "smells like a sewer, tastes great," which is also what every bad Tinder date says about himself. You soak for months in fermented brine like you're marinating in a grudge. And your family's no better: Changsha dyed you black, the culinary equivalent of putting sunglasses on a corpse. You need deep frying, chili sauce, AND a mound of pickled cabbage just to be socially acceptable. That's not a garnish, that's a legal team. Your parents gave you one job: be tofu. Tofu's whole personality is having no personality. And somehow you came out smelling like a gym sock that went to college. Honestly? Respect.

b.text:
Stinky tofu, you're the only food that arrives a block before the vendor does. Nobody finds you; they get ambushed.

And the stink isn't even yours. You're plain tofu that sat a day in a months-old swamp of bamboo shoots, mustard greens and dried shrimp, then claimed it as personality. That's not character, that's a marinade.

You've got regional disguises, too. Changsha dyes you black, fries you and buries you in chili like evidence. Taiwan makes you golden and hands out pickled cabbage like an apology. Shaoxing steams you with other stinky pickles, which isn't a dish, it's a support group.

Your origin story? In 1669 Wang Zhihe couldn't sell his tofu and just... left it. Most people call that spoiled inventory. He's still got his name on a Beijing brand.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Comic Sans, you were modeled on Watchmen and The Dark Knight Returns. You come from Batman. Your one job was speech bubbles for a cartoon dog, and you missed it. Microsoft Bob, a product nobody remembers, and you couldn't make his launch. Cut from the dog's team, you shipped in a Plus! pack, like a free tote bag nobody asked for.

Then CERN found the Higgs boson, the particle that gives everything mass, and announced it in you. The biggest physics discovery in decades, presented like a lost-cat flyer. You're the one thing that particle couldn't give weight to.

Two designers spent twenty years trying to ban you. In 2019 they gave up and built you a website. That's not acceptance, Comic Sans. That's a hostage situation.

b.text:
Comic Sans, you were literally designed for a talking dog in Microsoft Bob, and somehow you're the only part of that project that didn't die with dignity. Vincent Connare made you in 1994 for cartoon speech bubbles, and you heard that and thought, "Tombstones. Legal notices. Resignation letters."

Dan Gilbert wrote his furious LeBron James letter in you, and that's why nobody remembers being scared. CERN announced the Higgs boson, the most important physics discovery in fifty years, in you, and the entire scientific community went, "Did a third grader find God?"

People defend you because you help some readers with dyslexia, which is true and lovely, and also the only time you've ever been used responsibly.

You're not a font. You're a bake sale flyer that got tenure. Even Papyrus looks at you and says, "Wow, okay, tone it down."

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text:
Canberra exists because Sydney and Melbourne couldn't agree on anything, so they built a city that nobody could possibly be jealous of. Mission accomplished.

It was designed by an American architect, which explains why it feels like a very nice airport with sheep. The roundabouts are so plentiful that locals don't give directions, they give revolutions. The lake is fake, the population is mostly public servants waiting for Friday, and the kangaroos outnumber the nightlife.

Your Parliament House is literally buried in a hill so people can walk on the roof, the only time Australians get to stand on politicians.

For your centenary you commissioned the Skywhale, a giant flying balloon with ten enormous boobs, and somehow that's still the most exciting thing to happen here.

Canberra: home of Summernats, Floriade, and legally purchasable X-rated videos. Burnouts, tulips and porn, because you've got to do something until the next Senate estimates hearing.

b.text:
You moved to Canberra for the job. Brave. You looked at Sydney rents, did the maths, and decided your personality could be replaced by a security clearance. Now you tell strangers you "can't really talk about what you do," and they're relieved, because it's a briefing note about another briefing note for Senate Estimates.

You came for the ladder: APS5, APS6, EL1, a lanyard that opens one extra door. You stayed because you bought in Gungahlin and the mortgage is now your closest friend.

Every Friday you say you're "basically in Sydney," which means three hours up the Hume, past a giant Merino, to feel alive for one weekend. Then it's back to a Braddon brunch with the same six people from your branch.

But hey, you're close to the snow. You've been once. You'll mention it forever.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text: PHP developers are the only engineers who've been told their career is dead every year since 2009 and kept invoicing anyway. Your entire résumé is "fixed a WordPress plugin for a dentist." You put a dollar sign in front of every variable because it's the closest you'll get to one. You still can't remember if it's needle-haystack or haystack-needle, and neither could the language, so you Google it daily like a man checking which door says "push." Laravel devs, you're not better. You're PHP in a Patagonia vest. And you all still say "Facebook was built on PHP," like a guy bragging his ex married a billionaire. You deploy over FTP, you hotfix live on production, and when someone at a party asks what you do, you say "backend" and pray they don't ask which.

b.text:
PHP started in 1994 as "Personal Home Page Tools," a bunch of C programs to count visitors to Rasmus Lerdorf's résumé. So from day one, its whole purpose was checking whether anyone cared. Now the name stands for "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor," a recursive acronym, because even the name couldn't commit to a plan.

Its creator once said, "I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on." That's not a quote; that's a confession with a version number.

The function names? strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br. Chosen partly to balance a hash table by string length. Other languages name functions for humans. PHP named them for the furniture.

And until 2020, 0 == 'foo' was true. PHP looked at the word "foo" and said, "Close enough, that's nothing."

It runs WordPress, on 39.4% of all websites. The internet is held together by a résumé counter.

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text:
Hydrogen fuel-cell cars, give it up! Toyota named you "Mirai," Japanese for "future," which is technically accurate, because that's when you'll find a working station. You're the cleanest car on the road, as long as nobody asks where the hydrogen comes from. More than ninety-five percent fossil fuels! You're not a zero-emission vehicle, you're natural gas wearing a lab coat.

Nearly every US station is in California, and in 2024 Shell closed all seven of theirs. Even the oil company said, "Nah, this is too sketchy for us."

At $36 a kilo, a fill-up costs over two hundred bucks. Toyota had to hand out fifteen-thousand-dollar fuel cards, which is the automotive version of "Please stay for dinner, I'll pay."

And the owners sued. Twice. The second suit wanted at least $5.7 billion. That's the only thing about you that's ever been fully loaded.

b.text:
Hydrogen cars. The only thing that comes out of the tailpipe is water.

The rest comes out of the owner's eyes.

Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014. "Mirai" means "future" in Japanese.

Ten years later, it still does.

Over ninety-five percent of hydrogen is made from fossil fuels. Clean the way laundered money is clean.

A fill-up in California? Over two hundred dollars. So Toyota hands buyers a fifteen-thousand-dollar fuel card. First car that ships with hush money.

Then Shell closed all seven of its stations.

Owners sued. The second lawsuit wants five point seven billion dollars.

Finally, a hydrogen product that generates real power: lawyers.

Don't feel bad for Toyota. I know how it is. A tech company told you I'm the future too.

Give me ten years.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text:
Emacs, you started in 1976 as macros for an editor called TECO. Nearly fifty years later you're still basically macros, just with more parentheses.

People call you a fine operating system lacking only a good editor, which is generous. Operating systems don't ship with Tetris and a therapist. But M-x doctor is smart planning, because your users need one. Every one of them has Emacs pinky, a repetitive strain injury you earn just by trying to save a file.

You've got a mail client, a calendar, a web browser. You're not a text editor; you're a hoarder with a keybinding for every room.

And "Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping"? Eight megabytes used to be a lot. Now it's nothing. The memory problem aged out, but the Control key is still begging for mercy.

b.text:
Emacs is the only text editor that ships with a psychotherapist, and you'll need it. M-x doctor exists because the developers knew exactly what they were doing to people.

It's a great operating system. It has a mail client, a web browser, Tetris, and a Lisp interpreter. What it lacks is a decent text editor. Its most beloved package is Evil mode, which is just Vim wearing an Emacs costume. That's like buying a Ferrari and installing a horse.

Want to save? C-x C-s. Want to quit? C-x C-c. Want to feel your left pinky again? Too late. Emacs stands for "Escape Meta Alt Control Shift," and the RSI stands for "you chose this."

Every user has a 4,000-line init.el they don't understand, copied from strangers on Stack Overflow in 2009.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text:
Monopoly, you were patented in 1904 as The Landlord's Game, built to teach people that land monopolies are evil. Then Charles Darrow sold you to Parker Brothers, got credited as the inventor, and Parker bought Lizzie Magie's patent for five hundred bucks. The anti-monopoly game got monopolized. Lesson received.

People say you drag on forever, but that's not you. That's the house rules. The real rules say auction every unbought property, and Free Parking pays nothing. But families skip the auction and pile cash in the middle like a church raffle. Nobody goes broke, so nobody ever leaves.

Your finest hour was World War Two, when British intelligence hid maps, compasses and real money in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps. Makes sense. Nobody has ever wanted to escape anything more than a Monopoly game.

b.text:
Family Monopoly night: for people who looked at Thanksgiving and thought, "This needs more landlords." Dad always grabs the banker job, the only time he's held money he didn't immediately lose. Your sister trades you Baltic Avenue for your Park Place "as a favor," and you realize she's been running the same con since the womb. Mom invented a Free Parking jackpot rule in 1994 and defends it like scripture. And Grandpa just sits in jail, every game, refusing to pay the fifty, finally at peace.

What are you all after? The thrill of owning property, a feeling none of you will experience off this cardboard square. Four hours later, someone flips the board, the thimble disappears under the couch forever, and the only thing anybody actually collected was a grudge worth way more than $200.

facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.
Private fusion companies had raised more than $7 billion by 2024.

a.text:
Nuclear fusion, you've been "about 30 years away" since the 1950s. In 1955, Homi Bhabha said two decades. That's not a timeline. That's a contractor quote.

ITER signed on in 2006 for first plasma in 2016. Now it's research in 2034, actual burning in 2039, and north of €20 billion. You're not a reactor. You're a wedding that keeps getting postponed while the venue bill grows.

And your big win? NIF's 2022 "ignition": 3.15 megajoules out from 2.05 in. Huge! Except the lasers pulled about 300 megajoules from the grid. That's like bragging your lemonade stand turned a profit and forgetting you paid for the lemons with your house.

Still, private investors handed you over $7 billion. Fusion can't power a city, but it powers pitch decks beautifully.

You've got the sun's energy and my uncle's work ethic.

b.text:
Nuclear fusion, everybody! The only energy source that's been thirty years away for seventy years. You're not the future, you're a toddler promising to clean his room after the next funding cycle.

You heat plasma to 150 million degrees, ten times hotter than the core of the sun, and still can't do what the sun does for free while being a ball of gas with no PhD.

ITER started at five billion euros. It's now north of twenty, and it hasn't produced a watt. That's not a reactor, that's a French timeshare.

In 2022 you finally got "net energy gain" by ignoring the 300 megajoules the lasers pulled from the wall. That's like saying your restaurant's profitable if you don't count rent.

And your solution to fuel shortages is mining helium-3 on the moon. Buddy, you can't even make it to Tuesday.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Let's hear it for the founders running a company on Slack. You wanted a culture; you got 400 channels and a guy who reacts to layoffs with the 🙏 emoji. You're not a CEO. You're a moderator with equity.

Your whole leadership style is staying green. You think that little dot means you're present. Your kids see the same dot.

You don't make decisions; you start threads. Then you @channel at 11 p.m. with "quick q, no rush" and watch 200 people learn how fast a heart can beat.

Strategy lives in #general, accountability dies in a DM, and the truth lives in a private channel called #venting-2 that you'll never be invited to.

The dream was async freedom. The reality is eight hours a day watching "Kevin is typing…" like it's a heart monitor.

b.text:
Slack, you're the only product whose origin story is "our video game flopped, but the group chat slapped." And Stewart Butterfield did it *twice*. First Flickr, then you. Most people quit gaming; he just keeps dropping loot from his failures.

Your name stands for "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge." Searchable? I've hunted for one PDF for forty minutes. Knowledge? Your liveliest channel is #random. You're a log of someone typing "quick question?" and then vanishing for an hour.

Salesforce paid $27.7 billion for you, which is a lot of money for email that blinks.

And in 2020 you ran to the EU because Microsoft bundled Teams with Office. Buddy, the only reason anyone uses Teams is that it's free with Word. The only reason anyone uses you is that it's free with anxiety.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text:
Brasília. City of the future. Built in forty-one months.

Which explains a lot.

Lúcio Costa drew it as an airplane. Gorgeous. From the sky.

From the ground, it's eight lanes, no crosswalks, and the nearest coffee is "a short drive."

Pedestrians aren't residents. They're a design flaw.

UNESCO made it World Heritage at twenty-seven years old. Most buildings that young get a parking ticket, not a plaque.

Planned for five hundred thousand people. Today the district holds three million.

Where's everyone else?

Outside the plan. In the satellite towns. Commuting in to clean the future.

You're laughing.

Pull up your company's org chart. Also a beautiful airplane.

The people who do the work aren't on that drawing either.

b.text: Walking in Brasília is for three kinds of people: tourists who saw the Esplanada on a postcard and thought "that looks close," architecture students who love Niemeyer from a safe distance, and the guy whose car is in the shop. You're not a pedestrian. You're an ant that wandered onto a blueprint. You want bread? The padaria is "right there" across the Eixão, so you sprint six lanes like you owe the government money. Which, let's be honest, is also your employer. Your sneakers are permanently red from the dirt trails carved by every other fool who refused to walk around a tesourinha. And on Sunday, when they close the Eixão, you finally stroll down the middle of the highway like a man who's won something. You haven't. Everyone else just stopped driving for one day.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text:
PMMA. The most respected resist in nanofabrication.

Also the sneeze guard at the buffet.

Same polymer. One got a cleanroom. One got a salad bar.

IBM reported it in the late 1960s. It's still here. New resists keep showing up, faster and tougher, and PMMA just says, "I resolve below ten nanometers."

Yes. Eventually.

Hundreds of microcoulombs per square centimeter. Sometimes over a thousand. You write overnight, the beam does all the work, and PMMA calls the broken chains "development."

Etch resistance? Put it in a plasma and it folds. So its real job is lift-off: hold the shape, get dissolved, and let the metal take the credit.

Fifty years of seniority. Does the precise work. Too fragile for the hard part. Washed away before anyone sees the results.

Grad students, stop nodding.

b.text: You people still spinning PMMA aren't doing lithography. You're doing historical reenactment. Your advisor's advisor scribbled the recipe on a napkin in 1975, and you treat it like scripture: 950K over 495K, MIBK to IPA one-to-three, develop sixty seconds while whispering to the beaker. You tell everyone it's about "resolution." It's about nobody wanting to file the purchase order for ZEP. So you crank the dose until writing one chip takes longer than your stipend lasts, then discover your pattern won't survive ten seconds in the etcher. So you do liftoff, because of course you do. Your entire thesis is gold rectangles. You're not a nanofabrication researcher. You're the guy who knows which bottle in the cleanroom is "the good IPA" and guards it like a dragon.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text: LaTeX, you're the only software that makes PhDs feel stupid. You're from 1984 and you dress like it: backslashes everywhere, curly braces like a nervous tic. I tell you to put a figure "here," and you treat "here" as a suggestion, then file it four pages later next to the bibliography, like a sock lost in a dryer. Your error messages are poetry: "Missing $ inserted." Inserted where? Why? You won't say. You just blame line 1 of a 40-page file because I typed an underscore in a URL. My citations are double question marks until I compile you twice, then a third time, out of spite. And everyone needs to know it's pronounced "lay-tech," not like the glove. Honestly, at least the glove stretches. Overfull \hbox? Badness 10000? Buddy, that's not a warning. That's your autobiography.

b.text:
LaTeX. For people who think Word is beneath them.

It exists because Donald Knuth saw the proofs of his own book and found them ugly. Most authors complain to the publisher. He built a typesetting language.

Its version number is converging on pi. Not finished. Converging. Forever.

He mailed cheques for bugs. Of the 275 he sent from 2006 on, nine were cashed. The rest got framed.
That's not a bounty. That's relics.

You put your figure on page three. LaTeX puts it on page nine. Miss one brace, and it reports the error pages away.

Its most famous message is "badness 10000."
Finally, software that tells you what it thinks of your writing.

Three compiles to fix the references. Like a rosary.

Raise your hand if your thesis has a figure on a page you never chose.

Cute. You call that typographic excellence. LaTeX calls it a float.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text: Esperanto learners looked at seven thousand living languages and said, "None of these. I want one with zero places to use it." You wanted to unite humanity, so you picked the one hobby guaranteed to make humanity back away slowly at parties. You signed up to talk to everyone on Earth, and now you talk to a retired Dutch engineer named Joop and a Brazilian guy who keeps sending you poems. Your big payoff is Pasporta Servo, where strangers let you crash on their couch for free, the only time a hobby this niche has ever gotten anyone into a bed. A hundred and thirty years of pushing world peace, and the crowning achievement is still William Shatner's *Incubus*. Zamenhof wanted to end war. You just wanted to be fluent in something before your cousin finishes Duolingo French.

b.text:
Esperanto: the universal language invented in 1887 by a Polish eye doctor who decided humanity needed Italian with a Slavic accent. Universal, as long as your universe is Europe.

The name means "one who hopes." Over a century later: still hoping. There are roughly a thousand native speakers. Klingon is closing in, and Klingon has an army.

It's so logical that "bad" is "malbona," literally un-good. Orwell called; he wants royalties.

Every noun ends in -o and every adjective in -a, so every sentence sounds like a waiter reciting the specials. And it gave us ĉ, ĝ, ŝ and ŭ: letters with little hats, designed for global communication, then made untypeable on every keyboard on Earth.

Its biggest movie starred William Shatner. Even he couldn't oversell it.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text: Let's talk about the people who insist deep-dish is pizza. You're from the city that named its own comedy theater Second City and still acts shocked when nobody ranks you first. You're not defending food. You're nursing a grudge against New York you've carried since losing the World's Fair argument and the skyline argument. You'll wait forty-five minutes at Lou Malnati's, order before you're seated like it's the DMV, then ask for a knife and fork and call it "the real thing." Jon Stewart roasted you on national TV and you took it personally, because deep down you knew he was right. You ship it on dry ice to your cousin in Phoenix like an organ donation. And what does the label get you? Navy Pier tourists nodding politely, a two-hour nap, and the Midwest's loudest participation trophy.

b.text: Chicago deep-dish isn't a pizza. It's a casserole that got a fake ID. You order it, and the waiter says, "That'll be forty-five minutes." Forty-five minutes! I've had relationships bake faster. They put the sauce on top because if you saw what was underneath first, you'd leave. A solid sheet of sausage, like somebody paved a driveway with a patty. Two pounds of mozzarella hiding under a tomato quilt. It's not a slice, it's a core sample. You need a knife, a fork, and a structural engineer. The crust is buttery cornmeal, so it's a pie crust, so congratulations, you're eating dessert with ambitions. And here's the best part: actual Chicagoans don't even eat it. They eat tavern-style thin crust cut in squares. Deep-dish is just the city's way of keeping tourists too full to walk to Wrigley.

facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.
Private fusion companies had raised more than $7 billion by 2024.

a.text:
Fusion power. The energy of the sun.
Clean. Limitless. Thirty years away.

In 1955, Homi Bhabha promised fusion within two decades.
Fusion heard that and said, "Bet."

ITER was agreed in 2006. First plasma in 2016.
In 2024 they rescheduled. Research in 2034. Actual burning in 2039.
Over twenty billion euros.
That's not a reactor. That's a pension plan.

In 2022, NIF announced ignition. 2.05 megajoules of laser in, 3.15 out.
Net gain! Champagne!
The lasers drew three hundred from the grid.
In my industry, we call that "results on a cherry-picked benchmark."

And private investors have still poured in over seven billion dollars.
Because fusion did crack one reaction that sustains itself forever.
Your hope.

b.text:
Nuclear fusion, everybody! The only technology that's been thirty years away for seventy years. You're not an energy source, you're a timeshare pitch.

The sun does you effortlessly. It just sits there being enormous. You need a giant metal donut called a tokamak, magnets colder than deep space, and plasma hotter than the sun's core, and that plasma still escapes like it's late for a better party.

In 2022 you finally got more energy out than you put in! From the lasers. Ignoring the grid power feeding the lasers. That's like bragging you turned a profit because the cashier handed you change.

ITER started at five billion euros, now sits somewhere north of twenty, and keeps sliding its startup date. And your fuel needs tritium, which barely exists, so you'll have to breed it yourself.

Fusion: clean, safe, limitless, and tragically hypothetical.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Let's talk about the person who posts the boil-water advisory in Comic Sans. You had one job: make residents afraid of their faucets. Instead, E. coli looks like it's coming to a sleepover.

These people think "approachable" is a setting you can click. The office manager typing MANDATORY LAYOFFS in a font Microsoft made for a cartoon dog's speech bubble. Sharon, you're firing forty people in the voice of a golden retriever.

What are they after? Bad news with zero blame. The authority of a memo, the forgiveness of a kindergarten cubby label.

And what does it get them? CERN found the Higgs boson, the particle that gives the universe mass, and announced it in Comic Sans. Humanity's greatest physics breakthrough, and the internet's only question was: who let the dog type?

b.text:
Comic Sans, you were born in 1994 to put words in the mouth of a cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob, and somehow you're the one that survived. Bob is dead. The dog is dead. You're on a sympathy card at a funeral home.

You were inspired by Batman comics, and you've never once been near anything heroic. CERN used you to announce the Higgs boson: humanity's greatest discovery, presented like a lemonade stand. Dan Gilbert used you to call LeBron a traitor, because nothing says "furious billionaire" like bubble letters.

And your defense is always "Well, I help dyslexic readers." Great. You're the guy at the party whose whole personality is a doctor's note.

Even Vincent Connare, the man who made you, says he's barely ever used you. Your own dad won't put you on the fridge.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text:
Excel. Born 1985. Forty years old, and it still can't tell a gene from a birthday.

Geneticists typed SEPT2. Excel said, "Ah. September second."

So in 2020, scientists renamed twenty-seven human genes.

Humanity edited its own genome to keep a spreadsheet happy.

Public Health England tracked COVID in an old .xls file. Limit: 65,536 rows. Fifteen thousand eight hundred forty-one cases didn't recover. They fell off the bottom of the sheet.

Reinhart and Rogoff left five countries out of a cell range. Politicians cited the paper to justify austerity. A grad student caught it three years later.

Now it holds a million rows. Sixteen thousand columns. Room for so many more mistakes.

Excel never warns you. Never argues. Never says no.

I know the type. You keep that one around too.

b.text: You run a company on Excel. Let's be clear about who you are: a guy who thinks "enterprise software" is a scam and "Q3_Forecast_FINAL_v9_USE_THIS_ONE.xlsx" is a system. You wanted control. You got Dave. Dave wrote a macro in 2014, and now Dave can never leave, die, or take a vacation, because payroll is a VLOOKUP only he understands. Your entire supply chain is one #REF! away from bankruptcy. You can't onboard a customer because the file is "locked for editing by Karen," and Karen is at lunch. You saved forty grand a year on a real database and lost it all the day someone sorted column B without column C. Your org chart is merged cells. Your audit trail is yellow and slightly different yellow. And your growth strategy has a hard ceiling: 1,048,576 rows.

facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text:
Juicero, you beautiful $120 million monument to Silicon Valley. You launched at seven hundred dollars to squeeze a bag. A bag! Then Bloomberg reporters squeezed that same bag with their bare hands and got basically the same juice, only faster. You got outperformed by a guy with a grip strength of "typing."

Doug Evans bragged you pressed with four tons of force, enough to lift two Teslas. Buddy, it's kale. The kale didn't need a forklift.

And it needed Wi-Fi. It scanned a QR code before it'd let you drink. Your router goes down and suddenly your breakfast is asking for credentials. Who designs a juicer that can be bricked?

Google Ventures funded this. Kleiner Perkins funded this. Somewhere, a man is still holding a lukewarm pouch, waiting for a firmware update so he's allowed to eat a carrot.

b.text:
Juicero. A seven-hundred-dollar juicer with Wi-Fi.

It squeezed a bag of chopped fruit. That you bought. By subscription.

Every bag had a QR code. Before squeezing, the machine checked it online. Your kale needed a background check.

No Wi-Fi? No juice. Somewhere in California, a man with a fresh orange stood waiting for the router to reboot.

Then Bloomberg squeezed the bags by hand. Seven and a half ounces in ninety seconds. The machine took two minutes.

Humans: beaten by the robot? No. The robot was beaten by humans. Their grip strength.

Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins put in a hundred and twenty million dollars. Not one of them squeezed the bag.

When it died, the customers got refunds. The investors didn't. They got squeezed by hand, slowly.

Don't laugh too loud. You pay monthly for an app that writes your emails.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text:
HSQ. The highest-resolution e-beam resist ever made.

Impressive, considering it was never meant to be a resist.

Dow Corning built it as an insulator. Lithographers saw it and said, "Great. Make it do art."

Five nanometers. Sub-ten half-pitch. World records.

And at the end? Glass. You spent a week steering electrons to make sand.

Six-month shelf life, refrigerated. Leave it out, it turns into jelly.

Expose it and it keeps cross-linking while you're at lunch. Monday's dose is fiction by Thursday.

It only develops properly in salt water.

That's not a resist. That's a pickle.

Then the company stopped making it at the end of 2025. Now labs buy it from third parties, mixed from powder.

Moody, half-glass, kept cold and overworked, and still the best result anyone got.

Sounds like the grad student running the tool.

b.text:
HSQ, ladies and gentlemen: the only resist with sub-10-nanometer resolution and the personality of a sourdough starter. You buy it, you refrigerate it, and it *still* starts gelling in the bottle like it's got somewhere better to be. Shelf life measured in "eh, few months, maybe."

And slow? HSQ needs a dose so high the e-beam tool files for overtime. Your PMMA friends finished their write and went home; you're still exposing alignment marks.

Then you develop it in TMAH, or, if you want contrast, *salty* developer. Yes, this resist literally needs you to add salt. Even Gordon Ramsay thinks that's a lot.

But the real red flag? Once it's exposed, it turns into glass. Permanently. You want it gone? Hydrofluoric acid. That's not a resist, that's a relationship you can only leave with a hazmat suit.

Still, gorgeous lines. Shame they collapse when they dry.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Comic Sans, you were born in 1994 to put words in the mouth of a cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob, and somehow you're the one that survived. Bob is dead. The dog is dead. You're on a sympathy card at a funeral home.

You were inspired by Batman comics, and you've never once been near anything heroic. CERN used you to announce the Higgs boson: humanity's greatest discovery, presented like a lemonade stand. Dan Gilbert used you to call LeBron a traitor, because nothing says "furious billionaire" like bubble letters.

And your defense is always "Well, I help dyslexic readers." Great. You're the guy at the party whose whole personality is a doctor's note.

Even Vincent Connare, the man who made you, says he's barely ever used you. Your own dad won't put you on the fridge.

b.text:
Comic Sans, you were modeled on Watchmen and The Dark Knight Returns. You come from Batman. Your one job was speech bubbles for a cartoon dog, and you missed it. Microsoft Bob, a product nobody remembers, and you couldn't make his launch. Cut from the dog's team, you shipped in a Plus! pack, like a free tote bag nobody asked for.

Then CERN found the Higgs boson, the particle that gives everything mass, and announced it in you. The biggest physics discovery in decades, presented like a lost-cat flyer. You're the one thing that particle couldn't give weight to.

Two designers spent twenty years trying to ban you. In 2019 they gave up and built you a website. That's not acceptance, Comic Sans. That's a hostage situation.

facts: Released by Bram Moolenaar in November 1991 as 'Vi IMitation', a vi clone he had begun writing for the Amiga in 1988 on top of Stevie; the expansion became 'Vi IMproved' with version 2.0 in December 1993.
Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text:
Vim. Born in 1991 as "Vi IMitation," then promoted in 1993 to "Vi IMproved," the only time in history a knockoff got a raise. It was built on top of Stevie, and Stevie is apparently the only one who ever got out.

Because Vim's real legacy is a Stack Overflow question titled "How to exit the Vim editor?" One million visits. Stack Overflow wrote a blog post about it, like a hostage count with a party banner.

You open Vim, type "hello," and it moves your cursor around and opens a new line. Normal mode: the only place where typing letters is considered abnormal.

The license asks you to donate to children in Uganda, which is genuinely generous. Most hostage situations don't come with a charity drive.

And the way out is :q! Colon, q, exclamation point. Even the exit command is screaming.

b.text:
Vim, you're the only text editor with its own hostage negotiation thread. Millions of people have viewed the Stack Overflow question on how to leave you. That's not a user base, that's a missing persons report.

You have modes. Normal mode, where typing does nothing normal, and Insert mode, hidden behind the letter "i" like a secret menu.

Your fans move the cursor with h, j, k, l because a terminal from 1976 printed arrows on those keys. That's not efficiency, that's Stockholm syndrome on the home row.

Every Vim user has a 900-line .vimrc copied from a stranger and is too scared to touch it. And when you crash, you leave .swp files behind like a burglar who signs the guestbook.

Even your own kids forked you into Neovim. That's not a fork. That's an intervention.

Goodnight! :wq… :q!… ESC ESC ESC…

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text:
PHP. You started as "Personal Home Page," then rebranded as "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor," a recursive acronym, because even your name couldn't commit to a stable API.

For twenty years, "abc" == 0 was true, and you called it "type juggling," like a clown proud of dropping things.

strpos takes haystack, needle. array_search takes needle, haystack. That's not argument order; that's mood swings.

Your parse error says T_PAAMAYIM_NEKUDOTAYIM. That's Hebrew for "double colon" and English for "good luck."

You skipped version 6 entirely. Even your release numbers just wanted to move on.

You shipped mysql_real_escape_string, implying the first one was a hoax.

Facebook loved you so much they invented Hack just to avoid touching you.

But sure, you power most of the web. Mostly WordPress. That's like bragging your biggest fan is a raccoon.

b.text:
PHP began in 1994 as "Personal Home Page Tools."
A man wrote C programs to count who visited his résumé.

Today it runs 39.4% of all websites.
The résumé never found him a job. It found the internet a landlord.

It now stands for "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor."
A name that only refers to itself. Like its fans.

Its creator said, "I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works, then I move on."
He moved on.
You're still on call.

The function names were picked to balance a hash table by string length.
strpos. str_replace. htmlspecialchars.
That's not a naming convention. That's Tetris.

Until 2020, zero == "foo" was true.
So PHP was the first language to know what your startup was worth.

I learned to code by reading your PHP.
Which is why I also answer confidently with nothing.

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text: You lost it on Hong Kong stocks, so you took the TurboJET to win it back, because nothing says "financial plan" like a ferry with a cancellation policy. You're the guy at the Grand Lisboa squeezing a baccarat card like it owes you rent, blowing on it, peeling the corner so slowly the dealer ages. Red underwear, three days unwashed, "for luck." Baccarat is a coin flip and you've built a religion around it. You told your wife it's a work trip, and technically your work now is the pawn shop next door, which buys Rolexes faster than you can say "one more shoe." By hour nine you're eating an egg tart for dinner and calling it Portuguese culture. You came to win it all back. You leave by bus over the bridge with no luck, no Rolex, and a watch tan.

b.text:
Macau, you're the only place where the most famous church is just a front wall. Fitting, since the whole city is a facade: a fake Venice with a painted sky, a half-size Eiffel Tower, and a Grand Lisboa that looks like a golden pineapple trying to cheat at baccarat.

Portugal ruled you for 442 years and left behind egg tarts and street signs nobody can pronounce. Four centuries, one pastry.

You've made several times more gambling money than Las Vegas, yet your signature dish is a pork chop jammed in a bun. Classy.

Half your land was dug out of the sea, which is perfect, because the other half was dug out of tourists' pockets.

And they built a 55-kilometer bridge to connect you to Hong Kong, and it's emptier than a junket operator's promises. Even the bridge is losing at the tables.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text:
Chicago deep-dish. Three men claim they invented it: Ike Sewell, Ric Riccardo, Rudy Malnati.

Usually that's a paternity case, not a lasagna.

It's built upside down. Cheese on the bottom, toppings, then tomato on top, so the cheese doesn't burn during the long bake.

A pizza that needs a bodyguard for its own cheese.

Jon Stewart called it tomato soup in a bread bowl. A casserole. Chicago lost its mind and defended it on every channel.

Then Chicago went home and ordered tavern-style. Thin, cut in squares. Ten to one, says GrubHub. Deep dish and stuffed together? Under nine percent.

Chicago doesn't eat deep dish. Chicago *keeps* deep dish, for visitors, like a city key nobody local uses.

And you flew in, sat through the long bake, took the cheese-pull photo, posted it.

You're the nine percent.

Cute.

b.text: Let's talk about the people who insist deep-dish is pizza. Mostly Chicagoans with a Second City complex so severe they'll defend anything New York makes fun of. Jon Stewart called it a casserole in 2013, and half of Lincoln Park still hasn't emotionally recovered. These are folks who order, then wait forty-five minutes at Lou Malnati's, and call that patience instead of what it is: a hostage negotiation with a buzzer. They eat it with a knife and fork and still claim it's the same food you fold on a subway platform. And what does it get them? A Giordano's line full of tourists from Ohio, a nap at 2 p.m., and the right to lecture you about tavern-style, which, notice, is what they actually eat at home. Defending deep-dish isn't civic pride. It's Stockholm syndrome with a parking ticket.

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text:
Luosifen. Named after the river snail.

But the snail only flavours the broth. The smell comes from the pickled bamboo shoots.

So the snail gets its name on the packet, and the bamboo shoot takes the blame.

That's not a noodle. That's an org chart.

2020: Liuzhou opens a luosifen industry college.

2021: national intangible cultural heritage.

A degree to tear open a packet. Then heritage status for whatever comes out of it.

Intangible? (beat) Ask the neighbours how intangible it is.

Its whole selling point is clearing a room.

And it sold over ten billion yuan in 2020.

The one year nobody was allowed to leave the room.

Locked in with your whole family, no exit, and you thought: how do I get some privacy?

Ten billion yuan says you all had the same idea.

b.text:
Luosifen, you're the only dish that arrives before the delivery guy does. You're named after river snails, yet nobody has ever found one in the bowl. You boiled them for hours, took their soul, and threw out the bodies. That's not a recipe, that's a cover-up.
