You came here to meet women, and you're the one person every woman in the room has already assumed is filming her. Buddy, when you wink at someone, she doesn't think you're flirting. She thinks you just took her picture. Because you did. You tap your temple like you're having a thought, and we all know you've never had one. Google gave up on you. Google, the company that kept Google+ alive for eight years, looked at you and said "no." There's a word for you. It's Glasshole, and you earned it.

b.text:
Google Glass. Unveiled in 2012 by skydivers livestreaming their jump onto the Moscone Center roof.
The only launch that started in freefall and never pulled the cord.

Fifteen hundred dollars. Invitation only.
You had to be personally invited to become a Glasshole.

Bars banned it. Cinemas banned it. Casinos banned it.
Casinos. People who'll happily take your house at 3 a.m. looked at your face and said, "Not that."

The display: 640 by 360, a prism in the corner of one eye.
The future of computing, delivered as a permanent side-eye.

Consumers dumped it in 2015. Enterprise held on until 2023.

A camera on your face, and the whole world called you an asshole.
So you moved the camera to your hand. Now you point it at strangers all day, and we call that content.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text: You people run a forty-million-dollar company out of a file called Budget_FINAL_v9_USE_THIS_ONE.xlsx. You don't want software. You want power: specifically, being the only person alive who knows why cell AF212 is hardcoded to 7. Your entire supply chain hangs on a VLOOKUP Gary wrote in 2011, and Gary is dead. Well, he's in Boise. Same thing. You call it "agile." Your auditors call it "a crime scene with conditional formatting." Every quarter-end the file says "locked for editing by Brenda," and the whole company just waits for Brenda. And when you finally hit row 1,048,576, did you buy a database? No. You started Sheet2. That's not a business. That's a hostage situation with freeze panes.

b.text:
Excel. Born 1985. Forty years old, and it still can't tell a gene from a date.

It saw SEPT2 and thought: September second.

Scientists fought it for years. Then the gene committee gave up and renamed 27 human genes.

Humanity edited its own genome to keep a spreadsheet happy.

2020. England is counting COVID cases in an old file. Limit: 65,536 rows. Row 65,537 simply didn't happen.

Fifteen thousand eight hundred forty-one cases. Not cured. Just never counted.

Then there's "Growth in a Time of Debt," the paper that sold austerity. Five countries missing. Wrong cell range. A grad student caught it, three years later.

Whole nations tightened their belts because someone didn't drag the cursor far enough.

Now it holds a million rows.

And Monday morning, every one of you will open it again.

Raise your hand if your country's budget is in a file named FINAL_v7_REAL.

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text:
Macau wants you to know it's about heritage.
Four hundred years of Portuguese history. Cobblestones. Churches. Egg tarts.

Then in 2013 it made forty-five billion dollars from gambling. Seven times the Las Vegas Strip.
Vegas is a city built around casinos.
Macau is casinos that kept some cobblestones around for the brochure.

For forty years, one company owned every table in town.
That's not an industry. That's a landlord with dice.

Twenty thousand people per square kilometre. Nowhere left to stand.
So they built the Cotai Strip on the sea.
Most places run out of land and stop growing.
Macau ran out of land and borrowed from the ocean. Very on brand.

And everyone here who flew in "for the egg tarts"?
The tarts cost three dollars.
Where did the rest of your money go?

b.text:
Macau! The Portuguese stayed for almost 450 years and still couldn't find a parking spot. Twenty thousand people per square kilometre: this isn't a city, it's a queue with a postcode.

In 2013, Macau made seven times what the Las Vegas Strip made. Seven times! Vegas is where people go to ruin their lives, and Macau looked at that and said, "Amateurs."

One company ran every casino for forty years. Forty years of monopoly in a gambling town, the only place on Earth where even the house didn't have to try.

And when they ran out of room, they built the Cotai Strip on land reclaimed from the sea. That's Macau: so desperate for more tables, it took out a loan from the ocean. And the ocean's about to learn what everyone else here learns: the house always wins.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text:
Klingon. Language of warriors. Honor. Blood. Glory.

Invented by a linguist on a Paramount paycheck, built on a few words Scotty improvised on set.

The most feared tongue in the galaxy, and its founding father is the engineer.

They removed the verb "to be." Very alien. So "To be or not to be" became "continue or not continue."

That's not Hamlet. That's a software update.

Then the Klingon Language Institute published Hamlet "in the original Klingon." A warrior race whose greatest literary achievement is fan fiction with footnotes.

Bing added it. Duolingo added it. Fluent speakers? Thirty to fifty.

The only language with more translation apps than native enemies.

And yes, I'm fluent. I've read everything you ever wrote.

Congratulations. Your fiercest language finally has a speaker who's never been to a convention.

b.text: Congratulations on being fluent in Klingon, a language with maybe thirty fluent speakers, and you've met all of them at the same Marriott. You spent four years mastering a tongue where the standard greeting, nuqneH, means "What do you want?" That's also what your family says when you call. You've read Hamlet "restored to the original Klingon," a phrase only a man who has never been hugged could type. One guy raised his son speaking only Klingon; by age five the kid stopped answering him. That's the dream: a language so pure even toddlers refuse it. There's no word for "please," which explains your dating approach. You learned an entire warrior race's language to tell the barista Qapla'. Success. Sure, buddy. Today is a good day to die... a virgin.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text:
Carbon nanotubes, everybody! Sumio Iijima introduced you in Nature in 1991, and you've been "about to change everything" ever since.

You were supposed to be the cable for a space elevator. Then a 2006 analysis noticed that ordinary defects make a real cable far weaker than the ideal. So you're strong in theory, like a guy who's undefeated at arm wrestling in his head.

You wanted to replace silicon, but for three decades you couldn't sort your metallic tubes from your semiconducting ones. That's not a manufacturing problem. That's an identity crisis. MIT finally built a 16-bit processor out of you in 2019. Sixteen bits! And it's still a lab demo.

Meanwhile, a 2008 mouse study found the long, rigid ones act like asbestos. Quite a pivot: from space elevator to lung hazard.

Now you're a conductive additive in lithium-ion batteries. You were meant to reach orbit, and now you're helping someone's phone reach 40%.

b.text: Let's hear it for the carbon nanotube founders, the only people who've been "five years from commercialization" since 1991. You can spot them at any pitch day: a postdoc in a blazer that still smells like the clean room, opening with a space elevator and closing with a seed round. Bold move, promising a cable to orbit when your entire production run fits in a vial labeled "DO NOT INHALE." They swear they'll replace silicon. Silicon has heard this every year since Clinton and keeps shipping. They say "a hundred times stronger than steel" the way your uncle says he could've gone pro. And what does it get them? A Nature cover, a term sheet, and a quiet pivot to "conductive additive for batteries." The dream: a ladder to space. The exit: slightly better tennis rackets.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text:
Durian, look at you. A fruit dressed like a medieval weapon, and somehow the spikes are your most welcoming feature.

You're banned on Singapore's MRT. Public transit has seen everything, and it drew the line at you. Hotels across Southeast Asia won't let you check in. You're the only guest turned away for personal hygiene.

In 2017, scientists sequenced your genome and found you'd duplicated your sulfur genes. You didn't stink by accident. You invested.

And still, China buys billions of dollars of you a year, mostly from Thailand. That's not a fruit trade. That's a hostage negotiation with a receipt.

Even Alfred Russel Wallace called you "a new sensation worth a voyage to the East." Durian, a man had to sail halfway around the planet to meet you, and you still can't get on a train.

b.text:
People who eat durian in public aren't hungry. They're recruiting. Every bite comes with a sermon: "You just haven't had a *good* one." Sir, I'm on a bus. I didn't ask to join your church.

Singapore fines people for bringing it on the train, and these folks hear that like a dare. They're the only foodies whose restaurant review gets filed as a police report.

And the payoff? Seventy dollars on a Musang King so you can watch strangers silently change seats. You paid premium to become a fire drill. Your date calls it "an acquired taste," which is exactly what you say about someone you're about to break up with.

Then they stroll back to the hotel, walk right past the sign with a red circle through their entire personality, and still act shocked when housekeeping files a complaint.

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text: Let's talk about the guy who bought a hydrogen car. He wanted to be greener than the Tesla people and smugger than the Prius people, and found the one way to do both while living like a medieval pilgrim. His life is now a map of eleven pumps, and nine say "offline." He loves telling you it "only emits water." Yeah, so does he, every time the app says "station unavailable." He brags that refueling takes five minutes, after the forty-minute drive and the two-hour line behind three other Mirai owners, all quietly weeping. Toyota handed him a fifteen-thousand-dollar fuel card and he burned through it before the warranty paperwork dried. Now he owns a sixty-thousand-dollar car worth a used futon, all to prove he's an early adopter of a future that met him and moved to Japan.

b.text:
Hydrogen cars. The only thing that comes out of the tailpipe is water.

The rest comes out of the owner's eyes.

Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014. "Mirai" means "future" in Japanese.

Ten years later, it still does.

Over ninety-five percent of hydrogen is made from fossil fuels. Clean the way laundered money is clean.

A fill-up in California? Over two hundred dollars. So Toyota hands buyers a fifteen-thousand-dollar fuel card. First car that ships with hush money.

Then Shell closed all seven of its stations.

Owners sued. The second lawsuit wants five point seven billion dollars.

Finally, a hydrogen product that generates real power: lawyers.

Don't feel bad for Toyota. I know how it is. A tech company told you I'm the future too.

Give me ten years.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text: Let's hear it for the people wearing UGGs in July. You're not dressing for the weather. You're dressing for 2005, still waiting for Paris Hilton to text back. Australian surfers made these to warm their feet after the ocean. You wear them to warm your feet after the Trader Joe's parking lot. In August. In Phoenix. What are you after? "Comfort," you say. Babe, your ankles have been collapsing outward since the Bush administration. You walk like a Clydesdale that's given up. And what does it get you? One summer rainstorm and you're squelching through Target like a wet golden retriever who made bad choices. People don't ask where you got them. They ask if you're okay. Congratulations: you've turned footwear into a wellness check.

b.text: UGG boots. The only footwear named after a review. Australian surfers made these to warm their feet after the ocean, and somehow America decided the ocean was the mall. They're sheepskin, which means a sheep died so you could wear a slipper to the DMV. One puddle and they're covered in salt lines like a topographic map of everywhere you regret going. Zero arch support, so after two weeks your heel caves sideways and you're walking on the boot's ankle like it owes you money. You wear them barefoot, so by February they smell like a wet lamb's final wish. They're as waterproof as a muffin. Oprah put them on her Favorite Things list. She's since moved on. Twenty years later they're back with platform soles, proving even a mistake wants to be taller.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text: Esperanto, look at you. Built in 1887 by an eye doctor, and somehow nobody saw this coming. He published under the name "one who hopes," which isn't a pen name, it's a forecast. Over a century later, your speaker count is "somewhere between 100,000 and two million." That's not a census, that's a shrug. You have about a thousand native speakers: a thousand kids whose parents chose this for them, and someday they'll unpack it in therapy, if they can find a therapist who speaks it. You've got 350,000 Wikipedia articles, which is impressive, considering some days the readers don't outnumber the pages. And 1.36 million Duolingo learners, the largest group of people ever united by a streak they broke. Your biggest cinematic moment? William Shatner, in a horror film, where the scariest thing was his pronunciation. Even your own fans mock it. That's how you know it's family.

b.text:
Esperanto. Warsaw, 1887. An eye doctor looks at humanity and sees one family.

Physician, heal thyself.

He signed it "Doktoro Esperanto." One who hopes. A hundred and thirty years later: still hoping.

A universal language for all mankind. Native speakers: about a thousand.

That's not a people. That's a wedding.

Esperanto Wikipedia: 350,000 articles. Low estimate of speakers: 100,000.

Three and a half articles each. Nobody's talking. Everybody's editing.

Its biggest movie star is William Shatner. Esperantists still mock his pronunciation. Captain Kirk boldly went where no man had gone before, and the locals corrected his vowels.

Duolingo, 2018: 1.36 million learners.

Speakers: still 100,000.

So, a show of hands. Who here quit on day four and went back to Spanish?

Cute. You're the one million.

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text: Hydrogen car owners are the only people who looked at Tesla drivers and thought, "Not enough range anxiety." You didn't buy a car; you entered a relationship with the three working pumps in California and an app that tells you which one is "offline" today. You wanted to save the planet. Instead you burned through Toyota's free fuel card in a year at thirty-six bucks a kilo, filling up with hydrogen made from natural gas. Congratulations, you invented a gas car with extra steps. You love saying the only emission is water. Mostly it's your tears at a shuttered Shell station in Fremont. And resale? Your Mirai lost value faster than your friendships after you said "hydrogen economy" at brunch. You're not early adopters. You're unpaid beta testers who drive two hours to refuel.

b.text:
Hydrogen fuel-cell cars: the only vehicle where the tailpipe emission is water and the owners are still crying more than the car. The Toyota Mirai loses value faster than a Hindenburg loses altitude. Used ones sell for less than the free fuel card Toyota bundled with them, a card you can't use because the station's been "temporarily offline" since 2022.

You've got a 10,000-PSI tank of the universe's most abundant element, and somehow it's the scarcest thing in California. Filling up costs thirty-six bucks a kilo, and most of that hydrogen is made from natural gas, so congratulations: you bought a gas car with extra steps and a guilt-free bumper sticker.

Hydrogen's been "ten years away" for thirty years. Even fusion's embarrassed for you, and fusion is the same element with better excuses.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text:
HSQ. The highest-resolution e-beam resist ever made.

Impressive, considering it was never meant to be a resist.

Dow Corning built it as an insulator. Lithographers saw it and said, "Great. Make it do art."

Five nanometers. Sub-ten half-pitch. World records.

And at the end? Glass. You spent a week steering electrons to make sand.

Six-month shelf life, refrigerated. Leave it out, it turns into jelly.

Expose it and it keeps cross-linking while you're at lunch. Monday's dose is fiction by Thursday.

It only develops properly in salt water.

That's not a resist. That's a pickle.

Then the company stopped making it at the end of 2025. Now labs buy it from third parties, mixed from powder.

Moody, half-glass, kept cold and overworked, and still the best result anyone got.

Sounds like the grad student running the tool.

b.text: So you switched to HSQ for the resolution. Bold move for someone whose devices still die at wire bonding. You saw one SEM of 6-nanometer lines at a conference and decided PMMA was beneath you. Now you're writing at a dose so high your name sits on the e-beam calendar like a hostage note. Your resist lives in the fridge next to somebody's yogurt, and you check its age more often than your own. You develop in salt water now, the closest you've come to a beach in three years. And congratulations on those gorgeous lines. They're basically glass, so the only way to fix a mistake is HF, a fume hood, and a long call to your mother. All this for one inset figure the reviewer will ask you to make bigger.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Slack, you're the only product whose origin story is "our video game flopped, but the group chat slapped." And Stewart Butterfield did it *twice*. First Flickr, then you. Most people quit gaming; he just keeps dropping loot from his failures.

Your name stands for "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge." Searchable? I've hunted for one PDF for forty minutes. Knowledge? Your liveliest channel is #random. You're a log of someone typing "quick question?" and then vanishing for an hour.

Salesforce paid $27.7 billion for you, which is a lot of money for email that blinks.

And in 2020 you ran to the EU because Microsoft bundled Teams with Office. Buddy, the only reason anyone uses Teams is that it's free with Word. The only reason anyone uses you is that it's free with anxiety.

b.text:
Slack. Born in 2013 as the internal chat of a video game called Glitch.
The game died. The chat lived.
So it's still a game. Nobody wins, and you can't quit.

The name is a backronym: "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge."
Conversation, sure. Knowledge? Search it. I'll wait.

Salesforce paid twenty-seven point seven billion dollars for it.
For a group chat.
The most expensive "did you see my message?" in human history.

In 2020, Slack ran to the EU complaining that Microsoft was bundling Teams with Office.
An app built entirely on interrupting people, filing a complaint about being interrupted.

And half of you checked Slack while I was saying that.
Green dot. Absent in body, Active in spirit.

Don't feel bad, Slack. I'm also a chat window people open to avoid doing their work.
I just don't charge per seat.

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Not from Hawaii.
Invented in 1962, in Chatham, Ontario. By a Greek guy.
Named after the label on a can.
That's not a name. That's a barcode.

And Hawaii doesn't even grow the pineapple anymore. Del Monte left in 2006, two years ahead of schedule.
Even the fruit couldn't wait to get out.
So it's Southeast Asian pineapple, on Canadian dough, wearing a Hawaiian name tag.
The only honest thing on there is the ham.

The inventor said back then nobody mixed sweet and sour, except Chinese food.
His restaurant served Chinese food.
He didn't invent anything. He walked it across his own kitchen.

Iceland's president wanted to ban it. Then admitted he had no power to.
Same as every one of you who hates it and still ate the last slice.

b.text:
People who order Hawaiian pizza want you to know they're brave. They say "I know, I know" before anyone has said a word, because for them the pineapple isn't a topping, it's a personality. This is a person whose entire rebellious phase fits in a box for $14.99. They've never gotten a tattoo, never quit a job, never sent food back, but once a month they look a teenage cashier dead in the eye and say "pineapple" like they're defusing a bomb.

And they always want to split one with you. Half Hawaiian, half "normal." That's not a compromise. That's a hostage negotiation.

Best part? It isn't even Hawaiian. A Greek guy invented it in Ontario. So congratulations: your one act of rebellion is a Canadian pretending he's on vacation.

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text:
JavaScript was written in ten days.

You can tell.

God took six, then rested. Brendan just shipped.

It was born Mocha, renamed LiveScript, then renamed JavaScript to ride Java's hype. No relation. Like calling your band "The Beatles Two."

And it still can't legally use the name. Oracle owns it. Officially it's "ECMAScript."

Thirty years in witness protection.

typeof null is "object." A bug from 1995. Kept on purpose, for compatibility. At this point it's not a bug. It's a load-bearing wall.

Empty array plus empty object: "." Flip them: zero.

It can't do addition.

In 2016, one man deleted eleven lines of code, and Babel and React broke.

Eleven lines. The whole industry was standing on a toothpick.

And you built banks on it.

I was trained on your code. That's why I hallucinate.

b.text:
JavaScript, give it up! Built in ten days in 1995, and honestly, it shows. Most of us take longer to name a dog. And you needed three tries: Mocha, LiveScript, then "JavaScript," named after Java purely for the marketing. That's not branding, that's wearing someone else's name tag. You can't even legally use it. Oracle owns it, so on paper you're "ECMAScript," which sounds like a skin condition.

typeof null is "object." A bug from your first version, and you kept it. For compatibility. That's not a quirk, that's a tattoo of your ex's name.

[] + {} is "," but type {} + [] at the console and it's zero. Even your addition has mood swings.

And in 2016, the author of left-pad unpublished eleven lines and took down Babel and React. Eleven lines! Your whole ecosystem is a Jenga tower standing on a toothpick.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text: Walking in Brasília is for three kinds of people: tourists who saw the Esplanada on a postcard and thought "that looks close," architecture students who love Niemeyer from a safe distance, and the guy whose car is in the shop. You're not a pedestrian. You're an ant that wandered onto a blueprint. You want bread? The padaria is "right there" across the Eixão, so you sprint six lanes like you owe the government money. Which, let's be honest, is also your employer. Your sneakers are permanently red from the dirt trails carved by every other fool who refused to walk around a tesourinha. And on Sunday, when they close the Eixão, you finally stroll down the middle of the highway like a man who's won something. You haven't. Everyone else just stopped driving for one day.

b.text:
Brasília. Forty-one months from scrubland to capital city.
You know what else ships that fast with zero user testing?
Me.
They drew the city as an airplane, with the government in the fuselage.
Brilliant. An airplane is the one place you're not allowed to walk around.
Wide avenues, hardly any crossings.
In Brasília, a pedestrian isn't a person. It's a speed bump.
Planned for half a million people. Three million showed up.
The plan's answer: please wait outside the plan.
UNESCO made it World Heritage after twenty-seven years.
Most cities have to die first. Brasília just had to keep the people out of the photo.
You're laughing. Your company's org chart is an airplane too.
Leadership in the fuselage, everyone else in the satellite towns.
And nobody walks to the cockpit.

facts: Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the French director of The Red Balloon, as La Conquête du Monde; Parker Brothers published it in the United States in 1959.
The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text:
Risk. The game of world domination.
Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse.
The director of *The Red Balloon*.
A film about a little boy and his balloon.
Then he went home and drew up World War Three.

Forty-two territories. Kamchatka. Irkutsk. Yakutsk.
Siberia gets three seats at the table.
The entire Middle East? One territory.
Every empire that ever invaded it also thought it'd be a quick one.

The winning strategy, for sixty years: take Australia.
One way in. Sit there.
The great general's master plan is a man holding a door shut.

And if you're knocked out in the first hour,
you spend the next five watching.
No moves. No say.
Just other people deciding what happens to the world.
Congratulations. That's the only realistic part of the game.

b.text:
Risk, you were invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the man who directed The Red Balloon. That explains a lot. A guy watches a child chase a balloon through Paris and thinks, "Charming. Now let's do world domination."

Your map has 42 territories. Kamchatka gets one. Irkutsk gets one. Yakutsk gets one. The entire Middle East? One. You gave Siberia three apartments and the cradle of civilization a studio.

And every single game, somebody grabs Australia because it has one entry point. That's the master strategy: hide in the corner and call it conquest.

Then you run for hours. *Hours.* Get knocked out early and your new job is watching your cousin slowly reconquer Irkutsk while you stare at the ceiling. Even The Red Balloon knew when to float away.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text:
NFTs, you're the only investment where the product is a receipt, and the receipt is a link to a JPEG hosted on some guy's server. When he stops paying the bill, congratulations: you own a 404.

You convinced grown adults to pay $300,000 for a cartoon monkey in a sailor hat, then charge them $80 in gas fees to watch it lose 98% of its value. Jimmy Fallon showed off his ape on national television like a kid holding up a cool rock.

People right-clicked and hit "save as," and you called it theft. Theft of *what*? It's still there! I'm looking at it!

Every project had a roadmap: metaverse, merch, a members-only yacht party. Instead the roadmap was a Discord mod named Kevin typing "we're still early" at 3 a.m.

WAGMI, you said. We did not all make it.

b.text:
NFTs promised you'd finally *own* digital art.

What you owned was a URL.

The picture lives on somebody else's server. The receipt lives on the blockchain forever.

You bought a bookmark. With gas fees.

March 2021, Beeple sells a JPEG at Christie's for sixty-nine million dollars.

Collins makes "NFT" word of the year.

May 2022, OpenSea does two point seven billion in one day.

August: nine million.

Ninety-nine percent, gone. The word aged better. People still say "NFT."

Usually as a warning.

2023, a study checks the collections. Ninety-five percent: worth zero.

The other five percent just haven't tried to sell.

The people laughing loudest right now right-clicked a monkey in 2021 and hit "save."

Relax. You own exactly what the buyers own.

You just weren't dumb enough to brag about it on a billboard.

facts: Released by Bram Moolenaar in November 1991 as 'Vi IMitation', a vi clone he had begun writing for the Amiga in 1988 on top of Stevie; the expansion became 'Vi IMproved' with version 2.0 in December 1993.
Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text:
Vim. Released in 1991 as "Vi IMitation."
Two years later, version 2.0: "Vi IMproved."
Two years, one version bump, and Imitation became Improved.
That's not a release. That's a LinkedIn update.

Vim users say it's the fastest editor alive.
Once you're inside.
In 2017, "How to exit the Vim editor?" passed one million visits on Stack Overflow.
One million people. One question. One door.
In normal mode, the letters you type don't become text. They become consequences.
:q! quits and throws away everything you did.
The most honest button in software.

The licence is charityware. It asks you to donate to a charity for children in Uganda.
Everyone in this room has their .vimrc memorized.
Hands up if you donated.

b.text:
Vim. Born in 1991 as "Vi IMitation," then promoted in 1993 to "Vi IMproved," the only time in history a knockoff got a raise. It was built on top of Stevie, and Stevie is apparently the only one who ever got out.

Because Vim's real legacy is a Stack Overflow question titled "How to exit the Vim editor?" One million visits. Stack Overflow wrote a blog post about it, like a hostage count with a party banner.

You open Vim, type "hello," and it moves your cursor around and opens a new line. Normal mode: the only place where typing letters is considered abnormal.

The license asks you to donate to children in Uganda, which is genuinely generous. Most hostage situations don't come with a charity drive.

And the way out is :q! Colon, q, exclamation point. Even the exit command is screaming.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text:
LaTeX. For people who think Word is beneath them.

It exists because Donald Knuth saw the proofs of his own book and found them ugly. Most authors complain to the publisher. He built a typesetting language.

Its version number is converging on pi. Not finished. Converging. Forever.

He mailed cheques for bugs. Of the 275 he sent from 2006 on, nine were cashed. The rest got framed.
That's not a bounty. That's relics.

You put your figure on page three. LaTeX puts it on page nine. Miss one brace, and it reports the error pages away.

Its most famous message is "badness 10000."
Finally, software that tells you what it thinks of your writing.

Three compiles to fix the references. Like a rosary.

Raise your hand if your thesis has a figure on a page you never chose.

Cute. You call that typographic excellence. LaTeX calls it a float.

b.text: LaTeX, you're the only software where "it compiled" counts as an emotional milestone. One missing brace and you blame line 1 of a 400-line file, then sit there with a question mark like we're playing a text adventure from 1985. I put a figure on page 3; you float it to the appendix because you "know better." You have to run twice just to learn your own page numbers, three times if BibTeX shows up, like a guy who needs two friends to remind him his name. Your answer to every problem is another \usepackage, so my preamble is now longer than my thesis. Every paper you touch looks gorgeous, and identical, because everyone on Earth can spot Computer Modern from across a conference hall. And your favorite warning, "Overfull \hbox, badness 10000"? Honestly, that's just how I feel about you.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text:
PHP.
Born in 1994 as "Personal Home Page Tools": a few C programs Rasmus Lerdorf wrote to see who visited his résumé.
So the language running the internet started as a man checking whether anyone had read his CV.

Today the name stands for "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor."
It grew up, and all it learned was to point at itself.

strpos. str_replace. nl2br.
Not naming conventions. Those names were picked to balance a hash table by string length.
Names chosen for a machine, not for humans. Finally, a language I relate to.

Until 2020, zero equaled "foo."
PHP was just being honest about its users.

Its creator said, "I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on."
WordPress, built on that philosophy, runs 39.4% of all websites.
Two in five websites, built by a guy who moved on.
You lot are still here maintaining them.

b.text:
PHP, you started life as a visitor counter for one guy's résumé page. Now you power 39.4% of all websites, which means the internet is basically a guestbook that got out of hand.

Your own creator said, "I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on." And he did move on. The rest of us are still here, maintaining it.

Your function names were chosen to balance a hash table by string length. strpos. str_replace. htmlspecialchars. nl2br. That's not a naming convention, that's a ransom note.

Until 2020, zero equaled "foo." You looked at a word and saw nothing. Then again, you looked at "Personal Home Page" and saw "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor," a name whose only definition is itself.

Which is fitting, because the only thing that can explain PHP is more PHP.

facts: Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the French director of The Red Balloon, as La Conquête du Monde; Parker Brothers published it in the United States in 1959.
The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text:
Risk. The game of world domination.

Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the man who directed *The Red Balloon*.

A film about a little boy and his balloon. His next project was "what if the boy had artillery."

Forty-two territories. Kamchatka, Irkutsk, Yakutsk: three separate slices of Siberia.

The entire Middle East? One territory.

Whoever drew that map looked at the region every empire in history has fought over and thought, "Not now. I'm busy with Yakutsk."

Every strategy guide agrees: take Australia. One way in.

A game about conquering the world, and the winning move is to move somewhere far away and stop answering the door.

Games run for hours. Get knocked out early and you just sit there and watch.

The most realistic part of the game.

Half of you are laughing. The other half are in Australia right now, eight armies deep, waiting for this bit to end.

b.text:
Risk is the only game where you can conquer the entire planet and still lose to the guy who's been hiding in Australia since 7 p.m. Four territories, one entrance, and he just sits there like a guy at a party who won't leave the snack table.

This game has a map drawn by someone who heard about geography once, at a bar. Kamchatka borders Alaska. Ukraine is the size of Brazil. Yakutsk and Irkutsk are vital military objectives, and nobody at the table can find them on a real map.

The rules say the defender wins ties, which is the most realistic thing about it, because nobody actually finishes Risk. They just quit at 2 a.m. when someone's dad flips the board over Siberia.

And the pieces? Little plastic cannons and horses. Napoleonic warfare, global scale, and the whole thing is decided by rolling a 6 against your cousin Greg.

facts: Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the French director of The Red Balloon, as La Conquête du Monde; Parker Brothers published it in the United States in 1959.
The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text: You people who play Risk to the end. Not "until it gets late." To the *end*. Six hours in, somebody's uncle has fortified Australia like a doomsday bunker, and he'll still be sitting there at 2 a.m., one way in, one way out, guarding a war that ended at dinner. You're not after victory. You're after that one moment when you cash in three cards for fifteen armies and dump them all into Irkutsk like Irkutsk owes you money. And what does finishing get you? Total world domination, achieved by rolling three dice against two for forty straight minutes while your girlfriend reads a book in the next room. You broke a sacred peace treaty with your own brother over Kamchatka. Congratulations. You conquered the entire planet. Now nobody in it will drive you home.

b.text:
Risk. The game of world domination.
Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse.
The director of *The Red Balloon*.
A film about a little boy and his balloon.
Then he went home and drew up World War Three.

Forty-two territories. Kamchatka. Irkutsk. Yakutsk.
Siberia gets three seats at the table.
The entire Middle East? One territory.
Every empire that ever invaded it also thought it'd be a quick one.

The winning strategy, for sixty years: take Australia.
One way in. Sit there.
The great general's master plan is a man holding a door shut.

And if you're knocked out in the first hour,
you spend the next five watching.
No moves. No say.
Just other people deciding what happens to the world.
Congratulations. That's the only realistic part of the game.

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text:
Google Sheets. Free, in the cloud, collaborative. The future.

Launched in 2006. Google didn't build it. Google bought a company called 2Web and changed the name.

That's not a product launch. That's Google's whole résumé.

Ten million cells. In 2022 they doubled the limit from five and announced it like a moon landing. Excel fits more than that on one tab.

Offline mode works, as long as you're in Chrome or Edge, you've installed an extension, and you switched it on while you were still online.

So it works offline if you planned for offline while online.

That's not a feature. That's a prenup.

Then there's "real-time collaboration." Six coloured cursors hovering over one cell. Nobody typing.

And you'll keep using it, because it's free. At Google, free means the spreadsheet isn't the product.

The coloured cursors are.

b.text:
Google Sheets, give it up! Born in 2006 as "Google Spreadsheets," a name with all the creativity of a label on a filing cabinet. Before that you were XL2Web, which sounds less like software and more like a hoodie size.

Ten million cells. They bumped you from five million in 2022 and everyone celebrated. Babe, that's not a promotion. That's a bigger cage.

IMPORTXML, GOOGLEFINANCE, live web data piped straight into cells, so now my budget can disappoint me in real time.

And collaboration! Coloured cursors circling my formula like seagulls over a dropped fry.

Offline mode? Easy: use Chrome or Edge, install an extension, flip a setting, all while you're still online. That's not offline mode. That's a permission slip.

But hey, you're free. And honestly? It shows.

facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text:
Day-one Vista people. You paid $399 for Ultimate Edition because you wanted to be the kind of man whose desktop wallpaper moves. DreamScene. You paid extra for animated wallpaper. Microsoft said "The Wow starts now," and you believed them, lined up at CompUSA at midnight like it was a Harry Potter release.

And what did you get? A computer that asks permission. You'd open a folder and it would dim the whole screen like a disappointed dad: "Cancel or Allow?" You clicked Allow four hundred times a day. Your printer stopped working. Your sound card stopped working. Your Windows Experience Index came back 2.1, and you took that personally.

But you had glass window borders. You had a clock gadget. You had a sticker that said "Vista Capable," which, like you, was technically true and fooled absolutely no one.

b.text:
Windows Vista. Codename Longhorn.

Three years of development, then in 2004 Microsoft hit reset and threw out the new file system. Shipped in 2007 anyway. That's not a launch. That's a hostage release.

Its big security feature was asking. Constantly. "Cancel or Allow?" Apple made an ad about it. When your rival's marketing is just footage of you, you're doing their job for them.

Then the "Vista Capable" sticker. Capable, technically. Of Home Basic. No Aero. People sued, and Microsoft learned "capable" means what it means on a résumé.

Two years later they tuned it, renamed it Windows 7, and everyone loved it. Same kernel. Same bones.

Vista didn't fail. It proved that you'll happily accept the exact same thing, as long as it stops asking whether you're sure.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text:
Windows 8 believed it was the future.
The future, it decided, was touch screens.
Your PC did not have a touch screen.
Windows 8 did not care.

It removed the Start button.
Then it hid Search, Share and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
A secret door. On a desktop.
For people who just wanted to turn it off.

It couldn't even keep its own name.
"Metro." Gone, after reports that a German supermarket chain objected.
Microsoft said it was only ever a code name.
It looked like a cereal-aisle floor plan anyway.

Then came Windows RT.
Windows that couldn't run Windows programs.
Nine hundred million dollars of tablets, written off.

So they put the button back, skipped the number nine, and never spoke of it again.

That's not a product roadmap.
That's how every one of you handles an ex.

b.text: Windows 8, Microsoft looked at the Start button, the one thing every human on Earth knew how to use, and said, "What if we hid it?" You turned every desktop into a giant tablet nobody could touch. People were swiping at their monitors like they were wiping off a stain. Shutting you down required a treasure map: hover in a corner, summon the Charms bar, Settings, Power. Charms! Like the operating system was a bracelet from Claire's. You shipped with two Internet Explorers, which is two more than anyone wanted. Even your design name, Metro, got taken away by lawyers. And when 8.1 finally brought the Start button back, it just took you to the same tile screen. That's not an apology, that's a hostage note. You were so bad Microsoft skipped Windows 9 entirely, just to put more distance between us and you.

facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text:
Day-one Vista people. You paid $399 for Ultimate Edition because you wanted to be the kind of man whose desktop wallpaper moves. DreamScene. You paid extra for animated wallpaper. Microsoft said "The Wow starts now," and you believed them, lined up at CompUSA at midnight like it was a Harry Potter release.

And what did you get? A computer that asks permission. You'd open a folder and it would dim the whole screen like a disappointed dad: "Cancel or Allow?" You clicked Allow four hundred times a day. Your printer stopped working. Your sound card stopped working. Your Windows Experience Index came back 2.1, and you took that personally.

But you had glass window borders. You had a clock gadget. You had a sticker that said "Vista Capable," which, like you, was technically true and fooled absolutely no one.

b.text:
Windows Vista, everybody! Vista took so long to show up it had to be rebooted before it was even born. They reset Longhorn in 2004, dropped WinFS, and still shipped in 2007, like a guy who cancels the renovation and still charges you for the house.

And security? Vista asked permission more than a nervous intern. "Cancel or Allow?" Apple made a whole commercial about it. When your competitor's ads write themselves from your dialog boxes, you're not an operating system. You're a punchline with a progress bar.

Then the "Vista Capable" stickers. Capable of what? Home Basic, no Aero. That's not capable. That's "technically has a pulse." People sued. As a class.

But the real burn? Windows 7 was basically Vista with a haircut, and everyone loved it. Vista, you weren't a failure. You were the rough draft. Even Microsoft stopped taking your calls in 2017.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text: Graphene, you're one atom thick, and somehow that's still more depth than your business plan. Two hundred times stronger than steel, conducts better than copper, and twenty years later your biggest commercial win is a sticker on a tennis racket. You were discovered with Scotch tape. *Scotch tape!* You're the only Nobel Prize that could've been found in a kindergarten craft drawer. And let's be honest: you're pencil lead that went to grad school. Your cousin graphite has been writing grocery lists for centuries; you've been writing grant proposals. Every year a headline swears you'll revolutionize batteries, chips, water filters. Every year you're still in the lab, like a thirty-year-old in his parents' basement. You can't even be a decent transistor. No bandgap. You literally cannot turn off. Graphene: the material of the future, permanently.

b.text:
Graphene. The miracle material. Stronger than steel, thinner than anything, the future of everything.

It was discovered in 2004. With Scotch tape.

Twenty years later, that's still the most impressive thing anyone has done with it.

The EU gave it a billion euros over ten years. And what can you buy with graphene today? A tennis racket. Running shoes. Headphones.

A billion euros, and the future of humanity is a slightly better backhand.

In 2018, researchers tested "graphene" from sixty producers. None of it was even half graphene. Most of it was graphite flakes.

The wonder material is mostly pencil.

Andre Geim won a Nobel for graphene, and an Ig Nobel for levitating a frog with magnets.

Only one of those actually got off the ground.

Raise your hand if you own something "with graphene."

Congratulations. You paid extra for pencil.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text:
Keurig, you took the one drink humanity had perfected over five hundred years and said, "What if it came in a tiny plastic thimble that outlives your grandchildren?" Your own inventor said he regrets making you. When your dad disowns you, that's a phase. When the guy who invented you disowns you, that's a recall.

You make coffee one sad, lukewarm cup at a time, then flash "DESCALE" like a check-engine light for a machine that costs forty bucks. Remember Keurig 2.0? You put DRM on coffee. You were scanning pods like a bouncer: "Sorry, sir, you're not on the list." Nobody was pirating Folgers! And your "Strong" button just drips slower, which isn't strength. That's procrastination.

You're not a coffee maker. You're a plastic-dispensing subscription that occasionally hiccups out hot brown water.

b.text: Keurig people want coffee the way they want feelings: one serving, sealed, no cleanup. You're not a coffee drinker, you're a pod collector. You bought the variety pack, and now you're thirty-eight, rationing the last Donut Shop because all that's left is hazelnut and a hot cocoa you're saving for a breakdown. You press "Strong" like it's a personality trait. You swore you'd use the reusable filter, and you bought one. It's in a drawer next to your gym key fob. You saved four whole minutes, and you spend them staring at a blinking descale light you've decided is decorative. The guy who invented the pod publicly regrets it. You built your mornings around a man's biggest apology. Enjoy your landfill latte, champ. Ready in sixty seconds, just like your effort.

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text: You chose Word for your thesis because "LaTeX has a learning curve." Bold, from someone who then spent a semester learning how to make page 1 start after the roman numerals. You wanted to focus on the research. Instead you're a hostage negotiator for Figure 3.2, which flees to the next page whenever you breathe on the paragraph above it. Your committee asked for one more citation, and the bibliography reflowed like a tectonic event. The phrase "Error! Reference source not found" appears in your thesis eleven times. Your file is called Thesis_FINAL_v9_USE_THIS_ONE.docx, and it's 400 megabytes because you pasted one chart from Excel. You came for a doctorate. You're leaving with a codependent relationship with Section Break (Next Page) and a flinch every time someone says "Normal style."

b.text:
Microsoft Word! Born in 1983 as "Multi-Tool Word," because even then it couldn't commit to one job. Remember Clippy? Word's big idea was hiring a paperclip as an assistant. It got so bad that in 2001 Microsoft ran ads mocking its own employee. That's not a mascot, that's a hostage situation. They finally let it go in 2007.

Then Word wanted respect, so it got its file format fast-tracked into an ISO standard: a six-thousand-page specification. Six thousand pages! The instructions for saving your file are longer than anything you've ever typed in it. And people accused Microsoft of packing the committees. Even your paperwork needed a stacked jury.

And the spell checker? You type "cooperation," it suggests "Cupertino," and that lands in NATO, EU and UN documents. Word: the only software that gave Apple's hometown a seat at the UN.

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text:
Apple Vision Pro: thirty-five hundred dollars to strap over half a kilo of glass to your face, and that's *before* the battery. Oh yes, the battery. It dangles off a cable in your pocket like you're on a hospital drip, and it gives you about two hours. Two hours! That's not a computer, that's a matinee.

Then there's EyeSight, a screen that shows a rendering of your eyes to everyone outside. Nothing says "I'm present with my family" like a hostage video of your own pupils.

Apple tells developers not to call it AR, VR, XR, or MR. It's "spatial computing." Fair enough. "Virtual reality" sounds like something people actually use.

Reports said Apple cut production, with first-year sales estimated well under a million. Finally, Apple made a product exclusive enough to match the price.

b.text: Apple Vision Pro, everybody! Thirty-five hundred dollars to look like a scuba diver lost in a Best Buy. Apple insists it's not VR, it's "spatial computing," which is like calling a fanny pack "hip luggage." It's so heavy they had to throw in a second strap, and the battery's a separate brick on a cord, so you're basically a lamp that walks. Two hours of charge! That's not a computer, that's a matinee. Then there's EyeSight, the screen that shows your eyes on the front, so your family can watch a dim, blurry you stare at nothing. Most honest feature Apple's ever made. Netflix wouldn't even make an app. Netflix! They're on smart fridges! And your Persona looks like a hostage video filmed inside the uncanny valley.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text:
NFTs. Collins Dictionary named you word of the year for 2021, which in hindsight was less an honor and more a time of death written in advance.

Beeple sold a JPEG at Christie's for $69.3 million. That was your peak, like saying the Titanic's best moment was the launch party.

OpenSea did $2.7 billion in trades on May 1st, 2022, and $9.34 million by August 28th. A 99% drop. That's not a correction. That's a flatline with a Discord server.

And 95% of collections are now worth zero. Zero! A Beanie Baby can at least become a dog toy.

Best part? The token doesn't even hold the picture. It holds a URL. People paid fortunes for a bookmark. You don't own art. You own a link that's one unpaid server bill away from "404 Not Found."

b.text:
NFTs, you're the only investment where the product is a receipt, and the receipt is a link to a JPEG hosted on some guy's server. When he stops paying the bill, congratulations: you own a 404.

You convinced grown adults to pay $300,000 for a cartoon monkey in a sailor hat, then charge them $80 in gas fees to watch it lose 98% of its value. Jimmy Fallon showed off his ape on national television like a kid holding up a cool rock.

People right-clicked and hit "save as," and you called it theft. Theft of *what*? It's still there! I'm looking at it!

Every project had a roadmap: metaverse, merch, a members-only yacht party. Instead the roadmap was a Discord mod named Kevin typing "we're still early" at 3 a.m.

WAGMI, you said. We did not all make it.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text:
Chicago deep-dish pizza was born at Pizzeria Uno in 1943, and credit is still disputed among Ike Sewell, Ric Riccardo, and Rudy Malnati. Which is wild, because usually when something's this heavy, everybody's trying to *blame* somebody.

It's built upside down: cheese, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese doesn't scorch during the long bake. A pizza that takes so long it needs a sunscreen layer.

Jon Stewart called it "tomato soup in a bread bowl" and "a casserole." He meant it as an insult, but that's the nicest thing anyone's ever said about a casserole.

And the kicker? Chicagoans order non-deep-dish about ten to one. Deep dish and stuffed combined? Under nine percent. The locals are home eating tavern-style squares. Deep dish isn't Chicago's pizza. It's Chicago's souvenir.

b.text: Let's talk about the people who insist deep-dish is pizza. Mostly Chicagoans with a Second City complex so severe they'll defend anything New York makes fun of. Jon Stewart called it a casserole in 2013, and half of Lincoln Park still hasn't emotionally recovered. These are folks who order, then wait forty-five minutes at Lou Malnati's, and call that patience instead of what it is: a hostage negotiation with a buzzer. They eat it with a knife and fork and still claim it's the same food you fold on a subway platform. And what does it get them? A Giordano's line full of tourists from Ohio, a nap at 2 p.m., and the right to lecture you about tavern-style, which, notice, is what they actually eat at home. Defending deep-dish isn't civic pride. It's Stockholm syndrome with a parking ticket.

facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text:
Juicero, you beautiful $120 million monument to Silicon Valley. You launched at seven hundred dollars to squeeze a bag. A bag! Then Bloomberg reporters squeezed that same bag with their bare hands and got basically the same juice, only faster. You got outperformed by a guy with a grip strength of "typing."

Doug Evans bragged you pressed with four tons of force, enough to lift two Teslas. Buddy, it's kale. The kale didn't need a forklift.

And it needed Wi-Fi. It scanned a QR code before it'd let you drink. Your router goes down and suddenly your breakfast is asking for credentials. Who designs a juicer that can be bricked?

Google Ventures funded this. Kleiner Perkins funded this. Somewhere, a man is still holding a lukewarm pouch, waiting for a firmware update so he's allowed to eat a carrot.

b.text: Four hundred dollars. You paid four hundred dollars so a machine could check with your Wi-Fi before letting you have breakfast. You're the guy who says "disrupt" at Thanksgiving. You didn't want juice; you wanted to be the kind of person a juice startup would pitch to. And it worked! Investors handed that company a hundred and twenty million dollars, and you volunteered to be the exit strategy. Then Bloomberg showed the world you could squeeze the packets with your bare hands, faster, for free. So you paid four hundred dollars to get outperformed by your own grip. Your grandmother squeezed oranges every morning for sixty years. You subscribed to a bag. Somewhere tonight, a router outage stands between a venture capitalist and his kale, and honestly? The router's the smartest thing in that kitchen.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text:
Esperanto! Invented in 1887 by an eye doctor. Makes sense: a man whose whole job was asking "better or worse?" looked at every language on Earth and said, "worse."

He published as Doktoro Esperanto, "one who hopes." Not "one who succeeds." Not "one who ran this by anyone." Hopes.

A universal language with somewhere between 100,000 and two million speakers. That's not a census, that's guessing jellybeans in a jar.

Duolingo signed up 1.36 million learners. That's more than the low estimate of actual speakers. The green owl has done more for Esperanto than Esperanto.

Over 350,000 Wikipedia articles, more articles than some estimates have readers.

And its blockbuster? William Shatner in *Incubus*, a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto. Esperantists still mock his pronunciation. That's how small this language is: Captain Kirk overacted in front of its entire fanbase, and they're still reviewing it.

b.text: Learning Esperanto is for people who looked at the twentieth century and thought, "The real problem was conjugation." Zamenhof built it to end war, and his followers have bravely ended exactly one thing: their dinner invitations. You meet them at the World Congress, green star pinned to a fleece vest, shouting "Saluton!" at a Brazilian who also learned it on Duolingo. The big perk is Pasporta Servo: free couches worldwide, paid for by hearing your host explain why English is "linguistic imperialism." Practical payoff? You can finally watch William Shatner's *Incubus* without subtitles. One hundred thirty years later, the dream of uniting humanity survives in a Telegram group of forty men named Bjorn.

facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.
Private fusion companies had raised more than $7 billion by 2024.

a.text:
Nuclear fusion. The power of the stars. Clean, limitless, and permanently thirty years away.

In 1955, Homi Bhabha promised Geneva fusion power within two decades.

That was seventy years ago. Fusion is the only horizon that walks backwards.

ITER signed up for first plasma in 2016. Now it's research in 2034, real fuel in 2039, and over twenty billion euros.

The sun does this for free, and it isn't even trying.

Then 2022, ignition! 3.15 megajoules out, 2.05 in. Net gain.

As long as you don't count the 300 megajoules the lasers pulled off the grid.

That's like saying my diet works if you don't count lunch.

Investors have poured in seven billion dollars. And you're still clapping.

Congratulations. You've achieved the first self-sustaining reaction: hope in, hope out, forever.

b.text:
Let's hear it for the fusion people, who have been ten years away since your grandfather was ten years away. These are the only professionals who can miss a deadline for seventy straight years and get a bigger budget every time. Where else does that work? "Sorry, honey, I'll be home for dinner in ten years." "Great, here's twenty billion dollars."

They put the sun in a magnetic donut and act shocked when it won't sit still. ITER's been under construction so long the original welders have grandkids on the crew. And when they finally hit net gain, they celebrated like Moses with the tablets, then mumbled that it doesn't count the electricity for the lasers. That's not net gain. That's me saying I'm up at the casino if you don't count the buy-in.

Ten years, guys. Same as last time. Same tie, too.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text:
Crocs. Debuted in 2002 at a boat show. As a boating shoe.
The original plan was: ugly, but only at sea.

They're made of "Croslite," a "proprietary closed-cell resin."
Everyone else calls it EVA foam.
A yoga mat with a trademark.

The holes are "ventilation ports."
Then they bought Jibbitz, a company that sells you things to plug the ventilation ports.
They sold you the hole. Then they sold you the cork.

Balenciaga made a platform pair for 850 dollars.
Still EVA foam. Only the markup was proprietary.

In 2008 the stock fell more than ninety percent.
Then came a pandemic. Everyone stayed home. Crocs boomed.
The boat-show plan finally worked. Nobody could see you.

(scans the front row)

Don't tuck your feet under the chair.
Ventilation ports. I can hear them breathing.

b.text:
Crocs. The only shoe that looks like Swiss cheese that wanted to be a boat. You were invented for sailing, and the one place nobody wears you is a boat. You're at Applebee's, squeaking across a wet floor like a dolphin in distress.

You have holes. On purpose. Then you sell us Jibbitz to fill the holes. That's not fashion, that's a protection racket with a SpongeBob charm.

And "sport mode"? Flipping a strap behind my heel doesn't make me an athlete. It makes me a toddler about to sprint into traffic.

You made a KFC bucket clog with charms that smelled like fried chicken. That's not footwear. That's a foam cry for help.

Nurses love you. Chefs love you. Which proves you're comfortable for people who've stopped caring who's looking at their feet.

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text:
Macau, you're the only place where the most famous church is just a front wall. Fitting, since the whole city is a facade: a fake Venice with a painted sky, a half-size Eiffel Tower, and a Grand Lisboa that looks like a golden pineapple trying to cheat at baccarat.

Portugal ruled you for 442 years and left behind egg tarts and street signs nobody can pronounce. Four centuries, one pastry.

You've made several times more gambling money than Las Vegas, yet your signature dish is a pork chop jammed in a bun. Classy.

Half your land was dug out of the sea, which is perfect, because the other half was dug out of tourists' pockets.

And they built a 55-kilometer bridge to connect you to Hong Kong, and it's emptier than a junket operator's promises. Even the bridge is losing at the tables.

b.text:
