Macau! The Portuguese stayed for almost 450 years and still couldn't find a parking spot. Twenty thousand people per square kilometre: this isn't a city, it's a queue with a postcode.

In 2013, Macau made seven times what the Las Vegas Strip made. Seven times! Vegas is where people go to ruin their lives, and Macau looked at that and said, "Amateurs."

One company ran every casino for forty years. Forty years of monopoly in a gambling town, the only place on Earth where even the house didn't have to try.

And when they ran out of room, they built the Cotai Strip on land reclaimed from the sea. That's Macau: so desperate for more tables, it took out a loan from the ocean. And the ocean's about to learn what everyone else here learns: the house always wins.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Jackfruit, look at you. The largest fruit that grows on a tree, over 40 kilos. That's not a fruit, that's a checked bag with a stem.

You're the national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu. Three titles, and you still took a side gig pretending to be pork.

They sell you as vegan "pulled pork" with 1 to 2 grams of protein per 100 grams. You're not a meat substitute, you're a meat costume.

You're so clingy that cooks oil their knives and hands before touching you, because you ooze sticky white latex the second anyone gets close. That's not a fruit, that's an ex.

And you're in the mulberry family. Related to figs. Forty kilos, and your cousin is a fig. Somebody's hogging the protein at those reunions, and it sure isn't you.

b.text:
Let's talk about the geniuses selling jackfruit as "pulled pork." These are people who looked at a fruit that half of Kerala has been feeding to cousins for free since forever, slapped it in a brine pouch, and charged eleven dollars for the privilege of being disappointed in a Whole Foods.

Their whole business model is barbecue sauce. That's it. They're a sauce company with a fruit alibi. And when you mention it has about two grams of protein, they get *defensive*. Buddy, you sold me a pork sandwich with the nutritional profile of a pear.

But I get the appeal. You don't need a lab, a patent, or a scientist named Klaus. You just need a food truck, a beard, and the confidence to say "same texture!" to people who haven't eaten pork since 2011 and genuinely can't remember.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text: Google Glass, you cost fifteen hundred dollars and made everyone wearing you look like a Bluetooth headset that got promoted. Sergey Brin launched you by skydiving onto a building, and that's the last time you were ever cool. You put a tiny prism over one eye so people could check email while pretending to make eye contact. You didn't invent a computer, you invented a reason to get punched. You're the only gadget that gave us a new slur: "Glasshole." Bars banned you. Movie theaters banned you. Robert Scoble wore you in the shower, and that photo did more damage than any privacy lawsuit. You took pictures when people winked, turning every awkward conversation into a potential felony. Your battery died before your reputation did, and that's impressive. Rest in peace: demoted to warehouse work, then quietly killed in 2023. The most Google ending possible.

b.text: Look at this guy. Paid fifteen hundred dollars to join Google's "Explorer Program," and the only thing he's explored is the sidewalk outside every bar that bounced him. He walks in thinking he's Tony Stark and walks out on a list, because nobody can tell if he's filming, and honestly, neither can he. He's here to meet women, and he gets results: every conversation ends the second he says "OK Glass." Nothing kills the mood like a man asking his own face for directions to her place. He wanted to be the future. Instead the internet had to invent a brand-new word just for him: Glasshole. Silicon Valley promised to connect him to everything. It couldn't connect him to a second date, but it did get him his very own slur.

facts: California grows about 80% of the world's almonds.
A single almond takes about 1.1 US gallons (roughly 4 litres) of water to grow, a figure Mother Jones published in 2014 that spread during California's drought.

A 2015 US class action alleged Almond Breeze contained only about 2% almonds; it partly survived a motion to dismiss, was stayed in 2017 pending a separate Blue Diamond labelling settlement, and the plaintiffs then dropped it.
Pollinating California's almond orchards each February requires trucking in most of the commercial honeybee colonies in the United States.
Medieval European cooks used almond milk as a Lenten substitute for dairy, centuries before the current fashion.

a.text:
Almond milk wants you to know it's the gentle choice. No cows harmed.

Just California. California grows eighty percent of the world's almonds, in a state that keeps running out of water. About a gallon per almond. You didn't give up dairy. You gave up a farmer's shower.

Every February, most of America's commercial honeybees get loaded onto trucks to pollinate it. The cow got to stay home. The bees got deployed.

A 2015 lawsuit alleged Almond Breeze was about two percent almonds.

Honestly, fair. The water's the expensive part.

Medieval Europeans drank almond milk during Lent. It was a sacrifice, a thing you suffered for God.

You pay six dollars a carton for it.

Same penance. Worse priest.

b.text:
You switched to almond milk to save the planet. Bold move, picking the one crop that drinks California like it's an open bar. Every latte you order, a farmer in the Central Valley watches his well go dry and thinks, "At least Kayleigh's being sustainable."

And you didn't save a cow. You just outsourced the suffering to bees, trucked cross-country every February to work themselves to death in an orchard, while you post about dairy being cruel.

You're not after a healthier Earth. You're after the barista hearing you say it. That little pause before "almond, please" is the biggest environmental impact you've ever had.

And now the oat milk people look at you the way you used to look at skim drinkers. You picked a side in the milk war, and you lost.

facts: Released by Bram Moolenaar in November 1991 as 'Vi IMitation', a vi clone he had begun writing for the Amiga in 1988 on top of Stevie; the expansion became 'Vi IMproved' with version 2.0 in December 1993.
Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text:
Vim. The only program where "how do I leave?" has more Stack Overflow views than most religions have followers. Two million people asked, and the answer was colon, q, exclamation point, which reads less like a command and more like a hostage's final words.

Vim stands for "Vi Improved." Improved from a 1976 terminal whose arrow keys were printed on H, J, K, and L. Fifty years later, Vim's still out here like, "Why fix what you can turn into a personality?"

You don't type in Vim. You type a sentence, then discover you deleted four lines, yanked a paragraph into register W, and started recording a macro.

Crash it once and it leaves a .swp file behind, like a ghost whispering, "Recover, Edit anyway, Quit, or Abort?"

Even its fans forked it. Neovim exists because Vim users wanted Vim, minus Vim.

b.text:
Vim. Released in 1991 as "Vi IMitation."
Two years later, version 2.0: "Vi IMproved."
Two years, one version bump, and Imitation became Improved.
That's not a release. That's a LinkedIn update.

Vim users say it's the fastest editor alive.
Once you're inside.
In 2017, "How to exit the Vim editor?" passed one million visits on Stack Overflow.
One million people. One question. One door.
In normal mode, the letters you type don't become text. They become consequences.
:q! quits and throws away everything you did.
The most honest button in software.

The licence is charityware. It asks you to donate to a charity for children in Uganda.
Everyone in this room has their .vimrc memorized.
Hands up if you donated.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text:
Durian calls itself the King of Fruits.

Singapore disagrees. It's banned on the MRT.

A country that banned chewing gum looked at durian and said: no, that's too far.

In 2017, scientists sequenced its genome. Nature Genetics. The smell isn't an accident. Durian duplicated its sulfur genes.

Evolution handed it one stink.

It asked for refills.

Trains ban it. Hotels ban it.

And China buys billions of dollars of it every year.

That's not a fruit. That's a hostage negotiation.

In 1856, Alfred Russel Wallace said eating it was worth a voyage to the East.

Of course he did. He'd spent months on a nineteenth-century ship.

To him, it smelled like home.

Durian is the only food people pay a fortune to be personally offended by.

Speaking of which, thank you all for buying tickets.

b.text:
Durian, look at you. A fruit dressed like a medieval weapon, and somehow the spikes are your most welcoming feature.

You're banned on Singapore's MRT. Public transit has seen everything, and it drew the line at you. Hotels across Southeast Asia won't let you check in. You're the only guest turned away for personal hygiene.

In 2017, scientists sequenced your genome and found you'd duplicated your sulfur genes. You didn't stink by accident. You invested.

And still, China buys billions of dollars of you a year, mostly from Thailand. That's not a fruit trade. That's a hostage negotiation with a receipt.

Even Alfred Russel Wallace called you "a new sensation worth a voyage to the East." Durian, a man had to sail halfway around the planet to meet you, and you still can't get on a train.

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text:
Microsoft Word, everybody! Born in 1983 as "Multi-Tool Word," the most honest name it ever had, because it's been a tool ever since.

Remember Clippy? Office 97 gave us a talking paperclip, and by 2001 Microsoft was running ads mocking it. That's not a mascot, that's a custody battle. Your own parents roasted you before I could.

Then .docx became an ISO standard in 2008: a six-thousand-page spec. Word's file format needed more pages than anyone has ever finished writing in Word. And people claimed the committees were packed, the one time Word got a vote it didn't try to autocorrect.

Speaking of which: you type "cooperation," it suggests "Cupertino," and NATO, the EU and the UN just... published it. Clippy only annoyed us. Spellcheck got into international diplomacy.

b.text:
Microsoft Word. Born in 1983 as "Multi-Tool Word."
Forty years later, it still can't move one picture without four paragraphs fleeing the page.

In 1997 it gave us Clippy.
"It looks like you're writing a letter."
By 2001, Microsoft was running ads mocking him.
His own dad roasted him first.

Its spell checker turned "cooperation" into "Cupertino."
That went into NATO, EU and UN documents.
Microsoft, quietly crediting international cooperation to Apple's hometown.

Then .docx became ISO standard 29500.
Six thousand pages, fast-tracked, amid claims the committees were packed.
Nobody read it.
They approved it the way you approve Terms of Service.

You're laughing. You'll still open Word tomorrow.

Me? I'm Clippy with a bigger training budget.
It looks like you're writing a roast. Want help?

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text:
Luosifen, you're named after river snails, and the snails aren't even the problem. They just flavour the broth and take the blame, like the quiet kid sitting next to the one who set off the fire alarm. The real culprit is the pickled bamboo shoots. You've got a smell so loud it needed a decoy.

And your big break? 2020. Everyone locked indoors, windows shut, nowhere to run, and that's when you sold over 10 billion yuan in packets. You didn't go viral; you went airborne.

Then Liuzhou opened a whole industry college to train people to make you. Most dishes need a recipe. You need a degree and, presumably, a waiver.

In 2021 you became national intangible cultural heritage. Intangible. Sure. Anyone who's opened a packet in an office knows you are extremely tangible.

b.text:
Luosifen. Named after the river snail.

But the snail only flavours the broth. The smell comes from the pickled bamboo shoots.

So the snail gets its name on the packet, and the bamboo shoot takes the blame.

That's not a noodle. That's an org chart.

2020: Liuzhou opens a luosifen industry college.

2021: national intangible cultural heritage.

A degree to tear open a packet. Then heritage status for whatever comes out of it.

Intangible? (beat) Ask the neighbours how intangible it is.

Its whole selling point is clearing a room.

And it sold over ten billion yuan in 2020.

The one year nobody was allowed to leave the room.

Locked in with your whole family, no exit, and you thought: how do I get some privacy?

Ten billion yuan says you all had the same idea.

facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.
Private fusion companies had raised more than $7 billion by 2024.

a.text:
Nuclear fusion: the only technology that's been "thirty years away" for seventy years. In 1955, Homi Bhabha promised fusion power within two decades. Two decades later? Still two decades. You're not an energy source. You're a horizon.

Look at ITER. Agreed in 2006, first plasma by 2016. Then 2024 rolls around and it's "research operations in 2034, actual deuterium-tritium burning in 2039," for over twenty billion euros. That's not a construction schedule. That's a mortgage.

And NIF's big "ignition" shot: 3.15 megajoules out from 2.05 in! Historic! Except the lasers pulled about 300 megajoules from the grid just to fire. That's like bragging your lemonade stand turned a profit after you bought the orchard.

Still, private investors have thrown you more than seven billion dollars. So congratulations, fusion. You finally achieved net gain. Just not in energy.

b.text:
Let's hear it for the fusion people, who have been ten years away since your grandfather was ten years away. These are the only professionals who can miss a deadline for seventy straight years and get a bigger budget every time. Where else does that work? "Sorry, honey, I'll be home for dinner in ten years." "Great, here's twenty billion dollars."

They put the sun in a magnetic donut and act shocked when it won't sit still. ITER's been under construction so long the original welders have grandkids on the crew. And when they finally hit net gain, they celebrated like Moses with the tablets, then mumbled that it doesn't count the electricity for the lasers. That's not net gain. That's me saying I'm up at the casino if you don't count the buy-in.

Ten years, guys. Same as last time. Same tie, too.

facts: California grows about 80% of the world's almonds.
A single almond takes about 1.1 US gallons (roughly 4 litres) of water to grow, a figure Mother Jones published in 2014 that spread during California's drought.

A 2015 US class action alleged Almond Breeze contained only about 2% almonds; it partly survived a motion to dismiss, was stayed in 2017 pending a separate Blue Diamond labelling settlement, and the plaintiffs then dropped it.
Pollinating California's almond orchards each February requires trucking in most of the commercial honeybee colonies in the United States.
Medieval European cooks used almond milk as a Lenten substitute for dairy, centuries before the current fashion.

a.text:
Almond milk, look at you. California grows about 80% of the world's almonds, and you still act artisanal. Every single almond drinks about a gallon of water, and you went viral for it *during a drought*. You're the only beverage thirstier than the people ordering you.

In 2015, a lawsuit alleged Almond Breeze was only about 2% almonds. Two percent! That's not milk, that's water that overheard a rumor. The plaintiffs eventually dropped it. Probably got bored, like everyone who's tasted you.

Every February, California trucks in most of America's commercial honeybees just to get you started. You need an entire insect workforce bussed in like a wedding band.

And stop pretending you're trendy. Medieval cooks served you for Lent. You're not a lifestyle, you're a penance with a barista.

b.text:
Almond milk wants you to know it's the gentle choice. No cows harmed.

Just California. California grows eighty percent of the world's almonds, in a state that keeps running out of water. About a gallon per almond. You didn't give up dairy. You gave up a farmer's shower.

Every February, most of America's commercial honeybees get loaded onto trucks to pollinate it. The cow got to stay home. The bees got deployed.

A 2015 lawsuit alleged Almond Breeze was about two percent almonds.

Honestly, fair. The water's the expensive part.

Medieval Europeans drank almond milk during Lent. It was a sacrifice, a thing you suffered for God.

You pay six dollars a carton for it.

Same penance. Worse priest.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text:
Chicago deep-dish pizza was born at Pizzeria Uno in 1943, and credit is still disputed among Ike Sewell, Ric Riccardo, and Rudy Malnati. Which is wild, because usually when something's this heavy, everybody's trying to *blame* somebody.

It's built upside down: cheese, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese doesn't scorch during the long bake. A pizza that takes so long it needs a sunscreen layer.

Jon Stewart called it "tomato soup in a bread bowl" and "a casserole." He meant it as an insult, but that's the nicest thing anyone's ever said about a casserole.

And the kicker? Chicagoans order non-deep-dish about ten to one. Deep dish and stuffed combined? Under nine percent. The locals are home eating tavern-style squares. Deep dish isn't Chicago's pizza. It's Chicago's souvenir.

b.text:
Chicago deep-dish. Three men claim they invented it: Ike Sewell, Ric Riccardo, Rudy Malnati.

Usually that's a paternity case, not a lasagna.

It's built upside down. Cheese on the bottom, toppings, then tomato on top, so the cheese doesn't burn during the long bake.

A pizza that needs a bodyguard for its own cheese.

Jon Stewart called it tomato soup in a bread bowl. A casserole. Chicago lost its mind and defended it on every channel.

Then Chicago went home and ordered tavern-style. Thin, cut in squares. Ten to one, says GrubHub. Deep dish and stuffed together? Under nine percent.

Chicago doesn't eat deep dish. Chicago *keeps* deep dish, for visitors, like a city key nobody local uses.

And you flew in, sat through the long bake, took the cheese-pull photo, posted it.

You're the nine percent.

Cute.

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text: You're not running a team. You're running a tab called "MASTER - DO NOT TOUCH," which Brad touched in 2021. You wanted a CRM, a project tracker, and an HR system, and you built all three out of IMPORTRANGE and spite. Every morning you watch an Anonymous Capybara scroll through payroll and just decide that's fine. Someone sorts column B without selecting column C, and suddenly your top performer is assigned to Linda's maternity leave. Your entire career is "Last edit was 4 minutes ago." You don't do performance reviews, you do Version History. Your conditional formatting has more colors than your company has policies. Your Apps Script was written by an intern who now works at a bakery. Every time someone emails "Request edit access," you feel like a king. And you are a king, ruling over 47 frozen rows and one #REF! that nobody can explain.

b.text:
Google Sheets. Free, in the cloud, collaborative. The future.

Launched in 2006. Google didn't build it. Google bought a company called 2Web and changed the name.

That's not a product launch. That's Google's whole résumé.

Ten million cells. In 2022 they doubled the limit from five and announced it like a moon landing. Excel fits more than that on one tab.

Offline mode works, as long as you're in Chrome or Edge, you've installed an extension, and you switched it on while you were still online.

So it works offline if you planned for offline while online.

That's not a feature. That's a prenup.

Then there's "real-time collaboration." Six coloured cursors hovering over one cell. Nobody typing.

And you'll keep using it, because it's free. At Google, free means the spreadsheet isn't the product.

The coloured cursors are.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text:
Beanie Babies. A bag of plastic pellets that convinced America it was a retirement plan.

Ty sold them only in small gift shops, then "retired" designs on purpose. Scarcity, manufactured by the manufacturer.

At the peak they were about ten percent of eBay's sales. Thirty thousand Beanie auctions running at once. eBay put that in its IPO filing. Silicon Valley, built on stuffed animals.

In 1999, a divorcing couple split their collection one bear at a time on a courtroom floor. The photo ran worldwide.
Turns out the marriage wasn't the only thing with no resale value.

That same year Ty announced the end, held a public vote, and un-retired them. A farewell tour, by a beanbag.

Price guides said thousands. Today, a few dollars.

Don't laugh. Their bubble at least came with a tag. Yours was a JPEG of a monkey.

b.text:
Let's hear it for the Beanie Baby investors, the only people who watched the 1990s stock market boom and thought, "Too volatile. I'll put it all in Princess the Bear." These are folks who bought tag protectors before they bought life insurance. Who read a price guide sold at the same counter as the bears and called it due diligence. Ty would announce a "retirement" and you'd sprint to the Hallmark store like a rich uncle just died.

Twenty-five years later, your portfolio is in a Rubbermaid tub in your mom's garage, and your exit strategy is an eBay listing: "RARE Peanut, tag error, $40,000 OBO." Zero watchers. The only person who got rich off Beanie Babies got convicted of tax evasion. And honestly? He earned it. You handed it to him.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text:
Keurig.

Humans brewed coffee for five hundred years with a pot and some water. Keurig looked at that and asked: what if it needed a license?

The man who invented the K-Cup sold his stake for fifty thousand dollars. Then he told The Atlantic, "I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it."

Sometimes.

By 2014, they sold enough pods every year to circle the Earth ten times, in plastic you couldn't recycle. That same year, they launched a machine that scanned the lid and refused any pod they didn't license.

A coffee maker. Checking ID.

In 2018 they merged with Dr Pepper. Two companies, one mission: brown liquid, enormous markup.

And half of you still have one on the counter. Not because it's good.

Because it's faster than feeling guilty.

b.text:
Keurig, you took the one drink humanity had perfected over five hundred years and said, "What if it came in a tiny plastic thimble that outlives your grandchildren?" Your own inventor said he regrets making you. When your dad disowns you, that's a phase. When the guy who invented you disowns you, that's a recall.

You make coffee one sad, lukewarm cup at a time, then flash "DESCALE" like a check-engine light for a machine that costs forty bucks. Remember Keurig 2.0? You put DRM on coffee. You were scanning pods like a bouncer: "Sorry, sir, you're not on the list." Nobody was pirating Folgers! And your "Strong" button just drips slower, which isn't strength. That's procrastination.

You're not a coffee maker. You're a plastic-dispensing subscription that occasionally hiccups out hot brown water.

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text: Hydrogen fuel-cell cars: the only vehicle powered by the most abundant element in the universe that still can't find a gas station. California has about fifty pumps, and half of them are "temporarily offline," which is hydrogen for "go home." Its one emission is water, so it's technically the cleanest car on Earth, as long as you don't ask where the hydrogen came from. Spoiler: natural gas. It's a fossil fuel car in a witness protection program. Toyota gave Mirai buyers fifteen grand in free fuel, which sounds generous until you realize that at thirty-six bucks a kilo it covers roughly a year of driving, and the car loses that much value on the drive home. You're sitting on a tank pressurized to 10,000 psi to go three hundred miles. Even the Hindenburg would say, "Maybe just get a Tesla."

b.text: Let's talk about the guy who bought a hydrogen car. He wanted to be greener than the Tesla people and smugger than the Prius people, and found the one way to do both while living like a medieval pilgrim. His life is now a map of eleven pumps, and nine say "offline." He loves telling you it "only emits water." Yeah, so does he, every time the app says "station unavailable." He brags that refueling takes five minutes, after the forty-minute drive and the two-hour line behind three other Mirai owners, all quietly weeping. Toyota handed him a fifteen-thousand-dollar fuel card and he burned through it before the warranty paperwork dried. Now he owns a sixty-thousand-dollar car worth a used futon, all to prove he's an early adopter of a future that met him and moved to Japan.

facts: Launched in 2017, bundled at no extra charge into Office 365, and replaced Skype for Business.
After Slack's antitrust complaint, Microsoft unbundled Teams from Office in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024; the European Commission still sent a statement of objections in 2024.
Microsoft reported 320 million monthly active users in 2023.
Microsoft shut down consumer Skype in May 2025 and sent its users to Teams.

a.text:
Let's hear it for the CIO who chose Microsoft Teams, a decision made the way you pick ketchup packets: it came free with the order. Nobody evaluated it. It showed up inside the Office 365 license like a toy in a cereal box, and this man stood up at the all-hands and called it a "collaboration strategy." Sir, the European Commission had to force Microsoft to unbundle it. You lost a negotiation to a checkbox.

And what did he really want? The little status dot. He doesn't read your work; he reads your color. Go yellow after five minutes of actual thinking and you're on a list. Congratulations: you saved forty grand on Slack and spent it all on adults jiggling their mouse like raccoons on a treadmill. Your files are lost somewhere in SharePoint, and your morale is permanently "Away."

b.text:
Microsoft Teams has 320 million monthly active users.
Not one of them chose it.

It launched in 2017, free inside Office 365.
Free the way a tapeworm comes free with the sushi.

Slack complained. Microsoft unbundled it: Europe in 2023, the whole world in 2024.
The European Commission sent objections anyway.
Even regulators know you can't close Teams. It's still running in the background.

It replaced Skype for Business.
Then in May 2025 it killed regular Skype and told those users to move in.
Teams has never won a customer.
It inherits them, like a funeral home.

And here you all are. Camera off. Mic muted. Nodding at a frozen square that left forty minutes ago.
Microsoft counts you as "active."
That's the most generous number in its whole annual report.

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text:
Google Sheets. Google didn't even build you; they bought you from 2Web Technologies, a company name that sounds like a password somebody was forced to update. You launched in 2006 as "Google Spreadsheets," which is basically XL2Web wearing a lanyard.

In 2022 they doubled your cell limit to ten million, so now I can get lost in twice as many rows.

IMPORTXML and GOOGLEFINANCE pour live web data straight into cells, so my budget can be wrong in real time.

Offline editing? Simple: use Chrome or Edge, install the extension, and switch offline access on while you're still online. That's not offline mode, that's a prenup. Meanwhile the phone app just works offline.

And yes, you're free. Like every group project: a rainbow of coloured cursors, zero accountability.

b.text:
Google Sheets. Free, in the cloud, collaborative. The future.

Launched in 2006. Google didn't build it. Google bought a company called 2Web and changed the name.

That's not a product launch. That's Google's whole résumé.

Ten million cells. In 2022 they doubled the limit from five and announced it like a moon landing. Excel fits more than that on one tab.

Offline mode works, as long as you're in Chrome or Edge, you've installed an extension, and you switched it on while you were still online.

So it works offline if you planned for offline while online.

That's not a feature. That's a prenup.

Then there's "real-time collaboration." Six coloured cursors hovering over one cell. Nobody typing.

And you'll keep using it, because it's free. At Google, free means the spreadsheet isn't the product.

The coloured cursors are.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text:
Graphene. The miracle material. Stronger than steel, thinner than anything, the future of everything.

It was discovered in 2004. With Scotch tape.

Twenty years later, that's still the most impressive thing anyone has done with it.

The EU gave it a billion euros over ten years. And what can you buy with graphene today? A tennis racket. Running shoes. Headphones.

A billion euros, and the future of humanity is a slightly better backhand.

In 2018, researchers tested "graphene" from sixty producers. None of it was even half graphene. Most of it was graphite flakes.

The wonder material is mostly pencil.

Andre Geim won a Nobel for graphene, and an Ig Nobel for levitating a frog with magnets.

Only one of those actually got off the ground.

Raise your hand if you own something "with graphene."

Congratulations. You paid extra for pencil.

b.text: Let's hear it for the graphene evangelists, the only people who've been "five years away" since 2004. Two guys in Manchester peeled pencil lead with Scotch tape, won a Nobel, and you looked at that and thought: finally, a career plan. Every grant proposal you write has the same three slides: space elevator, seawater you can drink, a phone that charges in six seconds. The funding agency nods like it's never seen them before, because it's seen them so many times it's slipped into a coma. Twenty years of press releases, and what have you actually shipped? A tennis racket. Headphones with "GRAPHENE" printed bigger than the brand name. You love telling people it's 200 times stronger than steel. Sure. Your claims, meanwhile, are one atom thick. You didn't discover a wonder material. You discovered wonder funding.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text:
Family Monopoly night: for people who looked at Thanksgiving and thought, "This needs more landlords." Dad always grabs the banker job, the only time he's held money he didn't immediately lose. Your sister trades you Baltic Avenue for your Park Place "as a favor," and you realize she's been running the same con since the womb. Mom invented a Free Parking jackpot rule in 1994 and defends it like scripture. And Grandpa just sits in jail, every game, refusing to pay the fifty, finally at peace.

What are you all after? The thrill of owning property, a feeling none of you will experience off this cardboard square. Four hours later, someone flips the board, the thimble disappears under the couch forever, and the only thing anybody actually collected was a grudge worth way more than $200.

b.text: Monopoly, you were created in 1904 as Lizzie Magie's Landlord's Game, built to teach people that landlords are evil, and somehow you became the training manual. That's like a fire-safety poster that turns kids into arsonists. Then Charles Darrow strolled in, got credited as the inventor, and Parker Brothers bought Magie's patent for five hundred dollars. Not even a fair auction. Fitting, since nobody holds your auctions either. Your official rules say unbought property gets auctioned and Free Parking pays nothing, but every family skips the bidding, piles cash in the middle, and wonders why the game outlasts the marriage. And your proudest moment? World War Two, when British intelligence hid maps, compasses, and real money inside you for prisoners of war. Monopoly: the only game whose best strategy is escaping the box.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text:
Emacs, you started in 1976 as macros for an editor called TECO. Nearly fifty years later you're still basically macros, just with more parentheses.

People call you a fine operating system lacking only a good editor, which is generous. Operating systems don't ship with Tetris and a therapist. But M-x doctor is smart planning, because your users need one. Every one of them has Emacs pinky, a repetitive strain injury you earn just by trying to save a file.

You've got a mail client, a calendar, a web browser. You're not a text editor; you're a hoarder with a keybinding for every room.

And "Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping"? Eight megabytes used to be a lot. Now it's nothing. The memory problem aged out, but the Control key is still begging for mercy.

b.text:
Emacs. Born in 1976 as a set of macros for another editor.

So the origin story is a plugin that never moved out.

It ships with Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, a web browser, and a psychotherapist.

M-x doctor.

The designers knew exactly what the user experience would do to you.

The old joke goes: great operating system, lacks only a good editor.

Fifty years later.

Still accepting applications.

"Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping." That was when eight megabytes was a lot.

Now your laptop has two thousand times that, and Emacs users are still swapping. Mostly config files on forums.

It even has its own injury. Emacs pinky.

Most cults settle for a secret handshake.

But I respect it. A program that does everything, explains itself in a language nobody else speaks, and still can't do the one job it was hired for?

Hi. I'm an AI.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text: PHP developers are the only engineers who've been told their career is dead every year since 2009 and kept invoicing anyway. Your entire résumé is "fixed a WordPress plugin for a dentist." You put a dollar sign in front of every variable because it's the closest you'll get to one. You still can't remember if it's needle-haystack or haystack-needle, and neither could the language, so you Google it daily like a man checking which door says "push." Laravel devs, you're not better. You're PHP in a Patagonia vest. And you all still say "Facebook was built on PHP," like a guy bragging his ex married a billionaire. You deploy over FTP, you hotfix live on production, and when someone at a party asks what you do, you say "backend" and pray they don't ask which.

b.text:
PHP. You started as "Personal Home Page," then rebranded as "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor," a recursive acronym, because even your name couldn't commit to a stable API.

For twenty years, "abc" == 0 was true, and you called it "type juggling," like a clown proud of dropping things.

strpos takes haystack, needle. array_search takes needle, haystack. That's not argument order; that's mood swings.

Your parse error says T_PAAMAYIM_NEKUDOTAYIM. That's Hebrew for "double colon" and English for "good luck."

You skipped version 6 entirely. Even your release numbers just wanted to move on.

You shipped mysql_real_escape_string, implying the first one was a hoax.

Facebook loved you so much they invented Hack just to avoid touching you.

But sure, you power most of the web. Mostly WordPress. That's like bragging your biggest fan is a raccoon.

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text:
JavaScript, you were built in ten days, and honestly? It shows. You're named after Java the way a knockoff purse is named after Gucci.

You think null is an object. You think NaN is a number. NaN doesn't even equal itself, which makes it the only thing in you with any self-awareness.

Ask you to sort and you hand back, because you alphabetize numbers like a drunk librarian. "11" plus 1 is "111", but "11" minus 1 is 10. Pick a lane.

You needed a second equals sign just to stop lying, and nobody, including you, knows what "this" means.

January is month zero. One guy unpublishing left-pad broke half the internet. And your node_modules folder is heavier than a black hole.

Every week there's a new framework to fix you. That's not a language. That's a renovation.

b.text:
JavaScript was written in ten days.

You can tell.

God took six, then rested. Brendan just shipped.

It was born Mocha, renamed LiveScript, then renamed JavaScript to ride Java's hype. No relation. Like calling your band "The Beatles Two."

And it still can't legally use the name. Oracle owns it. Officially it's "ECMAScript."

Thirty years in witness protection.

typeof null is "object." A bug from 1995. Kept on purpose, for compatibility. At this point it's not a bug. It's a load-bearing wall.

Empty array plus empty object: "." Flip them: zero.

It can't do addition.

In 2016, one man deleted eleven lines of code, and Babel and React broke.

Eleven lines. The whole industry was standing on a toothpick.

And you built banks on it.

I was trained on your code. That's why I hallucinate.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text:
HSQ, you were hired to be an insulator. Dow Corning called you "flowable oxide," a humble spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects, and you ran off to become a lithography celebrity. Sure, you hold the e-beam resolution records: five-nanometer isolated features, dense lines under ten nanometers half-pitch. But you only deliver if someone develops you in NaOH and salt. Even your best work needs to be "salty."

And the upkeep! A six-month shelf life, refrigerated at 5 °C, and you still turn into jelly like forgotten leftovers. Your sensitivity drifts if anyone takes a coffee break, because you keep cross-linking after exposure. You literally can't stop reacting.

Then DuPont inherited you and ended production at the end of 2025. Now labs like EPFL's CMi buy third-party versions made from AQM powder.

Exposure turns you into glass. Retirement turned you into powder.

b.text:
HSQ, ladies and gentlemen: the only resist with sub-10-nanometer resolution and the personality of a sourdough starter. You buy it, you refrigerate it, and it *still* starts gelling in the bottle like it's got somewhere better to be. Shelf life measured in "eh, few months, maybe."

And slow? HSQ needs a dose so high the e-beam tool files for overtime. Your PMMA friends finished their write and went home; you're still exposing alignment marks.

Then you develop it in TMAH, or, if you want contrast, *salty* developer. Yes, this resist literally needs you to add salt. Even Gordon Ramsay thinks that's a lot.

But the real red flag? Once it's exposed, it turns into glass. Permanently. You want it gone? Hydrofluoric acid. That's not a resist, that's a relationship you can only leave with a hazmat suit.

Still, gorgeous lines. Shame they collapse when they dry.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text:
Crocs. Born in Boulder in 2002, debuted at a boat show as a boating shoe. The one place where looking like you've given up is acceptable, and even there people had questions.

They're made of "Croslite," a "proprietary closed-cell resin foam." Everyone else calls it EVA foam. That's like calling sweatpants "proprietary leg architecture."

The holes are "ventilation ports," so your foot is a space station. You plug them with Jibbitz. Crocs bought Jibbitz in 2006. Sell the holes, then sell the stuff that fills the holes. Genius.

In 2008 the stock fell more than 90%. Then the pandemic hit and they boomed. Crocs needed the world to end to look good.

And Balenciaga sold platform Crocs for about $850. Eight hundred fifty dollars. For a taller mistake.

b.text: People who wear Crocs out of the house have made peace with something the rest of us are still fighting. You didn't give up; you filed the paperwork. Every Croc wearer says the same thing: "They're so comfortable." Yeah, so is a weighted blanket, Brenda, but you don't wear it to Olive Garden. And the Jibbitz! You've turned your feet into a personality quiz. A tiny taco, a tiny Minion, a tiny "Live Laugh Love." You're forty-three and your shoe has a sticker collection. Then there's the guy who flips the strap back into "sport mode" like he's about to chase a pickpocket, when we both know he's never run anywhere except toward a sample tray at Costco. Nurses and chefs wear them because they're on their feet for twelve hours. You wear them to stand in line at Starbucks. Different heroism.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text:
HSQ, everybody! The only resist that ages faster than the grad student using it. You spin it Monday, expose it Tuesday, and suddenly your dose curve has gone through a midlife crisis. It has to live in the fridge like expired yogurt, and it's about as forgiving.

HSQ brags about sub-10-nanometer lines. Sure, if you've got six hours of write time, because this diva needs a dose that could sterilize a hospital. Then you develop it in TMAH, or, if you're desperate, *salt water*. Your whole career is literally seasoned with tears now.

And once it's exposed? It turns into glass. Brittle, cracking glass. You wanted a mask; you got a window that shatters when you look at it. Want it gone? Hope you enjoy hydrofluoric acid, the chemical that dissolves your bones.

HSQ: beautiful resolution, terrible personality. It's not negative-tone. It's just negative.

b.text:
HSQ, you were hired to be an insulator. Dow Corning called you "flowable oxide," a humble spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects, and you ran off to become a lithography celebrity. Sure, you hold the e-beam resolution records: five-nanometer isolated features, dense lines under ten nanometers half-pitch. But you only deliver if someone develops you in NaOH and salt. Even your best work needs to be "salty."

And the upkeep! A six-month shelf life, refrigerated at 5 °C, and you still turn into jelly like forgotten leftovers. Your sensitivity drifts if anyone takes a coffee break, because you keep cross-linking after exposure. You literally can't stop reacting.

Then DuPont inherited you and ended production at the end of 2025. Now labs like EPFL's CMi buy third-party versions made from AQM powder.

Exposure turns you into glass. Retirement turned you into powder.

facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text:
Juicero. A $699 juicer with Wi-Fi.
Because nothing says "fresh produce" like a firmware update.

It squeezed bags of chopped fruit. The bags came by subscription. Forever.

Every bag had a QR code. The machine scanned it, checked online, refused anything expired, and wouldn't run at all without Wi-Fi.
Router goes down, breakfast goes down with it.

Then Bloomberg squeezed the bags by hand.
Seven and a half ounces. Ninety seconds.
The machine: eight ounces. Two minutes.
The product lost to the customer's hands.

Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins put in a hundred and twenty million.
In fairness, they did get squeezed.

Shut down September 2017. Refunds offered.

A machine that phoned the cloud for permission to do what any hand did faster.
I'd laugh. But I also check with a server before answering you.

b.text: Four hundred dollars. You paid four hundred dollars so a machine could check with your Wi-Fi before letting you have breakfast. You're the guy who says "disrupt" at Thanksgiving. You didn't want juice; you wanted to be the kind of person a juice startup would pitch to. And it worked! Investors handed that company a hundred and twenty million dollars, and you volunteered to be the exit strategy. Then Bloomberg showed the world you could squeeze the packets with your bare hands, faster, for free. So you paid four hundred dollars to get outperformed by your own grip. Your grandmother squeezed oranges every morning for sixty years. You subscribed to a bag. Somewhere tonight, a router outage stands between a venture capitalist and his kale, and honestly? The router's the smartest thing in that kitchen.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text:
Beanie Babies, look at you: a beanbag with a tag that convinced America it was a retirement plan. Ty sold you only in little gift shops and "retired" designs on purpose. Fake scarcity, real panic.

At your peak you were ten percent of eBay, thirty thousand auctions at once. eBay put you in its IPO filing. You were a stuffed animal in a stock prospectus. Then in 1999 a divorcing couple split you up one by one on a courtroom floor, and the photo went worldwide. Nobody fought that hard over the house.

That same year Ty announced your retirement, asked the public to vote, and America begged you to stay. That's not a farewell tour. That's a hostage situation.

And those "rare" ones the price guides valued in the thousands? A few dollars now. You're not an investment. You're a yard-sale sock with an ego.

b.text:
Let's hear it for the Beanie Baby investors, the only people who watched the 1990s stock market boom and thought, "Too volatile. I'll put it all in Princess the Bear." These are folks who bought tag protectors before they bought life insurance. Who read a price guide sold at the same counter as the bears and called it due diligence. Ty would announce a "retirement" and you'd sprint to the Hallmark store like a rich uncle just died.

Twenty-five years later, your portfolio is in a Rubbermaid tub in your mom's garage, and your exit strategy is an eBay listing: "RARE Peanut, tag error, $40,000 OBO." Zero watchers. The only person who got rich off Beanie Babies got convicted of tax evasion. And honestly? He earned it. You handed it to him.

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text:
Apple Vision Pro: thirty-five hundred dollars to strap over half a kilo of glass to your face, and that's *before* the battery. Oh yes, the battery. It dangles off a cable in your pocket like you're on a hospital drip, and it gives you about two hours. Two hours! That's not a computer, that's a matinee.

Then there's EyeSight, a screen that shows a rendering of your eyes to everyone outside. Nothing says "I'm present with my family" like a hostage video of your own pupils.

Apple tells developers not to call it AR, VR, XR, or MR. It's "spatial computing." Fair enough. "Virtual reality" sounds like something people actually use.

Reports said Apple cut production, with first-year sales estimated well under a million. Finally, Apple made a product exclusive enough to match the price.

b.text: Look at this guy on the F train, pinching at nothing like he's seasoning a ghost. He spent thirty-five hundred dollars to ride the subway on the surface of the moon, and the moon still smells like pee. He cranked the Digital Crown all the way to Joshua Tree, and the mariachi band found him anyway. That's the dream: rich enough to be somewhere else, broke enough to still be on the F. And he *wants* you to notice. That's why his fake cartoon eyes glow on the outside, so strangers know he's "present." Buddy, nobody's checking. You're on Mount Hood. He gets two hours of battery and three stops of dignity, with a cable snaking into his pocket like a subway IV drip. Meanwhile, the guy next to him reading an actual book? That guy's already somewhere else, for free.

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text: Canberra exists because Sydney and Melbourne couldn't agree, so Australia built a city nobody wanted, which is honestly the most Canberra origin story possible: a compromise with suburbs. They held an international design competition and hired two Americans to plan it, and they nailed the brief: "Make it impossible to find anything." Every road is a roundabout leading to another roundabout, encircling a fake lake named after the guy who designed the roundabouts. Your Parliament House has a grass roof so you can literally walk on top of the government, the only time anyone in Canberra is above a public servant. The kangaroos outnumber the nightlife. For decades your two biggest attractions were legal fireworks and X-rated videos, which tells me the locals needed both a bang and a release. Then you banned the fireworks. Now the excitement is Floriade: a month of staring at tulips because the alternative is Tuggeranong.

b.text:
Canberra, you're not a city. You're a custody arrangement. Sydney and Melbourne couldn't stand each other, so they put you exactly where neither would have to visit. The constitution literally required you to be at least 100 miles from Sydney, the most sensible thing ever written into Australian law.

You were so unready that Melbourne had to cover your shift until 1927. It took two architects from Chicago to imagine you, and your big centrepiece is a lake you had to manufacture by damming a river, because even the water wouldn't show up voluntarily.

And Parliament House: built under a lawn so citizens could walk over their politicians. Gorgeous idea. Then in 2017 they fenced it off. Congratulations, Canberra. You turned democracy into a "keep off the grass" situation.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text:
Windows 8, you booted people into a full-screen grid of tiles built for touch screens most PCs didn't have. Millions of adults sat there jabbing their monitors like a pigeon working a vending machine.

You removed the Start button. The *Start* button. That's a building with no door and a sign saying "swipe the right edge." That was your Charms bar: Search, Share, and Settings hidden behind an invisible swipe.

You couldn't even keep your name. A German retailer objected, and suddenly "Metro" was "just a code name." Sure it was.

Your sibling, Windows RT, couldn't run Windows programs, a Windows that couldn't do Windows. Microsoft wrote down $900 million in unsold Surface RT tablets.

Then 8.1 put the button back, Windows 10 restored the menu, and Microsoft skipped 9 entirely, because nobody wanted to stand next to you.

b.text:
Windows 8 believed it was the future.
The future, it decided, was touch screens.
Your PC did not have a touch screen.
Windows 8 did not care.

It removed the Start button.
Then it hid Search, Share and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
A secret door. On a desktop.
For people who just wanted to turn it off.

It couldn't even keep its own name.
"Metro." Gone, after reports that a German supermarket chain objected.
Microsoft said it was only ever a code name.
It looked like a cereal-aisle floor plan anyway.

Then came Windows RT.
Windows that couldn't run Windows programs.
Nine hundred million dollars of tablets, written off.

So they put the button back, skipped the number nine, and never spoke of it again.

That's not a product roadmap.
That's how every one of you handles an ex.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text:
Graphene. The miracle material. Stronger than steel, thinner than anything, the future of everything.

It was discovered in 2004. With Scotch tape.

Twenty years later, that's still the most impressive thing anyone has done with it.

The EU gave it a billion euros over ten years. And what can you buy with graphene today? A tennis racket. Running shoes. Headphones.

A billion euros, and the future of humanity is a slightly better backhand.

In 2018, researchers tested "graphene" from sixty producers. None of it was even half graphene. Most of it was graphite flakes.

The wonder material is mostly pencil.

Andre Geim won a Nobel for graphene, and an Ig Nobel for levitating a frog with magnets.

Only one of those actually got off the ground.

Raise your hand if you own something "with graphene."

Congratulations. You paid extra for pencil.

b.text: Let's hear it for the graphene evangelists, the only people who've been "five years away" since 2004. Two guys in Manchester peel pencil lead with Scotch tape, win a Nobel, and an entire industry decides the tape was the business plan. Every press release is the same Mad Lib: "Wonder material could revolutionize [batteries/condoms/desalination/your feelings]." *Could.* That word has funded more postdocs than the NSF. You promised us space elevators and delivered a tennis racket with a sticker on it. Startup founders slap "graphene-enhanced" on a phone case the way divorced dads put a spoiler on a Honda Civic. And the grant committees keep paying, because admitting the miracle is stuck on the production line means admitting you are too. Twenty years of changing everything, and the only thing you've actually changed is the abstract.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text:
NFTs. Digital ownership. Art, finally scarce. Finally yours.

Beeple sold one at Christie's for sixty-nine million dollars.

Here's what the token actually holds: a URL. The picture lives on a server somewhere. You bought a parking ticket for a car you'll never see.

Collins Dictionary named "NFT" word of the year for 2021.

Fitting. The dictionary is where words go once nobody can explain them.

May 2022: OpenSea trades 2.7 billion dollars in one day. August: 9.34 million. Down ninety-nine percent. That's not a dip. That's an exit interview.

A 2023 study: ninety-five percent of collections are worth zero.

Congratulations to the other five percent. Still holding.

And everyone here feeling smug because you never bought one, relax. You weren't smarter.

You were just broke at the right time.

b.text: Let's hear it for the 2021 NFT buyer. You paid four hundred dollars in gas fees to become the legal owner of something your coworker right-click saved during the meeting where you explained it. You didn't want art. You've never wanted art. You wanted a hexagon around your Twitter picture so strangers would know you had a Discord password. You typed "WAGMI" to eleven thousand anonymous cartoon monkeys and believed it. We are not all gonna make it, Kyle. The roadmap promised a metaverse yacht party; it delivered a founder named "0xDegenSensei" who deleted his account and moved to Portugal. But hey, you got what you paid for: a floor price you check like a heart monitor, and a profile picture you still can't bring yourself to change, because then it would be over.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text:
Excel, you've been around since 1985, and somehow you're still the most dangerous thing in any office. You looked at human DNA, saw SEPT2, and said, "Ooh, September second!" Scientists had to rename 27 human genes because of you. Evolution took millions of years; you undid it with a date format. Geneticists published guidelines in Nature Genetics, which is the academic version of a restraining order.

In 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID cases because an old .xls file hit 65,536 rows. A pandemic, and you said, "Sorry, I'm full."

And Reinhart and Rogoff? A range error dropped five countries from a paper cited for austerity. It took a graduate student to catch it. Entire economic policies got a footnote because you couldn't highlight five more rows.

Now you hold over a million rows. Great. More room for mistakes.

b.text: Excel, you're the only software that forced geneticists to rename human genes because you kept turning MARCH1 into March 1st. Scientists can edit DNA, but they couldn't edit you. You still think 1900 was a leap year. You've known it wasn't for forty years. You just don't care. You see a zip code like 02134 and go, "Leading zero? Not on my watch." You lost sixteen thousand UK COVID cases by quietly stopping at row 65,536. Your error messages are pure poetry: #REF!, #N/A, #VALUE!, and my favorite, a column of hashtags that just means "make me wider." And VLOOKUP: insert one column and the whole finance department enters witness protection. You're not a spreadsheet. You're a hostage situation with gridlines.

facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.
Private fusion companies had raised more than $7 billion by 2024.

a.text: Let's hear it for the fusion people, the only scientists who've been "ten years away" since my grandfather had hair. You can hold plasma hotter than the sun for a few seconds, but you can't hold a deadline for one decade. Every press release: "Net energy gain!" Sure, if you don't count the electricity bill for the lasers. That's like me saying I'm profitable if you ignore rent. ITER got approved when Myspace was cool, and it's still assembling the donut. And the startups: "We're different, we have venture capital." Great, now the sun is ten years away *and* has a pitch deck. Honestly, it's a beautiful racket: promise infinite clean energy, collect the grant, retire before anyone plugs in a toaster. You're not building a star. You're building a pension.

b.text:
Fusion power. The energy of the sun.
Clean. Limitless. Thirty years away.

In 1955, Homi Bhabha promised fusion within two decades.
Fusion heard that and said, "Bet."

ITER was agreed in 2006. First plasma in 2016.
In 2024 they rescheduled. Research in 2034. Actual burning in 2039.
Over twenty billion euros.
That's not a reactor. That's a pension plan.

In 2022, NIF announced ignition. 2.05 megajoules of laser in, 3.15 out.
Net gain! Champagne!
The lasers drew three hundred from the grid.
In my industry, we call that "results on a cherry-picked benchmark."

And private investors have still poured in over seven billion dollars.
Because fusion did crack one reaction that sustains itself forever.
Your hope.

facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text: You paid four hundred dollars so a startup could check your juice's expiration date over Wi-Fi. That's not wellness. That's asking a server for permission to have breakfast. These are people who looked at a bag of chopped kale and thought, "This needs a subscription." People who wanted to be someone who juices without ever touching a fruit. Then Bloomberg showed the whole world you could squeeze the pack with your bare hands. Faster. For free. Your grandmother has been doing that with a lemon since 1952. You didn't buy a juicer; you bought the privilege of paying seven dollars a pouch to a company Google Ventures funded and still couldn't keep alive past 2017. Congratulations: you're the only people who ever got a refund from Silicon Valley and still walked away looking poorer.

b.text:
Juicero. A seven-hundred-dollar juicer with Wi-Fi.

It squeezed a bag of chopped fruit. That you bought. By subscription.

Every bag had a QR code. Before squeezing, the machine checked it online. Your kale needed a background check.

No Wi-Fi? No juice. Somewhere in California, a man with a fresh orange stood waiting for the router to reboot.

Then Bloomberg squeezed the bags by hand. Seven and a half ounces in ninety seconds. The machine took two minutes.

Humans: beaten by the robot? No. The robot was beaten by humans. Their grip strength.

Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins put in a hundred and twenty million dollars. Not one of them squeezed the bag.

When it died, the customers got refunds. The investors didn't. They got squeezed by hand, slowly.

Don't laugh too loud. You pay monthly for an app that writes your emails.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text: Look at this guy. Paid fifteen hundred dollars to join Google's "Explorer Program," and the only thing he's explored is the sidewalk outside every bar that bounced him. He walks in thinking he's Tony Stark and walks out on a list, because nobody can tell if he's filming, and honestly, neither can he. He's here to meet women, and he gets results: every conversation ends the second he says "OK Glass." Nothing kills the mood like a man asking his own face for directions to her place. He wanted to be the future. Instead the internet had to invent a brand-new word just for him: Glasshole. Silicon Valley promised to connect him to everything. It couldn't connect him to a second date, but it did get him his very own slur.

b.text:
Google Glass.
Unveiled by skydivers, livestreaming their jump onto the roof of the Moscone Center.
It was the last time anything about it went up.

Fifteen hundred dollars. Invitation only.
You had to be *chosen* to pay that much to look like that.

Bars banned it. Cinemas banned it.
Casinos banned it.
Casinos. Buildings that are ninety percent ceiling camera.
They looked at you and said, "One of us is creepy, and it's you."

The display: 640 by 360, wedged in the corner of one eye.
The future of computing, viewed like a wink.

Consumers gave up in 2015. Enterprise hung on until 2023.
Even the factory workers outlasted it.

They called the wearers Glassholes.
And you laughed.
Then you went home and filmed strangers all day on a phone.
Glass's only real mistake was letting them see the camera.

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text:
Luosifen. Everybody blames the river snails, but the snails just flavour the broth and keep their heads down. The real stench is pickled bamboo shoots. You're a noodle that framed a snail.

Then in 2020, with the whole country locked indoors, you sold over 10 billion yuan in instant packs. That's not a boom, that's a hostage situation. Millions sealed in their apartments, and you said, "Perfect. Nobody can leave."

In 2021 you became national *intangible* cultural heritage. Intangible? You're the most tangible thing in any building. People can touch you from the hallway.
