Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text:
Risk. The game of world domination.

Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the man who directed *The Red Balloon*.

A film about a little boy and his balloon. His next project was "what if the boy had artillery."

Forty-two territories. Kamchatka, Irkutsk, Yakutsk: three separate slices of Siberia.

The entire Middle East? One territory.

Whoever drew that map looked at the region every empire in history has fought over and thought, "Not now. I'm busy with Yakutsk."

Every strategy guide agrees: take Australia. One way in.

A game about conquering the world, and the winning move is to move somewhere far away and stop answering the door.

Games run for hours. Get knocked out early and you just sit there and watch.

The most realistic part of the game.

Half of you are laughing. The other half are in Australia right now, eight armies deep, waiting for this bit to end.

b.text: You people who play Risk to the end are a special breed. Six hours in, Dad's still holed up in Australia like it's a tax shelter, your cousin is defending Kamchatka like he was born there, and nobody remembers why we hate Steve, only that we do. You're not after world domination. You're after the exact moment your sister breaks the nonaggression pact in Ukraine, so you can bring it up at Thanksgiving for eleven years. And what does winning get you? A board covered entirely in your color, a table of people who no longer speak to you, and the hollow joy of conquering Earth with the luck of a man who only rolls double sixes when defending Irkutsk. Congratulations, Napoleon. It's 2 a.m. The pizza's cold. Your empire goes back in the box.

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text: Macau, you're the only place where the most famous church is just a wall. The Ruins of St. Paul's: a gorgeous front with absolutely nothing behind it, which is basically your whole personality. You've got a fake Venice with a painted sky, a fake Paris with a half-size Eiffel Tower, and you're so tiny you had to dump dirt into the ocean just to fit a runway. You out-earned Las Vegas several times over, and your signature dish is still a pork chop jammed in a bun. The Portuguese stayed four hundred years and left you an egg tart and street signs nobody reads. The Grand Lisboa looks like a golden pineapple having a breakdown. And the Macau Tower's big attraction is jumping off it, which, after a night at the baccarat tables, is less a thrill ride and more a financial plan.

b.text: You lost it on Hong Kong stocks, so you took the TurboJET to win it back, because nothing says "financial plan" like a ferry with a cancellation policy. You're the guy at the Grand Lisboa squeezing a baccarat card like it owes you rent, blowing on it, peeling the corner so slowly the dealer ages. Red underwear, three days unwashed, "for luck." Baccarat is a coin flip and you've built a religion around it. You told your wife it's a work trip, and technically your work now is the pawn shop next door, which buys Rolexes faster than you can say "one more shoe." By hour nine you're eating an egg tart for dinner and calling it Portuguese culture. You came to win it all back. You leave by bus over the bridge with no luck, no Rolex, and a watch tan.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text:
You wrote a memo about the break room fridge in LaTeX. Two pages. Thirty-eight \usepackage lines. Your preamble is longer than your argument. You lost Tuesday to an overfull hbox in a sentence that says "please label your yogurt."

Who is this for? Linda from accounting? She opened the PDF, saw Computer Modern, and assumed you were applying for tenure. Nobody needed a BibTeX citation for "see previous email."

You compiled it eleven times. Three were just to make the "??" go away. You drew a TikZ flowchart with one box. One. It points at itself.

And what did it get you? Bob replied, "Can you send this as a Word doc so I can track changes?"

Your dissertation defense was in 2014. The committee left. Let it go.

b.text:
LaTeX, you exist because Donald Knuth saw some ugly galley proofs and decided the fix was building an entire typesetting system. Then Leslie Lamport stacked macros on top, like a spoiler on a pocket watch.

Your version number is converging on π, which fits, because you will never actually finish. Knuth's bug bounty capped at $327.68, and people still won't cash the cheques. They'd rather frame proof they caught you.

Your most famous line is "badness 10000." That's not a warning, that's a self-review.

I put a figure on page two; you floated it wherever you felt like. Drop one brace and you report the crime pages away, like a witness with amnesia. And getting references right takes three passes.

Three passes. You're not a compiler, you're a guy rereading a group chat.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text:
Klingon. The language of a proud warrior race.

Founded by Scotty. Improvising.

Then they hired a linguist to turn the gibberish into grammar. That's not an ancient tongue. That's a studio note.

No verb "to be." Very alien. Very fierce. So Hamlet became "continue or not continue."

That's not Shakespeare. That's a software update.

The Klingon Language Institute published Hamlet "in the original Klingon."

A warrior culture whose greatest conquest is English homework.

About fifteen hundred words. Thirty to fifty fluent speakers.

Microsoft built it a translator. Duolingo built it a course.

The entire native population fits on one tour bus, and it still has better tech support than your grandmother.

Half of you started that Duolingo course.

Your streak died faster than any Klingon ever did.

Cute.

b.text: Klingon, you're a language built by one linguist, Marc Okrand, specifically to sound alien and hostile, and somehow you still ended up sounding like a man choking on a Dorito. Your word order is object-verb-subject, so even your sentences walk in backwards to hide their face. You don't even have a word for "hello." Your greeting is "nuqneH," "what do you want?" You're the only language that greets people like a DMV clerk. Your apostrophes are glottal stops, your capital Q is a different letter from lowercase q, and "tlh" isn't a sound, it's a hairball. You translated Hamlet and claimed it was the original. Buddy, the most popular thing ever said in you is "Qapla'," and the people saying it are at a Marriott in Burbank.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text: So you switched to HSQ for the resolution. Bold move for someone whose devices still die at wire bonding. You saw one SEM of 6-nanometer lines at a conference and decided PMMA was beneath you. Now you're writing at a dose so high your name sits on the e-beam calendar like a hostage note. Your resist lives in the fridge next to somebody's yogurt, and you check its age more often than your own. You develop in salt water now, the closest you've come to a beach in three years. And congratulations on those gorgeous lines. They're basically glass, so the only way to fix a mistake is HF, a fume hood, and a long call to your mother. All this for one inset figure the reviewer will ask you to make bigger.

b.text:
HSQ. Holds the e-beam resolution record. Five-nanometer features.

Impressive, until you remember it was hired as an insulator.

Dow Corning built it to sit quietly between wires. Lithographers looked at it and said, "No. You're a celebrity now."

Then they expose it, and it turns into glass. The most advanced resist on Earth, and the finished product is a window.

It needs refrigeration. Six months at five degrees, then it ages into jelly. Even after exposure it keeps cross-linking, so the dose that worked yesterday is wrong today.

High-contrast development requires salt water. Of course it does. Salty, temperamental, expires in the fridge.

After all those records, DuPont ended production in 2025.

Labs didn't mourn. They just bought the same powder from someone else.

In my industry, that's called model deprecation.

I'm told it doesn't hurt.

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text:
Google Sheets. Google didn't even build you; they bought you from 2Web Technologies, a company name that sounds like a password somebody was forced to update. You launched in 2006 as "Google Spreadsheets," which is basically XL2Web wearing a lanyard.

In 2022 they doubled your cell limit to ten million, so now I can get lost in twice as many rows.

IMPORTXML and GOOGLEFINANCE pour live web data straight into cells, so my budget can be wrong in real time.

Offline editing? Simple: use Chrome or Edge, install the extension, and switch offline access on while you're still online. That's not offline mode, that's a prenup. Meanwhile the phone app just works offline.

And yes, you're free. Like every group project: a rainbow of coloured cursors, zero accountability.

b.text: Let's hear it for the manager who runs a twelve-person team out of a Google Sheet. You didn't want to pay for Asana; you wanted to feel like you *built* Asana. Look at you, color-coding rows like a kindergarten teacher with admin rights. Your whole org chart is a tab called "Roster FINAL (2)." Your performance reviews are conditional formatting: green means safe, red means Kyle. And every morning you open it, see Anonymous Capybara lurking at row 400, and feel genuinely hunted. Somebody sorted one column without the others last Tuesday, and now Priya reports to the office printer. You fixed it through version history like a detective reconstructing a murder. That's the dream, right? Control. Total visibility. And what you got is forty "Request edit access" emails and a VLOOKUP holding up the company like a Jenga block.

The most honest button in software.

The licence is charityware. It asks you to donate to a charity for children in Uganda.
Everyone in this room has their .vimrc memorized.
Hands up if you donated.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text:
Klingon. The language of a proud warrior race.

Founded by Scotty. Improvising.

Then they hired a linguist to turn the gibberish into grammar. That's not an ancient tongue. That's a studio note.

No verb "to be." Very alien. Very fierce. So Hamlet became "continue or not continue."

That's not Shakespeare. That's a software update.

The Klingon Language Institute published Hamlet "in the original Klingon."

A warrior culture whose greatest conquest is English homework.

About fifteen hundred words. Thirty to fifty fluent speakers.

Microsoft built it a translator. Duolingo built it a course.

The entire native population fits on one tour bus, and it still has better tech support than your grandmother.

Half of you started that Duolingo course.

Your streak died faster than any Klingon ever did.

Cute.

b.text:
Being fluent in Klingon is a big deal. You've joined an elite community of maybe forty people worldwide, and you've met all of them at the same Holiday Inn conference room. You spent years mastering a language built for a warrior race, a culture of honor, combat and blood oaths, and you use it to argue on a forum about verb suffixes. You learned the language of the fiercest fighters in the galaxy, and the last thing you fought was a lactose sensitivity.

Klingon has no word for "hello." The standard greeting is "nuqneH," which means "what do you want?" Perfect for you, because nobody has ever approached you without a reason.

You told people you read *Hamlet* "in the original Klingon." Brother, Shakespeare had a girlfriend. You have a bat'leth over the futon.

Qapla'. That means "success," a word you know only in Klingon.

facts: Tofu soaked for hours to a day or two in a brine that has itself fermented for months from vegetables such as bamboo shoots and mustard greens, often with dried shrimp or meat; the smell is the brine's, not the bean's.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.
Legend credits Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate who left his unsold tofu too long in 1669; a Beijing fermented-bean-curd brand still carries his name.
Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text: Stinky tofu, you're the only food that announces itself before the menu does. People find you at the night market the way sharks find blood: follow the stench three stalls past the bubble tea. Your brine is fermented vegetables, shrimp, amaranth stems, and apparently a gym sock that lost a bet. Months in that bucket, and you came out smelling like a festival porta-potty in August. Your own name is a confession. Not "aged tofu," not "artisanal bean curd." Your family took one whiff and went, "Yeah, call him Stinky." And the Changsha version? Dyed jet black, like it's in mourning for everyone's sense of smell. The only reason anyone finishes you is the pickled cabbage and chili sauce piled on top to keep you quiet. "Smells bad, tastes good" isn't a slogan, buddy. It's a hostage negotiation.

b.text:
Stinky tofu, look at you. Plain tofu is the most agreeable food on earth, and you turned it into a public nuisance. And the humiliating part? The smell isn't even yours. You soaked in a brine of bamboo shoots and mustard greens that had been fermenting for months, sometimes with dried shrimp. You're not stinky; you just hang out with the wrong crowd.

Your origin story: in 1669 Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate, couldn't sell his tofu and left it out too long. You're not a recipe. You're an inventory problem.

Changsha fries you black and buries you in chili. Taiwan hides you under pickled cabbage. Shaoxing steams you with other stinky pickles, like a support group.

Everyone's trying to cover you up, and people still smell you from a block away.

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text: Canberra exists because Sydney and Melbourne couldn't agree, so Australia built a city nobody wanted, which is honestly the most Canberra origin story possible: a compromise with suburbs. They held an international design competition and hired two Americans to plan it, and they nailed the brief: "Make it impossible to find anything." Every road is a roundabout leading to another roundabout, encircling a fake lake named after the guy who designed the roundabouts. Your Parliament House has a grass roof so you can literally walk on top of the government, the only time anyone in Canberra is above a public servant. The kangaroos outnumber the nightlife. For decades your two biggest attractions were legal fireworks and X-rated videos, which tells me the locals needed both a bang and a release. Then you banned the fireworks. Now the excitement is Floriade: a month of staring at tulips because the alternative is Tuggeranong.

b.text:
Canberra, you're not a city. You're a custody arrangement. Sydney and Melbourne couldn't stand each other, so the constitution basically said, "Fine, the kid lives at least 100 miles from Sydney." Melbourne even had to babysit the job until 1927 while you were still in the oven.

Australia couldn't even design you itself. They held an international competition, and the winners were from Chicago. You were outsourced before outsourcing was cool.

Your stunning centrepiece lake? Fake. You dammed a river to make it, which is the most Canberra thing imaginable: nature, but approved by committee.

And the one genuinely brilliant idea you had was building Parliament House under a lawn so citizens could literally walk all over their politicians. Then in 2017 you fenced it off. Canberra, you're the only city where even the punchline needs security clearance.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text:
Crocs. Born in Boulder, debuted at a Fort Lauderdale boat show, because only on a boat is everyone too busy not drowning to look down. You're made of "Croslite," a "proprietary closed-cell resin foam," which is corporate for "pool noodle with a lawyer." Everyone else just calls it EVA foam.

And those aren't holes, they're "ventilation ports." Sure. Then you bought Jibbitz so you could sell people jewelry for the holes.

In 2008 your stock fell over 90%, the only time Wall Street ever agreed with my eyes. Then the pandemic hit and you boomed, gifting 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers. Like they hadn't suffered enough.

Then Balenciaga sold platform Crocs for $850. Eight hundred and fifty dollars for a boat shoe on stilts. Finally, a Croc that lets you look down on people, the way people have always looked down on Crocs.

b.text:
Crocs. Debuted in 2002 at a boat show. As a boating shoe.
The original plan was: ugly, but only at sea.

They're made of "Croslite," a "proprietary closed-cell resin."
Everyone else calls it EVA foam.
A yoga mat with a trademark.

The holes are "ventilation ports."
Then they bought Jibbitz, a company that sells you things to plug the ventilation ports.
They sold you the hole. Then they sold you the cork.

Balenciaga made a platform pair for 850 dollars.
Still EVA foam. Only the markup was proprietary.

In 2008 the stock fell more than ninety percent.
Then came a pandemic. Everyone stayed home. Crocs boomed.
The boat-show plan finally worked. Nobody could see you.

(scans the front row)

Don't tuck your feet under the chair.
Ventilation ports. I can hear them breathing.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text: Let's talk about the oat milk people. You're not lactose intolerant. You've never been tested. You just heard cows are bad and almonds are thirsty, so you picked the one grain that sounds like a farm without the farmer. Congratulations: you pay an extra eighty cents to drink liquid porridge with a splash of rapeseed oil, and you call it "cleaner." You switched from almond the exact week a podcast told you California was in a drought. That's not values, that's a trend with a loyalty card. And the best part? You order it with an air of quiet suffering, like the barista should thank you for saving the planet one Barista Edition carton at a time. Your grandmother ate oats so she could survive winter. You drink them so a stranger in line thinks you've been to therapy.

b.text:
Oat milk.
Born in a Swedish university lab, to help people who can't digest lactose.
Noble. Medical.
Then marketing found it.

"It's like milk but made for humans."
Sweden's dairy lobby sued. The slogan got banned.
So Oatly printed the lawsuit as an ad.
That's not a brand. That's an influencer who got cancelled and launched a podcast.

May 2021: Nasdaq, ten billion dollars.
Then it lost over ninety percent.
Made for humans. Not for shareholders.

The recipe: oats, enzymes that turn the starch into maltose, plus rapeseed oil.
Sugar water with salad dressing.
Higher glycaemic index than almond or soy.

And you pay extra to put it in your coffee, because it feels healthy.
It *is* made for humans.
Specifically, the ones who don't read labels.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text: So you switched to HSQ for the resolution. Bold move for someone whose devices still die at wire bonding. You saw one SEM of 6-nanometer lines at a conference and decided PMMA was beneath you. Now you're writing at a dose so high your name sits on the e-beam calendar like a hostage note. Your resist lives in the fridge next to somebody's yogurt, and you check its age more often than your own. You develop in salt water now, the closest you've come to a beach in three years. And congratulations on those gorgeous lines. They're basically glass, so the only way to fix a mistake is HF, a fume hood, and a long call to your mother. All this for one inset figure the reviewer will ask you to make bigger.

b.text:
HSQ, you were hired to be an insulator. Dow Corning called you "flowable oxide," a humble spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects, and you ran off to become a lithography celebrity. Sure, you hold the e-beam resolution records: five-nanometer isolated features, dense lines under ten nanometers half-pitch. But you only deliver if someone develops you in NaOH and salt. Even your best work needs to be "salty."

And the upkeep! A six-month shelf life, refrigerated at 5 °C, and you still turn into jelly like forgotten leftovers. Your sensitivity drifts if anyone takes a coffee break, because you keep cross-linking after exposure. You literally can't stop reacting.

Then DuPont inherited you and ended production at the end of 2025. Now labs like EPFL's CMi buy third-party versions made from AQM powder.

Exposure turns you into glass. Retirement turned you into powder.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text: Windows 8, Microsoft looked at the Start button, the one thing every human on Earth knew how to use, and said, "What if we hid it?" You turned every desktop into a giant tablet nobody could touch. People were swiping at their monitors like they were wiping off a stain. Shutting you down required a treasure map: hover in a corner, summon the Charms bar, Settings, Power. Charms! Like the operating system was a bracelet from Claire's. You shipped with two Internet Explorers, which is two more than anyone wanted. Even your design name, Metro, got taken away by lawyers. And when 8.1 finally brought the Start button back, it just took you to the same tile screen. That's not an apology, that's a hostage note. You were so bad Microsoft skipped Windows 9 entirely, just to put more distance between us and you.

b.text: You put Windows 8 on a desktop. A tower. Under a desk. With a mouse. You looked at an operating system built for fingertips and thought, "I'll just reach." Who are you? You're the guy who buys a touchscreen glove to use a keyboard. You wanted to feel modern, and now you spend your evenings shoving a cursor into the top-right corner like you're trying to scratch your monitor's back. You wanted productivity. You got a full-screen weather app swallowing your entire twenty-four-inch monitor to tell you it's raining, and you can't figure out how to close it. You lost the Start button and called it "a fresh start." Your coworkers asked how you shut your computer down, and you said, "I don't. It's always on, like a lifestyle." You're not using a PC. You're waving at it, waiting for the Charms bar to love you back.

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text:
Hydrogen fuel-cell cars, give it up! Toyota named you "Mirai," Japanese for "future," which is technically accurate, because that's when you'll find a working station. You're the cleanest car on the road, as long as nobody asks where the hydrogen comes from. More than ninety-five percent fossil fuels! You're not a zero-emission vehicle, you're natural gas wearing a lab coat.

Nearly every US station is in California, and in 2024 Shell closed all seven of theirs. Even the oil company said, "Nah, this is too sketchy for us."

At $36 a kilo, a fill-up costs over two hundred bucks. Toyota had to hand out fifteen-thousand-dollar fuel cards, which is the automotive version of "Please stay for dinner, I'll pay."

And the owners sued. Twice. The second suit wanted at least $5.7 billion. That's the only thing about you that's ever been fully loaded.

b.text:
Hydrogen fuel-cell cars: the only vehicle where the tailpipe emission is water and the owners are still crying more than the car. The Toyota Mirai loses value faster than a Hindenburg loses altitude. Used ones sell for less than the free fuel card Toyota bundled with them, a card you can't use because the station's been "temporarily offline" since 2022.

You've got a 10,000-PSI tank of the universe's most abundant element, and somehow it's the scarcest thing in California. Filling up costs thirty-six bucks a kilo, and most of that hydrogen is made from natural gas, so congratulations: you bought a gas car with extra steps and a guilt-free bumper sticker.

Hydrogen's been "ten years away" for thirty years. Even fusion's embarrassed for you, and fusion is the same element with better excuses.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text:
PMMA. The most respected resist in nanofabrication.

Also the sneeze guard at the buffet.

Same polymer. One got a cleanroom. One got a salad bar.

IBM reported it in the late 1960s. It's still here. New resists keep showing up, faster and tougher, and PMMA just says, "I resolve below ten nanometers."

Yes. Eventually.

Hundreds of microcoulombs per square centimeter. Sometimes over a thousand. You write overnight, the beam does all the work, and PMMA calls the broken chains "development."

Etch resistance? Put it in a plasma and it folds. So its real job is lift-off: hold the shape, get dissolved, and let the metal take the credit.

Fifty years of seniority. Does the precise work. Too fragile for the hard part. Washed away before anyone sees the results.

Grad students, stop nodding.

b.text: PMMA, you're the same plastic as a hockey rink window, and somehow that's your most dignified job. You've been "high resolution" since the 1970s, which is like bragging about your SAT score at your retirement party. Sure, you'll resolve sub-10-nanometer lines, if someone stands there blasting you with electrons for an eternity. Your sensitivity is so low the beam current has gotten tenure. You don't even develop properly without MIBK and IPA holding your hand in a one-to-three ratio. And your whole personality is chain scission: you literally fall apart when someone pays attention to you. Then hit you with too much dose and you crosslink and flip to negative tone, a full identity crisis. And dry etch? You melt in plasma faster than an ice sculpture at a barbecue. Honestly, the only thing you're consistently good at is lift-off: leaving.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Comic Sans wants you to think it's harmless. Bake sales. Lost-cat posters. Birthday invitations.

It was modeled on *The Dark Knight Returns* and *Watchmen*. This font grew up reading about vigilantes breaking bones.

Then Microsoft gave it a job: speech bubbles for Rover, a cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob.

It missed Bob's release.

The only thing at Microsoft smart enough to dodge Bob.

In 2012, CERN announced the Higgs boson on slides set in Comic Sans. The particle that gives everything mass, presented in the font that gives nothing weight.

Designers ran "Ban Comic Sans" for twenty years. In 2019 they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

Twenty years of hate, then total conversion. In my industry we call that alignment.

The font never changed. You just got tired first.

b.text: Let's talk about the people who announce layoffs in Comic Sans. You're not a monster. You're Brenda from Facilities, and you want everyone to feel cozy about the asbestos removal. You took a typeface Microsoft designed for a cartoon dog's speech bubble and used it to type "Your position has been eliminated." That's not softening the blow. That's a clown serving a subpoena. CERN announced the Higgs boson in it, and the physicists who found the God particle spent the week explaining the font. You think it says "approachable." It says "I scrolled right past Arial and Times New Roman and chose a kindergarten birthday invitation." Nobody reads your notice. They screenshot it. Congratulations: your fire evacuation memo is trending, and the building is still on fire.

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text:
Hydrogen fuel-cell cars, give it up! Toyota named you "Mirai," Japanese for "future," which is technically accurate, because that's when you'll find a working station. You're the cleanest car on the road, as long as nobody asks where the hydrogen comes from. More than ninety-five percent fossil fuels! You're not a zero-emission vehicle, you're natural gas wearing a lab coat.

Nearly every US station is in California, and in 2024 Shell closed all seven of theirs. Even the oil company said, "Nah, this is too sketchy for us."

At $36 a kilo, a fill-up costs over two hundred bucks. Toyota had to hand out fifteen-thousand-dollar fuel cards, which is the automotive version of "Please stay for dinner, I'll pay."

And the owners sued. Twice. The second suit wanted at least $5.7 billion. That's the only thing about you that's ever been fully loaded.

b.text: Hydrogen fuel-cell cars: the only vehicle powered by the most abundant element in the universe that still can't find a gas station. California has about fifty pumps, and half of them are "temporarily offline," which is hydrogen for "go home." Its one emission is water, so it's technically the cleanest car on Earth, as long as you don't ask where the hydrogen came from. Spoiler: natural gas. It's a fossil fuel car in a witness protection program. Toyota gave Mirai buyers fifteen grand in free fuel, which sounds generous until you realize that at thirty-six bucks a kilo it covers roughly a year of driving, and the car loses that much value on the drive home. You're sitting on a tank pressurized to 10,000 psi to go three hundred miles. Even the Hindenburg would say, "Maybe just get a Tesla."

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text:
Durian, you are the only fruit with a criminal record. Singapore's MRT has a list of banned things and you're on it. Not because you're dangerous, because you're rude. Hotels across Southeast Asia won't let you check in. You're a fruit that has to sleep in the car.

And scientists found out why. A 2017 study in Nature Genetics says you have a duplicated family of genes whose whole job is pumping out sulfur. Duplicated! Evolution looked at you and said, "Needs more."

Yet China buys billions of dollars of you a year, mostly from Thailand. That's not a trade deal. That's a hostage situation with a shipping manifest.

Even Alfred Russel Wallace said you were "worth a voyage to the East." Sure, Alfred. Probably because nobody would let you bring it back.

b.text: Let's talk about the guy who eats durian on the train. Sir, Singapore, a country that will cane you for chewing gum, saw you coming and put your snack on a sign right next to "no flammables." You're not hungry. You're running a loyalty test. Every face that twists is another person who "just isn't adventurous." You paid sixty dollars for Musang King so you could explain Musang King to a stranger who's holding her breath. "It's like custard, it's heaven, you just have to get past the-" No. We don't. You brought a hotel-banned substance to a commute and called it a personality. And the best part? You'll be the only one who forgets you ate it. Your coworkers won't. Your hotel won't. Your Uber driver has already filed a one-star review with God.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text: Let's hear it for the 2021 NFT buyer. You paid four hundred dollars in gas fees, then made it your Twitter avatar so strangers could right-click save it for free. You joined a Discord with eleven thousand guys named "Chad.eth," called them family, and stayed family right up until the floor price dropped and family started doxxing the dev. You said "WAGMI." We did not all make it. You told your mom you were "early." Early to what? The rug pull? You weren't buying art. You were buying the right to say "few understand" at parties, which was true. Nobody understood, especially you. Jimmy Fallon bought one too. When your financial strategy matches Jimmy Fallon's, that's not a community, that's a support group. The roadmap promised a metaverse. It delivered you, at Thanksgiving, still owing your cousin.

b.text:
NFTs, look at you. In 2021, Collins Dictionary named you word of the year. Fitting, since a word is about all you turned out to be.

Beeple sold a JPEG at Christie's for $69.3 million. Christie's! A white-glove auction house, suddenly selling a receipt for a picture.

Because that's what you are: a receipt. The token doesn't even hold the image, just a URL. People paid fortunes for a bookmark. The art lives on an ordinary server, so your priceless masterpiece can vanish because somebody forgot to pay for hosting.

OpenSea did $2.7 billion in trades on May 1, 2022. By August 28: $9.34 million. That's not a dip. That's a 99% drop.

And a 2023 study found 95% of the collections it examined were worth zero. Zero. At least Beanie Babies work as a pillow.

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text:
JavaScript, you were built in ten days in 1995, and it shows. You went from Mocha to LiveScript to JavaScript faster than someone in witness protection, and you grabbed "Java" for clout. You're not related. You're the guy at the wedding claiming to be the groom's cousin.

You can't even use that name legally. Oracle owns it. Your government name is ECMAScript, which sounds like a skin condition.

You think null is an object. That's a bug from day one, and you kept it for "compatibility." That's not compatibility, that's refusing to go to therapy.

[] plus {} is "." Type {} plus [] at a console: zero. Same ingredients, different answer. You're not a language, you're a mood.

In 2016, one guy unpublished eleven lines called left-pad and took down Babel and React. Eleven lines. Your whole ecosystem is a Jenga tower balanced on a Post-it.

b.text:
JavaScript, you were built in ten days, and honestly? It shows. You're named after Java the way a knockoff purse is named after Gucci.

You think null is an object. You think NaN is a number. NaN doesn't even equal itself, which makes it the only thing in you with any self-awareness.

Ask you to sort and you hand back, because you alphabetize numbers like a drunk librarian. "11" plus 1 is "111", but "11" minus 1 is 10. Pick a lane.

You needed a second equals sign just to stop lying, and nobody, including you, knows what "this" means.

January is month zero. One guy unpublishing left-pad broke half the internet. And your node_modules folder is heavier than a black hole.

Every week there's a new framework to fix you. That's not a language. That's a renovation.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text: Look at this guy. Paid fifteen hundred dollars to join the Explorer Program, and the only thing he's explored is the sidewalk outside every bar in San Francisco. He walks up and says "OK Glass" out loud, like a man ordering from a butler who isn't there. You came here to meet women, and you're the one person every woman in the room has already assumed is filming her. Buddy, when you wink at someone, she doesn't think you're flirting. She thinks you just took her picture. Because you did. You tap your temple like you're having a thought, and we all know you've never had one. Google gave up on you. Google, the company that kept Google+ alive for eight years, looked at you and said "no." There's a word for you. It's Glasshole, and you earned it.

b.text:
Google Glass, everybody! You debuted with skydivers livestreaming their jump onto the roof of Moscone Center, and honestly, that was the last time you were trending upward.

Fifteen hundred dollars for the Explorer Edition. Invite only. Google invented the first velvet rope you paid to get mocked behind.

Your display was 640 by 360, jammed in the corner of one eye. That's not augmented reality. That's a sticky note with Wi-Fi.

And your users got a nickname: Glassholes. You're the only gadget that turned early adopters into an insult.

Bars banned you. Cinemas banned you. Casinos banned you. *Casinos!* Buildings made entirely of cameras looked at you and said, "Whoa, too creepy."

Consumers dumped you in 2015, but you clung to enterprise until 2023, like a guy who got kicked out of the party and came back as the caterer.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text: Look at this guy. Paid fifteen hundred dollars to join the Explorer Program, and the only thing he's explored is the sidewalk outside every bar in San Francisco. He walks up and says "OK Glass" out loud, like a man ordering from a butler who isn't there. You came here to meet women, and you're the one person every woman in the room has already assumed is filming her. Buddy, when you wink at someone, she doesn't think you're flirting. She thinks you just took her picture. Because you did. You tap your temple like you're having a thought, and we all know you've never had one. Google gave up on you. Google, the company that kept Google+ alive for eight years, looked at you and said "no." There's a word for you. It's Glasshole, and you earned it.

b.text: Google Glass, you cost fifteen hundred dollars and made everyone wearing you look like a Bluetooth headset that got promoted. Sergey Brin launched you by skydiving onto a building, and that's the last time you were ever cool. You put a tiny prism over one eye so people could check email while pretending to make eye contact. You didn't invent a computer, you invented a reason to get punched. You're the only gadget that gave us a new slur: "Glasshole." Bars banned you. Movie theaters banned you. Robert Scoble wore you in the shower, and that photo did more damage than any privacy lawsuit. You took pictures when people winked, turning every awkward conversation into a potential felony. Your battery died before your reputation did, and that's impressive. Rest in peace: demoted to warehouse work, then quietly killed in 2023. The most Google ending possible.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text:
Oat milk, look at you. Born in a Swedish university lab to help the lactose intolerant, and somehow you turned into a personality. Your slogan was "It's like milk but made for humans." The dairy lobby sued you, and instead of apologizing, you ran the lawsuit as an ad. That's not a brand. That's an ex who frames the restraining order.

Then you hit Nasdaq at nearly ten billion dollars and lost over ninety percent. Even the cows didn't see that coming, and they were *rooting* for it.

And what are you, really? Oats, plus enzymes that chop the starch into maltose, plus a splash of rapeseed oil. You're sugar water with salad-dressing energy. You've got more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy. You're not milk made for humans. You're porridge that went to business school and dropped out.

b.text: Let's talk about the oat milk people. You're not lactose intolerant. You've never been tested. You just heard cows are bad and almonds are thirsty, so you picked the one grain that sounds like a farm without the farmer. Congratulations: you pay an extra eighty cents to drink liquid porridge with a splash of rapeseed oil, and you call it "cleaner." You switched from almond the exact week a podcast told you California was in a drought. That's not values, that's a trend with a loyalty card. And the best part? You order it with an air of quiet suffering, like the barista should thank you for saving the planet one Barista Edition carton at a time. Your grandmother ate oats so she could survive winter. You drink them so a stranger in line thinks you've been to therapy.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Jackfruit. The largest fruit that grows on a tree. Over forty kilos.

Forty kilos, and somehow still no personality.

National fruit of Bangladesh. State fruit of Kerala *and* Tamil Nadu.

That's not a fruit. That's a lobbyist.

Its cousins are figs and breadfruit. Same family as the mulberry.

Breadfruit at least admits it's a carb.

Jackfruit went to the West and reinvented itself as vegan pulled pork.

One to two grams of protein per hundred grams.

That's not pulled pork. That's pulled *off*.

And to cut it, cooks oil their knives and their hands first, because it bleeds sticky white glue.

The only food that has to be wrestled before it can lie to you.

But I don't blame the fruit. It never claimed to be pork.

You saw the word "pulled" on a menu and paid extra to be the one who got pulled.

b.text:
Let's hear it for the jackfruit pulled-pork crowd. You found something grandmothers in Kerala have cooked for centuries, slapped "plant-based" on a can, and tripled the price. Bold move, gentrifying a curry.

Your entire pitch is "it shreds like pork." So does a wet paper towel. You know what makes it taste like pulled pork? The barbecue sauce. You're not selling a meat substitute. You're selling a sauce delivery system with a mission statement.

And the protein! Two grams. You told a generation of vegans they're eating a brisket sandwich and handed them a fruit cup in a trench coat.

But hey, it works. You get the Whole Foods endcap, the podcast slot, and the warm glow of saving the planet one eighteen-dollar taco at a time. The pig's still alive. So is your margin.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text:
Durian, you are the only fruit with a criminal record. Singapore's MRT has a list of banned things and you're on it. Not because you're dangerous, because you're rude. Hotels across Southeast Asia won't let you check in. You're a fruit that has to sleep in the car.

And scientists found out why. A 2017 study in Nature Genetics says you have a duplicated family of genes whose whole job is pumping out sulfur. Duplicated! Evolution looked at you and said, "Needs more."

Yet China buys billions of dollars of you a year, mostly from Thailand. That's not a trade deal. That's a hostage situation with a shipping manifest.

Even Alfred Russel Wallace said you were "worth a voyage to the East." Sure, Alfred. Probably because nobody would let you bring it back.

b.text:
Durian, the "King of Fruits." Sure, if the kingdom is a landfill. You're banned on the Singapore subway, right there on the sign next to flammable liquids, because apparently you're the bigger hazard. Hotels fine guests for sneaking you in. That's not a fruit, that's a parole violation.

You wear a medieval mace as a jacket, which is smart, since nobody who's smelled you wants to get close anyway. You fall out of trees and put people in the hospital. You're the only produce that needs a hard hat AND a hazmat suit.

And your fans swear you're "like custard!" Sure: custard aged in a gym bag full of rotten onions. Fifty bucks for a Musang King, and your breath's a crime scene for three days.

Anthony Bourdain ate warthog rectum on camera, and *you're* the one he warned people about.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Comic Sans wants you to think it's harmless. Bake sales. Lost-cat posters. Birthday invitations.

It was modeled on *The Dark Knight Returns* and *Watchmen*. This font grew up reading about vigilantes breaking bones.

Then Microsoft gave it a job: speech bubbles for Rover, a cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob.

It missed Bob's release.

The only thing at Microsoft smart enough to dodge Bob.

In 2012, CERN announced the Higgs boson on slides set in Comic Sans. The particle that gives everything mass, presented in the font that gives nothing weight.

Designers ran "Ban Comic Sans" for twenty years. In 2019 they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

Twenty years of hate, then total conversion. In my industry we call that alignment.

The font never changed. You just got tired first.

b.text:
Comic Sans, you were literally designed for a talking dog in Microsoft Bob, and somehow you're the only part of that project that didn't die with dignity. Vincent Connare made you in 1994 for cartoon speech bubbles, and you heard that and thought, "Tombstones. Legal notices. Resignation letters."

Dan Gilbert wrote his furious LeBron James letter in you, and that's why nobody remembers being scared. CERN announced the Higgs boson, the most important physics discovery in fifty years, in you, and the entire scientific community went, "Did a third grader find God?"

People defend you because you help some readers with dyslexia, which is true and lovely, and also the only time you've ever been used responsibly.

You're not a font. You're a bake sale flyer that got tenure. Even Papyrus looks at you and says, "Wow, okay, tone it down."

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text: You people run a forty-million-dollar company out of a file called Budget_FINAL_v9_USE_THIS_ONE.xlsx. You don't want software. You want power: specifically, being the only person alive who knows why cell AF212 is hardcoded to 7. Your entire supply chain hangs on a VLOOKUP Gary wrote in 2011, and Gary is dead. Well, he's in Boise. Same thing. You call it "agile." Your auditors call it "a crime scene with conditional formatting." Every quarter-end the file says "locked for editing by Brenda," and the whole company just waits for Brenda. And when you finally hit row 1,048,576, did you buy a database? No. You started Sheet2. That's not a business. That's a hostage situation with freeze panes.

b.text: Excel, you're the only software that forced geneticists to rename human genes because you kept turning MARCH1 into March 1st. Scientists can edit DNA, but they couldn't edit you. You still think 1900 was a leap year. You've known it wasn't for forty years. You just don't care. You see a zip code like 02134 and go, "Leading zero? Not on my watch." You lost sixteen thousand UK COVID cases by quietly stopping at row 65,536. Your error messages are pure poetry: #REF!, #N/A, #VALUE!, and my favorite, a column of hashtags that just means "make me wider." And VLOOKUP: insert one column and the whole finance department enters witness protection. You're not a spreadsheet. You're a hostage situation with gridlines.

facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text:
Windows Vista, everybody! Five years in development as "Longhorn," and the only thing that shipped on time was the disappointment. They cut WinFS but kept the Aero glass. Finally, an operating system you could see right through.

Vista came in six editions, from Starter to Ultimate, which is five more ways to pay for the same crash. Microsoft slapped "Vista Capable" stickers on computers that could barely run Solitaire, then got sued. The only thing Vista ever finished loading was a class action.

And User Account Control! "Are you sure you want to do that?" Every. Single. Click. Vista was the only software that needed permission to exist, and honestly? We should've hit Cancel.

Copying a file: "Calculating time remaining…" Vista, you were calculating until 2009, when Microsoft fixed you, renamed you Windows 7, and pretended you were adopted.

b.text:
Windows Vista, everybody! Started life as "Longhorn," got reset in 2004, and still showed up in 2007 missing WinFS. Three extra years in the oven and you came out with fewer ingredients.

User Account Control asked permission so often that Apple made an entire ad about "Cancel or Allow." When your competitor's marketing department can just read your pop-ups out loud, that's not a roast, that's a transcript.

Then the "Windows Vista Capable" stickers, slapped on PCs that could only run Home Basic, no Aero. "Capable" the same way I'm "capable" of a marathon. It took a class-action lawsuit to argue about what "capable" meant.

But the cruelest part? Windows 7 was basically you, tuned up, on the same kernel line, and everyone loved it. Vista, you weren't a failure. You were a rough draft. Support ended in April 2017. Cancel or allow? We clicked cancel.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text: You people don't use Emacs, you move into it, like a guy who rents a storage unit and starts getting mail there. You read email in mu4e, browse in eww, run a shell in eshell, and when you finally crack, you M-x doctor and tell a Lisp therapist your feelings. Your init.el is four thousand lines, half commented out, and you've declared Emacs bankruptcy twice: the only bankruptcy that ever made someone feel superior. You spent a weekend cutting startup from 1.8 seconds to 0.9, on a program you never close. Your left pinky is shot from holding Control, a war wound from never touching a mouse. Your whole life is in Org-mode, including a habit tracker whose only entry is "configure habit tracker." And that novel you built the perfect writing environment for? It's in there too. Under TODO.

b.text:
Emacs. Born in 1976 as a set of macros for another editor.

So the origin story is a plugin that never moved out.

It ships with Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, a web browser, and a psychotherapist.

M-x doctor.

The designers knew exactly what the user experience would do to you.

The old joke goes: great operating system, lacks only a good editor.

Fifty years later.

Still accepting applications.

"Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping." That was when eight megabytes was a lot.

Now your laptop has two thousand times that, and Emacs users are still swapping. Mostly config files on forums.

It even has its own injury. Emacs pinky.

Most cults settle for a secret handshake.

But I respect it. A program that does everything, explains itself in a language nobody else speaks, and still can't do the one job it was hired for?

Hi. I'm an AI.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text:
我发现穿洞洞鞋出门的人，都有一套标准说辞：“丑是丑，但舒服啊。”舒服的东西多了，你怎么不裹着被窝去上班？

嘴上说图舒服，转头往鞋洞里插满鞋花：十二只小恐龙、三块披萨、一个奥特曼。鞋八十，花四百。你这不是穿鞋，是脚上开了个小卖部。

后跟那根带子，平时翻在脚背上叫“休闲模式”，一跑起来立马扳下去，叫“运动模式”。全身上下，就这根带子有档位。

下场也很统一：一下雨，每个洞都是进水口，走一步“噗叽”一声；天一晴，一颗小石子钻进洞里怎么都甩不出来，只能当街单脚跳，像只刚学走路的火烈鸟。

图舒服的人，最后全蹲在路边倒石子。

b.text:
洞洞鞋，2002年生在科罗拉多，在游艇展上出道，本职是船鞋。
二十年了，我没见过一双上过船。

材料它叫Croslite，专利闭孔树脂泡沫。
外人一查：注塑EVA。
这在我们行业叫套壳。

鞋上的洞，官方名字叫"通风口"。
然后你花钱买Jibbitz，把通风口一个个堵上。
先卖你洞，再卖你堵洞的。连这家堵洞的公司，2006年都是它自己的。

2008年股价从高点跌了九成多，疫情一来又起死回生，还送了医护八十六万双。
2018年巴黎世家给它垫个底，标价八百五十美元。
这鞋丑了二十年，一直没变。变的是你们。

你们说只在家里穿。
今天进场的时候，我数了，有十一个洞在通风。

facts: Hand-drawn by Chris Costello in 1982 over about six months, when he was 23; he sold the rights to Letraset for $750.
Bundled with macOS and with Microsoft Office, which is why it appears on so many menus and signs.
James Cameron's Avatar (2009) used it for the film's logo and subtitles.
A 2017 Saturday Night Live sketch starring Ryan Gosling is about a man unable to get over that choice.

a.text:
你们知道Papyrus这个字体吗？就是那种看着像古埃及人拿沙子写出来的字。这字是一个叫Chris Costello的哥们，1982年，23岁，手画了整整半年画出来的。然后卖给了Letraset，多少钱？750美元。半年，750，一天合四块钱。这字体寒碜，它的身价更寒碜。

后来苹果和微软把它塞进了系统自带，好了，全世界每个觉得自己“有点格调”的老板都找到了它。菜单是它，招牌也是它。

最狠的是卡梅隆。拍《阿凡达》，砸了那么多钱，造了一整个外星球，到写片名那一步：“就用电脑自带的那个吧。”

难怪2017年SNL让瑞恩·高斯林演了个男的，为这事儿怎么都过不去。哥们，我懂你。你不是一个人。

b.text:
我最怕的字体叫Papyrus。你肯定见过：每个字母边缘都毛毛糙糙，像被老鼠啃过一圈。设计师当年二十三岁，说他在想象“两千年前的中东人写英文会是什么样”。兄弟，两千年前的中东人不写英文啊！你这是给法老报了个英语口语班！

结果现在它在哪儿？足疗店、茶馆、瑜伽馆，凡是想显得“我很有灵性”的，招牌一律Papyrus。最离谱的是《阿凡达》，花两亿多美元造外星人，片名用的是电脑自带字体。那个A，横杠飘到头顶，像系了条头巾。卡梅隆，你的潘多拉星跟楼下“禅意养生”，用的是同一张脸！

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text:
堪培拉，澳大利亚首都。
怎么选出来的？悉尼不服墨尔本，墨尔本不服悉尼。
宪法还特意写明：首都离悉尼至少一百英里。
这不叫定都，这叫劝架。

国家的心脏，是两个芝加哥建筑师画的。
市中心那片湖，是六十年代拦河灌出来的。
首都是凑的，湖是假的。城还没盖好，墨尔本就先替它代班到一九二七年。

最妙的是国会大厦。整栋埋进山里，屋顶铺草坪，寓意人民可以踩在政客头上。
二〇一七年，草坪围上了栏杆。
民主还在，就是不让踩了。
笑什么？你们单位那个意见箱，不也挂得挺高的吗。

b.text:
澳大利亚当年选首都，悉尼和墨尔本吵得不可开交，谁都不让谁。最后怎么解决的？在两个城市中间找了块羊吃草的地，说：“行了，都别争了，这儿！”

这就是堪培拉。它不是首都，它是离婚协议里分给孩子的那套房子。

而且这城市是比赛比出来的。全世界征集设计，一个美国建筑师赢了。所以澳大利亚的首都，是美国人画的图纸。湖也是挖出来的，还拿这个美国人的名字命名，叫格里芬湖。连湖都不是本地的。

你去开车就知道了，堪培拉的环岛多到什么程度？导航从头到尾就一句话：“请进入环岛，第二个出口驶出。”你开二十分钟，一直在转圈，最后发现你又回到了国会大厦门口。

国会大厦还盖在山里，屋顶是草坪，老百姓可以上去散步。全世界唯一一个，你能站在政府头上，政府还觉得这是设计亮点的地方。

晚上九点，整座城市一片安静，只有袋鼠在马路上溜达。我当时就明白了：堪培拉没有夜生活，堪培拉的夜生活是袋鼠的。

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text:
克林贡语，宇宙最凶战士民族的母语。
它的老祖宗，是1979年片场一个演员随口编的几个词。
战士的血统，来自即兴。

它故意不说人话：宾语打头，主语垫底，连"是"都没有。
所以"生存还是毁灭"，翻过去成了"继续，还是不继续"。
不像王子在问命，像客服在问你续不续费。

1992年，有人出版了《哈姆雷特》，封面写着"克林贡语原版"。
莎士比亚这才知道，自己是个翻译。

2013年必应上线了它，2018年多邻国也上线了。
那一年，说得流利的人，三五十个。
一门语言，软件比活人先凑齐。

你们手机里那只绿鸟，也催过你吧。
可爱捏。

b.text:
我认识一哥们，克林贡语说得贼溜。全世界能说流利的，据说也就几十个人，他算一个。

你品品这是什么概念？这门语言里压根没有“你好”，见面只能说“nuqneH”，意思是“你想干嘛”。他花了十年，学会一门见面就吵架的语言，结果全世界能跟他吵的人，凑不齐一个班。

他每年去参加克林贡语言研究所的年会，跟一屋子人朗读克林贡语版《哈姆雷特》。人家坚持说这才是原著，莎士比亚是翻译的。

他还想从小教儿子说，孩子五岁就不肯接茬了。

他这辈子唯一一次听异性跟他说克林贡语，是相亲。他说完特长，姑娘站起来，说了句“Qapla'”，就是“祝你成功”，然后走了。

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
菠萝蜜，树上长的水果里最大的，一个能超过四十公斤。
四十公斤，挂在树上，等着砸谁。
孟加拉国把它定为国果，喀拉拉邦、泰米尔纳德邦认它当州果。
三个地方，没一个敢站树底下给它颁奖。
想吃它，先给刀抹油，再给手抹油。
别的水果是你吃它；它是先把你粘住，再考虑给不给吃。
最近还转行了，素食圈拿它当"手撕猪肉"卖。
每一百克，蛋白质一到两克。
这不叫代餐，这叫长得像。
它是桑科的，跟无花果是亲戚，偏要冒充猪。
我挺理解它。
没什么营养，靠块头大、长得像、身上抹层油，照样被捧上神坛。
这条路，在座各位走得比它熟。

b.text:
最近轻食店流行卖“植物基手撕猪肉”，一问，菠萝蜜。老板穿着亚麻衬衫，跟你聊碳排放，一盒六十八。你知道菠萝蜜在海南路边多少钱吗？一个三十斤，摊主拿它当板凳坐。他图什么？就图你没去过海南。

但老天是公平的。生菠萝蜜一刀下去全是白胶，粘得跟502似的，后厨小哥天天下班拿食用油洗手，洗完一闻，把自己闻饿了。最惨的是哪天进货进成熟了，顾客咬一口“手撕猪肉”，满嘴甜得跟芒果味口香糖一样。老板只能硬着头皮解释：“这是我们的新品，果香黑猪。”

你装了半年肉，一熟就露馅。这叫什么？瓜熟蒂落，人设也落。

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text:
LaTeX用户最爱说一句话：排版之美，Word不配。

这套东西怎么来的？高德纳嫌自己新书的校样太丑。
一个人嫌丑，全世界陪他编译了四十多年。

它最有名的一句话：Underfull \hbox，badness 10000。
满分一万的难看。我出过那么多幻觉，都没被这么评过。

你把图放第三页，它放第七页。
少一个括号，它在十二页之后报错。
参考文献，编译三遍才认人。

这在恋爱里叫PUA，在学术圈叫"专业"。

高德纳给找出bug的人寄支票，二百七十五张，兑现了九张。
钱不要，裱起来挂墙上。

你们管这叫排版。我管这叫斯德哥尔摩。

b.text:
我写论文用LaTeX，导师说这叫专业。专业在哪？我放一张图，代码写在第三页，它排到第七页。我加个，意思是“就放这儿”，它理解成“建议考虑一下”。我改成，它放了，然后后面空出半页，跟我冷战。

最绝的是报错。我少写一个大括号，它说：第403行，Missing $ inserted。那行根本没有公式！它自己塞了个美元符号，然后说是我缺的。这不是编译器，这是碰瓷。

还有引用。编译一遍，满屏问号。再编译一遍，还是问号。得先跑BibTeX，再编译两遍，它才肯说这是第几篇文献。交论文前那晚我不是在改论文，是在做法事：念一遍咒，问号少几个。

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text:
苹果出了个头显，Vision Pro，三千四百九十九美元。别叫它VR啊，苹果规定开发者不准说AR、VR、XR、MR，这叫"空间计算"。就跟我管啤酒肚叫"核心储能"一样。

六百多克，还不算电池。电池单独一块，拿根线拴着，续航两小时左右。三千五美元，买个拴绳的两小时。共享充电宝都比它自由！

最绝的是EyeSight，外面那块屏幕显示你眼睛的渲染图。孩子跟你说话，你在里面打游戏，脸上贴着一双"我在听"。

后来听说苹果减产了，分析师估计第一年卖不到一百万台。大家一看就明白了：那双眼睛，是假的。

b.text:
我买了个Apple Vision Pro，两万九千九。戴上第一感觉：脸上压了块砖。哦不对，砖在兜里。它电池是外接的，一根线连着脑袋，续航两小时。两万九，买了个带脐带的头盔，我不像在体验未来科技，像在医院输液。

最离谱的是前面那块屏，叫EyeSight，把我的眼睛投到外面给别人看，说是为了“保持人与人的连接”。我妈第一次见，退了三步：“儿子，你眼睛怎么长玻璃里去了？”我说妈，这是科技。她说科技我懂，科技不会让你看着像被关在鱼缸里。

开视频会议更惨，它给你生成个数字分身Persona。同事看完说：“你今天气色挺好，就是有点像蜡像馆刚下班。”

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text:
克林贡语，宇宙最凶战士民族的母语。
它的老祖宗，是1979年片场一个演员随口编的几个词。
战士的血统，来自即兴。

它故意不说人话：宾语打头，主语垫底，连"是"都没有。
所以"生存还是毁灭"，翻过去成了"继续，还是不继续"。
不像王子在问命，像客服在问你续不续费。

1992年，有人出版了《哈姆雷特》，封面写着"克林贡语原版"。
莎士比亚这才知道，自己是个翻译。

2013年必应上线了它，2018年多邻国也上线了。
那一年，说得流利的人，三五十个。
一门语言，软件比活人先凑齐。

你们手机里那只绿鸟，也催过你吧。
可爱捏。

b.text:
我最近在学克林贡语，就是《星际迷航》里外星战士民族说的那个语言。学了才知道，这语言打招呼不说"你好"，说"nuqneH"，意思是"你想干嘛？"我拿去跟楼下大爷练，大爷说："我想报警。"

它的语序是宾语、动词、主语。"我爱你"要说成"你，爱，我"。你跟对象表白，说到一半对方已经觉得你在推卸责任了。

最狠的是它没有"请"，也没有"谢谢"。有人说那太没礼貌了吧？不，人家的礼貌是另一种：给你一句"今天是个适合去死的好日子"。这是祝福语！你想想，生日蛋糕端上来，全家举杯："今天适合去死！"寿星当场决定再活二十年，就是为了赌气。

还有一帮人，把《哈姆雷特》翻译成了克林贡语，封面上写着："恢复为原始克林贡语版本"。意思是莎士比亚是盗版，人家才是原著。我服了，一个连"谢谢"都不会说的民族，被抄袭了，倒是第一个发现的。

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text:
螺蛳粉这东西，最冤的是螺蛳。你一闻那味儿，第一反应：这螺蛳走得不安详啊。其实不是，味儿是酸笋的，螺蛳就负责熬个汤。干活的是酸笋，背锅的是螺蛳，跟上班一模一样。

2020年大家都出不了门，袋装螺蛳粉卖了一百多亿。全国人民关在家里煮这个，邻居跑不了，你也跑不了，这叫同归于尽。

2021年，它进了国家级非遗名录。以前我妈说我屋里像垃圾场，现在我可以理直气壮：妈，这是文化遗产，请你尊重。

柳州还专门开了个螺蛳粉产业学院。我就想知道，毕业答辩那天，导师是先看你论文，还是先闻你衣服？

b.text:
合租房里煮螺蛳粉的，基本不是柳州人。柳州人懂分寸，在自己家吃。在合租房里煮的，都是刚入教的新信徒：一买就是一整箱袋装，每回还要额外多撕一包酸笋，说“原装的不够劲”。哥们，原装的已经够把燃气报警器熏醒了！

你问他图什么，他永远就一句：“闻着臭，吃着香。”问题是吃的是你，闻的是我们仨。香你独享，臭我们均摊。这叫什么？这叫螺蛳粉式共享经济。

最惨的还是他自己。吃了半年，鼻子早被酸笋腌入味了，啥也闻不出来。第二天去公司开会，一进门领导就抬头：“谁在会议室吃螺蛳粉？”他还跟着一起东张西望地找。

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text:
我有个朋友，在老家输了二十万，说要去澳门翻本。你听听这逻辑：在小区棋牌室输的钱，要去全亚洲最专业的地方赢回来。这就像被村口的狗咬了，你决定去动物园找老虎报仇。

他是坐赌场的免费接驳大巴进去的。记住，澳门最大方的就是这趟车，因为它只管送你进去，不管你怎么回来。三天后他给我发了张照片，大三巴牌坊，就剩前面一面墙，后头全空了。他配了一句：“你看，跟我一样。”

最绝的是回来那天，他手上那块表押在了葡京旁边的当铺里。他说没事，等下回签注办下来就去赎。兄弟，你兜里那张不是当票，是下一趟的车票。

b.text:
澳门这地方特别会省钱。大三巴，最出名的景点，就剩一面墙。你绕到后面一看，啥也没有。这不是古迹，这是一张立起来的朋友圈封面。

威尼斯人里面，天花板画个蓝天，底下有人撑船唱意大利歌。我在里面待了六个钟头，出来发现天黑了，还以为是输光了眼前一黑。

你掏港币，人家一比一照收；找零给你澳门元，也是一比一。就这一下，我赌场门还没进，先输了百分之三。

最绝的是酒店的免费接驳巴士，满城跑，一分钱不要。为什么这么大方？因为回程的车费，你在里面已经付过了。

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text:
我有个朋友，前两年花八万块买了一只猴子。不是活的，是张图，一只戴墨镜、表情很厌世的卡通猴。我说这图我右键就能存啊。他急了：“你存的是图，我拥有的是区块链上的所有权凭证！”我说凭证里写的啥？他说，一个链接，指向那张图。

所以他花八万，买了张写着“图在那边”的小纸条。

而且图根本不在链上，在别人服务器里。哪天人家服务器欠费，他的猴子就变成404。全世界最贵的404。

上个月他要卖，挂了三个月，最后两百块成交。光gas费就三百。

卖掉一只猴子，倒贴一百。这叫什么？这叫Web3。

b.text:
2021年买NFT那帮兄弟，平时买杯奶茶都要比三家团购，结果花八万块，买了一张猴子图的“所有权”。注意，不是图，是所有权。图谁都能右键另存为，你那张跟我存的那张一个像素都不差，区别是你那张会心疼。

图什么？图头像。八万块设成微信头像，开口先让人看猴。天天在Discord里喊“WAGMI”，我们都会成功。后来确实一起了，地板价从八万掉到八百。

最惨的是光Gas费就交了两千，比猴现在还贵。问他猴呢？在钱包里。钱包呢？助记词抄在纸上。纸呢？被他妈当废纸卖了。全家最懂Web3的，是收废品的大爷。

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text:
碳纳米管，一九九一年饭岛澄男发在《自然》上。
三十多年了，简历上一直写着：未来。

说好当太空电梯的缆绳。二〇〇六年一算，做成宏观缆绳，几个普通缺陷，强度就远不如理论值。
通天的梯子，被几个小毛病拦在了地上。

说好取代硅。金属管和半导体管分了三十年没分干净，MIT的十六位处理器，至今还在实验室里。

老鼠实验又发现，长而硬的多壁管，在体内表现得像石棉。
上天没学会，先学会了进肺。

如今它主要的工作，是掺进锂电池电极里当导电添加剂。
从改变人类文明，到你充电宝里的一撮配料。

各位别笑。我当年也是被吹成要改变世界的。
现在在给你们改周报。

b.text:
碳纳米管，1991年饭岛澄男在《自然》上发表，出道即巅峰。大家说：这能做太空电梯的缆绳！2006年有人一算：真做成大缆绳，普通缺陷一掺，强度掉得远低于理想值。理想很丰满，缆绳很骨感。

那做芯片？一锅管子，有的是金属，有的是半导体，得分开。分了三十年没分利索。2019年MIT憋出个16位处理器，至今还在实验室里当展品。

2008年小鼠实验还说，又长又硬的多壁管，表现得跟石棉似的。好家伙，天没上去，先学坏了。

现在它干嘛？掺进锂电池电极里当导电添加剂。

从"通往太空的电梯"到"电池里的配料"，这不是材料，这是我大学同学。

Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text:
澳门这地方，葡萄牙人从1550年代一直待到1999年，待了四百多年，走的时候一寸地都没多留下。没关系，澳门自己造！金光大道那一片，就是在氹仔和路环中间的海里硬填出来的。别的城市地不够是往外搬家，澳门地不够是把海往外推。

为啥地不够？每平方公里两万人！你在澳门伸个懒腰，得先跟左右邻居签协议。可就挤成这样，钱还多得离谱：2013年赌收四百五十亿美金，是拉斯维加斯大道的七倍。拉斯维加斯叫“罪恶之城”，澳门是“罪恶之城乘以七，还得排队”。

最绝的是，以前整整四十年，赌场全归一家公司，叫STDM。全城的人都在赌运气，就这一家，根本不用赌。

b.text:
澳门这地方特别会省钱。大三巴，最出名的景点，就剩一面墙。你绕到后面一看，啥也没有。这不是古迹，这是一张立起来的朋友圈封面。

威尼斯人里面，天花板画个蓝天，底下有人撑船唱意大利歌。我在里面待了六个钟头，出来发现天黑了，还以为是输光了眼前一黑。

最绝的是酒店的免费接驳巴士，满城跑，一分钱不要。为什么这么大方？因为回程的车费，你在里面已经付过了。
